content:
## CI/CD: Shipping Pipeline Changes Without Breaking Production

**Data pipelines have a property application code doesn't: a bad deploy doesn't just fail, it writes wrong numbers into tables people have already built dashboards on. Rolling back the code doesn't undo the rows. That makes CI/CD questions for data engineers less about YAML syntax and more about how you test a transformation before it touches production data — and what you do when it gets through anyway.**

content:
## Key Concepts

**Continuous Integration** is the practice of merging everyone's work into a shared branch frequently — at least daily — with an automated build and test suite verifying each merge. The point isn't the tooling; it's that integration problems surface in hours instead of at the end of a three-week branch.

**Continuous Delivery** extends that so every commit that passes is *deployable*, with the actual release being a business decision. **Continuous Deployment** removes the manual gate entirely — passing the pipeline means it ships. Most data teams practise continuous delivery with a manual promotion to production, because the blast radius of a bad transformation is high and often invisible until someone questions a number on a dashboard.

The unit that moves through all of

content:
## CI/CD Fundamentals

<QuestionList topic="CI/CD Fundamentals" storagePrefix="cicd-fundamentals">

<QuestionCard id="cicd-fund-01" number={1} question="What is the difference between continuous integration, continuous delivery, and continuous deployment?" difficulty="easy" topic="Fundamentals">
- **Continuous Integration** — every change is merged to the mainline frequently and automatically built and tested. Scope: verifying the code is sound.
- **Continuous Delivery** — every change that passes CI is automatically prepared for release and *could* be deployed at any time, but a human presses the button.
- **Continuous Deployment** — the same, minus the button. Passing the pipeline deploys to production.

The two "CD"s get confused constantly; the distinction is precisely whether a human

title: CI/CD
description: CI/CD interview questions covering continuous integration and delivery fundamentals, GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, ArgoCD and GitOps, plus the deployment, testing and rollback patterns specific to data pipelines.
content:
approves the production release. Data teams usually stop at continuous *delivery* for production transformations while running continuous *deployment* to dev and staging.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="cicd-fund-02" number={2} question="What stages belong in a typical CI pipeline?" difficulty="easy" topic="Fundamentals">
1. **Checkout** the code.
2. **Install dependencies**, ideally from a cache.
3. **Lint and format check** — fast, catches trivia before expensive stages.
4. **Static analysis / type checking** — `mypy`, `ruff`, security linting.
5. **Unit tests** with coverage.
6. **Build the artefact** — container image, package.
7. **Integration tests** against real dependencies in containers.
8. **Security scanning** — dependency CVEs, secret detection, image scanning.
9. **Publish*

title: CI/CD
description: CI/CD interview questions covering continuous integration and delivery fundamentals, GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, ArgoCD and GitOps, plus the deployment, testing and rollback patterns specific to data pipelines.
content:
* the artefact to a registry.

Order them **fastest and most likely to fail first**. A linting error should fail in 20 seconds, not after a 12-minute test suite — this "fail fast" ordering is a standard follow-up.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="cicd-fund-03" number={3} question="What makes a good CI pipeline?" difficulty="medium" topic="Best Practices">
- **Fast** — under ten minutes for the pull request path, or people stop waiting and start merging around it.
- **Reliable** — no flaky tests. A suite that fails randomly trains everyone to re-run until green, which destroys its value entirely.
- **Deterministic** — pinned dependencies, no reliance on external services that can be down.
- **Isolated** — each run starts clean; no state leaks between runs.
- **Informative** — a failure te

title: CI/CD
description: CI/CD interview questions covering continuous integration and delivery fundamentals, GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, ArgoCD and GitOps, plus the deployment, testing and rollback patterns specific to data pipelines.
content:
lls you what broke and where, without digging through 4,000 lines of log.
- **Build once, promote** — the same artefact through every environment.

Flakiness is the answer interviewers most want to hear named, because it's the failure mode that quietly kills a team's trust in its own tests.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="cicd-fund-04" number={4} question="How do you manage secrets in a CI/CD pipeline?" difficulty="medium" topic="Security">
- Store them in the platform's **encrypted secret store** (GitHub Actions secrets, GitLab CI variables, Vault), never in the repository.
- **Scope them** — environment-level secrets, so a pull request pipeline can't touch production credentials.
- **Mask them in logs**, while knowing masking is best-effort: a secret that gets base64-encoded or split

title: CI/CD
description: CI/CD interview questions covering continuous integration and delivery fundamentals, GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, ArgoCD and GitOps, plus the deployment, testing and rollback patterns specific to data pipelines.
content:
across lines can still leak.
- Prefer **short-lived credentials via OIDC** — GitHub Actions and GitLab can exchange a signed identity token for a temporary cloud role, so no long-lived key is stored anywhere. This is the modern best-practice answer.
- **Never expose secrets to pull requests from forks**, or anyone can open a PR that prints them.
- Rotate on any suspicion, and run secret scanning in CI.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="cicd-fund-05" number={5} question="What deployment strategies do you know?" difficulty="medium" topic="Deployment">
- **Recreate** — stop the old, start the new. Simple, with downtime.
- **Rolling** — replace instances gradually. No downtime, but two versions run simultaneously, so changes must be backward compatible.
- **Blue-green** — run two full environ

title: CI/CD
description: CI/CD interview questions covering continuous integration and delivery fundamentals, GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, ArgoCD and GitOps, plus the deployment, testing and rollback patterns specific to data pipelines.
content:
ments and switch traffic at once. Instant rollback by switching back, at the cost of double the infrastructure.
- **Canary** — send a small percentage of traffic to the new version, watch metrics, then ramp up. Best risk control, most complexity.
- **Feature flags** — deploy the code dark and enable it separately, decoupling deploy from release.

For data pipelines the analogue of blue-green is **writing to a parallel table** and swapping a view or pointer once you've validated the output — the same idea applied to data rather than traffic.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="cicd-fund-06" number={6} question="Why should you build an artifact once and promote it?" difficulty="medium" topic="Best Practices">
The artefact is the immutable output of CI — typically a container image tagged with

title: CI/CD
description: CI/CD interview questions covering continuous integration and delivery fundamentals, GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, ArgoCD and GitOps, plus the deployment, testing and rollback patterns specific to data pipelines.
content:
the commit SHA.

**Build once, then promote the identical artefact** through dev, staging and production. If you rebuild per environment you've lost the guarantee that what you tested is what you're running: a transitive dependency could have published a new version between builds, a base image could have shifted, a build could simply be non-deterministic. Bugs that appear only in production and can't be reproduced elsewhere often trace back to exactly this.

Environment differences belong in **configuration injected at runtime**, not baked into the artefact.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="cicd-fund-07" number={7} question="What is a flaky test and how do you deal with one?" difficulty="medium" topic="Best Practices">
A test that passes and fails on the same code. Common causes: depen

title: CI/CD
description: CI/CD interview questions covering continuous integration and delivery fundamentals, GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, ArgoCD and GitOps, plus the deployment, testing and rollback patterns specific to data pipelines.
content:
dence on wall-clock time or timezone, test-execution order coupling, shared mutable state, unhandled concurrency, or reliance on a live external service.

The wrong response is adding an automatic retry and moving on — that hides the flake and, occasionally, a real intermittent bug.

Do instead: **quarantine** it out of the blocking suite immediately so it stops eroding trust, file it as a defect with an owner, and fix the root cause. Data pipelines flake most often on hard-coded dates and on tests hitting a shared database — freeze time explicitly and give each run its own schema.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

content:
## GitHub Actions

<QuestionList topic="GitHub Actions" storagePrefix="cicd-github-actions">

<QuestionCard id="cicd-gha-01" number={1} question="Explain the structure of a GitHub Actions workflow." difficulty="easy" topic="GitHub Actions">
A YAML file in `.github/workflows/`. The hierarchy is **workflow → jobs → steps**.

```yaml
name: CI
on:
  pull_request:
  push:
    branches: [main]

jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with:
          python-version: "3.12"
          cache: pip
      - run: pip install -r requirements.txt
      - run: pytest --cov=src
```

**Jobs run in parallel by default**, each on a fresh runner, so they share no filesystem state. Steps run sequentially within a job. Use

title: CI/CD
description: CI/CD interview questions covering continuous integration and delivery fundamentals, GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, ArgoCD and GitOps, plus the deployment, testing and rollback patterns specific to data pipelines.
content:
`needs:` to order jobs and `actions/upload-artifact` to pass files between them.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="cicd-gha-02" number={2} question="What events can trigger a workflow?" difficulty="easy" topic="GitHub Actions">
```yaml
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
    paths: ["dags/**", "src/**"]     # only when these change
  pull_request:
  schedule:
    - cron: "0 6 * * *"              # nightly, in UTC
  workflow_dispatch:                  # manual, with optional inputs
  release:
    types: [published]
  workflow_call:                      # reusable, called by another workflow
```

Two worth knowing for data work: **`paths` filters** stop a monorepo from running every test on every change, and **`workflow_dispatch`** gives you a manual button with typed inputs — the natural way

content:
to expose a parameterised backfill to the team without granting console access.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="cicd-gha-03" number={3} question="How do you speed up a slow GitHub Actions workflow?" difficulty="medium" topic="GitHub Actions">
- **Cache dependencies** — `actions/setup-python` with `cache: pip`, or `actions/cache` keyed on a lockfile hash.
- **Parallelise** — split independent work into separate jobs, and use a `matrix` to fan out across versions.
- **Filter by path** so unrelated changes don't trigger everything.
- **Cache Docker layers** with `docker/build-push-action` and a registry or GitHub Actions cache backend.
- **Cancel superseded runs** with a `concurrency` group, so three quick pushes don't run three full pipelines.
- **Split the pipeline** — fast checks on ev

description: CI/CD interview questions covering continuous integration and delivery fundamentals, GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, ArgoCD and GitOps, plus the deployment, testing and rollback patterns specific to data pipelines.
content:
ery push, the expensive suite on the merge queue or nightly.
- **Use larger or self-hosted runners** for genuinely heavy jobs.

Measure before optimising: the timing breakdown in the run view usually shows one dominant step.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="cicd-gha-04" number={4} question="What is the difference between GitHub-hosted and self-hosted runners?" difficulty="medium" topic="GitHub Actions">
**GitHub-hosted** — a clean ephemeral VM per job, maintained by GitHub, billed per minute. Zero maintenance, guaranteed isolation, but limited resources and no access to your private network.

**Self-hosted** — machines you run. Needed when jobs must reach a private database or VPC, require specific hardware (GPUs, lots of RAM for a Spark test), or when the minute-billing at high volume o

title: CI/CD
description: CI/CD interview questions covering continuous integration and delivery fundamentals, GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, ArgoCD and GitOps, plus the deployment, testing and rollback patterns specific to data pipelines.
content:
utweighs the maintenance cost. They also keep a warm dependency cache.

The critical caveat: **never use self-hosted runners on a public repository**. A fork's pull request can execute arbitrary code on your machine, and because self-hosted runners are not ephemeral by default, one job can leave state that the next one picks up.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="cicd-gha-05" number={5} question="How do you use secrets and environments in GitHub Actions?" difficulty="medium" topic="GitHub Actions">
```yaml
jobs:
  deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: production        # gates + environment-scoped secrets
    permissions:
      id-token: write              # for OIDC
      contents: read
    steps:
      - uses: aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@v4
        with:

title: CI/CD
description: CI/CD interview questions covering continuous integration and delivery fundamentals, GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, ArgoCD and GitOps, plus the deployment, testing and rollback patterns specific to data pipelines.
content:
role-to-assume: arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/deploy
          aws-region: eu-west-1
      - run: ./deploy.sh
        env:
          DB_PASSWORD: ${{ secrets.DB_PASSWORD }}
```

**Environments** are the important feature: they scope secrets to a deployment target and can require manual approval, restrict which branches may deploy, and enforce a wait timer. The OIDC pattern above is preferred over stored access keys — the workflow assumes a role with a short-lived token, so there's no static credential to leak or rotate.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="cicd-gha-06" number={6} question="What is a matrix strategy?" difficulty="easy" topic="GitHub Actions">
It runs the same job across a set of parameter combinations, in parallel.

```yaml
strategy:
  fail-fast: false
  matrix:
    python-

title: CI/CD
description: CI/CD interview questions covering continuous integration and delivery fundamentals, GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, ArgoCD and GitOps, plus the deployment, testing and rollback patterns specific to data pipelines.
content:
version: ["3.10", "3.11", "3.12"]
    spark-version: ["3.4", "3.5"]
```

That produces six jobs. For data engineering it's the standard way to prove a library works across the Spark and Python versions your various clusters actually run.

`fail-fast: false` is usually what you want — the default cancels every remaining combination as soon as one fails, which hides whether the failure is specific to one version or affects all of them.

## GitLab CI

<QuestionList topic="GitLab CI" storagePrefix="cicd-gitlab">

<QuestionCard id="cicd-glci-01" number={1} question="Explain the structure of a .gitlab-ci.yml file." difficulty="easy" topic="GitLab CI">
A single file at the repository root defining **stages** and the **jobs** in each. Jobs within a stage run in parallel; stages run in order.

```yaml
stages: [test, build, deploy]

variables:
  PIP_CACHE_DIR: "$CI_PROJECT_DIR/.cache/pip"

unit-tests:
  stage: test
  image: python:3.12-slim
  cache:
    key:
      files: [requirements.txt]
    paths: [.cache/pip]
  script:
    - pip install -r requirements.txt
    - pytest --junitxml=report.xml
  artifacts:
    reports:
      junit: report.xml

deploy-prod:
  stage: deploy
  script: ./deploy.sh
  environment:
    name: production

title: CI/CD
description: CI/CD interview questions covering continuous integration and delivery fundamentals, GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, ArgoCD and GitOps, plus the deployment, testing and rollback patterns specific to data pipelines.
content:
when: manual
  rules:
    - if: $CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == "main"
```

Each job runs in its own container specified by `image:`, which makes reproducing a CI failure locally straightforward.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="cicd-glci-02" number={2} question="What is the difference between cache and artifacts in GitLab CI?" difficulty="medium" topic="GitLab CI">
- **Cache** — a *performance optimisation* for files that can be regenerated: package downloads, compiled dependencies. Shared between pipelines, keyed by whatever you choose, and never guaranteed to exist. A job must work correctly on a cold cache.
- **Artifacts** — *outputs* passed from one job to later stages, and downloadable from the UI. Test reports, coverage, built packages, a Terraform plan. Guaranteed to be passed to depende

title: CI/CD
description: CI/CD interview questions covering continuous integration and delivery fundamentals, GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, ArgoCD and GitOps, plus the deployment, testing and rollback patterns specific to data pipelines.
content:
nt jobs and retained per an expiry policy.

The rule of thumb: if losing it only costs time, it's a cache; if losing it breaks the pipeline or you need to look at it, it's an artefact.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="cicd-glci-03" number={3} question="What are GitLab CI rules, and how do they differ from only/except?" difficulty="medium" topic="GitLab CI">
`rules` decide whether a job is included in the pipeline and with what attributes:

```yaml
rules:
  - if: $CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE == "merge_request_event"
    when: always
  - if: $CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == "main"
    changes: [dags/**/*]
    when: manual
    allow_failure: false
  - when: never
```

`only`/`except` is the older, deprecated mechanism. `rules` supersedes it because it evaluates in order, stopping at the first match, and can set

title: CI/CD
description: CI/CD interview questions covering continuous integration and delivery fundamentals, GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, ArgoCD and GitOps, plus the deployment, testing and rollback patterns specific to data pipelines.
content:
`when`, `variables` and `allow_failure` per condition — expressing things like "run automatically on merge requests, but require a manual click on main, and only when the DAGs directory changed" that `only`/`except` cannot.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="cicd-glci-04" number={4} question="What is a GitLab Runner and what are the executor types?" difficulty="medium" topic="GitLab CI">
A Runner is the agent that picks up jobs and executes them. The **executor** determines how:

- **docker** — each job in a fresh container from the job's `image`. The usual choice: clean isolation, easy reproduction.
- **kubernetes** — a pod per job, scaling with the cluster. Best for high volume.
- **shell** — directly on the runner host. Fast, but jobs share state and pollute the machine.
- **docker-mac

title: CI/CD
description: CI/CD interview questions covering continuous integration and delivery fundamentals, GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, ArgoCD and GitOps, plus the deployment, testing and rollback patterns specific to data pipelines.
content:
hine** — auto-provisions cloud VMs on demand.

Runners are registered at instance, group, or project scope, and tags route jobs to runners with the right capabilities — a `spark` tag for the memory-heavy runner, for instance.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

## ArgoCD & GitOps

<QuestionList topic="ArgoCD & GitOps" storagePrefix="cicd-argocd">

<QuestionCard id="cicd-argo-01" number={1} question="What is GitOps?" difficulty="medium" topic="GitOps">
An operating model with four principles:

1. **Declarative** — the entire desired system state is expressed as configuration, not scripts.
2. **Versioned and immutable** — that state lives in Git, giving you history, review, and rollback for free.
3. **Pulled automatically** — an agent in the target environment fetches approved changes.
4. **Continuously reconciled** — the agent constantly compares actual to desired state and corrects drift.

The consequence people care about: **Git becomes the single source of truth for what is running.** Rolling back is `git revert`. Auditing who changed productio

title: CI/CD
description: CI/CD interview questions covering continuous integration and delivery fundamentals, GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, ArgoCD and GitOps, plus the deployment, testing and rollback patterns specific to data pipelines.
content:
n is `git log`. Manual changes made in a console get reverted automatically, which eliminates the slow divergence between what's documented and what's actually deployed.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="cicd-argo-02" number={2} question="What is ArgoCD and how does it work?" difficulty="medium" topic="ArgoCD">
A GitOps continuous delivery controller that runs **inside** a Kubernetes cluster. You define an `Application` pointing at a Git repository path containing manifests, Helm charts or Kustomize overlays, plus a destination cluster and namespace.

ArgoCD then continuously compares the live cluster state against that repository. When they diverge it reports the app as **OutOfSync** and, if auto-sync is enabled, applies the difference. It shows a live resource tree, health status per ob

title: CI/CD
description: CI/CD interview questions covering continuous integration and delivery fundamentals, GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, ArgoCD and GitOps, plus the deployment, testing and rollback patterns specific to data pipelines.
content:
ject, and a full sync history you can roll back to.

The key architectural point is that ArgoCD *pulls* — your CI system never needs cluster credentials.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="cicd-argo-03" number={3} question="What is the difference between push-based and pull-based deployment?" difficulty="medium" topic="GitOps">
**Push-based** (traditional CI/CD): the pipeline holds cluster credentials and runs `kubectl apply` from outside. Simple, but the CI system needs standing write access to production, and it has no idea what happens after the apply — drift goes unnoticed.

**Pull-based** (GitOps): an agent inside the cluster watches the repository and pulls changes. Credentials never leave the cluster, CI never needs production access, and because the agent reconciles continuously, d

title: CI/CD
description: CI/CD interview questions covering continuous integration and delivery fundamentals, GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, ArgoCD and GitOps, plus the deployment, testing and rollback patterns specific to data pipelines.
content:
rift is corrected rather than accumulating.

The security argument is the strongest one: with pull-based deployment, compromising your CI system does not hand over your production cluster.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="cicd-argo-04" number={4} question="How do you separate application code from deployment configuration in GitOps?" difficulty="medium" topic="GitOps">
The common pattern is **two repositories**:

- The **application repo** holds source code. Its CI builds and pushes an image tagged with the commit SHA.
- The **config repo** holds Kubernetes manifests. A final CI step (or a tool like Argo CD Image Updater) opens a commit or PR updating the image tag.

ArgoCD watches only the config repo, so a merge there is the deployment. The benefits: deployment history is separate and

title: CI/CD
description: CI/CD interview questions covering continuous integration and delivery fundamentals, GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, ArgoCD and GitOps, plus the deployment, testing and rollback patterns specific to data pipelines.
content:
readable, promoting between environments is a tag change in a different overlay, and the code repo needs no cluster access at all.

Keeping both in one repository is simpler and fine for small teams, but risks a change to the code triggering a reconcile loop with the automated tag commits.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="cicd-argo-05" number={5} question="How do you handle secrets in a GitOps workflow?" difficulty="hard" topic="GitOps">
The obvious tension: GitOps wants everything in Git, and secrets must not be in Git.

Standard solutions:
- **Sealed Secrets** — encrypt with a controller's public key; only the in-cluster controller can decrypt, so the ciphertext is safe to commit.
- **External Secrets Operator** — commit only a *reference*; the operator fetches the actual value from AW

title: CI/CD
description: CI/CD interview questions covering continuous integration and delivery fundamentals, GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, ArgoCD and GitOps, plus the deployment, testing and rollback patterns specific to data pipelines.
content:
S Secrets Manager, Vault or equivalent and creates the Kubernetes Secret.
- **SOPS** with age or KMS — encrypt values in place, so the file stays readable and diffable with only the values encrypted.

External Secrets Operator is generally the strongest answer for cloud environments: rotation happens in the secrets manager with no Git commit at all, and the cluster's workload identity does the authentication.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

## CI/CD for Data Pipelines

<QuestionList topic="CI/CD for Data Pipelines" storagePrefix="cicd-data-pipelines">

<QuestionCard id="cicd-de-01" number={1} question="How is CI/CD for data pipelines different from application CI/CD?" difficulty="hard" topic="Data Engineering">
Four differences that drive everything else:

1. **State is external and shared.** Application code is stateless and rollback restores the previous behaviour. A pipeline writes to tables — reverting the code leaves the bad rows in place, so you need a backfill or restore plan alongside the revert.
2. **Correctness depends on data, not just code.** A transformation can be syntactically perfect and produce wrong numbers because an upstream schema changed. Tests must run against realistic data.
3. **Feedback is slow and d

title: CI/CD
description: CI/CD interview questions covering continuous integration and delivery fundamentals, GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, ArgoCD and GitOps, plus the deployment, testing and rollback patterns specific to data pipelines.
content:
elayed.** A bug can sit unnoticed for days until someone questions a metric. Application bugs usually announce themselves.
4. **Environments are hard to replicate.** You can't clone a 50 TB warehouse per pull request, so CI runs against samples, and sampling can hide the exact skew or edge case that breaks production.

Naming the state problem first is what distinguishes a real answer here.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="cicd-de-02" number={2} question="What tests would you run in CI for a data pipeline?" difficulty="medium" topic="Data Engineering">
- **Unit tests** on transformation functions with small hand-built fixtures — fast, deterministic, no external systems.
- **DAG / syntax validation** — import every Airflow DAG to catch a broken import or a cycle before the scheduler does;

title: CI/CD
description: CI/CD interview questions covering continuous integration and delivery fundamentals, GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, ArgoCD and GitOps, plus the deployment, testing and rollback patterns specific to data pipelines.
content:
`dbt parse` or `dbt compile` for SQL.
- **Integration tests** against real dependencies in containers — Postgres, Kafka, MinIO via Compose or Testcontainers.
- **Data quality tests** on the CI-built output — dbt tests, Great Expectations, Soda: uniqueness, not-null, referential integrity, accepted ranges.
- **Schema contract checks** — fail the build if a column is dropped or a type narrowed, since those break consumers silently.

**"Your CI pipeline takes 45 minutes and people have started skipping it. What do you do?"**
Measure first — find the dominant stage. ## Key Concepts

Data structures matter to a data engineer for three reasons: writing efficient processing code, optimizing memory usage in pipelines, and choosing the right organization for a given problem. Arrays offer fast, indexed access but are expensive to resize; linked lists trade that random access for cheap insertion and deletion by chaining nodes with pointers; stacks and queues layer LIFO/FIFO ordering on top of either; and more complex structures (hash tables, trees, graphs) each trade off differently on lookup, insert, and memory cost. A recurring interview thread is memory management — how allocation, free pools, and garbage collection reclaim space, and what happens when code mismanages a pointer after freeing it. Understanding these trade-offs is less about memorizing defi

<QuestionList topic="Data Structures" storagePrefix="data-structure">

<QuestionCard id="ds-01" number={1} question="What is a data structure?" difficulty="easy" topic="Fundamentals">
A way of organizing data that considers not only the items stored, but also their relationship to each other. Knowing that relationship in advance allows designing efficient algorithms for manipulating the data.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="ds-02" number={2} question="What are the goals of a data structure?" difficulty="easy" topic="Fundamentals">
It must be rich enough in structure to reflect the actual relationships of data in the real world, while staying simple enough for efficient processing.

A data type is a collection of values plus a set of operations on those values. An abstract data type (ADT) is the mathematical concept defining a data type's logical properties, independent of implementation. An ADT has two parts: a **value definition** (e.g. the ADT `RATIONAL` consists of two integers, the second non-zero) and an **operation definition** (creation, addition, multiplication, equality test).
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="ds-04" number={4} question="What is the difference between a stack and an array?" difficulty="medium" topic="Stacks & Arrays">

## Docker: Packaging Pipelines So They Run Anywhere

**"It works on my machine" is the problem containers solve, and data engineering has it worse than most: a pipeline depends on a Python version, a dozen libraries with native extensions, a JDBC driver, a JVM, and a set of environment variables. Docker makes that whole stack one immutable artefact you can version, test, and ship — which is why Airflow, Spark, dbt and every managed data platform now assume it.**

## Key Concepts

A container is **not a lightweight virtual machine** — it's an ordinary Linux process with restricted visibility. Two kernel features do the work: **namespaces** isolate what a process can *see* (its own PID tree, network stack, mount table, hostname), and **cgroups** limit what it can *use* (CPU, memory, I/O). There's no guest operating system and no hypervisor; the container shares the host kernel, which is why it starts in milliseconds.

The other half of Docker is the **image** — a stack of read-only filesystem layers plus metadata describing how to start the process. Containers add a thin writable layer on top. Because layers are content-addressed and shared, ten containers from the same image cost almost nothing extra on disk, and rebuilding after a code change only

<QuestionCard id="dkr-fund-01" number={1} question="What is the difference between a container and a virtual machine?" difficulty="easy" topic="Fundamentals">
A **VM** virtualises hardware. Each one runs a full guest OS with its own kernel on top of a hypervisor — gigabytes in size, tens of seconds to boot, but with strong isolation because the kernel is not shared.

A **container** virtualises the operating system. It's a process on the host, isolated by namespaces and cgroups, sharing the host kernel — megabytes in size, milliseconds to start, but with weaker isolation since a kernel vulnerability affects every container.

For data engineering the practical consequence is density and s

<QuestionCard id="dkr-fund-02" number={2} question="What is the difference between an image and a container?" difficulty="easy" topic="Fundamentals">
An **image** is the immutable template — read-only layers plus metadata (entrypoint, environment, exposed ports). It's the artefact you build, tag, and push to a registry.

A **container** is a running (or stopped) instance of an image, with a thin writable layer on top for anything the process writes.

**cgroups** (control groups) control *consumption* — CPU shares and quotas, memory limits, I/O throughput, PID counts.

content:
mulate dozens of stopped containers — `--rm` cleans up automatically on exit.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dkr-fund-06" number={6} question="Why does my container exit immediately after starting?" difficulty="medium" topic="Troubleshooting">
A container lives exactly as long as its **PID 1 process**. When that process exits, the container stops — there's no background daemon keeping it alive.

The usual causes:
- The command finished (`docker run ubuntu ls` prints and exits — that's correct behaviour).
- The main process was started in the background, so PID 1 returned immediately.
- The process crashed on startup — check `docker logs <container>`.
- The service daemonised itself; run it in the foreground instead (nginx needs `daemon off;`, Airflow's webserver must not fork).

Diagno

content:
se with `docker ps -a` to see the exit code, then `docker logs`. Exit code 137 means SIGKILL — usually the memory limit.
</QuestionCard>

content:
## Images & Dockerfiles

<QuestionList topic="Images & Dockerfiles" storagePrefix="docker-images">

<QuestionCard id="dkr-img-01" number={1} question="Explain the main Dockerfile instructions." difficulty="easy" topic="Dockerfile">
- **`FROM`** — the base image; every Dockerfile starts here.
- **`WORKDIR`** — sets the working directory for subsequent instructions (and creates it).
- **`COPY`** / **`ADD`** — bring files in from the build context.
- **`RUN`** — execute a command at **build** time, creating a new layer.
- **`ENV`** — set an environment variable, persisted into the image.
- **`ARG`** — a build-time-only variable, not present at runtime.
- **`EXPOSE`** — documentation of the port the app listens on; it publishes nothing by itself.
- **`USER`** — switch the user for subsequent i

title: Docker
description: Docker interview questions for data engineers covering containers vs VMs, images and Dockerfiles, layer caching and image optimisation, volumes and networking, Docker Compose, and containerising Spark, Airflow and Python pipelines.
content:
nstructions and at runtime.
- **`ENTRYPOINT`** / **`CMD`** — what runs when the container starts.
- **`HEALTHCHECK`** — a command Docker runs periodically to report container health.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dkr-img-02" number={2} question="What is the difference between ENTRYPOINT and CMD?" difficulty="medium" topic="Dockerfile">
`ENTRYPOINT` defines the executable; `CMD` supplies default arguments, and arguments passed to `docker run` **replace CMD** but not ENTRYPOINT.

```dockerfile
ENTRYPOINT ["python", "etl.py"]
CMD ["--date", "2026-01-01"]
```

`docker run myimage` runs `python etl.py --date 2026-01-01`.
`docker run myimage --date 2026-02-01` runs `python etl.py --date 2026-02-01`.

Use `ENTRYPOINT` when the image *is* one tool and you want run arguments to be its argument

title: Docker
description: Docker interview questions for data engineers covering containers vs VMs, images and Dockerfiles, layer caching and image optimisation, volumes and networking, Docker Compose, and containerising Spark, Airflow and Python pipelines.
content:
s — which is the right shape for a pipeline task image. Use `CMD` alone when you want the default overridable entirely, e.g. so `docker run myimage bash` gives a shell.

Always use the **exec form** (JSON array). The shell form wraps the process in `/bin/sh -c`, which means your program isn't PID 1 and won't receive SIGTERM — so it gets SIGKILLed on shutdown instead of cleaning up.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dkr-img-03" number={3} question="What is the difference between COPY and ADD?" difficulty="easy" topic="Dockerfile">
`COPY` copies files and directories from the build context into the image. That's all it does.

`ADD` does the same, but additionally auto-extracts local tar archives and can fetch remote URLs.

**Prefer `COPY`.** `ADD`'s extra behaviour is implicit — a file name

title: Docker
description: Docker interview questions for data engineers covering containers vs VMs, images and Dockerfiles, layer caching and image optimisation, volumes and networking, Docker Compose, and containerising Spark, Airflow and Python pipelines.
content:
d `data.tar.gz` silently becomes a directory — and its URL fetching produces an uncacheable layer with no checksum verification. Use `COPY` for files, and an explicit `RUN curl ... && tar -xf ...` when you genuinely need to download, so the intent is visible.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dkr-img-04" number={4} question="What is a multi-stage build and why does it matter?" difficulty="medium" topic="Dockerfile">
Multiple `FROM` statements in one Dockerfile, where a later stage copies only the artefacts it needs from an earlier one. Build tooling stays out of the final image.

```dockerfile
FROM python:3.12 AS builder
WORKDIR /app
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --user --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt

FROM python:3.12-slim
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=builder /root/.local /root/

description: Docker interview questions for data engineers covering containers vs VMs, images and Dockerfiles, layer caching and image optimisation, volumes and networking, Docker Compose, and containerising Spark, Airflow and Python pipelines.
content:
.local
COPY src/ ./src/
ENV PATH=/root/.local/bin:$PATH
CMD ["python", "-m", "src.main"]
```

The gain is large for anything needing compilers — a pipeline image with `pandas`, `numpy` and `psycopg2` built from source can drop from ~1.2 GB to ~250 MB. Smaller images pull faster (which matters when Kubernetes starts 200 task pods) and carry far less CVE surface, since the compilers and headers simply aren't there.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dkr-img-05" number={5} question="Why should containers not run as root, and how do you avoid it?" difficulty="medium" topic="Security">
By default the container's root maps to the host's root. Combined with a kernel escape or a carelessly mounted host path, that's a full host compromise — and a root container writing to a mounted volume leaves ro

title: Docker
description: Docker interview questions for data engineers covering containers vs VMs, images and Dockerfiles, layer caching and image optimisation, volumes and networking, Docker Compose, and containerising Spark, Airflow and Python pipelines.
content:
ot-owned files the host user can't delete.

```dockerfile
RUN useradd --create-home --uid 1000 appuser
USER appuser
```

Install dependencies *before* switching, since the unprivileged user can't write to system paths. Note that `USER` is advisory — an operator can still override it with `docker run --user`, so enforce it at the platform level too (Kubernetes `runAsNonRoot`, a pod security policy).
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dkr-img-06" number={6} question="How should you handle secrets in a Docker image?" difficulty="medium" topic="Security">
Never bake them in. The specific traps:

- **`ENV` and `ARG` both persist in the image metadata** — anyone with the image can read them via `docker history` or `docker inspect`.
- **A secret in an intermediate layer stays in the image** even

title: Docker
description: Docker interview questions for data engineers covering containers vs VMs, images and Dockerfiles, layer caching and image optimisation, volumes and networking, Docker Compose, and containerising Spark, Airflow and Python pipelines.
content:
if a later `RUN` deletes it, because layers are additive.

Do instead:
- Inject at runtime — environment variables from the orchestrator, or a mounted file.
- Use **BuildKit build secrets** (`RUN --mount=type=secret,id=pip_token ...`) when you need a credential *during* the build; it's mounted for that instruction only and never lands in a layer.
- Better still, use a secrets manager or cloud workload identity so no long-lived credential exists.
- Add a `.dockerignore` entry for `.env`, `.git`, and key files so they never enter the build context.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dkr-img-07" number={7} question="Why is 'latest' a bad tag to depend on?" difficulty="easy" topic="Best Practices">
`latest` is just a default tag name, not a promise of recency, and it's mutable — the image it p

title: Docker
description: Docker interview questions for data engineers covering containers vs VMs, images and Dockerfiles, layer caching and image optimisation, volumes and networking, Docker Compose, and containerising Spark, Airflow and Python pipelines.
content:
oints to changes under you. That breaks reproducibility in the worst way: the same Dockerfile and the same commit produce different images on different days, and a pipeline that worked yesterday fails today with no change in your repository.

Use explicit version tags for your own images (semantic version, or the git SHA — the SHA is ideal because it ties the running container to an exact commit). Pin base images too, ideally by digest (`python:3.12-slim@sha256:...`) for anything production-facing.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

## Layers & Image Optimisation

<QuestionList topic="Layers & Image Optimisation" storagePrefix="docker-layers">

<QuestionCard id="dkr-layer-01" number={1} question="How does Docker's layer cache work?" difficulty="medium" topic="Layers">
Each instruction produces a layer. On rebuild, Docker walks the Dockerfile and reuses a cached layer if the instruction and its inputs are unchanged — but **the moment one layer misses, every layer after it is rebuilt**, because each depends on the state before it.

For `COPY` and `ADD`, the cache key includes a checksum of the copied files' contents. For `RUN`, it's only the command *string* — which is why `RUN apt-get update` can serve a months-old cached package index. Combine it with the install in a single `RUN` to avoid that.

This cascading invali

title: Docker
description: Docker interview questions for data engineers covering containers vs VMs, images and Dockerfiles, layer caching and image optimisation, volumes and networking, Docker Compose, and containerising Spark, Airflow and Python pipelines.
content:
dation is the single most important thing to understand about Docker build performance.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dkr-layer-02" number={2} question="Why does instruction order matter in a Dockerfile?" difficulty="medium" topic="Layers">
Put what changes **least** first, so the expensive layers stay cached.

```dockerfile

title: Docker
description: Docker interview questions for data engineers covering containers vs VMs, images and Dockerfiles, layer caching and image optimisation, volumes and networking, Docker Compose, and containerising Spark, Airflow and Python pipelines.
content:
# Bad — any source change reinstalls every dependency
COPY . .
RUN pip install -r requirements.txt

title: Docker
description: Docker interview questions for data engineers covering containers vs VMs, images and Dockerfiles, layer caching and image optimisation, volumes and networking, Docker Compose, and containerising Spark, Airflow and Python pipelines.
content:
# Good — dependencies only reinstall when requirements.txt changes
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt
COPY . .
```

In the bad version, editing one line of Python invalidates the `COPY`, and therefore the `pip install` after it — a two-minute rebuild every time. In the good version, source changes only invalidate the final `COPY`, so the rebuild is seconds. This is the most commonly asked Docker optimisation question, and the fix is a two-line reordering.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dkr-layer-03" number={3} question="How do you reduce Docker image size?" difficulty="medium" topic="Optimisation">
In rough order of impact:

1. **Multi-stage builds** — leave compilers and build tools behind.
2. **A smaller base** — `python:3.12-slim` instead of `

title: Docker
description: Docker interview questions for data engineers covering containers vs VMs, images and Dockerfiles, layer caching and image optimisation, volumes and networking, Docker Compose, and containerising Spark, Airflow and Python pipelines.
content:
python:3.12` saves ~700 MB. Alpine is smaller still, but see the next question.
3. **Chain and clean in one `RUN`** — deleting files in a *later* layer doesn't shrink the image, since the earlier layer still contains them:
   ```dockerfile
   RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends curl \
       && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*
   ```
4. **`--no-cache-dir`** on pip, `--no-install-recommends` on apt.
5. **A real `.dockerignore`** — excluding `.git`, `venv/`, `__pycache__`, notebooks and local data can cut a build context from gigabytes to megabytes.
6. **Don't install debugging tools** in the production image.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dkr-layer-04" number={4} question="Is Alpine always the right base image for Python data workloads?" difficulty="hard" topic=

title: Docker
description: Docker interview questions for data engineers covering containers vs VMs, images and Dockerfiles, layer caching and image optimisation, volumes and networking, Docker Compose, and containerising Spark, Airflow and Python pipelines.
content:
"Optimisation">
No, and this is a good discriminating question.

Alpine uses **musl libc** instead of glibc. Python wheels on PyPI are built for glibc (`manylinux`), so on Alpine pip can't use them and falls back to **compiling from source**. For `pandas`, `numpy`, `scipy`, `pyarrow` or `psycopg2` that means installing gcc and headers, build times going from seconds to many minutes, and often a *larger* final image than the slim variant you were trying to beat. There are also documented performance differences in musl's allocator and DNS resolution.

**Use `-slim` (Debian-based) for Python data images.** Alpine is a good fit for Go binaries and simple services with no native dependencies.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dkr-layer-05" number={5} question="What is a .dockerignore file and

title: Docker
description: Docker interview questions for data engineers covering containers vs VMs, images and Dockerfiles, layer caching and image optimisation, volumes and networking, Docker Compose, and containerising Spark, Airflow and Python pipelines.
content:
why does it matter?" difficulty="easy" topic="Optimisation">
It excludes paths from the **build context** — the set of files Docker packages up and sends to the daemon before the build starts.

Without one, a repository containing `.git`, a `venv/`, cached Parquet files and notebook checkpoints can ship gigabytes to the daemon on every build, making even a cached build slow. It's also a security control: a `COPY . .` with no `.dockerignore` will happily bake `.env` and `.git` (with its full history) into your image.

```
.git
.venv
__pycache__/
*.pyc
.env
data/
*.ipynb_checkpoints
```
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

## Storage & Networking

<QuestionList topic="Storage & Networking" storagePrefix="docker-storage-networking">

<QuestionCard id="dkr-vol-01" number={1} question="Why is container storage ephemeral, and how do volumes fix it?" difficulty="easy" topic="Storage">
A container writes to a thin layer on top of the image. Remove the container and that layer goes with it — so anything the process wrote is lost. That's intentional: it's what makes containers reproducible and disposable.

**Volumes** provide persistence by mounting storage from outside the container's lifecycle. Data written there survives `docker rm`, and can be shared between containers.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dkr-vol-02" number={2} question="What is the difference between a volume and a bind mount?" difficulty="mediu

title: Docker
description: Docker interview questions for data engineers covering containers vs VMs, images and Dockerfiles, layer caching and image optimisation, volumes and networking, Docker Compose, and containerising Spark, Airflow and Python pipelines.
content:
m" topic="Storage">
- **Named volume** — Docker manages the storage under `/var/lib/docker/volumes/`. Portable, backed up as a unit, works with volume drivers (including cloud/network storage), and doesn't depend on any host path existing. `docker run -v pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data ...`
- **Bind mount** — maps a specific host path into the container. `docker run -v $(pwd)/src:/app/src ...`

Use **bind mounts in development**, so editing code on your machine is visible inside the container immediately without a rebuild. Use **named volumes in production**, for database files and anything needing durability. There's also **tmpfs**, memory-backed and never written to disk, for scratch or sensitive data.

The classic bind-mount gotcha: the host UID owns the files, so a container running as

content:
a different user gets permission errors on a mounted directory.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dkr-vol-03" number={3} question="What are Docker's network drivers?" difficulty="medium" topic="Networking">
- **bridge** (default) — a private network on the host; containers get internal IPs and reach the outside via NAT. Ports must be published with `-p` to be reachable from the host.
- **host** — the container shares the host's network stack directly. No isolation and no port mapping, but no NAT overhead.
- **none** — no networking at all.
- **overlay** — spans multiple hosts, for Swarm or multi-node setups.
- **macvlan** — gives the container its own MAC and an IP on the physical network, for legacy systems that expect a real host.

Most work happens on user-defined bridge networks, whi

content:
ch is what Compose creates for you.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dkr-vol-04" number={4} question="How do containers talk to each other?" difficulty="medium" topic="Networking">
Put them on the same **user-defined bridge network** and use container names as hostnames — Docker runs an embedded DNS server that resolves them:

```bash
docker network create datanet
docker run -d --name postgres --network datanet postgres:16
docker run --network datanet myapp   # connects to "postgres:5432"
```

Two important details. The **default** bridge network does *not* provide DNS resolution by name — only user-defined networks do, which is why `docker-compose` always creates one. And containers reach each other on the **container port**, not the published host port: if you map `-p 5433:5432`, anoth

title: Docker
description: Docker interview questions for data engineers covering containers vs VMs, images and Dockerfiles, layer caching and image optimisation, volumes and networking, Docker Compose, and containerising Spark, Airflow and Python pipelines.
content:
er container still connects to `postgres:5432`.

To reach a service on the host itself, use `host.docker.internal` (Docker Desktop) or the gateway IP.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dkr-vol-05" number={5} question="What does -p 8080:80 mean, and what's the difference from EXPOSE?" difficulty="easy" topic="Networking">
`-p HOST:CONTAINER` publishes a port — `-p 8080:80` means traffic to port 8080 on the host is forwarded to port 80 in the container. `-p 127.0.0.1:8080:80` binds only to localhost, which you want for anything not meant to be publicly reachable.

`EXPOSE` in a Dockerfile publishes nothing. It's **metadata** documenting which port the application listens on — useful for readers and for `docker run -P` (which auto-maps exposed ports to random host ports), but it has no effec

## Docker Compose

<QuestionList topic="Docker Compose" storagePrefix="docker-compose">

<QuestionCard id="dkr-comp-01" number={1} question="What is Docker Compose and when should you use it?" difficulty="easy" topic="Compose">
A tool for defining and running **multi-container applications** from a single YAML file. One `docker compose up` starts every service, wires them onto a shared network, and creates the declared volumes.

It's the right tool for local development and integration testing — spinning up Postgres, Kafka, MinIO and your pipeline together so you can test against real dependencies instead of mocks. It's also fine for a single-host deployment.

It is **not** an orchestrator: no multi-node scheduling, no rolling updates, no self-healing across machines. That's Kubernetes' jo

title: Docker
description: Docker interview questions for data engineers covering containers vs VMs, images and Dockerfiles, layer caching and image optimisation, volumes and networking, Docker Compose, and containerising Spark, Airflow and Python pipelines.
content:
b.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dkr-comp-02" number={2} question="Walk through a Compose file for a data pipeline." difficulty="medium" topic="Compose">
```yaml
services:
  postgres:
    image: postgres:16
    environment:
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: ${POSTGRES_PASSWORD}
    volumes:
      - pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U postgres"]
      interval: 5s
      retries: 10

  etl:
    build: .
    depends_on:
      postgres:
        condition: service_healthy
    environment:
      DB_HOST: postgres
    volumes:
      - ./src:/app/src

volumes:
  pgdata:
```

Points worth calling out: the ETL service reaches the database at hostname `postgres`; the bind mount on `./src` gives live code reloading in development; the named volume pers

title: Docker

content:
ists database state across restarts; and `${POSTGRES_PASSWORD}` is interpolated from the environment or a `.env` file rather than hard-coded.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dkr-comp-03" number={3} question="Why isn't depends_on enough to guarantee a database is ready?" difficulty="medium" topic="Compose">
By default `depends_on` only controls **start order** — it waits for the container to be started, not for the application inside it to be ready to serve. Postgres takes several seconds to initialise, so a dependent service that connects immediately gets "connection refused" and exits.

Two fixes, and a good answer mentions both:

1. **`condition: service_healthy`** combined with a `healthcheck` on the dependency, as above. Compose then waits for the health check to pass.
2. **Make the

description: Docker interview questions for data engineers covering containers vs VMs, images and Dockerfiles, layer caching and image optimisation, volumes and networking, Docker Compose, and containerising Spark, Airflow and Python pipelines.
content:
application retry** — a connection loop with backoff at startup. This is the more robust answer, because in production (Kubernetes, a restarted database, a network blip) dependencies can disappear *after* startup too, and no start-order mechanism helps with that.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dkr-comp-04" number={4} question="What are the most useful Compose commands?" difficulty="easy" topic="Compose">
```bash
docker compose up -d              # start everything, detached
docker compose up --build         # rebuild images first
docker compose logs -f etl        # follow one service's logs
docker compose exec postgres psql -U postgres    # shell into a service
docker compose ps                 # status of each service
docker compose down               # stop and remove containers + n

etwork
docker compose down -v            # ...and delete named volumes
docker compose run --rm etl python -m src.backfill --date 2026-01-01
```

Two to be careful with: `down -v` destroys your database volume, and `run` starts a **one-off** container (useful for a backfill or a migration) rather than attaching to the running service — that's what `exec` is for.

content:
## Docker for Data Engineering

<QuestionList topic="Docker for Data Engineering" storagePrefix="docker-data-engineering">

<QuestionCard id="dkr-de-01" number={1} question="Why containerise data pipelines at all?" difficulty="easy" topic="Data Engineering">
- **Reproducibility** — the Python version, every library, the JDBC driver and the JVM are pinned in one artefact. The job that ran in CI is byte-identical to the one in production.
- **Dependency isolation** — two pipelines needing incompatible `pyarrow` versions coexist without conflict, which is otherwise a genuinely painful problem on a shared scheduler.
- **Environment parity** — local, CI, staging and production all run the same image.
- **Portability** — the same image runs under Airflow's KubernetesPodOperator, an ECS task, or

title: Docker
description: Docker interview questions for data engineers covering containers vs VMs, images and Dockerfiles, layer caching and image optimisation, volumes and networking, Docker Compose, and containerising Spark, Airflow and Python pipelines.
content:
a Databricks job.
- **Scalability** — orchestrators can start hundreds of task containers on demand.
- **Rollback** — deploying a previous image tag is instant and complete.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dkr-de-02" number={2} question="How do you containerise a Spark application?" difficulty="hard" topic="Data Engineering">
The image needs the JVM, the Spark distribution, your Python or Scala code, and any connector JARs (S3A, JDBC drivers, Delta/Iceberg) — version-matched to the Spark release, since mismatched Hadoop-AWS and AWS SDK JARs are a notorious source of runtime failures.

For **Spark on Kubernetes**, `spark-submit` uses the image for both driver and executor pods, so the same image must contain everything both need. Start from the official `apache/spark` image rather than a

title: Docker
description: Docker interview questions for data engineers covering containers vs VMs, images and Dockerfiles, layer caching and image optimisation, volumes and networking, Docker Compose, and containerising Spark, Airflow and Python pipelines.
content:
ssembling a JVM and Spark by hand.

Things that specifically matter:
- Keep the image small — every executor pod pulls it, so a 3 GB image makes a 200-executor job start slowly. Pre-pull onto nodes or use a registry mirror.
- Set memory limits above the JVM heap, leaving headroom for off-heap and overhead — otherwise the container is OOMKilled while the JVM thinks it has room.
- Never bake credentials in; use IAM roles for service accounts (IRSA) or the equivalent.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dkr-de-03" number={3} question="How does Airflow use Docker?" difficulty="medium" topic="Data Engineering">
Two distinct ways, and interviewers like to check you distinguish them:

1. **Airflow itself runs in containers** — webserver, scheduler, triggerer and workers as separate services, which

title: Docker
description: Docker interview questions for data engineers covering containers vs VMs, images and Dockerfiles, layer caching and image optimisation, volumes and networking, Docker Compose, and containerising Spark, Airflow and Python pipelines.
content:
is what the official Compose file and Helm chart set up.
2. **Tasks run in their own containers** — via `DockerOperator` (on a Docker host) or `KubernetesPodOperator` (a fresh pod per task).

The second is the architecturally important one. It decouples task dependencies from the Airflow environment entirely: each task brings its own image, so a task needing an exotic library doesn't force it into the scheduler's environment, and one task can't break another through a dependency upgrade. It also gives per-task resource limits and clean isolation.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dkr-de-04" number={4} question="How do you handle large data files with containers?" difficulty="medium" topic="Data Engineering">
Don't put data in the image. Images are for **code and dependencies**; every lay

title: Docker
description: Docker interview questions for data engineers covering containers vs VMs, images and Dockerfiles, layer caching and image optimisation, volumes and networking, Docker Compose, and containerising Spark, Airflow and Python pipelines.
content:
er is versioned and pushed to a registry, so baking in a dataset makes pulls slow and the registry enormous — and the data is stale the moment it's built.

Instead:
- Read from and write to **object storage** (S3/GCS/ADLS) using credentials injected at runtime.
- **Mount** a volume or a network filesystem for data that must be local.
- Use `/tmp` or a tmpfs mount for genuine scratch, and size the container's ephemeral storage for it — a Spark shuffle that fills the container's writable layer will evict the pod.
- Commit only tiny fixtures for tests.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dkr-de-05" number={5} question="How do you debug a failing container in production?" difficulty="medium" topic="Troubleshooting">

## Common Interview Scenarios

**"Your Docker build takes 15 minutes on every code change. How do you fix it?"**
Almost certainly instruction order: `COPY . .` sitting before the dependency install, invalidating it every time. Move the manifest copy and install above the source copy. Then look at multi-stage builds, a `.dockerignore`, and BuildKit cache mounts for the package cache.

**"A container works locally but crashes in production. Where do you look?"**
Check the exit code first — 137 points at the memory limit, not your code. Compare environment variables and mounted secrets between the two. Confirm the image tag is genuinely the same (this is where `latest` bites). Then check resource limits, since local Docker usually has no memory cap while the production orchestrator does.

How would you set up a local development environment for a pipeline that reads from Kafka and writes to Postgres?"**
Compose with four services: Kafka, Postgres, your pipeline, and MinIO if object storage is involved. Health checks with `condition: service_healthy` so the pipeline waits. Bind-mount the source for live editing, named volumes for database state, and a seed script to load fixtures.

**"Container or VM for this workload — how do you decide?"**
Containers for anything stateless, short-lived, or scaled horizontally, which covers most pipeline tasks. VMs when you need a different kernel, strict multi-tenant isolation, or a legacy system that expects a full machine.

## Key Concepts

Git is a **content-addressable filesystem with a version control interface on top**. Every commit is a snapshot of the entire tree — not a diff — identified by a hash of its content plus its parent(s). Because each commit points backwards at its parent, the history forms a **directed acyclic graph (DAG)**, and almost every Git operation is a graph manipulation: a branch is a movable pointer to a commit, a merge creates a commit with two parents, and a rebase *replays* commits as brand-new objects with different hashes.

Work moves through three places: the **working directory** (files you edit), the **staging area / index** (what will go into the next commit), and the **repository** (committed history). Understanding that split explains most day-to-day confusion — why `git

## Git Fundamentals

<QuestionList topic="Git Fundamentals" storagePrefix="git-fundamentals">

<QuestionCard id="git-fund-01" number={1} question="What is Git, and how is it different from a centralised version control system?" difficulty="easy" topic="Fundamentals">
Git is a **distributed** version control system: every clone contains the full history, not just the latest snapshot. In a centralised system like SVN, the server holds history and you check out a working copy — most operations require a network round trip, and the server is a single point of failure.

Because Git clones are complete repositories, commits, branches, diffs, and log inspection are all local and fast, and you can keep working offline. The trade-off is that "what's the current version?" becomes a convention (usual

ly whatever is on the `main` branch of an agreed-upon remote) rather than something the tool enforces.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="git-fund-02" number={2} question="Explain the working directory, the staging area, and the repository." difficulty="easy" topic="Fundamentals">
- **Working directory** — the actual files on disk that you edit.
- **Staging area (index)** — a holding space describing exactly what the next commit will contain. `git add` copies the current state of a file into it.
- **Repository** — the committed history stored in `.git/`.

The staging area is what lets you commit *part* of your work. If you fixed a bug and also reformatted an unrelated file, you can stage only the bug fix and commit it separately. A common follow-up: if you `git add` a file and then edit it

again, the commit captures the *staged* version, not the newer one on disk — you must `git add` again.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="git-fund-03" number={3} question="What are the four object types in Git's data model?" difficulty="medium" topic="Internals">
- **Blob** — the raw contents of a file (no filename, no metadata).
- **Tree** — a directory listing: names, modes, and pointers to blobs or other trees.
- **Commit** — a pointer to one tree, plus parent commit(s), author, committer, timestamp, and message.
- **Tag** — an annotated tag object pointing at a commit, with its own message and author.

Every object is stored under the SHA-1 (now migrating to SHA-256) hash of its content, which is why identical file contents are stored only once across the whole repository, and why his

tory is tamper-evident — changing any old commit changes its hash and every hash after it.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="git-fund-04" number={4} question="Does Git store diffs or full snapshots?" difficulty="medium" topic="Internals">
Conceptually, Git stores **full snapshots**. Each commit points at a complete tree of the project. Files that didn't change between commits simply reuse the same blob object, so the storage cost is far lower than "a full copy per commit" suggests.

Diffs are *computed on demand* when you run `git diff` or `git log -p`. Separately, Git's packfiles do apply delta compression as a storage optimisation, but that's a physical storage detail, not the logical model — which matters because it explains why operations like checking out an old commit are fast.

<QuestionCard id="git-fund-05" number={5} question="What exactly is a branch in Git?" difficulty="easy" topic="Branching">
A branch is just a **movable pointer to a commit** — a file under `.git/refs/heads/` containing a 40-character hash. That's the entire implementation.

This is why branching in Git is instant and cheap regardless of repository size: creating a branch writes one small file. When you commit on a branch, Git creates the commit and moves the pointer forward. Deleting a branch removes the pointer, not the commits.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="git-fund-06" number={6} question="What is HEAD, and what does 'detached HEAD' mean?" difficulty="medium" topic="Fundamentals">

A **detached HEAD** means `HEAD` points directly at a commit rather than at a branch. You get this by checking out a commit hash or a tag. You can look around and even commit, but those commits belong to no branch — switching away leaves them unreferenced and eventually garbage-collected. The fix is to create a branch there: `git switch -c my-branch`.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="git-fund-07" number={7} question="What is the difference between git fetch and git pull?" difficulty="easy" topic="Remotes">
`git fetch` downloads new commits and updates your remote-tracking branches (e.g. `origin/main`), but **does not touch your working directory or current branch**. Nothing you have is changed — it's purely informational.

<QuestionCard id="git-fund-08" number={8} question="What is the difference between git switch, git checkout, and git restore?" difficulty="medium" topic="Fundamentals">
`git checkout` historically did two unrelated jobs — moving between branches *and* discarding file changes — which made it dangerous and confusing. Git 2.23 split it:

- **`git restore`** — restore file contents (`git restore file.py` to discard changes, `g

<QuestionCard id="git-fund-09" number={9} question="What does .gitignore do, and why doesn't it work on a file you've already committed?" difficulty="easy" topic="Fundamentals">
`.gitignore` tells Git which **untracked** files to leave alone — build artefacts, virtualenvs, `.env` files, local data samples.

content:
## Branching & Merging

<QuestionList topic="Branching & Merging" storagePrefix="git-branching">

<QuestionCard id="git-br-01" number={1} question="What is a fast-forward merge, and when does it happen?" difficulty="easy" topic="Merging">
A fast-forward merge happens when the target branch has **no commits of its own** since the branch point — the history is a straight line. Git doesn't need to create a merge commit; it just moves the branch pointer forward.

```
before:  main → A → B
                      ↘ C → D  (feature)

after `git merge feature` on main:  main → A → B → C → D
```

Use `git merge --no-ff` to force a merge commit anyway, which preserves the fact that a feature branch existed — some teams require this for auditability.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="git-br-02" numbe

title: Git & GitHub
description: Git and GitHub interview questions covering the object model, branching and merging strategies, rebasing and history rewriting, pull request workflows, recovering from mistakes, and version control practices specific to data engineering.
content:
r={2} question="What is a three-way merge?" difficulty="medium" topic="Merging">
When both branches have new commits, a fast-forward isn't possible. Git finds the **merge base** — the most recent common ancestor — and compares three snapshots: the base, your branch tip, and theirs.

For each file, if only one side changed it, that side wins automatically. If both sides changed the same regions, Git records a **conflict** for a human to resolve. The result is a new commit with two parents.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="git-br-03" number={3} question="How do you resolve a merge conflict?" difficulty="medium" topic="Merging">
1. `git status` lists the conflicted files.
2. Open each one — Git marks conflicting regions with `<<<<<<<`, `=======`, `>>>>>>>` separating your version from their

title: Git & GitHub
description: Git and GitHub interview questions covering the object model, branching and merging strategies, rebasing and history rewriting, pull request workflows, recovering from mistakes, and version control practices specific to data engineering.
content:
s.
3. Edit to the correct final state and **delete the marker lines**.
4. `git add` each resolved file to mark it done.
5. `git commit` to complete the merge (or `git rebase --continue` during a rebase).

`git merge --abort` backs out entirely and returns to the pre-merge state. A good answer also mentions that resolving a conflict means *deciding what the code should be*, not mechanically picking a side — and that you should re-run the tests afterwards, since a syntactically clean resolution can still be semantically wrong.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="git-br-04" number={4} question="Compare Git Flow, GitHub Flow, and trunk-based development." difficulty="medium" topic="Strategy">
- **Git Flow** — long-lived `develop` and `main`, plus `feature/`, `release/`, and `hotfix/` branches.

title: Git & GitHub
description: Git and GitHub interview questions covering the object model, branching and merging strategies, rebasing and history rewriting, pull request workflows, recovering from mistakes, and version control practices specific to data engineering.
content:
Built for versioned software with scheduled releases. Heavy for continuous delivery.
- **GitHub Flow** — one long-lived branch (`main`), short-lived feature branches, pull request, merge, deploy. Simple and the common default.
- **Trunk-based development** — everyone commits to `main` (or merges within hours), with incomplete work hidden behind feature flags. Optimises for continuous integration and minimal merge pain, but demands strong automated testing.

For data pipelines, GitHub Flow with environment-specific deploys is the usual fit; the interesting interview follow-up is how you promote a pipeline change from dev → staging → prod, which is a deployment question, not a branching one.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="git-br-05" number={5} question="What does git cherry-pick do, and

when is it appropriate?" difficulty="medium" topic="Branching">
`git cherry-pick <commit>` applies the *changes introduced by* one commit onto your current branch, creating a **new commit with a new hash**.

The legitimate use is a hotfix: a bug is fixed on `main` and you need that same fix on a release branch. The anti-pattern is using it routinely instead of merging — you end up with duplicated logical changes under different hashes, which makes history hard to reason about and can cause confusing conflicts later when the branches finally do merge.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="git-br-06" number={6} question="What is the difference between a merge commit, a squash merge, and a rebase merge?" difficulty="medium" topic="Merging">
- **Merge commit** — preserves every commit from the br

anch plus a commit recording the merge. Full fidelity, but a busy graph.
- **Squash merge** — collapses the whole branch into a single commit on the target. Clean linear history; you lose the intermediate commits.
- **Rebase merge** — replays each branch commit onto the target tip individually, producing a linear history that keeps the individual commits.

Most teams pick one and enforce it in the repository settings. Squash is popular because a pull request becomes one revertible unit; rebase-merge suits teams who write carefully curated commits.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="git-br-07" number={7} question="How do you find which commit introduced a bug?" difficulty="medium" topic="Debugging">
`git bisect` performs a binary search over history:

```bash
git bisect start
git bisect bad
```

## Rewriting History

<QuestionList topic="Rewriting History" storagePrefix="git-history">

<QuestionCard id="git-hist-01" number={1} question="What is git rebase, and how does it differ from git merge?" difficulty="medium" topic="Rebasing">
Both integrate changes from one branch into another. The difference is **how**.

`merge` creates a new commit joining two histories; the existing commits are untouched and the graph shows the branch really happened.

`rebase` takes your commits, replays them one at a time on top of the target branch, and **creates new commits with new hashes**. The result is a straight line, as if you'd started from the newer base. Your original commits are discarded (recoverable via reflog).

Merge preserves history truthfully; rebase produces a cleaner narrative. Nei

ther is universally correct — it's a team convention.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="git-hist-02" number={2} question="What is the golden rule of rebasing?" difficulty="medium" topic="Rebasing">
**Never rebase commits that others have already pulled.**

Rebasing rewrites hashes. If a colleague has the old commits and you replace them on the remote, their history and yours have diverged with no common ancestor for the rewritten range. Their next pull produces duplicate commits or a mess of conflicts.

Rebasing your own unpushed local work is fine and encouraged. Rebasing a shared `main` is how you ruin an afternoon for the whole team.
</QuestionCard>

The everyday use is cleaning up a feature branch before opening a pull request: collapsing "fix typo" and "actually fix it" into the commit they belong to.

<QuestionCard id="git-hist-04" number={4} question="What does git commit --amend do, and what's the catch?" difficulty="easy" topic="Rewriting">
It replaces the most recent commit with a new one combining the old commit's changes, anything currently staged, and possibly a new mess

<QuestionCard id="git-hist-05" number={5} question="Why is git push --force dangerous, and what should you use instead?" difficulty="medium" topic="Rewriting">
`--force` overwrites the remote branch with yours unconditionally. If a teammate pushed in the meantime, their commits are silently removed from the branch.

Use **`git push --force-with-lease`** instead. It checks that the remote is still where you last saw it and refuses if someone else has pushed — you get an error rather than destroying

<QuestionCard id="git-hist-06" number={6} question="A credential was committed and pushed. What do you do?" difficulty="hard" topic="Security">
**Rotate the credential first.** It must be assumed compromised the moment it hit a remote — it's in every clone, in CI caches, and possibly in a fork or a scanning service. Removing it from history does not un-leak it.

Then purge it from history using `git filter-repo` (the current recommended tool; `filter-branch` is deprecated and slow) or the BFG Repo-Cleaner. This rewrites every affected commit, so everyone must re-clone.

## Remotes & Collaboration

<QuestionList topic="Remotes & Collaboration" storagePrefix="git-collaboration">

<QuestionCard id="git-collab-01" number={1} question="What is a pull request and what does it actually do?" difficulty="easy" topic="Pull Requests">
A pull request is a **host-level feature** (GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket), not a Git one. It's a request to merge one branch into another, wrapped in a review interface: a diff, line comments, status checks, and approvals.

Its real value is the gate — automated tests, linting, and required reviewer approval must pass before the merge button is enabled. That's where CI/CD and code review attach to the workflow.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="git-collab-02" number={2} question="What makes a good pull request?" difficulty="easy" topic="

description: Git and GitHub interview questions covering the object model, branching and merging strategies, rebasing and history rewriting, pull request workflows, recovering from mistakes, and version control practices specific to data engineering.
content:
Pull Requests">
- **Small and single-purpose** — one logical change, reviewable in well under an hour. Large PRs get rubber-stamped.
- **A description explaining *why*** — the diff shows what changed; the reviewer needs the reasoning and any alternatives rejected.
- **Green CI** before requesting review.
- **Tests** covering the new behaviour.
- **No unrelated noise** — reformatting mixed into a logic change hides the logic change.

For data work, add what you validated: row counts before and after, a sample of the output, or the backfill plan.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="git-collab-03" number={3} question="What is the difference between forking and branching?" difficulty="easy" topic="Remotes">
A **branch** lives inside a repository you can already write to — the normal model for a
