team.

A **fork** is a server-side copy of the whole repository under your own account. You have write access to your copy and propose changes upstream via a pull request across repositories. This is the open-source model: contributors need no write access to the original.

Some companies also use forks for tightly controlled repositories, but within a team, branches are the default.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="git-collab-04" number={4} question="What is a remote-tracking branch?" difficulty="medium" topic="Remotes">
A remote-tracking branch such as `origin/main` is a **local, read-only bookmark of where that branch was on the remote the last time you communicated with it**. You don't commit to it; `git fetch` updates it.

This is what makes Git's offline story work: `git log main.

content:
.origin/main` shows what you'd be pulling, and `git status` can say "your branch is ahead by 3 commits" without any network access — it's comparing against the cached pointer.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="git-collab-05" number={5} question="What are protected branches and branch protection rules?" difficulty="medium" topic="Governance">
Host-side rules on a branch (usually `main`) that block direct pushes and enforce a process. Typical settings:

- require a pull request before merging
- require N approving reviews, and dismiss stale approvals on new commits
- require status checks (tests, lint, build) to pass
- require the branch to be up to date with the base
- forbid force-pushes and deletion
- require signed commits

For data platforms this is often a compliance control as much a

</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="git-collab-06" number={6} question="What is a Git submodule, and what are the alternatives?" difficulty="medium" topic="Remotes">
A submodule embeds one repository inside another at a **pinned commit**. The parent repo stores a pointer, not the code. Useful for sharing a library across projects while controlling exactly which version each consumer gets.

The pain: clones need `--recurse-submodules`, updates are a two-step commit dance, and contributors routinely commit a parent change without the submodule bump.

Alternatives: publish the shared code as a proper versioned package (usually the right answer for Python), use a monorepo, or use `git subtree` if

## Undoing Mistakes

<QuestionList topic="Undoing Mistakes" storagePrefix="git-undoing">

<QuestionCard id="git-undo-01" number={1} question="What is the difference between git reset --soft, --mixed, and --hard?" difficulty="medium" topic="Undoing">
All three move the branch pointer to the commit you name. They differ in what they do to the staging area and working directory:

- **`--soft`** — moves the pointer only. Your changes stay staged, ready to recommit. Use to redo a commit message or recombine commits.
- **`--mixed`** (default) — moves the pointer and resets the index. Changes remain in the working directory but unstaged.
- **`--hard`** — moves the pointer and **discards everything**, staged and unstaged. Uncommitted work is gone for good.

`--hard` is the only genuinely destructi

title: Git & GitHub
description: Git and GitHub interview questions covering the object model, branching and merging strategies, rebasing and history rewriting, pull request workflows, recovering from mistakes, and version control practices specific to data engineering.
content:
ve one, and only for uncommitted work — anything committed is still findable in the reflog.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="git-undo-02" number={2} question="When should you use git revert instead of git reset?" difficulty="medium" topic="Undoing">
Use **`git revert`** on any branch others share. It creates a *new* commit that applies the inverse of a previous commit, so history is only ever added to — nobody's clone breaks, and the record shows both the mistake and the correction.

Use **`git reset`** only on local, unpushed commits, where rewriting is harmless.

The short rule: **`revert` for public history, `reset` for private history.** Reverting a merge commit is the tricky follow-up — it needs `-m 1` to specify which parent is the mainline.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="git-u

description: Git and GitHub interview questions covering the object model, branching and merging strategies, rebasing and history rewriting, pull request workflows, recovering from mistakes, and version control practices specific to data engineering.
content:
ndo-03" number={3} question="What is the reflog, and how does it save you?" difficulty="medium" topic="Recovery">
The reflog records **every movement of HEAD and of your branch pointers** in the local repository — commits, checkouts, resets, rebases, merges — even when the commits involved are no longer reachable from any branch.

That makes it the undo button for "I destroyed my work":

```bash
git reflog                    # find the hash from before the mistake
git reset --hard HEAD@{3}     # go back to it
```

It recovers from a bad `reset --hard`, a rebase gone wrong, or a deleted branch. Caveats: it's local only (not pushed, not in a fresh clone), and entries expire — 90 days by default for reachable commits, 30 for unreachable.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="git-undo-04" number=

{4} question="How do you temporarily set aside work in progress?" difficulty="easy" topic="Undoing">
`git stash` saves your uncommitted changes and returns the working directory to a clean state.

```bash
git stash push -m "wip: partial parser"
git stash list
git stash pop      # reapply and remove from the stash
git stash apply    # reapply but keep it in the stash
```

By default it stashes tracked files only — add `-u` to include untracked ones, which is the common gotcha when a brand-new file mysteriously stays behind. For anything you care about, a throwaway commit on a scratch branch is safer, since stashes are easy to forget and don't travel between machines.
</QuestionCard>

description: Git and GitHub interview questions covering the object model, branching and merging strategies, rebasing and history rewriting, pull request workflows, recovering from mistakes, and version control practices specific to data engineering.
content:
ranch. How do you fix it?" difficulty="medium" topic="Recovery">
Assuming you haven't pushed:

```bash
git branch feature-x        # point a new branch at the current commit
git reset --hard HEAD~1     # move main back one commit
git switch feature-x        # your commit is here
```

The commit itself never moves — you create a second pointer to it, then rewind `main`. If you had several commits to move, use `HEAD~n`.

If you already pushed to a protected `main`, don't rewrite it: `git revert` the commit on `main` and re-apply it properly on a branch.
</QuestionCard>

## Git for Data Engineering

<QuestionList topic="Git for Data Engineering" storagePrefix="git-data-engineering">

<QuestionCard id="git-de-01" number={1} question="Why shouldn't you commit large data files to Git, and what are the alternatives?" difficulty="medium" topic="Data Engineering">
Git stores every version of every file forever. A 500 MB CSV committed weekly makes the repository unusable within months — clones become enormous, and the history can't be trimmed without rewriting everything. Git also diffs and compresses text well but binary formats like Parquet poorly, so each version is stored close to in full.

Alternatives:
- **Object storage** (S3/GCS/ADLS) as the source of truth, with only the path and schema in Git.
- **Git LFS** — replaces large files with pointers, storing

title: Git & GitHub
description: Git and GitHub interview questions covering the object model, branching and merging strategies, rebasing and history rewriting, pull request workflows, recovering from mistakes, and version control practices specific to data engineering.
content:
content on a separate server. Works, but adds infrastructure and quota.
- **DVC** or **lakeFS** — data-versioning tools that give you Git-like semantics over data in object storage.

Commit small fixtures for tests, never production datasets.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="git-de-02" number={2} question="How do you handle secrets and environment configuration in a data pipeline repository?" difficulty="medium" topic="Data Engineering">
Never in the repository. The standard layering:

- **`.env` files ignored via `.gitignore`**, with a committed `.env.example` documenting the required keys and no real values.
- **A secrets manager** — AWS Secrets Manager, GCP Secret Manager, Azure Key Vault, or Vault — read at runtime by the job's identity.
- **CI/CD secrets** for deploy-time credential

content:
s, injected as masked environment variables.
- **Workload identity / IAM roles** instead of long-lived keys where the cloud supports it — nothing to leak.

Add a pre-commit hook (`gitleaks`, `detect-secrets`) and host-side push protection so a mistake is caught before it becomes a rotation incident.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="git-de-03" number={3} question="How do notebooks complicate version control, and how do you deal with it?" difficulty="medium" topic="Data Engineering">
A `.ipynb` file is JSON containing source, outputs, execution counts, and metadata. Two problems follow: diffs are unreadable, and every re-run produces changes even when no code changed — plus outputs may embed sample data or credentials.

Mitigations:
- **`nbstripout`** as a pre-commit hook to strip outputs

description: Git and GitHub interview questions covering the object model, branching and merging strategies, rebasing and history rewriting, pull request workflows, recovering from mistakes, and version control practices specific to data engineering.
content:
before committing.
- **`jupytext`** to pair each notebook with a plain `.py` file that is what actually gets reviewed.
- **`nbdime`** for notebook-aware diff and merge.
- Culturally: treat notebooks as exploration, and move anything production-bound into tested modules.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="git-de-04" number={4} question="How does version control fit into a dbt or SQL transformation workflow?" difficulty="medium" topic="Data Engineering">
dbt is designed around it: models are `.sql` files in a repository, so transformations get the same review, history, and rollback as application code.

The typical flow — a developer branches, changes a model, and dbt builds it into a **personal or CI schema** rather than production. CI runs `dbt build` against that schema, executing tests o

description: Git and GitHub interview questions covering the object model, branching and merging strategies, rebasing and history rewriting, pull request workflows, recovering from mistakes, and version control practices specific to data engineering.
content:
n real data. On merge to `main`, a scheduled or triggered job deploys to the production schema.

That gives you the property that matters: the state of `main` is the definition of what production should be, and any change to a metric is traceable to a reviewed commit.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="git-de-05" number={5} question="What belongs in a data engineering repository's CI checks?" difficulty="medium" topic="Data Engineering">
Beyond the usual lint and unit tests:

- **SQL/DAG parsing** — catch a broken Airflow DAG or malformed model before it reaches the scheduler.
- **Unit tests on transformation logic** with small fixtures, not live data.
- **Data quality tests** against a CI-built copy — dbt tests, Great Expectations suites.
- **Schema-change detection** — flag a column drop

title: Git & GitHub
description: Git and GitHub interview questions covering the object model, branching and merging strategies, rebasing and history rewriting, pull request workflows, recovering from mistakes, and version control practices specific to data engineering.
content:
or type change in a PR, since those break downstream consumers silently.
- **Secret scanning** and dependency vulnerability checks.
- **Plan output for IaC** posted to the pull request, so infrastructure changes are reviewable.

The theme: the pipeline is code, so the same gates apply — plus data-specific ones that application CI has no equivalent for.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="git-de-06" number={6} question="How do you structure a repository for multiple pipelines and shared code?" difficulty="medium" topic="Data Engineering">
There's no single right answer, and the interviewer usually wants your reasoning on the trade-off.

**Monorepo** — all pipelines plus shared libraries in one repository. Atomic changes across a library and its consumers, one CI config, easy discovery. Need

title: Git & GitHub
description: Git and GitHub interview questions covering the object model, branching and merging strategies, rebasing and history rewriting, pull request workflows, recovering from mistakes, and version control practices specific to data engineering.
content:
s path-based CI filtering so a one-line change doesn't run every test.

**Polyrepo** — one repository per pipeline or domain, with shared code published as versioned packages. Clean ownership boundaries and independent release cadence, at the cost of dependency-bump churn and duplicated tooling.

Most data teams below a certain size are better served by a monorepo, because pipelines share so much utility code and schema knowledge that coordinating versioned releases becomes the dominant cost.
</QuestionCard>

## Common Interview Scenarios

**"Walk me through what happens when you run `git pull` and get a conflict."**
Name the two phases — fetch updates `origin/main`, then merge tries to integrate it into your branch. The conflict is in the merge phase. Explain that Git found a region both sides modified since the common ancestor and needs a human decision. Then resolve, `git add`, commit, and re-run tests.

**"Your teammate force-pushed and your work has disappeared. What do you do?"**
Don't panic and don't re-clone — that would discard your local recovery options. Your commits are still in your local reflog. Find them with `git reflog`, create a branch pointing at your last good commit, then rebase or merge onto the new remote state. Follow up with the team about protecting the branch.

**"How

title: Git & GitHub
description: Git and GitHub interview questions covering the object model, branching and merging strategies, rebasing and history rewriting, pull request workflows, recovering from mistakes, and version control practices specific to data engineering.
content:
would you roll back a bad pipeline deploy?"**
Distinguish the code from the data. Reverting the commit and redeploying fixes future runs. It does not fix rows already written — you also need a backfill or restore plan for affected partitions. Mentioning that distinction unprompted signals real production experience.

**"Why does your team squash merge?"**
Any consistent answer works if you own the trade-off: squashing makes each PR one revertible unit and keeps `main` readable, at the cost of losing intermediate commits. The wrong answer is not knowing that it's a choice.

## Infrastructure as Code: Provisioning You Can Review and Roll Back

**Clicking through a cloud console to create an S3 bucket, a Glue job and an IAM role works exactly once. Six months later nobody remembers which settings were deliberate, staging has drifted from production, and the person who set it up has left. IaC turns infrastructure into reviewed, versioned, reproducible code — and for data platforms, where one pipeline touches storage, compute, networking and a dozen IAM policies, it stops being optional fairly quickly.**

content:
## Key Concepts

The central idea is **declarative desired state**. You describe what infrastructure should exist; the tool computes the difference against what does exist and makes the minimum set of changes to close the gap. That's fundamentally different from a shell script, which describes *steps* and has no idea what's already there.

Making that work requires the tool to track what it created — which is what **state** is. Terraform's state file maps each resource in your configuration to a real object in the cloud. Nearly every hard Terraform question is really a state question: drift, imports, locking, moving resources, and the various ways teams corrupt state by working around it.

The other property worth internalising is **idempotency**. Applying the same configuration twice must

title: Infrastructure as Code
description: Infrastructure as Code interview questions covering declarative vs imperative approaches, Terraform core workflow and state management, modules and environments, OpenTofu and AWS CDK, and provisioning data platform infrastructure.
content:
produce the same result, with the second run making no changes. That's what makes IaC safe to run from CI on every merge, and why "run it again" is a reasonable recovery strategy in a way it never was with provisioning scripts.

## IaC Fundamentals

<QuestionList topic="IaC Fundamentals" storagePrefix="iac-fundamentals">

<QuestionCard id="iac-fund-01" number={1} question="What is Infrastructure as Code and what problems does it solve?" difficulty="easy" topic="Fundamentals">
Defining and provisioning infrastructure through machine-readable configuration files rather than manual console work or ad-hoc scripts.

What it solves:
- **Reproducibility** — recreate an entire environment from scratch, identically.
- **Version control** — history, diffs, code review, and blame for infrastructure changes.
- **Consistency** — staging and production come from the same definitions, so "it worked in staging" means something.
- **Auditability** — every change is a reviewed commit, often a compliance requirement.
- **Disaster re

title: Infrastructure as Code
description: Infrastructure as Code interview questions covering declarative vs imperative approaches, Terraform core workflow and state management, modules and environments, OpenTofu and AWS CDK, and provisioning data platform infrastructure.
content:
covery** — rebuild in another region from code.
- **Documentation** — the configuration *is* the description of what exists, and it can't drift out of date the way a wiki page does.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="iac-fund-02" number={2} question="What is the difference between declarative and imperative IaC?" difficulty="medium" topic="Fundamentals">
**Imperative** specifies the steps: "create a VPC, then a subnet, then attach a gateway." A bash script with CLI calls. You control the order precisely, but you must handle every case yourself — what if the VPC already exists? What if the last run failed halfway?

**Declarative** specifies the end state: "there should be a VPC with these subnets." Terraform, CloudFormation and Kubernetes manifests all work this way. The tool determines wha

title: Infrastructure as Code
description: Infrastructure as Code interview questions covering declarative vs imperative approaches, Terraform core workflow and state management, modules and environments, OpenTofu and AWS CDK, and provisioning data platform infrastructure.
content:
t to create, update or destroy, and running it repeatedly converges on the same result.

Declarative is preferred for infrastructure because it's **idempotent** and self-healing against drift. Imperative still has a place for genuine one-offs — a data migration, a manual failover.

The nuance worth adding: tools like AWS CDK and Pulumi let you *write* imperative code that *generates* a declarative template, giving you loops and abstractions while keeping the declarative engine underneath.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="iac-fund-03" number={3} question="What is idempotency and why does it matter for IaC?" difficulty="medium" topic="Fundamentals">
An operation is idempotent if applying it many times has the same effect as applying it once.

For IaC this is what makes automation safe. You

content:
can run `terraform apply` on every merge without duplicating resources; if nothing changed, nothing happens. If a previous run failed halfway, re-running completes it rather than compounding the mess. And CI can continuously enforce that deployed state matches the code.

It's also why provisioning with a shell script is fragile — `aws s3 mb` on an existing bucket errors, so the script needs explicit existence checks everywhere, which is exactly the logic Terraform's state and diff engine provide for you.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="iac-fund-04" number={4} question="What is configuration drift, and how do you handle it?" difficulty="medium" topic="Fundamentals">
Drift is when real infrastructure diverges from what your code says — someone changed a setting in the console during an i

ncident, an autoscaler adjusted a value, or another tool modified a shared resource.

Detect it by running `terraform plan` on a schedule: a non-empty plan against an unchanged codebase is drift. Some teams fail a nightly CI job on exactly that.

Handle it by deciding which side is right. Usually you **re-apply to restore the code's version**. If the manual change was correct, codify and commit it. Prevent recurrence by restricting console write access in production so changes must go through the pipeline — this is where GitOps-style continuous reconciliation beats periodic applies, since it corrects drift automatically.
</QuestionCard>

Terraform** — declarative HCL, multi-cloud through a large provider ecosystem, external state file. The de facto standard for provisioning.
- **CloudFormation** — AWS-native, declarative YAML/JSON, state managed by AWS for you. Deep AWS integration and no state file to protect, but AWS-only.
- **Pulumi / AWS CDK** — infrastructure defined in a real programming language. You get loops, types and unit testing; the cost is that it's easier to build something too clever to review.
- **Ansible** — primarily *configuration management* (installing packages, editing config on existing machines) rather than provisioning, procedural by default, agentless over SSH.

The distinction that matters: Terraform and CloudFormation **provision** infrastructure; Ansible **configures** what runs on it. They're

## Terraform Core

<QuestionList topic="Terraform Core" storagePrefix="iac-terraform-core">

<QuestionCard id="iac-tf-01" number={1} question="Walk through the core Terraform workflow." difficulty="easy" topic="Terraform">
```bash
terraform init      # download providers, configure the backend
terraform fmt       # canonical formatting
terraform validate  # syntax and internal consistency
terraform plan      # show what would change — nothing is modified
terraform apply     # make it so
terraform destroy   # tear it all down
```

`init` is required after adding a provider or module, or changing the backend. `plan` is the safety mechanism and should be **saved and applied as a file** in automation:

```bash
terraform plan -out=tfplan
terraform apply tfplan
```

Otherwise `apply` re-plans at

content:
execution time and may do something different from what was reviewed — exactly what you don't want in a pipeline.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="iac-tf-02" number={2} question="What are the main block types in a Terraform configuration?" difficulty="easy" topic="Terraform">
- **`terraform`** — required version and backend configuration.
- **`provider`** — which cloud and how to authenticate.
- **`resource`** — something Terraform creates and manages.
- **`data`** — something that already exists, read-only, looked up at plan time.
- **`variable`** — an input, with optional type, default and validation.
- **`output`** — a value exported for humans or other configurations.
- **`locals`** — named intermediate expressions, for readability.
- **`module`** — a call to a reusable group of res

ources.

The `resource` vs `data` distinction is the one to be crisp about: `resource` means "Terraform owns this and will create and destroy it"; `data` means "this exists already, just tell me about it."
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="iac-tf-03" number={3} question="What is the difference between count and for_each?" difficulty="medium" topic="Terraform">
Both create multiple instances of a resource, but they key them differently — and that difference matters a lot.

**`count`** gives a numeric index: `aws_s3_bucket.data[0]`, `[1]`, `[2]`. Removing the *first* item from the list shifts every subsequent index, so Terraform plans to destroy and recreate everything after it.

**`for_each`** keys by a map key or set value: `aws_s3_bucket.data["raw"]`, `["curated"]`. Removing one entry af

fects only that resource.

```hcl
resource "aws_s3_bucket" "zone" {
  for_each = toset(["raw", "staging", "curated"])
  bucket   = "acme-lake-${each.key}"
}
```

**Prefer `for_each` for anything with an identity.** Reserve `count` for a simple on/off toggle (`count = var.enabled ? 1 : 0`).
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="iac-tf-04" number={4} question="What are provisioners and why are they discouraged?" difficulty="medium" topic="Terraform">
`local-exec` and `remote-exec` run scripts as part of resource creation. HashiCorp documents them explicitly as a **last resort**.

The problems: they're imperative escapes from the declarative model, so Terraform can't plan their effect or detect drift in what they did. They only run at create time, so changing the script does nothing until the re

**commit `.terraform.lock.hcl`**. It pins exact provider versions and checksums so every developer and CI run uses identical providers — the equivalent of an application lockfile. Without it, a provider release can change your plan output with no change in your code.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="iac-tf-06" number={6} question="What are lifecycle meta-arguments?" difficulty="medium" topic="Terraform">
```hcl
resource "aws_db_instance" "warehouse" {
  # ...
  lifecycle {
    prevent_destroy       = true
    create_before_destroy = true
    ignore_changes        = [tags["LastModified"]]
  }
}
```

- **`prevent_destroy`** — makes Terraform error rather than destroy. Put it on production databases and stateful storage; cheap insurance against a misplaced `terraform destroy`.
- **`create_

title: Infrastructure as Code
description: Infrastructure as Code interview questions covering declarative vs imperative approaches, Terraform core workflow and state management, modules and environments, OpenTofu and AWS CDK, and provisioning data platform infrastructure.
content:
before_destroy`** — build the replacement before removing the original, avoiding downtime when a change forces replacement.
- **`ignore_changes`** — stop fighting over attributes modified outside Terraform, such as tags applied by a cost-allocation tool or a count managed by an autoscaler.
- **`replace_triggered_by`** — force replacement when a referenced resource changes.
</QuestionCard>

description: Infrastructure as Code interview questions covering declarative vs imperative approaches, Terraform core workflow and state management, modules and environments, OpenTofu and AWS CDK, and provisioning data platform infrastructure.
content:
## State Management

<QuestionList topic="State Management" storagePrefix="iac-state">

<QuestionCard id="iac-state-01" number={1} question="What is Terraform state and why does it exist?" difficulty="medium" topic="State">
A JSON file mapping the resources in your configuration to real objects in the cloud, along with their last-known attributes and dependency relationships.

It exists because Terraform must answer "does this already exist, and did I create it?" Cloud APIs can list resources but can't tell you which ones *this configuration* is responsible for. State provides that mapping, lets Terraform detect drift by comparing recorded attributes against reality, and caches attributes so a plan doesn't need to re-read everything.

The consequence worth stating: **state is critical infr

title: Infrastructure as Code
description: Infrastructure as Code interview questions covering declarative vs imperative approaches, Terraform core workflow and state management, modules and environments, OpenTofu and AWS CDK, and provisioning data platform infrastructure.
content:
astructure.** Lose it and Terraform no longer knows it owns anything — the next apply tries to create everything from scratch, colliding with what's already there.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="iac-state-02" number={2} question="Why should state be remote, and how do you configure it?" difficulty="medium" topic="State">
Local state can't be shared, isn't backed up, and offers no locking — two engineers applying at once will corrupt it.

```hcl
terraform {
  backend "s3" {
    bucket       = "acme-terraform-state"
    key          = "data-platform/prod/terraform.tfstate"
    region       = "eu-west-1"
    encrypt      = true
    use_lockfile = true
  }
}
```

A production backend needs **versioning** (to recover a corrupted state), **encryption at rest**, **restricted access**, and **l

title: Infrastructure as Code
description: Infrastructure as Code interview questions covering declarative vs imperative approaches, Terraform core workflow and state management, modules and environments, OpenTofu and AWS CDK, and provisioning data platform infrastructure.
content:
ocking**. Equivalents exist for Azure Storage (blob leases), GCS, and Terraform Cloud. Older AWS setups used a DynamoDB table for locking; S3 now supports it natively.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="iac-state-03" number={3} question="What is state locking and why does it matter?" difficulty="medium" topic="State">
Before an operation that writes state, Terraform acquires a lock; a second run blocks or fails rather than proceeding.

Without it, two concurrent applies both read the same state, each makes changes, and the second write overwrites the first — leaving resources that exist in the cloud but appear nowhere in state, which are then invisible to Terraform and to your cost tracking.

If a run is killed mid-apply the lock can be left behind. `terraform force-unlock <LOCK_ID>` clear

title: Infrastructure as Code
description: Infrastructure as Code interview questions covering declarative vs imperative approaches, Terraform core workflow and state management, modules and environments, OpenTofu and AWS CDK, and provisioning data platform infrastructure.
content:
s it, but **verify no apply is genuinely still running first** — force-unlocking an active apply causes exactly the corruption locking exists to prevent.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="iac-state-04" number={4} question="Someone created a resource manually. How do you bring it under Terraform?" difficulty="medium" topic="State">
Write the configuration to match it, then import.

The modern approach is an **import block**, which is reviewable and works with `plan`:

```hcl
import {
  to = aws_s3_bucket.raw
  id = "acme-lake-raw"
}
```

Run `terraform plan` — it shows what would be imported and flags any mismatch between your config and reality. Adjust until the plan is clean, then apply. Terraform can also generate a starting configuration with `terraform plan -generate-config-out=genera

title: Infrastructure as Code
description: Infrastructure as Code interview questions covering declarative vs imperative approaches, Terraform core workflow and state management, modules and environments, OpenTofu and AWS CDK, and provisioning data platform infrastructure.
content:
ted.tf`.

The older `terraform import aws_s3_bucket.raw acme-lake-raw` still works but mutates state immediately with no review step. Either way, the goal is the same: **a subsequent plan showing no changes**, which proves your code accurately describes the resource.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="iac-state-05" number={5} question="How do you rename or move a resource without destroying it?" difficulty="medium" topic="State">
Terraform tracks resources by their address, so renaming one in code reads as "destroy the old, create the new" — catastrophic for a database.

Use a **`moved` block**, which lives in code and goes through review:

```hcl
moved {
  from = aws_s3_bucket.data
  to   = aws_s3_bucket.raw_zone
}
```

The plan then reports a move rather than a replacement. This also han

title: Infrastructure as Code
description: Infrastructure as Code interview questions covering declarative vs imperative approaches, Terraform core workflow and state management, modules and environments, OpenTofu and AWS CDK, and provisioning data platform infrastructure.
content:
dles moving resources into a module, which is the common case when refactoring.

`terraform state mv` does the same imperatively, but it's unreviewable and easy to get wrong. Prefer `moved` blocks, and delete them once everyone's state has been updated.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="iac-state-06" number={6} question="Why shouldn't state files be committed to Git, and what's in them?" difficulty="medium" topic="Security">
State contains **every attribute of every resource, including sensitive values in plaintext** — RDS passwords, generated access keys, private key material, connection strings. Marking a variable `sensitive = true` only hides it from CLI output; it's still in the state file.

So state must never be committed. It also shouldn't be, mechanically: it changes on every appl

title: Infrastructure as Code
description: Infrastructure as Code interview questions covering declarative vs imperative approaches, Terraform core workflow and state management, modules and environments, OpenTofu and AWS CDK, and provisioning data platform infrastructure.
content:
y, causing constant merge conflicts, and Git provides no locking.

Instead: a remote backend with encryption at rest, versioning, and tight IAM. Treat read access to the state bucket as equivalent to read access to every secret in your infrastructure, and prefer generating credentials outside Terraform (or into a secrets manager) so they never enter state at all.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="iac-state-07" number={7} question="How do you split state, and why would you?" difficulty="hard" topic="State">
A single state file for an entire platform becomes slow (every plan refreshes every resource), risky (one mistake can destroy unrelated things), and a bottleneck (one lock for all teams).

Split by **blast radius and change frequency** — commonly: networking, data storage, compute, and

title: Infrastructure as Code
description: Infrastructure as Code interview questions covering declarative vs imperative approaches, Terraform core workflow and state management, modules and environments, OpenTofu and AWS CDK, and provisioning data platform infrastructure.
content:
per-application stacks, each with its own state. Rarely-changing foundational layers stay separate from frequently-deployed pipeline code.

Share values between them with **`terraform_remote_state`** data sources, or better, publish stable identifiers to SSM Parameter Store / Secrets Manager and read those — that avoids coupling one configuration to another's internal structure.

The trade-off is real: more states means more coordination for cross-cutting changes. Split along ownership boundaries, not arbitrarily.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

content:
## Modules & Environments

<QuestionList topic="Modules & Environments" storagePrefix="iac-modules">

<QuestionCard id="iac-mod-01" number={1} question="What is a Terraform module and when should you write one?" difficulty="easy" topic="Modules">
A reusable, parameterised group of resources — any directory of `.tf` files can be a module, called with inputs and returning outputs.

```hcl
module "lake_bucket" {
  source  = "./modules/s3-data-zone"
  zone    = "raw"
  env     = var.env
  kms_key = aws_kms_key.lake.arn
}
```

Write one when the same **group** of resources appears repeatedly — an S3 bucket with its policy, encryption, lifecycle rules and logging is a good module because those pieces always travel together.

Don't write a module that wraps a single resource with no added logic;

title: Infrastructure as Code
description: Infrastructure as Code interview questions covering declarative vs imperative approaches, Terraform core workflow and state management, modules and environments, OpenTofu and AWS CDK, and provisioning data platform infrastructure.
content:
it just adds indirection. The other failure mode is over-parameterising: a module with 40 variables trying to cover every case is harder to use than the resources it wraps.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="iac-mod-02" number={2} question="What is the difference between a root module and a child module?" difficulty="easy" topic="Modules">
The **root module** is the directory where you run `terraform` — it holds the backend configuration and provider setup, and it's the entry point.

A **child module** is anything called via a `module` block. It cannot configure a backend, and it should generally **not** declare its own `provider` block; providers are configured in the root and inherited (or passed explicitly with `providers = {}`). A module with its own provider configuration can't be use

title: Infrastructure as Code
description: Infrastructure as Code interview questions covering declarative vs imperative approaches, Terraform core workflow and state management, modules and environments, OpenTofu and AWS CDK, and provisioning data platform infrastructure.
content:
d with `for_each` and is painful to remove later.

Structurally: root modules are thin — composition plus environment-specific values. Child modules hold the reusable logic.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="iac-mod-03" number={3} question="How do you manage multiple environments in Terraform?" difficulty="medium" topic="Environments">
Three common approaches:

1. **Directory per environment** — `envs/dev/`, `envs/prod/`, each a root module calling shared modules with different variables and its own state and backend. Verbose but explicit; the most common production choice because prod's configuration is visibly separate and can differ where it needs to.
2. **Workspaces** — one configuration, multiple states, switched with `terraform workspace select`. Least duplication, but the environme

title: Infrastructure as Code
description: Infrastructure as Code interview questions covering declarative vs imperative approaches, Terraform core workflow and state management, modules and environments, OpenTofu and AWS CDK, and provisioning data platform infrastructure.
content:
nts share one codebase with conditionals, and it's dangerously easy to apply to the wrong workspace. Better suited to ephemeral, identical environments than to dev/prod.
3. **Terragrunt** or similar — keeps configuration DRY while generating per-environment roots.

Whichever you choose, **prod must have its own state and its own credentials**, so a mistake in dev cannot reach it.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="iac-mod-04" number={4} question="How do you test Infrastructure as Code?" difficulty="hard" topic="Testing">
Layered, cheapest first:

- **`terraform fmt -check` and `validate`** — formatting and syntax, instant.
- **Static analysis** — `tflint` for provider-specific mistakes, `tfsec` / `checkov` / `trivy` for security misconfigurations like a public bucket or an unencrypted volu

title: Infrastructure as Code
description: Infrastructure as Code interview questions covering declarative vs imperative approaches, Terraform core workflow and state management, modules and environments, OpenTofu and AWS CDK, and provisioning data platform infrastructure.
content:
me.
- **Policy as code** — OPA/Conftest or Sentinel evaluating the *plan* against organisational rules ("every S3 bucket must be encrypted", "no instance larger than X outside prod").
- **`terraform test`** (native, 1.6+) — HCL-defined test files that can run plan-only assertions or apply real infrastructure and check outputs.
- **Terratest** — Go tests that provision real infrastructure, assert against it, and destroy it. Slow and costs money, so reserve it for critical modules.

Plan-based checks in CI catch most issues; the review of the plan output posted to the pull request is itself a key control.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="iac-mod-05" number={5} question="What does a good Terraform CI/CD pipeline look like?" difficulty="medium" topic="Automation">
On a pull request:
1. `terr

title: Infrastructure as Code
description: Infrastructure as Code interview questions covering declarative vs imperative approaches, Terraform core workflow and state management, modules and environments, OpenTofu and AWS CDK, and provisioning data platform infrastructure.
content:
aform fmt -check`, `validate`, `tflint`, `tfsec`.
2. `terraform plan -out=tfplan` against the target environment using a **read-only** role.
3. **Post the plan as a PR comment** so reviewers see exactly what will change — this is the single most valuable step.
4. Policy checks against the plan JSON.

On merge:
5. Apply the **saved plan file**, not a fresh plan, so what was approved is what runs.
6. Use OIDC for short-lived cloud credentials rather than stored keys.
7. Require manual approval for production (a GitHub environment gate).

A destroy plan should be loud — flag any PR whose plan includes deletions of stateful resources.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

## OpenTofu & AWS CDK

<QuestionList topic="OpenTofu & AWS CDK" storagePrefix="iac-alternatives">

<QuestionCard id="iac-alt-01" number={1} question="What is OpenTofu and why does it exist?" difficulty="easy" topic="OpenTofu">
An open-source fork of Terraform, created in 2023 after HashiCorp relicensed Terraform from the Mozilla Public License to the Business Source License — a source-available licence restricting competing commercial use. The fork was donated to the Linux Foundation and is community-governed.

It began as a drop-in replacement: same HCL, same provider ecosystem, same state format, so migration from Terraform 1.5.x was essentially swapping the binary. The projects have since diverged somewhat, with OpenTofu adding features like state encryption and early variable evaluatio

title: Infrastructure as Code
description: Infrastructure as Code interview questions covering declarative vs imperative approaches, Terraform core workflow and state management, modules and environments, OpenTofu and AWS CDK, and provisioning data platform infrastructure.
content:
n.

The honest interview answer: it's a licensing and governance decision more than a technical one. Terraform remains more widely used; OpenTofu matters if the BSL is a problem for your organisation or you want vendor-neutral governance.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="iac-alt-02" number={2} question="How do you decide between Terraform and OpenTofu?" difficulty="medium" topic="OpenTofu">
Considerations that actually differ:

- **Licence** — BSL restricts building a competing commercial product on Terraform. For most companies simply *using* it, this is not a practical constraint; for vendors and some legal departments, it is.
- **Governance** — Linux Foundation and open contribution versus single-vendor control.
- **Ecosystem** — providers and modules are shared, so this is rarely the

title: Infrastructure as Code
description: Infrastructure as Code interview questions covering declarative vs imperative approaches, Terraform core workflow and state management, modules and environments, OpenTofu and AWS CDK, and provisioning data platform infrastructure.
content:
deciding factor. Third-party tooling (Terraform Cloud, some CI integrations, some policy engines) is better tested against Terraform.
- **Feature divergence** — growing over time, so a "drop-in replacement" assumption weakens with each release.

For a greenfield data platform either is defensible. The bad answer is treating it as a purely technical superiority argument in either direction.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="iac-alt-03" number={3} question="What is AWS CDK and how does it differ from Terraform?" difficulty="medium" topic="AWS CDK">
The Cloud Development Kit lets you define AWS infrastructure in TypeScript, Python, Java, Go or C#. At synthesis time (`cdk synth`) it generates a CloudFormation template, which CloudFormation then deploys — so the execution engine is declarativ

title: Infrastructure as Code
description: Infrastructure as Code interview questions covering declarative vs imperative approaches, Terraform core workflow and state management, modules and environments, OpenTofu and AWS CDK, and provisioning data platform infrastructure.
content:
e even though your code isn't.

Differences from Terraform:
- **Real language** — loops, conditionals, classes, unit tests, IDE autocomplete and type checking.
- **Constructs** — L2/L3 constructs apply sensible defaults, so a few lines can produce a correctly wired VPC with subnets, route tables and gateways.
- **State** — managed by CloudFormation; there's no state file to protect, but also less control.
- **AWS only** (CDK for Terraform, `cdktf`, is the multi-cloud variant).

The trade-off is reviewability: a Terraform plan shows exactly what changes, while CDK code requires reading `cdk diff` on the synthesised template to see the real effect.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="iac-alt-04" number={4} question="When would you choose a general-purpose language over HCL?" difficulty="mediu

m" topic="AWS CDK">
Choose a **general-purpose language** (CDK, Pulumi) when the team is already strong in it, when you need genuine abstraction — a reusable "data pipeline" construct that expands into twenty correctly-configured resources — or when you want unit tests over your infrastructure logic.

Choose **HCL** when you value the constraint. HCL's limited expressiveness keeps configurations readable by people who aren't developers, makes plans easy to reason about, and prevents the drift toward a framework only its author understands. Multi-cloud and the breadth of the provider ecosystem also favour Terraform.

The failure mode to name: infrastructure code in a full programming language tends to accumulate abstraction until nobody can tell what will actually be created — which defeats

## IaC for Data Platforms

<QuestionList topic="IaC for Data Platforms" storagePrefix="iac-data-platforms">

<QuestionCard id="iac-de-01" number={1} question="What data platform infrastructure would you manage with Terraform?" difficulty="medium" topic="Data Engineering">
- **Storage** — S3/GCS/ADLS buckets with encryption, versioning, lifecycle rules to move cold partitions to cheaper tiers, and access policies.
- **Warehouses** — Redshift, BigQuery datasets, Snowflake (databases, warehouses, roles and grants via the Snowflake provider).
- **Processing** — EMR or Dataproc clusters, Glue jobs and crawlers, Databricks workspaces and job definitions.
- **Streaming** — MSK/Kafka clusters, Kinesis streams, Pub/Sub topics and subscriptions.
- **Orchestration** — MWAA or Cloud Composer environme

title: Infrastructure as Code
description: Infrastructure as Code interview questions covering declarative vs imperative approaches, Terraform core workflow and state management, modules and environments, OpenTofu and AWS CDK, and provisioning data platform infrastructure.
content:
nts, or the Kubernetes cluster Airflow runs on.
- **Catalog and governance** — Glue Data Catalog databases, Lake Formation permissions.
- **IAM** — roles and policies for every pipeline, which in practice is the bulk of the code.
- **Networking** — VPCs, subnets, security groups, private endpoints.

What generally does *not* belong: the pipeline logic itself, and the tables inside a warehouse (that's dbt or migrations).
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="iac-de-02" number={2} question="Where is the boundary between IaC and application deployment for a data platform?" difficulty="hard" topic="Data Engineering">
A useful rule: **IaC provisions the long-lived container; the application pipeline deploys what changes often.**

Terraform creates the MWAA environment, the S3 bucket it reads DAGs

title: Infrastructure as Code
description: Infrastructure as Code interview questions covering declarative vs imperative approaches, Terraform core workflow and state management, modules and environments, OpenTofu and AWS CDK, and provisioning data platform infrastructure.
content:
from, and the IAM roles. It does *not* deploy the DAGs — those change daily and belong to an application pipeline syncing to the bucket. Terraform creates the Databricks workspace and cluster policies; a separate pipeline deploys notebooks and jobs. Terraform creates the BigQuery dataset; dbt creates the tables inside it.

Mixing them produces two bad outcomes: a DAG change requiring a Terraform apply (slow, and now every developer needs infrastructure permissions), or infrastructure drifting because it's managed by an ad-hoc deploy script.

Rate of change is the practical test — if it changes weekly or faster, it probably isn't Terraform's job.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="iac-de-03" number={3} question="How do you manage IAM for data pipelines with Terraform?" difficulty="medium" t

opic="Data Engineering">
Define a **role per pipeline** with least-privilege policies rather than one shared role, so a compromised or buggy job has a bounded blast radius and CloudTrail attributes actions to a specific pipeline.

Practical patterns:
- Scope S3 policies to **prefixes**, not whole buckets — `arn:aws:s3:::lake/raw/orders/*`.
- Separate read and write: most jobs read from several zones and write to exactly one.
- Use **workload identity** (IRSA on EKS, GCP Workload Identity, Azure Managed Identity) so pods assume roles with no static credentials.
- Generate repetitive roles with `for_each` over a map of pipeline definitions rather than copying blocks.
- Enforce with policy-as-code in CI — fail any plan introducing a wildcard action or a public bucket.

Never create long-lived

access keys in Terraform; they land in state in plaintext.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="iac-de-04" number={4} question="What's the risk of running terraform apply against a data platform, and how do you reduce it?" difficulty="hard" topic="Data Engineering">
The specific danger is that data infrastructure is **stateful**. A change that forces replacement doesn't just cause downtime — it can destroy data. Changing a Redshift cluster's node type, an RDS engine version, or a bucket's name can all produce a replace plan, and Terraform will happily execute it.

Mitigations:
- **`prevent_destroy`** on every stateful resource — buckets, databases, catalogs.
- **Read the plan properly**, watching for `must be replaced` and the `-/+` marker rather than skimming to the summary.
- **Automated

title: Infrastructure as Code
description: Infrastructure as Code interview questions covering declarative vs imperative approaches, Terraform core workflow and state management, modules and environments, OpenTofu and AWS CDK, and provisioning data platform infrastructure.
content:
policy checks** that fail the pipeline on any deletion of a stateful resource type.
- **Separate state** so pipeline infrastructure and storage are never in the same apply.
- **Deletion protection** at the cloud level (RDS deletion protection, S3 MFA delete, bucket retention policies) as a second layer that Terraform cannot override.
- **Backups and versioning** independent of Terraform.
- Require manual approval for production applies.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="iac-de-05" number={5} question="How would you provision a complete environment for a new data product?" difficulty="hard" topic="Data Engineering">
Compose modules rather than writing resources directly:

```hcl
module "product" {
  source = "../../modules/data-product"

  name        = "orders"
  env         = var.env
  z

description: Infrastructure as Code interview questions covering declarative vs imperative approaches, Terraform core workflow and state management, modules and environments, OpenTofu and AWS CDK, and provisioning data platform infrastructure.
content:
ones       = ["raw", "staging", "curated"]
  retention   = { raw = 90, staging = 30, curated = 365 }
  catalog_db  = true
  airflow_role_arns = [module.orchestration.executor_role_arn]
}
```

The module creates the storage zones with lifecycle rules, the Glue Catalog database, the pipeline IAM role scoped to those prefixes, monitoring alarms, and cost-allocation tags — all consistently, because they come from one reviewed definition.

The payoff is that onboarding a new data product becomes a small pull request rather than a two-day console session, and every product ends up with the same encryption, retention and tagging standards by construction rather than by discipline.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

content:
## Common Interview Scenarios

**"Your `terraform apply` failed halfway through. What now?"**
State records what was created before the failure, so re-running continues rather than duplicating. Read the error first — a permissions problem or an invalid attribute needs a code fix. Watch for resources marked *tainted*, which will be replaced on the next apply. If the failure left the lock held, verify nothing is still running before force-unlocking.

**"A colleague deleted the state file. How bad is it, and what do you do?"**
Bad but usually recoverable. If the backend has versioning, restore the previous version — this is the whole reason versioning is non-negotiable. If not, you must re-import every resource by hand, which for a real platform is days of work. Meanwhile do not run `apply`,

title: Infrastructure as Code
description: Infrastructure as Code interview questions covering declarative vs imperative approaches, Terraform core workflow and state management, modules and environments, OpenTofu and AWS CDK, and provisioning data platform infrastructure.
content:
since Terraform will try to create everything that already exists.

**"How do you give a new team member the ability to deploy without giving them production access?"**
Separate the plan and apply credentials: a read-only role for the PR plan, which anyone can trigger, and an apply role only the CI pipeline can assume via OIDC. Humans review plans; the pipeline applies them. Nobody needs standing write access to production.

**"How do you know your Terraform code matches what's actually deployed?"**
A scheduled plan against unchanged code — an empty plan means no drift. Fail the job when it isn't empty. Mention that this is periodic rather than continuous, and that a reconciliation-based tool closes the window further.

content:
## Linux: The Environment Every Pipeline Runs On

**Your Spark jobs run on Linux. Your Airflow scheduler runs on Linux. Your container images are Linux. When a job dies at 3am, the difference between a five-minute fix and a two-hour outage is usually whether you can read a log, check disk usage, find the process eating the memory, and kill it cleanly — which is exactly what these questions test.**

## Key Concepts

Linux's organising idea is that **everything is a file** — regular files, directories, devices, sockets, and even running-process metadata under `/proc` all present the same read/write interface. That's what makes shell pipelines so powerful: any tool that reads bytes from standard input can be composed with any tool that writes bytes to standard output, regardless of what's on either end.

Three ideas underpin most interview questions. **Processes** are isolated execution contexts with a PID, a parent, an owner, and a working directory; they communicate through signals, pipes, and files. **Permissions** are a triple of read/write/execute bits for owner, group, and everyone else, checked on every access. And **streams** — stdin (0), stdout (1), stderr (2) — are what redire

## Filesystem & Navigation

<QuestionList topic="Filesystem & Navigation" storagePrefix="linux-filesystem">

<QuestionCard id="lnx-fs-01" number={1} question="Describe the standard Linux directory layout." difficulty="easy" topic="Filesystem">
- **`/`** — root of the single unified tree; there are no drive letters.
- **`/etc`** — system and application configuration files.
- **`/var`** — variable data: logs (`/var/log`), spools, caches. Usually the first mount to fill up.
- **`/home`** — user home directories.
- **`/tmp`** — world-writable scratch space, typically cleared on reboot.
- **`/opt`**, **`/usr/local`** — third-party and locally installed software.
- **`/proc`**, **`/sys`** — virtual filesystems exposing kernel and process state as files.
- **`/dev`** — device nodes.

For a data

content:
engineer, `/var/log` and `/tmp` are the two that matter most in practice — the first is where you look when a job fails, the second is where a Spark shuffle quietly consumes 200 GB.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="lnx-fs-02" number={2} question="What is the difference between a hard link and a symbolic link?" difficulty="medium" topic="Filesystem">
A **hard link** is a second directory entry pointing at the same inode. Both names are equally "the file"; deleting one leaves the data intact until the last link is gone. Hard links can't cross filesystems and can't point at directories.

A **symbolic link** (`ln -s`) is a small file containing a *path*. It can cross filesystems and point at directories, but breaks if the target is moved or deleted — a dangling symlink.

<QuestionCard id="lnx-fs-03" number={3} question="How do you find files on a system?" difficulty="easy" topic="Filesystem">
```bash
find /var/log -name "*.log" -mtime +7          # modified more than 7 days ago
find /data -type f -size +1G                   # files over 1 GB
find /tmp -type f -mtime +30 -delete           # clean up old scratch files
find . -name "*.parquet" -exec ls -lh {} \;    # run a command per match
```

`find` walks the tree live, so it's accurate but slow on huge trees. `locate` queries a prebuilt database — near-instant but only as fresh as the last `updatedb`. `which` and `type` find executables on your `PATH`.
</QuestionCard>

stionCard id="lnx-fs-04" number={4} question="How do you check disk usage, and why do df and du sometimes disagree?" difficulty="medium" topic="Filesystem">
```bash
df -h              # free space per mounted filesystem
du -sh /var/log/*  # size of each item, summarised
du -h --max-depth=1 /data | sort -rh | head    # biggest subdirectories
```

They disagree most often because a **deleted file is still held open by a running process**. `du` walks directory entries and no longer sees it; `df` asks the filesystem, which can't reclaim the blocks until the last file descriptor closes. Find the culprit with `lsof +L1`, then restart the process.

```bash
tail -n 100 app.log          # last 100 lines
```

## Permissions & Ownership

<QuestionList topic="Permissions & Ownership" storagePrefix="linux-permissions">

<QuestionCard id="lnx-perm-01" number={1} question="How do Linux file permissions work?" difficulty="easy" topic="Permissions">
Every file has an owner, a group, and three permission triples — for **owner**, **group**, and **others** — each with read (r=4), write (w=2), execute (x=1).

`ls -l` shows `-rwxr-xr--`: the leading character is the type (`-` file, `d` directory, `l` symlink), then the three triples. That example is `754`.

On a **directory** the bits mean something different and this is a favourite follow-up: `r` lists the contents, `w` creates and deletes entries within it, and `x` allows traversing into it. You need `x` on every directory in a path to reach a file, whic

</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="lnx-perm-02" number={2} question="What do chmod 755 and chmod 644 mean, and when do you use each?" difficulty="easy" topic="Permissions">
- **755** (`rwxr-xr-x`) — owner can read/write/execute, everyone else can read and execute. The default for **directories and executable scripts**.
- **644** (`rw-r--r--`) — owner can read and write, everyone else can read. The default for **regular files**.
- **600** (`rw-------`) — owner only. Required for SSH private keys and credential files; SSH refuses to use a key that's group- or world-readable.

Symbolic form is often clearer for a single change: `chmod +x deploy.sh`, `chmod g-w config.yaml`.
</QuestionCard>

hat is the difference between chmod, chown, and chgrp?" difficulty="easy" topic="Permissions">
- **`chmod`** — changes the permission bits.
- **`chown`** — changes the owning user (`chown airflow file.py`), and optionally the group with `chown airflow:data file.py`.
- **`chgrp`** — changes only the group.

Add `-R` to recurse. Only root can give a file away to another user, which is why `chown` in a deploy script usually runs under `sudo`.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="lnx-perm-04" number={4} question="What is umask?" difficulty="medium" topic="Permissions">
`umask` is a mask of permission bits to **withhold** from newly created files. With the common default `022`, a new file gets `666 - 022 = 644` and a new directory `777 - 022 = 755`.

It matters in shared pipeline environments: if

<QuestionCard id="lnx-perm-05" number={5} question="What are the setuid, setgid, and sticky bits?" difficulty="hard" topic="Permissions">
- **setuid** (`chmod u+s`) — an executable runs with the *owner's* privileges rather than the caller's. Powerful and a classic privilege-escalation vector; avoid unless you must.
- **setgid** on a directory (`chmod g+s`) — new files inside inherit the directory's **group** instead of the creator's primary group. Genuinely useful for shared data directories, since it keeps group ownersh

<QuestionCard id="lnx-perm-06" number={6} question="What is sudo and how does it differ from logging in as root?" difficulty="easy" topic="Security">
`sudo` runs a single command as another user (root by default) after authenticating as *yourself*, subject to rules in `/etc/sudoers`. Every invocation is logged with who ran what.

Compared to a shared root login, that gives you accountability, least privilege (grant only specific commands), and no shared password to rotate. `sudo -i` opens a root shell when you genuinely need a session. On managed infrastructure, prefer

## Processes & Signals

<QuestionList topic="Processes & Signals" storagePrefix="linux-processes">

<QuestionCard id="lnx-proc-01" number={1} question="How do you list and inspect running processes?" difficulty="easy" topic="Processes">
```bash
ps aux                      # every process, with user, CPU, memory
ps -ef --forest             # tree view showing parent/child
top                         # live, sorted by CPU
htop                        # nicer interactive version
pgrep -af spark             # PIDs plus command line, matching a pattern
```

Read `ps aux` columns in this order for triage: `%MEM` and `RSS` (real memory used), `%CPU`, `STAT` (state), and `START`/`TIME` (how long it's been burning CPU). `RSS` is the number that matters when you're hunting an out-of-memory kill.
</Qu

<QuestionCard id="lnx-proc-02" number={2} question="What is the difference between SIGTERM and SIGKILL?" difficulty="medium" topic="Signals">
**SIGTERM (15)** is the polite request, and the default for `kill`. The process receives it and can run a handler — flush buffers, commit an offset, close a database connection, remove a lock file — then exit cleanly.

**SIGKILL (9)** is handled by the kernel; the process never sees it and cannot trap or ignore it. It dies immediately with no cleanup, which for a data job can mean a half-written file, an uncommitted Kafka offset, or a stale lock.

Always send SIGTERM first, wait, and escalate to SIGKILL only if the process is genuinely stuck. Reaching for `kill -9` reflexively is a red flag in an interview.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard

id="lnx-proc-03" number={3} question="What other signals should you know?" difficulty="medium" topic="Signals">
- **SIGHUP (1)** — originally "terminal closed"; conventionally repurposed by daemons to mean *reload your configuration* without restarting.
- **SIGINT (2)** — what Ctrl+C sends; catchable, so a script can clean up.
- **SIGSTOP / SIGCONT (19/18)** — suspend and resume; SIGSTOP is uncatchable like SIGKILL.
- **SIGQUIT (3)** — quit and dump core. On a JVM process it triggers a **thread dump**, which is the quickest way to see where a hung Spark driver is stuck.
- **SIGPIPE (13)** — write to a closed pipe. This is why `head` on a long pipeline kills the upstream command.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="lnx-proc-04" number={4} question="What is a zombie process, and how do you g

content:
et rid of one?" difficulty="medium" topic="Processes">
A zombie (`STAT` of `Z`) has already exited, but its parent hasn't called `wait()` to collect the exit status, so the kernel keeps a small entry in the process table.

Zombies use no CPU or memory — just a table slot. A handful is harmless; thousands mean a buggy parent that isn't reaping children, and can exhaust the PID table.

You cannot kill a zombie, since it's already dead. **Kill or fix the parent** — when the parent exits, the zombies are re-parented to init/systemd, which reaps them immediately. This is exactly why containers need proper init handling (`--init`, or `tini`) when PID 1 is an application that doesn't reap.
</QuestionCard>

```bash
nohup python etl.py > etl.log 2>&1 &     # ignore SIGHUP, redirect output
```

`nohup ... &` is fine for fire-and-forget. **tmux** is better for anything you want to watch, because you can detach (`Ctrl+b d`) and reattach later (`tmux attach -t etl`) with the terminal still live.

The real answer for production, though, is neither: use **systemd**, a scheduler like Airflow, or a container orchestrator, so the job is supervised, restarted on failure, and logged centrally rather than depending on someone's laptop staying connected.
</QuestionCard>

The nice value ranges from **-20 (highest priority)** to **19 (lowest)**, defaulting to 0. Higher niceness means the process is "nicer" to others and yields CPU more readily.


Only root can set a negative value. Useful for keeping a large backfill from starving interactive queries on a shared box — though note it only affects **CPU** scheduling. For I/O contention, `ionice` is the equivalent knob.

<QuestionCard id="lnx-text-02" number={2} question="When would you use awk over grep or cut?" difficulty="medium" topic="awk">

```bash

awk 'NR % 100 == 0' huge.csv                     # sample every 100th line
awk -F',' '{count[$2]++} END {for (k in count) print k, count[k]}' data.csv
```

Use `cut` for simple fixed-delimiter extraction, `grep` for matching, `awk`

## Shell Scripting

<QuestionList topic="Shell Scripting" storagePrefix="linux-shell-scripting">

<QuestionCard id="lnx-shell-01" number={1} question="What is a shebang, and why does it matter?" difficulty="easy" topic="Scripting">
The first line of a script, telling the kernel which interpreter to run it with:

```bash
#!/bin/bash
#!/usr/bin/env python3
```

The `env` form searches your `PATH`, so it picks up the Python in an active virtualenv rather than a hard-coded system path — which is why it's preferred for Python. The script also needs the execute bit (`chmod +x`) for the shebang to be used at all.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="lnx-shell-02" number={2} question="What does set -euo pipefail do, and why should every production script start with it?" difficulty="medium" topic="Sc

ripting">
```bash
set -euo pipefail
```

- **`-e`** — exit immediately if any command returns non-zero.
- **`-u`** — treat an unset variable as an error rather than an empty string.
- **`-o pipefail`** — a pipeline fails if *any* stage fails, not just the last one.

Without these, a script silently continues after a failed step. The `pipefail` part is the one people miss: `curl bad-url | psql` would otherwise report success because `psql` exited 0. Without `-u`, a typo in a variable name expands to an empty string — and `rm -rf "$PREFIX/"` with an unset prefix is how people delete root.
</QuestionCard>

```bash
python etl.py || { echo "ETL failed" >&2; exit 1; }
```

Schedulers depend on this entirely — Airflow, cron, and Kubernetes all decide success or failure from the exit code. A script that catches an error, prints a message, and then exits 0 is invisible to your scheduler, which is one of the more common ways a broken pipeline goes unnoticed for a week.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="lnx-shell-05" number={5} question="How do you make a script clean up after itself, even on failure?" difficulty="medium" topic="Scripting">
Use `trap` to run a handler on exit or on a signal:

```bash
#!/bin/bash
set -euo pipefail

TMPDIR=$(mktemp -d)
cleanup() {
  rm -rf "$TMPDIR"
}
trap cleanup EXIT
```

`trap ... EXIT` fires on normal exit, on an error under `set -e`, and on SIGTERM — s

content:
o the temp directory is removed no matter how the script ends. Without it, a failing job leaves scratch files behind and eventually fills the disk, which is a genuinely common production incident.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="lnx-shell-06" number={6} question="How do you make a scheduled script safe to run twice concurrently?" difficulty="hard" topic="Scripting">
Use a lock so the second instance refuses to start:

```bash
exec 200>/var/lock/etl.lock
flock -n 200 || { echo "Already running"; exit 0; }
```

`flock` takes a lock on a file descriptor and releases it automatically when the process exits — including on a crash, unlike a hand-rolled PID file that goes stale.

This matters because a cron job scheduled every 15 minutes that occasionally takes 20 will overlap itself, and two

content:
concurrent writers to the same output partition produce duplicates or corruption. Exiting 0 when the lock is held (rather than 1) avoids alert noise for what is expected behaviour.

## Cron & Scheduling

<QuestionList topic="Cron & Scheduling" storagePrefix="linux-cron">

<QuestionCard id="lnx-cron-01" number={1} question="Explain cron syntax." difficulty="easy" topic="cron">
Five time fields, then the command:

```
┌── minute (0-59)
│ ┌── hour (0-23)
│ │ ┌── day of month (1-31)
│ │ │ ┌── month (1-12)
│ │ │ │ ┌── day of week (0-7, 0 and 7 are Sunday)
│ │ │ │ │
* * * * *  command
```

```bash
0 2 * * *        # daily at 02:00
*/15 * * * *     # every 15 minutes
0 9 * * 1-5      # 09:00 on weekdays
0 0 1 * *        # midnight on the 1st of each month
```

The gotcha: if **both** day-of-month and day-of-week are restricted, cron runs when *either* matches, not both.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="lnx-cron-02" number={2} question="Why does a script work in your shell

title: Linux
description: Linux interview questions for data engineers covering the filesystem, permissions, processes and signals, text processing with grep/awk/sed, shell scripting, cron scheduling, and diagnosing disk, memory and CPU problems on production servers.
content:
but fail under cron?" difficulty="medium" topic="cron">
Because **cron runs with a minimal environment**. It's the single most common cron problem.

Your interactive shell sources `.bashrc`/`.profile`, so it has a full `PATH`, an activated virtualenv, and exported credentials. Cron typically gives you `PATH=/usr/bin:/bin`, no virtualenv, and none of your exports.

Fixes: use absolute paths for every binary and file, set the variables you need explicitly at the top of the crontab, or have the cron entry source an environment file first. Debug it by capturing everything — `* * * * * /path/script.sh >> /tmp/cron.log 2>&1` — and comparing `env` output between the two contexts.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="lnx-cron-03" number={3} question="How do you manage and inspect cron jobs?" difficu

title: Linux
description: Linux interview questions for data engineers covering the filesystem, permissions, processes and signals, text processing with grep/awk/sed, shell scripting, cron scheduling, and diagnosing disk, memory and CPU problems on production servers.
content:
lty="easy" topic="cron">
```bash
crontab -l           # list the current user's jobs
crontab -e           # edit them
crontab -r           # remove ALL of them — dangerously adjacent to -e
sudo crontab -l -u airflow    # another user's jobs
```

System-wide jobs also live in `/etc/crontab`, `/etc/cron.d/`, and the `/etc/cron.{hourly,daily,weekly}` directories — worth checking when hunting a mystery job, since `crontab -l` won't show them. Logs are usually in `/var/log/syslog` or `/var/log/cron`.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="lnx-cron-04" number={4} question="What are the limitations of cron for data pipelines, and what would you use instead?" difficulty="medium" topic="Scheduling">
Cron has no concept of:

- **Dependencies** — it can't express "run this only after the ingest finishes.

title: Linux
description: Linux interview questions for data engineers covering the filesystem, permissions, processes and signals, text processing with grep/awk/sed, shell scripting, cron scheduling, and diagnosing disk, memory and CPU problems on production servers.
content:
"
- **Retries** or backoff on failure.
- **Backfills** — no way to re-run a date range.
- **Visibility** — no run history, no UI, no lineage.
- **Alerting** — a failure is silent unless you build it yourself.
- **Overlap protection** — you must add `flock` by hand.
- **Distribution** — it's tied to one machine, which is a single point of failure.

For real pipelines use **Airflow**, **Dagster**, or **Prefect**, which are built around exactly these gaps. Cron is still fine for simple, independent, self-contained maintenance tasks — and `systemd` timers are a better cron than cron, with proper logging and dependency handling.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="lnx-cron-05" number={5} question="What is a systemd timer and why might you prefer it to cron?" difficulty="medium" topic="Scheduling

title: Linux
description: Linux interview questions for data engineers covering the filesystem, permissions, processes and signals, text processing with grep/awk/sed, shell scripting, cron scheduling, and diagnosing disk, memory and CPU problems on production servers.
content:
">
A systemd timer unit triggers a service unit on a schedule. Compared to cron it gives you:

- **Centralised logging** through journald (`journalctl -u myjob.service`).
- **Dependency ordering** — start only after the network or a mount is ready.
- **`Persistent=true`** — runs a missed job after the machine was off, which cron never does.
- **Resource limits** — CPU and memory caps per job.
- **Randomised delays** to avoid a thundering herd across a fleet.
- Real status inspection with `systemctl status`.

The cost is more configuration: two unit files instead of one crontab line.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

## Troubleshooting & Performance

<QuestionList topic="Troubleshooting & Performance" storagePrefix="linux-troubleshooting">

<QuestionCard id="lnx-diag-01" number={1} question="A production server is slow. How do you diagnose it?" difficulty="hard" topic="Troubleshooting">
Work through the four resources in order:

1. **Load and CPU** — `uptime` for the 1/5/15-minute load averages, `top` for the biggest consumers. Compare load to core count (`nproc`): load 8 on 8 cores is saturated, on 32 cores it's fine.
2. **Memory** — `free -h`. Check whether swap is in use; heavy swapping is usually the real cause. Then `dmesg | grep -i "killed process"` for OOM kills.
3. **Disk** — `df -h` for space, `df -i` for inodes, `iostat -x 1` for utilisation and await. High `%util` with high `await` means the

title: Linux
description: Linux interview questions for data engineers covering the filesystem, permissions, processes and signals, text processing with grep/awk/sed, shell scripting, cron scheduling, and diagnosing disk, memory and CPU problems on production servers.
content:
disk is the bottleneck.
4. **Network** — `ss -s` for socket summary, `ss -tunap` for what's connected.

The structure matters more than the specific commands: name the resource, name the tool, name what number would confirm it.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="lnx-diag-02" number={2} question="How do you read load average?" difficulty="medium" topic="Troubleshooting">
`uptime` shows three numbers — the average number of processes **running or waiting** over the last 1, 5, and 15 minutes.

Interpret it relative to core count: 4.0 on a 4-core machine means fully utilised; 16.0 on 4 cores means heavily oversubscribed. The three values show the trend — 1-minute far above 15-minute means the problem is growing right now.

The subtlety that distinguishes a strong answer: on Linux, load includ

title: Linux
description: Linux interview questions for data engineers covering the filesystem, permissions, processes and signals, text processing with grep/awk/sed, shell scripting, cron scheduling, and diagnosing disk, memory and CPU problems on production servers.
content:
es processes blocked in **uninterruptible I/O wait**, not just CPU. So a machine with idle CPUs can still show a load of 20 if it's stuck on a slow disk or a hung NFS mount.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="lnx-diag-03" number={3} question="How do you interpret the output of free -h?" difficulty="medium" topic="Memory">
The number people misread is **`free`**. Linux deliberately uses spare RAM for the page cache, so `free` is usually small on a healthy long-running server — that's good, not bad.

Look at **`available`** instead: it estimates what a new process could get, including reclaimable cache. If `available` is healthy, you have memory.

Then check the **swap** row. Steady swap usage with active paging (visible as `si`/`so` in `vmstat 1`) is genuine memory pressure and will destroy

title: Linux
description: Linux interview questions for data engineers covering the filesystem, permissions, processes and signals, text processing with grep/awk/sed, shell scripting, cron scheduling, and diagnosing disk, memory and CPU problems on production servers.
content:
your job's performance.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="lnx-diag-04" number={4} question="Your Spark job was killed but the logs show no error. What happened?" difficulty="hard" topic="Troubleshooting">
Most likely the **OOM killer**. When the kernel can't satisfy an allocation, it picks a victim by score — usually the largest-memory process, which is your executor — and sends an uncatchable SIGKILL. The application gets no chance to log anything, so its own logs simply stop.

Confirm with:

```bash
dmesg -T | grep -i "killed process"
grep -i "out of memory" /var/log/syslog
```

In Kubernetes or YARN the equivalent is a container exceeding its memory limit, showing up as exit code **137** (128 + 9, i.e. SIGKILL) and a reason of `OOMKilled`.

Fixes depend on the cause: raise the executo
