title: JOIN Queries
description: Interview questions on SQL JOIN types — INNER, LEFT, RIGHT, FULL OUTER, Self, and Cross Join — with what each returns and when to use it.
content:
## RIGHT JOIN

<QuestionList topic="RIGHT JOIN" storagePrefix="join-queries-right-join">

<QuestionCard id="rj-01" number={1} question="What does RIGHT JOIN return?" difficulty="easy" topic="RIGHT JOIN">
`RIGHT JOIN` (or `RIGHT OUTER JOIN`) is the mirror image of `LEFT JOIN`: it returns every row from the right table, whether or not it has a match in the left table, filling the left table's columns with `NULL` where there's no match.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="rj-02" number={2} question="Why is RIGHT JOIN used far less often than LEFT JOIN in practice, even though they're logically equivalent?" difficulty="medium" topic="RIGHT JOIN">
Anything expressible with `RIGHT JOIN` can be rewritten as a `LEFT JOIN` by swapping the table order, and most people find it more readable to keep th

title: JOIN Queries
description: Interview questions on SQL JOIN types — INNER, LEFT, RIGHT, FULL OUTER, Self, and Cross Join — with what each returns and when to use it.
content:
e "table I want everything from" consistently on the left rather than switching join direction mid-query. As a matter of convention, many style guides and codebases simply standardize on `LEFT JOIN` and avoid `RIGHT JOIN` entirely.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="rj-03" number={3} question="Rewrite `A RIGHT JOIN B ON A.id = B.a_id` as an equivalent LEFT JOIN." difficulty="easy" topic="RIGHT JOIN">
`B LEFT JOIN A ON A.id = B.a_id` — swapping which table is written first and switching `RIGHT` to `LEFT` produces an identical result set, since both express "keep every row from B, matched or not."
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

---

title: JOIN Queries
description: Interview questions on SQL JOIN types — INNER, LEFT, RIGHT, FULL OUTER, Self, and Cross Join — with what each returns and when to use it.
content:
## FULL OUTER JOIN

<QuestionList topic="FULL OUTER JOIN" storagePrefix="join-queries-full-outer-join">

<QuestionCard id="foj-01" number={1} question="What does FULL OUTER JOIN return?" difficulty="easy" topic="FULL OUTER JOIN">
`FULL OUTER JOIN` returns every row from both tables — matched rows combined normally, and unmatched rows from either side kept with `NULL` filling in the columns from whichever table didn't have a match. It's the union of what `LEFT JOIN` and `RIGHT JOIN` would each return.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="foj-02" number={2} question="What's a realistic use case for FULL OUTER JOIN?" difficulty="medium" topic="FULL OUTER JOIN">
Reconciliation between two datasets that should mostly overlap but might not — comparing a source system's records against a destinatio

title: JOIN Queries
description: Interview questions on SQL JOIN types — INNER, LEFT, RIGHT, FULL OUTER, Self, and Cross Join — with what each returns and when to use it.
content:
n system's after a migration, for example, to surface rows that exist only on one side (data that failed to migrate, or was added only in the new system) alongside the rows that matched correctly.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="foj-03" number={3} question="Not every database supports FULL OUTER JOIN directly — how would you emulate it?" difficulty="hard" topic="FULL OUTER JOIN">
MySQL, notably, doesn't support `FULL OUTER JOIN` directly. It can be emulated with a `UNION` of a `LEFT JOIN` and a `RIGHT JOIN` (or a `LEFT JOIN` and a second `LEFT JOIN` with the tables swapped), since `UNION` naturally deduplicates the rows that both queries would otherwise return twice.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

---

title: JOIN Queries
description: Interview questions on SQL JOIN types — INNER, LEFT, RIGHT, FULL OUTER, Self, and Cross Join — with what each returns and when to use it.
content:
## Self Join

<QuestionList topic="Self Join" storagePrefix="join-queries-self-join">

<QuestionCard id="sj-01" number={1} question="What is a self join, and why does it require table aliases?" difficulty="easy" topic="Self Join">
A self join joins a table to itself, treating it as if it were two separate tables — used when rows in a table relate to other rows in the *same* table, like an `employees` table where each row has a `manager_id` pointing to another employee. It requires aliases (`employees e1 JOIN employees e2 ON ...`) because the database needs a way to distinguish which "copy" of the table a given column reference belongs to.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="sj-03" number={3} question="What's another common use case for a self join besides hierarchical data?" difficulty="medium" topic="Self Join">

## Cross Join

<QuestionList topic="Cross Join" storagePrefix="join-queries-cross-join">

<QuestionCard id="cj-01" number={1} question="What does CROSS JOIN return?" difficulty="easy" topic="Cross Join">
`CROSS JOIN` returns the Cartesian product of two tables — every row from the first table paired with every row from the second, with no matching condition at all. A 10-row table cross joined with a 5-row table produces 50 rows.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="cj-02" number={2} question="What's a legitimate use case for CROSS JOIN, as opposed to it being an accidental mistake?" difficulty="medium" topic="Cross Join">
Generating every combination of two sets deliberately — for example, cross joining a table of products with a table of sizes to generate every possible product-size SKU com

content:
bination, or cross joining a date-range table with a table of stores to build a complete "every store, every day" scaffold for a report before left-joining in actual sales data.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="cj-03" number={3} question="Why is CROSS JOIN often the accidental result of a missing join condition rather than an intentional choice?" difficulty="medium" topic="Cross Join">
The old-style implicit join syntax (`FROM a, b`) is silently equivalent to a `CROSS JOIN` if the corresponding `WHERE` condition linking the tables is forgotten — producing a result set that's the product of both tables' row counts instead of the intended matched pairs, often without an obvious error, just a suspiciously huge and duplicated-looking result.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

content:
## Performance Optimization: Making Queries Run Faster at Scale

**Performance work always starts the same way — measure before you guess — and everything downstream (which index to add, which join strategy to expect, which subquery to rewrite) is really just acting on what a query plan already told you.**

description: Interview questions on SQL performance optimization — query analysis, effective indexing, join optimization, reducing subqueries, and selective projection.
content:

title: Performance Optimization
description: Interview questions on SQL performance optimization — query analysis, effective indexing, join optimization, reducing subqueries, and selective projection.
content:
## Key Concepts

SQL performance tuning is a diagnose-then-fix loop: use `EXPLAIN`/`EXPLAIN ANALYZE` to see what the query actually does (not what you assume it does), find the expensive step, then apply a targeted fix — an index, a rewritten join, a restructured subquery, or simply requesting less data. The fixes on this page all reduce to the same underlying goal: **do less work, and do it against less data**, whether that's avoiding a full table scan (indexing), choosing a cheaper join algorithm (join optimization), avoiding per-row re-execution (rewriting subqueries), or not transferring columns nobody asked for (selective projection).

---

title: Performance Optimization
description: Interview questions on SQL performance optimization — query analysis, effective indexing, join optimization, reducing subqueries, and selective projection.
content:
## Query Analysis Techniques

<QuestionList topic="Query Analysis Techniques" storagePrefix="perf-opt-query-analysis">

<QuestionCard id="qat-01" number={1} question="What's the first step in diagnosing a slow query?" difficulty="easy" topic="Query Analysis">
Run `EXPLAIN` (or `EXPLAIN ANALYZE`, which also executes the query and reports real timings) to see the actual execution plan — which scans, joins, and sorts the database is performing, and in what order — rather than guessing at the cause from the query text alone.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="qat-02" number={2} question="What is a sequential scan, and when is seeing one in a query plan a red flag versus expected?" difficulty="medium" topic="Query Analysis">
A sequential (full table) scan reads every row rather than using an in

title: Performance Optimization
description: Interview questions on SQL performance optimization — query analysis, effective indexing, join optimization, reducing subqueries, and selective projection.
content:
dex to jump to matching ones. It's expected and often the *optimal* choice on a small table, or when a query matches a large fraction of the table's rows — an index lookup plus a trip back to the table can be more expensive than just scanning. It's a red flag specifically when it appears on a large table for a highly selective condition that should have used an available index.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

For a deeper look at how the planner decides between a scan and an index, see [Indexes](/level-1-foundations/sql/indexes/#query-optimization-with-indexes).

## Using Indexes Effectively

<QuestionList topic="Using Indexes Effectively" storagePrefix="perf-opt-using-indexes">

<QuestionCard id="uie-01" number={1} question="What is index selectivity, and why does it matter for whether an index actually helps?" difficulty="medium" topic="Using Indexes">
Selectivity is the fraction of rows a condition on the indexed column actually excludes — a highly selective condition (matching a small percentage of rows) benefits enormously from an index, while a low-selectivity condition (matching most of the table) gains little, since the database ends up fetching most rows anyway.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="uie-02" number={2} question="Why might indexing a low-cardinality column, like a boolean is_active flag, provide little benefit?" difficulty="med

title: Performance Optimization
description: Interview questions on SQL performance optimization — query analysis, effective indexing, join optimization, reducing subqueries, and selective projection.
content:
ium" topic="Using Indexes">
A boolean column has only two possible values, so a condition like `WHERE is_active = true` typically still matches a huge fraction of the table — low selectivity, in other words. The planner often reasonably decides a full scan is cheaper than the overhead of using such an index, since the index barely narrows down the search at all.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

For composite indexes, partial indexes, and covering indexes, see [Indexes](/level-1-foundations/sql/indexes/#managing-indexes).

content:
## Optimizing Joins

<QuestionList topic="Optimizing Joins" storagePrefix="perf-opt-optimizing-joins">

<QuestionCard id="oj-01" number={1} question="What are the three main physical join algorithms, and when does each tend to be chosen?" difficulty="hard" topic="Optimizing Joins">
**Nested loop join** — for each row in the outer table, scan (or index-lookup) the inner table; efficient when one side is small or a good index exists on the join column. **Hash join** — builds an in-memory hash table from one side, then probes it with the other; efficient for large, unsorted inputs without a useful index. **Merge join** — walks two already-sorted inputs in tandem; efficient when both sides are already sorted on the join key, or an index provides that order cheaply.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCa

title: Performance Optimization
description: Interview questions on SQL performance optimization — query analysis, effective indexing, join optimization, reducing subqueries, and selective projection.
content:
rd id="oj-02" number={2} question="Why does join order matter for performance, and who usually decides it?" difficulty="medium" topic="Optimizing Joins">
Joining tables in a different order can produce very different sizes of intermediate results — starting with the most selective filter/smallest resulting set reduces the amount of data every subsequent join has to process. The query optimizer usually decides join order automatically based on table statistics, not the order tables are written in the `FROM`/`JOIN` clauses, though it can get this wrong when statistics are stale.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="oj-03" number={3} question="How does the size of the tables being joined affect which join algorithm the optimizer picks?" difficulty="medium" topic="Optimizing Joins">
Nested loop

title: Performance Optimization
description: Interview questions on SQL performance optimization — query analysis, effective indexing, join optimization, reducing subqueries, and selective projection.
content:
joins scale poorly as both sides grow large, since the cost grows roughly with the product of the two sizes without a good index. Hash and merge joins scale better for large inputs, which is why the optimizer tends to favor them once table sizes cross a certain threshold — the "right" algorithm is fundamentally a function of data volume, not a fixed preference.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="oj-04" number={4} question="What's a common join-related performance mistake, and how would you spot it in a query plan?" difficulty="medium" topic="Optimizing Joins">
Joining on columns of mismatched data types (e.g., an indexed `INT` column joined against a `VARCHAR` column), which can silently prevent the optimizer from using an index on the join, or force an implicit cast per row. In a query pl

content:
an, this often shows up as an unexpectedly expensive sequential scan or a type-conversion function wrapped around the join column that wouldn't be there for a properly typed join.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

content:
## Reducing Subqueries

<QuestionList topic="Reducing Subqueries" storagePrefix="perf-opt-reducing-subqueries">

<QuestionCard id="rs-01" number={1} question="Why are correlated subqueries often a performance concern, and what's the general rewrite strategy?" difficulty="medium" topic="Reducing Subqueries">
A correlated subquery conceptually re-runs once per outer row, which scales poorly on large tables if the optimizer can't rewrite it internally. The general strategy is to rewrite it as an equivalent `JOIN` (often with `GROUP BY` if an aggregate was involved), which lets the optimizer consider set-based join algorithms instead of implicit per-row execution.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="rs-02" number={2} question="Rewrite a correlated EXISTS subquery as an equivalent JOIN." difficu

title: Performance Optimization
description: Interview questions on SQL performance optimization — query analysis, effective indexing, join optimization, reducing subqueries, and selective projection.
content:
lty="medium" topic="Reducing Subqueries">
```sql
-- Correlated subquery
SELECT c.* FROM customers c
WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id);

-- Equivalent JOIN
SELECT DISTINCT c.* FROM customers c
JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id;
```
The `DISTINCT` is necessary in the join version to avoid duplicating a customer once per matching order — a detail the `EXISTS` version handles implicitly, which is worth watching for when doing this kind of rewrite.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="rs-03" number={3} question="When would you use a CTE instead of a subquery purely for performance, not just readability?" difficulty="hard" topic="Reducing Subqueries">
It depends on the database: some materialize a CTE's result once and reuse it, which helps if the same CTE is ref

title: Performance Optimization
description: Interview questions on SQL performance optimization — query analysis, effective indexing, join optimization, reducing subqueries, and selective projection.
content:
erenced multiple times in the outer query — avoiding recomputation a repeated subquery would incur. Others (PostgreSQL since version 12, for example) treat CTEs as optimization fences only in specific cases and may inline them like a subquery by default — so this is a "check your specific database's behavior" answer, not a universal rule.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

## Selective Projection

<QuestionList topic="Selective Projection" storagePrefix="perf-opt-selective-projection">

<QuestionCard id="selproj-01" number={1} question="Beyond readability, what concrete costs does SELECT * add in production?" difficulty="easy" topic="Selective Projection">
More data transferred over the network and materialized in memory than the application actually uses, and it silently changes behavior if columns are added, removed, or reordered upstream — a query that worked fine can break or slow down after a schema change it never explicitly referenced.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="selproj-02" number={2} question="How does selecting only needed columns interact with covering indexes?" difficulty="medium" topic="Selective Projection">
A covering index includes eve

title: Performance Optimization
description: Interview questions on SQL performance optimization — query analysis, effective indexing, join optimization, reducing subqueries, and selective projection.
content:
ry column a query needs, letting the database satisfy it entirely from the index without a separate lookup back to the table ("index-only scan"). `SELECT *` defeats this almost by definition — it's very unlikely every column in the table is also in the covering index — so selecting only the columns actually needed is often a prerequisite for that optimization to even be possible.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

See [Basic SQL Syntax](/level-1-foundations/sql/basic-syntax/#select) for `SELECT *`'s broader readability and maintainability trade-offs.

<QuestionCard id="sql-prac-rank-01" number={100} question="How would you find the second-highest salary in an Employee table?" difficulty="medium" topic="Ranking">
Given an `Employee` table (`ID`, `Salary`), there are several ways to do this.

**Option 1 — subquery with `NOT IN`:** find the max, exclude it, find the new max.
```sql
SELECT MAX(Salary) AS SecondHighestSalary
FROM Employee
WHERE Salary NOT IN (SELECT MAX(Salary) FROM Employee);
```

**Option 2 — not-equal operator**, efficient when excluding a single top value:
```sql
SELECT MAX(Salary) AS SecondHighestSalary
FROM Employee
WHERE

```

**Option 3 — `LIMIT`/`OFFSET`** (best for row ordering); `DISTINCT` avoids ties breaking the logic:
```sql
SELECT DISTINCT Salary AS SecondHighestSalary
FROM Employee
ORDER BY Salary DESC
LIMIT 1 OFFSET 1;
```
*(SQL Server: `OFFSET 1 ROWS FETCH NEXT 1 ROWS ONLY`.)*
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="sql-prac-rank-02" number={101} question="How would you find the maximum salary by department, including departments with no employees?" difficulty="medium" topic="Ranking">
Given `Employee(ID, Salary, DeptID)` and `Department(ID, DeptName)` — **this is a trick question**: ask the interviewer whether departments with no employees should still appear. If yes, use `LEFT OUTER JOIN` (`NULL` salary for empty departments); if no, `INNER JOIN` is enou

## Filtering, Sets & Duplicates

Set comparisons between tables, and finding rows that don't belong.

<QuestionList topic="Filtering, Sets & Duplicates" storagePrefix="sql-prac-filter">

<QuestionCard id="sql-prac-filter-01" number={104} question="How would you select every other (alternate odd/even) record from a table?" difficulty="medium" topic="Filtering">
Assign a row number with `ROW_NUMBER()`, then filter with modulo:

```sql
-- Even-numbered records
SELECT * FROM (
    SELECT *, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY (SELECT NULL)) AS row_num
    FROM Employee
) AS Subquery
WHERE MOD(row_num, 2) = 0;

-- Odd-numbered: WHERE MOD(row_num, 2) = 1
```
*(No `MOD()` support? Use `WHERE row_num % 2 = 0`.)*
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="sql-prac-filter-02" number={105} question="How would you fi

title: SQL Practice | Core Concepts

content:
nd records in Table A that don't exist in Table B, without using NOT IN?" difficulty="medium" topic="Filtering">
**Set operators** — standard SQL/SQL Server/PostgreSQL/MySQL use `EXCEPT`, Oracle uses `MINUS`:
```sql
SELECT * FROM Table_A EXCEPT SELECT * FROM Table_B;   -- Oracle: MINUS instead of EXCEPT
```

**`LEFT JOIN`** (most universal — works across all SQL databases):
```sql
SELECT Table_A.* FROM Table_A
LEFT JOIN Table_B ON Table_A.ID = Table_B.ID
WHERE Table_B.ID IS NULL;
```
*(`NOT IN` is avoided here because it silently returns no rows if the subquery contains even one `NULL`.)*
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="sql-prac-dates-05" number={114} question="How do you limit the number of rows returned by a query, and how does pagination build on that?" difficulty="easy" topic="Result Shaping">
```sql
-- Standard SQL
SELECT * FROM table_name FETCH FIRST 10 ROWS ONLY;
-- MySQL
SELECT * FROM table_name LIMIT 10;

-- Pagination: skip 3, take next 6
SELECT * FROM table_name OFFSET 3 ROWS FETCH NEXT 6 ROWS ONLY;   -- MySQL: LIMIT 3, 6
```
Always pair `LIMIT`/`FETCH` with `ORDER BY` — without it, row order (and your results) are unpredictable.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

title: RDBMS Benefits & Limitations
description: Interview questions on RDBMS benefits and limitations — ACID properties, vertical vs horizontal scaling trade-offs, and when to choose a relational database.
content:
## RDBMS Benefits and Limitations: When to Choose (and Outgrow) a Relational Database

**An RDBMS trades some flexibility and horizontal scalability for strong consistency guarantees and a rigorously enforced schema — a trade that's right for most transactional systems and starts to strain only at a specific kind of scale.**

title: RDBMS Benefits & Limitations
description: Interview questions on RDBMS benefits and limitations — ACID properties, vertical vs horizontal scaling trade-offs, and when to choose a relational database.
content:
## Table of Contents
- [Key Concepts](#key-concepts)
- [Interview Questions](#interview-questions)
- [Common Interview Scenarios](#common-interview-scenarios)
- [Further Reading](#further-reading)

---

title: RDBMS Benefits & Limitations
description: Interview questions on RDBMS benefits and limitations — ACID properties, vertical vs horizontal scaling trade-offs, and when to choose a relational database.
content:
## Key Concepts

The core benefit of an RDBMS is **ACID** — Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability — the set of guarantees that make a transaction either fully happen or not happen at all, even under concurrent access or a crash mid-write. That's paired with a **fixed, enforced schema** (bad data gets rejected at write time, not discovered later) and a mature, standardized query language with decades of tooling, optimizers, and operational experience behind it. The limitations show up as scale grows past what a single, more powerful machine can handle: RDBMSs traditionally scale **vertically** (a bigger server) rather than **horizontally** (more servers), a rigid schema makes fast-changing or semi-structured data awkward to model, and enforcing strong consistency across many machine

title: RDBMS Benefits & Limitations
description: Interview questions on RDBMS benefits and limitations — ACID properties, vertical vs horizontal scaling trade-offs, and when to choose a relational database.
content:
s gets expensive — which is exactly the gap NoSQL and distributed systems were built to fill.

---

title: RDBMS Benefits & Limitations
description: Interview questions on RDBMS benefits and limitations — ACID properties, vertical vs horizontal scaling trade-offs, and when to choose a relational database.
content:
## Interview Questions

<QuestionList topic="RDBMS Benefits & Limitations" storagePrefix="rdbms-benefits-and-limitations">

<QuestionCard id="rbl-01" number={1} question="What are the core benefits of using an RDBMS?" difficulty="easy" topic="Benefits">
Strong consistency guarantees through ACID transactions, a schema that's enforced at write time rather than discovered as a runtime error later, a standardized and widely-known query language (SQL), and decades of mature tooling — query optimizers, replication, backup/recovery, monitoring — built around the relational model.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="rbl-02" number={2} question="What does ACID stand for, and why does it matter?" difficulty="easy" topic="ACID">
**Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability.** Together they guarant

title: RDBMS Benefits & Limitations
description: Interview questions on RDBMS benefits and limitations — ACID properties, vertical vs horizontal scaling trade-offs, and when to choose a relational database.
content:
ee that a transaction either fully completes or has no effect at all, that the database moves from one valid state to another, that concurrent transactions don't corrupt each other's view of the data, and that a committed transaction survives a crash. It matters because it's what lets application code trust the database instead of re-implementing that safety itself.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="rbl-03" number={3} question="Explain atomicity with an example." difficulty="medium" topic="ACID">
Atomicity means a transaction is all-or-nothing. Classic example: transferring money between two bank accounts requires debiting one account and crediting another — atomicity guarantees that if the crediting step fails, the debit is rolled back too, so the transaction never leaves money "in trans

title: RDBMS Benefits & Limitations
description: Interview questions on RDBMS benefits and limitations — ACID properties, vertical vs horizontal scaling trade-offs, and when to choose a relational database.
content:
it" or duplicated.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="rbl-04" number={4} question="Explain consistency in ACID." difficulty="medium" topic="ACID">
Consistency means a transaction can only bring the database from one valid state to another valid state — it can't violate constraints, foreign keys, or defined rules, even temporarily as far as anything outside the transaction can observe. If a transaction would break a constraint (e.g., insert an order for a customer that doesn't exist), the whole transaction is rejected rather than partially applied.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="rbl-05" number={5} question="Explain isolation and why isolation levels exist." difficulty="medium" topic="ACID">
Isolation means concurrent transactions shouldn't see each other's uncommitted changes, so the ou

title: RDBMS Benefits & Limitations
description: Interview questions on RDBMS benefits and limitations — ACID properties, vertical vs horizontal scaling trade-offs, and when to choose a relational database.
content:
tcome looks as if transactions ran one at a time even though they actually overlapped. Isolation levels (`READ COMMITTED`, `REPEATABLE READ`, `SERIALIZABLE`, etc.) exist because full isolation is expensive — each level trades some strictness for performance, and picking the right one depends on what anomalies (dirty reads, non-repeatable reads, phantom reads) a given workload can tolerate.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="rbl-06" number={6} question="Explain durability." difficulty="easy" topic="ACID">
Durability means once a transaction is committed, its changes survive — even a power loss or crash immediately afterward won't lose it. RDBMSs typically achieve this by writing to a write-ahead log (WAL) on durable storage before acknowledging the commit, so the change can be replayed from

title: RDBMS Benefits & Limitations
description: Interview questions on RDBMS benefits and limitations — ACID properties, vertical vs horizontal scaling trade-offs, and when to choose a relational database.
content:
the log if the in-memory state is lost.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="rbl-07" number={7} question="What are the main limitations of an RDBMS at scale?" difficulty="medium" topic="Limitations">
Traditional RDBMSs scale vertically more naturally than horizontally, so there's a ceiling set by how large a single machine can get. A fixed schema makes it awkward to store fast-changing, semi-structured, or highly variable data. And maintaining strong consistency across many nodes (if you do try to distribute an RDBMS) adds coordination overhead that limits write throughput compared to systems designed for eventual consistency.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="rbl-08" number={8} question="What's the difference between vertical and horizontal scaling, and why do RDBMSs traditionally favor v

title: RDBMS Benefits & Limitations
description: Interview questions on RDBMS benefits and limitations — ACID properties, vertical vs horizontal scaling trade-offs, and when to choose a relational database.
content:
ertical?" difficulty="medium" topic="Scaling">
Vertical scaling means adding more resources (CPU, RAM, faster disks) to a single machine; horizontal scaling means adding more machines and distributing the load across them. RDBMSs traditionally favor vertical scaling because ACID transactions and joins are much simpler to guarantee on a single node — distributing them across machines while preserving the same consistency guarantees is a genuinely hard distributed-systems problem, one that only some newer distributed SQL systems (e.g., CockroachDB, Google Spanner) have solved.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="rbl-09" number={9} question="When would you choose an RDBMS over a NoSQL system, and vice versa?" difficulty="medium" topic="Trade-offs">
Choose an RDBMS when data is structured, rela

title: RDBMS Benefits & Limitations
description: Interview questions on RDBMS benefits and limitations — ACID properties, vertical vs horizontal scaling trade-offs, and when to choose a relational database.
content:
tionships matter (foreign keys, joins), and transactional correctness is critical — financial records, order systems, anything where "partially applied" is unacceptable. Lean toward NoSQL when the schema is highly variable or evolving fast, write throughput needs to scale horizontally beyond what a single machine can handle, or the access pattern is simple enough (key-value lookups, for example) that relational features add overhead without adding value.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

---

title: RDBMS Benefits & Limitations
description: Interview questions on RDBMS benefits and limitations — ACID properties, vertical vs horizontal scaling trade-offs, and when to choose a relational database.
content:
## Common Interview Scenarios

- **"Walk me through what ACID actually protects against, one letter at a time."** Use a concrete transaction (a bank transfer, an order placement) and show what specifically breaks if each property is missing.
- **"Your RDBMS is hitting a scaling wall — what are your options before rearchitecting to NoSQL?"** Talk through read replicas, caching, connection pooling, query/index optimization, and vertical scaling headroom before jumping to "switch databases."
- **"When would you deliberately choose a weaker isolation level than SERIALIZABLE?"** Explain the performance trade-off — most workloads use `READ COMMITTED` because full serializability adds locking overhead the application doesn't actually need.

---

title: Relational Databases
description: Interview questions on what relational databases are, the relational model, tables, primary and foreign keys, and referential integrity.
content:
## What Are Relational Databases: Tables, Keys, and the Relational Model

**A relational database organizes data into tables of rows and columns, linked to each other through keys rather than duplicated everywhere they're needed — the structural idea every SQL query and every RDBMS is ultimately built on top of.**

title: Relational Databases
description: Interview questions on what relational databases are, the relational model, tables, primary and foreign keys, and referential integrity.
content:
## Table of Contents
- [Key Concepts](#key-concepts)
- [Interview Questions](#interview-questions)
- [Common Interview Scenarios](#common-interview-scenarios)
- [Further Reading](#further-reading)

---

title: Relational Databases
description: Interview questions on what relational databases are, the relational model, tables, primary and foreign keys, and referential integrity.
content:
## Key Concepts

The **relational model**, introduced by Edgar Codd in 1970, represents data as **tables** (also called relations) — each table a fixed set of columns (attributes) and any number of rows (records). A **primary key** uniquely identifies each row in a table, and a **foreign key** in one table points to a primary key in another, which is what lets related data live in separate tables instead of being duplicated everywhere it's needed. That separation is deliberate: it's how a relational database enforces **referential integrity** — the guarantee that a foreign key always points to a row that actually exists — and how it avoids the update anomalies that come from copying the same fact into a dozen places. Relationships between tables come in a few shapes: **one-to-many** (one d

title: Relational Databases
description: Interview questions on what relational databases are, the relational model, tables, primary and foreign keys, and referential integrity.
content:
epartment, many employees) needs only a foreign key on the "many" side, while **many-to-many** (students and courses) needs a third junction table holding a foreign key to each side.

---

title: Relational Databases
description: Interview questions on what relational databases are, the relational model, tables, primary and foreign keys, and referential integrity.
content:
## Interview Questions

<QuestionList topic="Relational Databases" storagePrefix="relational-databases">

<QuestionCard id="rdb-01" number={1} question="What is a relational database?" difficulty="easy" topic="Fundamentals">
A relational database is a database that stores data in tables — structured collections of rows and columns — and represents relationships between different pieces of data through keys rather than by nesting or duplicating data. It's the model underlying virtually every SQL database: PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQL Server, Oracle, and the managed cloud warehouses built on similar principles.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="rdb-02" number={2} question="Who introduced the relational model, and what problem was it solving?" difficulty="easy" topic="Fundamentals">
Edgar F. Codd

title: Relational Databases
description: Interview questions on what relational databases are, the relational model, tables, primary and foreign keys, and referential integrity.
content:
introduced the relational model in a 1970 paper while at IBM. Before it, databases were typically hierarchical or network-based, requiring applications to know the physical structure and navigation paths of the data. Codd's insight was that data could be represented purely as tables with logical relationships, letting a query language describe *what* data you want without specifying *how* to physically traverse it to get there.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="rdb-03" number={3} question="What are tables, rows, and columns in the relational model?" difficulty="easy" topic="Fundamentals">
A **table** represents one entity type (e.g., `employees`). Each **column** defines an attribute of that entity with a fixed data type (e.g., `name`, `hire_date`, `salary`). Each **row** is one instance

title: Relational Databases
description: Interview questions on what relational databases are, the relational model, tables, primary and foreign keys, and referential integrity.
content:
of that entity — one specific employee, with a value for every column. Every row in a table shares the same columns, which is what makes the table queryable as a uniform set.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="rdb-04" number={4} question="What is a primary key, and why must it be unique?" difficulty="easy" topic="Keys">
A primary key is one or more columns whose value uniquely identifies a row within a table — no two rows can share the same primary key value, and it can't be `NULL`. It has to be unique because it's the handle every other part of the system uses to refer to that exact row: foreign keys reference it, indexes are frequently built on it, and joins rely on it resolving to exactly one row.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="rdb-05" number={5} question="What is a foreign key, and

title: Relational Databases
description: Interview questions on what relational databases are, the relational model, tables, primary and foreign keys, and referential integrity.
content:
what does it enforce?" difficulty="easy" topic="Keys">
A foreign key is a column (or columns) in one table that references the primary key of another table — for example, an `orders.customer_id` column referencing `customers.id`. It enforces **referential integrity**: the database won't let you insert an order with a `customer_id` that doesn't exist in the `customers` table, and by default won't let you delete a customer that still has orders referencing them (unless a cascade rule says otherwise).
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="rdb-06" number={6} question="What's the difference between a one-to-many and a many-to-many relationship, and how is many-to-many implemented?" difficulty="medium" topic="Relationships">
A one-to-many relationship (one department has many employees) is impleme

title: Relational Databases
description: Interview questions on what relational databases are, the relational model, tables, primary and foreign keys, and referential integrity.
content:
nted with a single foreign key on the "many" side — `employees.department_id`. A many-to-many relationship (students enroll in many courses, courses have many students) can't be represented with a single foreign key on either side, since neither table has one row per relationship; instead it requires a **junction table** (e.g., `enrollments`) holding a foreign key to each side, with each row representing one specific student-course pairing.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="rdb-07" number={7} question="What is a schema, and why does defining one upfront matter?" difficulty="medium" topic="Fundamentals">
A schema is the definition of a table's structure — its columns, their data types, and its constraints (primary key, foreign keys, `NOT NULL`, etc.) — declared before any data is inserted.

title: Relational Databases
description: Interview questions on what relational databases are, the relational model, tables, primary and foreign keys, and referential integrity.
content:
Defining it upfront matters because the database then enforces it on every write: a row that violates the schema (wrong type, missing required value, duplicate key) is rejected at insert time rather than silently corrupting downstream data.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="rdb-08" number={8} question="Why store data across multiple related tables instead of one big table?" difficulty="medium" topic="Design">
Splitting data across related tables — normalization — avoids duplicating the same fact in many places. If a customer's address lived on every one of their orders instead of once in a `customers` table, updating it would mean rewriting every order row, and a partial update would leave the data inconsistent. Separate, related tables mean each fact is stored once and referenced everyw

title: Relational Databases
description: Interview questions on what relational databases are, the relational model, tables, primary and foreign keys, and referential integrity.
content:
here it's needed.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="rdb-09" number={9} question="What is referential integrity?" difficulty="medium" topic="Keys">
Referential integrity is the guarantee that a foreign key value always corresponds to an existing row in the referenced table — no "dangling" foreign keys pointing at rows that were deleted or never existed. The database enforces it automatically once a foreign key constraint is declared, rejecting inserts/updates that would violate it and controlling what happens on delete via rules like `ON DELETE CASCADE` or `ON DELETE RESTRICT`.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

---

title: Relational Databases
description: Interview questions on what relational databases are, the relational model, tables, primary and foreign keys, and referential integrity.
content:
## Common Interview Scenarios

- **"Design a simple schema for an e-commerce system with customers, orders, and products."** Walk through identifying the entities, their primary keys, the one-to-many relationships (customer → orders), and the many-to-many relationship (orders ↔ products) that needs a junction table (`order_items`).
- **"What happens if you try to delete a customer who still has orders?"** Explain referential integrity — the database blocks the delete by default, unless a cascade or set-null rule was explicitly configured on the foreign key.
- **"Why not just store everything in one giant table?"** Use it to explain normalization's payoff: avoiding duplicated facts and the update anomalies that come with them, at the cost of needing joins to reassemble the full picture.

--

content:
## SQL Data Types: Numeric, String, Date, and Beyond

**Every column in a relational table has a declared data type, and that choice isn't a formality — it determines how much space a value takes, what operations are valid on it, and whether bad data gets rejected at the door or silently corrupts a downstream calculation.**

title: SQL Data Types
description: Interview questions on SQL data types — numeric, string, date/time, boolean, vendor-specific types, and how type choice affects storage and correctness.
content:
## Table of Contents
- [Key Concepts](#key-concepts)
- [Interview Questions](#interview-questions)
- [Common Interview Scenarios](#common-interview-scenarios)
- [Further Reading](#further-reading)

---

title: SQL Data Types
description: Interview questions on SQL data types — numeric, string, date/time, boolean, vendor-specific types, and how type choice affects storage and correctness.
content:
## Key Concepts

SQL data types fall into a few core families: **numeric** (`INT`, `DECIMAL`, `FLOAT` — whole numbers, exact decimals, and approximate floating-point respectively), **string** (`CHAR`, `VARCHAR`, `TEXT` — fixed-length, variable-length, and unbounded text), **date/time** (`DATE`, `DATETIME`/`TIMESTAMP` — a calendar date versus a specific instant), and **boolean** (true/false, though not every SQL dialect has a native boolean type). The choice between similar-looking types has real consequences: `DECIMAL` stores an exact value while `FLOAT` stores an approximation, which matters enormously for money; `CHAR` pads to a fixed length while `VARCHAR` doesn't, trading a little flexibility for storage predictability. Most databases also offer **vendor-specific types** beyond the SQL

title: SQL Data Types
description: Interview questions on SQL data types — numeric, string, date/time, boolean, vendor-specific types, and how type choice affects storage and correctness.
content:
standard — PostgreSQL's `JSONB` and `ARRAY` being common examples — for cases the standard types don't cover well.

---

title: SQL Data Types
description: Interview questions on SQL data types — numeric, string, date/time, boolean, vendor-specific types, and how type choice affects storage and correctness.
content:
## Interview Questions

<QuestionList topic="SQL Data Types" storagePrefix="sql-data-types">

<QuestionCard id="dt-01" number={1} question="What are the main categories of SQL data types?" difficulty="easy" topic="Fundamentals">
**Numeric** (`INT`, `DECIMAL`, `FLOAT`), **string/character** (`CHAR`, `VARCHAR`, `TEXT`), **date/time** (`DATE`, `DATETIME`, `TIMESTAMP`), and **boolean** (`BOOLEAN`, though support varies by database). Most vendors also add their own extended types — JSON, arrays, UUIDs — layered on top of this common core.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dt-02" number={2} question="What's the difference between INT and DECIMAL, and when would you use DECIMAL over FLOAT?" difficulty="medium" topic="Numeric Types">
`INT` stores whole numbers with no fractional component. `DECIM

title: SQL Data Types
description: Interview questions on SQL data types — numeric, string, date/time, boolean, vendor-specific types, and how type choice affects storage and correctness.
content:
AL(precision, scale)` stores an exact fixed-point number — no rounding error — which is why it's the right choice for money and anything requiring exact arithmetic. `FLOAT` stores an approximate floating-point value, which is faster and more compact but can introduce tiny rounding errors that make it unsuitable for financial calculations.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dt-03" number={3} question="What's the difference between CHAR, VARCHAR, and TEXT?" difficulty="easy" topic="String Types">
`CHAR(n)` is fixed-length — a value shorter than `n` is padded with spaces, and storage is always exactly `n` characters. `VARCHAR(n)` is variable-length up to a maximum of `n`, storing only the actual length used. `TEXT` stores effectively unbounded-length text with no declared maximum, generally u

title: SQL Data Types
description: Interview questions on SQL data types — numeric, string, date/time, boolean, vendor-specific types, and how type choice affects storage and correctness.
content:
sed for large free-form content like descriptions or comments.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dt-04" number={4} question="What date/time types does SQL typically offer, and how do DATE and DATETIME/TIMESTAMP differ?" difficulty="medium" topic="Date/Time Types">
`DATE` stores just a calendar date (year, month, day) with no time component. `DATETIME`/`TIMESTAMP` stores a specific date and time down to some precision, and in some databases `TIMESTAMP` additionally tracks time zone information while `DATETIME` doesn't — the exact behavior varies by vendor, which is worth checking before assuming.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dt-05" number={5} question="How does BOOLEAN work across different SQL dialects?" difficulty="medium" topic="Boolean">
PostgreSQL has a native `BOOLEAN` type. My

title: SQL Data Types
description: Interview questions on SQL data types — numeric, string, date/time, boolean, vendor-specific types, and how type choice affects storage and correctness.
content:
SQL doesn't — it typically represents booleans as `TINYINT(1)` (0 or 1) under the hood, with `BOOLEAN` accepted as a synonym. This is a common source of confusion when porting schemas between databases, since code that assumes a real boolean type may behave differently against a database emulating one with an integer.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dt-06" number={6} question="What happens if you insert a value that doesn't match a column's data type?" difficulty="easy" topic="Fundamentals">
Depends on the database and the mismatch: many databases reject the insert outright with a type error (e.g., inserting text into an `INT` column). Some perform implicit conversion when it's unambiguous (e.g., inserting the string `'5'` into an `INT` column). Relying on implicit conversion is general

title: SQL Data Types
description: Interview questions on SQL data types — numeric, string, date/time, boolean, vendor-specific types, and how type choice affects storage and correctness.
content:
ly discouraged — it's a common source of subtle bugs when the conversion doesn't behave the way you'd expect.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dt-07" number={7} question="Why does picking the right data type matter for storage and query performance?" difficulty="medium" topic="Performance">
A narrower, well-chosen type takes less disk space and memory, which means more rows fit in a page and more of the working set fits in cache — both directly speed up scans and index lookups. Using an oversized type "just in case" (e.g., `BIGINT` for a column that will only ever hold small numbers) wastes space across every row and every index built on that column, at scale.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dt-08" number={8} question="What are vendor-specific data types, and give an example." difficu

title: SQL Data Types
description: Interview questions on SQL data types — numeric, string, date/time, boolean, vendor-specific types, and how type choice affects storage and correctness.
content:
lty="medium" topic="Vendor Types">
Types beyond the ANSI SQL standard that a specific database vendor adds to cover cases the standard types handle poorly. PostgreSQL's `JSONB` (binary-indexed JSON, queryable with operators) and `ARRAY` (a column holding a list of values) are common examples — both let you store semi-structured or multi-valued data inside an otherwise relational table without a separate junction table.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dt-09" number={9} question="What's the difference between implicit and explicit type conversion?" difficulty="medium" topic="Fundamentals">
Implicit conversion happens automatically when the database can unambiguously reinterpret a value as another type (e.g., comparing an `INT` column to the string `'5'`). Explicit conversion uses a functi

title: SQL Data Types
description: Interview questions on SQL data types — numeric, string, date/time, boolean, vendor-specific types, and how type choice affects storage and correctness.
content:
on like `CAST(value AS type)` or `value::type` to convert deliberately. Explicit conversion is generally preferred in production code because it makes the intent visible and avoids relying on a database's specific implicit-conversion rules, which differ across vendors.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

title: SQL Data Types
description: Interview questions on SQL data types — numeric, string, date/time, boolean, vendor-specific types, and how type choice affects storage and correctness.

**Every SQL keyword falls into one of a small number of categories based on what it actually changes — schema, data, permissions, or transaction state — and recognizing which bucket a statement belongs to is a fast way to reason about its blast radius before running it.**

## Key Concepts

SQL keywords are **reserved words** the database parser assigns special meaning to — they can't be used as ordinary identifiers (table or column names) without special quoting, because the parser needs to recognize them unambiguously. The category matters practically, not just academically: DDL statements typically auto-commit and can't be rolled back th

## Common Interview Scenarios

- **"Categorize these five keywords: CREATE, SELECT, GRANT, COMMIT, DELETE."** A quick fluency check — `CREATE` is DDL, `SELECT` is DML/DQL, `GRANT` is DCL, `COMMIT` is TCL, `DELETE` is DML.
- **"Why might TRUNCATE be riskier to run in production than DELETE, even though both remove data?"** Explain that `TRUNCATE`'s DDL status often means it can't be rolled back the same way, may skip row-level triggers, and removes everything at once with no `WHERE` clause to scope it.

## SQL Operators: Comparison, Logical, and Pattern Matching

**Operators are what turn a SQL statement's raw values into the conditions that decide which rows get selected, updated, or deleted — and a surprising number of query bugs trace back to a single operator behaving differently than expected, especially around NULL.**

title: SQL Operators
description: Interview questions on SQL operators — arithmetic, comparison, logical, BETWEEN, IN, LIKE wildcards, and NULL-safe comparisons.

## Table of Contents
- [Key Concepts](#key-concepts)
- [Interview Questions](#interview-questions)

- [Further Reading](#further-reading)

title: SQL Operators
description: Interview questions on SQL operators — arithmetic, comparison, logical, BETWEEN, IN, LIKE wildcards, and NULL-safe comparisons.
content:
## Key Concepts

SQL operators split into a few functional groups: **arithmetic** (`+ - * / %`) for numeric calculation, **comparison** (`= <> < > <= >=`) for evaluating conditions, **logical** (`AND`, `OR`, `NOT`) for combining conditions, and a set of purpose-built operators for common filtering patterns — `BETWEEN` for inclusive ranges, `IN` for membership in a list, and `LIKE` with wildcards (`%`, `_`) for pattern matching on text. The one recurring trap across almost all of them is **NULL**: it represents "unknown," not a value, so any comparison against `NULL` using `=` or `<>` evaluates to unknown (effectively excluded) rather than true or false — which is why SQL provides the dedicated `IS NULL` / `IS NOT NULL` operators instead of relying on standard comparison.

---

</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="op-02" number={2} question="What are the arithmetic operators, and where do they commonly show up in queries?" difficulty="easy" topic="Arithmetic">
`+`, `-`, `*`, `/` for addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division, and `%` (or `MOD`) for remainder. They show up most often in computed

<QuestionCard id="op-03" number={3} question="What are the comparison operators, and how does NULL interact with them?" difficulty="medium" topic="Comparison">
`=`, `<>`/`!=`, `<`, `>`, `<=`, `>=` compare two values. `NULL` breaks the usual true/false logic: `NULL = NULL` does not evaluate to true — it evaluates to unknown, because `NULL` represents an unknown value, and comparing two unknowns can't logically resolve to "equal." Any row where a comparison involving `NULL` evaluates to unknown gets excluded from the result, which surprises people who expect `WHERE col = NULL` to match NULL rows.
</QuestionCard>

`IN (v1, v2, v3, ...)` matches a column against any value in a given list — shorthand for `col = v1 OR col = v2 OR col = v3`. `LIKE` performs pattern matching on text. `%` matches any sequence of characters (including zero), and `_` matches exactly one character. `name LIKE 'A%'` matches any name starting with "A"; `name LIKE '_ohn'` matches any 4-character name ending in "ohn" (like "John"). ## SQL vs NoSQL Databases: Choosing the Right Data Model

**SQL and NoSQL aren't two competing databases — they're different families of data model, each suited to a different shape of data and access pattern, and most real systems at scale end up using more than one.**

title: SQL vs NoSQL Databases

## Key Concepts

**SQL databases** are relational: fixed schema, tables linked by keys, strong ACID consistency. **NoSQL databases** cover four broad, distinct data models rather than one alternative: **document** stores (MongoDB — flexible, JSON-like records), **key-value** stores (Redis, DynamoDB — the simplest and fastest lookup pattern), **column-family/wide-column** stores (Cassandra, BigTable — optimized for high write throughput and horizontal scale), and **graph** databases (Neo4j — optimized for traversing relationships). The real trade-off isn't "SQL is better" or "NoSQL is better" — it's schema flexibility and horizontal scalability (NoSQL's strengths) against strong consistency and relational query power (SQL's strengths). Most systems past a certain size practice **polyglot pe

SQL databases default to strong consistency — a read always sees the latest committed write. content:
## Common Interview Scenarios

- **"You're designing a system that needs both a product catalog and a real-time recommendation engine — what database(s) would you use?"** Talk through a relational or document store for the catalog and a graph database for the relationship-heavy recommendation traversals — a natural polyglot persistence case.

## Stored Procedures & Functions: Reusable Server-Side Logic

**Stored procedures and functions both let you save logic inside the database instead of the application layer, but they answer different questions — a procedure performs an action, a function computes and returns a value — and that distinction determines where each one can legally be used in a query.**

title: Stored Procedures & Functions

## Key Concepts

A **stored procedure** is a saved block of logic invoked with `CALL`/`EXEC` — it can perform multiple actions, have side effects (inserts, updates, sending output parameters), and doesn't have to return anything at all. A **function** must return a value (or a set of rows) and, in most databases, is restricted from certain side effects specifically so it's safe to call from inside a query — a `SELECT` list, a `WHERE` clause, a `FROM` clause. That "usable inside a query" property is what separates the three function types on this page: a **scalar function** returns one value, a **table-valued function** returns a whole result set (usable like a table in `FROM`), and **row-level functions** compute something per row — the same conceptual foundation window functions are later

A scalar function takes some input and returns exactly one value — built-in examples include `UPPER()`, `ROUND()`, and `LEN()`. Because it resolves to a single value, it can be used anywhere a literal value could go: a `SELECT` list, a `WHERE` condition, an `ORDER BY` expression.

<QuestionCard id="tvf-01" number={1} question="What is a table-valued function, and how is it different from a scalar function?" difficulty="easy" topic="Table-valued Functions">
A table-valued function returns a full result set — rows and columns — rather than a single value, and can be used directly in a `FROM` clause like a table: `SELECT * FROM get_orders_for_customer(123)`. A scalar function, by contrast, only ever resolves to one value and can never stand in for a table.

An **inline** table-valued function is essentially a parameterized view — a single `SELECT` statement wrapped in a function definition, which the optimizer can often expand and optimize as if it were inlined directly into the calling query. A **multi-statement** table-valued function builds its result across multiple statements into a table variable before returning it, which is more flexible (loops, conditional logic) but generally harder for the optimizer to see through, often performing worse as a result.

## Row & Column Functions

<QuestionList topic="Row & Column Functions" storagePrefix="stored-procs-row-column">

<QuestionCard id="rcf-01" number={1} question="What are row-level functions, and how do they differ from aggregate functions?" difficulty="medium" topic="Row & Column Functions">
Row-level functions compute a value independently for each row, producing one output per input row — `UPPER(name)`, `price * quantity`, `DATEDIFF(ship_date, order_date)`. Aggregate functions (`SUM`, `AVG`, `COUNT`) instead collapse many rows into one summary value per group. Both can appear in a `SELECT` list, but they operate at fundamentally different granularities.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="rcf-02" number={2} question="How do row-level functions relate to window functions?" difficulty="medi

Window functions are, conceptually, an extension of row-level computation — they still produce one output value per input row (unlike an aggregate collapsing a group into one row), but that value is computed using a *window* of related rows (via `OVER`/`PARTITION BY`) rather than that row's own columns alone. Understanding plain row-level expressions first is what makes window functions' "per-row, but aware of other rows" behavior click.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="rcf-03" number={3} question="Give an example of a per-row computed column using a row-level expression." difficulty="easy" topic="Row & Column Functions">
```sql

FROM order_items;
```

## Subqueries: Nested, Correlated, and Scalar

**A subquery is a query nested inside another query, and what makes the three flavors distinct isn't syntax so much as *when* and *how many times* the inner query actually runs relative to the outer one.**

## Key Concepts

A **nested (non-correlated) subquery** runs independently of the outer query — once, producing a fixed result the outer query then filters or joins against, commonly with `IN`, `EXISTS`, `ANY`, or `ALL`. A **correlated subquery** references a column from the outer query inside its own `WHERE` clause, which means it can't be evaluated once up front — conceptually, it re-runs once per outer row, checking something specific to that row. A **scalar subquery** is defined by its *shape*, not its independence: it's any subquery guaranteed to return exactly one row and one column, which is what lets it be used anywhere a single value is expected — in a `SELECT` list, or on either side of a comparison. These categories aren't mutually exclusive: a subquery can be both scalar and co

A nested subquery is a `SELECT` statement embedded inside another query, most commonly in the `WHERE` clause (`WHERE id IN (SELECT ...)`), but also valid in `HAVING`, `FROM` (as a derived table), or the `SELECT` list itself. It's evaluated as a self-contained unit — the database can run it independently of the outer query's rows.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionList topic="Correlated Subqueries" storagePrefix="subqueries-correlated">

<QuestionCard id="cs-01" number={1} question="What is a correlated subquery, and how is it different from a regular nested subquery?" difficulty="medium" topic="Correlated Subqueries">
A correlated subquery references a column from the *outer* query inside its own `WHERE` clause, so it can't be evaluated as one independent, standalone result the way a regular nested subquery can — conceptually, it needs to be re-evaluated for each row the outer query considers, using that row's specific value.
</QuestionCard>

A scalar subquery is any subquery that's guaranteed to return exactly one row and one column — a single value. That single-value guarantee is what lets it be used anywhere a literal value could go: in a `SELECT` list, or on either side of a comparison operator like `=` or `>`.

content:
## Quick Reference

A refresher on the syntax the questions below assume. For a from-scratch walkthrough of SQL, see the [SQL Roadmap](/roadmaps/sql/) — this page focuses on what interviewers ask, not how to learn SQL from zero.

title: SQL Theory | Core Concepts
description: Master SQL fundamentals, advanced queries, database design, and optimization for data engineering interviews. Interactive Q&A with progress tracking.
content:
### Reading data
`SELECT` retrieves columns, `WHERE` filters rows, `ORDER BY` sorts, `GROUP BY`/`HAVING` aggregate and filter groups, `LIMIT`/`OFFSET` paginate:

```sql
SELECT department, COUNT(*) AS employee_count, AVG(salary) AS avg_salary
FROM employees
WHERE hire_date >= '2020-01-01'
GROUP BY department
HAVING COUNT(*) > 5
ORDER BY avg_salary DESC
LIMIT 10;
```

title: SQL Theory | Core Concepts
description: Master SQL fundamentals, advanced queries, database design, and optimization for data engineering interviews. Interactive Q&A with progress tracking.
content:
### Joins
`INNER JOIN` returns only matching rows; `LEFT`/`RIGHT JOIN` keep all rows from one side (NULL where unmatched); `FULL OUTER JOIN` keeps all rows from both; `CROSS JOIN` produces a Cartesian product; a self join joins a table to itself via an alias.

```sql
SELECT e.employee_name, d.department_name
FROM employees e
LEFT JOIN departments d ON e.department_id = d.id;
```

title: SQL Theory | Core Concepts
description: Master SQL fundamentals, advanced queries, database design, and optimization for data engineering interviews. Interactive Q&A with progress tracking.
content:
### Modifying data & schema
`INSERT`, `UPDATE`, `DELETE` (DML) manipulate rows; `CREATE TABLE`, `ALTER TABLE`, `DROP TABLE` (DDL) manage schema. Always scope `UPDATE`/`DELETE` with `WHERE` — omitting it applies to every row.

```sql
CREATE TABLE employees (
    employee_id INT PRIMARY KEY AUTO_INCREMENT,
    name VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
    salary DECIMAL(10, 2),
    department_id INT,
    FOREIGN KEY (department_id) REFERENCES departments(id)
);

UPDATE employees SET salary = salary * 1.10 WHERE department_id = 2;
```

title: SQL Theory | Core Concepts
description: Master SQL fundamentals, advanced queries, database design, and optimization for data engineering interviews. Interactive Q&A with progress tracking.
content:
### Constraints & data types
`PRIMARY KEY` (unique row identifier), `FOREIGN KEY` (referential integrity), `UNIQUE`, `NOT NULL`, `CHECK` (validates values), `DEFAULT`. Common types: `INT`, `VARCHAR(n)`, `DECIMAL(precision, scale)`, `DATE`, `DATETIME`, `BOOLEAN`, `TEXT`.

title: SQL Theory | Core Concepts
description: Master SQL fundamentals, advanced queries, database design, and optimization for data engineering interviews. Interactive Q&A with progress tracking.
content:
### Common mistakes

| Mistake | Problem | Fix |
|---------|---------|-----|
| `WHERE col = NULL` | Always returns no rows | Use `WHERE col IS NULL` |
| Missing `WHERE` on `UPDATE`/`DELETE` | Modifies/deletes every row | Always scope with `WHERE` |
| `SELECT *` on large tables | Slow, excess data transfer | Select only needed columns |
| Using a column alias in `WHERE` | Alias isn't resolved yet at that stage | Only usable in `ORDER BY`/`SELECT` |

## Relational Database Fundamentals

Before the command-level questions below, interviewers sometimes start one level up — what a relational database actually is, and why you'd reach for one over the alternatives.

<QuestionList topic="Relational Database Fundamentals" storagePrefix="sql-relational-db">

<QuestionCard id="sql-rdb-01" number={1} question="What is a relational database, and what does the relational model organize data into?" difficulty="easy" topic="Fundamentals">
A relational database stores data in **tables** made up of rows (records) and columns (attributes), based on the relational model Edgar Codd introduced in 1970. Relationships between tables are expressed through keys — a **primary key** uniquely identifies a row, and a **foreign key** in one table references a prim

title: SQL Theory | Core Concepts
description: Master SQL fundamentals, advanced queries, database design, and optimization for data engineering interviews. Interactive Q&A with progress tracking.
content:
ary key in another — which is what lets you split data across tables without duplicating it and still reconstruct any relationship through a join.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="sql-rdb-02" number={2} question="What are the main benefits of an RDBMS, and where does it start to show its limitations?" difficulty="medium" topic="Fundamentals">
The core benefits are **ACID guarantees** (reliable transactions), a **fixed schema** that enforces data consistency at write time, and a mature, standardized query language (SQL) with decades of tooling built around it. The limitations show up at scale: RDBMSs traditionally scale **vertically** (a bigger machine) rather than horizontally, a rigid schema makes fast-changing or semi-structured data awkward to model, and very high write throughput or

title: SQL Theory | Core Concepts
description: Master SQL fundamentals, advanced queries, database design, and optimization for data engineering interviews. Interactive Q&A with progress tracking.
content:
massive horizontal scale is where NoSQL and distributed systems typically take over.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="sql-rdb-03" number={3} question="How are SQL keywords typically categorized, and what does each category do?" difficulty="easy" topic="Fundamentals">
SQL keywords fall into four categories: **DDL** (Data Definition Language — `CREATE`, `ALTER`, `DROP`, which manage schema), **DML** (Data Manipulation Language — `SELECT`, `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, `DELETE`, which manage rows), **DCL** (Data Control Language — `GRANT`, `REVOKE`, which manage permissions), and **TCL** (Transaction Control Language — `COMMIT`, `ROLLBACK`, `SAVEPOINT`, which manage transaction boundaries). Recognizing which bucket a keyword falls into is a quick way to reason about what a statement actually affects

content:
— schema, data, access, or transaction state.
</QuestionCard>

## SQL Fundamentals

<QuestionCard id="sql-fund-01" number={1} question="What is SQL and what is it used for?" difficulty="easy" topic="Fundamentals">
SQL (Structured Query Language) is the standard programming language for managing relational databases. It enables data professionals to create, read, update, and delete data (CRUD), manage schemas, and perform data analysis.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="sql-fund-02" number={2} question="Describe the difference between SQL and NoSQL databases." difficulty="easy" topic="Fundamentals">
- **SQL** — relational, structured schema, ACID compliance, tables with rows/columns
- **NoSQL** — non-relational,

<QuestionCard id="sql-fund-03" number={3} question="What are the different types of SQL commands?" difficulty="easy" topic="Fundamentals">
- **DDL** — Data Definition (`CREATE`, `ALTER`, `DROP`)
- **DML** — Data Manipulation (`SELECT`, `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, `DELETE`)
- **DCL** — Data Control (`GRANT`, `REVOKE`)
- **TCL** — Transaction Control (`COMMIT`, `ROLLBACK`, `SAVEPOINT`)
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="sql-fund-04" number={4} question="Explain the purpose of the SELECT statement." difficulty="easy" topic="Fundamentals">
Retrieves data from tables.

```sql
SELECT columns FROM table WHERE conditions ORDER BY columns;
```
</QuestionCard>

- **`WHERE`** — filters rows *before* `GROUP BY`
- **`HAVING`** — filters groups *after* aggregation

<QuestionCard id="sql-fund-06" number={6} question="Define what a JOIN is in SQL and list its types." difficulty="easy" topic="Joins">
JOINs combine rows based on related columns.

- **`INNER JOIN`** — matching rows only
- **`LEFT`/`RIGHT JOIN`** — all rows from one side + matching from the other
- **`FULL OUTER JOIN`** — all rows from both tables
- **`CROSS JOIN`** — Cartesian product
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="sql-fund-08" number={8} question="Explain what a foreign key is and how it is used." difficulty="easy" topic="Fundamentals">
A column referencing another table's primary key. Enforces referential integrity and creates relationships between tables.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="sql-fund-09" number={9} question="How can you prevent SQL injections?" difficulty="medium" topic="Security">
Parameterized queries (prepared statements), input validation, least-privilege database accounts, and stored procedures used cautiously — never build queries by concatenating raw user input.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="sql-fund-11" number={11} question="Describe the concept of denormalization and when you would use it." difficulty="medium" topic="Data Modeling">
Deliberately adding redundant data to improve read performance, at the cost of write complexity and storage. Common in data warehouses and read-heavy applications where join cost outweighs storage cost.

<QuestionCard id="sql-fund-13" number={13} question="Explain the purpose of the GROUP BY clause." difficulty="easy" topic="Fundamentals">

Inclusive of both endpoints.

Produces the Cartesian product of two tables (every row of A paired with every row of B). Used for generating test data or combining independent dimensions (e.g. all product/color combinations).
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="sql-design-03" number={43} question="What are Stored Procedures and how are they beneficial?" difficulty="medium" topic="Database Objects">
Precompiled, named blocks of SQL stored in the database. Benefits: reduced network round trips, centralized/reusable logic, tighter access control, and execution plan caching.

Reading execution plans and making queries faster.

<QuestionList topic="SQL Optimization and Performance" storagePrefix="sql-optimization">

<QuestionCard id="sql-opt-01" number={51} question="How do you identify and optimize slow-running queries?" difficulty="medium" topic="Optimization">
Use `EXPLAIN`/`EXPLAIN ANALYZE` to find the bottleneck, add targeted indexes, avoid `SELECT *`, and restructure `JOIN`s so the database can use indexes and smaller intermediate result sets.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="sql-opt-04" number={54} question="How can indexing affect performance both positively and negatively?" difficulty="medium" topic="Optimization">

## SQL Security

Protecting access to data.

<QuestionList topic="SQL Security" storagePrefix="sql-security">

<QuestionCard id="sql-sec-01" number={58} question="How do you implement database encryption in SQL?" difficulty="medium" topic="Security">
**TDE** (Transparent Data Encryption) for data at rest, column-level encryption for specific sensitive fields, and **SSL/TLS** for data in transit.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="sql-sec-02" number={59} question="What are roles and how do they manage database access?" difficulty="easy" topic="Security">
Named collections of privileges. Users are assigned roles and inherit the underlying permissions — simplifies access control at scale versus granting permissions per-user.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionCard>

An atomic unit of work that either commits fully or rolls back fully, preserving the database's ACID guarantees.
</QuestionCard>

**ACID**: Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability.

<QuestionCard id="sql-txn-04" number={68} question="How do you manage transaction isolation levels?" difficulty="hard" topic="Transactions">

content:
## Transactions: Grouping Statements Into Atomic Units of Work

**A transaction bundles a sequence of statements so they succeed or fail together — the control statements (BEGIN, COMMIT, ROLLBACK, SAVEPOINT) are the mechanics, and the isolation level is what decides how much of that in-progress work other concurrent transactions are allowed to see.**

## Key Concepts

A transaction is a sequence of statements treated as one atomic unit: `BEGIN` starts it, `COMMIT` makes its changes permanent, and `ROLLBACK` undoes everything since it started. `SAVEPOINT` adds a partial checkpoint inside a longer transaction, letting you undo just the recent part without discarding everything. These control statements are what *deliver* the ACID guarantees in practice — but ACID also depends on **isolation level**, which governs how much of one transaction's in-progress, uncommitted work a concurrent transaction is allowed to see. That's a separate knob from the control statements themselves: two transactions can both correctly `COMMIT`/`ROLLBACK`, and still produce different results depending on whether the isolation level let them see each other's unco

## BEGIN

<QuestionList topic="BEGIN" storagePrefix="transactions-begin">

<QuestionCard id="bg-01" number={1} question="What does BEGIN do, and what's the difference between implicit and explicit transaction management?" difficulty="easy" topic="BEGIN">
`BEGIN` (or `START TRANSACTION`) explicitly starts a new transaction, after which subsequent statements are grouped together until a `COMMIT` or `ROLLBACK`. Without an explicit `BEGIN`, most databases run in **autocommit** mode by default — each individual statement is implicitly its own complete transaction, committed immediately if it succeeds.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="bg-02" number={2} question="What happens to statements run before an explicit BEGIN in autocommit mode?" difficulty="medium" topic="BEGIN">
Each one commits imme

content:
diately on its own as soon as it completes successfully — there's no window to roll multiple of them back together, since autocommit treats every individual statement as a self-contained transaction. This is why any operation that needs several statements to succeed or fail as a unit must start with an explicit `BEGIN` first.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="bg-03" number={3} question="Can you start a transaction inside another already-open transaction?" difficulty="hard" topic="BEGIN">
Standard SQL doesn't support true nested transactions — calling `BEGIN` again while a transaction is already open typically either raises an error, is silently ignored, or (in some databases) is treated as an implicit `SAVEPOINT` rather than a genuinely independent inner transaction. `SAVEPOINT` is the st

description: Interview questions on SQL transactions — BEGIN, COMMIT, ROLLBACK, SAVEPOINT, ACID guarantees, and transaction isolation levels.
content:
## COMMIT

<QuestionList topic="COMMIT" storagePrefix="transactions-commit">

<QuestionCard id="cm-01" number={1} question="What does COMMIT do?" difficulty="easy" topic="COMMIT">
`COMMIT` permanently applies every change made since the transaction began, making it visible to other connections and durable against a crash. Until `COMMIT` runs, the changes are only visible within the transaction that made them (at most isolation levels).
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="cm-02" number={2} question="What happens if the connection is lost before a COMMIT is issued?" difficulty="medium" topic="COMMIT">
The transaction is left uncommitted, and the database automatically rolls it back — none of its changes take effect. This is a safety property, not a bug: a transaction that never reached `COMMI

title: Transactions
description: Interview questions on SQL transactions — BEGIN, COMMIT, ROLLBACK, SAVEPOINT, ACID guarantees, and transaction isolation levels.
content:
T` shouldn't be able to leave partial changes behind just because the client disconnected.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="cm-03" number={3} question="Once a transaction is committed, can it still be rolled back?" difficulty="easy" topic="COMMIT">
No — `COMMIT` is the point of no return for that transaction; `ROLLBACK` only works on a still-open transaction. Undoing a mistake that's already been committed requires a new, separate transaction that explicitly reverses the change (or a restore from backup/point-in-time recovery for larger-scale mistakes).
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

---

title: Transactions
description: Interview questions on SQL transactions — BEGIN, COMMIT, ROLLBACK, SAVEPOINT, ACID guarantees, and transaction isolation levels.
content:
## ROLLBACK

<QuestionList topic="ROLLBACK" storagePrefix="transactions-rollback">

<QuestionCard id="rb-01" number={1} question="What does ROLLBACK do?" difficulty="easy" topic="ROLLBACK">
`ROLLBACK` undoes every change made since the transaction began (or since a specified `SAVEPOINT`), as if none of those statements had run. It's only meaningful on a transaction that hasn't been committed yet.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="rb-02" number={2} question="What's the difference between rolling back to a SAVEPOINT and rolling back the entire transaction?" difficulty="medium" topic="ROLLBACK">
`ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT name` undoes only the changes made after that specific savepoint, leaving everything before it (including the transaction itself) still open and intact. A plain `ROLLBACK` with

title: Transactions
description: Interview questions on SQL transactions — BEGIN, COMMIT, ROLLBACK, SAVEPOINT, ACID guarantees, and transaction isolation levels.
content:
no savepoint discards the entire transaction from its very start.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="rb-03" number={3} question="Can DDL statements be rolled back the same way DML can?" difficulty="hard" topic="ROLLBACK">
It depends on the database: PostgreSQL supports transactional DDL, so a `CREATE TABLE` or `ALTER TABLE` inside an open transaction can be rolled back like any DML statement. Many other databases (MySQL among them) auto-commit DDL immediately, meaning it takes effect right away and can't be undone with `ROLLBACK` — this is a meaningful, vendor-specific difference worth knowing before assuming DDL is always safely reversible.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>
