<QuestionCard id="sp-01" number={1} question="What is a SAVEPOINT, and why would you use one instead of just rolling back everything?" difficulty="easy" topic="SAVEPOINT">
A `SAVEPOINT` marks a named point within an open transaction that you can later roll back to, without discarding the whole transaction. It's useful when a long transaction has several logically separate steps, and a failure partway through should only undo the failed step — not the earlier, successful work.
</QuestionCard>

## ACID

<QuestionList topic="ACID" storagePrefix="transactions-acid">

<QuestionCard id="acid-01" number={1} question="What do the four ACID properties guarantee, at a high level?" difficulty="easy" topic="ACID">
**Atomicity** — the transaction is all-or-nothing. **Consistency** — it can only move the database from one valid state to another. **Isolation** — concurrent transactions don't see each other's uncommitted work. **Durability** — once committed, changes survive a crash. Together, they're what let application code trust the database instead of re-implementing that safety itself.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="acid-02" number={2} question="How do BEGIN, COMMIT, and ROLLBACK specifically deliver atomicity?" difficulty="medium" topic="ACID">
Atomicity requires an all-or-nothing o

content:
utcome, and the transaction control statements are exactly what implement that: `BEGIN` marks where the "all" starts, `COMMIT` is the point where "all" becomes permanent, and `ROLLBACK` is the mechanism that enforces "nothing" if any part fails before that point — without these statements, there would be no way to group several writes into one atomic unit at all.
</QuestionCard>

title: Transactions
description: Interview questions on SQL transactions — BEGIN, COMMIT, ROLLBACK, SAVEPOINT, ACID guarantees, and transaction isolation levels.
content:
## Transaction Isolation Levels

<QuestionList topic="Transaction Isolation Levels" storagePrefix="transactions-isolation">

<QuestionCard id="iso-01" number={1} question="What are the four standard transaction isolation levels, from least to most strict?" difficulty="medium" topic="Isolation Levels">
`READ UNCOMMITTED` (weakest — can see other transactions' uncommitted changes), `READ COMMITTED` (only sees committed data, but a value can change between two reads in the same transaction), `REPEATABLE READ` (the same row read twice within a transaction returns the same value), and `SERIALIZABLE` (strongest — transactions behave as if run one at a time, with no concurrency anomalies at all).
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="iso-02" number={2} question="What is a dirty read, and which isola

title: Transactions
description: Interview questions on SQL transactions — BEGIN, COMMIT, ROLLBACK, SAVEPOINT, ACID guarantees, and transaction isolation levels.
content:
tion level allows it?" difficulty="medium" topic="Isolation Levels">
A dirty read happens when a transaction reads data that another transaction has written but not yet committed — if that other transaction then rolls back, the first transaction acted on data that never actually existed. Only `READ UNCOMMITTED` allows dirty reads; every stricter level prevents them.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="iso-03" number={3} question="What's the difference between a non-repeatable read and a phantom read, and which levels prevent each?" difficulty="hard" topic="Isolation Levels">
A **non-repeatable read** is when re-reading the *same row* within a transaction returns a different value, because another transaction updated and committed it in between — prevented starting at `REPEATABLE READ`. A **

title: Transactions
description: Interview questions on SQL transactions — BEGIN, COMMIT, ROLLBACK, SAVEPOINT, ACID guarantees, and transaction isolation levels.
content:
phantom read** is when re-running the *same query* returns a different *set of rows* (not just changed values), because another transaction inserted or deleted rows matching the condition in between — only fully prevented at `SERIALIZABLE` in the standard definition, though some databases prevent it earlier through their specific implementation (e.g., PostgreSQL's `REPEATABLE READ`).
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="iso-04" number={4} question="Why would you deliberately choose a lower isolation level than SERIALIZABLE?" difficulty="medium" topic="Isolation Levels">
Stronger isolation requires more locking or version-tracking overhead, which reduces concurrency and throughput. Most application workloads default to `READ COMMITTED` because the anomalies it doesn't prevent (non-repeatable

title: Transactions
description: Interview questions on SQL transactions — BEGIN, COMMIT, ROLLBACK, SAVEPOINT, ACID guarantees, and transaction isolation levels.
content:
and phantom reads) simply don't matter for most queries — reserving `SERIALIZABLE` for the specific operations where getting a stale or shifting view of the data would actually cause a correctness problem, like financial reconciliation.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

description: Interview questions on SQL views — creating, modifying, and dropping views, updatable views, and how views differ from materialized views.
content:
## Key Concepts

A view is a named, saved `SELECT` query that can be queried as if it were a table — `CREATE VIEW active_customers AS SELECT ... FROM customers WHERE status = 'active'` lets anyone write `SELECT * FROM active_customers` afterward without repeating the underlying logic. Critically, a standard view stores no data of its own: every time it's queried, the database re-runs the underlying `SELECT` against the current state of the base tables. That makes views useful for two main things — **simplifying repeated complex logic** (hiding a messy multi-table join behind a simple name) and **access control** (granting a user permission to query a view that only exposes certain columns or rows, without granting access to the full underlying table). It's also the key difference from a **

content:
materialized view**, which does store its result physically and needs to be refreshed — trading some staleness for real performance gains a plain view can't offer.

## Creating Views

<QuestionList topic="Creating Views" storagePrefix="views-creating">

<QuestionCard id="cv-01" number={1} question="What is a view, and what problem does it solve?" difficulty="easy" topic="Creating Views">
A view is a saved `SELECT` query, stored under a name, that can be queried like a table. It solves the problem of repeating the same complex join or filtering logic across many queries — wrapping it once behind a view means every consumer writes a simple `SELECT * FROM view_name` instead of re-deriving the same multi-table logic each time.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="cv-02" number={2} question="Write a CREATE VIEW statement that wraps a join into a reusable object." difficulty="medium" topic="Creating Views">
```sql
CREATE VIEW customer_order_summary AS
SELECT
```

## Modifying Views

<QuestionList topic="Modifying Views" storagePrefix="views-modifying">

<QuestionCard id="mv-01" number={1} question="How do you modify an existing view's definition?" difficulty="easy" topic="Modifying Views">
Most databases support `CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW view_name AS <new query>`, which redefines the view in place. Some databases instead require (or additionally support) `ALTER VIEW`, and if neither is available, the fallback is `DROP VIEW` followed by a fresh `CREATE VIEW`.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="mv-02" number={2} question="What's the difference between CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW and DROP + CREATE VIEW?" difficulty="medium" topic="Modifying Views">
`CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW` updates the definition while preserving the view's existing permissions and any depend

</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="mv-03" number={3} question="What restrictions typically exist on CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW?" difficulty="hard" topic="Modifying Views">
Many databases only allow the replacement if the new query's output columns are compatible with the original — commonly requiring the same column names and types, in the same order, with new columns only allowed to be appended at the end. ## Dropping Views

<QuestionList topic="Dropping Views" storagePrefix="views-dropping">

<QuestionCard id="dv-01" number={1} question="What does DROP VIEW do, and does it affect the underlying tables?" difficulty="easy" topic="Dropping Views">
`DROP VIEW view_name` removes the view's saved definition. It has no effect whatsoever on the underlying base tables or their data — a view is just a stored query, so dropping it only removes that stored query, not anything it reads from.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dv-02" number={2} question="What happens if you try to DROP a view that other views depend on?" difficulty="medium" topic="Dropping Views">
Depending on the database, it either blocks the drop (protecting the dependent view from suddenly referencing something that no longer exists)

title: Views
description: Interview questions on SQL views — creating, modifying, and dropping views, updatable views, and how views differ from materialized views.
content:
or requires `CASCADE` to explicitly drop the dependent views along with it — the same referential-safety pattern used for foreign keys and dependent tables.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dv-03" number={3} question="Can you insert, update, or delete through a view, and what limits that?" difficulty="hard" topic="Dropping Views">
Simple views based on a single table with no aggregation, `DISTINCT`, or `GROUP BY` are often updatable — a write through the view passes through to the underlying table. Views involving joins, aggregates, or set operations usually aren't updatable, because there's no unambiguous way to translate a change to the view's output back into a specific change on the underlying base table(s).
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

## Common Interview Scenarios

- **"Why would you use a view instead of just saving the query text somewhere for people to copy?"** Discuss reusability, centralized logic (one place to fix a bug or change a definition), and access control — none of which a copy-pasted query provides.
- **"A view used to expose columns A, B, C — a teammate wants to remove column B. What's the safest way to do that?"** Walk through why `CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW` often can't remove or reorder columns, and why `DROP` + `CREATE` (with attention to re-granting permissions) is usually required instead.
- **"When would you reach for a materialized view instead of a regular view?"** Discuss the trade-off: a materialized view trades some data freshness (it needs refreshing) for real performance gains on an expensive u

- **"Design a view that lets a support team see customer contact info but not payment details."** A practical access-control scenario: a view exposing only the permitted columns, with `GRANT SELECT` on the view instead of the underlying table.

## Choosing the Right Technologies: A Trade-Off Framework

**Picking a data technology is rarely about which tool is "best" in the abstract — it's about matching a tool's trade-offs (managed vs. self-hosted, cost vs. control, latency vs. complexity) against a team's actual scale, skill set, and budget, which is why the same problem can have a different right answer at two different companies.**

## Key Concepts

Every technology choice in data engineering trades off along a handful of recurring axes: **managed vs. self-hosted** (operational burden vs. cost and control), **build vs. buy** (engineering time vs. vendor lock-in and licensing cost), **open source vs. proprietary** (flexibility and no licensing fees vs. official support and polish), and workload-specific trade-offs like **batch vs. streaming** (simplicity vs. latency) and **warehouse vs. lake vs. lakehouse** (query performance and cost vs. flexibility with raw and unstructured data). None of these trade-offs resolve the same way twice — a five-person startup and a 500-engineer platform team will reasonably land on opposite answers for the same question, because team size, existing skill set, and how much operational ove

## Interview Questions

<QuestionList topic="Choosing the Right Technologies" storagePrefix="choosing-the-right-technologies">

<QuestionCard id="crt-01" number={1} question="What's the core trade-off between a managed service and a self-hosted one?" difficulty="easy" topic="Managed vs Self-Hosted">
A managed service (e.g., a cloud data warehouse, a managed Kafka offering) trades cost and some control for lower operational burden — the vendor handles scaling, patching, and uptime. Self-hosting trades that convenience for full control and often lower direct cost at scale, at the price of needing the in-house expertise to operate it reliably.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="crt-02" number={2} question="When does self-hosting a technology like Kafka or Spark actually make sense over a mana

It makes sense when the team already has deep operational expertise in that system, when usage is large and steady enough that managed pricing becomes disproportionately expensive, or when specific configuration/tuning needs aren't well supported by the managed version. For most teams without dedicated platform engineers, though, the operational cost of self-hosting outweighs the savings.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="crt-03" number={3} question="How should a team think about the build vs. buy decision for data tooling?" difficulty="medium" topic="Build vs Buy">
Buy (or use an existing open-source tool) by default — building custom tooling only pays off when the problem is genuinely core to the business or when no exis

Proprietary tools trade that flexibility for official support, more polished tooling, and often faster time-to-value — at the cost of licensing spend and less control over the roadmap.

<QuestionCard id="crt-09" number={9} question="What role does cost play in choosing a technology, beyond just the sticker price of a service?" difficulty="medium" topic="Cost">
Total cost includes compute and storage pricing, but also engineering time to operate it, the cost of mistakes during a learning curve, and migration cost if the choice turns out wrong. A cheaper-looking managed service can be more expensive overall if it requires significant custom tooling to fit the team's workflow, and a "free" open-source tool isn't free once the engineering hours to run it reliably are counted.

Choosing for current scale keeps complexity proportional to actual need — over-engineering for hypothetical future scale (e.g., adopting Kafka before there's any streaming use case) adds operational burden with no present payoff. Choosing with growth in mind matters when a migration later would be genuinely painful (e.g., a storage format or schema convention that's expensive to change retroactively) — those decisions deserve more forward-looking weight than ones that are cheap to revisit.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="crt-11" number={11} question="Why can the same technology decision reasonably go two different ways at two different companies?" difficulty="hard" topic="Team Fit">

A five-person startup optimizing for speed and low overhead will often reasonably choose a fully managed stack, while a large platform team with dedicated infrastructure engineers may reasonably self-host the same category of tool for cost and control at scale. Neither is wrong; they're solving for different constraints.

**Data engineering and data science are closely related but distinct disciplines — data engineers build the infrastructure that data scientists rely on, while data scientists extract insights and build models from that data.**

## Key Concepts

The two roles split along a clear line: data engineers focus on **infrastructure and pipelines**, data scientists focus on **analysis and modeling**. That difference shows up in their tools (SQL, Python, Spark, and Airflow for engineers; Python, R, Jupyter, and ML libraries for scientists), their goals (reliable data flow vs. insights and predictions), and their output (clean, structured datasets vs. models, reports, and dashboards). Neither role is self-sufficient: data engineers provide the clean, reliable datasets data scientists need, and data scientists feed data requirements back to engineers, forming a feedback loop that turns raw data into business value. They're closely related but distinct disciplines. Data engineers build the infrastructure that data scientists rely on — pipelines, storage, and processing systems. Data scientists extract insights and build models from that data — statistical analysis, machine learning, and experimentation. One makes data available and trustworthy; the other turns it into decisions.

There's real overlap (both use SQL and Python heavily), but the surrounding toolchain diverges.

## Data Engineering Lifecycle: From Raw Data to Business Decisions

**The data engineering lifecycle is the repeatable journey data takes from where it's created to where it's used — generation, ingestion, processing, storage, serving, and consumption — and each stage's output is the next stage's input, so a failure anywhere upstream propagates through everything downstream of it.**

title: Data Engineering Lifecycle
description: Interview questions on the data engineering lifecycle — generation, ingestion, processing, storage, serving, and consumption — and how failures propagate between stages.
content:
## Key Concepts

The lifecycle runs in one direction: **Generation → Ingestion → Processing → Storage → Serving → Consumption**. Data is *generated* by source systems (application databases, APIs, logs, IoT devices), *ingested* into the platform in batch or streaming mode, *processed* through cleaning, transformation, and enrichment, *stored* in a warehouse, lake, or lakehouse suited to how it'll be queried, *served* to consumers through query engines or APIs, and finally *consumed* by analysts, data scientists, and applications. Two ideas cut across every stage: **each handoff is a contract** — a schema, a freshness expectation, a grain — that the next stage relies on, so quietly changing it upstream breaks things downstream without warning; and **the lifecycle isn't strictly linear in pr

content:
actice** — processing can happen before or after storage (ETL vs. ELT), and modern platforms increasingly blend batch and streaming ingestion rather than choosing one exclusively.

## Interview Questions

<QuestionList topic="Data Engineering Lifecycle" storagePrefix="data-engineering-lifecycle">

<QuestionCard id="del-01" number={1} question="What are the six stages of the data engineering lifecycle, in order?" difficulty="easy" topic="Fundamentals">
**Generation → Ingestion → Processing → Storage → Serving → Consumption.** Data is created in a source system, brought into the platform, cleaned and transformed, stored in a queryable form, exposed to consumers, and finally used by people or applications to make decisions.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="del-02" number={2} question="What happens at the generation stage, and why does a data engineer need to understand the source system, not just the data it produces?" difficulty="easy" topic="Generation">
Generation

is where data is created — application databases, third-party APIs, application logs, IoT/sensor devices. Understanding the source system matters because it determines *how* data can be reliably extracted: a database with no change-tracking forces expensive full scans, while one with change data capture support enables efficient incremental ingestion.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="del-03" number={3} question="What's the difference between batch and streaming ingestion, and how do teams typically decide between them?" difficulty="medium" topic="Ingestion">
Batch ingestion collects and moves data on a schedule (hourly, daily); streaming ingestion moves each event as it happens, typically through a message broker like Kafka. The decision comes down to latency requirements versus complexi

</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="del-04" number={4} question="What kinds of work happen during the processing stage?" difficulty="medium" topic="Processing">
Cleaning (deduplication, handling nulls and malformed records), transformation (reshaping data into the schema consumers need), and enrichment (joining in reference data or computing derived fields). This is also where business logic gets encoded — the definition of a "completed order" or an "active user" typically lives in this stage's transformation code.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="del-05"

number={5} question="What's the difference between ETL and ELT, and why has ELT become more common?" difficulty="medium" topic="Processing">
ETL transforms data *before* loading it into the destination; ELT loads raw data first and transforms it *inside* the destination (typically a warehouse) using SQL. ELT has become more common because modern cloud warehouses have enough compute to make in-warehouse transformation cheap and fast, and keeping raw data around makes it possible to re-derive a transformation without re-extracting from the source.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="del-06" number={6} question="How do you decide where processed data should be stored — warehouse, lake, or lakehouse?" difficulty="medium" topic="Storage">

The choice is really about matching storage cost and query pattern, not picking whichever is newest.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="del-07" number={7} question="What does the serving stage involve, and who or what is it built for?" difficulty="easy" topic="Serving">
Serving is making stored data available to whoever needs to consume it — through a query engine for ad hoc SQL, a BI tool's semantic layer for dashboards, or an API for applications that need low-latency lookups. It's built for very different access patterns depending on the consum

<QuestionCard id="del-08" number={8} question="Who consumes data at the final stage, and what do their needs typically look like?" difficulty="easy" topic="Consumption">
Analysts consume it through dashboards and ad hoc queries, data scientists consume it as training data or feature inputs, and applications consume it through APIs to power product features. Each has different tolerance for latency and different expectations about data freshness and schema stability — which is why "the pipeline is done" doesn't mean the same thing for every consumer.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="del-09" number={9} question="Why is it said that a data quality issue early in the lifecycle propagat

Because each stage's output feeds the next stage as input — a bad value that enters at generation or ingestion gets copied, joined, and aggregated at every later stage, showing up in a dashboard or model far removed from where it originated. That's why fixing quality issues as close to the source as possible is far cheaper than catching them downstream, where the same bad value has already multiplied into dozens of derived tables.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="del-10" number={10} question="What's a schema change at the source, and why is it one of the most common ways the lifecycle breaks in practice?" difficulty="medium" topic="Fundamentals">

It's a common failure point because ingestion, processing, and storage all implicitly depend on the previous schema; an unannounced change can silently drop data, break a transformation, or corrupt a downstream metric.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="del-11" number={11} question="Is the lifecycle always strictly linear in a real system?" difficulty="hard" topic="Fundamentals">
No — real platforms often blend patterns. Processing can happen before storage (ETL) or after (ELT); some data streams through processing and serving nearly simultaneously for near-real-time use cases while other data sits raw for hours before a scheduled batch job touches it. The six st

## Common Interview Scenarios

- **"Walk me through what happens to a single event, from the moment it's generated to the moment an analyst sees it in a dashboard."** Trace all six stages in order, naming a concrete tool or pattern at each step (e.g., CDC at ingestion, dbt at processing, a warehouse at storage).
- **"A dashboard shows a number that doesn't match what a stakeholder expects — how do you find where in the lifecycle it went wrong?"** Describe working backward from consumption through serving, storage, processing, ingestion, to generation, checking each handoff's contract (schema, freshness, grain) until the mismatch is isolated.
- **"When would you choose streaming ingestion over batch for a new pipeline?"** Anchor the answer in the actual latency requirement of the downstream

content:
use case, not a general preference — streaming is only worth its added operational complexity when near-real-time data genuinely changes what a consumer can do with it.
- **"How would you design a pipeline to be resilient to an upstream schema change?"** Talk through schema validation at ingestion, alerting on unexpected structure changes, and treating raw/landed data as immutable so a broken transformation can be fixed and rerun without re-extracting from the source.

content:
## Key Concepts

Governance starts with clear ownership: a **data owner** is accountable for a dataset's business meaning, a **data steward** maintains its quality and metadata day to day, and a **data custodian** operates the underlying platform. On top of ownership sits access control — **RBAC** grants permissions to roles, while **ABAC** evaluates dynamic attributes (department, region, sensitivity) for more flexible but harder-to-manage policies — plus finer-grained row- and column-level security for multi-tenant and PII-heavy datasets. A **data catalog** ties it together by making datasets discoverable, with lineage, owners, and freshness in one place, while a **business glossary** aligns what terms actually mean. Governance also has to answer compliance questions: how PII/PHI gets ma

content:
## Interview Questions

<QuestionList topic="Data Governance" storagePrefix="data-governance">

<QuestionCard id="dg-01" number={1} question="What is data governance and why does it matter?" difficulty="easy" topic="Fundamentals">
Data governance is the set of processes, policies, and responsibilities that ensure data is discoverable, trusted, secure, and used correctly. It matters because data platforms scale to many teams; without governance, definitions diverge, access becomes risky, and compliance issues appear. Good governance enables faster, safer self-service analytics.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dg-02" number={2} question="What is the difference between governance and security?" difficulty="medium" topic="Fundamentals">
Security focuses on preventing unauthorized access and

title: Data Governance
description: Data governance interview questions covering ownership, RBAC/ABAC, PII handling, data mesh, policy-as-code, GDPR/CCPA compliance, and governance maturity.
content:
ensuring confidentiality/integrity (access controls, encryption). Governance includes security but also covers ownership, definitions, quality, lifecycle, and change management. Governance answers "who owns this data and what does it mean," not just "who can access it."
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dg-03" number={3} question="What are common roles in data governance (owner/steward/custodian)?" difficulty="easy" topic="Roles">
Common roles are:

- **data owner** — accountable for the dataset and its business definition
- **data steward** — maintains quality, metadata, and processes
- **data custodian** — operates the technical platform (storage, access, backups)

Clear roles prevent "nobody owns it" incidents.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dg-04" number={4} question="What is a d

ata catalog and what should it contain?" difficulty="easy" topic="Cataloging">
A data catalog is an inventory of datasets with searchable metadata. It typically contains dataset descriptions, owners, lineage, classifications, freshness/SLA, schema, and links to dashboards. A good catalog reduces time to discovery and improves trust and reuse.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dg-05" number={5} question="What is business glossary vs. technical metadata?" difficulty="medium" topic="Metadata">
A business glossary defines business terms (for example "active user," "net revenue") and their approved definitions. Technical metadata describes datasets and fields (schemas, types, partitions, lineage). Both are needed: glossary aligns meaning, technical metadata enables implementation and discovery

content:
.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dg-06" number={6} question="RBAC vs. ABAC: what is the difference?" difficulty="medium" topic="Access Control">
RBAC (Role-Based Access Control) grants permissions to roles (analyst, engineer) and assigns users to roles. ABAC (Attribute-Based Access Control) uses attributes (department, region, sensitivity) to evaluate policies dynamically. ABAC is more flexible but can be harder to manage without good tooling.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dg-07" number={7} question="What is row-level and column-level security?" difficulty="medium" topic="Access Control">
Row-level security restricts which rows a user can see (for example only their region). Column-level security restricts which columns are visible (for example hide salary or PII). These controls

description: Data governance interview questions covering ownership, RBAC/ABAC, PII handling, data mesh, policy-as-code, GDPR/CCPA compliance, and governance maturity.
content:
are important for multi-tenant analytics and compliance.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dg-08" number={8} question="How do you handle PII/PHI data in analytics platforms?" difficulty="hard" topic="Compliance">
You classify sensitive fields, minimize exposure, and enforce least privilege. Common controls include encryption, masking/tokenization, column-level access, and auditing. You also ensure downstream marts only include necessary fields and implement secure sharing patterns.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dg-09" number={9} question="What is data masking and tokenization?" difficulty="medium" topic="Compliance">
Masking hides sensitive values (for example showing only the last 4 digits) while keeping the dataset usable. Tokenization replaces sensitive values with tokens that can

title: Data Governance
description: Data governance interview questions covering ownership, RBAC/ABAC, PII handling, data mesh, policy-as-code, GDPR/CCPA compliance, and governance maturity.
content:
be detokenized only with access to a secure mapping. Tokenization is useful when analytics needs stable identifiers without exposing raw PII.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dg-10" number={10} question="How do you implement auditability for data access?" difficulty="medium" topic="Auditing">
You log access events (who queried what, when, from where) and retain logs per policy. You also track permission changes and administrative actions. Audit logs should be queryable for investigations and compliance reporting.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dg-11" number={11} question="How do you handle GDPR “right to be forgotten” in a lakehouse/warehouse?" difficulty="hard" topic="Compliance">
You need a process to delete or anonymize personal data across raw, derived, and serving layers. This

title: Data Governance
description: Data governance interview questions covering ownership, RBAC/ABAC, PII handling, data mesh, policy-as-code, GDPR/CCPA compliance, and governance maturity.
content:
can involve targeted deletes (where supported), reprocessing from raw logs without the user, or storing personal data separately to allow deletion without rewriting large datasets. You also document what is feasible given retention and legal constraints.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dg-12" number={12} question="What are data retention policies and how do you enforce them?" difficulty="medium" topic="Retention">
Retention policies define how long data is kept and when it must be deleted or archived. Enforcement can be implemented with partition expiry jobs, lifecycle rules on object storage, snapshot expiration, and access reviews. Retention must align with legal requirements and business needs.
</QuestionCard>

## Classification & Modern Governance Models

How sensitivity gets labeled, and how governance changes shape once a platform grows past one central team.

<QuestionList topic="Classification & Modern Models" storagePrefix="dg-modern">

<QuestionCard id="dg-13" number={13} question="What is data classification, and what tiers does a typical scheme use?" difficulty="easy" topic="Classification">
Data classification labels datasets (or individual columns) by sensitivity, so access controls, masking rules, and retention policies can be applied consistently based on that label rather than decided ad hoc per table. A common scheme: **Public** (no restriction), **Internal** (company-only), **Confidential** (restricted to specific teams/roles), and **Restricted** (PII/PHI, tightest controls, often

title: Data Governance
description: Data governance interview questions covering ownership, RBAC/ABAC, PII handling, data mesh, policy-as-code, GDPR/CCPA compliance, and governance maturity.
content:
legally regulated) — each tier mapping to a concrete, enforced set of access and handling rules.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dg-14" number={14} question="What is data mesh, and how does it change the governance model compared to a centralized team?" difficulty="hard" topic="Data Mesh">
Data mesh distributes data ownership to the domain teams that actually produce the data (treating each domain's output as a "data product" they're responsible for), instead of a single central data team owning ingestion, quality, and governance for everything. Governance shifts from "the central team enforces every rule" to **federated computational governance** — global standards (security, compliance, interoperability) are defined centrally, but enforced automatically through shared tooling/platfor

title: Data Governance
description: Data governance interview questions covering ownership, RBAC/ABAC, PII handling, data mesh, policy-as-code, GDPR/CCPA compliance, and governance maturity.
content:
ms, while domain-specific decisions stay with the domain teams.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dg-15" number={15} question="What is federated computational governance in a data mesh?" difficulty="hard" topic="Data Mesh">
It's the mechanism that keeps a decentralized data mesh from becoming ungoverned chaos: a small set of global rules (schema standards, security policies, PII handling) are defined once by a federated group (representatives from each domain, not one central authority), then **enforced automatically** by the platform itself — automated policy checks, standardized catalog registration — rather than manually policed for every domain's every dataset.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dg-16" number={16} question="What's the difference between anonymization and pseudonymizat

title: Data Governance
description: Data governance interview questions covering ownership, RBAC/ABAC, PII handling, data mesh, policy-as-code, GDPR/CCPA compliance, and governance maturity.
content:
ion?" difficulty="hard" topic="Compliance">
**Anonymization** irreversibly removes the ability to re-identify an individual — done correctly, the data falls outside the scope of regulations like GDPR entirely, but it's often destructive to analytical value and genuinely hard to guarantee (re-identification via combining "anonymized" fields is a known risk). **Pseudonymization** replaces identifying fields with a token or key, but the mapping back to the real identity still exists somewhere — it reduces risk and is often required by regulation, but the data is still considered personal data because re-identification remains possible.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dg-17" number={17} question="What is a data product, and how does governance apply differently to it than to a raw table?" d

description: Data governance interview questions covering ownership, RBAC/ABAC, PII handling, data mesh, policy-as-code, GDPR/CCPA compliance, and governance maturity.
content:
ifficulty="medium" topic="Data Mesh">
A data product is a dataset treated with the same discipline as a customer-facing product: it has a defined owner, a documented interface (schema/contract), quality SLAs, and discoverability — not just "a table that happens to exist." Governance for a data product is largely self-contained and owned by the producing domain (they're accountable for its contract and quality), whereas governance for an ungoverned raw table typically falls back to whatever central policy applies by default, with no one specifically accountable for its fitness for use.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

## Tooling & Automation

Turning governance from documented policy into something the platform actually enforces.

<QuestionList topic="Tooling & Automation" storagePrefix="dg-tooling">

<QuestionCard id="dg-18" number={18} question="What do data catalog tools like DataHub or Collibra actually provide beyond a spreadsheet of tables?" difficulty="medium" topic="Tooling">
They automatically ingest metadata (schemas, ownership, usage stats) directly from the warehouse/pipelines rather than relying on someone to manually maintain a document, so the catalog doesn't silently go stale the way a spreadsheet does. They also add lineage graphs connecting datasets to their upstream/downstream dependencies, search and discovery, and often plug into access-request workflows and classification tagging —

description: Data governance interview questions covering ownership, RBAC/ABAC, PII handling, data mesh, policy-as-code, GDPR/CCPA compliance, and governance maturity.

turning a static inventory into a live, queryable system of record.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dg-19" number={19} question="What is policy-as-code, and how does it apply to access governance?" difficulty="hard" topic="Automation">
```yaml

title: Data Governance
description: Data governance interview questions covering ownership, RBAC/ABAC, PII handling, data mesh, policy-as-code, GDPR/CCPA compliance, and governance maturity.

# example: an access policy defined declaratively, not granted manually
policy: deny
  if: resource.classification == "restricted"
     and not user.has_role("data-steward")
```
Policy-as-code defines access rules as version-controlled, testable configuration (often using a tool like Open Policy Agent) rather than permissions granted manually through a UI. This makes access policy reviewable in the same pull-request process as any other code change, consistently enforced across every system that respects it, and auditable — you can see exactly when and why a rule changed, not just infer it from who currently has access.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dg-20" number={20} question="How would you automate detection of PII in a dataset you didn't design?" difficulty="medium" topic="Automati

on">
Combine pattern-based scanning (regexes for emails, SSNs, phone numbers, credit card formats) with column-name heuristics (`email`, `ssn`, `dob`) and, for higher confidence, a trained classifier on sampled values. Automated scanning is a starting point, not a final answer — it needs a human review step for ambiguous cases, since it will both miss context-dependent PII and occasionally flag something that isn't (a column named `user_id` that's actually a random UUID, not identifying on its own).
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dg-21" number={21} question="What is an access request/approval workflow, and why not just grant broad access upfront?" difficulty="easy" topic="Access Control">
An access request workflow requires someone to explicitly request access to a specific dataset, wi

th an owner or steward approving it (often time-bound, sometimes requiring a business justification), rather than everyone getting broad default access. Granting broad access upfront is simpler operationally but violates least-privilege — it makes audits meaningless (everyone can see everything, so "who accessed this" tells you nothing useful) and makes revoking access when someone changes teams or leaves nearly impossible to reason about.

## Compliance Frameworks & Process

Beyond GDPR — comparing regulatory regimes, and the organizational processes that make governance stick.

<QuestionList topic="Compliance & Process" storagePrefix="dg-compliance">

<QuestionCard id="dg-22" number={22} question="How does GDPR differ from CCPA from a data engineering perspective?" difficulty="hard" topic="Compliance">
Both require honoring deletion and access requests, but **GDPR** (EU) is opt-in by default (you generally need a lawful basis and often explicit consent to process personal data at all) and applies more broadly to "personal data." **CCPA** (California) is more opt-out oriented (processing is generally allowed unless the consumer opts out, particularly of *sale* of their data) and is narrower in some respects but still require

title: Data Governance

content:
s similar underlying capabilities — knowing what personal data you hold about someone and being able to delete or export it on request.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dg-23" number={23} question="What is consent management, and how does it affect what a pipeline is allowed to process?" difficulty="medium" topic="Compliance">
Consent management tracks what each user has actually agreed to (marketing use, analytics, third-party sharing) as its own structured, queryable data — not just a one-time checkbox that's forgotten. A pipeline that ingests or transforms personal data needs to check current consent state before processing for a given purpose, and needs to handle consent being **withdrawn** after the fact, which usually means the same deletion/reprocessing machinery used for a "right

title: Data Governance
description: Data governance interview questions covering ownership, RBAC/ABAC, PII handling, data mesh, policy-as-code, GDPR/CCPA compliance, and governance maturity.
content:
to be forgotten" request.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dg-24" number={24} question="What is a Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA), and when is one required?" difficulty="hard" topic="Compliance">
A DPIA is a structured assessment of the privacy risk a new system or process introduces before it launches — what personal data it touches, what could go wrong, and what mitigations are in place — required under GDPR for processing likely to result in high risk to individuals (large-scale sensitive data processing, systematic profiling). For a data engineering team, this means privacy review becomes a design-time gate for certain new pipelines, not something bolted on after the fact.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dg-25" number={25} question="How do you measure whether a governanc

content:
e program is actually working?" difficulty="medium" topic="Governance Maturity">
Track concrete, observable signals rather than "we wrote a policy document": percentage of datasets with an assigned owner and complete catalog metadata, time-to-fulfill for access requests and deletion requests, number of datasets with an enforced classification tag, and audit findings from access reviews. A governance program with no metrics is one nobody can tell is failing until an incident (a compliance violation, a "nobody owns this" fire drill) forces the question.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dg-26" number={26} question="How would you design a RACI matrix for a new data domain?" difficulty="medium" topic="Process">
A RACI matrix maps each governance activity (defining the schema, approving access

, responding to a quality incident, honoring a deletion request) to who is **R**esponsible (does the work), **A**ccountable (final approval, usually the data owner), **C**onsulted (has input beforehand), and **I**nformed (told after the fact) — for a new domain, this is worth doing explicitly up front specifically to avoid the common failure mode where an incident happens and three teams each assume another team owns the response.

- **"Two teams have different definitions of 'active user' in their dashboards — how do you fix that at the platform level?"** Tests business glossary thinking and conformed definitions.
- **"Design the ownership model for a new data domain with three producing teams and ten consuming teams."** Tests owner/steward/custodian role design.

content:
## The Data Lifecycle: Generation to Serving

**Almost every data engineering interview has a stage where you have to design something end to end, and the lifecycle is the frame that keeps that answer organised. Where does data come from, how does it land, where does it live, how is it shaped, and who consumes it — with the undercurrents of governance, quality and cost running through all five. Candidates who answer stage by stage sound structured; candidates who jump straight to "I'd use Kafka" don't.**

title: The Data Lifecycle
description: Data lifecycle interview questions covering data generation and source systems, storage architecture, ingestion, transformation and serving — the end-to-end journey data takes through a platform.
content:

title: The Data Lifecycle
description: Data lifecycle interview questions covering data generation and source systems, storage architecture, ingestion, transformation and serving — the end-to-end journey data takes through a platform.
content:
## Key Concepts

The lifecycle has five stages — **generation, storage, ingestion, transformation, serving** — but storage is not really a stage. It's the substrate every other stage touches, which is why it appears in the middle of most diagrams and everywhere in practice.

Running underneath are the **undercurrents**: security, data management and governance, DataOps, architecture, orchestration and software engineering. They're not phases you do once; they're concerns that apply at every stage, and the phrase is worth knowing because it comes directly from *Fundamentals of Data Engineering*, which many interviewers have read.

The most useful thing this framing gives you is a **place to put trade-offs**. Latency requirements are decided at ingestion. Cost is dominated by storage and by

title: The Data Lifecycle
description: Data lifecycle interview questions covering data generation and source systems, storage architecture, ingestion, transformation and serving — the end-to-end journey data takes through a platform.
content:
how much data each transformation reads. Trust is established by quality checks between transformation and serving. When an interviewer asks "how would you build X", walking the stages in order surfaces the decisions rather than jumping to a tool.

title: The Data Lifecycle
description: Data lifecycle interview questions covering data generation and source systems, storage architecture, ingestion, transformation and serving — the end-to-end journey data takes through a platform.
content:
## Data Generation

<QuestionList topic="Data Generation" storagePrefix="data-lifecycle-generation">

<QuestionCard id="dlc-gen-01" number={1} question="What are the main types of source system, and what does each imply?" difficulty="medium" topic="Generation">
- **Transactional databases (OLTP)** — the application's own store. Authoritative and current, but you must extract without disrupting it, which pushes you toward replicas, snapshots or CDC.
- **Application events** — emitted deliberately for analytics. High volume, schema you control, and the best source when it exists.
- **Logs** — often semi-structured and enormous. Parsing and volume management are the work.
- **APIs (third party)** — rate-limited, paginated, and subject to change without notice. Assume you'll need retries, incr

title: The Data Lifecycle
description: Data lifecycle interview questions covering data generation and source systems, storage architecture, ingestion, transformation and serving — the end-to-end journey data takes through a platform.
content:
emental pulls and monitoring for silent schema changes.
- **Files from partners** — SFTP or object drops. Irregular arrival, inconsistent formats, and the most common source of "the file didn't arrive" incidents.
- **IoT and devices** — very high volume, out-of-order arrival, intermittent connectivity.

The question to ask of any source: **who owns it, can they change it without telling you, and what happens when it's late or wrong?** That's usually more important than its technical shape.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dlc-gen-02" number={2} question="What is a data contract, and why does it matter?" difficulty="hard" topic="Generation">
An explicit, versioned agreement between a data producer and its consumers covering **schema**, **semantics** (what each field actually means), **qua

title: The Data Lifecycle
description: Data lifecycle interview questions covering data generation and source systems, storage architecture, ingestion, transformation and serving — the end-to-end journey data takes through a platform.
content:
lity guarantees**, **freshness SLAs**, and a **change process**.

The problem it solves is the most common cause of broken pipelines: an application team renames a column or changes a unit, ships it on a Tuesday, and discovers a week later that three dashboards were wrong. Nobody did anything malicious — there was simply no agreement that the field was an interface.

In practice a contract is a schema definition in version control (Avro, Protobuf, JSON Schema, or a dbt/Soda spec), enforced in the producer's CI so a breaking change fails their build, plus runtime validation at ingestion.

The organisational point matters as much as the technical one: a contract makes the producer **accountable** for the data as a product, rather than data engineering absorbing every upstream change silently

title: The Data Lifecycle
description: Data lifecycle interview questions covering data generation and source systems, storage architecture, ingestion, transformation and serving — the end-to-end journey data takes through a platform.
content:
.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dlc-gen-03" number={3} question="What is schema evolution, and how do you handle it?" difficulty="medium" topic="Generation">
Source schemas change. The question is which changes you can absorb and which must break loudly.

- **Backward compatible** — adding an optional field, widening a type. Old consumers keep working. Should flow through automatically.
- **Forward compatible** — new consumers can read old data.
- **Breaking** — removing a field, renaming, narrowing a type, changing units or semantics. Must be caught, not absorbed.

Handling it: a **schema registry** (Confluent, Glue, or a repo of contract files) with compatibility rules enforced at publish time; **explicit schemas on read** rather than inference, so a change errors instead of silentl

title: The Data Lifecycle
description: Data lifecycle interview questions covering data generation and source systems, storage architecture, ingestion, transformation and serving — the end-to-end journey data takes through a platform.
content:
y producing nulls; a **raw landing zone** that stores data as received so you can reprocess after fixing a mapping; and **alerting on unexpected columns** rather than dropping them.

The failure to name is silent coercion — a numeric column arriving as a string, being cast to null, and aggregations quietly reading low.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

title: The Data Lifecycle
description: Data lifecycle interview questions covering data generation and source systems, storage architecture, ingestion, transformation and serving — the end-to-end journey data takes through a platform.
content:
## Data Storage

<QuestionList topic="Data Storage" storagePrefix="data-lifecycle-storage">

<QuestionCard id="dlc-sto-01" number={1} question="What are the storage options, and how do you choose?" difficulty="medium" topic="Storage">
- **Object storage** (S3, GCS, ADLS) — cheap, effectively unlimited, decoupled from compute. **The default for a lake.**
- **Data warehouse** (Snowflake, BigQuery, Redshift) — columnar, optimised for SQL analytics at high concurrency.
- **Lakehouse** — open table formats (Iceberg, Delta, Hudi) over object storage, giving warehouse semantics without the lock-in.
- **OLTP database** — row-oriented, for serving applications, not analytics.
- **Key-value / wide-column** (DynamoDB, Bigtable) — millisecond lookups by key at high write throughput.
- **Cache** (Redis

title: The Data Lifecycle
description: Data lifecycle interview questions covering data generation and source systems, storage architecture, ingestion, transformation and serving — the end-to-end journey data takes through a platform.
content:
) — sub-millisecond, volatile.
- **Search** (OpenSearch) — full-text and log analytics.

The choice follows the **access pattern**, not the data's size. Scan-and-aggregate wants columnar; lookup-by-key wants key-value; full-text wants an inverted index. Most platforms need two or three, and the mistake is forcing one store to serve every pattern.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dlc-sto-02" number={2} question="What is the difference between a data lake, a warehouse and a lakehouse?" difficulty="medium" topic="Storage">
- **Data warehouse** — structured, schema-on-write, curated and modelled before loading. Excellent SQL performance and governance; expensive, and rigid about semi-structured or unanticipated data.
- **Data lake** — raw files in object storage, schema-on-read. Cheap and fl

title: The Data Lifecycle
description: Data lifecycle interview questions covering data generation and source systems, storage architecture, ingestion, transformation and serving — the end-to-end journey data takes through a platform.
content:
exible for any format; without discipline it becomes a **data swamp**, with no ACID guarantees, no reliable schema and no idea what's trustworthy.
- **Lakehouse** — open table formats over the lake, adding **ACID transactions, schema enforcement, time travel and upserts** to cheap object storage, queryable by multiple engines.

The lakehouse exists because the earlier choice was a false dilemma: teams ran a lake *and* a warehouse, copied data between them, and reconciled the two. Keeping one copy in an open format that both batch engines and SQL engines can read removes that duplication.

Naming the **transaction log** as the mechanism — Delta's `_delta_log`, Iceberg's metadata tree — is what separates a real answer from a marketing one.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dlc-sto-03" numbe

title: The Data Lifecycle
description: Data lifecycle interview questions covering data generation and source systems, storage architecture, ingestion, transformation and serving — the end-to-end journey data takes through a platform.
content:
r={3} question="Why organise a lake into zones?" difficulty="medium" topic="Storage">
Typically three, under various names — raw/staging/curated, bronze/silver/gold, landing/conformed/consumption:

- **Raw** — exactly as received, immutable, append-only. It's your ability to **reprocess** when you find a bug six months later, and your audit record of what a source actually sent.
- **Staging / silver** — cleaned, deduplicated, typed, conformed. Quality gates live at this boundary.
- **Curated / gold** — modelled for consumption: dimensional models, aggregates, feature tables.

What the separation buys: a clear **contract about trust** (consumers know gold is safe and raw is not), the ability to rebuild everything downstream from raw, and a natural place for lifecycle policies — raw tiers to

title: The Data Lifecycle
description: Data lifecycle interview questions covering data generation and source systems, storage architecture, ingestion, transformation and serving — the end-to-end journey data takes through a platform.
content:
cheap storage, staging is reproducible so it can simply expire, curated stays hot.

The zone people skip is raw, and it's the one that saves you.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dlc-sto-04" number={4} question="How do partitioning and file layout affect everything downstream?" difficulty="hard" topic="Storage">
More than almost any code decision. Query engines prune whole partitions before reading, so layout determines how much data every downstream query touches — and on per-byte pricing, that is the bill.

The principles:
- **Partition on what queries filter by**, usually a date.
- **Not too fine** — partitioning by hour or by user ID creates the **small files problem**: per-file request overhead, slow listing, ineffective compression and statistics, and a task per tiny file.
- **Tar

title: The Data Lifecycle
description: Data lifecycle interview questions covering data generation and source systems, storage architecture, ingestion, transformation and serving — the end-to-end journey data takes through a platform.
content:
get 128 MB–1 GB files**, with scheduled compaction.
- **Columnar format** (Parquet) so column pruning and predicate pushdown work.
- **Sort or cluster within partitions** on high-cardinality filter columns.

The reason this belongs in a lifecycle discussion: it's decided once during storage design and every transformation and query pays for it afterwards. Fixing layout is frequently a bigger win than any tuning of the code reading it.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

title: The Data Lifecycle
description: Data lifecycle interview questions covering data generation and source systems, storage architecture, ingestion, transformation and serving — the end-to-end journey data takes through a platform.
content:
## Data Ingestion

<QuestionList topic="Data Ingestion" storagePrefix="data-lifecycle-ingestion">

<QuestionCard id="dlc-ing-01" number={1} question="What is the difference between ETL and ELT?" difficulty="easy" topic="Ingestion">
**ETL** — extract, transform, then load the transformed result. Transformation happens in a separate engine before data reaches the warehouse. Historically necessary because warehouse compute was expensive and scarce.

**ELT** — extract, load raw, then transform **inside** the destination using its compute. The modern default, because cloud warehouses have cheap elastic compute and separating storage from compute made loading raw data affordable.

Why ELT usually wins now: you keep the raw data, so you can re-transform when requirements change without re-extract

title: The Data Lifecycle
description: Data lifecycle interview questions covering data generation and source systems, storage architecture, ingestion, transformation and serving — the end-to-end journey data takes through a platform.
content:
ing from source; transformations are SQL, which more people can read and review; and tools like dbt make the transformation layer version-controlled and testable.

ETL still applies when data must be **masked or filtered before landing** for compliance, when the destination can't transform efficiently, or when the source's volume needs reducing before transfer.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dlc-ing-02" number={2} question="How do you decide between full and incremental loads?" difficulty="medium" topic="Ingestion">
**Full load** — replace everything each run. Simple, self-healing (a bad run is fixed by the next one), and immune to missed changes. Impractical once volume grows.

**Incremental** — move only what changed, by a watermark, by CDC, or by partition. Fast and cheap, but it ca

title: The Data Lifecycle
description: Data lifecycle interview questions covering data generation and source systems, storage architecture, ingestion, transformation and serving — the end-to-end journey data takes through a platform.
content:
n miss deletes, depends on a reliable change indicator, and drifts if a run fails silently.

The pragmatic combination most teams land on: **incremental daily, full weekly or monthly**, so drift is bounded and self-corrects without paying full-load cost every day.

The details that decide correctness: how you capture **deletes** (a timestamp-based incremental pull can't see them — CDC or a periodic reconciliation can), whether the load is **idempotent** so a retry can't duplicate, and whether **late-arriving data** for an already-processed partition is handled.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dlc-ing-03" number={3} question="What makes an ingestion pipeline reliable?" difficulty="hard" topic="Ingestion">
- **Idempotency** — re-running produces the same result. Every scheduler retries, s

title: The Data Lifecycle
description: Data lifecycle interview questions covering data generation and source systems, storage architecture, ingestion, transformation and serving — the end-to-end journey data takes through a platform.
content:
o without this a transient failure becomes duplicated rows.
- **Checkpointing** — record what's been processed so a restart resumes rather than repeating.
- **Retries with backoff and jitter** on transient failures, and fail-fast on permanent ones (a 4xx is not retryable).
- **Dead-letter handling** so one bad record can't block the stream forever.
- **Schema validation at the boundary**, failing loudly rather than coercing silently.
- **Monitoring on freshness and volume**, not just job success — the classic silent failure is a job that succeeds having loaded zero rows.
- **A raw landing zone**, so reprocessing never requires going back to the source.

If asked to pick one, choose **idempotency**. It's the property that makes everything else — retries, backfills, replays — safe.
</Questio

content:
## Transformation & Serving

<QuestionList topic="Transformation & Serving" storagePrefix="data-lifecycle-serving">

<QuestionCard id="dlc-srv-01" number={1} question="What happens in the transformation stage?" difficulty="medium" topic="Transformation">
Turning raw data into something trustworthy and useful:

- **Cleaning** — types, nulls, deduplication, standardising formats and units.
- **Conforming** — reconciling the same entity across sources, so `customer` means one thing.
- **Enriching** — joining reference data, deriving fields, geocoding.
- **Modelling** — dimensional models, Data Vault, or wide denormalised tables shaped for consumption.
- **Aggregating** — pre-computing what consumers query repeatedly.
- **Quality checks** — uniqueness, referential integrity, accepted ranges, r

title: The Data Lifecycle
description: Data lifecycle interview questions covering data generation and source systems, storage architecture, ingestion, transformation and serving — the end-to-end journey data takes through a platform.
content:
ow-count deltas.

The architectural point: transformation is where **business logic lives**, so it needs the same treatment as application code — version control, review, tests and CI. That's precisely what dbt made normal, and why "transformations as reviewed code" is now the expected answer rather than a differentiator.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dlc-srv-02" number={2} question="Who are the consumers of a data platform, and what does each need?" difficulty="medium" topic="Serving">
- **BI and analysts** — dimensional models, consistent metric definitions, fast interactive queries, and a semantic layer so "revenue" means one thing everywhere.
- **Data scientists** — access to granular and raw data, reproducibility, and history rather than only current state.
- **ML systems** — fea

title: The Data Lifecycle
description: Data lifecycle interview questions covering data generation and source systems, storage architecture, ingestion, transformation and serving — the end-to-end journey data takes through a platform.
content:
ture tables, with the **same** transformations available offline for training and online for serving, or you get training-serving skew.
- **Applications** — low-latency lookups, which means a serving store (key-value, cache), not the warehouse.
- **Reverse ETL to operational tools** — data pushed back into CRM, marketing and support systems.
- **Other teams' pipelines** — stable schemas and contracts, since your output is their input.

The mistake to name: serving every consumer from the same table. An analyst's dimensional model and an application's millisecond lookup have genuinely incompatible requirements.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dlc-srv-03" number={3} question="What are the undercurrents of the data lifecycle?" difficulty="medium" topic="Fundamentals">
Concerns that apply a

title: The Data Lifecycle
description: Data lifecycle interview questions covering data generation and source systems, storage architecture, ingestion, transformation and serving — the end-to-end journey data takes through a platform.
content:
t **every** stage rather than being a stage themselves — the framing from *Fundamentals of Data Engineering*:

- **Security** — least privilege, encryption in transit and at rest, PII handling at each hop.
- **Data management** — governance, cataloguing, lineage, quality, master data, privacy and retention.
- **DataOps** — automation, observability, incident response, and treating pipelines as production systems.
- **Data architecture** — the trade-off decisions that make the whole thing coherent.
- **Orchestration** — dependencies, scheduling, retries and backfills across stages.
- **Software engineering** — testing, version control, CI/CD, code review.

Why it's worth naming in an interview: it demonstrates you see data engineering as a discipline rather than a set of tools, and it gives

title: The Data Lifecycle
description: Data lifecycle interview questions covering data generation and source systems, storage architecture, ingestion, transformation and serving — the end-to-end journey data takes through a platform.
content:
you a checklist for any design question — "and here's how governance and observability apply at each stage" is a strong closing move.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dlc-srv-04" number={4} question="Walk through the lifecycle for a concrete example." difficulty="hard" topic="Fundamentals">
Say daily revenue reporting for an e-commerce business:

1. **Generation** — orders in a Postgres OLTP database; clickstream events from the web app; a product catalogue from a partner via SFTP.
2. **Ingestion** — CDC from Postgres via Debezium or DMS (captures deletes, no load on the primary); events to Kafka; the partner file triggering a job on arrival.
3. **Storage** — all three land in object storage as raw, partitioned by date, in an open table format. Retained for reprocessing.
4. **Transforma

title: The Data Lifecycle
description: Data lifecycle interview questions covering data generation and source systems, storage architecture, ingestion, transformation and serving — the end-to-end journey data takes through a platform.
content:
tion** — dbt models: clean and conform in staging, then a `fact_orders` and conformed dimensions in curated, with tests for uniqueness on order ID, referential integrity to customers, and non-negative amounts.
5. **Serving** — the warehouse for BI, with a semantic layer defining "revenue"; aggregates for the executive dashboard; reverse ETL pushing customer lifetime value into the CRM.
6. **Undercurrents throughout** — Airflow orchestrating with retries and backfill; freshness and volume monitoring per table; PII masked in non-production; lineage so an upstream schema change shows its blast radius.

Answering in this order is the point — it demonstrates structure and surfaces the trade-offs at each step.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

content:
## Common Interview Scenarios

**"Design a data platform for [some business]."** — walk the lifecycle in order. Sources and their ownership, ingestion mode driven by latency requirements, zoned storage with a partitioning strategy, transformation as reviewed code with quality gates, then serving shaped per consumer. Close with the undercurrents.

**"Where would you spend the most effort?"** — storage layout and ingestion reliability. Layout determines the cost of every query afterwards, and idempotent ingestion is what makes retries, backfills and replays safe. Both are expensive to change later.

**"An upstream team changed a column and broke your pipeline. How do you prevent recurrence?"** — data contracts enforced in the producer's CI, schema validation at ingestion that fails loudly, a

title: The Data Lifecycle
description: Data lifecycle interview questions covering data generation and source systems, storage architecture, ingestion, transformation and serving — the end-to-end journey data takes through a platform.
content:
raw zone so you can reprocess, and lineage so the blast radius is known immediately.

**"ETL or ELT?"** — ELT by default with cloud warehouses, because you keep raw data and can re-transform. ETL when compliance requires masking before landing, or when volume must be reduced before transfer.

## Data Modeling: Schema Design for Analytics

content:
## Key Concepts

Everything in analytical data modeling starts with **grain** — the level of detail a table represents (one row per order line, one row per user per day). Get grain wrong and every downstream join or aggregation is suspect. From there, the **star schema** (a central fact table surrounded by dimension tables) is the default shape for analytics: facts hold measurable events and foreign keys, dimensions hold descriptive context. **Slowly Changing Dimensions (SCD)** define how you handle attribute changes over time, and patterns like **conformed dimensions**, **bridge tables**, and **degenerate dimensions** solve for consistency, many-to-many relationships, and drill-through respectively.

## Interview Questions

<QuestionList topic="Data Modeling" storagePrefix="data-modeling">

<QuestionCard id="dm-01" number={1} question="What is data modeling in analytics and why does it matter?" difficulty="easy" topic="Fundamentals">
Data modeling in analytics is the process of structuring data so it can be queried reliably and efficiently for business questions. A good model makes metrics consistent, reduces complexity for consumers, and improves performance by aligning storage with query patterns. A bad model leads to inconsistent KPIs, confusing joins, and expensive queries.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dm-02" number={2} question="What is grain and why is it the first question to answer?" difficulty="easy" topic="Fundamentals">
Grain is the level of detail of a table — for exa

mple "one row per order line" or "one row per user per day." It determines which metrics are additive, how joins behave, and what can be uniquely identified. If grain is unclear, you get duplicates, incorrect aggregations, and ambiguous keys.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dm-03" number={3} question="What is the difference between fact and dimension tables?" difficulty="easy" topic="Star Schema">
Facts store measurable events (orders, payments, clicks) and typically contain foreign keys to dimensions. Dimensions store descriptive attributes (user, product, date) that provide context for slicing and filtering. Facts answer "what happened," dimensions answer "who/what/where/when."
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dm-04" number={4} question="What is a star schema and what are its benefi

ts?" difficulty="easy" topic="Star Schema">
A star schema has a central fact table connected to multiple dimension tables. Benefits include simpler queries, clear join paths, and good performance because joins are typically fact-to-dimension (many-to-one). It also encourages consistent definitions of metrics and attributes.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dm-05" number={5} question="Star schema vs snowflake schema: what are the trade-offs?" difficulty="medium" topic="Star Schema">
A snowflake schema normalizes dimensions into multiple related tables. It can reduce redundancy and improve dimension maintainability, but it increases join complexity and can hurt performance. Star schemas are usually preferred for BI and ad-hoc analytics because they're easier for users and tools to work wit

h.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dm-06" number={6} question="What are the main types of fact tables?" difficulty="medium" topic="Fact Tables">
- **Transactional** — one row per business event (order, payment)
- **Periodic snapshot** — one row per entity per period (daily account balance)
- **Accumulating snapshot** — one row that gets updated as a process progresses (order lifecycle)

Choosing the right type depends on the questions you need to answer.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dm-07" number={7} question="What is a surrogate key and when should you use it?" difficulty="medium" topic="Keys">
A surrogate key is a synthetic identifier used instead of a natural key. It's useful when natural keys aren't stable, when you need SCD history, or when integrating multiple sources with d

description: Data modeling interview questions covering star schema, SCD, Data Vault, NoSQL and dbt-style modeling, advanced dimension patterns, and schema evolution.
content:
ifferent key systems. Surrogate keys also allow consistent joins even if source keys change.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dm-08" number={8} question="What is a conformed dimension?" difficulty="medium" topic="Dimensions">
A conformed dimension is a dimension shared consistently across multiple fact tables or data marts — for example, the same "customer" dimension used for orders and support tickets. Conformed dimensions enable consistent reporting and cross-domain analysis.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dm-09" number={9} question="What is SCD (Slowly Changing Dimension)?" difficulty="medium" topic="SCD">
SCD describes how you handle changes in dimension attributes over time (for example, a user changing address).

- **Type 1** — overwrites history
- **Type 2** — tracks history w

content:
ith multiple rows and effective dates
- **Type 3** — keeps limited history in additional columns

The choice depends on whether "as-of" reporting is required.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dm-10" number={10} question="How do you implement SCD Type 2?" difficulty="hard" topic="SCD">
SCD2 typically stores:

- a surrogate key
- the natural/business key
- `effective_start` and `effective_end` timestamps (or `end_date`)
- a `current_flag`

On change, you "close" the previous record and insert a new version. You must define how to detect changes and handle late-arriving updates.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dm-11" number={11} question="What is a factless fact table?" difficulty="medium" topic="Fact Tables">
A factless fact table records events that don't have numeric measures — for ex

content:
ample, "student attended class" or "user is eligible for campaign." The fact itself can be counted, and the table is useful for coverage, eligibility, and relationship tracking.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dm-12" number={12} question="What is a bridge table and when do you need it?" difficulty="hard" topic="Dimensions">
A bridge table resolves many-to-many relationships — for example, products belonging to multiple categories, or users having multiple roles. It can also store weights for allocation (for example, revenue split). Without a bridge table, joins can explode row counts and break aggregations.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dm-13" number={13} question="What are degenerate dimensions?" difficulty="medium" topic="Dimensions">
Degenerate dimensions are identifiers stored

content:

</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dm-14" number={14} question="How do you prevent double counting in analytical models?" difficulty="hard" topic="Data Quality">
You prevent double counting by enforcing correct grain, using proper join keys (many-to-one), and avoiding many-to-many joins without a bridge table. You also define metric rules (sum vs. distinct count vs. last value) and test them with reconciliation queries.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dm-15" number={15} question="How do you validate a data model after changes?" difficulty="medium" topic="Data Quality">
Typical validation include

- row count and key uniqueness checks at each layer
- reconciliation of totals against source systems
- sampling and drill-through checks on known entities
- regression tests for key business metrics

This catches subtle issues like join duplication or missing late data.
</QuestionCard>
