## Data Vault Modeling

An alternative to Kimball dimensional modeling, built for integrating many source systems with strong auditability and resilience to change.

<QuestionList topic="Data Vault" storagePrefix="dm-vault">

<QuestionCard id="dm-16" number={16} question="What is Data Vault modeling, and when would you choose it over Kimball dimensional modeling?" difficulty="medium" topic="Data Vault">
Data Vault is a modeling methodology designed for auditability, scalability, and flexibility when integrating many source systems, especially where schemas and sources change often. Unlike Kimball's business-facing star schemas, Data Vault separates raw structural integration (hubs/links/satellites) from the business-friendly reporting layer built on top of it. Choose Data Vault when you ne

title: Data Modeling
description: Data modeling interview questions covering star schema, SCD, Data Vault, NoSQL and dbt-style modeling, advanced dimension patterns, and schema evolution.
content:
ed strong historization, parallel loading, and resilience to upstream changes; choose Kimball when the priority is fast, simple BI consumption.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dm-17" number={17} question="What are hubs, links, and satellites in Data Vault modeling?" difficulty="medium" topic="Data Vault">
- **Hub** — stores a list of unique business keys for a core entity (e.g., customer), never descriptive attributes.
- **Link** — represents a relationship or transaction between hubs (e.g., customer-to-order), storing only foreign keys.
- **Satellite** — holds descriptive, time-stamped attributes for a hub or link (e.g., customer address history), enabling full historization.

This separation lets you add new attributes or sources without redesigning existing structures.
</QuestionCard

title: Data Modeling
description: Data modeling interview questions covering star schema, SCD, Data Vault, NoSQL and dbt-style modeling, advanced dimension patterns, and schema evolution.
content:
>

<QuestionCard id="dm-18" number={18} question="How does Data Vault handle history compared to SCD Type 2?" difficulty="hard" topic="Data Vault">
Satellites are inherently append-only and timestamped on load, so every change becomes a new satellite row automatically, without the explicit "close old row, insert new row" logic SCD Type 2 needs. Because history lives in every satellite rather than one dimension table, Data Vault captures history at a more granular level, at the cost of needing more joins to reconstruct a point-in-time view.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dm-19" number={19} question="What is a Point-of-Time (PIT) table in Data Vault, and why is it needed?" difficulty="hard" topic="Data Vault">
A PIT table pre-joins hubs to their satellites at defined snapshot points (e.g

title: Data Modeling
description: Data modeling interview questions covering star schema, SCD, Data Vault, NoSQL and dbt-style modeling, advanced dimension patterns, and schema evolution.
content:
., daily), storing the relevant satellite keys for each point in time. It exists because querying multiple satellites directly for an "as of" report requires expensive multi-way joins with date-range logic — a PIT table pre-computes those joins so downstream BI queries stay fast and simple.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dm-20" number={20} question="What are the main trade-offs of Data Vault versus Kimball dimensional modeling?" difficulty="medium" topic="Data Vault">
Data Vault trades query simplicity for load flexibility and auditability — it's easier to onboard new sources and preserve full history, but raw Data Vault tables are rarely queried directly by business users; you typically build a Kimball-style mart on top. Kimball is simpler to query and understand but harder to evolve

without redesign when sources or business rules change significantly. Many organizations use Data Vault as the integration layer and Kimball as the presentation layer.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

## NoSQL & Modern Analytics-Engineering Modeling

Modeling principles shift once you leave the relational world, or once "modeling" means organizing dbt/lakehouse transformation layers rather than table schemas.

<QuestionList topic="Modern Modeling" storagePrefix="dm-modern">

<QuestionCard id="dm-21" number={21} question="How does data modeling for NoSQL databases differ from relational modeling?" difficulty="medium" topic="NoSQL">
Relational modeling starts from the data's structure and normalizes to avoid redundancy; NoSQL modeling starts from your application's access patterns and denormalizes deliberately so the most common queries need no joins. You often duplicate data across documents or wide rows, trading storage and update complexity for read performance and horizontal scalabili

<QuestionCard id="dm-22" number={22} question="Embedding vs. referencing in document store modeling: how do you decide?" difficulty="medium" topic="NoSQL">
Embed related data inside a document when it's read together, doesn't grow unbounded, and isn't queried independently (an order's line items inside the order document). Reference — store an ID and look up separately — when the related data is large, shared across many parents, updated independently, or would push a document past size limits (a product referenced by thousands of orders).
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dm-23" number={23} question="How do you model data for a wide-column store like Cassandra or BigTable?" difficulty="hard" topic="NoSQL">
Design the table around your query patterns first — a partiti

content:
on key that distributes data evenly and matches your most common lookup, and a clustering key that gives the sort order your queries need. Since these stores don't support arbitrary joins or efficient secondary indexes, you typically denormalize and maintain multiple query-specific tables ("one table per query") rather than one normalized source of truth.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dm-24" number={24} question="What is denormalization, and when is it the right modeling choice?" difficulty="easy" topic="NoSQL">
Denormalization intentionally duplicates or pre-joins data to avoid expensive joins or lookups at query time. It's the right choice when read performance matters more than storage cost or update complexity — typical in analytics/BI tables, NoSQL access-pattern modeling, and ca

ching layers — but it pushes the burden of keeping duplicated data consistent onto your write/ETL logic.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dm-25" number={25} question="What are dbt's staging, intermediate, and marts layers, and why keep them separate?" difficulty="medium" topic="Analytics Engineering">
- **Staging** — one model per source table, doing only light renaming/type-casting: a 1:1 clean mirror of the source.
- **Intermediate** — business logic and joins not yet ready to expose to end users, reused across multiple marts.
- **Marts** — final, business-facing models (often dimensionally shaped) that BI tools query directly.

Separating them keeps transformations testable and traceable, and lets source-level details change without rewriting business logic.
</QuestionCard>

<Question

Bronze holds raw, unprocessed data as ingested; silver holds cleaned, conformed, deduplicated data (often still fairly normalized); gold holds business-level, aggregated, typically dimensionally-modeled data ready for consumption. It maps loosely onto staging/intermediate/marts, but is framed around data-quality stages rather than dbt's specific tooling layers, and is common in lakehouse architectures.
</QuestionCard>

OBT denormalizes a fact and all its dimensions into a single wide table, avoiding joins entirely at query time. It makes sense when your BI tool or query engine handles wide tables well, joins are the actual bottleneck, or a single well-defined use case doesn't need reusable conformed dimensions. The trade-off is duplicated dimension data and harder-to-maintain consistency if you need several OBTs.

## Advanced Dimension Patterns

Beyond the basic star schema — patterns for specific dimensional-modeling problems that come up once a warehouse matures.

<QuestionList topic="Advanced Patterns" storagePrefix="dm-advanced">

<QuestionCard id="dm-29" number={29} question="What is a role-playing dimension?" difficulty="medium" topic="Dimensions">
A role-playing dimension is a single physical dimension table used multiple times in the same fact table through different foreign keys and views, representing different roles it plays. The classic example is one Date dimension joined three times to represent order_date, ship_date, and delivery_date — each presented to users as if it were a separate dimension.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dm-30" number={30} question="What is a mini-dimension,

title: Data Modeling
description: Data modeling interview questions covering star schema, SCD, Data Vault, NoSQL and dbt-style modeling, advanced dimension patterns, and schema evolution.
content:
and when do you need one?" difficulty="hard" topic="Dimensions">
A mini-dimension splits frequently-changing or high-cardinality attributes out of a large dimension into their own smaller dimension — for example, pulling "customer age band" and "income band" out of a Customer dimension. It's used when those attributes change often enough that SCD Type 2 on the full dimension would create excessive row churn, or when the attribute combination is small enough to enumerate as its own table.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dm-31" number={31} question="What is an outrigger dimension?" difficulty="hard" topic="Dimensions">
An outrigger dimension is a dimension table that itself has a foreign key to another dimension table — for example, a Customer dimension referencing a separate Geography di

title: Data Modeling
description: Data modeling interview questions covering star schema, SCD, Data Vault, NoSQL and dbt-style modeling, advanced dimension patterns, and schema evolution.
content:
mension. It's a controlled exception to the "dimensions don't join to other dimensions" star-schema rule, used sparingly when a shared sub-dimension like geography or a calendar is reused across several dimensions.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dm-32" number={32} question="How do you model ragged or unbalanced hierarchies?" difficulty="hard" topic="Hierarchies">
A ragged hierarchy is one where branches have different depths — an org chart where some employees report directly to the CEO and others sit five levels down. Common approaches are a **recursive/parent-child** table (self-referencing foreign key) queried with recursive CTEs, or a **bridge table** that flattens every ancestor-descendant pair with a depth column, trading modeling simplicity for query-time convenience.
</Question

description: Data modeling interview questions covering star schema, SCD, Data Vault, NoSQL and dbt-style modeling, advanced dimension patterns, and schema evolution.
content:
Card>

<QuestionCard id="dm-33" number={33} question="How do you design a date or time dimension?" difficulty="easy" topic="Dimensions">
A date dimension has one row per calendar day, often pre-populated for decades, with pre-computed attributes like day-of-week, month name, fiscal period, holiday flags, and quarter — so BI tools can filter and group by these without date-function logic in every query. Time-of-day is usually modeled separately (a small dimension or a plain column), since a date dimension is already large enough without every second of the day multiplying it further.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dm-34" number={34} question="What is SCD Type 4, and how does it differ from Type 2?" difficulty="hard" topic="SCD">
SCD Type 4 splits a dimension into a current-values table

content:
and a separate history table, rather than keeping both current and historical rows in one table with effective dates like Type 2. This keeps the current table small and fast for typical queries, while the larger, less-frequently-queried history table absorbs the historical churn — useful when a dimension changes very frequently and Type 2's row growth becomes a performance problem.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

## Schema Evolution, Contracts & Relationships

How a model survives change over time — both in schema shape and in the relationships it represents.

<QuestionList topic="Schema Evolution" storagePrefix="dm-evolution">

<QuestionCard id="dm-35" number={35} question="What is schema evolution, and why is it risky in analytics pipelines?" difficulty="medium" topic="Schema Evolution">
Schema evolution is how a table's structure changes over time — new columns, renamed fields, changed types. It's risky because downstream consumers (dashboards, ML models, other pipelines) often assume a fixed shape; an unannounced column removal or type change can silently break queries or, worse, silently produce wrong numbers if a type change alters aggregation behavior without erroring.
</QuestionCard>

<Ques

title: Data Modeling
description: Data modeling interview questions covering star schema, SCD, Data Vault, NoSQL and dbt-style modeling, advanced dimension patterns, and schema evolution.
content:
tionCard id="dm-36" number={36} question="What is a data contract, and how does it help manage schema evolution?" difficulty="medium" topic="Schema Evolution">
A data contract is an explicit, versioned agreement between a data producer and its consumers about a dataset's schema, semantics, and change process, often enforced with validation in CI/CD. It helps by making breaking changes a deliberate, communicated decision — bump a version, notify consumers — rather than a surprise, shifting schema evolution from "discovered when something breaks" to "planned and reviewed."
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dm-37" number={37} question="What's the difference between a backward-compatible and a forward-compatible schema change?" difficulty="hard" topic="Schema Evolution">
A **backward-compatib

title: Data Modeling
description: Data modeling interview questions covering star schema, SCD, Data Vault, NoSQL and dbt-style modeling, advanced dimension patterns, and schema evolution.
content:
le** change means new data still works with code written against the old schema (adding a new optional column — old readers just ignore it). A **forward-compatible** change means old data still works with code written against the new schema (a new required field needs a default so historical rows without it don't break). Designing for both lets producers and consumers deploy independently without a synchronized rollout.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dm-38" number={38} question="What is cardinality in ER modeling, and why does it matter for a data model?" difficulty="easy" topic="Relationships">
Cardinality describes how many instances of one entity relate to instances of another — one-to-one, one-to-many, or many-to-many. Getting it wrong is a common source of grain-mismatch bugs: ass

title: Data Modeling
description: Data modeling interview questions covering star schema, SCD, Data Vault, NoSQL and dbt-style modeling, advanced dimension patterns, and schema evolution.
content:
uming a one-to-many relationship is actually one-to-one silently drops rows or picks an arbitrary one on a join, while missing a many-to-many relationship (no bridge table) silently duplicates rows and inflates metrics.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dm-39" number={39} question="How do you model recursive or self-referencing relationships, like an org chart or category tree?" difficulty="medium" topic="Relationships">
The standard relational approach is a self-referencing foreign key (`employee.manager_id -> employee.employee_id`), queried with a recursive CTE to walk up or down the hierarchy. For read-heavy analytical use, this is often paired with a flattened path or bridge-table representation so BI tools don't need to run recursive queries themselves.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard

description: Data modeling interview questions covering star schema, SCD, Data Vault, NoSQL and dbt-style modeling, advanced dimension patterns, and schema evolution.
content:
id="dm-40" number={40} question="How do you handle unknown or missing dimension members?" difficulty="medium" topic="Relationships">
Rather than allowing NULL foreign keys — which silently exclude rows from inner joins and complicate filtering — the standard pattern is to insert an explicit "Unknown" or "Not Applicable" row into the dimension with a reserved surrogate key, and point unresolved facts at that row. This keeps joins simple (always an inner join) and makes missing-data volume visible and reportable instead of hidden.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dm-41" number={41} question="What questions should you ask before modeling a new fact table for a new business domain?" difficulty="medium" topic="Fact Tables">
Start with grain — what does one row represent? Then: what dimension

description: Data modeling interview questions covering star schema, SCD, Data Vault, NoSQL and dbt-style modeling, advanced dimension patterns, and schema evolution.
content:
s does this event naturally relate to, are any of them new or already covered by existing conformed dimensions, what measures are actually additive at this grain, how will corrections or cancellations be handled (a new fact vs. mutating a row), and what's the expected volume and update frequency. Answering these up front avoids the most common rework: discovering the grain was wrong after the table's already in production.
</QuestionCard>

## Common Interview Scenarios

- **"Design a fact table for e-commerce orders."** Start by nailing down grain (order? order line?), then identify dimensions (customer, product, date, promotion) and decide how to handle returns or cancellations — usually a separate fact or a status dimension rather than mutating the original row.
- **"Our revenue metric doesn't match between two dashboards."** This is almost always a grain or join-fan-out problem. Walk through checking for many-to-many joins without a bridge table, duplicate rows from a non-conformed dimension, or inconsistent aggregation rules (sum vs. distinct count) between the two queries.
- **"A dimension's attributes change over time — how do you model it?"** Identify whether the business needs point-in-time history (SCD Type 2) or on

ly the current value (SCD Type 1), then talk through the surrogate key, effective-dating, and how late-arriving changes get handled.
- **"We're integrating 12 source systems that all change independently — how would you model this?"** This is a Data Vault signal: talk through hubs for the shared business keys, links for how the systems' entities relate, and satellites absorbing each source's own attributes and change cadence, with a Kimball-style mart built on top for actual reporting.
- **"Design a schema for a document store instead of a relational database."** Walk through identifying the application's actual read patterns first, then decide what gets embedded (read together, bounded size) versus referenced (shared, independently updated, unbounded growth) — the opposite starting point

## Data Quality: Accuracy, Completeness & Trust

**Data quality is the practice of ensuring data is correct, complete, consistent, and timely enough that downstream consumers can trust it — a mix of pipeline engineering (checks, contracts, monitoring) and product thinking (clear definitions and ownership).**

## Key Concepts

Data quality means data is fit for its intended use, which usually breaks down into six dimensions: completeness, validity, accuracy, consistency, timeliness/freshness, and uniqueness. Checks operate at two levels — **row-level checks** (`not_null`, regex, range constraints on individual records) and **aggregate checks** (row counts, distinct counts, distribution shifts across the whole dataset) — and both are needed because aggregate checks catch issues row-level rules miss, like a missing partition. Upstream, **data contracts** and schema-drift detection prevent producers from silently breaking consumers; downstream, **quarantine patterns** let bad rows get isolated with an error reason while the pipeline keeps running for valid data. A common failure mode is alert fatig

## Interview Questions

<QuestionList topic="Data Quality" storagePrefix="data-quality">

<QuestionCard id="dq-01" number={1} question="What does data quality mean in data engineering?" difficulty="easy" topic="Fundamentals">
Data quality means the data is fit for its intended use. In practice, it means data is correct, complete, consistent, timely, and well-defined so downstream consumers can trust metrics. Data quality is both a technical problem (pipelines) and a product problem (definitions and contracts).
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dq-02" number={2} question="What are common dimensions of data quality?" difficulty="easy" topic="Fundamentals">
Common dimensions include:

- completeness (missing rows/fields)
- validity (values in allowed ranges/domains)
- accuracy (matches real-

content:
world or source truth)
- consistency (no contradictions across tables)
- timeliness/freshness (arrives within SLA)
- uniqueness (no duplicates where keys should be unique)
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dq-03" number={3} question="What is data freshness and how do you measure it?" difficulty="easy" topic="Freshness">
Freshness is how recently data was updated relative to expected cadence. You can measure it by comparing the maximum event/ingestion timestamp in a table to current time, and alert when it exceeds an SLA threshold. Freshness should be defined per dataset because "daily" and "real-time" pipelines differ.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dq-04" number={4} question="What is the difference between data validation and data reconciliation?" difficulty="medium" topic="Validatio

Validation checks whether a dataset satisfies rules (types, constraints, ranges). Reconciliation compares datasets to ensure they match expected totals or invariants (for example source row count vs. target row count, or `sum(amount)` in source vs. warehouse). Reconciliation is important when multiple systems can drift.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dq-05" number={5} question="What are row-level checks and aggregate checks?" difficulty="medium" topic="Checks">
Row-level checks validate each record (for example `not_null`, regex, range constraints). Aggregate checks validate the dataset as a whole (row counts, distinct counts, distribution checks, totals). Aggregate checks often catch issues that row-level rules miss, like missing partitions.
</QuestionCard>

Checks should be scoped to the incremental window and also protect the full table invariants. For example, validate uniqueness on the keys in the new batch, validate that the batch size is within expected bounds, and validate that total counts change consistently. You also need idempotency checks to detect duplicates on retries.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dq-07" number={7} question="How do you handle late arriving data from a quality perspective?" difficulty="hard" topic="Pipelines">
You define allowed lateness (for example 7 days), track completeness by event time, and implement backfills to "close" historical partitions. Quality checks should consider both ing

</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dq-08" number={8} question="How do you detect schema drift and breaking changes?" difficulty="medium" topic="Schema">
You compare incoming schemas to an expected contract (column names, types, nullability) and alert on changes. Additive changes can be allowed with policy, but breaking changes (rename/type change) should fail fast. Many teams use CI checks and schema registries to enforce compatibility.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dq-09" number={9} question="What are data contracts?" difficulty="medium" topic="Contracts">
Data contracts are explicit agreements between producers and consumers about schema, semantics, SLAs, and ownership. Contracts reduce surprises by defining what can

</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dq-10" number={10} question="How do you avoid noisy alerts (false positives) in data quality monitoring?" difficulty="medium" topic="Alerting">
Use dynamic thresholds, seasonality-aware baselines, and multi-signal alerts (freshness + volume + error rate). Also route alerts by severity and dataset criticality, and suppress alerts during known maintenance windows. Good alerting includes a runbook and clear ownership.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dq-11" number={11} question="What is anomaly detection for metrics and when is it useful?" difficulty="medium" topic="Monitoring">
Anomaly detection flags unusual changes in metrics

<QuestionCard id="dq-12" number={12} question="How do you quarantine bad data without blocking the entire pipeline?" difficulty="hard" topic="Pipelines">
A common pattern is to split data into "good" and "quarantine" outputs based on validation rules. You can store bad rows with error reasons for debugging while allowing the pipeline to continue for valid data. For critical datasets, you may still block publishing to marts while keeping raw ingestion running.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dq-14" number={14} question="What is the minimum set of checks you would add to every table?" difficulty="easy" topic="Checks">

- freshness (max timestamp within SLA)

## Tooling & Frameworks

The actual libraries and workflows teams use to define and run checks, rather than writing ad-hoc validation SQL every time.

<QuestionList topic="Tooling & Frameworks" storagePrefix="dq-tools">

<QuestionCard id="dq-16" number={16} question="What is Great Expectations, and what problem does it solve?" difficulty="medium" topic="Tooling">
Great Expectations is a Python framework for defining data quality rules ("expectations" — `expect_column_values_to_not_be_null`, `expect_column_values_to_be_between`) as declarative, version-controllable code rather than one-off SQL scripts. Expectations are grouped into **suites** and run via **checkpoints**, producing a human-readable validation report — it solves the problem of quality checks living as tribal knowledge or scat

title: Data Quality
description: Data quality interview questions covering dimensions, validation, Great Expectations and dbt tests, deduplication, distribution drift, and quality ownership.
content:
tered scripts by making them a first-class, testable, shareable artifact.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dq-17" number={17} question="How do dbt's built-in tests (unique, not_null, relationships, accepted_values) work?" difficulty="easy" topic="Tooling">
```yaml
models:
  - name: orders
    columns:
      - name: order_id
        tests: [unique, not_null]
      - name: status
        tests:
          - accepted_values: {values: ["pending", "shipped", "cancelled"]}
      - name: customer_id
        tests:
          - relationships: {to: ref('customers'), field: customer_id}
```
Each test compiles to a SQL query that should return **zero rows** if the data is valid — `dbt test` runs them after a build and fails the run if any query returns rows. They're declared alongside the model defin

title: Data Quality
description: Data quality interview questions covering dimensions, validation, Great Expectations and dbt tests, deduplication, distribution drift, and quality ownership.
content:
ition, so the quality rule lives right next to the transformation it's validating.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dq-18" number={18} question="When would you choose a dedicated framework like Great Expectations over dbt tests?" difficulty="medium" topic="Tooling">
dbt tests are ideal when checks are simple, SQL-expressible, and already living inside a dbt project — low friction, no extra tooling. Reach for Great Expectations (or a similar dedicated framework) when you need checks outside a dbt-managed warehouse (raw files, a data lake, a non-dbt pipeline), richer statistical expectations, or standalone validation reports/documentation independent of any single transformation tool.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dq-19" number={19} question="How do you integrate data quality checks i

title: Data Quality
description: Data quality interview questions covering dimensions, validation, Great Expectations and dbt tests, deduplication, distribution drift, and quality ownership.
content:
nto a CI/CD pipeline?" difficulty="medium" topic="Tooling">
Run checks against a representative sample or a full staging dataset as part of the build/deploy pipeline — for dbt, `dbt build` runs models and tests together, failing the pipeline before a broken model reaches production. The key design decision is *what blocks deployment versus what just alerts*: schema-breaking changes and critical table failures should block merges, while softer statistical checks (mild distribution shifts) are often better as warnings that don't halt every deploy.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dq-20" number={20} question="What is data profiling, and why is it the first step before writing quality checks for a new dataset?" difficulty="easy" topic="Profiling">
Profiling means computing summary statistics

title: Data Quality

content:
on a dataset before you know what to check — null rates per column, distinct value counts, min/max/mean, common patterns in string columns. It matters because you can't write meaningful checks (what's a "normal" null rate? what values are actually valid?) without first understanding what the data actually looks like; skipping profiling leads to either checks that are too loose to catch real problems or so strict they fail on legitimate data.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

content:
## Practical Validation Techniques

Specific problems that come up once you move past "check for nulls" into real production datasets.

<QuestionList topic="Practical Validation Techniques" storagePrefix="dq-practical">

<QuestionCard id="dq-21" number={21} question="How do you check referential integrity in a warehouse that doesn't enforce foreign keys?" difficulty="medium" topic="Referential Integrity">
Most analytical warehouses accept (but don't enforce) foreign key declarations, so referential integrity has to be checked explicitly — typically an anti-join: rows in the child table whose key doesn't exist in the parent table.

```sql
SELECT o.customer_id
FROM orders o
LEFT JOIN customers c ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
WHERE c.customer_id IS NULL   -- orphaned foreign keys
```

Run

title: Data Quality
description: Data quality interview questions covering dimensions, validation, Great Expectations and dbt tests, deduplication, distribution drift, and quality ownership.
content:
this as a scheduled check (or a dbt `relationships` test) rather than relying on the database to reject bad writes, since the warehouse itself won't.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dq-22" number={22} question="What techniques do you use to detect duplicate records at scale?" difficulty="hard" topic="Deduplication">
For exact duplicates, hash the row's relevant columns and check for repeated hash values — cheaper than comparing every column pairwise. For duplicates that differ slightly (a retry that changed a timestamp), define a business key (the columns that should uniquely identify a record) and check *that* for uniqueness instead of the whole row. At large scale, a window function is the standard SQL pattern for both detecting and resolving duplicates:

```sql
SELECT *, ROW_NUMBER()

title: Data Quality
description: Data quality interview questions covering dimensions, validation, Great Expectations and dbt tests, deduplication, distribution drift, and quality ownership.
content:
OVER (PARTITION BY business_key ORDER BY updated_at DESC) AS rn
FROM table
QUALIFY rn = 1   -- keep only the most recent version of each key
```
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dq-23" number={23} question="How do you detect distribution drift in a column's values over time?" difficulty="hard" topic="Statistical Checks">
Compare a statistical summary of today's batch against a rolling historical baseline — mean/median/standard deviation for numeric columns, or the distribution of category frequencies for categorical ones — and alert when the difference exceeds a threshold (a fixed percentage, or a statistical distance measure like population stability index for more rigorous setups). This catches problems row-level checks can't: every row can individually be "valid" while the overall sh

title: Data Quality
description: Data quality interview questions covering dimensions, validation, Great Expectations and dbt tests, deduplication, distribution drift, and quality ownership.
content:
ape of the data has still shifted in a way that signals an upstream change.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dq-24" number={24} question="What data quality challenges are unique to streaming pipelines compared to batch?" difficulty="hard" topic="Streaming">
Batch checks run against a complete, stable dataset; streaming checks have to work against data that's still arriving, with no natural "batch is done" moment to validate against. This means checks need to run over rolling windows rather than a fixed dataset, tolerate legitimately late/out-of-order events without false-alarming, and use approximate techniques (sketches for distinct counts, running aggregates) since holding the full stream in memory to validate it isn't an option.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dq-25" number={25} qu

content:
estion="How do you decide between NULL, an empty string, and a sentinel value for missing data?" difficulty="medium" topic="Data Modeling">
Use **NULL** for "value doesn't exist / unknown," reserving it for genuine absence rather than overloading it with multiple meanings. Use an **empty string** only when "known to be empty" is itself meaningful and distinct from "unknown" (a middle name field where you've confirmed the person has none, vs. one you simply haven't collected). Avoid ad-hoc **sentinel values** ("N/A", -1, 9999) in the data itself wherever possible — they're invisible to standard NULL-handling logic (COUNT, aggregates, joins) and silently corrupt results unless every downstream consumer knows to filter them out; if you need a placeholder in a dimension for exactly this reason

content:
, use the "Unknown member" pattern instead.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dq-26" number={26} question="Where in a medallion (bronze/silver/gold) pipeline should quality gates actually enforce checks?" difficulty="medium" topic="Pipeline Design">
Light structural checks (can it be parsed, does it match the expected raw schema) belong at bronze, right on ingestion, so malformed source data is caught immediately rather than propagating. The bulk of validation — not-null, referential integrity, business rules, deduplication — belongs at the bronze-to-silver transition, since silver is meant to be the clean, trusted layer everything else builds on. Gold-layer checks are usually reconciliation-style (do these aggregates tie back to silver correctly) rather than re-validating row-level rules

content:
that should have already been caught upstream.
</QuestionCard>

## Metrics, Ownership & Trust

Beyond individual checks — how you decide how much quality investment a dataset deserves, and who's responsible when it fails.

<QuestionList topic="Metrics, Ownership & Trust" storagePrefix="dq-trust">

<QuestionCard id="dq-27" number={27} question="How do you build a data quality score, and what would it be based on?" difficulty="medium" topic="Metrics">
A simple, defensible approach: weight each quality dimension (completeness, validity, freshness, uniqueness) by how much it matters for that specific dataset, compute a pass rate for each from your existing checks, and combine into a single 0-100 score per table. The value isn't the exact number — it's giving stakeholders a trend line ("this table's score dropped from 98 to 85 last week") that's easier to a

title: Data Quality
description: Data quality interview questions covering dimensions, validation, Great Expectations and dbt tests, deduplication, distribution drift, and quality ownership.
content:
ct on than a wall of individual pass/fail check results.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dq-28" number={28} question="How do you decide how much quality investment a dataset actually needs?" difficulty="medium" topic="Prioritization">
Scale checks to the dataset's actual blast radius: a table feeding an executive dashboard or a financial report justifies deep validation, reconciliation, and tight SLAs; an internal exploratory table a few analysts use occasionally doesn't need the same investment. Treating every table as equally critical is how quality programs burn effort on low-value checks while genuinely important tables stay under-covered — usage and downstream dependency count are the practical signals for where to spend the effort.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dq-29" number=

title: Data Quality
description: Data quality interview questions covering dimensions, validation, Great Expectations and dbt tests, deduplication, distribution drift, and quality ownership.
content:
{29} question="Who should own a data quality failure — the producing team or the consuming team?" difficulty="medium" topic="Ownership">
The producing team owns fixing the *source* of the problem (a broken upstream job, a schema change that wasn't communicated), since they're the only ones who can actually correct it at the root. The consuming team typically owns detecting and surfacing the failure fast (their checks, their dashboards break first) and communicating impact — a data contract is what ties these together in advance, so this isn't negotiated fresh during every incident.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dq-30" number={30} question="How do you build stakeholder trust in data after a high-profile quality incident?" difficulty="medium" topic="Trust">
Be transparent about what hap

title: Data Quality
description: Data quality interview questions covering dimensions, validation, Great Expectations and dbt tests, deduplication, distribution drift, and quality ownership.
content:
pened and why, rather than quietly fixing it — a short incident writeup (what broke, what was affected, what's changing) does more for trust than silence. Follow up with a durable fix (a new check that would have caught it, not just a one-time patch), and make quality *visible* going forward — a quality score, a status page, or a badge on documented tables — so trust is rebuilt on demonstrated reliability over time rather than a single reassurance.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

nership.

## Data Warehousing: Architecture, Schemas & ETL

**A data warehouse is the architectural layer that turns raw, write-optimized operational data into a structure built for fast, reliable analytics — this page covers OLAP/OLTP fundamentals, star and snowflake schema design, ETL, dimensional modeling, and the platform-level trade-offs data engineers are expected to reason through in interviews.**

content:
## Key Concepts

A data warehouse exists to answer one question well: how do you turn scattered, write-optimized operational data into a structure that's fast and reliable to query for analytics? The foundational split is **OLTP vs. OLAP** — OLTP systems (the applications generating your data) are normalized and optimized for many small, concurrent writes; OLAP systems are denormalized and optimized for large, read-heavy aggregations across history. Warehouses exist because running analytical queries directly against an OLTP system either degrades it or gives you an incomplete, historyless answer.

Getting data from source to warehouse is the job of **ETL/ELT** — extract from source systems, transform (clean, conform, apply business rules), and load into the warehouse, or in the ELT varian

title: Data Warehousing
description: Data warehousing interview questions covering OLAP vs OLTP, star/snowflake schemas, ETL, dimensional modeling, and warehouse architecture for data engineers.
content:
t, load raw and transform inside the warehouse using its own compute. Once data lands, **dimensional modeling** — star and snowflake schemas, fact/dimension tables, slowly changing dimensions — is the standard way warehouses organize data for query performance and business usability; see the [Data Modeling](/level-2-core-concepts/data-modeling/) page for schema-design specifics, since this page stays at the platform and architecture layer around it.

The landscape has also evolved beyond a single "data warehouse" box: **data lakes** store raw, schema-on-read data cheaply at scale, and **lakehouses** try to combine lake economics with warehouse-style transactions and performance. Vendor-specific implementation details for Snowflake, BigQuery, Redshift, and Databricks live on their own pages

The following are the stages of data warehousing:

- **Offline Data Warehouse** — in this stage, data warehouses are updated from data in the OS, and the data warehouse's data is stored in a structure designed for facilitating reports.
- **Real-time Data Warehouse** — the data warehouse is updated whenever the OS performs a transaction.
- **Integrated Data Warehouse** — the data warehouse is updated by the OS at the time of performing a transaction; transactions are then generated and passed back into the operational systems.

There are two common methods for loading data into dimension tables:

- **Conventional load (slower)** — every constraint and key is validated against the incoming data *before* it is loaded, so data integrity is guaranteed throughout the load.
- **Direct load (faster)** — all constraints and keys are disabled before loading. Once loaded, the data is validated against the constraints; any rows found invalid are excluded from indexing and skipped in downstream processing.

Database normalization is a data design and organization process applied to data structures based on rules that help build relational databases. In relational database design, the process of organizing data to minimize redundancy. Normalization usually involves dividing a database into two or more tables and defining relationships between the tables. The objective is to isolate data so that additions, deletions, and modifications of a field can be made in just one table and then propagated through the rest of the database via the defined relationships

- 1NF: Eliminate Repeating Groups Make a separate table for each set of related attributes, and give each table a primary key. Each field contains at most one value from its attribute domain.
- 2NF: Eliminate Redundant Data If an attribute depends on only part of a multi-valued key, remove it to a separate table.
- 3NF: Eliminate Columns Not Dependent On Key If attributes do not contribute to a description of the key, remove them to a separate table. All attributes must be directly dependent on the primary key.
- BCNF: Boyce-Codd Normal Form If there are non-trivial dependencies between candidate key attributes, separate them out into di

- 5NF: Isolate Semantically Related Multiple Relationships There may be practical constrains on information that justify separating logically related many-to-many relationships.
- ONF: Optimal Normal Form A model limited to only simple (elemental) facts, as expressed in Object Role Model notation.
- DKNF: Domain-Key Normal Form A model free from all modification anomalies. Remember, these normalization guidelines are cumulative. For a database to be in 3NF, it must first fulfill all the criteria of a 2NF and 1NF database.

ty="medium" topic="DBMS Internals">
The ROWID is a unique database-wide physical address for every row on every table. Once assigned (when the row is first inserted into the database), it never changes until the row is deleted or the table is dropped.
The ROWID consists of the following three components, the combination of which uniquely identifies the physical storage location of the row.
Oracle database file number, which contains the block with the rows
Oracle block address, which contains the row
The row within the block (because each block can hold many rows)
The ROWID is used internally in indexes as a quick means of retrieving rows with a particular key value. Application developers also use it in SQL statements as a quick way to access a row once they know the ROWID.

There are three levels of abstraction:

- **View level** — the highest level of abstraction, describes only part of the entire database.

Logical Data Independence: Modification in logical level should affect the view level.

Triggers are used to maintain the referential integrity of data by changing the data in a systematic fashion. A trigger cannot be called or executed; the DBMS automatically fires the trigger as a result of a data modification to the associated table. Triggers can be viewed as similar to stored procedures in that both consist of procedural logic that is stored at the database level. Stored procedures, however, are not event-drive and are not attached to a specific table as triggers are. Stored procedures are explicitly executed by invoking a CALL to the procedure while triggers are implicitly executed. In addition, triggers can also execute stored procedures.
</QuestionCard>

## Common Interview Scenarios

- **"Design a data warehouse for a retail company's sales reporting."** Start by nailing down the source systems and grain, then walk through staging, a star schema for the sales fact table (product, store, date, promotion dimensions), and how OLTP data gets denormalized for reporting performance.
- **"Our OLAP queries are slow — where do you start?"** Probe fact table grain, aggregation/rollup strategy, indexing choice (bitmap vs. B-tree), and whether the underlying MOLAP/ROLAP/HOLAP trade-offs actually fit the data volume and query patterns.
- **"How would you choose between a data warehouse, a data lake, and a lakehouse for a new analytics platform?"** Talk through schema-on-write vs. schema-on-read, cost profile, data variety, and the query patterns each

is actually good at.
- **"A dimension needs to track history — how do you model that, and how does it flow through the ETL?"** Walk through SCD Type 2 (or a hybrid approach) plus the load logic — surrogate keys, effective-dating, detecting changes — that keeps it correct.
- **"How would you migrate an on-prem warehouse to the cloud without breaking downstream BI reports?"** Discuss re-architecting ETL/ELT, keeping schema parity during the transition, and a reconciliation/validation strategy before cutting reports over.

This section covers the core concepts and disciplines that define modern data engineering. These topics are essential for building reliable, scalable data systems.

content:
## Topics Covered

- **Data Modeling**: Designing effective data models with star schemas, dimension tables, and slowly changing dimensions
- **Data Warehousing**: Architecture and design patterns for building data warehouses and marts
- **Data Quality**: Ensuring data reliability through validation, testing, and monitoring
- **Data Governance**: Managing data responsibly with policies, catalogs, and access controls

A strong understanding of these concepts is necessary for designing and managing enterprise data systems.

## Reverse ETL: Getting Data Out of the Warehouse and Back Into the Business

**The warehouse is where all your data ends up, and for years that was also where it stopped — visible on a dashboard nobody acts on. Reverse ETL closes that loop by syncing modelled data back into the operational tools people actually work in: the CRM, the support desk, the ad platform. It's a small category with a specific set of hard problems — API rate limits, idempotent upserts against systems you don't control, and deciding who owns a field once two systems both write to it.**

title: Reverse ETL
description: Reverse ETL interview questions covering how it differs from ETL, operational analytics use cases, tools like Hightouch, Census and Segment, data interoperability, and the sync, idempotency and API rate-limit problems it creates.
content:
## Key Concepts

Reverse ETL moves data **from the warehouse into operational systems** — the opposite direction to the pipelines that filled it. The category exists because the warehouse became the only place where data from every source is joined, modelled and agreed upon, which makes it the natural source of truth for things like customer lifetime value or churn risk. Those calculations are useless sitting in a table if the salesperson can't see them in Salesforce.

The term for what this enables is **operational analytics**: putting analytical output in front of the person or system making a decision, in the tool they already use, rather than expecting them to open a dashboard.

The engineering problems are genuinely different from normal ETL. Destinations are **third-party APIs** with

title: Reverse ETL
description: Reverse ETL interview questions covering how it differs from ETL, operational analytics use cases, tools like Hightouch, Census and Segment, data interoperability, and the sync, idempotency and API rate-limit problems it creates.
content:
rate limits, bespoke object models and their own validation — not a warehouse you control. Writes must be **idempotent upserts** keyed on an external identifier, since retries are certain. And because a sync **writes into a system of record**, a bug doesn't produce a wrong dashboard, it produces wrong data in front of customers, which raises the stakes on testing and rollback considerably.

content:
## ETL vs Reverse ETL

<QuestionList topic="ETL vs Reverse ETL" storagePrefix="reverse-etl-comparison">

<QuestionCard id="retl-cmp-01" number={1} question="What is reverse ETL, and how does it differ from ETL?" difficulty="easy" topic="Fundamentals">
**ETL/ELT** moves data **into** the warehouse: many operational sources → one analytical store, so it can be joined, modelled and analysed.

**Reverse ETL** moves modelled data **out of** the warehouse into operational tools — CRM, marketing automation, support desk, ad platforms — so it can be acted on.

The differences that matter technically:

| | ETL | Reverse ETL |
|---|---|---|
| Direction | sources → warehouse | warehouse → SaaS tools |
| Destination | one you control | third-party APIs |
| Volume | large, bulk | small, incremental del

title: Reverse ETL
description: Reverse ETL interview questions covering how it differs from ETL, operational analytics use cases, tools like Hightouch, Census and Segment, data interoperability, and the sync, idempotency and API rate-limit problems it creates.
content:
tas |
| Constraint | source impact | **API rate limits** |
| Write shape | append or partition overwrite | **upsert by external key** |
| Blast radius | a wrong dashboard | wrong data in a customer-facing system |

That last row is the one worth emphasising: reverse ETL writes into systems people and customers see directly.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="retl-cmp-02" number={2} question="Why did reverse ETL emerge as a category?" difficulty="medium" topic="Fundamentals">
Three things converged.

**The warehouse became the source of truth.** Cheap cloud storage and ELT meant every source landed in one place, so the warehouse became the only system with a complete, joined view of a customer. The best definition of "lifetime value" now lives there, not in any single application.

**Dashbo

title: Reverse ETL
description: Reverse ETL interview questions covering how it differs from ETL, operational analytics use cases, tools like Hightouch, Census and Segment, data interoperability, and the sync, idempotency and API rate-limit problems it creates.
content:
ards proved insufficient.** Analytical output that requires someone to open a BI tool and interpret it mostly doesn't change behaviour. The value is realised when the number appears in the workflow — next to the customer record the sales rep is already looking at.

**Point-to-point integrations didn't scale.** Before this, syncing a computed field into Salesforce meant a bespoke script per destination, each with its own auth, pagination and error handling. As tool counts grew, N sources × M destinations became unmaintainable.

Reverse ETL tools productised the M side: model once in the warehouse, sync anywhere.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="retl-cmp-03" number={3} question="How does reverse ETL relate to CDP and iPaaS?" difficulty="medium" topic="Fundamentals">
They overlap, and inter

title: Reverse ETL
description: Reverse ETL interview questions covering how it differs from ETL, operational analytics use cases, tools like Hightouch, Census and Segment, data interoperability, and the sync, idempotency and API rate-limit problems it creates.
content:
viewers sometimes probe whether you can distinguish them.

- **CDP (Customer Data Platform)** — Segment, mParticle. Collects customer events, builds unified profiles in **its own store**, and activates them to destinations. It owns the data model.
- **Reverse ETL** — Hightouch, Census. The **warehouse is the source of truth**; the tool only syncs from it. No separate store, no duplicated modelling.
- **iPaaS** — Workato, Zapier, MuleSoft. General app-to-app integration and workflow automation, not warehouse-centric and not built for bulk data sync.

The distinction that matters: a CDP maintains its own copy and its own definition of a customer; reverse ETL deliberately doesn't, so there's **one definition** of every metric, maintained in dbt alongside everything else.

That's why the indus

content:
try moved toward the "**composable CDP**" — warehouse plus reverse ETL, rather than a separate platform holding a second copy of the truth.

## Use Cases

<QuestionList topic="Use Cases" storagePrefix="reverse-etl-use-cases">

<QuestionCard id="retl-uc-01" number={1} question="What are the main reverse ETL use cases?" difficulty="easy" topic="Use Cases">
- **Sales enablement** — push lead scores, product usage, health scores and lifetime value into Salesforce or HubSpot, so reps prioritise using real signals rather than intuition.
- **Marketing activation** — sync audience segments to ad platforms and email tools, so campaigns target warehouse-defined cohorts rather than a marketer's approximation.
- **Customer support** — surface account tier, usage and open issues in Zendesk or Intercom, so agents have context without switching systems.
- **Product** — feed computed attributes back into the application for personalisation or

title: Reverse ETL
description: Reverse ETL interview questions covering how it differs from ETL, operational analytics use cases, tools like Hightouch, Census and Segment, data interoperability, and the sync, idempotency and API rate-limit problems it creates.
content:
feature gating.
- **Finance and ops** — push usage-based billing figures into the billing system.
- **Alerting** — notify Slack when an account's health score drops.

The common thread: **the decision-maker already lives in a specific tool**, and the analytical output needs to reach them there.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="retl-uc-02" number={2} question="When is reverse ETL the wrong solution?" difficulty="medium" topic="Use Cases">
- **When latency needs are sub-minute.** Reverse ETL syncs on a schedule — typically every 15 to 60 minutes. Real-time personalisation needs an event stream or a direct API, not a warehouse sync.
- **When the destination should own the data.** Syncing a field the destination system also writes creates a conflict you must resolve; better to leave ownershi

title: Reverse ETL
description: Reverse ETL interview questions covering how it differs from ETL, operational analytics use cases, tools like Hightouch, Census and Segment, data interoperability, and the sync, idempotency and API rate-limit problems it creates.
content:
p where it belongs.
- **When it's a one-off.** A single export doesn't justify a tool.
- **When the volume is huge.** Millions of records against a rate-limited API will take days; a bulk import or a direct database connection is more appropriate.
- **When the data isn't trustworthy yet.** Reverse ETL amplifies quality problems — a wrong dashboard is embarrassing, a wrong email to 50,000 customers is an incident.

That last point is the strongest answer: **don't activate data you don't yet trust.** Quality gates should come before the sync, not after.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="retl-uc-03" number={3} question="What is operational analytics?" difficulty="medium" topic="Use Cases">
Using analytical data to drive **operational action**, rather than to inform a periodic human review.

title: Reverse ETL
description: Reverse ETL interview questions covering how it differs from ETL, operational analytics use cases, tools like Hightouch, Census and Segment, data interoperability, and the sync, idempotency and API rate-limit problems it creates.
content:
The contrast: traditional analytics answers "how did we do last quarter" for a person reading a report. Operational analytics answers "which accounts should this rep call today" and puts the answer in the rep's queue.

Characteristics: the consumer is often a **system or a workflow** rather than an analyst; freshness matters because the data drives an action now; and the output is a **field in a tool**, not a chart.

Why it matters for a data engineer: it changes the reliability requirements. A dashboard that's stale for a day is annoying. A sync feeding a customer-facing workflow that's stale or wrong for a day causes real damage — so operational data products need monitoring, alerting and rollback plans much closer to application software than to reporting.
</QuestionCard>

content:
## Tools & Implementation

<QuestionList topic="Tools & Implementation" storagePrefix="reverse-etl-tools">

<QuestionCard id="retl-tool-01" number={1} question="What do Hightouch, Census and Segment each do?" difficulty="medium" topic="Tools">
- **Hightouch** — warehouse-native reverse ETL. Define a model in SQL or dbt, map columns to destination fields, and sync to 200+ destinations. Adds audience building for marketers and identity resolution.
- **Census** — the same category and shape, with strong dbt integration and a focus on syncing dbt models directly.
- **Segment** — historically a **CDP**: an SDK collects events client-side, builds profiles in Segment's own store, and fans them out to destinations. It has added warehouse-sourced sync, blurring the line.

The architectural distinct

title: Reverse ETL
description: Reverse ETL interview questions covering how it differs from ETL, operational analytics use cases, tools like Hightouch, Census and Segment, data interoperability, and the sync, idempotency and API rate-limit problems it creates.
content:
ion to state: Hightouch and Census treat the **warehouse as the source of truth** and hold no copy. Segment's original model owns the data and its own definition of a customer.

Beyond the vendors, the alternatives are **building it yourself** (a scheduled job calling destination APIs) or Airbyte's reverse-ETL connectors — both viable when you have one or two destinations and don't want another SaaS bill.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="retl-tool-02" number={2} question="How would you build reverse ETL yourself, and what would you need to handle?" difficulty="hard" topic="Implementation">
The pipeline itself is a scheduled job: query the warehouse for a model, diff against what was last sent, and call the destination's API for changed records.

What makes it harder than it sounds:

- **

title: Reverse ETL
description: Reverse ETL interview questions covering how it differs from ETL, operational analytics use cases, tools like Hightouch, Census and Segment, data interoperability, and the sync, idempotency and API rate-limit problems it creates.
content:
Change detection.** Sending everything every run wastes API quota and can trigger spurious downstream notifications. You need a state table of what was last synced per record, or a hash comparison.
- **Idempotent upserts** keyed on an **external ID** the destination understands, so retries don't create duplicate contacts.
- **Rate limits** — respect documented limits, honour `Retry-After` on 429s, and back off with jitter. This is the dominant constraint.
- **Batching** — most APIs accept bulk operations; per-record calls will not finish.
- **Partial failure** — 900 of 1,000 records succeed. You need per-record error capture, not a failed job.
- **Field mapping and type coercion** to the destination's model, including its validation rules.
- **Observability** — records synced, failed and r

title: Reverse ETL
description: Reverse ETL interview questions covering how it differs from ETL, operational analytics use cases, tools like Hightouch, Census and Segment, data interoperability, and the sync, idempotency and API rate-limit problems it creates.
content:
ejected, per destination.

Roughly 80% of the work is error handling and rate limiting, which is exactly why the tools exist.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="retl-tool-03" number={3} question="How do you make a reverse ETL sync safe to re-run?" difficulty="hard" topic="Implementation">
Everything hinges on **upsert by a stable external key**.

- Choose a key the destination system can match on — email, an external ID, or the CRM's own record ID stored back in the warehouse. Never rely on positional or generated identifiers.
- Use the destination's **upsert endpoint** where one exists, so an existing record is updated rather than duplicated.
- **Track sync state** — a table of record key, last-synced hash and timestamp — so a re-run sends only genuine changes.
- **Make the transformation

title: Reverse ETL
description: Reverse ETL interview questions covering how it differs from ETL, operational analytics use cases, tools like Hightouch, Census and Segment, data interoperability, and the sync, idempotency and API rate-limit problems it creates.
content:
deterministic**, so the same warehouse state always produces the same payload.
- **Guard against mass updates** — a threshold that halts the sync if it would change more than N% of records, since that usually means an upstream bug rather than a genuine change.

That last control is the one experienced practitioners add after being burned: a model change that suddenly marks every account as churn-risk will happily propagate to 50,000 customer records unless something stops it.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="retl-tool-04" number={4} question="How do you test and monitor a reverse ETL pipeline?" difficulty="medium" topic="Implementation">
Because the destination is a live business system, the testing story matters more than for a normal pipeline.

- **Test the model, not just the sync**

title: Reverse ETL
description: Reverse ETL interview questions covering how it differs from ETL, operational analytics use cases, tools like Hightouch, Census and Segment, data interoperability, and the sync, idempotency and API rate-limit problems it creates.
content:
— dbt tests on the source model catch bad data before it leaves the warehouse. This is the highest-value gate.
- **Use a sandbox destination** — most SaaS tools offer one. Sync there in CI.
- **Dry-run mode** showing what would change, reviewed before the first production run.
- **Start with a small segment** — sync 100 records, verify in the destination, then widen.
- **Monitor** rows synced, rejected and errored, plus sync duration and freshness. Alert on rejection-rate spikes.
- **Keep a rollback path** — the previous value of each field, so a bad sync can be reversed rather than manually repaired.

The rollback point is worth stating explicitly: unlike a warehouse table, you usually **cannot restore a third-party system from a snapshot**, so the ability to reverse a sync has to be desi

</QuestionCard>

content:
## Data Interoperability

<QuestionList topic="Data Interoperability" storagePrefix="reverse-etl-interoperability">

<QuestionCard id="retl-int-01" number={1} question="What is data interoperability, and why is it hard?" difficulty="medium" topic="Interoperability">
The ability of systems to exchange data and interpret it **consistently** — not just move bytes, but agree on what they mean.

Why it's hard in practice:
- **Schema mismatch** — the warehouse has `customer_id`, Salesforce has `AccountId`, Zendesk has `organization_id`, and none of them are the same key.
- **Semantic mismatch** — "active customer" means something different in each system, so a synced boolean carries a definition the destination doesn't share.
- **Format and type differences** — date formats, timezone assumptions

title: Reverse ETL
description: Reverse ETL interview questions covering how it differs from ETL, operational analytics use cases, tools like Hightouch, Census and Segment, data interoperability, and the sync, idempotency and API rate-limit problems it creates.
content:
, precision, enumerations with different allowed values.
- **Identity resolution** — deciding that a record here and a record there are the same entity, when the only shared field is an email that may have changed.
- **Ownership ambiguity** — once two systems write the same field, which wins?

The mitigations are **conformed dimensions and a shared identity spine** in the warehouse, plus explicit documented mappings per destination — treating the mapping as an artefact to review, not a config someone set once.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="retl-int-02" number={2} question="How do you handle conflicts when two systems write the same field?" difficulty="hard" topic="Interoperability">
First, try to avoid it: **define a single owner per field**. The warehouse owns computed attributes (li

title: Reverse ETL
description: Reverse ETL interview questions covering how it differs from ETL, operational analytics use cases, tools like Hightouch, Census and Segment, data interoperability, and the sync, idempotency and API rate-limit problems it creates.
content:
fetime value, churn score, segment); the CRM owns what sales reps type (notes, stage, next action). Documented ownership eliminates most conflicts before they exist.

When a field genuinely must be bidirectional:
- **Last-write-wins with a timestamp** — simple, and silently loses one side's change.
- **Source-of-truth precedence** — one system always wins for that field, with the other's write discarded and logged.
- **Field-level merge rules** — different owners for different fields on the same object, which is usually the practical answer.
- **Conflict surfacing** — flag rather than resolve, and let a human decide. Appropriate for high-value records.

The failure mode to describe: an unmanaged bidirectional sync creates a **loop**, where each system's write triggers the other's, and reco

title: Reverse ETL
description: Reverse ETL interview questions covering how it differs from ETL, operational analytics use cases, tools like Hightouch, Census and Segment, data interoperability, and the sync, idempotency and API rate-limit problems it creates.
content:
rds churn indefinitely. Loop detection or a strict one-way flow per field prevents it, and it's the thing to raise unprompted.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="retl-int-03" number={3} question="What role do standards and identifiers play?" difficulty="medium" topic="Interoperability">
Interoperability gets much easier when systems agree on **identifiers and formats** up front rather than mapping after the fact.

- **A canonical entity ID** minted in the warehouse and written back into every destination as an external ID field. This is the single most valuable thing you can do — it turns fuzzy matching into an exact join.
- **Standard formats** — ISO 8601 timestamps in UTC, ISO country and currency codes, E.164 phone numbers. Sounds trivial; prevents a large class of silent mismatch.
- **

title: Reverse ETL
description: Reverse ETL interview questions covering how it differs from ETL, operational analytics use cases, tools like Hightouch, Census and Segment, data interoperability, and the sync, idempotency and API rate-limit problems it creates.
content:
Schema definitions** — Avro, Protobuf or JSON Schema as contracts, with a registry enforcing compatibility.
- **Open table formats** (Iceberg, Delta) so multiple engines read the same data without export.
- **Event specifications** where a shared taxonomy of event names and properties is agreed across producers.

The theme is the same as data contracts: **agree the interface explicitly**, rather than each consumer reverse-engineering the producer's intent and breaking when it changes.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

## Common Interview Scenarios

**"Sales wants lead scores in Salesforce. How do you build it?"** — model the score in dbt with tests, sync with Hightouch or Census keyed on an external ID, upsert not insert, start with a small segment, and add a threshold that halts the sync if it would change an implausible proportion of records.

**"Your sync created duplicate contacts in the CRM."** — inserting rather than upserting, or matching on an unstable key. Fix with the destination's upsert endpoint keyed on a stable external ID written back from the warehouse.

**"How do you avoid hitting the destination's API rate limit?"** — batch operations rather than per-record calls, sync only genuine changes via state tracking, honour `Retry-After`, back off with jitter, and schedule large syncs outside

description: Reverse ETL interview questions covering how it differs from ETL, operational analytics use cases, tools like Hightouch, Census and Segment, data interoperability, and the sync, idempotency and API rate-limit problems it creates.
content:
peak windows.

**"Marketing emailed the wrong segment because of a bad sync."** — this is why quality gates belong before activation, not after. dbt tests on the model, a dry run, a staged rollout, a mass-change threshold, and a documented rollback path.

## Skills and Responsibilities: What a Data Engineer Actually Owns

**A data engineer's skill set splits into two halves — the technical toolkit (SQL, a general-purpose language, cloud platforms, data modeling, distributed systems) and the operational ownership (infrastructure, pipelines, data quality, performance) that toolkit is used to deliver — and interviewers probe both, not just the first.**

content:
## Key Concepts

The technical skill set breaks into a few layers: **query and transformation languages** (SQL is non-negotiable, Python is the default scripting language, Java/Scala matter when working directly with JVM-based engines like Spark or Kafka), **cloud platform fluency** (AWS, GCP, or Azure — whichever the org runs on, since modern data infrastructure is rarely on-prem anymore), and **systems knowledge** (data modeling for structuring data well, distributed systems fundamentals like partitioning and consistency for reasoning about scale and failure). Responsibility, meanwhile, isn't static — it scales with seniority. A junior data engineer typically owns well-scoped pipeline tasks inside an existing architecture; a senior or staff engineer owns architectural decisions, cross-te

am data contracts, and the operational health (on-call, incident response) of the platforms other teams depend on. Soft skills — communicating trade-offs to non-technical stakeholders, writing documentation, negotiating data contracts with upstream/downstream teams — are what separates someone who can write a pipeline from someone who can be trusted to own one.

<QuestionCard id="sar-01" number={1} question="What are the core technical skill areas a data engineer needs?" difficulty="easy" topic="Skills">
Four areas cover most of the job: **query/transformation languages** (SQL always, Python almost always), **a general-purpose or JVM language** for building and operating pipeline code, **cloud platform skills** (storage, compute, managed data services), and **systems knowledge** — data modeling and distributed systems fundamentals for reasoning about scale, consistency, and failure modes.

A data engineer who can't write efficient SQL can't reason about query plans, can't debug slow transformations, and can't communicate with analysts and scientists in the language they already use.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="sar-03" number={3} question="Why is Python usually the default language, and when does that default change?" difficulty="easy" topic="Skills">

<QuestionCard id="sar-04" number={4} question="What cloud platform skills matter, and why can't they be treated as optional?" difficulty="medium" topic="Skills">

Partitioning (splitting data/work across nodes), replication, consistency models, and the CAP theorem's trade-offs matter because most data infrastructure at any real scale is a distributed system. ## Key Concepts

At its core, data engineering is about **building and maintaining data pipelines** — systems that move data from source systems through transformation layers so it's reliably available for analysis, reporting, and machine learning. That work spans four recurring responsibilities: **data infrastructure** (reliable, scalable storage and processing systems), **pipeline architecture** (designing the ETL/ELT workflows that move data), **data quality** (ensuring accuracy and consistency), and **performance optimization** (keeping queries and transformations efficient as volume grows). The role leans on a specific skill set — SQL, Python, cloud platforms, data modeling, and system design — and the work itself follows a repeatable lifecycle: data is generated, ingested, processed,

title: Hadoop
description: Interview questions on Hadoop covering HDFS architecture, MapReduce, NameNode/DataNode roles, replication, rack awareness, and cluster administration.
content:
## Hadoop: Distributed Processing Framework

**Hadoop is a framework for storing and processing very large datasets across clusters of commodity hardware — HDFS handles distributed storage and MapReduce/YARN handle distributed computation, with fault tolerance built in through replication rather than expensive hardware.**

title: Hadoop
description: Interview questions on Hadoop covering HDFS architecture, MapReduce, NameNode/DataNode roles, replication, rack awareness, and cluster administration.
content:
## Table of Contents
- [Key Concepts](#key-concepts)
- [Interview Questions](#interview-questions)
- [Common Interview Scenarios](#common-interview-scenarios)
- [Further Reading](#further-reading)

---

title: Hadoop
description: Interview questions on Hadoop covering HDFS architecture, MapReduce, NameNode/DataNode roles, replication, rack awareness, and cluster administration.
content:
## Key Concepts

Hadoop is built around two ideas: distribute the data, and move the computation to where the data already lives rather than moving data to the computation. **HDFS** breaks files into fixed-size blocks (64MB or 128MB) and replicates each block — three copies by default — across **DataNodes**, using rack-aware placement (two replicas on one rack, a third on a different rack) so that a single node or rack failure never loses data. A single **NameNode** holds all filesystem metadata (the directory tree and block locations) in memory; it never stores actual file data. DataNodes report their health back to the NameNode via periodic **heartbeats** and **block reports**, and a **Secondary/Checkpoint NameNode** periodically merges the edit log into the filesystem image so restarts

title: Hadoop
description: Interview questions on Hadoop covering HDFS architecture, MapReduce, NameNode/DataNode roles, replication, rack awareness, and cluster administration.
content:
stay fast — but it is *not* a hot standby, which made the NameNode a single point of failure in Hadoop 1.

**MapReduce** processes data in phases: an optional input split, a map phase (filter/transform), an optional combiner (local pre-aggregation to cut network traffic), a shuffle-and-sort phase (group by key), and a reduce phase (aggregate). In Hadoop 1 this was coordinated by a single **JobTracker** and per-node **TaskTrackers**; YARN later generalized resource management beyond just MapReduce. Across almost every question below, the recurring themes are: how fault tolerance is achieved through replication and heartbeats, why data locality drives performance, and where the classic single points of failure sit.
