### DDL, Tables, Views & Partitioning

Creating, altering, and managing tables, views, partitions, and buckets.

<QuestionList topic="DDL, Tables, Views & Partitioning" storagePrefix="hive-ddl">

<QuestionCard id="hive-ddl-01" number={23} question="How do you change the data type of a column in Hive?" difficulty="medium" topic="DDL">
Use the `ALTER TABLE ... REPLACE COLUMNS` statement:

```sql
ALTER TABLE tableName REPLACE COLUMNS (columnName newDataType);
```
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="hive-ddl-02" number={24} question="Can a table be renamed in Hive, and how would you rename one without using ALTER?" difficulty="medium" topic="DDL">
Yes, a table can be renamed directly:

```sql
ALTER TABLE table_name RENAME TO new_name;
```

To rename a table **without** `ALTER`, export it and re

title: Hive
description: Apache Hive interview questions covering HiveQL, the metastore, partitioning and bucketing, file formats, joins, and performance optimization for data engineers.
content:
-import it under a new name:

```sql
EXPORT TABLE tableName TO 'TEMP_LOCATION';
IMPORT TABLE newTableName FROM 'TEMP_LOCATION';
```
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="hive-ddl-03" number={25} question="What is the use of the IF EXISTS clause in Hive statements, including when dropping a table?" difficulty="easy" topic="DDL">
`IF EXISTS` is used with statements like `DROP TABLE` to avoid an error when the target doesn't actually exist. Without it, `DROP TABLE tableName` throws an error if the table isn't there; with `DROP TABLE IF EXISTS tableName`, the statement succeeds silently even if the table was never created — useful when a script can't be sure the table exists.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="hive-ddl-04" number={26} question="What is the use of PURGE in a Hive DROP statement?"

title: Hive
description: Apache Hive interview questions covering HiveQL, the metastore, partitioning and bucketing, file formats, joins, and performance optimization for data engineers.
content:
difficulty="medium" topic="DDL">
`PURGE` is used when you're certain you want to permanently delete a table's data:

```sql
DROP TABLE tableName PURGE;
```

With `PURGE`, the data skips the trash folder entirely, so it can't be recovered if the `DROP` turns out to have been accidental.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="hive-ddl-05" number={27} question="Can we use the same name for a TABLE and a VIEW in Hive?" difficulty="easy" topic="Views">
No. A view's name must be unique across all tables and views in the same database, so you can't reuse a table name for a view (or vice versa).
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="hive-ddl-06" number={28} question="Can we load data into a VIEW in Hive?" difficulty="easy" topic="Views">
No — this is a common trick question. A view can never be the targe

content:
t of an `INSERT` or `LOAD` statement in Hive; data can only be loaded into an actual table.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="hive-ddl-07" number={29} question="What is bucketing in Hive?" difficulty="medium" topic="Bucketing">
Bucketing divides a dataset into a fixed, manageable number of parts based on the hash of a column — conceptually similar to hashing. Unlike partitioning, the number of buckets stays fixed regardless of how much the underlying data grows, and bucketing also enables efficient map-side joins.

For example, with `date` as a first-level partition and `user_id` as a second-level partition, millions of distinct `user_id` values would create millions of tiny partitions/files. Bucketing `user_id` instead uses a hash function to distribute users across a manageable, fixed n

title: Hive
description: Apache Hive interview questions covering HiveQL, the metastore, partitioning and bucketing, file formats, joins, and performance optimization for data engineers.
content:
umber of buckets rather than creating a new partition per user.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="hive-ddl-08" number={30} question="What is the use of the CLUSTERED BY clause during table creation in Hive?" difficulty="medium" topic="Bucketing">
`CLUSTERED BY` is Hive's mechanism for bucketing a table, and behaves like combining `DISTRIBUTE BY` and `SORT BY`: it first distributes rows across a set of reducers using a hash function, then sorts the data within each. It must be specified at table creation time, but its benefit shows up later, in more efficient querying.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="hive-ddl-09" number={31} question="What is a skewed table in Hive?" difficulty="hard" topic="Performance">
A skewed table is a table where some values in a column occur far more often than

title: Hive
description: Apache Hive interview questions covering HiveQL, the metastore, partitioning and bucketing, file formats, joins, and performance optimization for data engineers.
content:
others, producing a skewed distribution. Declaring a table `SKEWED` at creation time tells Hive to write the skewed values into separate files from the remaining values:

```sql
CREATE TABLE tableName (column1 STRING, column2 STRING)
SKEWED BY (column1) ON (value1);
```

This isolation gives better query performance against tables that would otherwise have a few very "hot" values dominating processing time.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="hive-ddl-10" number={32} question="What is a managed table in Hive?" difficulty="medium" topic="Tables">
A managed table is one whose files, metadata, and statistics are all controlled by Hive's internal processes — this is the default table type Hive creates. Dropping a managed table (or one of its partitions) deletes both its metadata and its underly

title: Hive
description: Apache Hive interview questions covering HiveQL, the metastore, partitioning and bucketing, file formats, joins, and performance optimization for data engineers.
content:
ing data. Managed tables are the right choice when you want Hive to own the table's full lifecycle, including for temporary tables. Running `DESCRIBE FORMATTED tableName` shows whether a table is `MANAGED_TABLE` or `EXTERNAL_TABLE`.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="hive-ddl-11" number={33} question="What are the different types of tables available in Hive?" difficulty="medium" topic="Tables">
There are two types:

- **Managed table** — both the data and the schema are under Hive's control; dropping the table deletes both.
- **External table** — only the schema is under Hive's control; the data lives independently, and dropping the table leaves the underlying files untouched.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="hive-ddl-12" number={34} question="How does the OVERWRITE clause work in a Hive

description: Apache Hive interview questions covering HiveQL, the metastore, partitioning and bucketing, file formats, joins, and performance optimization for data engineers.
content:
CREATE TABLE / LOAD statement, and what happens if it's omitted?" difficulty="medium" topic="DDL">
`OVERWRITE` deletes the existing data in the target and replaces it with the new data being written — as the name suggests, it overwrites rather than appends.

If `OVERWRITE` is **omitted** when loading data: new incoming files are simply added to the target directory, and any existing file whose name matches an incoming file is overwritten; files whose names don't match any incoming file are left alone. Adding `OVERWRITE` instead deletes all existing data in the directory before writing the new data.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="hive-ddl-13" number={35} question="How do you prevent data from being dropped or queried from a partition in Hive?" difficulty="hard" topic="Partitioning">

`ALTER TABLE table_name ENABLE NO_DROP` — prevents the partition from being dropped.
- `ALTER TABLE table_name ENABLE OFFLINE` — prevents the partition from being queried (its metadata is still accessible while offline).
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="hive-ddl-14" number={36} question="What is the use of TOUCH in an ALTER statement?" difficulty="medium" topic="Partitioning">
`TOUCH` reads a partition's metadata and writes it back, which updates the partition's last-accessed time. It also triggers any POST and PRE hooks configured on that table partition. It can't be used to create a table or partition that doesn't already exist.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="hive-ddl-15" number={37} question="How do you check if a particular partition exists?" difficulty="medium" topic="Partitioni

```sql

```
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="hive-ddl-16" number={38} question="When you point a partition of a Hive table to a new directory, what happens to the data?" difficulty="medium" topic="Partitioning">
The data itself stays in its old location — repointing the partition only updates the metastore's pointer to a new directory. Moving the actual data has to be done manually.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="hive-ddl-17" number={39} question="Write a query to insert a new column new_col of type INT into a Hive table at a position before an existing column x_col." difficulty="medium" topic="DDL">
```sql
ALTER TABLE table_name CHANGE COLUMN new_col new_col INT BEFORE x_col;
```
</QuestionCard>

content:
onCard id="hive-ddl-18" number={40} question="What are the pros and cons of archiving a partition in Hive, and does it save space in HDFS?" difficulty="hard" topic="Partitioning">
A partition can be archived to reduce the number of files Hive is managing for it.

- **Advantage** — fewer files means less metadata for the NameNode to track, which helps NameNode scalability. Archived partitions can still be queried.
- **Disadvantage** — queries against an archived partition become slower and less efficient.
- **Space savings** — archiving does **not** save storage space in HDFS. It only reduces the number of files; the underlying data volume is unchanged.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="hive-ddl-19" number={41} question="What types of costs are associated with creating an index in Hive tab

An index consumes additional storage space, and there's a processing cost incurred while building and maintaining the sorted index structure over the indexed column's values.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="hive-ddl-20" number={42} question="How do you specify the table creator's name when creating a table in Hive?" difficulty="easy" topic="DDL">
Use the `TBLPROPERTIES` clause:

```sql
TBLPROPERTIES ('creator' = 'Joan')
```
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="hive-ddl-21" number={43} question="How can you delete a database property (DBPROPERTY) in Hive?" difficulty="medium" topic="DDL">
You can't. Hive provides no way to delete a DBPROPERTY once it's set.
</QuestionCard>

### HiveQL Queries, Functions & Joins

Query syntax, string/table-generating functions, and join behavior.

<QuestionList topic="HiveQL Queries, Functions & Joins" storagePrefix="hive-query">

<QuestionCard id="hive-query-01" number={44} question="What is the difference between SORT BY and ORDER BY in Hive?" difficulty="medium" topic="Query Syntax">
- **`SORT BY`** — sorts data within each reducer; multiple reducers can be used, so the result is only locally sorted per reducer, not globally.
- **`ORDER BY`** — sorts all data through a single reducer, guaranteeing total (global) order in the output, at the cost of parallelism.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="hive-query-02" number={45} question="How does the CONCAT function work in Hive?" difficulty="easy" topic="Functions">
`CONCAT` conc

content:
atenates a comma-separated list of input strings. Hive also provides `CONCAT_WS`, which takes a custom delimiter to insert between the concatenated strings.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="hive-query-03" number={46} question="How do the TRIM and RPAD/LPAD functions work in Hive?" difficulty="easy" topic="Functions">
- **`TRIM`** — removes leading and trailing spaces from a string, useful for cleaning up user input that may have stray whitespace. `LTRIM`/`RTRIM` do the same but only from the left or right side respectively. E.g. `TRIM('  Smith  ')` → `'Smith'`.
- **`RPAD`** — pads a string with extra characters on the right so it reaches a target length; `LPAD` does the same on the left. Both accept an optional custom padding character. E.g. `LPAD('Hello', 8, ' ')` → `'   Hello'`.
</Ques

<QuestionCard id="hive-query-04" number={47} question="What is the RLIKE operator in Hive, and how does it differ from LIKE?" difficulty="medium" topic="Functions">
`LIKE` matches simple SQL string patterns, e.g. `user_name LIKE '%Smith'`. `RLIKE` supports full Java regular expressions for more advanced pattern matching, e.g.:

```sql
user_name RLIKE '.*(Smith|Sam).*'
```

This returns rows where `user_name` contains either "Smith" or "Sam" anywhere in the string — something plain `LIKE` can't express in a single condition.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="hive-query-05" number={48} question="What is a table-generating function in Hive?" difficulty="medium" topic="Functions">
A table-generating function takes a single row (often a single column) and expands it into multiple ro

content:
ws or columns — the opposite of an aggregate function. Common examples:

- `EXPLODE(array)` and `EXPLODE(map)` — expand each array/map element into its own row
- `STACK()` — builds multiple rows from a flat list of values
- `JSON_TUPLE()` — extracts multiple fields from a JSON string in a single call
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="hive-query-06" number={49} question="What does the STREAMTABLE hint do in Hive?" difficulty="hard" topic="Optimization">
`STREAMTABLE` is a query hint used with `JOIN` to control which table is streamed (rather than fully buffered) during the map/reduce stage of the join — a query optimization technique:

```sql
SELECT /*+ STREAMTABLE(table1) */ table1.val, table2.val
FROM table1 JOIN table2 ON (table1.key = table2.key);
```

If no `STREAMTABLE` hint is given

description: Apache Hive interview questions covering HiveQL, the metastore, partitioning and bucketing, file formats, joins, and performance optimization for data engineers.
content:
, Hive streams the rightmost table in the `JOIN` by default.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="hive-query-07" number={50} question="Is it possible to create a Cartesian join between two tables using Hive?" difficulty="medium" topic="Joins">
No — a Cartesian (cross) join isn't supported in this context because it can't be implemented efficiently in a MapReduce-style execution model.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="hive-query-08" number={51} question="As part of optimizing queries in Hive, what should be the order of table size in a JOIN query?" difficulty="medium" topic="Optimization">
Put the smallest table first and the largest table last in the `JOIN` — Hive's join execution is optimized to stream the last (largest) table rather than buffer it in memory.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCar

d id="hive-query-09" number={52} question="How do you resolve an out-of-memory error while running a JOIN query?" difficulty="hard" topic="Optimization">
A `JOIN` over large tables can hold too much data in memory and trigger an out-of-memory error. A simple mitigation is to switch a `RIGHT OUTER JOIN` to a `LEFT OUTER JOIN` and make sure the table with the largest number of rows is positioned rightmost in the join — consistent with Hive's general join-ordering guidance of smallest-to-largest, left-to-right.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="hive-query-10" number={53} question="What is the usefulness of the DISTRIBUTE BY clause in Hive?" difficulty="medium" topic="Query Syntax">

<QuestionCard id="hive-query-11" number={54} question="What is a Generic UDF in Hive?" difficulty="hard" topic="Functions">
A Generic UDF is a user-defined function written in Java to cover functionality not available in Hive's built-in function set. Unlike a simple UDF, it can inspect the type of its input arguments programmatically at runtime and return an appropriately typed response, making it more flexible for polymorphic or complex-type inputs.

### Configuration, Sessions & Operations

CLI usage, session/config precedence, and day-to-day operational commands.

<QuestionList topic="Configuration, Sessions & Operations" storagePrefix="hive-ops">

<QuestionCard id="hive-ops-01" number={56} question="What is the use of the .hiverc file in Hive?" difficulty="easy" topic="Configuration">
`.hiverc` is Hive's initialization file — it's loaded automatically whenever the Hive CLI starts, and it's the natural place to set initial parameter values or run startup commands, such as putting the session into strict mode by default.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="hive-ops-02" number={57} question="How do you run Unix shell commands from Hive?" difficulty="easy" topic="Operations">
Prefix the command with `!` in the Hive shell. For example, `!

title: Hive
description: Apache Hive interview questions covering HiveQL, the metastore, partitioning and bucketing, file formats, joins, and performance optimization for data engineers.
content:
pwd` at the `hive>` prompt lists the current directory, and `!date` runs the `date` command.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="hive-ops-03" number={58} question="What is the purpose of the USE command in Hive?" difficulty="easy" topic="Operations">
`USE` sets the current/active database that subsequent Hive queries in the session will run against — `USE default` switches to the default database, or `USE database_name` switches to a specific one. It's typically called before running other queries so they resolve against the intended database.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="hive-ops-04" number={59} question="What is the precedence order for Hive configuration properties?" difficulty="hard" topic="Configuration">
From highest to lowest priority:

1. Hive `SET` command (highest priority)

2. `-hiveconf` option on the Hive command line
3. `hive-site.xml`
4. `hive-default.xml`
5. `hadoop-site.xml`
6. `hadoop-default.xml`
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="hive-ops-05" number={60} question="How do you display a header row with the results of a Hive query?" difficulty="easy" topic="Configuration">
Set the `hive.cli.print.header` property:

```sql
set hive.cli.print.header=true;
```
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="hive-ops-06" number={61} question="How do you change the settings of a Hive session?" difficulty="easy" topic="Configuration">
Use the `SET` command — it can change session-level settings as well as settings for the underlying MapReduce job. Calling `SET` with just a property name returns its current value, and `SET -v` lists every property in the system, including

Hadoop's defaults.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="hive-ops-07" number={62} question="What is the use of strict mode in Hive?" difficulty="medium" topic="Performance">
Strict mode guards against accidentally running a full table scan against a very large table. Setting `hive.mapred.mode=strict` puts Hive into this mode:

```sql
set hive.mapred.mode=strict;
```

In strict mode, any query that would require a full table scan throws an error instead of running — for example, a query against a partitioned table is rejected unless it includes a `WHERE` clause that lets Hive prune partitions. This helps avoid unexpectedly slow, expensive jobs.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="hive-ops-08" number={63} question="How do you recursively access sub-directories in Hive?" difficulty="medium" topic

Set both of the following to `true`:

```sql
set mapred.input.dir.recursive=true;
set hive.mapred.supports.subdirectories=true;
```

Once set, Hive's MapReduce jobs will recursively read sub-directories of a given input directory.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="hive-ops-09" number={64} question="What optimization can be done for a SELECT * query in Hive?" difficulty="medium" topic="Performance">
Hive can convert certain `SELECT` queries into a single FETCH task instead of launching a full job, cutting query latency. This is controlled by `hive.fetch.task.conversion`, which accepts:

- `0` — FETCH conversion disabled
- `1` (minimal) — applies to `SELECT *`, filters on partition columns (`WHERE`/`HAVING`), and `LIMIT` only
- `2` (more) — extends to general `SELECT`, `FI

description: Apache Hive interview questions covering HiveQL, the metastore, partitioning and bucketing, file formats, joins, and performance optimization for data engineers.
content:
LTER`, and `LIMIT` (including virtual columns), and can even handle UDF expressions in the `SELECT` clause
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="hive-ops-10" number={65} question="What is the use of ORC format tables in Hive?" difficulty="medium" topic="File Formats">
ORC (Optimized Row Columnar) is a file format built for efficient storage, reading, writing, and processing in Hive. Benefits include:

- A single output file per task, which reduces load on the NameNode.
- Support for complex types — date/time, decimal, struct, map, and more.
- Lightweight indexes stored within the file itself, enabling skip-scans.
- Bounded memory usage during read/write.
- Metadata stored with Protocol Buffers, which supports adding/removing fields over time.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="hive-ops-16" number={71} question="How would you improve the performance of a program in Hive?" difficulty="medium" topic="Performance">
General good-practice principles apply on top of Hive-specific tuning (partitioning, bucketing, ORC/Parquet, strict mode):

- **Data structure** — pick the right table layout and file format for the access pattern you actually need.
- **Standard library** — prefer built-in Hive functions over hand-rolled UDF logic where possible; built-ins are typically much better optimized than custom implementations.
- **Abstraction** — excessive layers of views/subqueries can hide inefficiency; simplify redundant indirection in a query.

## Common Interview Scenarios

- **"A Hive query against a huge fact table is scanning the entire dataset — how do you speed it up?"** Walk through partitioning on the most common filter column (e.g. date), bucketing a high-cardinality join key, switching to ORC/Parquet for columnar pruning and predicate pushdown, and enabling strict mode so accidental full scans fail fast instead of running for hours.
- **"Design a Hive table for clickstream data that's queried both by date range and by user."** Discuss partitioning by date (coarse, filters most queries immediately) combined with bucketing by `user_id` (fine-grained, keeps partition count sane and enables map-side joins against a user dimension).
- **"Two teams query the same raw files but need different schemas — how would you support th

at in Hive?"** Explain schema-on-read: multiple Hive table definitions can point at the same underlying HDFS files, each interpreting the data through its own schema, without duplicating storage.
- **"A JOIN between two large tables keeps running out of memory — what do you check first?"** Table ordering (smallest to largest, left to right), whether a `RIGHT OUTER JOIN` should become a `LEFT OUTER JOIN`, and whether a skew in the join key calls for a skewed table or a different join strategy.

## Advanced RDD & DataFrame Transformations: Less Common, Still Important

**These transformations don't come up in every pipeline, but each one solves a specific problem the basic map/filter/select vocabulary can't — amortizing per-partition setup cost, reading less data than what's on disk, reshaping between wide and long formats, or turning nested data into something queryable.**

title: Spark Advanced Transformations

content:
## Key Concepts

Most of these patterns exist to avoid doing more work than necessary: **`mapPartitions`** amortizes expensive per-partition setup (like opening a connection) instead of paying that cost per row. **Predicate pushdown** avoids reading data that a filter would discard anyway, by pushing the condition down into the source scan itself. **Sampling** and **set operations** avoid processing a full dataset when a subset or a comparison is all that's needed. **Pivoting** and **exploding** are the odd ones out — not optimizations, but genuine reshaping operations, turning data between row-oriented and column-oriented, or between nested and flat, to match what a downstream consumer actually expects.

content:
## mapPartitions and mapPartitionsWithIndex

<QuestionList topic="mapPartitions and mapPartitionsWithIndex" storagePrefix="spark-adv-map-partitions">

<QuestionCard id="mpi-01" number={1} question="What does mapPartitions do differently from map?" difficulty="medium" topic="mapPartitions">
`map` applies a function to each element individually, one call per row. `mapPartitions` applies a function once per *partition*, receiving an iterator over that partition's rows and returning an iterator of results — any setup work inside the function runs once per partition instead of once per row.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="mpi-02" number={2} question="What's a practical example where mapPartitions meaningfully outperforms map?" difficulty="medium" topic="mapPartitions">
Opening a database con

description: Interview questions on advanced Spark transformations — mapPartitions, predicate pushdown, set operations, pivoting, sampling, and exploding nested structures.

nection or an HTTP client to enrich each row with external data. With `map`, that connection would be created and torn down once per row — enormously wasteful. With `mapPartitions`, it's created once per partition, reused for every row in that partition, and closed once at the end.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="mpi-03" number={3} question="What does mapPartitionsWithIndex add, and when would you need the partition index?" difficulty="medium" topic="mapPartitions">
It provides the partition's index alongside its iterator of rows. It's useful when the logic needs to know *which* partition it's processing — for example, generating IDs that must be unique and deterministic across the whole dataset by combining the partition index with a per-row counter, without any coordination between pa

content:
## Filter and Predicate Pushdown

<QuestionList topic="Filter and Predicate Pushdown" storagePrefix="spark-adv-predicate-pushdown">

<QuestionCard id="fpp-01" number={1} question="What is predicate pushdown?" difficulty="medium" topic="Predicate Pushdown">
Predicate pushdown moves a filter condition from after the data is read into the read itself — the data source only returns rows (or blocks of rows) that could actually match, rather than Spark reading everything and filtering afterward. Less data crosses the network and gets deserialized in the first place.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="fpp-02" number={2} question="Why does predicate pushdown work especially well with Parquet?" difficulty="medium" topic="Predicate Pushdown">
Parquet stores column-level statistics (min/max values) p

title: Spark Advanced Transformations
description: Interview questions on advanced Spark transformations — mapPartitions, predicate pushdown, set operations, pivoting, sampling, and exploding nested structures.
content:
er row group. If a filter's range doesn't overlap a row group's min/max for that column, Spark can skip reading that entire row group without decompressing or scanning a single row inside it — a much coarser, cheaper form of pushdown than row-by-row filtering.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="fpp-03" number={3} question="When does predicate pushdown NOT happen, even though a filter is present?" difficulty="hard" topic="Predicate Pushdown">
When the filter wraps the column in a function (`WHERE UPPER(name) = 'X'`), since the source usually can't evaluate arbitrary transformations during a scan — only direct comparisons on raw column values. It also doesn't apply to data sources that don't support it at all (plain text files, most databases without a pushdown-capable JDBC driver setup), an

content:
d won't help if the filter references a column not present in the source's own statistics.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

content:
## Set-Based Operations

<QuestionList topic="Set-Based Operations" storagePrefix="spark-adv-set-ops">

<QuestionCard id="sbo-01" number={1} question="What do union, intersect, and except do, and what do they require of the two DataFrames?" difficulty="easy" topic="Set Operations">
`union` combines the rows of two DataFrames into one. `intersect` returns only rows present in both. `except` returns rows present in the first but not the second. All three require both DataFrames to have the same number of columns with compatible types — they match columns by *position*, not by name.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="sbo-02" number={2} question="What's the difference between union and unionByName?" difficulty="medium" topic="Set Operations">
`union` matches columns purely by position — if the

title: Spark Advanced Transformations
description: Interview questions on advanced Spark transformations — mapPartitions, predicate pushdown, set operations, pivoting, sampling, and exploding nested structures.
content:
two DataFrames' columns are in a different order, the result silently mismatches data under the wrong column names. `unionByName` matches columns by name instead, which is safer whenever there's any chance the two DataFrames' column ordering doesn't line up exactly.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="sbo-03" number={3} question="Does union remove duplicate rows the way a SQL UNION (without ALL) does?" difficulty="medium" topic="Set Operations">
No — Spark's `union` behaves like SQL's `UNION ALL`: it keeps duplicates. To deduplicate the combined result, you have to explicitly call `.distinct()` afterward, since `union` alone won't do it for you.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

## Pivoting and Unpivoting Data

<QuestionList topic="Pivoting and Unpivoting Data" storagePrefix="spark-adv-pivot">

<QuestionCard id="piv-01" number={1} question="What does pivot() do, and what's the basic syntax?" difficulty="medium" topic="Pivoting">
`pivot()` turns distinct values from one column into separate output columns, typically paired with an aggregate — reshaping row-oriented data into a cross-tab layout: `df.groupBy("product").pivot("month").sum("sales")` produces one row per product with a separate column for each distinct month's total sales.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="piv-02" number={2} question="Why is it recommended to pass an explicit list of pivot values when possible?" difficulty="hard" topic="Pivoting">
Without an explicit list, Spark has to first scan the d

content:
ata to discover all distinct values of the pivot column before it can even plan the output columns — an extra, potentially expensive pass. Passing the values explicitly (`pivot("month", Seq("Jan", "Feb", "Mar"))`) skips that discovery scan entirely, and also guarantees a stable, predictable set of output columns.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="piv-03" number={3} question="How do you unpivot (turn columns back into rows) in Spark?" difficulty="medium" topic="Pivoting">
Spark's DataFrame API doesn't have a single built-in `unpivot` the way `pivot` exists (newer versions added `unpivot`/`melt` in Spark 3.4+); the common approach in earlier versions is a `stack()` SQL expression: `selectExpr("id", "stack(3, 'Jan', jan, 'Feb', feb, 'Mar', mar) AS (month, value)")`, which explicitly maps eac

h column into a `(month, value)` row pair.
</QuestionCard>

## Sampling and Data Splitting

<QuestionList topic="Sampling and Data Splitting" storagePrefix="spark-adv-sampling">

<QuestionCard id="sds-01" number={1} question="What does sample() do, and what's the difference between sampling with and without replacement?" difficulty="easy" topic="Sampling">
`sample(withReplacement, fraction, seed)` draws a random subset of rows. Without replacement, each row can be selected at most once. With replacement, the same row can theoretically be selected multiple times (each row is independently considered, potentially more than once) — used less often for DataFrames than in classic statistical bootstrapping contexts.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="sds-02" number={2} question="What does randomSplit() do, and what's a common use case?" difficulty="easy"

description: Interview questions on advanced Spark transformations — mapPartitions, predicate pushdown, set operations, pivoting, sampling, and exploding nested structures.

topic="Sampling">
`randomSplit(weights, seed)` partitions a DataFrame into multiple DataFrames based on given weights, e.g. `df.randomSplit(Array(0.8, 0.2))` for an 80/20 split. The most common use case is generating train/test (or train/validation/test) splits for a machine learning workflow directly on a distributed dataset.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="sds-03" number={3} question="Why might randomSplit()'s actual split sizes not exactly match the requested weights?" difficulty="hard" topic="Sampling">
The split is implemented probabilistically per row rather than by an exact global count — each row is independently assigned to a bucket based on the weights, so on a smaller dataset the actual proportions can deviate noticeably from the requested ones purely by chance, converging c

description: Interview questions on advanced Spark transformations — mapPartitions, predicate pushdown, set operations, pivoting, sampling, and exploding nested structures.

loser to the exact weights only as the dataset grows large.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

## Exploding and Flattening Nested/Array Structures

<QuestionList topic="Exploding and Flattening Nested/Array Structures" storagePrefix="spark-adv-explode">

<QuestionCard id="efn-01" number={1} question="What does explode() do?" difficulty="easy" topic="Exploding">
`explode(column)` takes an array or map column and produces one output row per element — a row with an array of 3 items becomes 3 separate rows, each with one of those items and every other original column duplicated across them. It's the standard way to turn nested, repeated data into a flat, queryable row-per-item shape.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="efn-02" number={2} question="What's the difference between explode() and explode_outer()?" difficulty="medium" topic="Exploding">
`explode()` drops the row entirely if the

title: Spark Advanced Transformations
description: Interview questions on advanced Spark transformations — mapPartitions, predicate pushdown, set operations, pivoting, sampling, and exploding nested structures.
content:
array/map column is `NULL` or empty. `explode_outer()` keeps it, producing a single row with `NULL` in the exploded column's place — the same distinction as an inner join versus a left outer join, applied to array unpacking.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="efn-03" number={3} question="How do you flatten a nested struct column into top-level columns?" difficulty="medium" topic="Exploding">
`df.select("id", "address.street", "address.city")` (or `col("address.*")` to expand every field of the struct at once) pulls a struct's nested fields up to the top level of the output. This differs from `explode`, which is for arrays/maps with a variable number of elements — struct flattening is for a fixed, known set of nested fields.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

content:
## Key Concepts

Spark reaches cloud object stores through Hadoop-compatible filesystem connectors — **S3A** for S3, the GCS connector, **ABFS** for ADLS — each emulating filesystem semantics (directories, atomic renames) over storage that's natively just a flat key-value object namespace. Relational databases are reached through **JDBC**, which — unlike a purpose-built distributed connector — has no native concept of Spark partitions, so Spark has to parallelize a JDBC read itself by splitting a query into concurrent range-bounded sub-queries. Across every connector, the same two concerns repeat: **pushing filters down** to the source so less data crosses the network, and keeping **credentials** out of hardcoded configuration in favor of IAM roles, secret managers, or credential providers

<QuestionList topic="S3, GCS, and ADLS Integration" storagePrefix="spark-cloud-object-stores">

<QuestionCard id="sga-01" number={1} question="How does Spark access cloud object stores like S3, GCS, and ADLS?" difficulty="easy" topic="Object Store Integration">
Through Hadoop-compatible filesystem connectors bundled or added as dependencies — the S3A connector for S3, the GCS connector for Google Cloud Storage, and ABFS for Azure Data Lake Storage — each translating standard Hadoop filesystem calls into the specific cloud provider's storage API underneath.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="sga-02" number={2} question="What URI schemes does Spark use for each, and why do they differ from a plain filesystem path?" difficulty="easy" topic="Object Store Integ

`s3a://bucket/path` for S3, `gs://bucket/path` for GCS, `abfss://container@account.dfs.core.windows.net/path` for ADLS. The scheme tells Spark which connector implementation to use to resolve the rest of the path — unlike a local or HDFS path, these encode the specific cloud service and bucket/container as part of the address itself.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="sga-03" number={3} question="What's a key architectural difference between an object store and HDFS that Spark's connectors have to work around?" difficulty="hard" topic="Object Store Integration">
Object stores have a **flat namespace** — what looks like a directory is really just a common prefix shared by object keys, with no native directory or atomic-rename operation the way a real filesystem has. Connectors have

<QuestionCard id="s3a-01" number={1} question="What is the S3A connector, and what does 'emulates a filesystem' mean given S3's actual object model?" difficulty="medium" topic="S3A">
S3A is the Hadoop-compatible connector that lets Spark treat S3 as if it were a hierarchical filesystem, even though S3 itself only understands flat object keys. It translates filesystem-style operations (listing a "directory," checking if a "file" exists) into the equivalent S3 API calls over that flat key space.

S3 committers (like the S3A committer or EMRFS's committer) manage how Spark's distributed write tasks land their output reliably and atomically on S3, working around the lack of a true atomic directory rename. Without a proper committer, a failed or retried task can leave partial or duplicate output behind, since S3 has no native equivalent to the atomic "rename temp directory to final directory" trick a real filesystem write commit typically relies on.

<QuestionCard id="pdr-01" number={1} question="What is Hive-style partitioning, and how does Spark use it when reading?" difficulty="easy" topic="Partitioned Directories">
Hive-style partitioning encodes column values directly into the directory path — `s3a://bucket/table/year=2024/month=01/`. When Spark reads such a path, it can infer the partition columns (`year`, `month`) from the directory structure itself, without those values needing to be stored in the file data.

## JDBC Drivers and Connection Pooling

<QuestionList topic="JDBC Drivers and Connection Pooling" storagePrefix="spark-cloud-jdbc">

<QuestionCard id="jdc-01" number={1} question="What do you need to set up before spark.read.jdbc will work?" difficulty="easy" topic="JDBC">
The appropriate JDBC driver JAR for the target database (PostgreSQL, MySQL, etc.) has to be on Spark's classpath — added via `--jars` or `spark.jars.packages` at submission time — since Spark itself doesn't bundle database-specific drivers.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="jdc-02" number={2} question="Does Spark pool JDBC connections across tasks by default?" difficulty="medium" topic="JDBC">

<QuestionCard id="ppd-01" number={1} question="How does predicate pushdown work for a JDBC source?" difficulty="medium" topic="JDBC Pushdown">
Spark translates supported filter predicates from the DataFrame query into the equivalent `WHERE` clause sent to the source database as part of the underlying SQL query — filtering happens inside the database before rows are even sent back to Spark, rather than Spark pulling the whole table across and filtering afterward.

<QuestionCard id="pdw-01" number={1} question="How does Spark parallelize a JDBC read across multiple tasks?" difficulty="medium" topic="JDBC Partitioning">
It splits a numeric (or otherwise orderable) `partitionColumn`'s range (`lowerBound` to `upperBound`) into `numPartitions` roughly equal sub-ranges, and issues one query per task, each scoped to its own `WHERE partitionColumn BETWEEN ... Hardcoded credentials end up in code repositories, logs, and job configuration files, all of which have a wider audience and longer retention than a credential's intended lifetime — a significant, avoidable exposure risk compared to credentials that are resolved dynamically at runtime and never persisted in plaintext anywhere.

<QuestionCard id="hfi-01" number={1} question="How does Spark read and write HDFS, and what does it inherit from doing so?" difficulty="easy" topic="HDFS">
Natively, via the `hdfs://` URI scheme — Spark talks to HDFS directly as a first-class Hadoop-ecosystem citizen, inheriting HDFS's built-in data locality awareness and block replication for fault tolerance, without needing an emulation layer the way object store connectors do.

**Every major cloud offers a managed Spark platform for the same reason — provisioning, patching, and scaling a cluster is undifferentiated operational work — and the real interview-relevant differences between them come down to how storage integrates, how clusters start and stop, and how aggressively they'll use cheap, interruptible compute.**

## Key Concepts

**AWS EMR**, **Google Cloud Dataproc**, and **Azure Synapse Spark pools** all solve the same core problem — provisioning and managing Spark clusters without operating the underlying infrastructure — but with different philosophies: EMR leans toward long-running, S3-integrated clusters; Dataproc emphasizes fast startup and **ephemeral clusters** spun up per job and torn down after; Synapse integrates Spark directly into a broader analytics workspace alongside notebooks and pipelines. All three, plus Databricks, offer **managed autoscaling** and **spot/preemptible instance** support, trading some interruption risk for meaningfully lower compute cost on workloads that can tolerate it.

question="What's the risk of autoscaling reacting too slowly or too aggressively to load changes?" difficulty="hard" topic="Autoscaling">
Too slow: a sudden spike in workload sits queued waiting for new capacity to provision, hurting latency-sensitive jobs. Too aggressive: the platform scales up and down repeatedly for short-lived load fluctuations, incurring the overhead (and cost) of constantly provisioning and deprovisioning nodes without ever settling into a stable, efficient state — most platforms let you tune scaling sensitivity/cooldown specifically to avoid this thrashing.

Beyond simply picking a cluster manager, deploying Spark in a shared environment means solving for **multi-tenancy** — making sure one team's job can't starve or crash another's — which each platform handles differently: YARN through **capacity/fair scheduler queues**, Kubernetes through **namespaces and resource quotas**. **Docker containerization** has become the common thread across modern deployments, since it's how Spark ships consistently to Kubernetes (and increasingly to containerized YARN) regardless of which specific cluster manager sits underneath.

## YARN Deployment and Queue Management

<QuestionList topic="YARN Deployment and Queue Management" storagePrefix="spark-deploy-yarn">

<QuestionCard id="ydq-01" number={1} question="How does Spark run as a YARN application, and what's the practical benefit of that model?" difficulty="medium" topic="YARN Deployment">
Spark submits itself as a YARN application, with YARN's ResourceManager allocating containers for the driver (in cluster mode) and executors, the same way it would for any other YARN workload. The benefit is resource sharing — Spark jobs coexist on the same cluster as other Hadoop-ecosystem workloads (Hive, MapReduce), governed by the same central resource allocation.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="ydq-02" number={2} question="What is queue management, and why does it matt

er for running Spark on a shared YARN cluster?" difficulty="medium" topic="YARN Deployment">
YARN's Capacity Scheduler or Fair Scheduler lets administrators define queues with guaranteed and maximum resource shares, and jobs are submitted into a specific queue (`--queue` flag) rather than competing for the whole cluster unconstrained. This matters because without queues, a single large or runaway Spark job could consume the entire cluster's capacity, starving every other team's workload.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="ydq-03" number={3} question="What's the practical difference between the Capacity Scheduler and the Fair Scheduler?" difficulty="hard" topic="YARN Deployment">
The Capacity Scheduler guarantees each queue a configured minimum share of cluster capacity, allowing queues to

The Fair Scheduler instead aims to give all running applications roughly equal resource shares over time, rebalancing dynamically as jobs start and finish — geared more toward fairness across many smaller, shorter jobs.
</QuestionCard>

## Multi-Tenancy and Resource Queue Isolation

<QuestionList topic="Multi-Tenancy and Resource Queue Isolation" storagePrefix="spark-deploy-multi-tenancy">

<QuestionCard id="mtq-01" number={1} question="What does multi-tenancy mean for a shared Spark platform, and why does it need explicit isolation mechanisms?" difficulty="medium" topic="Multi-Tenancy">
Multi-tenancy means multiple teams or applications share the same underlying cluster infrastructure. Without explicit isolation, one team's misbehaving or resource-hungry job can degrade or starve every other team's workload running on the same shared capacity — isolation mechanisms exist specifically to prevent that "noisy neighbor" problem.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="mtq-02" number={2} question="What are the concrete isolation m

echanisms available on YARN versus Kubernetes?" difficulty="medium" topic="Multi-Tenancy">
On YARN: queues (Capacity or Fair Scheduler) with guaranteed and maximum resource shares per team/queue. On Kubernetes: namespaces per team combined with resource quotas capping how much CPU/memory a namespace's workloads can consume in total, plus network policies restricting cross-namespace communication if needed.
</QuestionCard>

## Key Concepts

Every Spark application starts from a **`SparkSession`** — the single, unified entry point since Spark 2.0 — and is launched via **`spark-submit`**, whose flags control everything from resource sizing to which cluster manager to target. Configuration itself is **layered**: code-level `SparkConf` settings, `spark-defaults.conf`, `spark-submit` flags, and environment variables like `SPARK_HOME` each apply at different points, with a defined precedence when they conflict. Once running, an application is observable two ways: **logs** (controlled via `log4j2`, separately for driver and executor output) for detailed, line-by-line diagnostics, and the **Spark UI** for a live, structured view of jobs, stages, and resource usage. **Spark Connect** is the newest piece of this pictur

<QuestionCard id="ssc-01" number={1} question="What is SparkSession, and why did it replace having separate context objects?" difficulty="easy" topic="SparkSession">
`SparkSession` is the single, unified entry point for a Spark application since Spark 2.0, replacing what used to require separately creating a `SparkContext`, `SQLContext`, and `HiveContext` depending on what functionality was needed. It consolidates DataFrame, SQL, streaming, and Hive access behind one object, removing the earlier confusion of which context to reach for.

In modern code, `SparkSession` is what you interact with directly; `SparkContext` mostly operates underneath it.

`spark-submit` is the command-line tool used to launch a Spark application against a cluster, regardless of which cluster manager is in use. ## Spark Configuration and Environment Variables

<QuestionList topic="Spark Configuration and Environment Variables" storagePrefix="spark-cf-config">

<QuestionCard id="sce-01" number={1} question="What are the different ways to configure a Spark application, and what's their precedence order?" difficulty="medium" topic="Configuration">
From lowest to highest precedence: **`spark-defaults.conf`** (cluster-wide defaults), then **environment variables**, then **`SparkConf` set in application code**, then **`spark-submit` command-line flags**, which override everything else. In practice, this means a flag passed at submission time always wins over a setting baked into the code or the cluster's defaults.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="sce-02" number={2} question="What's the difference bet

`SparkConf` is set programmatically inside the application itself (`SparkConf().set("spark.executor.memory", "4g")`), scoped to that one application. `spark-defaults.conf` is a cluster-level file providing default values every application submitted to that cluster inherits unless it explicitly overrides them.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="sce-03" number={3} question="What do SPARK_HOME and JAVA_HOME environment variables control, and why do they matter?" difficulty="easy" topic="Configuration">
`SPARK_HOME` points to the Spark installation directory, which tools like `spark-submit` and `pyspark` rely on to locate Spark's own libraries and scripts. `JAVA_HOME` points to the JVM installation Sp

## Logging Level Configuration

<QuestionList topic="Logging Level Configuration" storagePrefix="spark-cf-logging">

<QuestionCard id="llc-01" number={1} question="How do you control Spark's logging verbosity?" difficulty="easy" topic="Logging">
Through `log4j2` properties files (`log4j2.properties`, typically placed in `$SPARK_HOME/conf`), which let you set logging thresholds (`INFO`, `WARN`, `ERROR`, etc.) globally or per package/class — for example, quieting Spark's own internal chatter while keeping application-level logs at `INFO`.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="llc-02" number={2} question="Why would you want to separate driver and executor log output?" difficulty="medium" topic="Logging">
Driver and executor logs live on different machines/processes and cover different concerns —

Keeping them separately accessible (rather than interleaved) makes it much easier to trace a specific failure back to whether it originated in driver-side logic or in a specific executor's task.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="llc-03" number={3} question="Why might you want to raise the log level for noisy packages instead of globally?" difficulty="medium" topic="Logging">
Spark's own internal components can log a large volume of routine `INFO`-level detail that drowns out application-specific log messages. Targeting specific noisy packages (e.g., setting `org.apache.spark` to `WARN` while leaving your own application's logger at `INFO`)

<QuestionList topic="Spark UI Monitoring Basics" storagePrefix="spark-cf-ui">

<QuestionCard id="sum-01" number={1} question="What is the Spark UI, and where do you find it?" difficulty="easy" topic="Spark UI">
The Spark UI is a web interface, provided automatically by `SparkContext`, for inspecting a running (or, via event logs, completed) application — available at `http://<driver-host>:4040` by default, with the port incrementing if multiple applications are running on the same machine.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="sum-02" number={2} question="What do the Jobs, Stages, and SQL tabs each show?" difficulty="medium" topic="Spark UI">
The **Jobs** tab lists jobs triggered by actions, with overall progress and duration. The **Stages** tab drills into each

<QuestionCard id="sum-03" number={3} question="What does the Storage tab show, and why is it useful for debugging caching issues?" difficulty="medium" topic="Spark UI">
The Storage tab lists every RDD/DataFrame currently persisted (via `.cache()`/`.persist()`), showing how much of it is actually cached in memory versus spilled to disk, and across how many partitions. ## Spark Connect Client-Server Architecture

<QuestionList topic="Spark Connect Client-Server Architecture" storagePrefix="spark-cf-connect">

<QuestionCard id="scc-01" number={1} question="What is Spark Connect, and what problem does it solve?" difficulty="medium" topic="Spark Connect">
Spark Connect is a client-server architecture, introduced in Spark 3.4, that lets a client application submit DataFrame/SQL query plans to a remote Spark cluster over a gRPC protocol — without that client needing a local Spark installation, matching JVM version, or direct network access to the cluster's internals. It solves the friction of embedding a full Spark runtime just to write client code that talks to Spark.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="scc-02" number={2} question="How does Spark Connect's ar

title: Spark Core Fundamentals
description: Interview questions on getting a Spark application up, configured, and observable — SparkSession, spark-submit, configuration precedence, logging, the Spark UI, and Spark Connect.
content:
chitecture differ from the traditional driver model?" difficulty="hard" topic="Spark Connect">
In the traditional model, the client application *is* effectively the driver (or launches one directly) — tightly coupled to the cluster, requiring a compatible Spark install locally. With Spark Connect, the client is a thin, separate process that only builds and sends a logical query plan over gRPC; the actual driver runs remotely on the cluster and executes that plan, decoupling the client's environment entirely from the cluster's.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="scc-03" number={3} question="What's a practical benefit of Spark Connect for application development?" difficulty="medium" topic="Spark Connect">
It lets lightweight applications — a web backend, a notebook environment, an IDE plugi

n — interact with a remote Spark cluster using just a small client library, without pulling in Spark's full dependency footprint or requiring the client's JVM/language version to match the cluster's exactly. It also allows a client to reconnect to a running session without losing its state, which the traditional tightly-coupled driver model doesn't support.
</QuestionCard>

## Data Quality Engineering: Validating Correctness on Spark

**Data quality tooling on Spark answers three questions in sequence — is this data structurally what we expect (schema), does it satisfy the rules we've declared (constraints/expectations), and if something's wrong, can we trace it back to where it actually broke (lineage) — with alerting as the thread connecting a failed check to someone actually finding out.**

## Key Concepts

**Deequ** and **Great Expectations** both let you declare data quality rules rather than hand-write validation logic, but they come from different lineages: Deequ is Amazon's library, purpose-built as scalable Spark aggregations for exactly this use case, while Great Expectations is a broader, engine-agnostic framework that happens to support a Spark backend among several others. **Schema enforcement** is the narrowest, cheapest check — catching structural drift before it even reaches row-level validation. **Statistical anomaly detection** catches the failures neither constraint checks nor schema enforcement would — data that's structurally valid and individually plausible, but collectively off from the norm. ## Deequ Constraint-Based Testing

<QuestionList topic="Deequ Constraint-Based Testing" storagePrefix="spark-dq-deequ">

<QuestionCard id="dcb-01" number={1} question="What is Deequ, and how does it differ from a general-purpose testing framework?" difficulty="medium" topic="Deequ">
Deequ is Amazon's open-source library for defining declarative data quality constraints — completeness, uniqueness, value ranges, statistical properties — computed directly as Spark aggregations over a DataFrame. Unlike a general testing framework bolted onto Spark, it was purpose-built for this use case, so its checks scale natively with the same distributed execution model as the rest of a Spark pipeline.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dcb-02" number={2} question="Write an example of a Deequ constraint ch

```scala
val result = VerificationSuite()
  .onData(df)
  .addCheck(
    Check(CheckLevel.Error, "Data quality checks")
      .isComplete("customer_id")
      .isUnique("order_id")
      .hasMin("amount", _ >= 0)
  )
  .run()
```
Each constraint declares an expectation; Deequ computes the relevant Spark aggregation to evaluate it and reports pass/fail per constraint rather than requiring hand-written validation SQL for each rule.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dcb-03" number={3} question="Why is Deequ described as 'computed as scalable Spark aggregations'?" difficulty="medium" topic="Deequ">
Under the hood, a Deequ check like `isComplete` or `hasMin` translates into standard Spark aggregate operations (counts, min

Great Expectations supports a Spark execution engine backend, letting you run the same declarative "expectations" (e.g., `expect_column_values_to_not_be_null`) directly against a Spark DataFrame — the expectations themselves are engine-agnostic, but execution against Spark data scales the same way any other Spark computation would.

## Statistical Anomaly Detection

<QuestionList topic="Statistical Anomaly Detection" storagePrefix="spark-dq-anomaly">

<QuestionCard id="sad-01" number={1} question="What does statistical anomaly detection look for in a Spark pipeline context?" difficulty="medium" topic="Anomaly Detection">
It flags rows or entire batches whose statistical properties — mean, standard deviation, null rate, row count — deviate significantly from a learned baseline of what's normal for that dataset, catching problems that are structurally valid but collectively suspicious, like a sudden spike in null values or a batch with dramatically fewer rows than usual.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="sad-02" number={2} question="Why is anomaly detection often computed incrementally per run rather than against the f

description: Interview questions on Spark data quality tooling — Deequ, Great Expectations, statistical anomaly detection, schema enforcement, lineage verification, and pipeline alerting.
content:
ull historical dataset each time?" difficulty="hard" topic="Anomaly Detection">
Recomputing baseline statistics over the entire historical dataset on every run gets more expensive as the dataset grows, and isn't necessary if the baseline itself is a rolling or incrementally-updated summary — computing per-run metrics and comparing them against a maintained running baseline is far cheaper and still catches the same class of drift.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

For anomaly detection as a general data quality monitoring concept, see [Data Quality](/level-2-core-concepts/data-quality/).

## Schema Enforcement and Evolution Policies

<QuestionList topic="Schema Enforcement and Evolution Policies" storagePrefix="spark-dq-schema-policy">

<QuestionCard id="sep-01" number={1} question="What does schema enforcement mean in a Spark write context, and what's the default behavior?" difficulty="medium" topic="Schema Policy">
Schema enforcement means rejecting a write whose schema doesn't match the target table's expected schema, rather than silently accepting it. On formats like Delta, this is the default: an incoming DataFrame with an unexpected extra column, missing column, or mismatched type fails the write outright unless schema evolution is explicitly enabled.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="sep-02" number={2} question="What does mergeSchema do, and why is it not the defaul

content:
t?" difficulty="medium" topic="Schema Policy">
`mergeSchema = true` tells Spark to reconcile a divergent incoming schema with the target table's schema automatically (typically adding new columns) rather than rejecting the write. It's not the default because automatic schema changes bypass any review — an unintended upstream change (a typo'd column, an unexpected new field) could silently and permanently alter a production table's schema without anyone deciding that should happen.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="sep-03" number={3} question="How would you design a policy that rejects breaking schema changes but allows additive ones automatically?" difficulty="hard" topic="Schema Policy">
Enable schema evolution only for strictly additive, backward-compatible changes (new nullable columns

## Data Lineage Verification

<QuestionList topic="Data Lineage Verification" storagePrefix="spark-dq-lineage">

<QuestionCard id="dlv-01" number={1} question="What is data lineage, and why does it matter for root-causing quality issues?" difficulty="easy" topic="Lineage">
Lineage is the tracked record of which upstream sources and transformations produced a given dataset. It matters for root-causing quality issues because when a downstream quality check fails, lineage is what lets you trace backward through the pipeline to find exactly where the bad data was introduced, instead of guessing across every upstream step.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dlv-02" number={2} question="How can lineage be captured automatically versus manually documented?" difficulty="medium" topic="Lineage">
Au

tomatic capture typically comes from instrumenting the pipeline framework itself — Spark's query execution listeners, or a catalog/governance layer (like Unity Catalog) that records column- and table-level lineage from actual query execution. Manual documentation (diagrams, wikis) is easier to start with but reliably goes stale as pipelines change, since nothing forces it to stay in sync with what the code actually does.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dlv-03" number={3} question="Give an example of how lineage helps trace a downstream quality issue back to its source." difficulty="medium" topic="Lineage">
A dashboard metric looks wrong; lineage shows it's derived from a specific aggregate table, which in turn was built from three upstream tables through a specific transformation job —

</QuestionCard>

## Pipeline Alerting on Quality Metrics

<QuestionList topic="Pipeline Alerting on Quality Metrics" storagePrefix="spark-dq-alerting">

<QuestionCard id="pam-01" number={1} question="Why should a quality check failure stop or flag a pipeline rather than just being logged?" difficulty="easy" topic="Alerting">
A logged-only failure only gets noticed if someone happens to go looking for it — which usually means bad data has already reached downstream consumers by the time anyone investigates. Failing loudly (blocking the pipeline, or at minimum triggering an active alert) is what actually prevents shipping known-bad data silently.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="pam-02" number={2} question="What's the risk of alerting on every quality check failure without any triage or severity levels?" d

title: Spark Data Quality Engineering
description: Interview questions on Spark data quality tooling — Deequ, Great Expectations, statistical anomaly detection, schema enforcement, lineage verification, and pipeline alerting.
content:
ifficulty="medium" topic="Alerting">
Alert fatigue — if minor, low-impact check failures page someone with the same urgency as a genuinely critical one, people start ignoring or muting alerts altogether, which defeats the purpose of alerting in the first place. Severity levels (warn vs. block, for example) let teams distinguish "worth investigating this week" from "stop the pipeline right now."
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="pam-03" number={3} question="How would you wire a Deequ or Great Expectations failure into an actual alerting system?" difficulty="medium" topic="Alerting">
Capture the check result (pass/fail, and which specific constraints failed) in the pipeline's orchestration layer, and have a failure trigger a notification through whatever the team already uses for on-call —

title: Spark Data Quality Engineering
description: Interview questions on Spark data quality tooling — Deequ, Great Expectations, statistical anomaly detection, schema enforcement, lineage verification, and pipeline alerting.
content:
Slack, PagerDuty, email — ideally including enough context (which table, which constraint, sample failing rows) that someone can start investigating without first having to dig through logs to understand what actually failed.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

## Key Concepts

A DataFrame is a distributed collection organized into **named, typed columns** — the schema is what lets the Catalyst optimizer reason about a query instead of treating it as an opaque function over unstructured records the way it must for RDDs. Working with DataFrames means working through the **Column API** (`col()`, `expr()`, `withColumn()`) to build expressions, being deliberate about **schema** (inferred at a scan cost, or declared upfront via `StructType` for stability and speed), and explicitly handling **`NULL`** and **type mismatches** rather than letting them fail silently downstream. <QuestionCard id="ceo-01" number={1} question="What is the Column API, and what's the difference between col() and expr()?" difficulty="medium" topic="Column API">
The Column API represents a column or a computed expression over one, usable in `select`, `withColumn`, `filter`, and similar. `col("price")` references an existing column by name. `expr("price * 1.1")` parses a SQL-like string expression, letting you write arithmetic, function calls, or conditional logic without chaining multiple Column API method calls.

## Schema Definition and Inference

<QuestionList topic="Schema Definition and Inference" storagePrefix="spark-df-schema">

<QuestionCard id="sdi-01" number={1} question="What's the difference between schema inference and an explicit schema?" difficulty="easy" topic="Schema">
Inference lets Spark scan the data (or a sample of it) to guess each column's type automatically — convenient, but it costs an extra pass over the data and can guess wrong on ambiguous or messy input. An explicit schema, defined via `StructType`/`StructField`, is declared upfront in code, skipping that scan entirely and guaranteeing the types Spark uses match exactly what you intended.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="sdi-02" number={2} question="Why is an explicit schema generally recommended for production pipelin

es over inference?" difficulty="medium" topic="Schema">
It avoids the inference scan's performance cost (which can be significant on large datasets or many small files), and it makes the pipeline's behavior stable and predictable — inference can silently produce a different schema if the input data's shape shifts slightly between runs, while an explicit schema either matches or fails loudly.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

For how inference and explicit schemas trade off in practice, see [Apache Spark](/level-3-technologies/batch-processing/spark/#dataframes-datasets--spark-sql).

## Null Handling Strategies

<QuestionList topic="Null Handling Strategies" storagePrefix="spark-df-nulls">

<QuestionCard id="nhs-01" number={1} question="What are the main tools for detecting and handling NULLs in a DataFrame?" difficulty="easy" topic="Null Handling">
`isNull`/`isNotNull` for filtering based on nullness, `na.drop()` to remove rows containing nulls (optionally scoped to specific columns or a minimum non-null threshold), `na.fill(value)` to substitute a default for nulls, and `coalesce(col1, col2, ...)` to return the first non-null value across several columns.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="nhs-02" number={2} question="What's the difference between na.drop() and na.drop('all')?" difficulty="medium" topic="Null Handling">
The default `na.drop()` removes a row if **any*

description: Interview questions on Spark's structured APIs — DataFrame creation, column expressions, schemas, null handling, type casting, Datasets, encoders, and pandas API on Spark.
content:
* column is null. `na.drop("all")` only removes a row if **every** column is null — a much more conservative filter, useful when a row with some missing fields is still meaningful but a completely empty row isn't.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="nhs-03" number={3} question="How would you fill nulls with different default values per column?" difficulty="medium" topic="Null Handling">
`na.fill(Map("age" -> 0, "name" -> "Unknown"))` — passing a map lets you specify a different fallback value per column in a single call, rather than chaining several single-column `na.fill` calls.
</QuestionCard>

## Column Type Casting

<QuestionList topic="Column Type Casting" storagePrefix="spark-df-casting">

<QuestionCard id="ctc-01" number={1} question="How do you explicitly cast a column's type, and why prefer that over relying on implicit conversion?" difficulty="easy" topic="Type Casting">
`df.withColumn("price", col("price").cast("double"))` (or `.astype()` in PySpark). Explicit casting is preferred because relying on implicit conversion means the actual comparison or arithmetic behavior depends on Spark's specific conversion rules, which can silently produce `NULL` or an unexpected value instead of failing loudly when types don't line up as assumed.
</QuestionCard>

## Dataset API and Type Safety

<QuestionList topic="Dataset API and Type Safety" storagePrefix="spark-df-dataset-api">

<QuestionCard id="dts-01" number={1} question="What does the Dataset API add on top of DataFrame, and in which languages is it available?" difficulty="medium" topic="Dataset API">
The Dataset API adds compile-time type safety — operations are checked against a known JVM type at compile time instead of only being validated against the schema at runtime. It's only available in Scala and Java, since Python and R are dynamically typed and have no compile-time type-checking phase for Spark to hook into; DataFrame in Python is effectively `Dataset[Row]` without the added type safety.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dts-02" number={2} question="What's a concrete example of a

Referencing a nonexistent or misspelled field on a typed case class — `ds.map(_.naem)` where the case class only has `name` — fails to compile with a Dataset, since the type checker knows the class's real fields. The equivalent DataFrame mistake, `df.select("naem")`, only fails at runtime, once that code path actually executes against the schema.

<QuestionList topic="Encoders and Compile-Time Checks" storagePrefix="spark-df-encoders">

<QuestionCard id="enc-01" number={1} question="What is an Encoder, and why does the Dataset API need one?" difficulty="medium" topic="Encoders">
An Encoder converts between JVM objects (like a Scala case class instance) and Spark's internal binary row format (Tungsten). The Dataset API needs one because it exposes a typed, object-oriented view over data that's actually stored internally in Spark's optimized binary layout, not as live JVM objects — the encoder is what bridges those two representations efficiently.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="enc-02" number={2} question="How do encoders enable efficiency gains beyond just type conversion?" difficulty="hard" t

Spark's built-in encoders can generate bytecode that accesses individual fields of the binary representation directly, without first fully deserializing the whole object into a live JVM instance — useful when an operation only needs one or two fields out of a larger record. This avoids both the CPU cost of full deserialization and the extra memory pressure of materializing complete objects that aren't fully needed.
</QuestionCard>

## Distributed Computing Fundamentals: How Spark Spreads Work Across a Cluster

**Every Spark application is really a small distributed system — one driver coordinating many executors across worker nodes, brokered by a cluster manager — and understanding that shape is what makes the rest of Spark (partitioning, shuffling, fault tolerance) make sense.**

title: Spark Distributed Computing
description: Interview questions on Spark's distributed computing fundamentals — driver, workers, executors, task slots, cluster managers, resource allocation, and heartbeats.
content:
## Key Concepts

A Spark application has exactly one **driver** — the process running `main()`, building the execution plan, and coordinating everything else — and many **executors**, JVM processes on **worker nodes** that actually run tasks and cache data. A **cluster manager** (Standalone, YARN, Mesos, or Kubernetes) sits between them, deciding which worker nodes get to launch executors for a given application. None of this is free-form: executors expose a fixed number of **task slots** (based on allocated cores), resources are claimed either **statically** up front or **dynamically** as demand changes, and the whole system stays coordinated through periodic **heartbeats** the driver uses to know an executor is still alive.

---

content:
## Driver Node Responsibilities

<QuestionList topic="Driver Node Responsibilities" storagePrefix="spark-dcf-driver">

<QuestionCard id="dnr-01" number={1} question="What is the Spark driver, and what does it actually do?" difficulty="easy" topic="Driver">
The driver is the process that runs the application's `main()` method. It creates the `SparkSession`/`SparkContext`, builds the DAG of transformations as the code executes, negotiates resources with the cluster manager, splits work into stages and tasks, and schedules those tasks onto executors — then collects and processes whatever results come back.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dnr-02" number={2} question="Why does the driver need to stay reachable throughout the application's lifetime?" difficulty="medium" topic="Driver">
Execut

description: Interview questions on Spark's distributed computing fundamentals — driver, workers, executors, task slots, cluster managers, resource allocation, and heartbeats.
content:
ors continuously communicate with the driver — sending heartbeats, task status updates, and results — and the driver schedules new tasks onto executors as prior ones finish. If the driver becomes unreachable, the whole application effectively stalls or fails, since there's no other process holding the DAG and coordinating what runs next.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dnr-03" number={3} question="What's the practical risk of a driver running out of memory, and what commonly causes it?" difficulty="medium" topic="Driver">
A driver OOM crashes the entire application, not just one task. It's commonly caused by actions that pull large amounts of data back to the driver — `collect()` on a big RDD/DataFrame, or accumulating too much state in driver-side variables — rather than letting the da

ta stay distributed across executors and only bringing back a small, aggregated result.
</QuestionCard>

## Worker Node Architecture

<QuestionList topic="Worker Node Architecture" storagePrefix="spark-dcf-worker">

<QuestionCard id="wna-01" number={1} question="What is a worker node, and what resources does it provide?" difficulty="easy" topic="Worker Nodes">
A worker node is any machine (physical or virtual) in the cluster capable of running Spark application code. It contributes its CPU cores, memory, and local disk to the cluster — resources that executors launched on that node draw from to run tasks and cache data.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="wna-02" number={2} question="Can a single worker node run more than one executor?" difficulty="medium" topic="Worker Nodes">
Yes — a worker node's resources can be divided across multiple executor processes, either from the same application o

content:
r different ones, depending on how the cluster manager schedules them and how the node's total capacity is configured. This is distinct from a worker node running multiple *worker processes* (e.g., via `SPARK_WORKER_INSTANCES` in Standalone mode), which is a separate, less common configuration.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="wna-03" number={3} question="What's the relationship between a worker node and the cluster manager?" difficulty="medium" topic="Worker Nodes">
The worker node reports its available resources to the cluster manager and, once allocated, hosts the executor processes the cluster manager launches on the driver's behalf. The worker node itself doesn't decide what work to run — it provides capacity, and the cluster manager (informed by the driver's requests) decides how t

content:
## Executor Processes and Task Slots

<QuestionList topic="Executor Processes and Task Slots" storagePrefix="spark-dcf-executor">

<QuestionCard id="ept-01" number={1} question="What is a Spark executor, and what two jobs does it perform?" difficulty="easy" topic="Executors">
An executor is a JVM process launched on a worker node for a specific Spark application. It performs two jobs: running the tasks the driver assigns it, and caching data (in memory or on disk) so repeated access to the same RDD/DataFrame partitions doesn't require recomputing or re-reading them.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="ept-02" number={2} question="What is a task slot, and how is the number of slots per executor determined?" difficulty="medium" topic="Executors">
A task slot is a unit of parallelism within an

title: Spark Distributed Computing
description: Interview questions on Spark's distributed computing fundamentals — driver, workers, executors, task slots, cluster managers, resource allocation, and heartbeats.
content:
executor — roughly, one core allocated to that executor can run one task at a time. The number of slots is generally set by `spark.executor.cores`: an executor configured with 4 cores can run 4 tasks concurrently, one per slot.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="ept-03" number={3} question="What happens if an executor is lost during a job?" difficulty="medium" topic="Executors">
The driver detects the loss (via missed heartbeats), marks any tasks that were running on it as failed, and reschedules them onto other executors. Any cached data that only existed on the lost executor is gone and gets recomputed from lineage the next time it's needed, rather than the whole job failing outright.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>
