description: Interview questions on Spark's distributed computing fundamentals — driver, workers, executors, task slots, cluster managers, resource allocation, and heartbeats.
content:
## Cluster Manager Concepts

<QuestionList topic="Cluster Manager Concepts" storagePrefix="spark-dcf-cluster-manager">

<QuestionCard id="cmc-01" number={1} question="What is a cluster manager's role in a Spark application?" difficulty="easy" topic="Cluster Managers">
The cluster manager is a pluggable component that allocates cluster resources on Spark's behalf — deciding which worker nodes launch executors for a given application, and how many resources each gets. Spark itself doesn't manage the cluster's physical resources directly; it delegates that entirely to whichever cluster manager is configured.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="cmc-02" number={2} question="Compare Standalone, YARN, Mesos, and Kubernetes as Spark cluster managers." difficulty="medium" topic="Cluster Managers">
*

title: Spark Distributed Computing
description: Interview questions on Spark's distributed computing fundamentals — driver, workers, executors, task slots, cluster managers, resource allocation, and heartbeats.
content:
*Standalone** is Spark's own simple, bundled cluster manager — easy to set up, fewer features. **YARN** is Hadoop's resource manager, common in clusters that already run Hadoop workloads alongside Spark. **Mesos** is a general-purpose cluster resource manager that can share a cluster across many different frameworks, not just Spark. **Kubernetes** runs each Spark executor as its own pod, leaning on Kubernetes' own scheduling, isolation, and container ecosystem rather than a Spark- or Hadoop-specific manager.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="cmc-03" number={3} question="Why has Kubernetes become an increasingly common choice for running Spark?" difficulty="medium" topic="Cluster Managers">
Many organizations already run Kubernetes for everything else, so running Spark on it avoids maintai

title: Spark Distributed Computing
description: Interview questions on Spark's distributed computing fundamentals — driver, workers, executors, task slots, cluster managers, resource allocation, and heartbeats.
content:
ning a separate Hadoop/YARN stack just for one workload. It also brings Spark into the same container-based deployment, resource isolation, and autoscaling tooling used for the rest of the infrastructure, rather than treating Spark's cluster management as a separate concern.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="cmc-04" number={4} question="What's the difference between client mode and cluster mode, and does it apply across all cluster managers?" difficulty="medium" topic="Cluster Managers">
In **client mode**, the driver runs on the machine that submitted the job (outside the cluster manager's control) — simple, but the job dies if that machine disconnects. In **cluster mode**, the driver itself runs as a process inside the cluster, managed the same way executors are — more resilient, since

title: Spark Distributed Computing
description: Interview questions on Spark's distributed computing fundamentals — driver, workers, executors, task slots, cluster managers, resource allocation, and heartbeats.
content:
the submitting machine can disconnect without killing the job. The distinction applies to YARN, Mesos, and Kubernetes; Standalone supports both too, though client mode is more common for quick, local-to-cluster submissions.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

## Spark Master and Worker Roles

<QuestionList topic="Spark Master and Worker Roles" storagePrefix="spark-dcf-master-worker">

<QuestionCard id="smw-01" number={1} question="In Standalone mode, what does the Spark master do?" difficulty="easy" topic="Master/Worker">
The Spark master is Standalone mode's own cluster manager process — it arbitrates resources across the applications submitted to the cluster, keeping track of which workers are available and deciding how to allocate them, analogous to the role YARN's ResourceManager or Mesos' master plays for those cluster managers.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="smw-02" number={2} question="How do workers register with the master, and what happens after that?" difficulty="medium" topic="Master/Worker">
Each worker process registers itself

title: Spark Distributed Computing
description: Interview questions on Spark's distributed computing fundamentals — driver, workers, executors, task slots, cluster managers, resource allocation, and heartbeats.
content:
with the master on startup, reporting its available resources (cores, memory). Once registered, the master can launch executors on that worker in response to application requests, and the worker continues reporting status back so the master's view of cluster capacity stays current.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="smw-03" number={3} question="What happens to running applications if the Standalone master goes down, and how is that mitigated?" difficulty="hard" topic="Master/Worker">
Without high availability configured, losing the master means no new applications can be scheduled and existing ones may be affected, since there's no longer a coordinator for cluster resources. Spark mitigates this with **standby masters coordinated through Apache ZooKeeper** — if the active master fails, a

standby is elected to take over, or with simpler **single-node recovery** using local filesystem state for smaller, less critical deployments.
</QuestionCard>

## Resource Allocation Strategies

<QuestionList topic="Resource Allocation Strategies" storagePrefix="spark-dcf-resource-alloc">

<QuestionCard id="ras-01" number={1} question="What is static resource allocation, and what's its main drawback?" difficulty="easy" topic="Resource Allocation">
Static allocation reserves a fixed number of executors (and their cores/memory) for the entire lifetime of an application, set at submission time. Its main drawback is inefficiency: those resources stay reserved even during periods where the job has little or no work to do, unavailable to any other application that could have used them.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="ras-02" number={2} question="What does per-job configuration mean in the context of resource allocation?" difficulty="medium" topic="R

esource Allocation">
It means explicitly tuning `--num-executors`, `--executor-cores`, and `--executor-memory` for each specific job's known workload, rather than relying on cluster-wide defaults. It trades the convenience of a one-size-fits-all setting for resource usage that actually matches what a given job needs — assuming someone characterizes that job's needs correctly.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="ras-03" number={3} question="How would you decide how many executors and cores to allocate to a Spark job?" difficulty="hard" topic="Resource Allocation">
Base it on the data volume and partition count (enough parallelism to keep executors busy without so many tiny tasks that scheduling overhead dominates), the cluster's total available capacity (leaving room for other jobs), and emp

## Dynamic Resource Allocation

<QuestionList topic="Dynamic Resource Allocation" storagePrefix="spark-dcf-dynamic-alloc">

<QuestionCard id="dra-01" number={1} question="What is dynamic resource allocation, and what problem does it solve?" difficulty="medium" topic="Dynamic Allocation">
Dynamic allocation lets Spark scale the number of executors for an application up and down at runtime based on actual workload, rather than holding a fixed count for the whole job. It solves static allocation's core inefficiency — a job with bursty or uneven work no longer has to either over-provision for its peak or under-provision and bottleneck.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dra-02" number={2} question="What triggers Spark to request additional executors under dynamic allocation?" difficulty="mediu

A backlog of pending tasks that existing executors can't get to fast enough — when the scheduler sees more runnable tasks than available task slots for longer than a configured timeout, it requests more executors from the cluster manager. When executors sit idle past a separate configured timeout with no tasks to run, they're released back to the cluster.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dra-03" number={3} question="What are the trade-offs or risks of enabling dynamic allocation?" difficulty="hard" topic="Dynamic Allocation">
Releasing an executor that's holding cached data means that data has to be recomputed later if it's needed again, which can undercut the benefit of caching in workloads that rely heavily on it — mitigated in some setups by external shu

## Node Heartbeats and Health Checks

<QuestionList topic="Node Heartbeats and Health Checks" storagePrefix="spark-dcf-heartbeats">

<QuestionCard id="nhh-01" number={1} question="What is a heartbeat in the context of Spark's cluster architecture?" difficulty="easy" topic="Heartbeats">
A heartbeat is a periodic signal an executor sends back to the driver, confirming it's still alive and reporting status information like block/cache updates. It's the mechanism the driver relies on to distinguish "this executor is just busy" from "this executor has failed."
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="nhh-02" number={2} question="What happens when the driver misses heartbeats from an executor?" difficulty="medium" topic="Heartbeats">
After a configured timeout with no heartbeat, the driver considers t

content:
hat executor lost. It marks the executor's in-flight tasks as failed and reschedules them elsewhere, and treats any data cached only on that executor as gone — to be recomputed from lineage if it's needed again.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="nhh-03" number={3} question="Why do heartbeats matter for both fault tolerance and metrics/monitoring?" difficulty="medium" topic="Heartbeats">
For fault tolerance, they're the detection mechanism that makes recovering from a lost executor possible at all — without them, the driver would have no reliable way to know a failure occurred. For monitoring, the same heartbeat channel carries the status and metrics data that powers the Spark UI's live view of executor and task state, so heartbeats double as the system's basic health-check and telemetry p

## Cluster Architecture & Execution Lifecycle: From Action to Task

**Every Spark action sets off the same chain of translation — job, into stages, into tasks — and the one decision that shapes that chain more than any other is whether a transformation can pipeline within a stage or forces a shuffle and a brand-new one.**

title: Spark Execution Lifecycle
description: Interview questions on how a Spark application is scheduled and executed — job/stage/task hierarchy, the DAG scheduler, dependencies, data locality, and shuffle mechanics.
content:
## Key Concepts

An **action** (like `collect()` or `count()`) triggers one **job**. The **DAG scheduler** walks that job's chain of transformations backward and splits it into **stages**, cutting a new stage boundary every time it hits a **wide dependency** — a transformation like `groupBy` or `join` that needs data from other partitions, forcing a **shuffle**. Transformations with only **narrow dependencies** (`map`, `filter`) don't need a shuffle and get pipelined together inside the same stage. Each stage then becomes a set of parallel **tasks**, one per partition, handed to the **task scheduler**, which assigns them to executor cores with a strong preference for **data locality** — running a task where its data already lives, to avoid moving data over the network at all.

## Job, Stage, and Task Hierarchy

<QuestionList topic="Job, Stage, and Task Hierarchy" storagePrefix="spark-el-job-stage-task">

<QuestionCard id="jst-01" number={1} question="What are jobs, stages, and tasks, and how do they relate to each other?" difficulty="easy" topic="Job/Stage/Task">
A **job** is the full unit of work triggered by one action. The DAG scheduler splits a job into **stages**, each stage a group of transformations that can run without a shuffle between them. Each stage is then broken into **tasks** — one task per partition — which are the actual units of work sent to executors. The hierarchy is strictly top-down: one job contains many stages, and each stage contains many tasks.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="jst-02" number={2} question="What triggers a new job in Sp

Calling several actions on the same lineage triggers several separate jobs, each potentially recomputing shared upstream work unless it was cached.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="jst-03" number={3} question="How many tasks does a single stage typically create, and what determines that number?" difficulty="medium" topic="Job/Stage/Task">

## DAG Scheduler Flow

<QuestionList topic="DAG Scheduler Flow" storagePrefix="spark-el-dag-scheduler">

<QuestionCard id="dsf-01" number={1} question="What does the DAG scheduler do?" difficulty="medium" topic="DAG Scheduler">
It translates the logical plan of RDD/DataFrame transformations — built up lazily as the application code runs — into a physical execution plan: a directed acyclic graph of stages, with dependencies between them tracked explicitly. It's the component responsible for deciding *where* stage boundaries go, before anything is actually scheduled onto executors.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dsf-02" number={2} question="How does the DAG scheduler decide where to split a job into stages?" difficulty="medium" topic="DAG Scheduler">

<QuestionCard id="dsf-03" number={3} question="What happens when the DAG scheduler detects a failed stage?" difficulty="hard" topic="DAG Scheduler">
It resubmits the failed stage — and, if needed, any earlier stages whose output the failed stage depended on but is no longer available (e.g., shuffle output lost along with an executor). ## Narrow versus Wide Dependencies

<QuestionList topic="Narrow versus Wide Dependencies" storagePrefix="spark-el-dependencies">

<QuestionCard id="nwd-01" number={1} question="What's the difference between a narrow and a wide dependency?" difficulty="easy" topic="Dependencies">
A **narrow dependency** means each output partition depends on a known, small (often single) number of input partitions — no data needs to move between partitions, so it can be computed independently and in parallel without a shuffle. A **wide dependency** means an output partition can depend on data from *any* input partition, which can only be resolved by shuffling data across the cluster first.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="nwd-02" number={2} question="Give examples of transformations that create narrow ver

description: Interview questions on how a Spark application is scheduled and executed — job/stage/task hierarchy, the DAG scheduler, dependencies, data locality, and shuffle mechanics.
content:
sus wide dependencies." difficulty="easy" topic="Dependencies">
**Narrow**: `map`, `filter`, `union`, `mapPartitions` — each output partition is computed purely from its corresponding input partition(s). **Wide**: `groupByKey`, `reduceByKey`, `join` (on non-co-partitioned data), `distinct`, `repartition` — any operation that needs to bring together records that could be scattered across every partition, keyed by something other than their current partitioning.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="nwd-03" number={3} question="Why do wide dependencies force a new stage boundary?" difficulty="medium" topic="Dependencies">
Because satisfying a wide dependency requires a shuffle — every upstream partition's relevant output has to be written out and made available before any downstream partition c

## Task Scheduling and Parallelism

<QuestionList topic="Task Scheduling and Parallelism" storagePrefix="spark-el-task-scheduling">

<QuestionCard id="tsp-01" number={1} question="What does the task scheduler do, once the DAG scheduler has produced stages?" difficulty="medium" topic="Task Scheduling">
The task scheduler takes each stage's set of tasks and assigns them to available executor task slots, submitting them to the cluster manager for actual execution. Where the DAG scheduler decides *what* work needs doing and in what order, the task scheduler decides *which executor* runs each specific task, and when.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="tsp-02" number={2} question="How does the task scheduler decide which executor to assign a task to?" difficulty="medium" topic="Task Scheduling">

title: Spark Execution Lifecycle
description: Interview questions on how a Spark application is scheduled and executed — job/stage/task hierarchy, the DAG scheduler, dependencies, data locality, and shuffle mechanics.
content:
Primarily by data locality — preferring an executor on the same node (or rack) as the task's input data, to avoid transferring it over the network. It also accounts for executor availability (open task slots) and any prior failures, retrying a task on a different executor if it previously failed there.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="tsp-03" number={3} question="What happens when there are more runnable tasks than available task slots?" difficulty="easy" topic="Task Scheduling">
The excess tasks queue, waiting for a slot to free up as running tasks complete. This queued backlog is exactly the signal dynamic resource allocation watches for — a sustained backlog past a configured threshold is what triggers Spark to request additional executors from the cluster manager.
</QuestionCard>

## Data Locality Awareness

<QuestionList topic="Data Locality Awareness" storagePrefix="spark-el-data-locality">

<QuestionCard id="dla-01" number={1} question="What is data locality, and why does Spark care about it?" difficulty="easy" topic="Data Locality">
Data locality is how close a task's assigned execution location is to the data it needs to process. Spark cares because network transfer is far slower than reading local (or in-process) data — scheduling tasks where their data already resides is one of the cheapest, most impactful performance optimizations available, requiring no code changes at all.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dla-02" number={2} question="What are the data locality levels, from most to least preferred?" difficulty="medium" topic="Data Locality">
`PROCESS_LOCA

description: Interview questions on how a Spark application is scheduled and executed — job/stage/task hierarchy, the DAG scheduler, dependencies, data locality, and shuffle mechanics.

L` (data is in the same JVM/executor — fastest), `NODE_LOCAL` (data is on the same physical node, different process), `RACK_LOCAL` (same rack, different node), `NO_PREF` (no locality preference applies), and `ANY` (data is elsewhere on the network — slowest, last resort).
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dla-03" number={3} question="What happens if Spark can't schedule a task at its preferred locality level quickly enough?" difficulty="hard" topic="Data Locality">
Spark waits a short, configurable amount of time (`spark.locality.wait`) hoping a preferred slot frees up, then falls back to progressively less-preferred locality levels rather than waiting indefinitely. This is a deliberate trade-off between locality (less network I/O) and simply keeping executors busy (less idle time) — wait

## Threading Models within Executors

<QuestionList topic="Threading Models within Executors" storagePrefix="spark-el-threading">

<QuestionCard id="twe-01" number={1} question="How do executors run multiple tasks concurrently?" difficulty="medium" topic="Threading">
Each executor is a single JVM process, and it runs multiple tasks concurrently as separate **threads** within that one process — one thread per task slot — rather than launching a separate process per task. This avoids the overhead of starting a new JVM for every task, at the cost of tasks sharing the same process-level resources.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="twe-02" number={2} question="What's shared between tasks running in the same executor, and what's isolated?" difficulty="medium" topic="Threading">
They share the e

title: Spark Execution Lifecycle
description: Interview questions on how a Spark application is scheduled and executed — job/stage/task hierarchy, the DAG scheduler, dependencies, data locality, and shuffle mechanics.
content:
xecutor's JVM heap (including cached RDD/DataFrame partitions and broadcast variables — one copy serves every task in that executor) and its connection pool to external systems. What's isolated is each task's own thread-local execution state — its local variables and call stack don't interfere with other concurrently running tasks' state.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="twe-03" number={3} question="Why can a single misbehaving task affect other tasks in the same executor?" difficulty="hard" topic="Threading">
Because they share the same JVM heap and garbage collector — a task with a memory leak or an unusually large intermediate result can trigger heap pressure or long GC pauses that slow down or destabilize every other task running in that same executor, even though those tasks are oth

content:
erwise logically independent. This shared-fate risk is part of why executor memory tuning matters beyond just "give it more RAM."
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

## Shuffle Phases and Mechanics

<QuestionList topic="Shuffle Phases and Mechanics" storagePrefix="spark-el-shuffle-mechanics">

<QuestionCard id="spm-01" number={1} question="What are the two sides of a shuffle, and what does each do?" difficulty="medium" topic="Shuffle Mechanics">
The **map (write) side**: each upstream task partitions its output records by destination (typically by hashing a key) and writes them to local shuffle files. The **reduce (read) side**: each downstream task fetches the relevant blocks from every upstream task's shuffle output, then merges them into the input it needs to proceed.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="spm-02" number={2} question="What happens during the map (write) side of a shuffle?" difficulty="medium" topic="Shuffle Mechanics">
Each task in the

title: Spark Execution Lifecycle
description: Interview questions on how a Spark application is scheduled and executed — job/stage/task hierarchy, the DAG scheduler, dependencies, data locality, and shuffle mechanics.
content:
upstream stage processes its partition and, instead of passing output directly downstream, writes it to local disk, organized so a downstream task can later fetch exactly the records it needs. If the data to write exceeds available memory, it spills to disk in sorted runs that get merged, which is one of the reasons shuffles are I/O-heavy.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="spm-03" number={3} question="What happens during the reduce (read) side of a shuffle?" difficulty="medium" topic="Shuffle Mechanics">
Each downstream task requests its relevant shuffle blocks from every upstream task that produced output for it — potentially many small network fetches across the cluster — then merges the results into the format the next computation needs (e.g., grouped by key). This fan-in, all-to-all f

description: Interview questions on how a Spark application is scheduled and executed — job/stage/task hierarchy, the DAG scheduler, dependencies, data locality, and shuffle mechanics.
content:
etch pattern is what makes shuffles expensive relative to a task that only touches its own single input partition.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

## Data Serialization during Shuffle

<QuestionList topic="Data Serialization during Shuffle" storagePrefix="spark-el-serialization">

<QuestionCard id="dss-01" number={1} question="Why does data need to be serialized during a shuffle?" difficulty="easy" topic="Serialization">
Shuffle data is written to disk and transferred over the network between JVM processes, and neither of those is possible with live, in-memory JVM objects directly — the data has to be converted into a byte format (serialized) to write and transmit, then converted back (deserialized) once read on the other side.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dss-02" number={2} question="What's the difference between Java serialization and Kryo serialization in Spark?" difficulty="medium" topic="Serialization">
Java serialization

title: Spark Execution Lifecycle
description: Interview questions on how a Spark application is scheduled and executed — job/stage/task hierarchy, the DAG scheduler, dependencies, data locality, and shuffle mechanics.

is Spark's default — broadly compatible, requiring no extra setup, but relatively slow and produces larger serialized output. Kryo serialization is significantly faster and more compact, but requires classes to be registered (or accepts a small correctness/compatibility risk if not) and isn't the out-of-the-box default, so it has to be explicitly enabled via `spark.serializer`.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dss-03" number={3} question="What's a practical consequence of choosing the wrong serialization format?" difficulty="medium" topic="Serialization">
Slower shuffles and higher memory/CPU overhead across every shuffle-heavy stage in the application — since serialization happens on the write side and deserialization on the read side of every single shuffle, a suboptimal choice compoun

description: Interview questions on how a Spark application is scheduled and executed — job/stage/task hierarchy, the DAG scheduler, dependencies, data locality, and shuffle mechanics.
content:
ds across the whole job rather than costing something once. This is why switching to Kryo is one of the standard early recommendations for tuning a shuffle-heavy Spark workload.
</QuestionCard>

## Common Interview Scenarios

- **"Walk me through what happens, stage by stage, when you call `df.groupBy(...).count()` and then `.collect()`."** Trace the full chain: transformations recorded lazily, `collect()` triggers a job, the DAG scheduler splits it at the `groupBy`'s wide dependency into two stages, tasks run per partition, a shuffle happens between the stages, and results return to the driver.
- **"A job has way more stages than you expected — how would you investigate why?"** Point to the Spark UI's stage graph, and look for wide-dependency operations (joins, groupBys, repartitions) that might not have been obvious from the code, including ones introduced implicitly by certain join strategies.
- **"Why might increasing `spark.sql.shuffle.partitions` help a slow shuffle-heavy jo

content:
b, and when could it hurt?"** Discuss more partitions meaning smaller, more parallel shuffle tasks (helpful up to a point) versus scheduling overhead and small-file proliferation if pushed too far.
- **"Explain why data locality matters, using PROCESS_LOCAL vs ANY as your example."** A direct test of understanding why "run the task where the data is" is one of Spark's cheapest optimizations.

## ORC File Structure and Benefits

<QuestionList topic="ORC File Structure and Benefits" storagePrefix="spark-storage-orc">

<QuestionCard id="orc-01" number={1} question="What is ORC, and what's its basic file structure?" difficulty="easy" topic="ORC">
ORC (Optimized Row Columnar) is a columnar storage format, organized into **stripes** (large chunks of rows, typically ~250MB), each holding column data plus lightweight per-stripe indexes, with a **file footer** at the end summarizing stripe locations, row counts, and column statistics.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="orc-02" number={2} question="What benefits does ORC offer, and where did it originate?" difficulty="medium" topic="ORC">
Built-in lightweight indexes at the stripe and row-group level, strong compression, and native suppo

title: Spark File Formats & Storage Optimization
description: Interview questions on ORC file structure, schema evolution across formats, the small file problem, and metadata/footer caching in Spark.
content:
rt for complex/nested types — originally developed to speed up Hive workloads, which is why it remains especially popular in Hive-centric data platforms, though Spark reads and writes it natively as well.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="orc-03" number={3} question="How does ORC's predicate pushdown differ mechanically from Parquet's?" difficulty="hard" topic="ORC">
Both use min/max statistics to skip data that can't match a filter, but ORC additionally maintains lightweight **row-level indexes** within each stripe, letting it skip at a finer granularity (within a stripe, not just between stripes/row groups) in some cases — the practical difference is usually small and workload-dependent, but it's the mechanical distinction worth knowing.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

## Schema Evolution Across Formats

<QuestionList topic="Schema Evolution Across Formats" storagePrefix="spark-storage-schema-evolution">

<QuestionCard id="sef-01" number={1} question="How does Avro handle schema evolution?" difficulty="medium" topic="Schema Evolution">
Avro embeds the schema used to write each file, and readers apply **schema resolution** between that writer schema and their own reader schema — reconciling renamed, added, or removed fields according to compatibility rules (e.g., a new field needs a default value to remain backward-compatible). This makes Avro a strong fit for streaming pipelines where producers and consumers evolve independently.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="sef-02" number={2} question="How does Parquet handle schema evolution, and how is that diff

## Small File Problem and Compaction Strategies

<QuestionList topic="Small File Problem and Compaction Strategies" storagePrefix="spark-storage-small-files">

<QuestionCard id="sfp-01" number={1} question="What is the small file problem, and why does it hurt Spark specifically?" difficulty="medium" topic="Small Files">
Having a very large number of tiny files (well below a typical block/row-group size) overloads two things: the driver's file-listing step (enumerating and planning against thousands of small files is itself expensive) and task-scheduling overhead (launching a task per tiny file wastes far more time on scheduling than the task itself takes to run).
</QuestionCard>

**A join type (inner, outer, semi, anti) describes *what* result you want; a join strategy (broadcast, sort-merge, shuffle hash) describes *how* Spark physically produces it — and the optimizer's job is picking the cheapest strategy for whatever type and data sizes it's actually looking at.**

content:
## Key Concepts

Spark separates **join type** (what rows end up in the result — inner, outer, semi, anti) from **join strategy** (how those rows are physically computed — broadcast hash, sort-merge, shuffle hash). The optimizer picks a strategy based on estimated table sizes and configuration thresholds: **broadcast hash join** when one side is small enough to ship to every executor, **sort-merge join** as the default for two large tables, and **shuffle hash join** as a less commonly chosen alternative. Whatever strategy is picked, **data skew** — a few keys with disproportionately more rows than the rest — can overload individual tasks regardless of which strategy is theoretically correct, which is why skew mitigation is treated as its own topic.

## Inner, Outer, Semi, and Anti Joins

<QuestionList topic="Inner, Outer, Semi, and Anti Joins" storagePrefix="spark-joins-types">

<QuestionCard id="ioa-01" number={1} question="What do inner, left/right/full outer joins each return in Spark?" difficulty="easy" topic="Join Types">
`inner` keeps only rows with a match on both sides. `left_outer` keeps every row from the left DataFrame, filling right-side columns with `NULL` where unmatched. `right_outer` is the mirror image. `full_outer` keeps unmatched rows from both sides at once, `NULL`-filling whichever side didn't match.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="ioa-02" number={2} question="What is a left semi join, and how is it different from an inner join?" difficulty="medium" topic="Join Types">
`left_semi` returns rows from the left Dat

</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="ioa-03" number={3} question="What is a left anti join, and what's a common use case for it?" difficulty="medium" topic="Join Types">
`left_anti` returns rows from the left DataFrame that have **no** match at all in the right DataFrame — the logical opposite of semi join. A common use case: finding customers who have never placed an order (`customers.join(orders, "customer_id", "left_anti")`), or identifying records present in a source system but missing from a destination after a m

<QuestionCard id="ccp-01" number={1} question="What is a cross join, and why does Spark require it to be explicit?" difficulty="easy" topic="Cross Joins">
A cross join pairs every row of one DataFrame with every row of the other — the Cartesian product, with no join condition at all. Spark SQL requires it to be explicitly written as `CROSS JOIN` (or via `.crossJoin()` in the DataFrame API) rather than allowing it to happen accidentally from a join with no condition, specifically to prevent an unintentional, extremely expensive result.

## Shuffle Hash Join

<QuestionList topic="Shuffle Hash Join" storagePrefix="spark-joins-shuffle-hash">

<QuestionCard id="shj-01" number={1} question="What does a shuffle hash join do, step by step?" difficulty="medium" topic="Shuffle Hash Join">
Both sides of the join are shuffled and hash-partitioned by the join key, so matching keys land on the same executor. Then, for each partition pair, Spark builds an in-memory hash table from the smaller side and probes it with rows from the larger side to find matches.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="shj-02" number={2} question="When does Spark's optimizer choose a shuffle hash join over other strategies?" difficulty="medium" topic="Shuffle Hash Join">

<QuestionCard id="shj-03" number={3} question="What's a risk of shuffle hash join if the 'smaller' side isn't actually small enough to fit in memory?" difficulty="hard" topic="Shuffle Hash Join">
Building the hash table requires holding that side's partition in memory — if it's larger than expected (bad size estimates, skew, or a stale statistic), the executor can run out of memory or spill excessively, which is a meaningfully worse failure mode than sort-merge join, whose sort-based approach doesn't require one side to fit fully in memory at once.

## Sort-Merge Join

<QuestionList topic="Sort-Merge Join" storagePrefix="spark-joins-sort-merge">

<QuestionCard id="smj-01" number={1} question="What does a sort-merge join do, step by step?" difficulty="medium" topic="Sort-Merge Join">
Both sides are shuffled and hash-partitioned by the join key, then **sorted** by that key within each partition, and finally merged in a single linear pass — since both sides are sorted, matching rows can be found by walking through them together without needing to build a full hash table in memory.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="smj-02" number={2} question="Why is sort-merge join Spark SQL's default strategy for large-large joins?" difficulty="medium" topic="Sort-Merge Join">
It doesn't require either side to fit entirely in memory — the sorted merge

pass processes data incrementally, spilling to disk as needed — which makes it reliably scalable to two genuinely large tables where broadcasting isn't an option and a full in-memory hash table (as shuffle hash join needs) risks memory pressure.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="smj-03" number={3} question="What's the cost of the sort step, and when might it be avoided?" difficulty="hard" topic="Sort-Merge Join">
Sorting is an extra CPU and I/O cost layered on top of the shuffle itself. It can be skipped if the data is already known to be sorted and co-partitioned by the join key — for example, from a prior sort-merge join or a bucketed table read — letting Spark merge directly without re-sorting.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

<QuestionList topic="Broadcast Hash Join" storagePrefix="spark-joins-broadcast">

<QuestionCard id="bhj-01" number={1} question="What does a broadcast hash join do?" difficulty="easy" topic="Broadcast Hash Join">
It ships an entire copy of the smaller table to every executor (instead of shuffling it), builds an in-memory hash table from it locally on each executor, and then joins the large table's partitions against that local hash table — avoiding a shuffle of the large side entirely.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="bhj-02" number={2} question="What controls whether Spark automatically uses a broadcast join, and how do you force one?" difficulty="medium" topic="Broadcast Hash Join">

</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="bhj-03" number={3} question="What's the risk of broadcasting a table that turns out to be larger than expected?" difficulty="hard" topic="Broadcast Hash Join">
Every executor has to hold a full copy of the broadcast table in memory — if it's much larger than estimated (stale statistics, an unexpectedly large filtered result, or a manually forced hint on a table that grew), it can cause widespread executor out-of-memory errors across the whole cluster simultaneously, since the oversized data is duplicated everywhere at once.

It estimates each side's size from table/column statistics (if collected) or file metadata, checks whether either side is small enough to broadcast, and otherwise defaults toward sort-merge join for two large sides — essentially a cost-based decision, though it can go wrong when statistics are missing or stale.

## Handling Data Skew in Joins

<QuestionList topic="Handling Data Skew in Joins" storagePrefix="spark-joins-skew">

<QuestionCard id="dsj-01" number={1} question="What is data skew in the context of a join, and why does it hurt performance?" difficulty="medium" topic="Data Skew">
Skew is when a small number of join key values have disproportionately many rows compared to the rest — a hash-partitioned shuffle sends all of one key's rows to a single task, so a heavily skewed key overloads just that one task while every other task finishes quickly and sits idle, dragging out the whole job's completion time.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dsj-03" number={3} question="How does AQE's skew join optimization handle this automatically?" difficulty="medium" topic="Data Skew">

All three lakehouse formats solve the same core problem — bringing ACID transactions, upserts, and schema management to plain object storage — but each does it with a different metadata mechanism: Delta's linear `_delta_log` commit sequence, Iceberg's snapshot/manifest hierarchy, and Hudi's timeline plus Copy-on-Write/Merge-on-Read table types. That difference in *how* metadata is tracked is what underlies every capability on this page: **time travel** works because each format keeps enough history to reconstruct an old table state, **schema evolution** rules depend on how strictly each format validates a write against the tracked schema, and **`MERGE INTO`** is the SQL-level upsert pattern every format ultimately supports, even though the physical mechanics of applying it

<QuestionCard id="ttq-01" number={1} question="What is time travel, and what mechanism underlies it across Delta, Iceberg, and Hudi?" difficulty="easy" topic="Time Travel">
Time travel means querying a table as it existed at a past version or timestamp, rather than only its current state. It's possible because each format retains historical metadata pointing at the exact set of files that made up the table at each prior commit — Delta's transaction log, Iceberg's snapshot history, and Hudi's timeline all serve this same purpose, just structured differently.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="ttq-02" number={2} question="How do you query a table as of a past

Delta: `SELECT * FROM table VERSION AS OF 12` or `TIMESTAMP AS OF '2024-01-01'`. Iceberg: `SELECT * FROM table.snapshots` to inspect history, then `SELECT * FROM table FOR VERSION AS OF <snapshot_id>` or `FOR TIMESTAMP AS OF ...`. The concepts are identical; the exact SQL syntax and the underlying identifier (Delta's version number vs. Iceberg's snapshot ID) differ.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="ttq-03" number={3} question="What's the practical retention trade-off that limits how far back time travel can go?" difficulty="medium" topic="Time Travel">
Retaining every historical version indefinitely means keeping every file that was ever part of any past snapshot, which grows storage cost

## Schema Evolution Strategies

<QuestionList topic="Schema Evolution Strategies" storagePrefix="spark-lakehouse-schema-evolution">

<QuestionCard id="ses-01" number={1} question="What schema changes are typically 'safe'/automatic across lakehouse formats, and which require explicit action?" difficulty="medium" topic="Schema Evolution">
Generally safe and often automatic: adding a new nullable column, widening a numeric type (e.g., `int` to `long`). Generally requiring explicit action or migration: renaming a column, narrowing a type, or removing a column — changes that could silently break existing readers or lose data if applied without deliberate intent.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="ses-02" number={2} question="How does Delta's schema enforcement + evolution flag differ from Icebe

rg's approach to schema changes?" difficulty="hard" topic="Schema Evolution">
Delta enforces the existing schema strictly by default (a write with an unexpected column fails), and schema evolution has to be explicitly opted into per write (`mergeSchema` option, or `ALTER TABLE`). Iceberg tracks schema changes as first-class, versioned metadata operations (`ALTER TABLE ... ADD COLUMN`, tracked with its own history) and identifies columns by a stable ID rather than by name/position, which makes some evolution operations (like column renames) safer and more explicit than in formats that match columns positionally.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="ses-03" number={3} question="What's the risk of allowing unrestricted automatic schema evolution in a production table?" difficulty="medium" topic

An upstream producer's unintentional change — a typo'd column name, an unexpected new field — can silently alter the table's schema without review, potentially breaking downstream consumers that expected a stable contract or introducing columns nobody intended to add permanently. This is why most teams treat automatic schema evolution as something to enable deliberately per-table rather than as a blanket default.

## MERGE INTO Syntax and Upsert Patterns

<QuestionList topic="MERGE INTO Syntax and Upsert Patterns" storagePrefix="spark-lakehouse-merge-into">

<QuestionCard id="mip-01" number={1} question="What does a MERGE INTO statement express, and why is it the standard upsert pattern on lakehouse tables?" difficulty="medium" topic="MERGE INTO">
`MERGE INTO` expresses conditional insert/update/delete logic against a target table in one atomic statement, based on matching rows from a source against the target by a key. It's the standard upsert pattern because it replaces what would otherwise require separate, non-atomic `UPDATE` and `INSERT` statements (with the risk of a race or partial failure between them) with one all-or-nothing operation.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="mip-02" number={2} q

title: Spark Lakehouse Table Formats
description: Interview questions comparing time travel, schema evolution, MERGE INTO upsert patterns, and table maintenance across Delta Lake, Iceberg, and Hudi.
content:
uestion="Write a basic MERGE INTO example implementing an upsert." difficulty="medium" topic="MERGE INTO">
```sql
MERGE INTO target_table t
USING source_updates s
ON t.id = s.id
WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET t.value = s.value, t.updated_at = s.updated_at
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT (id, value, updated_at) VALUES (s.id, s.value, s.updated_at);
```
Rows matching on `id` get updated in place; rows in the source with no matching target row get inserted as new — the classic "upsert" shape, expressed declaratively rather than as separate imperative steps.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="mip-03" number={3} question="Why is MERGE INTO's atomicity important compared to doing a separate UPDATE and INSERT as two statements?" difficulty="hard" topic="MERGE INTO">
Two separate statements create a wi

title: Spark Lakehouse Table Formats
description: Interview questions comparing time travel, schema evolution, MERGE INTO upsert patterns, and table maintenance across Delta Lake, Iceberg, and Hudi.
content:
ndow where a concurrent reader could see a partially-applied change (updates done, inserts not yet), or where a failure between the two statements leaves the table in an inconsistent, half-migrated state. `MERGE INTO`'s single-transaction atomicity guarantees readers only ever see the table either fully before or fully after the merge, never a partial mix of the two.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

## Table Maintenance

<QuestionList topic="Table Maintenance" storagePrefix="spark-lakehouse-maintenance">

<QuestionCard id="tmc-01" number={1} question="What does compaction do, and why do lakehouse tables need it regularly?" difficulty="medium" topic="Table Maintenance">
Compaction rewrites many small files into fewer, larger ones. Lakehouse tables accumulate small files naturally from frequent small writes (streaming micro-batches, incremental `MERGE` operations), and without periodic compaction, query performance degrades as file count grows — the same small-file problem that affects any Spark-read dataset, just compounded by these formats' typically higher write frequency.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="tmc-02" number={2} question="What does VACUUM do, and why is a retention wind

title: Spark Lakehouse Table Formats
description: Interview questions comparing time travel, schema evolution, MERGE INTO upsert patterns, and table maintenance across Delta Lake, Iceberg, and Hudi.
content:
ow important before deleting old files?" difficulty="medium" topic="Table Maintenance">
`VACUUM` permanently deletes files that are no longer referenced by any current or recently-retained historical version — freeing storage that old, superseded data versions were holding onto. The retention window (default commonly 7 days) matters because a file being physically deleted also permanently forecloses time travel to any version that depended on it, and could break a long-running query that started reading before the vacuum but hasn't finished.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="tmc-03" number={3} question="What does Z-ordering/OPTIMIZE do, and how is it different from a table's underlying partitioning scheme?" difficulty="hard" topic="Table Maintenance">
Z-ordering co-locates related data wi

title: Spark Lakehouse Table Formats
description: Interview questions comparing time travel, schema evolution, MERGE INTO upsert patterns, and table maintenance across Delta Lake, Iceberg, and Hudi.
content:
thin files based on the values of one or more columns, so a filter on those columns can skip more files/row-groups than it otherwise would — it's a *physical layout* optimization applied within and across files, distinct from partitioning, which is a *directory-level* organizational scheme. Z-ordering is particularly useful for filter columns that aren't good partition-key candidates (too high cardinality to partition by directly, but still worth co-locating for filter efficiency).
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

<QuestionCard id="esr-01" number={1} question="What is a schema registry, and why does it matter specifically for streaming/Avro pipelines?" difficulty="medium" topic="Schema Registries">
A schema registry (Confluent Schema Registry, AWS Glue Schema Registry) is a centralized service that stores and versions schemas — typically Avro or Protobuf — separately from the messages themselves. It matters for streaming because a continuous stream of messages has no natural place to embed a full schema per message cheaply, and producers/consumers need a shared, evolving contract without redeploying in lockstep.

**MLlib and GraphFrames both apply the same underlying idea — describe a computation as a composable pipeline of DataFrame operations and let Spark distribute it — to two workloads that don't look anything like typical ETL: fitting a model across many iterations, and traversing a graph's relationships at scale.**

title: Spark Machine Learning & Graph Processing
description: Interview questions on MLlib's Pipeline API, feature engineering, hyperparameter tuning, model persistence, and GraphFrames graph algorithms.
content:
## Key Concepts

MLlib's **Pipeline API** chains **Transformers** (stateless, `transform()`-only feature steps) and **Estimators** (`fit()`-producing algorithms, including the feature-engineering steps that need to learn something from the data first, like `StringIndexer`) into one reusable, serializable object — the same Pipeline that trains a model is what gets saved and later loaded for **serving**. **GraphFrames** applies the equivalent idea to graphs: it's the DataFrame-based successor to the older, RDD-based GraphX, representing vertices and edges as DataFrames so graph algorithms (**PageRank**, connected components, shortest paths) and ordinary relational operations can be freely mixed in the same query, instead of living in a separate graph-only API.

## MLlib Pipeline API

<QuestionList topic="MLlib Pipeline API" storagePrefix="spark-ml-pipeline-api">

<QuestionCard id="mpa-01" number={1} question="What are Transformers and Estimators, and how do they compose into a Pipeline?" difficulty="medium" topic="Pipeline API">
A **Transformer** implements `transform()`, converting one DataFrame into another — typically by appending a new column (a feature vector, a prediction). An **Estimator** implements `fit()`, learning from a DataFrame and producing a Model (itself a Transformer). A `Pipeline` is an ordered sequence of these stages, run in order, with each stage's output DataFrame feeding into the next.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="mpa-02" number={2} question="Why does chaining stages into a single Pipeline object matter beyond just c

content:
alling each step manually?" difficulty="medium" topic="Pipeline API">
A Pipeline can be fit, evaluated, and — critically — **saved and reloaded as one unit**, guaranteeing that the exact same sequence of feature transformations used during training is applied identically at inference time. Calling each step manually risks the training and serving code silently drifting apart over time, which is a common and hard-to-debug source of model quality issues in production.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="mpa-03" number={3} question="What happens when you call fit() on a Pipeline containing both Transformers and Estimators?" difficulty="hard" topic="Pipeline API">
Each stage runs in order: a plain Transformer stage just applies its `transform()` and passes the result on, while an Estimator stag

## Feature Engineering at Scale

<QuestionList topic="Feature Engineering at Scale" storagePrefix="spark-ml-feature-eng">

<QuestionCard id="fes-01" number={1} question="What does VectorAssembler do, and why do most MLlib algorithms require it?" difficulty="medium" topic="Feature Engineering">
`VectorAssembler` combines multiple individual columns into a single feature vector column — most MLlib algorithms expect exactly one vector column as their feature input, not a set of separate scalar columns, so `VectorAssembler` is almost always the final feature-prep step immediately before model training.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="fes-02" number={2} question="What's the difference between StringIndexer and OneHotEncoder, and why are they often used together?" difficulty="medium" topic="F

eature Engineering">
`StringIndexer` converts a categorical string column into numeric indices (by frequency). `OneHotEncoder` then converts those numeric indices into a sparse binary vector, avoiding the false sense of ordinal relationship a raw numeric index would otherwise imply to an algorithm (e.g., "category 3" isn't meaningfully "more" than "category 1"). They're typically chained: string → index → one-hot vector.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="fes-03" number={3} question="Why are these feature engineering steps implemented as Pipeline stages rather than one-off DataFrame transformations?" difficulty="hard" topic="Feature Engineering">
`StringIndexer` and similar steps are Estimators — they need to `fit()` on the training data first (learning the category-to-index mapping, for e

xample) before they can `transform()` anything, including new data at inference time. Wrapping them as Pipeline stages ensures that learned mapping is captured, saved, and reapplied consistently, rather than being silently re-derived (and potentially different) each time the transformation logic runs.
</QuestionCard>

## Model Training and Hyperparameter Tuning

<QuestionList topic="Model Training and Hyperparameter Tuning" storagePrefix="spark-ml-tuning">

<QuestionCard id="mht-01" number={1} question="What does CrossValidator do, and how does it differ from TrainValidationSplit?" difficulty="medium" topic="Hyperparameter Tuning">
`CrossValidator` splits the training data into k folds and evaluates each candidate parameter combination across all k, averaging the results for a more robust estimate. `TrainValidationSplit` instead uses a single train/validation split — faster and cheaper, but a noisier, less reliable estimate of how well a given parameter combination will generalize.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="mht-02" number={2} question="How does a parameter grid work with CrossValidator?" diffic

title: Spark Machine Learning & Graph Processing
description: Interview questions on MLlib's Pipeline API, feature engineering, hyperparameter tuning, model persistence, and GraphFrames graph algorithms.
content:
ulty="medium" topic="Hyperparameter Tuning">
A `ParamGridBuilder` defines the specific values to try for each hyperparameter (e.g., regularization strength, tree depth), and `CrossValidator` exhaustively evaluates every combination in that grid across all folds — the total number of model fits is `(grid combinations) × (number of folds)`, which grows quickly as either dimension increases.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="mht-03" number={3} question="Why does hyperparameter tuning via CrossValidator get expensive quickly, and how does Spark parallelize it?" difficulty="hard" topic="Hyperparameter Tuning">
Every combination-fold pair requires a full model fit, so a modest grid (say, 4 parameters × 3 values each) with 5-fold cross-validation means potentially hundreds of full training runs.

title: Spark Machine Learning & Graph Processing
description: Interview questions on MLlib's Pipeline API, feature engineering, hyperparameter tuning, model persistence, and GraphFrames graph algorithms.
content:
Spark can run multiple of these fits in parallel across the cluster (`parallelism` parameter on `CrossValidator`) rather than strictly sequentially, trading cluster resource usage for faster overall tuning time.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

## Model Persistence and Serving

<QuestionList topic="Model Persistence and Serving" storagePrefix="spark-ml-persistence">

<QuestionCard id="mps-01" number={1} question="How do you save and load a trained Pipeline in Spark?" difficulty="easy" topic="Model Persistence">
`pipelineModel.write.overwrite().save(path)` persists the fitted pipeline (including every stage's learned state) to storage, and `PipelineModel.load(path)` reconstructs it later — the same saved artifact can be loaded back into a fresh Spark session for either continued evaluation or inference.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="mps-02" number={2} question="What's the difference between serving a model by loading it back into Spark versus exporting it to a lighter runtime?" difficulty="medium" topic="Model Persistence">
L

title: Spark Machine Learning & Graph Processing
description: Interview questions on MLlib's Pipeline API, feature engineering, hyperparameter tuning, model persistence, and GraphFrames graph algorithms.
content:
oading it back into Spark means inference still runs through a full Spark application — appropriate for large-batch scoring jobs, but heavyweight (JVM startup, cluster resources) for a single low-latency prediction request. Exporting to a lighter runtime (via formats like ONNX or MLeap) lets a small, fast, dependency-light process serve predictions without needing Spark running at all.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="mps-03" number={3} question="Why might exporting to a lighter runtime be preferred for low-latency inference specifically?" difficulty="medium" topic="Model Persistence">
A live request-response API (a website recommending a product in real time, for example) can't tolerate Spark's startup and per-request overhead — a lightweight serving runtime can respond in single-digit

milliseconds, where invoking a Spark job per request would be orders of magnitude slower and far more resource-intensive for what's ultimately a single small computation.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

## GraphFrames for Graph Processing

<QuestionList topic="GraphFrames for Graph Processing" storagePrefix="spark-ml-graphframes">

<QuestionCard id="gfp-01" number={1} question="What is GraphFrames, and how does it differ from GraphX?" difficulty="medium" topic="GraphFrames">
GraphFrames is a DataFrame-based graph processing library, layered on top of GraphX, that represents a graph's vertices and edges as ordinary DataFrames rather than RDDs. It differs from GraphX the same way DataFrames differ from RDDs generally — schema awareness, Catalyst optimization, and a higher-level, more approachable API, at the cost of being a separate library rather than Spark-core built-in.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="gfp-02" number={2} question="How are vertices and edges represented in GraphFrames?"

As two DataFrames: a vertices DataFrame with (at minimum) an `id` column plus any vertex properties as additional columns, and an edges DataFrame with `src` and `dst` columns (referencing vertex IDs) plus any edge properties — a `GraphFrame` is constructed from this pair: `GraphFrame(verticesDF, edgesDF)`.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="gfp-03" number={3} question="What's the practical benefit of graph and relational (DataFrame) operations being able to mix freely?" difficulty="medium" topic="GraphFrames">
A real analysis often needs both — filtering vertices/edges with ordinary DataFrame `WHERE` conditions, joining in external attributes, then running a graph algorithm on the result — and GraphFrames lets all of that happen in one coherent pipel

<QuestionCard id="gap-01" number={1} question="What does the connected components algorithm compute, and what's a real use case?" difficulty="medium" topic="Graph Algorithms">
It finds groups of vertices that are all reachable from each other through some path of edges, assigning each vertex a component ID. A real use case: entity resolution — treating records that share an identifying attribute (same email, same phone number) as edges, connected components groups all records that ultimately trace back to the same underlying entity, even through indirect chains of shared attributes.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="gap-03" number={3} question="How do these built-in algorithms scale across a cluster compared to a hand-written iterative implementation?" difficulty="hard" topic="Graph Algorithms">
They're implemented using GraphFrames'/GraphX's distributed message-passing model (built on Pregel-style iteration), so the same algorithm runs correctly whether the graph fits on one machine or spans a large cluster — a naive hand-writte

## Key Concepts

Both connectors share a design philosophy: don't treat the source as a generic remote table — mirror its native physical layout to make reads and writes efficient. The **Spark Cassandra Connector** aligns Spark partitions to Cassandra's own **token ranges**, so each task reads from data that's already co-located on specific replicas. The **MongoDB Spark Connector** converts **BSON** documents into Spark's `Row`/schema representation, and can push **aggregation pipeline** stages down to MongoDB itself rather than pulling raw documents across the wire. Both also expose the source database's own consistency knobs — Cassandra's **consistency levels**, MongoDB's **write concern** — directly through connector configuration, since neither source has a JDBC-style universal semanti

<QuestionCard id="cap-01" number={1} question="How does the connector decide how to partition data when reading from Cassandra?" difficulty="medium" topic="Cassandra Partitioning">

## Cassandra Write Consistency Levels

<QuestionList topic="Cassandra Write Consistency Levels" storagePrefix="spark-nosql-cassandra-consistency">

<QuestionCard id="cwc-01" number={1} question="What consistency level does the Spark Cassandra Connector use for writes, and how do you change it?" difficulty="medium" topic="Write Consistency">
It's configurable via the `spark.cassandra.output.consistency.level` option (or per-write via DataFrame writer options), accepting the same levels Cassandra itself supports — `ONE`, `QUORUM`, `ALL`, and others — controlling how many replicas must acknowledge each write before the connector considers it successful.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="cwc-02" number={2} question="Why might you choose a weaker consistency level specifically for a large batc

title: Spark NoSQL Database Integration
description: Interview questions on connecting Spark to Cassandra and MongoDB — connector setup, token-range-aware partitioning, consistency/write concern, pipeline pushdown, and schema conversion.
content:
h write from Spark?" difficulty="medium" topic="Write Consistency">
A large distributed write job issues an enormous number of individual writes; requiring `ALL` replica acknowledgment on every single one adds latency that compounds across millions of rows. A weaker level like `ONE` or `LOCAL_QUORUM` trades some durability guarantee for meaningfully faster bulk load throughput — a trade-off that's often acceptable for a full reload where correctness can be re-verified afterward, but worth being deliberate about.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

For a deeper look at what Cassandra's consistency levels mean and how the CAP theorem trade-off plays out, see [Cassandra](/level-3-technologies/databases/cassandra/).

<QuestionCard id="cro-01" number={1} question="What does 'cluster-aware' read optimization mean for the connector?" difficulty="medium" topic="Cluster-Aware Reads">
The connector routes each read request directly to the Cassandra replica node(s) that actually hold the relevant token range, rather than going through an arbitrary coordinator node for every request — it has direct knowledge of the cluster's topology and data placement, not just a generic connection to "the database."

<QuestionCard id="mwc-01" number={1} question="How do you configure write concern when writing a DataFrame back to MongoDB via the connector?" difficulty="easy" topic="Write Concern">
Through connector write options, e.g. `df.write.format("mongodb").option("writeConcern.w", "majority").save()` — controlling how many nodes must acknowledge each write (`w:1` for a single node, `majority` for a quorum) before it's considered successful, the same write concern levels MongoDB itself exposes.

The same durability-versus-throughput trade-off as Cassandra's consistency levels: `majority` write concern gives stronger durability guarantees per write but adds latency that compounds across a large distributed job's total write volume, while a lighter concern (`w:1`) writes faster in bulk at the cost of a smaller acknowledgment guarantee per row.

<QuestionCard id="stc-01" number={1} question="Why is reconciling a NoSQL store's flexible schema with Spark's strict schema a real engineering problem?" difficulty="medium" topic="Schema Conversion">
NoSQL document and wide-column stores intentionally don't enforce a single fixed schema across all rows/documents, while Spark's DataFrame model expects a consistent schema for the whole dataset — the connector has to bridge that gap, which means real decisions about how to handle missing fields, type conflicts, and structural inconsistency rather than a clean one-to-one mapping.

content:
## Key Concepts

An executor's JVM heap is split between **execution memory** (shuffles, joins, sorts) and **storage memory** (cached data) under a **unified memory model** that lets one borrow from the other under pressure — the first place to look when an executor is unstable. Beyond the heap itself, **off-heap memory**, **memory overhead**, and **GC tuning** each address a different flavor of memory pressure. Separately, **shuffle partition sizing**, **data skew**, and **broadcast thresholds** all govern how evenly (and how much) data actually moves across the network during a shuffle — usually the second place to look once memory itself isn't the bottleneck.

---

content:
## Execution Memory versus Storage Memory

<QuestionList topic="Execution Memory versus Storage Memory" storagePrefix="spark-perf-exec-storage-mem">

<QuestionCard id="evm-01" number={1} question="What's the difference between execution memory and storage memory?" difficulty="medium" topic="Memory Model">
Execution memory is used for computation that needs working space — shuffles, joins, sorts, aggregations. Storage memory holds cached/persisted RDDs and DataFrames. Both draw from the same overall executor heap region under Spark's unified memory manager, rather than being fixed, separately-sized pools.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="evm-02" number={2} question="How does the unified memory model let these two share one region?" difficulty="medium" topic="Memory Model">
Rather than sta

description: Interview questions on Spark performance tuning — unified memory model, GC tuning, off-heap memory, OOM troubleshooting, shuffle partitioning, skew, and I/O optimization.
content:
tically partitioning memory into separate execution and storage pools (as older Spark versions did), the unified model lets either side use more of the shared region when the other isn't using its share, up to configurable boundaries (`spark.memory.fraction`, `spark.memory.storageFraction`) — dynamically adapting to whichever workload actually needs more space at a given moment.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="evm-03" number={3} question="What happens when execution memory needs more space but storage memory (cached data) is using it?" difficulty="hard" topic="Memory Model">
Execution memory can **evict cached blocks** to reclaim space, since execution (an in-progress computation that must complete) takes priority over storage (cached data that can always be recomputed from lineage if e

content:

</QuestionCard>

## Garbage Collection Tuning

<QuestionList topic="Garbage Collection Tuning" storagePrefix="spark-perf-gc">

<QuestionCard id="gct-01" number={1} question="Why does GC tuning matter specifically for Spark executors?" difficulty="medium" topic="GC Tuning">
Executors often run with large heaps holding significant cached and in-flight data, and a long garbage collection pause on an executor stalls every task running on it simultaneously — at scale, GC pauses are a common, meaningful contributor to overall job latency, not just a background JVM concern.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="gct-02" number={2} question="What's the difference between G1GC and Parallel GC?" difficulty="medium" topic="GC Tuning">
**G1GC** targets predictable, bounded pause times even on large heaps by collecting inc

title: Spark Performance Tuning & Memory Management
description: Interview questions on Spark performance tuning — unified memory model, GC tuning, off-heap memory, OOM troubleshooting, shuffle partitioning, skew, and I/O optimization.
content:
rementally across regions — the modern default for most Spark deployments. **Parallel GC** instead maximizes overall throughput, using multiple threads for collection but with longer stop-the-world pauses — a reasonable choice when raw throughput matters more than pause-time predictability.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="gct-03" number={3} question="What symptom in the Spark UI suggests GC is a real bottleneck?" difficulty="medium" topic="GC Tuning">
A high proportion of task time reported as "GC Time" relative to total task duration in the Stages tab — if a meaningful fraction of executor time is spent collecting garbage rather than doing actual work, that's a direct, measurable signal to look at heap sizing, caching behavior, or the collector choice itself.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionList topic="Memory Overhead Limits and OOM Troubleshooting" storagePrefix="spark-perf-oom">

<QuestionCard id="moo-01" number={1} question="What does spark.executor.memoryOverhead reserve space for?" difficulty="medium" topic="OOM Troubleshooting">
Memory beyond the JVM heap that the executor process still needs — JVM overhead itself (thread stacks, metaspace), off-heap allocations, native library memory (e.g., for Python UDFs or certain connectors), and other non-heap usage the cluster manager's container limit still has to account for.
</QuestionCard>

The executor's *container* gets killed by the cluster manager (YARN, Kubernetes) for exceeding its total memory limit — even though the JVM heap itself never technically ran out — because the overhead portion (outside the heap) exceeded what was reserved for it. This often shows up as a cryptic "container killed by YARN for exceeding memory limits" error rather than a standard Java `OutOfMemoryError`.
</QuestionCard>

## Shuffle Partition Sizing

<QuestionList topic="Shuffle Partition Sizing" storagePrefix="spark-perf-shuffle-partitions">

<QuestionCard id="sps-01" number={1} question="What does spark.sql.shuffle.partitions control, and what's its default?" difficulty="easy" topic="Shuffle Partitioning">
It sets the number of partitions Spark uses for shuffle operations (joins, aggregations) in DataFrame/SQL queries, defaulting to 200 — a fixed number applied regardless of the actual data volume involved, unless AQE's dynamic partition coalescing is enabled to adjust it at runtime.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="sps-02" number={2} question="What happens if shuffle partitions are set too low for the data volume?" difficulty="medium" topic="Shuffle Partitioning">
Each partition ends up holding more da

title: Spark Performance Tuning & Memory Management
description: Interview questions on Spark performance tuning — unified memory model, GC tuning, off-heap memory, OOM troubleshooting, shuffle partitioning, skew, and I/O optimization.
content:
ta than it comfortably should, increasing memory pressure per task and raising the risk of spills or executor OOMs — too few, overly large partitions is a common root cause when a shuffle-heavy stage is both slow and unstable.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="sps-03" number={3} question="What happens if shuffle partitions are set too high?" difficulty="medium" topic="Shuffle Partitioning">
Each partition holds too little data to justify its own task, so scheduling overhead (launching, tracking, and finalizing a huge number of tiny tasks) starts to dominate over actual useful work — a different, opposite failure mode from setting the count too low, but also a real performance drag.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

## Data Skew Mitigation and Salting Techniques

<QuestionList topic="Data Skew Mitigation and Salting Techniques" storagePrefix="spark-perf-skew">

<QuestionCard id="dsm-01" number={1} question="Beyond joins, where else does data skew commonly cause problems in a Spark job?" difficulty="medium" topic="Data Skew">
`groupBy`/aggregation operations on a skewed key have the same fundamental problem as a skewed join — one key's rows all land on one task, overloading it while other tasks finish quickly. Any shuffle-based operation keyed on a column with an uneven value distribution is susceptible, not just joins specifically.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dsm-02" number={2} question="How does salting work as a general technique, not just for joins?" difficulty="hard" topic="Data Skew">
The

title: Spark Performance Tuning & Memory Management
description: Interview questions on Spark performance tuning — unified memory model, GC tuning, off-heap memory, OOM troubleshooting, shuffle partitioning, skew, and I/O optimization.
content:
same idea applies beyond joins: append a random suffix to a skewed key before grouping, spreading what would have been one overloaded partition's rows across several artificial sub-keys, then combine the partial results in a second aggregation step afterward — trading one extra aggregation pass for eliminating the single-task bottleneck.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

For the join-specific version of this problem — including AQE's automatic skew join optimization — see [Spark Joins](/level-3-technologies/batch-processing/spark-joins/#handling-data-skew-in-joins).

## Speculative Execution

<QuestionList topic="Speculative Execution" storagePrefix="spark-perf-speculative">

<QuestionCard id="spx-01" number={1} question="What is speculative execution, and what problem does it solve?" difficulty="medium" topic="Speculative Execution">
When a task runs noticeably slower than the median of already-completed tasks in the same stage, Spark launches a duplicate copy of it on a different executor and keeps whichever finishes first, killing the other. It solves the straggler problem — a single slow or partially-failing node dragging out an entire stage's completion time, even though every other task finished long ago.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="spx-02" number={2} question="What are the risks of enabling speculative execution too aggressively?" difficu

description: Interview questions on Spark performance tuning — unified memory model, GC tuning, off-heap memory, OOM troubleshooting, shuffle partitioning, skew, and I/O optimization.
content:
lty="hard" topic="Speculative Execution">
Wasted cluster resources running duplicate work for tasks that were simply doing more work legitimately (not actually stragglers due to a failing node), and — critically — correctness risk for any task with side effects that aren't idempotent (writing to an external system, for example), where running the same logical task twice could cause duplicate writes if not handled carefully.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

## Task Concurrency and Core Allocation Tuning

<QuestionList topic="Task Concurrency and Core Allocation Tuning" storagePrefix="spark-perf-concurrency">

<QuestionCard id="tca-01" number={1} question="What's the relationship between executor cores, task slots, and concurrency?" difficulty="medium" topic="Task Concurrency">
`spark.executor.cores` sets how many task slots an executor has, and each slot can run one task concurrently — so an executor with 4 cores runs up to 4 tasks in parallel. Total cluster-wide concurrency is roughly `(cores per executor) × (number of executors)`.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="tca-02" number={2} question="Why doesn't simply maximizing cores per executor always improve throughput?" difficulty="hard" topic="Task Concurrency">
More cores per executor mean

title: Spark Performance Tuning & Memory Management
description: Interview questions on Spark performance tuning — unified memory model, GC tuning, off-heap memory, OOM troubleshooting, shuffle partitioning, skew, and I/O optimization.
content:
s more tasks sharing that executor's single JVM heap and garbage collector concurrently, which can increase GC pressure and memory contention past a certain point — very large executors (many cores, huge heap) can actually perform worse than a larger number of moderately-sized executors, which is why a common rule of thumb caps executor cores around 4-5 rather than maximizing them.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

For how this same executor-sizing trade-off applies at the cluster resource-request level, see [Spark Distributed Computing](/level-3-technologies/batch-processing/spark-distributed-computing-fundamentals/#resource-allocation-strategies).

<QuestionCard id="cct-01" number={1} question="What compression codecs does Spark commonly use for shuffle and storage, and how do they trade off?" difficulty="medium" topic="Compression">
`lz4` and `snappy` prioritize decompression speed with modest compression ratios — good defaults for interactive, latency-sensitive workloads. `zstd` (Zstandard) achieves meaningfully better compression ratios at somewhat higher CPU cost — a good fit when I/O/network is the bottleneck and CPU headroom is available.

## Network and Shuffle I/O Optimization

<QuestionList topic="Network and Shuffle I/O Optimization" storagePrefix="spark-perf-network-io">

<QuestionCard id="nsi-01" number={1} question="What is the external shuffle service, and what problem does it solve?" difficulty="medium" topic="Network I/O">
The external shuffle service runs shuffle-serving independently of individual executor processes, so shuffle output an executor produced remains available for other tasks to fetch even after that executor is removed or lost — without it, losing an executor mid-job means its shuffle output has to be recomputed from scratch, not just re-fetched.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="nsi-02" number={2} question="What shuffle-related settings would you tune to reduce network round-trips?" difficulty="ha

Increasing shuffle fetch buffer sizes to pull more data per network request rather than many small ones, tuning the number of concurrent fetch connections, and enabling shuffle compression to reduce the actual bytes transferred per request — all aimed at the same goal of getting more useful data per network round-trip rather than paying per-request overhead repeatedly.
</QuestionCard>

title: Spark RDD API
description: Interview questions on Spark's RDD API — creation, transformations, actions, lazy evaluation, lineage, persistence, checkpointing, broadcast variables, and custom partitioning.
content:
## Key Concepts

An RDD is an immutable, partitioned, fault-tolerant collection distributed across a cluster. It supports two kinds of operations — **transformations** (lazy, build up a plan) and **actions** (trigger real computation) — and its fault tolerance comes from **lineage**: instead of replicating data, Spark remembers the chain of transformations that produced each RDD, so a lost partition is simply recomputed rather than restored from a copy. Everything else on this page builds on that: **persistence** trades memory for avoiding recomputation, **checkpointing** trims a lineage chain that's gotten too long to recompute cheaply, and **broadcast variables**/**accumulators** are the two escape hatches for sharing state across tasks without an actual shuffle.

<QuestionList topic="RDD Creation Methods" storagePrefix="spark-rdd-api-creation">

<QuestionCard id="rcm-01" number={1} question="What are the ways to create an RDD?" difficulty="easy" topic="Creation">
Three ways: **parallelizing** an existing driver-side collection (`sc.parallelize(list)`), **reading from external storage** (HDFS, S3, a local filesystem — `sc.textFile(path)`), or **transforming an existing RDD** into a new one via a transformation like `map` or `filter`.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="rcm-02" number={2} question="How many partitions does an RDD get by default when read from external storage?" difficulty="medium" topic="Creation">
Typically one partition per block of the source file (e.g., one per 128 MB HDFS block), unless a minimum partitio
