content:
n count is passed explicitly — `sc.textFile(path, minPartitions)`. Requesting more partitions than blocks splits each block further; too few relative to cluster size under-utilizes available parallelism.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

## Transformation Operations

<QuestionList topic="Transformation Operations" storagePrefix="spark-rdd-api-transformations">

<QuestionCard id="tro-01" number={1} question="What is a transformation, and why is it lazy?" difficulty="easy" topic="Transformations">
A transformation (`map`, `filter`, `flatMap`, `groupByKey`, and similar) takes an RDD and returns a new RDD, without modifying the original. It's lazy because Spark doesn't execute it immediately — it only records the operation into the DAG, deferring actual computation until an action forces it, which gives Spark the chance to optimize the whole chain before running any of it.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="tro-02" number={2} question="Why does chaining many transformations together not cost anything until an action runs?" dif

ficulty="medium" topic="Transformations">
Because each transformation just appends to the lineage graph rather than touching data — `rdd.map(f).filter(g).map(h)` builds a three-step plan with zero computation performed, regardless of how large the underlying dataset is. The cost only materializes once an action triggers the DAG scheduler to actually execute that plan against real data.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

## Action Operations

<QuestionList topic="Action Operations" storagePrefix="spark-rdd-api-actions">

<QuestionCard id="aco-01" number={1} question="What is an action, and how is it different from a transformation?" difficulty="easy" topic="Actions">
An action (`collect`, `count`, `reduce`, `take`, `foreach`, `saveAsTextFile`) triggers execution of the RDD's full lineage and returns a real result — to the driver, or written to storage. Where a transformation returns another RDD (still just a plan), an action returns a concrete value or performs a concrete side effect.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="aco-02" number={2} question="Why is calling collect() on a very large RDD dangerous?" difficulty="medium" topic="Actions">
`collect()` pulls every element of the (potentially huge, cluster-d

description: Interview questions on Spark's RDD API — creation, transformations, actions, lazy evaluation, lineage, persistence, checkpointing, broadcast variables, and custom partitioning.
content:
istributed) RDD back into the driver's single-process memory — if the dataset is larger than the driver can hold, it crashes the driver with an out-of-memory error, taking down the whole application. Actions like `take(n)` or writing directly to storage (`saveAsTextFile`) avoid that risk by never requiring the full dataset to live in one place.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

## Lazy Evaluation Model

<QuestionList topic="Lazy Evaluation Model" storagePrefix="spark-rdd-api-lazy-eval">

<QuestionCard id="lem-01" number={1} question="What is lazy evaluation, and what does it let Spark do that eager execution couldn't?" difficulty="medium" topic="Lazy Evaluation">
Lazy evaluation delays running any transformation until an action forces it, building up a full DAG of pending work first. That upfront visibility lets Spark optimize the entire pipeline as a whole — reordering, combining, or eliminating steps — rather than executing and optimizing one operation at a time in isolation, the way eager execution would be forced to.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="lem-02" number={2} question="What's a practical debugging consequence of lazy evaluation?" difficulty="medium

" topic="Lazy Evaluation">
An error inside a transformation (e.g., a bad `map` function) doesn't surface at the line where the transformation was written — it only surfaces later, when an action finally triggers execution, potentially far away in the code from where the actual mistake was introduced. This makes stack traces from Spark errors sometimes point to the action call rather than the transformation that logically caused the problem.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

## Dependency Graphs and Lineage

<QuestionList topic="Dependency Graphs and Lineage" storagePrefix="spark-rdd-api-lineage">

<QuestionCard id="dgl-01" number={1} question="What is RDD lineage, and what is it used for?" difficulty="easy" topic="Lineage">
Lineage is the record of an RDD's parent RDD(s) and the specific transformation that produced it from them, chained all the way back to the original data source. It's what Spark uses for fault recovery: if a partition is lost, Spark replays just the relevant portion of the lineage to rebuild it, instead of needing a replicated copy the way Hadoop does.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dgl-02" number={2} question="What's the cost of a very long, unbroken lineage chain?" difficulty="hard" topic="Lineage">
Recomputing from a very long linea

title: Spark RDD API
description: Interview questions on Spark's RDD API — creation, transformations, actions, lazy evaluation, lineage, persistence, checkpointing, broadcast variables, and custom partitioning.
content:
ge chain after a failure gets progressively more expensive, since it means replaying many transformations, potentially from the very beginning of the pipeline. In extreme cases (very deep iterative algorithms), an excessively long lineage graph can even cause stack overflow issues in the driver when Spark tries to process it — which is exactly the problem checkpointing exists to solve.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

## Persistence and Storage Levels

<QuestionList topic="Persistence and Storage Levels" storagePrefix="spark-rdd-api-persistence">

<QuestionCard id="psl-01" number={1} question="What's the difference between cache() and persist(), and what storage levels are available?" difficulty="medium" topic="Persistence">
`cache()` is shorthand for `persist()` using the default storage level, `MEMORY_ONLY`. `persist()` lets you choose explicitly among levels like `MEMORY_ONLY`, `MEMORY_AND_DISK` (spills to disk if it doesn't fit in memory), `MEMORY_ONLY_SER`/`MEMORY_AND_DISK_SER` (serialized, more space-efficient), and `DISK_ONLY`, plus off-heap and replicated variants.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="psl-02" number={2} question="When would you choose MEMORY_AND_DISK over MEMORY_ONLY?" difficulty=

title: Spark RDD API
description: Interview questions on Spark's RDD API — creation, transformations, actions, lazy evaluation, lineage, persistence, checkpointing, broadcast variables, and custom partitioning.
content:
"medium" topic="Persistence">
When the dataset doesn't reliably fit entirely in available memory — `MEMORY_ONLY` simply recomputes whatever doesn't fit (from lineage) every time it's needed again, while `MEMORY_AND_DISK` spills the overflow to disk instead, trading some read speed for avoiding repeated, potentially expensive recomputation.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

For the full trade-off table across all storage levels and how to pick one, see [Apache Spark](/level-3-technologies/batch-processing/spark/#memory-management--persistence).

## RDD Checkpointing and Lineage Truncation

<QuestionList topic="RDD Checkpointing and Lineage Truncation" storagePrefix="spark-rdd-api-checkpointing">

<QuestionCard id="rct-01" number={1} question="What does checkpointing do, and how is it different from persistence?" difficulty="medium" topic="Checkpointing">
Checkpointing writes an RDD's actual data to reliable, durable storage (like HDFS or S3) and, critically, **truncates its lineage** — the checkpointed RDD forgets how it was derived and is treated as a fresh source going forward. Persistence (`cache`/`persist`) only keeps data around for reuse; it doesn't touch or shorten the lineage graph at all.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="rct-02" number={2} question="Why does truncating lineage matter, beyond just saving recomputation ti

title: Spark RDD API
description: Interview questions on Spark's RDD API — creation, transformations, actions, lazy evaluation, lineage, persistence, checkpointing, broadcast variables, and custom partitioning.
content:
me?" difficulty="hard" topic="Checkpointing">
An extremely long, unbroken lineage chain (common in iterative algorithms that repeatedly transform the same RDD) can grow large enough that Spark itself struggles to process the lineage graph, sometimes triggering driver-side stack overflow errors. Checkpointing periodically resets that chain to a short, known-good starting point, preventing lineage from growing unbounded over a long iterative job.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="rct-03" number={3} question="How do you decide what to checkpoint, and when?" difficulty="medium" topic="Checkpointing">
Checkpointing isn't automatic — the developer decides what's worth it, typically RDDs with long lineage chains and wide (shuffle-requiring) dependencies, where recomputation from scratch would be

content:
expensive. It's commonly applied periodically in iterative algorithms (every N iterations) rather than on every single RDD, since checkpointing itself has a real I/O cost.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

## Recovering Failed Tasks and Executor Loss Mitigation

<QuestionList topic="Recovering Failed Tasks and Executor Loss Mitigation" storagePrefix="spark-rdd-api-recovery">

<QuestionCard id="rft-01" number={1} question="What happens when a single task fails, as opposed to an entire executor being lost?" difficulty="medium" topic="Recovery">
A single failed task is simply retried, typically on a different executor, up to a configured retry limit (`spark.task.maxFailures`) before the whole job is failed. An executor loss is more disruptive — every task that was running on it is marked failed and rescheduled, and any data that was only cached on that executor has to be recomputed from lineage.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="rft-02" number={2} question="What role does lineage play specific

title: Spark RDD API
description: Interview questions on Spark's RDD API — creation, transformations, actions, lazy evaluation, lineage, persistence, checkpointing, broadcast variables, and custom partitioning.
content:
ally in recovering from executor loss, versus just retrying a task?" difficulty="medium" topic="Recovery">
Retrying a task only replays that one task's own logic. Recovering a *lost partition* that was only cached on the failed executor requires lineage — Spark walks back through the transformations that originally produced that partition and recomputes just it, on a healthy executor, rather than needing to redo the entire job from the start.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

## Broadcast Variables

<QuestionList topic="Broadcast Variables" storagePrefix="spark-rdd-api-broadcast">

<QuestionCard id="bcv-01" number={1} question="What is a broadcast variable, and what problem does it solve?" difficulty="easy" topic="Broadcast Variables">
A broadcast variable caches a read-only value on every executor once, instead of Spark shipping a fresh serialized copy of it with every individual task. It solves the redundant-transfer cost of using a large lookup table or set of join keys inside a closure that many tasks reference — without broadcasting, that same data would be re-sent over and over.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="bcv-02" number={2} question="When is a broadcast variable specifically useful for joins?" difficulty="medium" topic="Broadcast Variables">
When

description: Interview questions on Spark's RDD API — creation, transformations, actions, lazy evaluation, lineage, persistence, checkpointing, broadcast variables, and custom partitioning.
content:
joining a large RDD/DataFrame with a much smaller one — broadcasting the small side to every executor lets the join happen locally against in-memory data, avoiding a full shuffle of the large side entirely. This is the same underlying idea behind Spark SQL's broadcast hash join strategy.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

## Accumulator Usage Patterns

<QuestionList topic="Accumulator Usage Patterns" storagePrefix="spark-rdd-api-accumulators">

<QuestionCard id="aup-01" number={1} question="What is an accumulator, and what operations must it support?" difficulty="easy" topic="Accumulators">
An accumulator is a shared variable that tasks running across the cluster can add to, but generally only the driver can read the final value from. It requires the combining operation to be associative and commutative, so it produces the same result regardless of the order tasks happen to run or retry in.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="aup-02" number={2} question="What's a common pitfall when using accumulators for anything beyond simple counters?" difficulty="hard" topic="Accumulators">
Relying on an accumulator's va

title: Spark RDD API
description: Interview questions on Spark's RDD API — creation, transformations, actions, lazy evaluation, lineage, persistence, checkpointing, broadcast variables, and custom partitioning.
content:
lue being updated exactly once per element inside a *transformation* is unsafe — if a task is retried or recomputed (due to a failure, or lazy re-evaluation), the accumulator update inside that transformation can be applied more than once. Accumulator updates inside *actions* are guaranteed exactly-once; the safe pattern is to only rely on accumulators for approximate debugging/monitoring counters, not for values that must be exactly correct.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

## Custom Partitioning (Hash and Range)

<QuestionList topic="Custom Partitioning (Hash and Range)" storagePrefix="spark-rdd-api-partitioning">

<QuestionCard id="cph-01" number={1} question="What is a Partitioner, and what does it guarantee?" difficulty="medium" topic="Custom Partitioning">
A `Partitioner` defines how key-value pairs are distributed across an RDD's partitions, mapping each key to a partition ID. Its core guarantee is that every record for a given key always lands in the same partition — which is what lets operations like `join` and `reduceByKey` avoid a shuffle when both sides already share the same partitioner.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="cph-02" number={2} question="What's the difference between HashPartitioner and RangePartitioner?" difficulty="medium" topic="Cu

</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="cph-03" number={3} question="When would you write a custom Partitioner instead of using the built-in Hash or Range partitioners?" difficulty="hard" topic="Custom Partitioning">
When the data has a known structure the built-in partitioners can't exploit well — for example, deliberately co-locating related keys tha

## Key Concepts

A query moves through four phases before it runs: **analysis** (resolve references against the catalog, validate types), **logical optimization** (apply a fixed set of rewrite rules), **physical planning** (generate candidate execution strategies and pick one, ideally cost-informed), and **code generation** (compile the chosen plan into fused JVM bytecode). That whole pipeline runs *before* any data is touched — it's all planning based on estimates. **Adaptive Query Execution (AQE)** is the newer layer on top: instead of trusting upfront estimates for the whole query, Spark pauses at shuffle boundaries and re-optimizes the *remaining* plan using real, observed statistics — which is how it can coalesce partitions, downgrade a join strategy, or split a skewed partition after

## Logical Plan Analysis and Validation

<QuestionList topic="Logical Plan Analysis and Validation" storagePrefix="spark-catalyst-analysis">

<QuestionCard id="lpa-01" number={1} question="What does the Analyzer do, and what does an 'unresolved' logical plan mean?" difficulty="medium" topic="Analysis">
When a query is first parsed, column and table references are just names — the plan doesn't yet know if `orders` refers to a real table or if `customer_id` is a valid column, which makes it "unresolved." The Analyzer resolves those references against the catalog (checking tables and columns actually exist), and validates types, turning the unresolved plan into a validated logical plan — or failing with an analysis error if something doesn't check out.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="lpa-0

An `AnalysisException`, raised during the analysis phase — before any actual computation runs, since resolving column references against the catalog happens as part of building the validated logical plan, not at execution time. This is why a misspelled column name fails fast, even under Spark's generally lazy execution model.

<QuestionList topic="Rule-Based Logical Plan Optimization" storagePrefix="spark-catalyst-rule-based">

<QuestionCard id="rbo-01" number={1} question="What is rule-based logical plan optimization?" difficulty="medium" topic="Rule-Based Optimization">
Once a logical plan is validated, Catalyst applies a fixed set of rewrite rules to transform it into an equivalent but cheaper plan — without yet considering the actual data or cost. It's "rule-based" because each rule fires whenever its pattern matches, regardless of how large the tables involved actually are.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="rbo-02" number={2} question="Name a few common rule-based optimizations Catalyst applies." difficulty="medium" topic="Rule-Based Optimization">

</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="rbo-03" number={3} question="Why can rule-based optimization alone sometimes make a suboptimal choice?" difficulty="hard" topic="Rule-Based Optimization">
Because it applies rules mechanically without weighing actual cost — a rule that's usually beneficial can occasionally produce a worse plan for a specific data shape it has no visibility into (e.g., reordering joins without knowing which table is actually smaller). ## Physical Plan Generation and Selection

<QuestionList topic="Physical Plan Generation and Selection" storagePrefix="spark-catalyst-physical-plan">

<QuestionCard id="pgs-01" number={1} question="What happens during physical plan generation?" difficulty="medium" topic="Physical Planning">
The optimized logical plan (still an abstract description of *what* to compute) is turned into one or more concrete physical plans describing *how* to compute it — for example, choosing among broadcast hash join, sort-merge join, or shuffle hash join for a given join in the query.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="pgs-02" number={2} question="How does the planner pick among multiple candidate physical plans?" difficulty="medium" topic="Physical Planning">
By estimated cost — using whatever statistics a

## Cost-Based Optimization (CBO)

<QuestionList topic="Cost-Based Optimization (CBO)" storagePrefix="spark-catalyst-cbo">

<QuestionCard id="cbo-01" number={1} question="What is cost-based optimization, and how does it differ from rule-based optimization?" difficulty="medium" topic="CBO">
CBO uses collected table and column statistics (row counts, distinct value counts, min/max, null counts) to estimate the actual cost of different plan choices, then picks the cheapest. Rule-based optimization applies fixed heuristics regardless of data size; CBO makes data-size-aware decisions — most usefully, choosing a better join order or join strategy than a blind heuristic would.
</QuestionCard>

## Whole-Stage Code Generation

<QuestionList topic="Whole-Stage Code Generation" storagePrefix="spark-catalyst-codegen">

<QuestionCard id="wcg-01" number={1} question="What is whole-stage code generation?" difficulty="medium" topic="Code Generation">
It fuses multiple physical operators in a stage (a filter, a projection, an aggregation) into a single generated Java function, compiled and executed as one unit — instead of each operator processing a row and passing it to the next operator through a chain of virtual function calls.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="wcg-02" number={2} question="What overhead does whole-stage code generation eliminate?" difficulty="medium" topic="Code Generation">
The per-row, per-operator virtual function call overhead of the traditional "Volcano" iterator

title: Spark SQL Catalyst Optimizer
description: Interview questions on Spark's Catalyst optimizer — logical/physical plan optimization, CBO, whole-stage codegen, vectorized execution, AQE, plan caching, and explain plans.
content:
model, where each row passes through a `next()` call at every operator boundary. Fusing operators into one generated function lets the JVM optimize the whole sequence as straight-line code, closer to what a hand-written loop would look like.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="wcg-03" number={3} question="Why can't whole-stage code generation extend across a UDF?" difficulty="hard" topic="Code Generation">
Because a UDF's logic is arbitrary, opaque code — the code generator has no visibility into what it does, so it can't be inlined into the generated function the way built-in operators can. The UDF has to be called as a separate, un-fused black-box step, which breaks the otherwise fused pipeline at that point.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

## Vectorized Execution

<QuestionList topic="Vectorized Execution" storagePrefix="spark-catalyst-vectorized">

<QuestionCard id="vex-01" number={1} question="What is vectorized execution?" difficulty="medium" topic="Vectorized Execution">
Processing columnar batches of rows at once, rather than one row at a time — commonly used for reading columnar formats like Parquet, where a whole batch of values for a column can be decoded and processed together as a contiguous block instead of individually.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="vex-02" number={2} question="Why does vectorized execution perform better than row-at-a-time processing?" difficulty="hard" topic="Vectorized Execution">
Processing data in contiguous, columnar batches makes much better use of CPU cache locality and enables SIMD

(single-instruction-multiple-data) style operations on modern hardware, since the same operation is applied uniformly across many values in a tight loop — something a row-at-a-time model, jumping between different fields of different rows, can't exploit nearly as well.
</QuestionCard>

## Adaptive Query Execution (AQE)

<QuestionList topic="Adaptive Query Execution (AQE)" storagePrefix="spark-catalyst-aqe">

<QuestionCard id="aqe-01" number={1} question="What is Adaptive Query Execution, and why does it exist alongside CBO?" difficulty="medium" topic="AQE">
AQE re-optimizes the physical plan **at runtime**, using actual statistics gathered from completed shuffle stages — rather than relying purely on upfront estimates the way CBO does. It exists because even good statistics collected ahead of time can be wrong by the time a query actually runs (stale stats, filters that narrow data more than estimated), and AQE can correct for that using real, observed numbers.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="aqe-02" number={2} question="At what point in query execution does AQE actua

At shuffle boundaries — since a shuffle is already a natural synchronization point where all of a stage's output has to be materialized before the next stage can start, Spark can pause there, inspect the real size and distribution of that output, and adjust the remaining plan accordingly before continuing.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="aqe-03" number={3} question="What are the three main things AQE can do once it re-optimizes?" difficulty="medium" topic="AQE">
**Coalesce** small post-shuffle partitions into larger ones, **switch join strategies** (e.g., downgrade a planned sort-merge join to a broadcast join once actual output size is known to be small), and **split skewed partitions** into smaller sub-partitions to avoid a single str

## Dynamic Partition Coalescing

<QuestionList topic="Dynamic Partition Coalescing" storagePrefix="spark-catalyst-partition-coalescing">

<QuestionCard id="dpc-01" number={1} question="What problem does dynamic partition coalescing solve?" difficulty="medium" topic="Partition Coalescing">
A statically configured shuffle partition count (`spark.sql.shuffle.partitions`) is a single number applied regardless of how much data actually ends up in each partition after filtering — too high a count on a smaller-than-expected result produces many tiny, wasteful tasks with scheduling overhead disproportionate to the actual work.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dpc-02" number={2} question="How does AQE merge small partitions at runtime?" difficulty="medium" topic="Partition Coalescing">
After a sh

</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="djs-01" number={1} question="What is dynamic join strategy switching?" difficulty="medium" topic="Join Strategy Switching">
AQE can change a join's execution strategy at runtime — most commonly, downgrading a planned sort-merge join to a broadcast hash join once it observes that one side's actual post-shuffle output is small enough to broadcast, even though the upfront size estimate didn't indicate that.

## Skew Join Optimization

<QuestionList topic="Skew Join Optimization" storagePrefix="spark-catalyst-skew-join">

<QuestionCard id="sjo-01" number={1} question="What does AQE's skew join optimization do?" difficulty="medium" topic="Skew Join">
It detects shuffle partitions that are disproportionately larger than the rest (a sign of data skew on the join key) using real post-shuffle size statistics, and splits those oversized partitions into smaller sub-partitions that are joined separately against the corresponding data on the other side.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="sjo-02" number={2} question="How is this different from manually salting a skewed key?" difficulty="hard" topic="Skew Join">
Salting requires the developer to identify which keys are skewed and manually rewrite the join

logic to split them. AQE's skew join optimization does this automatically at runtime, based on actually observed partition sizes, without needing the skewed keys to be known or hand-coded around in advance — though manual salting can still be useful in cases or Spark versions where AQE's detection doesn't apply.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionList topic="Plan Caching" storagePrefix="spark-catalyst-plan-caching">

<QuestionCard id="plc-01" number={1} question="What does plan caching do?" difficulty="medium" topic="Plan Caching">
Spark caches parsed and analyzed logical plans for repeated query shapes, so a query executed many times (or with only its literal parameter values changing) doesn't have to re-run the full parser and analyzer from scratch on every single execution.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="plc-02" number={2} question="Why does plan caching matter more for some workloads than others?" difficulty="medium" topic="Plan Caching">
It matters most for workloads that execute the same or very similar query shape a large number of times in a short period — a BI tool or application issuing param

<QuestionCard id="rep-01" number={1} question="What does explain() show, and what are its main variants?" difficulty="medium" topic="Explain Plans">
`explain()` prints the physical plan by default. `explain("extended")` (or `explain(true)`) shows all four stages — parsed, analyzed, optimized logical plan, and physical plan — letting you see exactly what each phase of the pipeline did. `explain("cost")` additionally includes cost estimates where statistics are available; `explain("formatted")` gives a more structured, readable layout.
</QuestionCard>

## Key Concepts

By default, Structured Streaming runs on the **micro-batch** engine — treating an unbounded stream as a sequence of small, discrete batch jobs, each one a normal Spark SQL execution under the hood. **Watermarking** is the mechanism that makes stateful operations (windowed aggregations, deduplication) tractable at all: it declares how late data is allowed to arrive relative to event time, letting Spark eventually drop old state instead of buffering forever. Every one of the ten subtopics on this page ultimately serves one goal — processing a stream **exactly like a batch DataFrame**, with the same API, while still delivering the fault tolerance (**checkpointing**), correctness (**output modes**, **watermarks**), and scale (**state stores**, **joins**) a genuinely unbounded

## Micro-Batch Processing Model

<QuestionList topic="Micro-Batch Processing Model" storagePrefix="spark-streaming-microbatch">

<QuestionCard id="mbp-01" number={1} question="What is the micro-batch processing model in Structured Streaming?" difficulty="easy" topic="Micro-Batch">
Structured Streaming's default engine treats the incoming stream as a sequence of small batch jobs — each trigger interval, it processes whatever new data has arrived since the last batch, using the exact same Spark SQL execution engine and query plan as a batch job would.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="mbp-02" number={2} question="What latency and consistency guarantees does the micro-batch model provide?" difficulty="medium" topic="Micro-Batch">
Latencies typically in the ~100ms range (bounded by how often

title: Spark Structured Streaming
description: Interview questions on Structured Streaming — micro-batch and continuous processing, sources/sinks, Kafka integration, watermarking, state stores, output modes, and streaming joins.
content:
a micro-batch can be triggered and completed), paired with strong exactly-once processing guarantees end-to-end — each micro-batch either fully commits its results and offsets together, or the whole batch is retried, avoiding both duplicate and lost processing.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="mbp-03" number={3} question="What determines how often a micro-batch triggers?" difficulty="medium" topic="Micro-Batch">
The configured trigger interval (`Trigger.ProcessingTime("10 seconds")`, for example) — or, with no trigger explicitly specified, Spark starts a new micro-batch as soon as the previous one finishes, processing continuously back-to-back rather than on a fixed schedule.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

<QuestionCard id="clp-01" number={1} question="What is Continuous Processing mode, and how does it differ from micro-batch?" difficulty="medium" topic="Continuous Mode">
An experimental engine that processes each record as it arrives, rather than grouping records into discrete micro-batches — targeting latencies around ~1ms instead of the ~100ms typical of the micro-batch model, by removing the batch-boundary overhead entirely.
</QuestionCard>

It only provides at-least-once guarant

## Event-Time Watermarking

<QuestionList topic="Event-Time Watermarking" storagePrefix="spark-streaming-watermarking">

<QuestionCard id="etw-01" number={1} question="What is a watermark, and what problem does it solve?" difficulty="medium" topic="Watermarking">
A watermark declares how late data is allowed to arrive, relative to the maximum event time seen so far, before Spark considers it too late to affect existing results. It solves the problem of unbounded state growth — without a watermark, a windowed aggregation would have to keep state for every open window forever, since data could theoretically still arrive for it.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="etw-02" number={2} question="Write an example declaring a watermark on an event-time column." difficulty="medium" topic="Watermarki

```scala
df.withWatermark("event_time", "10 minutes")
  .groupBy(window(col("event_time"), "5 minutes"))
  .count()
```
This tells Spark it can safely drop state for any window more than 10 minutes older than the latest event time it's seen, bounding how long windowed aggregation state has to be kept around.

<QuestionCard id="etw-03" number={3} question="What's the trade-off in choosing a watermark threshold that's too short versus too long?" difficulty="hard" topic="Watermarking">
Too short: legitimately late (but not malicious or broken) data gets dropped and excluded from aggregations, silently producing incomplete results. Too long: state is retained far longer than necessary, growing memory/storage usage and increasing the latency before a window's result is cons

## Stateful Stream Processing and State Stores

<QuestionList topic="Stateful Stream Processing and State Stores" storagePrefix="spark-streaming-state-stores">

<QuestionCard id="ssp-01" number={1} question="What is a state store, and what operations require one?" difficulty="medium" topic="State Stores">
A state store is a versioned, checkpointed key-value store that Structured Streaming uses to persist running state across micro-batches — required by operations like streaming aggregations, deduplication, and `mapGroupsWithState`/`flatMapGroupsWithState`, all of which need to remember something from prior batches to process the current one correctly.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="ssp-02" number={2} question="What state store backends does Spark support, and why would you choose Rocks

DB over the default?" difficulty="medium" topic="State Stores">
The default is an in-memory HDFS-backed state store; RocksDB is an alternative backend that stores state on local disk instead of purely in the JVM heap. RocksDB is chosen for large state sizes that would otherwise strain executor memory or trigger excessive GC pauses — trading some access latency for much better scalability of state size.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="ssp-03" number={3} question="How is state store data made fault-tolerant across micro-batches?" difficulty="hard" topic="State Stores">
State changes are checkpointed to durable storage (alongside offsets) after each micro-batch, so if an executor or the whole application fails, the state store can be reconstructed from the last successful checkpoint rather

<QuestionList topic="Late Data Handling" storagePrefix="spark-streaming-late-data">

<QuestionCard id="ldh-01" number={1} question="What counts as 'late data' in Structured Streaming, and what happens to it?" difficulty="medium" topic="Late Data">
Data whose event time falls before the current watermark — meaning Spark has already decided any window it would belong to is closed and its state discarded. Such records are dropped from windowed aggregations rather than reopening already-finalized results.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="ldh-02" number={2} question="How does late data handling relate to watermarking specifically?" difficulty="medium" topic="Late Data">

## Output Modes

<QuestionList topic="Output Modes" storagePrefix="spark-streaming-output-modes">

<QuestionCard id="omd-01" number={1} question="What do append, update, and complete output modes each emit?" difficulty="medium" topic="Output Modes">
**Append** emits only new rows added since the last trigger (rows already emitted are never modified). **Update** emits rows that are new or have changed since the last trigger. **Complete** re-emits the entire, current result table every single trigger, regardless of what changed.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="omd-02" number={2} question="Which output modes are compatible with which kinds of queries?" difficulty="hard" topic="Output Modes">
Simple, non-aggregating streaming queries (a filter, a map) generally only support `append`. Aggreg

</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="omd-03" number={3} question="Why can't append mode be used with an aggregation that has no watermark?" difficulty="hard" topic="Output Modes">
Append mode promises a row, once emitted, will never be updated — but without a watermark, Spark has no way to know when an aggregate result is truly final, since late-arriving data could theoretically still update any existing group's result at any point. Emitting it under `append` would risk contradicting that "never changes again" guarantee.

<QuestionCard id="ssj-01" number={1} question="What is a stream-static join, and how does it behave each micro-batch?" difficulty="medium" topic="Streaming Joins">
Joining a streaming DataFrame against a static (batch-sourced) DataFrame — the static side is effectively re-scanned (or re-read, depending on caching) each micro-batch, joined against whatever new streaming rows arrived in that batch. It's the simpler of the two join types, since only one side has unbounded state concerns.

content:
## Key Concepts

Good Spark testing practice mirrors the standard test pyramid: fast, isolated **unit tests** on individual transformation functions using small fixture DataFrames and **mocked sources**, sitting on top of a **shared local-mode SparkSession** so the test suite doesn't pay startup overhead per test; fewer, slower **integration tests** running a fuller pipeline against realistic data to catch what unit tests structurally can't. All of that only has value if it's actually run automatically — **CI/CD** packages, tests, and promotes the job across environments — and stays reliable only if **configuration** (paths, credentials, cluster sizing) is externalized so the exact same code runs unmodified from dev through production.

## Shared SparkSession Test Fixtures

<QuestionList topic="Shared SparkSession Test Fixtures" storagePrefix="spark-testing-fixtures">

<QuestionCard id="ssf-01" number={1} question="Why use a single shared SparkSession across a test suite instead of creating one per test?" difficulty="medium" topic="Test Fixtures">
Starting a `SparkSession` has real overhead (JVM startup, session initialization), and creating a fresh one per test multiplies that cost across potentially hundreds of tests — a session-scoped fixture (created once, reused across the whole suite or module) keeps the test suite fast, which matters a lot for a test suite that's meant to be run constantly during development.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="ssf-02" number={2} question="What are the risks of sharing state across

Temp views, cached DataFrames, or configuration changes made in one test can leak into and affect a later test if not explicitly cleaned up between tests — a common source of flaky, order-dependent test failures. Good practice clears temp views and unpersists cached data in a teardown step, or scopes fixtures narrowly enough that this kind of cross-test leakage can't happen.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

It tests that a specific transformation function, given a small, known input DataFrame, produces the expected output DataFrame — verifying the transformation's logic in isolation, run in local mode against tiny in-memory fixtures rather than real cluster-scale data.

<QuestionList topic="Integration Testing for Pipelines" storagePrefix="spark-testing-integration">

<QuestionCard id="itp-01" number={1} question="What does integration testing add that unit tests on individual transformations don't catch?" difficulty="medium" topic="Integration Testing">
Issues that only appear when transformations are chained together and run against real (or realistic) sources and sinks — schema mismatches between stages, configuration problems, connector behavior, and interactions between transformations that each pass their own unit tests individually but don't compose correctly end-to-end.
</QuestionCard>

Real external sources make tests slow, flaky (dependent on network and external service availability), and hard to control precisely (you can't easily construct every edge case in a real Kafka topic). ## Performance Regression and Scalability Benchmarking

<QuestionList topic="Performance Regression and Scalability Benchmarking" storagePrefix="spark-testing-perf-regression">

<QuestionCard id="prb-01" number={1} question="What does performance regression benchmarking track, and why track it over time rather than just once?" difficulty="medium" topic="Performance Benchmarking">
It tracks job runtime and resource usage (and often specific stage/shuffle metrics) against a historical baseline, run repeatedly over time — a one-time performance check only tells you about that specific moment, while ongoing tracking catches a gradual or sudden regression introduced by a later code change or data volume growth before it becomes a production incident.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="prb-02" n

umber={2} question="What kind of change commonly causes an undetected performance regression in a Spark job?" difficulty="medium" topic="Performance Benchmarking">
A seemingly innocuous code change that unintentionally introduces a shuffle where none existed before (a repartition, a join that used to be broadcast but no longer qualifies as data grew), or a change that quietly disables a previously-effective optimization (breaking predicate pushdown by wrapping a filter column in a function, for example) — changes that don't affect correctness at all, so they'd never be caught by functional tests alone.
</QuestionCard>

Running the unit (and often integration) test suite on every change, building/packaging the application artifact (fat JAR, wheel), and — on merge to a release branch — deploying that artifact and promoting it through environments (dev → staging → prod), often with some form of approval gate before production.

## Notebook Development Environments

<QuestionList topic="Notebook Development Environments" storagePrefix="spark-testing-notebooks">

<QuestionCard id="nde-01" number={1} question="What role do notebooks play in a Spark development workflow, and what are their limits for production?" difficulty="easy" topic="Notebooks">
Jupyter and Zeppelin provide interactive, cell-based development against a live `SparkSession` — excellent for exploration, iterating on transformation logic, and visualizing intermediate results. Their limits for production: no built-in versioning/testing discipline, execution order that can silently diverge from the visible cell order, and no natural path to scheduled, automated, or parameterized execution the way a packaged job has.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="n

de-02" number={2} question="What's the risk of 'productionizing' code that was only ever tested interactively in a notebook?" difficulty="medium" topic="Notebooks">
Interactive notebook execution can hide state dependencies — a cell that only works because an earlier cell (possibly since deleted or reordered) set up some prerequisite state — that don't surface until the code is run as a clean, linear script in production and behaves differently or fails outright. Converting notebook exploration into a properly tested, linearly-executable job is a real, necessary step, not just a copy-paste.
</QuestionCard>

## Packaging Dependencies

<QuestionList topic="Packaging Dependencies" storagePrefix="spark-testing-packaging">

<QuestionCard id="pdj-01" number={1} question="What is a fat/uber JAR, and why is it needed for Scala/Java Spark applications?" difficulty="medium" topic="Packaging">
A fat (or "uber") JAR bundles the application's compiled code together with all of its non-Spark-provided dependencies into a single JAR file, so `spark-submit` can run the application without separately needing to locate and provide each dependency — since the cluster's executors need consistent access to every library the code references.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="pdj-03" number={3} question="What's a common failure mode from inconsistent packaging across environments?" difficulty="hard" topic="Packaging">
A version of a library differs between what was used in development/testing and what's actually available on the cluster's executors at runtime — producing behavior that "worked in testing" but fails or behaves subtly differently in production, often surfacing as a confusing runtime erro

## User Defined Functions (UDFs): Extending Spark SQL, and What It Costs

**A UDF lets you write custom logic Spark SQL can't express natively, but that convenience has a real price — Catalyst can't see inside it, can't optimize through it, and (in Python especially) it pays a serialization tax the built-in functions never do.**

## Key Concepts

A **scalar UDF** is the simplest extension point — custom row-at-a-time logic registered and used like any built-in function — but Spark SQL's optimizer treats it as an **opaque black box**: no predicate pushdown through it, no whole-stage code generation across it, none of Catalyst's usual tricks. For Python specifically, a regular UDF pays an even steeper cost: each row crosses the JVM/Python process boundary, serialized and deserialized on the way. **Pandas UDFs** (vectorized, using **Apache Arrow** for the data transfer) close most of that gap by operating on batches instead of single rows. **Higher-order functions** (`transform`, `filter`, `exists`) sidestep the whole trade-off for array/map columns by expressing the logic natively in Spark SQL, no UDF required at all

## Arrow-Based Data Transfer for UDFs

<QuestionList topic="Arrow-Based Data Transfer for UDFs" storagePrefix="spark-udf-arrow">

<QuestionCard id="abd-01" number={1} question="What is Apache Arrow, and what role does it play in Spark?" difficulty="medium" topic="Arrow">
Apache Arrow is a language-independent, columnar in-memory data format designed for efficient data interchange between systems without needing to serialize into an intermediate format each time. In Spark, it's used to move batches of data between the JVM and a Python process for Pandas UDFs, avoiding the row-by-row serialization a regular Python UDF requires.
</QuestionCard>

## Python versus JVM Execution Overhead

<QuestionList topic="Python versus JVM Execution Overhead" storagePrefix="spark-udf-python-jvm">

<QuestionCard id="pjo-01" number={1} question="Why do Python UDFs incur overhead that Scala/Java UDFs don't?" difficulty="medium" topic="Python vs JVM">
Spark itself runs on the JVM. A Scala/Java UDF executes directly inside that same JVM process, with no boundary to cross. A Python UDF requires data to leave the JVM, be serialized, handed to a separate Python worker process, deserialized, processed, and sent back the other way — an entire extra layer of overhead the JVM-native path simply doesn't have.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="pjo-03" number={3} question="How does this overhead compound on a large dataset with many rows?" difficulty="medium" topic="Python vs JVM">
For a regular (non-vectorized) Python UDF, that boundary-crossing cost is paid once *per row*, so it scales linearly with row count and can dominate total runtime on large datasets, even if the actual per-row logic is trivial. ## Built-in Functions versus Custom UDFs

<QuestionList topic="Built-in Functions versus Custom UDFs" storagePrefix="spark-udf-builtin-vs-custom">

<QuestionCard id="bvc-01" number={1} question="Why do built-in Spark SQL functions typically outperform an equivalent UDF?" difficulty="medium" topic="Built-in vs UDF">
Built-in functions run inside Catalyst's optimized execution path — eligible for whole-stage code generation, predicate pushdown, and other Catalyst optimizations the planner can reason about ahead of time. A UDF is opaque to all of that; the optimizer treats it as a fixed, unoptimizable black box it has to work around rather than through.

Whole-stage code generation fuses several physical operators into a single generated Java function per stage, eliminating the virtual-function-call overhead of processing rows through separate operator objects one at a time. It can't extend across a UDF because the UDF's logic is arbitrary, opaque code the code generator has no visibility into — it has to be called as a black-box step, breaking the fused pipeline at that point.

<QuestionCard id="hof-01" number={1} question="What are higher-order functions in Spark SQL, and name a few?" difficulty="medium" topic="Higher-Order Functions">
They're built-in functions that take a lambda expression as an argument and operate directly on array or map columns: `transform` (apply a function to each element), `filter` (keep elements matching a condition), `exists` (check if any element matches), and `aggregate` (reduce an array to a single value) — all native, optimizer-visible operations, not UDFs.

<QuestionCard id="die-01" number={1} question="Why do Python UDF environments need dependency isolation across executors?" difficulty="medium" topic="Dependency Isolation">
A Python UDF's code (and any libraries it imports) has to run identically on every executor's Python worker process. If executors have inconsistent package versions — or the driver's environment doesn't match the executors' — a UDF can behave differently, fail unpredictably, or throw serialization errors depending on which executor happens to run it.

</QuestionCard>

Every window function is evaluated over a **`WindowSpec`** — defined via `Window.partitionBy(...).orderBy(...)`, optionally with a frame boundary — which describes exactly which other rows are "in view" when computing each row's value. `partitionBy` splits rows into independent groups (like `GROUP BY`, but without collapsing them), `orderBy` establishes a sequence within each partition (required for ranking and `lead`/`lag`, optional for plain aggregates), and the **frame** narrows the window further to a specific range of rows relative to the current one — which is what turns a plain partition-wide aggregate into a running total or moving average.

## Ranking Functions

<QuestionList topic="Ranking Functions" storagePrefix="spark-wf-ranking">

<QuestionCard id="rnk-01" number={1} question="What's the difference between rank(), dense_rank(), and row_number()?" difficulty="medium" topic="Ranking Functions">
`row_number()` assigns a strictly unique, sequential number regardless of ties. `rank()` gives tied rows the same rank, then skips the next rank number by the count of ties (1, 2, 2, 4). `dense_rank()` also ties rows together, but doesn't skip the next number (1, 2, 2, 3).
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="rnk-02" number={2} question="Write a query to find the top 3 highest-paid employees per department." difficulty="medium" topic="Ranking Functions">
```scala
val spec = Window.partitionBy("department").orderBy(col("salary").desc)

df.withColumn("rn", row_number().over(spec))
  .filter(col("rn") <= 3)
```
`row_number()` guarantees exactly 3 rows per department even with tied salaries; `rank()` could return more than 3 if the 3rd-place salary is tied with a 4th.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="rnk-03" number={3} question="Why might row_number() be preferred over rank() when deduplicating rows?" difficulty="medium" topic="Ranking Functions">
Deduplication typically wants exactly one "winning" row per group (e.g., the latest record per key) — `row_number()`'s guaranteed uniqueness makes `WHERE rn = 1` deterministic. `rank()` can leave multiple rows tied for rank 1, which means the "deduplicated" result could still contain duplicates if there's a tie in the ordering column.
</QuestionCard>

## Lead and Lag Operations

<QuestionList topic="Lead and Lag Operations" storagePrefix="spark-wf-lead-lag">

<QuestionCard id="lgo-01" number={1} question="What do lead() and lag() do?" difficulty="easy" topic="LEAD / LAG">
`lag(col, n)` returns the value of `col` from `n` rows before the current row within its partition (default `n = 1`). `lead(col, n)` returns the value from `n` rows after. Both require an `orderBy` in the window spec, since "before" and "after" only make sense relative to a defined sequence.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="lgo-02" number={2} question="Write a query using lag() to compute month-over-month change." difficulty="medium" topic="LEAD / LAG">
```scala
val spec = Window.partitionBy("product").orderBy("month")
df.withColumn("prev_revenue", lag("revenue", 1).

  .withColumn("mom_change", col("revenue") - col("prev_revenue"))
```
This avoids a self-join entirely — the "previous row's value" is pulled directly into the current row via the window function.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="lgo-03" number={3} question="What do lead()/lag() return at partition boundaries, and how do you handle it?" difficulty="medium" topic="LEAD / LAG">
`NULL` by default — the first row in a partition has no prior row for `lag`, and the last has no next row for `lead`. Both accept an optional third argument specifying a default value to use instead of `NULL`: `lag("revenue", 1, 0)`.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionList topic="Range versus Row Frames" storagePrefix="spark-wf-frames">

<QuestionCard id="rvf-01" number={1} question="What's the difference between a ROWS frame and a RANGE frame?" difficulty="hard" topic="Frames">
`ROWS` defines the frame by physical row position — "the 2 rows before this one," counted strictly by position. `RANGE` defines it by logical value in the `orderBy` column — "all rows within a certain value distance," treating rows with equal order-by values as peers included together, regardless of how many of them there are.
</QuestionCard>

## Apache Spark: Unified Engine for Big Data Processing

**Apache Spark is a unified, in-memory analytics engine for large-scale data processing — combining batch, SQL, streaming, machine learning, and graph workloads on a single fault-tolerant execution model built around RDDs and DataFrames.**

content:
## Key Concepts

Spark's foundational abstraction is the **RDD (Resilient Distributed Dataset)** — an immutable, partitioned collection of records spread across a cluster that can be rebuilt from its **lineage** (the graph of transformations that produced it) if a partition is lost, instead of relying on replication like Hadoop. **DataFrames** and **Datasets** sit on top of RDDs, adding schema and a Catalyst-optimized execution plan, which is why they usually outperform raw RDDs for structured data.

Every operation on an RDD/DataFrame is either a **transformation** (map, filter, join — lazy, returns a new dataset) or an **action** (count, collect, save — triggers execution). Because of **lazy evaluation**, Spark doesn't run anything until an action forces it to, which lets the engine buil

title: Apache Spark
description: Apache Spark interview questions covering RDDs, DataFrames, Spark SQL, partitioning, shuffling, memory management, streaming, MLlib, GraphX, and deployment.
content:
d a DAG of the whole computation and optimize it before running a single task. That DAG is split into **stages** at shuffle boundaries and scheduled by the **driver**, which runs the user's `main()`, tracks RDD lineage, and hands tasks to **executors** — worker processes that actually run computations and cache data, coordinated through a **cluster manager** (Standalone, YARN, or Mesos).

Data is split into **partitions**, the unit of parallelism; operations that need to regroup data by key (`groupByKey`, `join`, `reduceByKey`) trigger a **shuffle** — an expensive all-to-all redistribution of data across the network — which is usually the first thing to look at when tuning a slow Spark job.

<QuestionCard id="spark-core-11" number={11} question="What are the main languages supported by Apache Spark, and why is JDBC popular with it?" difficulty="medium" topic="Ecosystem">
Spark supports four languages — **Scala, Java, Python, and R** — plus SQL, with Scala being the most widely used since Spark itself is written in Scala. **JDBC (Java Database Connectivity)** is a popular way to connect to data because Spark runs on the JVM, and Hadoop, Hive, and MySQL all interface easily with Spark cl

title: Apache Spark
description: Apache Spark interview questions covering RDDs, DataFrames, Spark SQL, partitioning, shuffling, memory management, streaming, MLlib, GraphX, and deployment.
content:
usters over it. JDBC also lets Spark's Catalyst optimizer push predicates (the `WHERE` clause) down into the source database, so filtering happens before data ever crosses the network — less data transferred, and fewer records for Spark to process.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="spark-core-12" number={12} question="What are the security options in Apache Spark?" difficulty="medium" topic="Security">
- **Encryption** — SSL support for encrypted data transfer (HTTPS), configured via `spark.ssl` parameters.
- **Authentication** — shared-secret authentication configured via `spark.authenticate`.
- **Event logging** — access control is enforced by setting permissions on the directory where event logs are stored.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

content:
### Architecture & Execution Model

<QuestionList topic="Spark Architecture" storagePrefix="spark-arch">

<QuestionCard id="spark-arch-01" number={13} question="What is Spark Core, and what functions does it perform?" difficulty="easy" topic="Architecture">
Spark Core is the base engine for large-scale parallel and distributed data processing — the distributed execution engine underlying the Java, Scala, and Python APIs. It's responsible for:
- Memory management and storage-system interaction
- Fault recovery
- Job scheduling, distribution, and monitoring
- Basic I/O functions

All the additional libraries (SQL, Streaming, MLlib, GraphX) are built on top of Spark Core.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="spark-arch-02" number={14} question="What does the Spark Engine do?" difficulty="easy"

title: Apache Spark
description: Apache Spark interview questions covering RDDs, DataFrames, Spark SQL, partitioning, shuffling, memory management, streaming, MLlib, GraphX, and deployment.
content:
topic="Architecture">
The Spark Engine is responsible for scheduling, distributing, and monitoring the data application across the cluster.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="spark-arch-03" number={15} question="What is a Spark Driver?" difficulty="easy" topic="Architecture">
The Spark Driver is the process that runs on the master/client machine and executes the application's `main()` method. It creates the `SparkContext`/`SparkSession`, declares all transformations and actions on RDDs, and splits the application into tasks that it schedules on executors via the cluster manager. Launching the Spark Shell effectively creates a driver program; when the driver terminates, the application finishes.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="spark-arch-04" number={16} question="What is a Spark Executor

title: Apache Spark
description: Apache Spark interview questions covering RDDs, DataFrames, Spark SQL, partitioning, shuffling, memory management, streaming, MLlib, GraphX, and deployment.
content:
?" difficulty="easy" topic="Architecture">
When `SparkContext` connects to a cluster manager, it acquires executors on the cluster's nodes. Executors are the processes that run computations and hold data (in memory or on disk) for a Spark application; the driver sends them the final tasks for execution and they report results back.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="spark-arch-05" number={17} question="What is a worker node?" difficulty="easy" topic="Architecture">
A worker node is any cluster node that can run Spark application code. A worker node can run more than one worker process, configured via the `SPARK_WORKER_INSTANCES` property in `spark-env.sh` (only one worker starts if it isn't set). Worker nodes do the actual data processing and report resource usage back to the master, which

title: Apache Spark
description: Apache Spark interview questions covering RDDs, DataFrames, Spark SQL, partitioning, shuffling, memory management, streaming, MLlib, GraphX, and deployment.
content:
decides how to allocate and schedule work across them.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="spark-arch-06" number={18} question="What are the core components of a distributed Spark application?" difficulty="medium" topic="Architecture">
- **Driver** — runs the `main()` method, creates RDDs, and performs transformations/actions on them.
- **Cluster Manager** — a pluggable component (Standalone, YARN, or Mesos) responsible for launching drivers and executors across nodes.
- **Executor** — a worker-node process that runs individual tasks and provides in-memory/disk storage for cached RDDs.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="spark-arch-07" number={19} question="Explain the runtime/working architecture of Spark." difficulty="medium" topic="Architecture">
Spark applications run as independent pro

title: Apache Spark
description: Apache Spark interview questions covering RDDs, DataFrames, Spark SQL, partitioning, shuffling, memory management, streaming, MLlib, GraphX, and deployment.
content:
cesses coordinated by the driver through a `SparkSession`. The cluster/resource manager assigns tasks to worker nodes on a one-task-per-partition basis. Iterative algorithms repeatedly apply the same operations to data, so Spark caches datasets across iterations where possible. Each task applies its unit of work to the data in its own partition, producing a new partitioned dataset; results are sent back to the driver for further processing or persisted to disk.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="spark-arch-08" number={20} question="What is the working of a DAG in Spark?" difficulty="hard" topic="Architecture">
DAG stands for **Directed Acyclic Graph** — a set of vertices (RDDs) and edges (the operations applied to them, in sequence).

1. The interpreter (e.g., the Scala interpreter for Sca

title: Apache Spark
description: Apache Spark interview questions covering RDDs, DataFrames, Spark SQL, partitioning, shuffling, memory management, streaming, MLlib, GraphX, and deployment.
content:
la code) parses the code entered in the Spark console.
2. Spark builds an **operator graph** as the code is entered.
3. When an action is called on an RDD, that operator graph is submitted to the **DAG Scheduler**.
4. The DAG Scheduler splits the graph into **stages** of tasks based on the transformations involved, pipelining operators together within a stage.
5. Stages are handed to the **Task Scheduler**, which launches tasks via the cluster manager; stages without dependencies between them can run independently.
6. **Worker nodes** execute the tasks.

Each RDD keeps a pointer back to its parent RDD(s) and its relationship to them — for example, `val childB = parentA.map()` gives `childB` a reference back to `parentA` — and this chain is the RDD's **lineage**.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionC

content:
ard id="spark-arch-09" number={21} question="What is the use of SparkContext in Apache Spark?" difficulty="easy" topic="Architecture">
`SparkContext` is the central, entry-point object that coordinates a Spark application and connects it to a cluster manager, which in turn allocates resources to the application. It's created from a `SparkConf` object holding the application's configuration, and it's what you use to create RDDs. The Spark Shell provides a default `SparkContext` automatically.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="spark-arch-10" number={22} question="How will you monitor Apache Spark?" difficulty="easy" topic="Operations">
- The **Web UI** provided by `SparkContext`, available on port `4040` by default, showing scheduler stages/tasks, RDD sizes and memory usage, environment inf

o, and executor details.
- The **Metrics library**, which can push Spark runtime information to HTTP endpoints, JMX, CSV files, or another monitoring dashboard.
- In **standalone mode**, Spark also has a web UI for cluster/job statistics, and per-job logs are written to each worker node's work directory.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="spark-arch-11" number={23} question="What is the use of Akka in Apache Spark?" difficulty="easy" topic="Architecture">
Akka was historically used internally by Spark for scheduling, and for messaging between workers and the master/driver.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="spark-arch-12" number={24} question="Which internal daemons does Apache Spark use?" difficulty="medium" topic="Architecture">
Some important internal daemons include: `BlockManager`, `M

emoryStore`, `DAGScheduler`, `Driver`, `Worker`, `Executor`, and `Tasks`.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="spark-arch-13" number={25} question="Do we need HDFS to run a Spark application?" difficulty="easy" topic="Architecture">
No — this is a bit of a trick question. Spark supports multiple filesystems (HDFS, HBase, local filesystem, S3, Cassandra, and more), so HDFS is just one option, not a requirement.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="spark-arch-14" number={26} question="What filesystems does Spark support?" difficulty="easy" topic="Architecture">
Some of the popular filesystems Spark can read from and write to: HDFS, Amazon S3, the local filesystem, Cassandra, OpenStack Swift, and the MapR filesystem.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="spark-arch-15" number={27} question="What is

the way Spark stores data?" difficulty="easy" topic="Architecture">
Apache Spark itself is an analytics/processing engine with no built-in storage engine — it retrieves and persists data via other storage systems, such as HDFS or S3.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="spark-arch-16" number={28} question="What is the use of the FileSystem API in Apache Spark?" difficulty="easy" topic="Architecture">
The FileSystem API is what Spark uses to read data from various storage backends, such as HDFS, S3, or the local filesystem.
</QuestionCard>

### Cluster Management & Deployment

<QuestionList topic="Cluster Management" storagePrefix="spark-deploy">

<QuestionCard id="spark-deploy-01" number={29} question="What are the different Cluster Managers / deployment modes in Apache Spark?" difficulty="medium" topic="Deployment">
- **Standalone** — the simple cluster manager bundled with Spark; you start it manually.
- **YARN (Hadoop NextGen)** — Hadoop's resource manager. In *cluster mode* the Spark driver runs inside a YARN-managed master process on the cluster; in *client mode* the driver runs in the client process and an application master requests resources from YARN.
- **Mesos** — the Mesos master replaces the Spark master as cluster manager; when the driver creates a job, Mesos decides which machine handles each task.
- **Cloud (e

title: Apache Spark
description: Apache Spark interview questions covering RDDs, DataFrames, Spark SQL, partitioning, shuffling, memory management, streaming, MLlib, GraphX, and deployment.
content:
.g., Amazon EC2)** — deploying and running a Spark cluster on cloud infrastructure.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="spark-deploy-02" number={30} question="What is YARN, and what role does it play for Spark?" difficulty="easy" topic="Deployment">
YARN is Hadoop's central resource-management platform for delivering scalable operations across a cluster — a distributed container manager, similar in role to Mesos. Spark is a data-processing tool that can run *on top of* YARN the same way Hadoop MapReduce does; doing so requires a Spark binary distribution built with YARN support.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="spark-deploy-03" number={31} question="Do you need to install Spark on all nodes of a YARN cluster?" difficulty="easy" topic="Deployment">
No — Spark runs on top of YARN and doesn'

title: Apache Spark
description: Apache Spark interview questions covering RDDs, DataFrames, Spark SQL, partitioning, shuffling, memory management, streaming, MLlib, GraphX, and deployment.
content:
t need to be installed on every cluster node; it runs independently of its installation location. Spark exposes YARN-specific options for dispatching jobs rather than using its own built-in manager or Mesos, including `master`, `deploy-mode`, `driver-memory`, `executor-memory`, `executor-cores`, and `queue`.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="spark-deploy-04" number={32} question="Is it possible to run Apache Spark on Apache Mesos?" difficulty="easy" topic="Deployment">
Yes — Spark can run on hardware clusters managed by Mesos.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="spark-deploy-05" number={33} question="How can you connect Spark to Apache Mesos?" difficulty="medium" topic="Deployment">
1. Configure the Spark driver program to connect to Mesos.
2. Set a path/location for the Spark binary packa

title: Apache Spark
description: Apache Spark interview questions covering RDDs, DataFrames, Spark SQL, partitioning, shuffling, memory management, streaming, MLlib, GraphX, and deployment.
content:
ge so it's accessible by Mesos.
3. Install Apache Spark in the same location on each machine as Apache Mesos, and configure `spark.mesos.executor.home` to point to that install location.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="spark-deploy-06" number={34} question="What are the benefits of using Spark with Apache Mesos?" difficulty="easy" topic="Deployment">
Mesos provides scalable partitioning among multiple Spark instances, and dynamic partitioning between Spark and other big-data frameworks sharing the same cluster.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="spark-deploy-07" number={35} question="Can Apache Spark be used along with Hadoop? If so, how?" difficulty="medium" topic="vs Hadoop">
Yes — Hadoop compatibility is one of Spark's core strengths, letting you combine Spark's processing speed with

title: Apache Spark
description: Apache Spark interview questions covering RDDs, DataFrames, Spark SQL, partitioning, shuffling, memory management, streaming, MLlib, GraphX, and deployment.
content:
Hadoop's YARN and HDFS. Common integration patterns:
- **HDFS** — Spark runs on top of HDFS to use its distributed, replicated storage.
- **MapReduce** — Spark can run alongside MapReduce in the same or a different processing framework/cluster, e.g. Spark for real-time and MapReduce for batch.
- **YARN** — Spark applications run under YARN as the cluster management framework.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="spark-deploy-08" number={36} question="Hadoop uses replication to achieve fault tolerance — how does Spark achieve it?" difficulty="medium" topic="Fault Tolerance">
Spark's data storage model is built on RDDs, which achieve fault tolerance through **lineage** rather than replication. An RDD always knows how it was built from other datasets, so if a partition is lost to a failure, Sp

title: Apache Spark
description: Apache Spark interview questions covering RDDs, DataFrames, Spark SQL, partitioning, shuffling, memory management, streaming, MLlib, GraphX, and deployment.
content:
ark uses the lineage graph to rebuild only that lost partition instead of restoring the whole dataset from a replica.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="spark-deploy-09" number={37} question="How can you achieve High Availability in Apache Spark?" difficulty="medium" topic="Fault Tolerance">
- Single-node recovery using the local filesystem.
- Standby masters coordinated via Apache ZooKeeper.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="spark-deploy-10" number={38} question="Does Apache Spark provide checkpointing?" difficulty="medium" topic="Fault Tolerance">
Lineage graphs are always useful for recovering RDDs after a failure, but recomputation gets expensive if the lineage chain is long. Spark provides a checkpointing API — a `REPLICATE` flag passed to `persist()` — that lets you save an RDD to r

title: Apache Spark
description: Apache Spark interview questions covering RDDs, DataFrames, Spark SQL, partitioning, shuffling, memory management, streaming, MLlib, GraphX, and deployment.
content:
eliable storage. The decision of what to checkpoint is left to the user; it's most valuable for long lineage chains with wide dependencies.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="spark-deploy-11" number={39} question="How can you launch Spark jobs inside Hadoop MapReduce?" difficulty="medium" topic="Deployment">
Using **SIMR** (Spark in MapReduce), you can run any Spark job inside MapReduce without needing admin rights on the cluster.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="spark-deploy-12" number={40} question="What do you understand by speculative execution in Apache Spark?" difficulty="hard" topic="Fault Tolerance">
A speculative task is a health-check mechanism for stragglers — a task running noticeably slower than the median of already-completed tasks in the same stage. Spark submits a duplica

title: Apache Spark
description: Apache Spark interview questions covering RDDs, DataFrames, Spark SQL, partitioning, shuffling, memory management, streaming, MLlib, GraphX, and deployment.
content:
te copy of that task to another worker and runs it in parallel rather than waiting on (or killing) the slow original. In cluster mode this is driven by a `TaskSchedulerImpl` thread, enabled via `spark.speculation`, checking periodically at intervals set by `spark.speculation.interval`.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="spark-deploy-13" number={41} question="Which Spark library allows reliable file sharing at memory speed across different cluster frameworks?" difficulty="easy" topic="Ecosystem">
**Tachyon** — it provides reliable, memory-speed file sharing across different cluster computing frameworks.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="spark-deploy-14" number={42} question="Why is BlinkDB used?" difficulty="medium" topic="Ecosystem">
BlinkDB is a query engine for running interactive SQL q

title: Apache Spark
description: Apache Spark interview questions covering RDDs, DataFrames, Spark SQL, partitioning, shuffling, memory management, streaming, MLlib, GraphX, and deployment.
content:
ueries on huge volumes of data. It trades a small amount of accuracy for much lower latency, returning results annotated with meaningful error bars so users can balance query accuracy against response time.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="spark-deploy-15" number={43} question="How does Spark compare to Hadoop in terms of ease of use?" difficulty="easy" topic="vs Hadoop">
Hadoop MapReduce requires programming directly in Java, which is difficult — Pig and Hive make it easier, but learning their syntax still takes time. Spark offers interactive APIs in Java, Python, and Scala, plus Spark SQL (originally "Shark") for SQL users, making it comparatively easier to pick up than Hadoop.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="spark-deploy-16" number={44} question="Under what scenarios do you use Cli

title: Apache Spark
description: Apache Spark interview questions covering RDDs, DataFrames, Spark SQL, partitioning, shuffling, memory management, streaming, MLlib, GraphX, and deployment.
content:
ent mode vs. Cluster mode for deployment?" difficulty="medium" topic="Deployment">
Use **Cluster mode** when the client machine isn't close to the cluster — it avoids the network latency that Client mode would incur between executors and a distant driver, and the job survives even if the client machine goes offline (since the driver runs on the cluster). Use **Client mode** when the client machine is already inside the cluster — there's no added network latency, and since the cluster is already maintained, there's less to worry about on failure.
</QuestionCard>
