content:
### RDDs: Transformations & Actions

<QuestionList topic="RDDs" storagePrefix="spark-rdd">

<QuestionCard id="spark-rdd-01" number={45} question="What is an RDD (Resilient Distributed Dataset)?" difficulty="easy" topic="RDD">
An RDD is a fault-tolerant collection of operational elements that run in parallel — a distributed and resilient collection of records spread across many partitions.
- **Distributed** — data lives across multiple nodes.
- **Resilient** — fault-tolerant; on node failure, Spark recomputes lost data from lineage instead of losing it.
- **Dataset** — a collection of data, similar to a Scala collection.
- **Immutable** — data in an RDD can't be modified after creation, only transformed into a new RDD.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="spark-rdd-02" number={46} question="W

title: Apache Spark
description: Apache Spark interview questions covering RDDs, DataFrames, Spark SQL, partitioning, shuffling, memory management, streaming, MLlib, GraphX, and deployment.
content:
hat are the different types of RDD?" difficulty="easy" topic="RDD">
Primarily two: **parallelized collections** (an existing collection parallelized from the driver program) and **Hadoop datasets** (RDDs built by running a function on each record in a file stored in HDFS or another storage system).
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="spark-rdd-03" number={47} question="What are the methods/ways of creating RDDs in Spark?" difficulty="easy" topic="RDD">
- **Parallelizing a collection** in the driver program, using `SparkContext`'s `parallelize` method.
- **Loading an external dataset** from external storage such as HDFS, HBase, or a shared filesystem.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="spark-rdd-04" number={48} question="What operations does an RDD support?" difficulty="easy" topic="RDD">
An

title: Apache Spark
description: Apache Spark interview questions covering RDDs, DataFrames, Spark SQL, partitioning, shuffling, memory management, streaming, MLlib, GraphX, and deployment.
content:
RDD is Spark's main logical data unit — a distributed, immutable (read-only) collection split across partitions, each of which can live in memory or on disk on a different cluster machine. You can't mutate an RDD, only transform it into a new one. RDDs support two kinds of operations:
- **Transformations** — create a new RDD from an existing one (e.g. `map`, `filter`, `reduceByKey`); computed lazily, on demand.
- **Actions** — return the final result of an RDD computation, triggering execution of the lineage graph (loading data, running intermediate transformations) and returning results to the driver or writing them to a filesystem.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="spark-rdd-05" number={49} question="What is a Transformation in Apache Spark?" difficulty="easy" topic="RDD">
A transforma

title: Apache Spark
description: Apache Spark interview questions covering RDDs, DataFrames, Spark SQL, partitioning, shuffling, memory management, streaming, MLlib, GraphX, and deployment.
content:
tion is a function applied to an RDD whose output is another RDD. It's a lazy operation — it doesn't execute until an action is called — and it never modifies the input RDD. You can chain multiple transformations into a pipeline to build a larger data flow:

```scala
val rawData = sc.textFile("path/to/movies.txt")
val moviesData = rawData.map(x => x.split("  "))
```

Here, `rawData` is transformed into `moviesData`, and neither transformation actually runs until an action is triggered.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="spark-rdd-06" number={50} question="What are some common Transformations in Apache Spark?" difficulty="medium" topic="RDD">
- **`map(func)`** — returns a new dataset by passing each element through `func`.
- **`filter(func)`** — returns a new dataset of only the elements fo

title: Apache Spark
description: Apache Spark interview questions covering RDDs, DataFrames, Spark SQL, partitioning, shuffling, memory management, streaming, MLlib, GraphX, and deployment.
content:
r which `func` returns true.
- **`union(otherDataset)`** — combines two datasets into their union.
- **`intersection(otherDataset)`** — returns only the elements common to both datasets.
- **`pipe(command, [envVars])`** — pipes each partition of the dataset through an external shell command.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="spark-rdd-07" number={51} question="What are Actions in Spark?" difficulty="easy" topic="RDD">
An action brings data back from an RDD to the driver/local machine. Executing an action triggers the lineage graph — loading the original data and running every intermediate transformation — and returns the final result to the driver or writes it to a filesystem. `reduce()`, for example, repeatedly applies a function until a single value is left, while `take()` pulls a set o

title: Apache Spark
description: Apache Spark interview questions covering RDDs, DataFrames, Spark SQL, partitioning, shuffling, memory management, streaming, MLlib, GraphX, and deployment.
content:
f values back to the driver.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="spark-rdd-08" number={52} question="What are some common Actions in Apache Spark?" difficulty="medium" topic="RDD">
- **`reduce(func)`** — aggregates all elements using `func`.
- **`count()`** — total number of elements in the dataset.
- **`collect()`** — returns all elements as an array to the driver.
- **`first()`** — returns the first element.
- **`take(n)`** — returns the first `n` elements.
- **`foreach(func)`** — runs `func` on every element.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="spark-rdd-09" number={53} question="What is RDD Lineage (a Lineage Graph)?" difficulty="medium" topic="RDD">
RDD lineage is the graph of all the parent RDDs that a given RDD depends on. Since Spark doesn't replicate data across the cluster, a lost

title: Apache Spark
description: Apache Spark interview questions covering RDDs, DataFrames, Spark SQL, partitioning, shuffling, memory management, streaming, MLlib, GraphX, and deployment.
content:
partition would otherwise mean lost data — lineage lets Spark reconstruct exactly the lost data by replaying the transformations that produced it, rather than restarting the whole computation. This is central to both Spark's fault tolerance and its performance.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="spark-rdd-10" number={54} question="What do you understand by a Pair RDD?" difficulty="medium" topic="RDD">
Special operations can be performed on RDDs of key/value pairs — these are called Pair RDDs (`PairRDDFunctions[K, V]`). They let you access each key in parallel, and provide methods like `reduceByKey()` (aggregates data per key) and `join()` (combines two RDDs by matching keys).
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="spark-rdd-11" number={55} question="What is the difference between RDD and Distr

title: Apache Spark
description: Apache Spark interview questions covering RDDs, DataFrames, Spark SQL, partitioning, shuffling, memory management, streaming, MLlib, GraphX, and deployment.
content:
ibuted Shared Memory (DSM)?" difficulty="hard" topic="RDD">
| Aspect | RDD | Distributed Shared Memory |
|---|---|---|
| **Read** | Coarse-grained or fine-grained — coarse-grained transforms a whole dataset at once, fine-grained transforms individual elements | Fine-grained only |
| **Write** | Coarse-grained | Fine-grained |
| **Consistency** | Trivially consistent — RDDs are immutable, so changes can't be rolled back and are always permanent | Consistent only if the programmer follows the memory model's rules; results of memory operations are predictable |
| **Fault recovery** | Uses the lineage graph to find and rebuild lost data at any point | Uses checkpointing — applications roll back to the last checkpoint rather than restarting |
| **Straggler mitigation** | Possible, via backup ta

description: Apache Spark interview questions covering RDDs, DataFrames, Spark SQL, partitioning, shuffling, memory management, streaming, MLlib, GraphX, and deployment.
content:
sks | Difficult to achieve |
| **Behavior when RAM is full** | Spills excess RDD data to disk | Performance degrades as RAM runs out |
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="spark-rdd-12" number={56} question="Explain the first() operation in Apache Spark RDD." difficulty="easy" topic="RDD">
`first()` is an action that returns the first element of the RDD.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="spark-rdd-13" number={57} question="Describe the join operation. How is outer join supported?" difficulty="hard" topic="RDD">
`join()` is a transformation, defined in `org.apache.spark.rdd.PairRDDFunctions`:

```scala
def join[W](other: RDD[(K, W)]): RDD[(K, (V, W))]
```

Called on datasets of type `(K, V)` and `(K, W)`, it returns a dataset of `(K, (V, W))` pairs — one pair per matching key across both RDD

title: Apache Spark
description: Apache Spark interview questions covering RDDs, DataFrames, Spark SQL, partitioning, shuffling, memory management, streaming, MLlib, GraphX, and deployment.
content:
s — implemented as a hash join across the cluster. Outer joins are supported through separate methods: `leftOuterJoin`, `rightOuterJoin`, and `fullOuterJoin`.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="spark-rdd-14" number={58} question="How can you remove the elements with a key present in any other RDD?" difficulty="easy" topic="RDD">
Use the `subtractByKey()` function.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="spark-rdd-15" number={59} question="What do you understand by piping in Spark?" difficulty="medium" topic="RDD">
Spark's `pipe()` method on RDDs lets you compose a transformation that runs an external UNIX command — in any language — as part of the RDD pipeline, per the UNIX standard-streams convention. It reads each RDD element as a `String`, hands it to the piped command, and returns the comma

title: Apache Spark
description: Apache Spark interview questions covering RDDs, DataFrames, Spark SQL, partitioning, shuffling, memory management, streaming, MLlib, GraphX, and deployment.
content:
nd's output, also as a `String`.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="spark-rdd-16" number={60} question="How will you pass functions to Apache Spark?" difficulty="easy" topic="RDD">
- **Anonymous function syntax** — for passing short pieces of code inline.
- **Static methods on a singleton object** — define the function as a static method of a single-instance object, and pass that object (with its methods) to the cluster nodes.

### Partitioning, Shuffling & Performance

<QuestionList topic="Performance" storagePrefix="spark-perf">

<QuestionCard id="spark-perf-01" number={63} question="Define partitions in Apache Spark." difficulty="easy" topic="Partitioning">
A partition is a smaller, logical division of data, similar to a split in MapReduce — a logical chunk of a large distributed dataset. Partitioning derives these logical units to speed up processing; everything in Spark is, in effect, a partitioned RDD. By default, Spark tries to read data into an RDD from nodes close to it, and creates one partition per HDFS block unless told otherwise.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="spark-perf-02" number={64} question="Describe Partition and Partitioner in Apache Spark." difficulty="hard" topic="Partitioning">
A **part

title: Apache Spark
description: Apache Spark interview questions covering RDDs, DataFrames, Spark SQL, partitioning, shuffling, memory management, streaming, MLlib, GraphX, and deployment.
content:
ition** is the basic unit of parallelism — a logical division of data stored on a cluster node, similar to an HDFS split; RDDs are collections of partitions, and Spark launches one task per partition when an action runs. If `spark.default.parallelism` is set, Spark uses that value; otherwise it uses the max number of upstream partitions (or matches the largest upstream RDD), which is least likely to cause out-of-memory errors.

A **partitioner** is an object that defines how key-value pairs are distributed across partitions — it maps each key to a partition ID between `0` and `numPartitions - 1`, and its contract guarantees that all records for a given key live on a single partition. This lets the scheduler optimize downstream operations. Spark has three kinds:
- **Hash Partitioner** — spr

title: Apache Spark
description: Apache Spark interview questions covering RDDs, DataFrames, Spark SQL, partitioning, shuffling, memory management, streaming, MLlib, GraphX, and deployment.
content:
eads data evenly across partitions based on a hash of the key.
- **Range Partitioner** — keys within the same range land on the same partition.
- **Custom Partitioner** — user-defined partitioning logic.

You can set one explicitly via `partitionBy()`, or get one implicitly from a transformation that preserves partitioning. For cogroup-like operations, Spark prefers an existing partitioner on one of the RDDs, falling back to a default `HashPartitioner` otherwise.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="spark-perf-03" number={65} question="How can you manually partition an RDD?" difficulty="medium" topic="Partitioning">
By default, Spark creates one partition per HDFS block — a 1280 MB file with 128 MB blocks becomes 10 partitions:

```scala
val data = context.textFile("/user/dataflair/file-name

")
```

To request more partitions than there are blocks, pass a partition count explicitly:

```scala
val data = context.textFile("/user/dataflair/file-name", 20)
```

This creates 20 partitions (2 per block, in this example). Having somewhat more partitions than blocks is generally recommended for better performance.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="spark-perf-04" number={66} question="What is the difference between repartition and coalesce?" difficulty="medium" topic="Partitioning">
- **`repartition`** — can both increase and decrease the number of partitions; it creates entirely new partitions and does a full shuffle to evenly redistribute the data. It internally calls `coalesce` with the shuffle flag set, which makes it slower than `coalesce`.
- **`coalesce`** — can only *reduce* th

title: Apache Spark
description: Apache Spark interview questions covering RDDs, DataFrames, Spark SQL, partitioning, shuffling, memory management, streaming, MLlib, GraphX, and deployment.
content:
e number of partitions; it reuses existing partitions to minimize (though not eliminate) the amount of data shuffled. It's generally faster than `repartition`, though speed can suffer if the input partitions are very unevenly sized.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="spark-perf-05" number={67} question="Describe the coalesce operation. When can you coalesce to a larger number of partitions?" difficulty="hard" topic="Partitioning">
`coalesce` is a transformation, in `org.apache.spark.rdd.ShuffledRDD`, that returns a new RDD reduced to `numPartitions` partitions:

```scala
def coalesce(numPartitions: Int, shuffle: Boolean = false): RDD[T]
```

Going from, say, 1000 partitions to 100 creates a **narrow dependency** — no shuffle occurs, since each of the 100 new partitions simply claims 10 of

title: Apache Spark
description: Apache Spark interview questions covering RDDs, DataFrames, Spark SQL, partitioning, shuffling, memory management, streaming, MLlib, GraphX, and deployment.
content:
the existing ones. But a drastic coalesce (e.g., down to `numPartitions = 1`) can leave your computation running on far fewer nodes than you'd like. Passing `shuffle = true` adds a shuffle step so the current upstream partitions still run in parallel.

With `shuffle = true`, you can actually coalesce *up* to a larger number of partitions too — useful if you have a small number of partitions (say 100), some of which are abnormally large: `coalesce(1000, shuffle = true)` redistributes the data across 1000 partitions using a hash partitioner. `coalesce` is generally an optimized `repartition` for the specific case of reducing partition count, and runs more efficiently after filtering has shrunk a large dataset.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="spark-perf-06" number={68} question="What is a

title: Apache Spark
description: Apache Spark interview questions covering RDDs, DataFrames, Spark SQL, partitioning, shuffling, memory management, streaming, MLlib, GraphX, and deployment.
content:
shuffle operation in Spark, and when does it occur?" difficulty="medium" topic="Shuffling">
Shuffling is the redistribution of data across partitions — an all-to-all operation that may or may not move data between JVM processes/executors on different machines. Spark has no control over exactly which partition a given record ends up on. It's costly because, unlike most Spark tasks (which operate on one partition), a shuffle has to touch every partition. Shuffles are triggered by operations like `join`, `groupByKey`, and `reduceByKey`. Two configuration parameters affect shuffle compression: `spark.shuffle.compress` (whether to compress shuffle map output) and `spark.shuffle.spill.compress` (whether to compress intermediate spill files).
</QuestionCard>

`repartition`, `coalesce` (with `shuffle = true`), `groupByKey`, `reduceByKey`, `cogroup`, and `join`.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="spark-perf-08" number={70} question="How will you minimize data transfer while working with Apache Spark?" difficulty="medium" topic="Optimization">
- **Broadcast variables** — cache a read-only variable on every machine instead of shipping a copy with every task; improves the efficiency of joins between a large and a small RDD, and reduces communication cost via Spark's broadcast algorithm.
- **Accumulators** — update a shared variable's value in parallel across executors (e.g. counters/sums) without shuffling data around to do it.
- **Avoid `ByKey` ope

content:
rations, `repartition`, and other shuffle-triggering calls** where they aren't necessary.
- **Enable shuffle compression** — set `spark.shuffle.compress = true` to reduce the volume of data transferred when a shuffle is unavoidable.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="spark-perf-09" number={71} question="What is the default level of parallelism in Apache Spark?" difficulty="easy" topic="Optimization">
When not explicitly configured, the default level of parallelism is simply the number of partitions in the RDD being operated on.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="spark-perf-10" number={72} question="What is lazy evaluation in Apache Spark?" difficulty="easy" topic="Optimization">
Lazy evaluation ("call-by-need") delays execution until a result is actually required. Transformations on an RDD

title: Apache Spark
description: Apache Spark interview questions covering RDDs, DataFrames, Spark SQL, partitioning, shuffling, memory management, streaming, MLlib, GraphX, and deployment.
content:
aren't run when they're called — Spark just records what has to happen, building a DAG of pending work. Only when an action is called does Spark execute that DAG. This means data isn't loaded until it's actually needed, and Spark gets the chance to optimize the whole pipeline before running any of it.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="spark-perf-11" number={73} question="What are the benefits of lazy evaluation?" difficulty="medium" topic="Optimization">
- Increases the manageability of the program by letting Spark reason about the whole computation graph at once.
- Reduces computation overhead and increases overall system speed.
- Reduces time and space complexity.
- Enables optimization by reducing the number of passes/queries needed over the data.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="sp

ark-perf-12" number={74} question="What is a Broadcast variable in Spark, and why do we need it?" difficulty="medium" topic="Optimization">
A broadcast variable lets you keep a read-only value cached on every machine, instead of shipping a fresh copy of it with every task — created via `SparkContext.broadcast(v)` and read via `.value`. Spark distributes it using an efficient broadcast algorithm to reduce communication cost. It's especially useful in shuffle operations that need the same reference data everywhere (e.g. join keys), and is recommended over a plain closure variable whenever the same data is needed by many tasks running on a cluster. The data is serialized before distribution and deserialized before use.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="spark-perf-13" number={75} question="Wh

title: Apache Spark
description: Apache Spark interview questions covering RDDs, DataFrames, Spark SQL, partitioning, shuffling, memory management, streaming, MLlib, GraphX, and deployment.
content:
at is an Accumulator in Apache Spark?" difficulty="medium" topic="Optimization">
An accumulator is a variable that can only be updated through an associative and commutative operation, making it safe to add to in parallel across executors — commonly used to implement counters or running sums. Workers only ever write to it; the driver reads the final value. Spark provides numeric accumulators out of the box (`SparkContext.longAccumulator()`, `SparkContext.doubleAccumulator()`), and accumulators can be named or unnamed.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="spark-perf-14" number={76} question="How are automatic clean-ups triggered in Spark to handle accumulated metadata?" difficulty="medium" topic="Optimization">
Clean-up can be triggered automatically by setting the `spark.cleaner.ttl` paramet

title: Apache Spark
description: Apache Spark interview questions covering RDDs, DataFrames, Spark SQL, partitioning, shuffling, memory management, streaming, MLlib, GraphX, and deployment.
content:
er (a periodic cleaner; the default is infinite, meaning metadata is remembered indefinitely). Metadata older than the configured duration is dropped, which is what lets long-running Spark applications keep running for many hours without accumulating unbounded metadata. Alternatively, you can batch-divide long-running jobs and write intermediary results to disk periodically.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="spark-sql-01" number={77} question="What is the purpose of Spark SQL?" difficulty="easy" topic="Spark SQL">
Spark SQL is Spark's module for running SQL queries and for interacting with structured data through the Dataset API — both use the same underlying computation engine, which gives Spark visibility into both the structure of the data and the computation being performed. It can also read data from an existing Hive installation, and it can be accessed via the JDBC/ODBC API or the command line, not just from within a Spark program.

<QuestionCard id="spark-mem-01" number={99} question="How will you do memory tuning in Spark?" difficulty="hard" topic="Memory">
Memory tuning has to account for the amount of memory objects consume, the cost of accessing them, and garbage-collection overhead. Since Spark caches objects in memory, start by measuring usage: cache a representative RDD and check its size on the Storage page of the Web UI, then estimate memory needs from there. To reduce usage where needed:
- Prefer arrays of primitives/objects over linked lists or `HashMap`s — the `fastutil` library provides convenient primitive-friendly collection classes for Java.

- Pass the JVM flag `-XX:+UseCompressedOops` to shrink pointers from eight bytes to four.

<QuestionCard id="spark-mem-02" number={100} question="What is the difference between cache() and persist()?" difficulty="easy" topic="Persistence">
Both persist an RDD in memory across operations. The difference is that `persist()` lets you choose the storage level explicitly, while `cache()` always uses the default storage level, `MEMORY_ONLY`.
</QuestionCard>

`DISK_ONLY`** — stored only on disk.

<QuestionCard id="spark-mem-05" number={103} question="How will you select the storage level in Apache Spark?" difficulty="medium" topic="Persistence">
The choice is a trade-off between CPU efficiency and memory usage. If your RDD fits comfortably in memory, use `MEMORY_ONLY` for the best performance. If it doesn't fit, try `MEMORY_ONLY_SER` with a compact serialization library — still fast, with real space savings. If there's a big gap between available memory and total object size, fall back to `MEMORY_AND_DISK`. Where fast fault recovery matters, replicate objects across multiple partitions.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="spark-mem-06" number={104} question="What do you mean by Persistence in Spark?" difficulty="medium" topic="Pe

title: Apache Spark
description: Apache Spark interview questions covering RDDs, DataFrames, Spark SQL, partitioning, shuffling, memory management, streaming, MLlib, GraphX, and deployment.
content:
rsistence">
RDD persistence is an optimization technique that saves the result of evaluating an RDD so it can be reused, avoiding recomputation and reducing overall computation overhead. It's implemented via `cache()` and `persist()`, and is a key tool for iterative algorithms: once persisted, each node keeps in memory whatever partitions of the RDD it computed, ready for reuse — which can speed up subsequent computations by roughly 10x.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="spark-mem-07" number={105} question="What is Executor Memory in a Spark application, and how do you calculate it?" difficulty="hard" topic="Memory">
Every Spark application has a fixed heap size and fixed core count per executor — the heap size is the **executor memory**, controlled by the `spark.executor.memory` property

title: Apache Spark
description: Apache Spark interview questions covering RDDs, DataFrames, Spark SQL, partitioning, shuffling, memory management, streaming, MLlib, GraphX, and deployment.
content:
(or the `--executor-memory` flag), and each worker node runs one executor per application. It's effectively a measure of how much of a worker node's memory the application is allowed to use.

**Worked example** — given 10 nodes, 15 cores per node, and 61 GB RAM per node, with a rule-of-thumb target of 5 concurrent tasks per executor:

```text
Number of executors per node = cores per node / concurrent tasks = 15 / 5 = 3
Total executors for the job   = nodes × executors per node = 10 × 3 = 30
```
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="spark-mem-08" number={106} question="What is spark.executor.memory in a Spark application?" difficulty="easy" topic="Memory">
`spark.executor.memory` sets the amount of memory used per executor process; its default value is 1 GB.
</QuestionCard>

### Spark Streaming

<QuestionList topic="Spark Streaming" storagePrefix="spark-stream">

<QuestionCard id="spark-stream-01" number={107} question="What is Spark Streaming?" difficulty="easy" topic="Streaming">
Spark Streaming is an extension of the core Spark API for processing live data streams with high throughput and fault tolerance. It ingests data from sources like Kafka, Kinesis, and Flume, lets you apply familiar Spark functions (`map`, `reduce`, `join`, etc.) to the incoming data, and writes the processed results to a filesystem, a database, or a live dashboard.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="spark-stream-02" number={108} question="How does Spark Streaming work internally?" difficulty="medium" topic="Streaming">
Spark Streaming listens to live data streams from various sources

title: Apache Spark
description: Apache Spark interview questions covering RDDs, DataFrames, Spark SQL, partitioning, shuffling, memory management, streaming, MLlib, GraphX, and deployment.
content:
and, as data arrives, divides it into small batches the Spark engine can handle. Internally, this uses an abstraction called a **DStream** (discretized stream) — a continuous stream of data that is, under the hood, simply a sequence of RDDs. Spark applies the usual transformations and actions to that sequence of RDDs to produce a resulting output stream.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="spark-stream-03" number={109} question="What is a DStream (Discretized Stream)?" difficulty="easy" topic="Streaming">
A DStream is the high-level abstraction Spark Streaming uses to represent a continuous stream of data — internally, just a sequence of RDDs. You can create a DStream either from a source like Kafka, Flume, or Kinesis, or by applying transformations to another DStream.
</QuestionCard>

<Qu

title: Apache Spark
description: Apache Spark interview questions covering RDDs, DataFrames, Spark SQL, partitioning, shuffling, memory management, streaming, MLlib, GraphX, and deployment.
content:
estionCard id="spark-stream-04" number={110} question="What are the different types of transformations on DStreams?" difficulty="medium" topic="Streaming">
- **Stateless transformations** — processing of the current batch doesn't depend on the output of the previous batch. Examples: `map()`, `filter()`, `reduceByKey()`.
- **Stateful transformations** — processing depends on the intermediary results of the previous batch, such as transformations built on sliding windows.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="spark-stream-05" number={111} question="What are receivers in Apache Spark Streaming?" difficulty="medium" topic="Streaming">
Receivers consume data from external sources and hand it off to Spark for processing. They're created as long-running tasks scheduled by the streaming context in a

title: Apache Spark
description: Apache Spark interview questions covering RDDs, DataFrames, Spark SQL, partitioning, shuffling, memory management, streaming, MLlib, GraphX, and deployment.
content:
round-robin fashion across executors, with each receiver using a single core. There are two kinds:
- **Reliable receivers** — send an acknowledgment back to the data source once the data has been received and replicated in Spark's storage.
- **Unreliable receivers** — send no acknowledgment.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="spark-stream-06" number={112} question="What is Structured Streaming in Apache Spark?" difficulty="medium" topic="Streaming">
Introduced in Spark 2.1, Structured Streaming is a scalable, fault-tolerant stream-processing engine built directly on the Spark SQL engine. You express streaming aggregations, event-time windows, and similar logic using the Dataset/DataFrame API, and the computation runs on the same optimized Spark SQL execution engine used for batch queries.

content:
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="spark-stream-07" number={113} question="What is Checkpointing in Spark Streaming?" difficulty="hard" topic="Streaming">
Checkpointing adds resiliency to a streaming application so it can recover after a failure. There are two types:
- **Metadata checkpointing** — saves the configuration and other information that defines the streaming application (configuration, DStream operations, incomplete batches), used to recover the driver after a failure.
- **Data checkpointing** — saves RDDs themselves to reliable storage; useful for stateful transformations where a generated RDD depends on the RDD from the previous batch, since that dependency chain can otherwise grow very long. Checkpointing intermediate RDDs bounds the recovery time.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionC

description: Apache Spark interview questions covering RDDs, DataFrames, Spark SQL, partitioning, shuffling, memory management, streaming, MLlib, GraphX, and deployment.
content:
ard id="spark-stream-08" number={114} question="What is Write-Ahead Logging (WAL) / journaling in Spark Streaming?" difficulty="hard" topic="Streaming">
There are two kinds of failure in a Spark job: driver failure and worker failure. When a **worker** fails, its executor processes are killed and their scheduled tasks are automatically moved to other running worker nodes. When the **driver** fails, every associated executor is killed along with whatever data was sitting in its memory — in a streaming application, that data hasn't necessarily been persisted anywhere yet, so it can be lost for good, unlike batch jobs reading from a reliable filesystem like HDFS (where zero data loss is guaranteed since the data can always be re-read).

**Write-Ahead Logging**, introduced in Spark 1.2, solves

title: Apache Spark
description: Apache Spark interview questions covering RDDs, DataFrames, Spark SQL, partitioning, shuffling, memory management, streaming, MLlib, GraphX, and deployment.
content:
this: the intent of every operation is first written to a log file, so if the driver fails and restarts, it can replay the logged operations against the data. For streaming sources like Kafka or Flume, receivers also write the data they receive into these log files, not just into executor memory. Enable it with:
1. `streamingContext.checkpoint(path)` — sets the checkpoint directory.
2. `spark.stream.receiver.WriteAheadLog.enable = true` — enables WAL logging.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="spark-stream-09" number={115} question="How is caching relevant in Spark Streaming?" difficulty="medium" topic="Streaming">
Spark Streaming divides a data stream into DStream batches, and those batches can be cached in memory — very useful when the same DStream feeds multiple downstream computations

title: Apache Spark
description: Apache Spark interview questions covering RDDs, DataFrames, Spark SQL, partitioning, shuffling, memory management, streaming, MLlib, GraphX, and deployment.
content:
. Caching uses `cache()` or `persist(StorageLevel)`:

```scala
val cacheDf   = dframe.cache()
val persistDf = dframe.persist(StorageLevel.MEMORY_ONLY)
```

For network-based input streams (Kafka, Flume, etc.), the default persistence level replicates data to 2 nodes for fault tolerance. Caching's main advantages: cost efficiency (avoids recomputation), time efficiency, and more jobs completed per unit of time since worker nodes spend less time recomputing.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="spark-stream-10" number={116} question="What is the significance of the Sliding Window operation?" difficulty="medium" topic="Streaming">
Spark Streaming's windowed computations apply transformations over a sliding window of RDDs rather than a single batch. As the window slides, the RDDs that fall insid

title: Apache Spark
description: Apache Spark interview questions covering RDDs, DataFrames, Spark SQL, partitioning, shuffling, memory management, streaming, MLlib, GraphX, and deployment.
content:
e it are combined and processed together, producing new RDDs for the windowed DStream — useful for aggregations that need to look back over a recent time span rather than just the latest micro-batch.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="spark-stream-11" number={117} question="Explain the level of parallelism in Spark Streaming." difficulty="medium" topic="Streaming">
To reduce processing time, you generally need to increase parallelism, in one of three ways:
- **Increase the number of receivers** — if a single receiver can't read and distribute records fast enough, it becomes a bottleneck; add more receivers as the scenario demands.
- **Re-partition the received data** — if you can't add more receivers, redistribute the data you already have by re-partitioning it.
- **Increase parallelism in

title: Apache Spark
description: Apache Spark interview questions covering RDDs, DataFrames, Spark SQL, partitioning, shuffling, memory management, streaming, MLlib, GraphX, and deployment.
content:
aggregation** — raise the parallelism of the aggregation stage itself.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="spark-stream-12" number={118} question="Which companies use Spark Streaming?" difficulty="easy" topic="Streaming">
Well-known adopters include Uber, Netflix, and Pinterest.
</QuestionCard>

GraphX uses a **vertex-cut** approach to distributed graph partitioning: instead of splitting a graph along its edges, it partitions along vertices, which can then span multiple machines. Edges are assigned to partitions according to whichever partition strategy is selected. This reduces communication and storage overhead compared to edge-cut partitioning.

PageRank measures the importance of each vertex in a graph, treating an edge from `u` to `v` as `u` endorsing `v`'s importance — a Twitter user followed by many others ends up ranked highly, for instance. <QuestionCard id="spark-ml-15" number={133} question="What makes Apache Spark well-suited to low-latency workloads like graph processing and machine learning?" difficulty="medium" topic="MLlib">
Spark keeps data in memory, which speeds up both model building/training and graph traversal — machine learning algorithms typically need multiple iterations to converge on an optimal model, and graph algorithms need to traverse all nodes and edges, often repeatedly. Workloads that require many iterations benefit the most from Spark's in-memory model: less disk access and more controlled network traffic make a large difference once there's a meaningful amount of data to process.

## Key Concepts

Looker's defining trait is that it doesn't store or move data — it's a semantic layer written in **LookML** that defines dimensions, measures, and relationships between tables, then compiles user interactions in an **Explore** into SQL run directly against the underlying warehouse. That "push-down" architecture explains most of Looker's trade-offs: it inherits the warehouse's scalability and real-time limits rather than imposing its own, relies on the warehouse (or **PDTs** — Persistent Derived Tables — materialized back into it) for performance, and depends on the warehouse's own security and partitioning features rather than reinventing them. Governance in Looker is mostly about **access control** (roles, Explore permissions, row-level filters) and **change management**

## Key Concepts

Superset is built on Python and Flask, and stores its own **metadata** (dashboards, charts, connections, users) in a metadata database that's separate from the databases it queries. Every visualization starts as a **slice** — a single chart tied to a dataset — and slices are composed into **dashboards**. Two workflows feed slices: the drag-and-drop **Explore** view for point-and-click chart building, and **SQL Lab**, a full SQL IDE for ad-hoc querying, complete with query history and a saved-query workflow. Because Superset connects via SQLAlchemy, it can talk to most relational databases and several NoSQL/OLAP engines with SQL-like interfaces — including **Druid**, historically the go-to backend for fast, real-time-ish analytics on top of Superset. Security is role-based

content:
(RBAC), extendable to **row-level security** for restricting which rows a given user's queries can return. As with most BI tools, performance is largely inherited from the underlying database, with Superset's own caching layer sitting on top to avoid re-running identical queries.

**Tableau is a drag-and-drop business intelligence platform built around fast, associative in-memory querying — the interview bar is less about syntax and more about knowing when to use a calculated field vs. an LOD expression, a join vs. a blend, and a live connection vs. an extract.**

content:
## Key Concepts

Tableau organizes every data source into **measures** (numeric values to aggregate) and **dimensions** (qualitative attributes to slice by), and every field as **continuous** (plotted on an axis) or **discrete** (plotted as a header). Getting data in happens two ways: a **live connection** queries the source directly for up-to-date results, while an **extract** snapshots the data into Tableau's own fast columnar engine (`.hyper`/`.tde`) for speed and offline use. Combining multiple tables is either a **join** (same data source) or a **blend** (across data sources, via a common field). On top of that foundation sit three tiers of calculation — basic calculated fields, **Level of Detail (LOD)** expressions for granularity that doesn't match the view, and **table calculations

### Data Connections, Joins & Files

<QuestionCard id="tableau-data-01" number={8} question="What are the different types of joins in Tableau?" difficulty="medium" topic="Joins">
Tableau's join types mirror SQL:

- **Left Outer Join** — all records from the left table plus matching rows from the right
- **Right Outer Join** — all records from the right table plus matching rows from the left
- **Full Outer Join** — all records from both tables, with `NULL` where there's no match
- **Inner Join** — only records that match in both tables

<QuestionCard id="tableau-data-02" number={9} question="What are the different connection types you can make with a dataset?" difficulty="medium" topic="Connections

### Data Modeling & Calculations

<QuestionList topic="Tableau Calculations" storagePrefix="tableau-calc">

<QuestionCard id="tableau-calc-01" number={16} question="What is a parameter in Tableau?" difficulty="medium" topic="Parameters">
A parameter is a variable — a number, string, or date — created to replace a constant value used in a calculation, filter, or reference line. For example, instead of hard-coding a field that flags sales above 30,000, you'd create a parameter so that threshold can be changed dynamically. Parameters accept values as:

- **All** — a free-text field
- **List** — a predefined list of selectable values
- **Range** — values constrained to a specified range
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="tableau-calc-02" number={17} question="Tell me about measures and dimensi

title: Tableau
description: Tableau interview questions covering data visualization, calculated fields, LOD expressions, joins vs. blending, dashboards, and server administration.
content:
ons in Tableau." difficulty="easy" topic="Data Modeling">
When you connect a new data source, every field is mapped as either a measure or a dimension, each with a data type (integer, string, and so on) and a role (discrete dimension or continuous measure). **Measures** hold numeric values you aggregate and analyze against a dimension. **Dimensions** hold qualitative values — names, dates, geography — that define the attributes used to categorize, segment, and add detail to the data.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="tableau-calc-03" number={18} question="What are continuous and discrete field types?" difficulty="medium" topic="Data Modeling">
Continuous and discrete are mathematical terms: continuous means unbroken, discrete means individually separate values. Tableau color-codes them —

title: Tableau
description: Tableau interview questions covering data visualization, calculated fields, LOD expressions, joins vs. blending, dashboards, and server administration.
content:
**blue** for discrete, **green** for continuous. A discrete field renders as a header you can sort; a continuous field defines an axis on the graph and can't be sorted the same way.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="tableau-calc-04" number={19} question="What is aggregation and disaggregation of data?" difficulty="medium" topic="Data Modeling">
**Aggregation** displays measures and dimensions in summarized form, using functions like:

- `SUM(expression)` — adds all values (numeric only)
- `AVG(expression)` — averages all values (numeric only)
- `MEDIAN(expression)` — computes the median (numeric only)
- `COUNT(expression)` — counts non-null values
- `COUNT(DISTINCT expression)` — counts unique values

Tableau also lets you change the aggregation type applied to a view. **Disaggregation**,

title: Tableau
description: Tableau interview questions covering data visualization, calculated fields, LOD expressions, joins vs. blending, dashboards, and server administration.
content:
by contrast, shows every individual data record rather than a summarized value.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="tableau-calc-05" number={20} question="What data types does Tableau support?" difficulty="easy" topic="Data Modeling">
| Data Type | Example |
|---|---|
| Boolean | `True` / `False` |
| Date | December 28, 2016 |
| Date & Time | December 28, 2016, 06:00:00 PM |
| Geographical | Beijing, Mumbai |
| Text/String | Any string value |
| Number (Decimal) | 8.00 |
| Number (Whole) | 5 |
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="tableau-calc-06" number={21} question="What are sets in Tableau?" difficulty="medium" topic="Sets">
Sets are custom fields that define a subset of data in your workbook. They can be computed dynamically based on a condition, or created manually from the dimensions i

n your data source. For example, you could define a set of customers whose revenue exceeds some threshold — a computed set updates automatically as the underlying data changes.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="tableau-calc-07" number={22} question="What are groups in Tableau?" difficulty="easy" topic="Groups">
Groups combine related members of a dimension into a larger category for analysis. You define a group's own field values to categorize members of that specific dimension however makes sense for the report.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="tableau-calc-08" number={23} question="How do you use groups in a calculated field?" difficulty="medium" topic="Groups">
- You can reference a saved group directly inside a calculation, but **not** an ad-hoc group created on the fly in the view.

- To reuse a group in another workbook, copy the calculation that defines it and paste it into the new workbook.

<QuestionCard id="tableau-calc-09" number={24} question="What are the various types of filters in Tableau?" difficulty="medium" topic="Filters">
Tableau has 6 filter types:

- **Extract Filter** — retrieves only a subset of the source data
- **Dimension Filter** — filters non-aggregated (discrete) data
- **Data Source Filter** — hides sensitive information at the source connection level, reducing what's fed into the workbook
- **Context Filter** — a preset filter that other filters are applied on top of
- **Measure Filter** — filters

based on aggregate operations like sum, median, or average
- **Table Calculation Filter** — applied after the view has already been constructed
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="tableau-calc-10" number={25} question="What is a Calculated Field, and how do you create one?" difficulty="medium" topic="Calculated Fields">
A calculated field is a new field derived via a formula built on top of other fields — it doesn't exist in the source data until you define it. Common uses:

- Segmenting data
- Converting a field's data type (e.g., string to date)
- Aggregating data
- Filtering results
- Calculating ratios

There are three main calculation types:

- **Basic Calculations** — transform field values at the source level
- **Level of Detail (LOD) Expressions** — also transform values at the sour

ce level, but at a more granular level of control than basic calculations
- **Table Calculations** — transform values only at the visualization level, based on what's already in the view

To create one: go to **Analysis > Create Calculated Field**, enter your formula in the calculation editor, and save.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="tableau-calc-11" number={26} question="How can you display the top five and bottom five sales in the same view?" difficulty="hard" topic="Calculated Fields">
1. Drag **Customer Name** to Rows and **Sales** to Columns.
2. Sort `SUM(Sales)` in descending order.
3. Create a calculated field for the **Rank of Sales**, then filter or combine two rank-based calculations (top N and bottom N) into the same view.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="tableau-calc-12"

number={27} question="What is the Rank function in Tableau?" difficulty="medium" topic="Functions">
`RANK` assigns positions to values in a measure. Tableau offers several variants:

- **`RANK`** — takes an aggregated measure and an optional sort order (default descending)
- **`RANK_DENSE`** — assigns the same rank to equal values but keeps incrementing the next rank without gaps: `10, 20, 20, 30` ranks as `1, 2, 2, 3`
- **`RANK_MODIFIED`** — assigns the same rank to equal values, similar to dense rank but with different gap behavior
- **`RANK_UNIQUE`** — assigns a distinct rank to every value, even ties: `10, 20, 20, 30` ranks as `1, 2, 3, 4`
</QuestionCard>

Dual axes let you analyze two different measures at two different scales on the same graph, comparing multiple attributes with two independent axes layered on top of each other. To add a measure as a dual axis, drag the field to the right edge of the view until a black dashed line appears — or right-click the measure on the Columns/Rows shelf and choose **Dual Axis**.

A **treemap** visualizes a hierarchy as nested rectangles, with hierarchy levels shown from larger rectangles down to smaller ones — for example, aggregated sales totals broken out across product categories.

A story combines a sequence of worksheets to walk viewers through a narrative built from your visualizations. to webpages?" difficulty="medium" topic="Publishing">
Interactive views from Tableau Server or Tableau Online can be embedded into webpages, blogs, web apps, or portals. Viewers typically need a Tableau Server account to see the embedded content. To embed a view, click **Share** at the top of the view and copy the embed code onto the target page — you can also customize the embed code or use the Tableau JavaScript API for more control.
</QuestionCard>

The Tableau data engine is an analytical database that computes near-instant query responses and handles predictive analysis and integrated data. It's used whenever you create, refresh, or query extracts, and it

## AWS Analytics: Building the Lake and Querying It

**This is the heart of AWS for a data engineer. Glue catalogues and transforms, Athena queries S3 without infrastructure, EMR runs Spark at scale, Kinesis and MSK move streams, and Lake Formation governs the lot. The interview questions that separate candidates aren't "what is Glue" — they're "why is this Athena query scanning 4 TB", "when would you use EMR over Glue", and "how do you get exactly-once from Kinesis".**

description: AWS analytics interview questions covering Athena, EMR, Glue and the Data Catalog, Lake Formation, Kinesis and MSK for streaming, OpenSearch, and building a lakehouse on S3.
content:
## Key Concepts

The AWS analytics stack is built on **separating storage from compute**. Data lives in S3 as open-format files — Parquet, and increasingly Iceberg or Delta tables. The **Glue Data Catalog** provides the shared schema layer, so the same table definition is visible to Athena, EMR, Redshift Spectrum, Glue jobs and Lake Formation. Compute engines come and go without touching the data.

That means the **table metadata is the integration point**, and getting it right — partitions registered, schema accurate, statistics current — determines whether queries are fast and cheap or slow and expensive.

The cost model follows directly. Athena and Redshift Spectrum bill **per terabyte scanned**, so partitioning, columnar formats and predicate pushdown aren't optimisations — they're the

title: AWS Analytics Services
description: AWS analytics interview questions covering Athena, EMR, Glue and the Data Catalog, Lake Formation, Kinesis and MSK for streaming, OpenSearch, and building a lakehouse on S3.
content:
difference between a query costing cents and costing hundreds of dollars. Almost every AWS analytics performance question ultimately reduces to "how do you scan less data."

title: AWS Analytics Services
description: AWS analytics interview questions covering Athena, EMR, Glue and the Data Catalog, Lake Formation, Kinesis and MSK for streaming, OpenSearch, and building a lakehouse on S3.
content:
## Amazon Athena

<QuestionList topic="Amazon Athena" storagePrefix="aws-analytics-athena">

<QuestionCard id="awsan-ath-01" number={1} question="What is Athena and how is it priced?" difficulty="easy" topic="Athena">
Serverless interactive SQL over data in S3, built on Trino (formerly Presto). No infrastructure to provision — you point it at a table in the Glue Data Catalog and query.

Pricing is **per terabyte of data scanned**, with a 10 MB minimum per query. Nothing is charged when idle, which makes it ideal for ad-hoc and intermittent analysis.

That pricing model drives every optimisation: since you pay for bytes read, the entire game is reading fewer bytes. `SELECT *` on an unpartitioned CSV table is the worst case in both cost and latency.

**Athena for Apache Spark** also exists f

title: AWS Analytics Services
description: AWS analytics interview questions covering Athena, EMR, Glue and the Data Catalog, Lake Formation, Kinesis and MSK for streaming, OpenSearch, and building a lakehouse on S3.
content:
or notebook-style Spark without a cluster, and there's a provisioned-capacity option that bills per hour instead if you want predictable cost.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="awsan-ath-02" number={2} question="How do you reduce Athena cost and improve performance?" difficulty="hard" topic="Athena">
All of these reduce bytes scanned:

1. **Partition** on the columns you filter on — usually date. A query hitting one day of a year's data scans 1/365th.
2. **Columnar format** — Parquet or ORC. A query touching 3 of 100 columns reads only those.
3. **Compress** — Snappy or ZSTD; less data on disk means fewer bytes scanned.
4. **Select only the columns you need** — never `SELECT *` in production.
5. **Right-size files** — 128 MB to 1 GB. Small files add per-file overhead; huge ones limit para

title: AWS Analytics Services
description: AWS analytics interview questions covering Athena, EMR, Glue and the Data Catalog, Lake Formation, Kinesis and MSK for streaming, OpenSearch, and building a lakehouse on S3.
content:
llelism.
6. **Partition projection** — for tables with many partitions, this avoids the metadata lookup entirely and is dramatically faster than repeated `MSCK REPAIR`.
7. **Bucketing / sorting** on high-cardinality filter columns for further pruning.
8. **`LIMIT` doesn't help** — Athena still scans the data; only predicates on partition columns prune.

That last point is the one people get wrong: adding `LIMIT 10` to a query over an unpartitioned table costs exactly the same.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="awsan-ath-03" number={3} question="What is partition projection?" difficulty="hard" topic="Athena">
Instead of reading partition metadata from the Glue Catalog, Athena **calculates** the partition values from a configured pattern in the table properties.

```sql
'projection.enabled'

title: AWS Analytics Services
description: AWS analytics interview questions covering Athena, EMR, Glue and the Data Catalog, Lake Formation, Kinesis and MSK for streaming, OpenSearch, and building a lakehouse on S3.
content:
='true',
'projection.dt.type'='date',
'projection.dt.range'='2020-01-01,NOW',
'projection.dt.format'='yyyy-MM-dd',
'storage.location.template'='s3://lake/orders/dt=${dt}/'
```

Why it matters: a table with hundreds of thousands of partitions spends significant query time just retrieving partition metadata, and `MSCK REPAIR TABLE` on such a table becomes painfully slow. Projection eliminates both — there's nothing to register, so **new partitions are queryable immediately** without any catalog update.

The trade: the layout must be predictable and regular. It suits time-partitioned data perfectly, and doesn't suit arbitrary partition values.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="awsan-ath-04" number={4} question="What are Athena workgroups?" difficulty="medium" topic="Athena">
Logical grouping

title: AWS Analytics Services
description: AWS analytics interview questions covering Athena, EMR, Glue and the Data Catalog, Lake Formation, Kinesis and MSK for streaming, OpenSearch, and building a lakehouse on S3.
content:
s that separate query execution by team or workload, providing:

- **Cost controls** — per-query and per-workgroup **data scanned limits**, which can cancel a runaway query before it scans 50 TB.
- **Separate result locations** in S3.
- **Cost attribution** via tags, so you can see which team is spending.
- **Enforced settings**, such as requiring encryption of results.
- **Separate CloudWatch metrics**.

The per-query data scan limit is the feature worth naming in an interview — it's the practical guard against a single bad `SELECT *` on a petabyte table, which is otherwise a very expensive accident with no natural ceiling.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

title: AWS Analytics Services
description: AWS analytics interview questions covering Athena, EMR, Glue and the Data Catalog, Lake Formation, Kinesis and MSK for streaming, OpenSearch, and building a lakehouse on S3.
content:
## AWS Glue

<QuestionList topic="AWS Glue" storagePrefix="aws-analytics-glue">

<QuestionCard id="awsan-glue-01" number={1} question="What are the components of AWS Glue?" difficulty="medium" topic="Glue">
- **Data Catalog** — a central metastore (Hive-compatible) of databases, tables, schemas and partitions, shared by Athena, EMR, Redshift Spectrum, Lake Formation and Glue jobs.
- **Crawlers** — scan S3 (or JDBC sources), infer schema and partitions, and populate the catalog.
- **ETL jobs** — serverless Spark (or Python shell for small tasks), billed per DPU-hour.
- **Glue Studio** — a visual job authoring interface.
- **Workflows and triggers** — basic orchestration of crawlers and jobs.
- **Glue DataBrew** — visual data preparation for analysts, no code.
- **Glue Data Quality** — rule-

title: AWS Analytics Services
description: AWS analytics interview questions covering Athena, EMR, Glue and the Data Catalog, Lake Formation, Kinesis and MSK for streaming, OpenSearch, and building a lakehouse on S3.
content:
based quality checks, with rules expressible in DQDL and the ability to suggest rules from data.
- **Schema Registry** — schema management and evolution for streaming.

The **Data Catalog** is the piece that matters most architecturally — it's the shared schema layer the whole AWS analytics stack reads from.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="awsan-glue-02" number={2} question="What is a Glue crawler, and when should you avoid using one?" difficulty="medium" topic="Glue">
A crawler samples files in a path, infers a schema and partition structure, and creates or updates catalog tables.

It's convenient for discovery and for genuinely unknown data. But for production tables, many teams **avoid crawlers** because:

- **Inference is unreliable** — sampling can misread a column as `bigint` that

title: AWS Analytics Services
description: AWS analytics interview questions covering Athena, EMR, Glue and the Data Catalog, Lake Formation, Kinesis and MSK for streaming, OpenSearch, and building a lakehouse on S3.
content:
later contains a value requiring `string`, and schema changes can silently alter the table.
- **They cost money and time** on large buckets.
- **They can be destructive** — a bad run can change column types under live queries.
- **They're unnecessary** when you already know the schema.

The mature pattern is to **define tables explicitly** in code (Terraform, or DDL in your pipeline) so the schema is version-controlled and reviewed, and use **partition projection** or explicit `ALTER TABLE ADD PARTITION` instead of repeated crawling.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="awsan-glue-03" number={3} question="What are DynamicFrames and how do they differ from Spark DataFrames?" difficulty="medium" topic="Glue">
A Glue-specific abstraction over Spark DataFrames designed for messy, schema-inconsi

title: AWS Analytics Services
description: AWS analytics interview questions covering Athena, EMR, Glue and the Data Catalog, Lake Formation, Kinesis and MSK for streaming, OpenSearch, and building a lakehouse on S3.
content:
stent data.

The differences:
- **Self-describing** — no schema required up front, inferred per record.
- **Choice types** — when a field is sometimes an `int` and sometimes a `string`, a DynamicFrame records both rather than failing or coercing. `ResolveChoice` then lets you decide what to do.
- **Built-in transforms** — `Relationalize` flattens nested structures into related tables, `ApplyMapping` renames and casts.

`toDF()` and `fromDF()` convert between the two.

Practical guidance: use DynamicFrames at the **ingestion edge** where data is unpredictable, then convert to a DataFrame for the actual transformation work — the DataFrame API is richer, better documented, and better optimised. Many teams use plain Spark throughout and only use DynamicFrames for the connectors.
</QuestionCard

title: AWS Analytics Services
description: AWS analytics interview questions covering Athena, EMR, Glue and the Data Catalog, Lake Formation, Kinesis and MSK for streaming, OpenSearch, and building a lakehouse on S3.
content:
>

<QuestionCard id="awsan-glue-04" number={4} question="What are Glue job bookmarks?" difficulty="medium" topic="Glue">
State that tracks what a job has already processed, so subsequent runs handle only new data — the mechanism for incremental ETL.

For S3 sources it tracks object keys and timestamps; for JDBC it tracks a bounded key column.

The caveats that catch people:
- **They only work with supported sources and formats**, and require the job to use Glue's own read methods.
- **A bookmark can be stale or wrong** after a failed run, so you may need to reset or pause it — `job.commit()` must be called for the bookmark to advance.
- **Modified files aren't reprocessed** — bookmarks track new objects, so an overwritten file is skipped.
- **They complicate backfills**, since you must res

title: AWS Analytics Services
description: AWS analytics interview questions covering Athena, EMR, Glue and the Data Catalog, Lake Formation, Kinesis and MSK for streaming, OpenSearch, and building a lakehouse on S3.
content:
et the bookmark for the range you're re-running.

Many teams prefer explicit watermarking — storing the last processed partition themselves — because it's visible, debuggable, and works the same across engines.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="awsan-glue-05" number={5} question="When would you use Glue versus EMR?" difficulty="hard" topic="Glue">
**Glue** — serverless Spark. No cluster to manage, per-second billing with a 1-minute minimum, integrated catalog and bookmarks. Best for **scheduled, moderate ETL** where you don't want infrastructure and can live with Glue's Spark version and configuration limits.

**EMR** — a real Hadoop/Spark cluster you configure. Best when you need **control**: a specific Spark version, custom JARs and tuning, other frameworks (Flink, Trino, HBase), long-r

title: AWS Analytics Services
description: AWS analytics interview questions covering Athena, EMR, Glue and the Data Catalog, Lake Formation, Kinesis and MSK for streaming, OpenSearch, and building a lakehouse on S3.
content:
unning clusters, notebooks, or genuinely large jobs where Spot pricing on a managed cluster is far cheaper.

Cost crossover: Glue's per-DPU-hour rate is high relative to Spot EC2, so **at sustained scale EMR is significantly cheaper**; at low duty cycle Glue wins because idle costs nothing.

**EMR Serverless** sits between them — Spark and Hive without cluster management, more configurable than Glue, and often the best default for new workloads today.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

title: AWS Analytics Services
description: AWS analytics interview questions covering Athena, EMR, Glue and the Data Catalog, Lake Formation, Kinesis and MSK for streaming, OpenSearch, and building a lakehouse on S3.
content:
## Amazon EMR

<QuestionList topic="Amazon EMR" storagePrefix="aws-analytics-emr">

<QuestionCard id="awsan-emr-01" number={1} question="What is EMR and what node types does a cluster have?" difficulty="medium" topic="EMR">
A managed cluster platform for open-source big data frameworks — Spark, Hive, Trino, HBase, Flink, Presto — on EC2, EKS, or serverless.

Node types:
- **Primary (master)** — runs the resource manager and coordinates. A single point of failure unless you use multi-master.
- **Core** — run tasks **and** store HDFS data. Losing one risks data loss, so they're normally On-Demand.
- **Task** — compute only, no HDFS. **Ideal for Spot**, because losing one only costs re-computation.

The standard cost-optimised shape is **primary and core On-Demand, task nodes on Spot with a d

title: AWS Analytics Services
description: AWS analytics interview questions covering Athena, EMR, Glue and the Data Catalog, Lake Formation, Kinesis and MSK for streaming, OpenSearch, and building a lakehouse on S3.
content:
iversified instance fleet.** With EMRFS reading from S3 rather than HDFS, core node storage matters less, which pushes even more capacity onto cheap task nodes.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="awsan-emr-02" number={2} question="What are transient versus long-running clusters?" difficulty="medium" topic="EMR">
**Transient** — created for a job, terminated when it completes (`--auto-terminate`). You pay only for the run, and every job gets a clean, correctly-sized cluster. The default for scheduled batch work.

**Long-running** — persists, serving many jobs and interactive users. Justified by notebook and ad-hoc query workloads, HBase, or when startup latency (5–10 minutes) is unacceptable.

The cost failure mode is the classic one: a long-running cluster provisioned for peak, idle most o

title: AWS Analytics Services
description: AWS analytics interview questions covering Athena, EMR, Glue and the Data Catalog, Lake Formation, Kinesis and MSK for streaming, OpenSearch, and building a lakehouse on S3.
content:
f the night and all weekend. Auto-termination on idle and managed scaling address it.

**EMR Serverless** removes the choice — you submit a job and pay for the resources it uses — which is why it's increasingly the default for batch.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="awsan-emr-03" number={3} question="What is EMRFS, and why not use HDFS?" difficulty="medium" topic="EMR">
**EMRFS** is EMR's implementation of the Hadoop filesystem API backed by **S3**, so `s3://` paths work as a filesystem to Spark and Hive.

Using S3 rather than cluster HDFS is the standard architecture because it **decouples storage from compute**: clusters become disposable, multiple clusters read the same data, and you don't pay to keep a cluster alive just to hold data. It's also cheaper and more durable than HDFS on E

title: AWS Analytics Services
description: AWS analytics interview questions covering Athena, EMR, Glue and the Data Catalog, Lake Formation, Kinesis and MSK for streaming, OpenSearch, and building a lakehouse on S3.
content:
BS.

HDFS on the cluster is still used for **intermediate data** — shuffle spill and temporary output — where the local NVMe of storage-optimised instances is much faster than S3.

Historical note worth knowing: EMRFS consistent view existed to work around S3's eventual consistency for listings. Since S3 became strongly consistent in 2020, it's unnecessary.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="awsan-emr-04" number={4} question="How do you tune a Spark job on EMR?" difficulty="hard" topic="EMR">
Diagnose first, in the Spark UI. The usual findings, in order of frequency:

1. **Data skew** — a handful of tasks running far longer than the rest. Fix with salting, broadcast joins for small sides, or Adaptive Query Execution's skew join handling.
2. **Too much data scanned** — bad partitioning, CSV

title: AWS Analytics Services
description: AWS analytics interview questions covering Athena, EMR, Glue and the Data Catalog, Lake Formation, Kinesis and MSK for streaming, OpenSearch, and building a lakehouse on S3.
content:
instead of Parquet, no predicate pushdown. Usually the biggest single win, and it's a storage-layout fix.
3. **Small files** — thousands of tasks doing almost nothing. Compact the input, tune the output partition count.
4. **Executor sizing** — a few large executors generally beat many tiny ones; leave headroom for off-heap and overhead or YARN kills the container.
5. **Shuffle spilling to EBS** — use an instance type with local NVMe.
6. **Unnecessary shuffles** — repartitioning where a coalesce would do, or a join that could be broadcast.

Enable **AQE** and **dynamic allocation**; they handle several of these automatically on modern Spark.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

title: AWS Analytics Services
description: AWS analytics interview questions covering Athena, EMR, Glue and the Data Catalog, Lake Formation, Kinesis and MSK for streaming, OpenSearch, and building a lakehouse on S3.
content:
## Streaming: Kinesis & MSK

<QuestionList topic="Streaming: Kinesis & MSK" storagePrefix="aws-analytics-streaming">

<QuestionCard id="awsan-kin-01" number={1} question="What are the Kinesis services and how do they differ?" difficulty="medium" topic="Kinesis">
- **Kinesis Data Streams** — a durable, ordered, replayable stream of records in **shards**. You control consumers and offsets; retention is 24 hours up to 365 days. Use it when you need **replay**, multiple independent consumers, or ordering.
- **Kinesis Data Firehose** — a fully managed **delivery** stream to S3, Redshift, OpenSearch or a third party, with buffering, format conversion to Parquet, compression and optional Lambda transformation. **No replay, no consumer offsets** — it's a pipe, not a log.
- **Managed Service for Ap

title: AWS Analytics Services
description: AWS analytics interview questions covering Athena, EMR, Glue and the Data Catalog, Lake Formation, Kinesis and MSK for streaming, OpenSearch, and building a lakehouse on S3.
content:
ache Flink** (formerly Kinesis Data Analytics) — stateful stream processing with SQL or the Flink API.
- **Kinesis Video Streams** — media; irrelevant to most data engineering.

The distinction interviewers probe: **Streams when you need to consume and replay; Firehose when you just need it landed in S3.** Firehose is dramatically less work if delivery is all you need.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="awsan-kin-02" number={2} question="How do shards work, and what limits should you know?" difficulty="hard" topic="Kinesis">
A shard is the unit of capacity and ordering. Per shard:

- **1 MB/s or 1,000 records/s** ingress
- **2 MB/s** egress shared across standard consumers, or 2 MB/s **per consumer** with enhanced fan-out
- **Ordering is guaranteed within a shard**, not across the stream

title: AWS Analytics Services
description: AWS analytics interview questions covering Athena, EMR, Glue and the Data Catalog, Lake Formation, Kinesis and MSK for streaming, OpenSearch, and building a lakehouse on S3.
content:
Records are assigned to shards by **partition key** hash — so a poorly chosen key creates a **hot shard** that throttles while others idle, exactly like DynamoDB.

Scaling means **resharding** (splitting or merging), which changes shard IDs and forces consumers to handle the transition. **On-demand mode** removes this by scaling automatically, at higher per-GB cost — usually the right choice unless volume is steady and well understood.

With more than a few consumers, use **enhanced fan-out** so they don't compete for the shared 2 MB/s.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="awsan-kin-03" number={3} question="What is MSK, and when would you choose it over Kinesis?" difficulty="medium" topic="MSK">
**Managed Streaming for Apache Kafka** — real Kafka, with AWS handling provisioning, patching, an

title: AWS Analytics Services
description: AWS analytics interview questions covering Athena, EMR, Glue and the Data Catalog, Lake Formation, Kinesis and MSK for streaming, OpenSearch, and building a lakehouse on S3.
content:
d broker replacement. MSK Serverless removes capacity planning too.

Choose **MSK** when:
- You need the **Kafka ecosystem** — Kafka Connect, Kafka Streams, ksqlDB, Schema Registry, Debezium for CDC.
- You want **portability** — the same code runs on-premises or on another cloud.
- You have existing Kafka expertise or applications.
- You need finer control over retention, compaction, and partitioning.

Choose **Kinesis** when you want the least operational surface, tight AWS integration (Firehose to S3 in a few clicks, native Lambda triggers), and don't need Kafka specifics.

The honest summary: Kinesis is simpler and more integrated; MSK is more capable and portable. Log compaction and Connect are the features that most often force MSK.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="awsan-kin-04" num

title: AWS Analytics Services
description: AWS analytics interview questions covering Athena, EMR, Glue and the Data Catalog, Lake Formation, Kinesis and MSK for streaming, OpenSearch, and building a lakehouse on S3.
content:
ber={4} question="How do you get exactly-once semantics in a streaming pipeline?" difficulty="hard" topic="Streaming">
Strictly, exactly-once *delivery* is impossible across a network; what you achieve is **effectively-once processing** through idempotency.

The mechanisms:
- **Idempotent writes** — key the output by a deterministic ID (`stream+shard+sequence_number`) so a reprocessed record overwrites rather than duplicates. An upsert on a primary key, or `MERGE` into a Delta/Iceberg table.
- **Deduplication** — track processed record IDs in DynamoDB or a Redis set within a time window.
- **Transactional checkpointing** — commit the offset and the output atomically. Flink's checkpoint barriers and Spark Structured Streaming's checkpoint plus idempotent sink do this.
- **Kafka transactions

title: AWS Analytics Services
description: AWS analytics interview questions covering Athena, EMR, Glue and the Data Catalog, Lake Formation, Kinesis and MSK for streaming, OpenSearch, and building a lakehouse on S3.
content:
** — for Kafka-to-Kafka, producers and consumers can participate in a transaction giving exactly-once within Kafka.

The point to make: **design the sink to be idempotent** rather than trying to guarantee the stream delivers once. That's the only approach that survives retries, restarts and replays.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

content:
## Governance & Search

<QuestionList topic="Governance & Search" storagePrefix="aws-analytics-governance">

<QuestionCard id="awsan-lf-01" number={1} question="What is Lake Formation and what does it add over IAM?" difficulty="medium" topic="Lake Formation">
A governance layer over the lake providing **fine-grained permissions on catalog objects** — database, table, **column**, row and cell level — enforced across Athena, Redshift Spectrum, EMR, Glue and QuickSight.

IAM alone controls access to **S3 prefixes**, which is coarse: you can grant a bucket path, but you can't say "this analyst may query the orders table but not the `email` or `ssn` columns," or "this team sees only EU rows."

Lake Formation adds that, plus **tag-based access control** (LF-Tags) so permissions are granted to ta

It also handles cross-account sharing of catalog resources cleanly, which is the foundation for a data mesh arrangement where domains publish tables to each other.

Architecturally the important part is **where** it runs: as a gate **before publishing** to the curated zone, so bad data never reaches consumers, plus a monitoring check on the way in so upstream drift is visible. Failing loudly at the boundary is far cheaper than discovering wrong numbers on a dashboard a week later.

Alternatives worth naming: Deequ (which Glue DQ builds on), Great Expectations, and dbt tests.

<QuestionCard id="awsan-os-01" number={3} question="What is Amazon OpenSearch Service used for in a data platform?" difficulty="medium" topic="OpenSearch">
Managed OpenSearch (the fork of Elasticsearch) — a distributed search and analytics engine over an inverted index.

In a data platform it appears for:
- **Log analytics and observability** — pipeli

- **Full-text search** over documents and product catalogues.
- **Near-real-time operational dashboards**, where a warehouse's latency is too high.

Where it does *not* belong: as a data warehouse. It's expensive per GB, has no joins, and its aggregations are approximate at scale. Teams that used it as a general analytics store usually regret it.

The typical pattern is **Firehose → OpenSearch for the hot, searchable window** (say 30 days) with the full history in S3 for analytical queries via Athena.

- **Ingestion** — Kinesis/MSK for streams,

- **Storage** — S3 with zones: `raw` (immutable, as-received), `staging` (cleaned, reproducible), `curated` (modelled, consumed).

- **Orchestration** — MWAA or Step Functions.

content:
## Key Concepts

Most AWS comparisons reduce to one of four axes. **Access shape** — object, block or file; key-value or relational; scan or point lookup. **Managed versus controlled** — how much AWS operates, and what you give up in exchange. **Elasticity versus committed capacity** — serverless costs nothing at idle and more per unit of work, provisioned is the reverse. And **coupling** — how tightly the choice ties you to AWS.

The strongest interview technique is to **name the axis first**, then place both services on it. "S3 versus EBS" is really "object storage accessed over HTTP by many clients versus block storage attached to one instance" — and once that's said, every difference in durability, sharing, pricing and performance follows.

The second technique is knowing when to **rej

ect the premise**. A question like "Redshift or Athena?" often has the answer "both, for different query patterns," and "RDS or DynamoDB?" is frequently "RDS, because the access pattern isn't actually key-value." Volunteering that is a stronger answer than picking a side.

## Storage Comparisons

<QuestionList topic="Storage Comparisons" storagePrefix="aws-comparisons-storage">

<QuestionCard id="awscmp-st-01" number={1} question="S3 vs EBS vs EFS — how do you choose?" difficulty="medium" topic="Storage">
| | **S3** | **EBS** | **EFS** |
|---|---|---|---|
| Type | object | block | file (NFS) |
| Access | HTTP API, from anywhere | one instance at a time | many instances concurrently |
| Scale | unlimited | up to 64 TiB per volume | petabytes, elastic |
| Durability | 11 nines, multi-AZ | single AZ (snapshots to S3) | multi-AZ |
| Cost | cheapest | middle | most expensive per GB |
| Latency | tens of ms | sub-ms | low ms |

**S3** for the data lake, backups, static content — anything analytical. **EBS** for a database's data directory or an instance's boot vol

title: AWS Service Comparisons

content:
ume. **EFS** when multiple instances genuinely need shared POSIX access, such as a shared Airflow DAGs folder.

For a data engineer the default is overwhelmingly **S3**; the analytics ecosystem is built on it, and putting a lake on EFS is an expensive anti-pattern.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="awscmp-st-02" number={2} question="S3 vs S3 Glacier — and which Glacier tier?" difficulty="medium" topic="Storage">
The trade is **storage cost against retrieval cost and latency**.

- **S3 Standard** — immediate access, highest storage price, no retrieval fee.
- **Glacier Instant Retrieval** — much cheaper storage, **milliseconds** access, retrieval fee. Best for archives you occasionally need immediately.
- **Glacier Flexible Retrieval** — cheaper again; minutes (expedited) to hours (bulk).
-

content:
**Glacier Deep Archive** — cheapest, up to 12 hours. For compliance retention you hope never to read.

The traps: **minimum storage durations** (90 days for Flexible, 180 for Deep Archive) mean early deletion is billed for the full period, and a **128 KB minimum billable object size** makes archiving millions of small files cost *more* than leaving them in Standard.

Rule of thumb for a lake: raw data to IA at 30 days and Flexible at 90; keep curated data queryable in Standard or IA.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="awscmp-st-03" number={3} question="S3 Standard vs Standard-IA vs One Zone-IA?" difficulty="medium" topic="Storage">
All three give **immediate access**; they differ in storage price, retrieval fee, and resilience.

- **Standard** — no retrieval fee, multi-AZ. For frequently-
