- **Standard-IA** — roughly 45% cheaper storage, **plus a per-GB retrieval fee**, multi-AZ. Break-even is roughly one read per month; read more often and it costs *more* than Standard.
- **One Zone-IA** — about 20% cheaper than Standard-IA, but stored in a **single AZ**. If that AZ is lost, the data is lost.

One Zone-IA is only appropriate for **reproducible** data — a derived table you can rebuild, a secondary copy, staging output. Never for raw ingested data you can't recreate.

If access patterns are unknown, **Intelligent-Tiering** avoids the retrieval-fee gamble entirely for a small monitoring charge — though it's a poor fit for buckets of tiny objects.
</QuestionCard>

**SSD** types optimise for **IOPS** (many small random operations); **HDD** types optimise for **throughput** (large sequential reads).

- **gp3** — general purpose SSD, 3,000 baseline IOPS and 125 MB/s, with IOPS and throughput provisioned **independently of size**. The default, and cheaper than gp2.
- **io2 / io2 Block Express** — provisioned IOPS up to 256,000, higher durability. For latency-sensitive databases only; it's expensive.
- **st1** — throughput-optimised HDD. Cheap sequential throughput, poor random access. Good for log processing and big scans.
- **sc1** — cold HDD, cheapest, infrequent access.

The rule: **random small I/O needs SSD; large sequential reads can use HDD.** Booting from st1 or running a transactional database on it will be miserable,

All three are managed shared filesystems, differing by protocol and purpose.

- **EFS** — NFS, Linux, elastic, multi-AZ, no capacity planning. The general-purpose choice for Linux workloads needing shared POSIX access.
- **FSx for Windows File Server** — SMB, with Active Directory integration, Windows ACLs and DFS. For Windows applications; EFS can't serve them properly.
- **FSx for Lustre** — a high-performance parallel filesystem delivering hundreds of GB/s, and — the feature that matters for data engineering — it can be **linked to an S3 bucket**, presenting objects as files and writing results back.

The

Lustre-plus-S3 pattern is the one to name: keep data in S3 as the durable, cheap source of truth, and mount it through Lustre for the duration of an HPC or ML training job that needs POSIX speed.

## Database Comparisons

<QuestionList topic="Database Comparisons" storagePrefix="aws-comparisons-databases">

<QuestionCard id="awscmp-db-01" number={1} question="RDS vs DynamoDB — how do you decide?" difficulty="hard" topic="Databases">
The axis is **whether your access patterns are known and key-based**.

**RDS** — relational, SQL, joins, transactions, ad-hoc queries, strong consistency, flexible schema evolution. Scales vertically, plus read replicas. Choose it when queries are varied or unknown, when relationships matter, or when the team needs SQL.

**DynamoDB** — key-value and document, single-digit millisecond latency, effectively unlimited horizontal scale, serverless. Choose it for very high write throughput, predictable key-based access, and when you want zero operational overh

content:
ead.

The mistake to name: teams pick DynamoDB for scale, then discover they need ad-hoc queries and joins, and end up doing expensive `Scan`s or exporting to S3 anyway. **If you can't enumerate your access patterns up front, that's evidence for RDS.**

Most applications are better served by Postgres than they think, and the burden of proof is on leaving it.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="awscmp-db-02" number={2} question="Aurora vs RDS — when is the premium worth it?" difficulty="medium" topic="Databases">
Aurora is MySQL/PostgreSQL-compatible with a rewritten distributed storage layer. It costs more per hour, so the question is what you get.

Worth it when you need:
- **Read scale** — up to 15 replicas sharing storage, with **millisecond replica lag** versus RDS's seconds. Important

title: AWS Service Comparisons

content:
if pipelines read replicas and care about freshness.
- **Throughput** — commonly 3–5× MySQL, 2–3× PostgreSQL.
- **Storage that auto-scales** to 128 TB with no provisioning.
- **Fast failover and crash recovery**.
- **Backtrack** — rewind the cluster in place, without a restore.
- **Serverless v2** — fine-grained autoscaling for variable load.
- **Zero-ETL to Redshift** — a managed continuous replication into the warehouse.

Not worth it for a small, steady database where standard RDS already performs fine. Also note Aurora isn't available for every engine — Oracle and SQL Server are RDS-only.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="awscmp-db-03" number={3} question="Global Secondary Index vs Local Secondary Index in DynamoDB?" difficulty="medium" topic="Databases">

|---|

**GSIs are what you use in practice.** They enable genuinely different access patterns, can be added as requirements evolve, and scale independently.

**LSIs** are constrained by two hard rules — create-time only, and the 10 GB per-partition-key ceiling — that make them risky. Getting the design wrong means recreating the table.

<QuestionCard id="awscmp-db-04" number={4} question="ElastiCache Redis vs Memcached, and Redis cluster mode?" difficulty="medium" topic="Databases">
**Memcached** — multi-threaded, simple key-value, no persistence, no replication. Scales by adding nodes with client-side sharding. Choose it only for a plain, high-throughput cache with large values where multi-threading helps.

**Redis** — richer data types (sorted sets, hashes, streams), replication, automatic failover, snapshots, pub/sub, Lua. Single-threaded per shard but very fast. **The default choice**, because the capability is free and matters as soon as the cache becomes load-bearing.

**Cluster mode disabled** — one shard, one primary plus up to five replicas. Scale reads by adding repl

title: AWS Service Comparisons
description: Head-to-head AWS service comparisons that come up constantly in data engineering interviews — S3 vs EBS vs EFS, RDS vs DynamoDB, Aurora vs RDS, Kinesis stream types, SQS vs SNS vs Step Functions, ECS vs EKS vs Lambda, and storage class trade-offs.
content:
icas, scale writes only vertically. Simpler.

**Cluster mode enabled** — data sharded across up to 500 shards, each with replicas. Scales writes and storage horizontally, but multi-key operations must stay within a hash slot, and clients must be cluster-aware.

Start with cluster mode disabled; enable it when you outgrow one node's memory or write capacity.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="awscmp-db-05" number={5} question="Redis persistence: AOF vs snapshots vs replication?" difficulty="hard" topic="Databases">
Three different guarantees, often conflated.

- **RDB snapshots** — a point-in-time dump on a schedule. Fast restart, compact, but you lose everything written since the last snapshot.
- **AOF (append-only file)** — logs every write, replayed on restart. Much less data loss (down

title: AWS Service Comparisons
description: Head-to-head AWS service comparisons that come up constantly in data engineering interviews — S3 vs EBS vs EFS, RDS vs DynamoDB, Aurora vs RDS, Kinesis stream types, SQS vs SNS vs Step Functions, ECS vs EKS vs Lambda, and storage class trade-offs.
content:
to one second with `everysec`), at the cost of larger files, slower restarts, and a write-throughput penalty.
- **Replication** — a replica in another AZ, promoted on failure. Protects against **node failure**, not against a logical error, because a bad `FLUSHALL` replicates instantly.

The important distinction: **replication is availability, persistence is durability.** They protect against different things, and a design needs to say which it requires.

For a cache, none of it matters much — rebuild from source. For anything where Redis is the source of truth, **MemoryDB** is the better answer than tuning AOF on ElastiCache.
</QuestionCard>

## Compute Comparisons

<QuestionList topic="Compute Comparisons" storagePrefix="aws-comparisons-compute">

<QuestionCard id="awscmp-cp-01" number={1} question="ECS vs EKS — which container orchestrator?" difficulty="medium" topic="Compute">
**ECS** — AWS's own orchestrator. No control plane fee, simpler concepts (task definitions and services rather than pods, deployments and ingresses), and deep native integration with IAM, ALB, CloudWatch and Fargate. Faster to adopt, less to operate.

**EKS** — managed Kubernetes. You get the standard API and the entire ecosystem: Helm charts, operators, Spark on Kubernetes, Airflow's KubernetesExecutor, Karpenter, service meshes. Costs a control plane fee per cluster and real operational effort — upgrades, networking, IRSA, resource quotas.

Choose **

content:
ECS** if you're committed to AWS and value simplicity. Choose **EKS** if you need the Kubernetes ecosystem, want portability across clouds or on-premises, or already run Kubernetes and want one operational model.

For data platforms specifically, EKS wins more often than it otherwise would, because Spark and Airflow have first-class Kubernetes support.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="awscmp-cp-02" number={2} question="ECS vs Lambda — when does a container beat a function?" difficulty="medium" topic="Compute">
**Lambda** wins for short, event-driven, spiky work: under 15 minutes, no server management, scales to zero, pay per millisecond. Ideal for reacting to an S3 event, transforming a small record, or triggering a job.

**ECS/Fargate** wins for:
- **Anything over 15 minutes** — a hard

content:
Lambda limit.
- **Sustained load** — at high duty cycle, containers are substantially cheaper per unit of compute.
- **Large dependencies** — a container image handles a heavy ML or Spark stack better than a Lambda package.
- **Long-lived processes** — a streaming consumer that should stay connected.
- **More resources** — beyond Lambda's 10 GB memory.
- **Custom runtimes and system libraries**.

The heuristic: **spiky and short → Lambda; steady or long → containers.** The crossover is usually somewhere around a few hours of daily execution.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="awscmp-cp-03" number={3} question="EC2 vs Fargate for data workloads?" difficulty="medium" topic="Compute">

## AWS Compute: Where Your Pipeline Actually Runs

**Every AWS data pipeline eventually reduces to a compute choice. A Glue job is Spark on managed compute; an Airflow task is a container somewhere; a Lambda is a 15-minute box you can't exceed. Interviewers use compute questions to test whether you understand the cost and constraint model underneath the managed services — because "why is this pipeline expensive" and "why does this job keep timing out" both have compute answers.**

## Key Concepts

AWS compute is a spectrum of **how much you manage versus how much you control**. EC2 gives you a virtual machine and every decision that comes with it. ECS and EKS abstract to containers. Fargate removes the servers underneath those containers. Lambda removes everything except a function and a 15-minute ceiling.

The axis that matters for data engineering is **workload shape**. Long-running, memory-hungry, stateful work — a Spark job shuffling 2 TB — wants EC2 or containers on EC2 with instance types chosen deliberately. Short, bursty, event-driven work — a file lands, transform it — wants Lambda. Embarrassingly parallel batch work with variable duration wants Batch.

The cost lever that dominates all of them is **purchasing model**. The same EC2 capacity can cost 100%, 6

0% or 20% of On-Demand depending on whether you use Savings Plans or Spot. For fault-tolerant, restartable data processing, Spot is the single largest cost reduction available in AWS — often 70% off, and it's the reason EMR and Spark clusters are so often Spot-backed.

## EC2

<QuestionList topic="EC2" storagePrefix="aws-compute-ec2">

<QuestionCard id="awscm-ec2-01" number={1} question="What are the EC2 instance families, and which matter for data workloads?" difficulty="easy" topic="EC2">
Families are named by purpose, then generation, then size — `r6g.4xlarge` is memory-optimised, 6th generation, Graviton, 4xlarge.

- **General purpose (M, T)** — balanced CPU to memory. T instances are burstable, which makes them a trap for sustained work.
- **Compute optimised (C)** — high CPU per GB. Good for CPU-bound transforms and compression.
- **Memory optimised (R, X, Z)** — high RAM per vCPU. **The default for Spark**, since shuffle and caching are memory-bound.
- **Storage optimised (I, D)** — large local NVMe. Excellent for shuffle-heavy Spark and for Kafka

content:
brokers.
- **Accelerated (P, G, Inf)** — GPUs, for ML rather than ETL.

For data engineering the two to name are **R for Spark executors** and **I for shuffle-heavy or local-disk workloads**. `g` in the name means **Graviton** (ARM), typically 20–40% better price-performance if your dependencies have ARM builds.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="awscm-ec2-02" number={2} question="Explain the EC2 purchasing options." difficulty="medium" topic="EC2">
- **On-Demand** — pay per second, no commitment. Baseline price, maximum flexibility.
- **Reserved Instances** — 1 or 3 year commitment to a specific instance type for up to ~72% off. Largely superseded by Savings Plans.
- **Savings Plans** — commit to a dollar-per-hour spend for 1 or 3 years, up to ~72% off. **Compute Savings Plans** apply ac

content:
ross instance families, regions, and even Fargate and Lambda, which makes them much more flexible than RIs.
- **Spot** — spare capacity at up to **90% off**, reclaimed with a **2-minute warning**.
- **Dedicated Hosts / Instances** — physical isolation, for licensing or compliance.

The data engineering answer: **Savings Plans for the always-on baseline** (orchestrator, metastore, streaming consumers), **Spot for the elastic batch layer** (Spark executors, EMR task nodes), On-Demand only for what can't tolerate interruption.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="awscm-ec2-03" number={3} question="How do you use Spot instances safely for data processing?" difficulty="hard" topic="EC2">
Spot is reclaimed with two minutes' notice, so the work must be **restartable**.

Practices that make it safe:

title: AWS Compute for Data Workloads
description: AWS compute interview questions for data engineers covering EC2 instance families and purchasing models, Lambda, ECS, EKS, Fargate and AWS Batch — and choosing between them for ETL, streaming and orchestration workloads.
content:
- **Keep the driver/master On-Demand, executors on Spot.** Losing an executor costs a re-computed partition; losing the driver kills the job. This is exactly how EMR instance fleets are usually configured.
- **Diversify across instance types and AZs** — a capacity-optimised allocation strategy across ten types is far less likely to be fully reclaimed than one type.
- **Handle the interruption notice** — drain gracefully, checkpoint, deregister from the load balancer.
- **Checkpoint long jobs** so a full restart doesn't lose hours.
- **Never put stateful services on Spot** — a Kafka broker or a database is the wrong workload.

Typical saving is 60–80%, which on a large EMR fleet is often the biggest single line item you can move.
</QuestionCard>

question="What are EBS-optimised instances and instance store, and when does the difference matter?" difficulty="medium" topic="EC2">
**Instance store** is physically attached NVMe — very fast, and **ephemeral**: the data is gone when the instance stops or fails. **EBS** is network-attached block storage that persists independently of the instance.

For data workloads the distinction is sharp. **Spark shuffle and temporary spill should go to instance store** — it's dramatically faster and the data is worthless after the job. Anything that must survive (a database's data directory, a checkpoint) belongs on EBS or S3.

**EBS-optimised** means dedicated bandwidth between the instance and EBS, so storage traffic doesn't contend with network traffic. It's the default on current-generation insta

nces.

The common mistake is running a shuffle-heavy job on an instance type with no local NVMe, so all shuffle spills to EBS and the job becomes I/O-bound.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="awscm-ec2-05" number={5} question="What is an AMI, and how does it fit a data platform?" difficulty="easy" topic="EC2">
An **Amazon Machine Image** is the template an instance boots from — OS, pre-installed software, and configuration.

For data platforms it's used to bake in what would otherwise be installed at boot: JDK version, Spark and connector JARs, monitoring agents, security agents, and the CA bundle. That turns a three-minute bootstrap into a fast start, which matters when an autoscaling group adds fifty nodes.

## AWS Lambda

<QuestionList topic="AWS Lambda" storagePrefix="aws-compute-lambda">

<QuestionCard id="awscm-lam-01" number={1} question="What are Lambda's limits, and how do they shape data pipeline design?" difficulty="medium" topic="Lambda">
The ones that decide whether Lambda fits:

- **15-minute maximum execution.** The hard ceiling — anything longer must be split or moved to Batch/ECS.
- **10 GB memory**, with vCPU allocated proportionally, so memory is also the CPU dial.
- **512 MB `/tmp`** by default, configurable to 10 GB — the constraint when processing files locally.
- **6 MB synchronous payload**, 256 KB asynchronous.
- **1,000 concurrent executions** per account by default (a soft limit).

The design consequence: Lambda suits **per-event or per-small-file** work — validate and

title: AWS Compute for Data Workloads
description: AWS compute interview questions for data engineers covering EC2 instance families and purchasing models, Lambda, ECS, EKS, Fargate and AWS Batch — and choosing between them for ETL, streaming and orchestration workloads.
content:
route a record, trigger a job, transform a file that fits in memory. It does not suit a full-table transform. A common pattern is Lambda as the **trigger** (S3 event fires, Lambda starts a Glue or Step Functions job) rather than the worker.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="awscm-lam-02" number={2} question="What is a cold start, and how do you reduce it?" difficulty="medium" topic="Lambda">
When no warm execution environment is available, Lambda must provision one, download your code, and initialise the runtime before your handler runs. That adds latency — tens of milliseconds for a small Python function, seconds for a large package or a JVM.

Reductions:
- **Shrink the deployment package** — this is the biggest lever. A function importing all of pandas pays for it on every cold start.

title: AWS Compute for Data Workloads
description: AWS compute interview questions for data engineers covering EC2 instance families and purchasing models, Lambda, ECS, EKS, Fargate and AWS Batch — and choosing between them for ETL, streaming and orchestration workloads.
content:
- **Initialise outside the handler** — database connections and clients created at module level are reused across invocations in the same environment.
- **Provisioned Concurrency** — keeps N environments warm. Effective and not free.
- **Avoid VPC attachment unless needed** — much improved since Hyperplane ENIs, but still an extra consideration.
- **Choose a lighter runtime** — Python and Node start faster than JVM.

For asynchronous data pipelines, cold starts usually don't matter. They matter for user-facing APIs.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="awscm-lam-03" number={3} question="How does Lambda integrate with data services?" difficulty="medium" topic="Lambda">
Event source mappings and triggers do most of the work:

- **S3 events** — an object lands, Lambda fires. The canonical inges

tion trigger.
- **Kinesis and DynamoDB Streams** — Lambda polls shards and invokes with batches, with configurable batch size and window.
- **SQS** — Lambda polls the queue; failures return the message for retry, and a DLQ catches poison messages.
- **MSK / self-managed Kafka** — consume topics directly.
- **EventBridge** — schedule (replacing cron) or react to service events.
- **Firehose transformation** — transform records in-flight before they land.

The important operational detail for stream sources: a **failing batch blocks the shard** by default, because ordering must be preserved. Configure `BisectBatchOnFunctionError`, a maximum retry age, and an on-failure destination, or one poison record stalls the partition indefinitely.
</QuestionCard>

={4} question="How is Lambda priced, and when does it become expensive?" difficulty="medium" topic="Lambda">
You pay per **request** plus **GB-seconds** — memory allocated multiplied by duration, billed per millisecond.

Because vCPU scales with memory, more memory can be *cheaper*: doubling memory that halves duration costs the same, and often less once you account for fewer retries. Tuning memory is a real optimisation, and AWS Lambda Power Tuning automates finding the sweet spot.

It becomes expensive when used as sustained compute. A function running continuously at high concurrency costs far more than an equivalent EC2 or Fargate task, because you're paying a premium for elasticity you aren't using.

The rule of thumb: Lambda wins for **spiky, low-duty-cycle** workloads. For steady th

## Containers: ECS, EKS & Fargate

<QuestionList topic="Containers: ECS, EKS & Fargate" storagePrefix="aws-compute-containers">

<QuestionCard id="awscm-cnt-01" number={1} question="What is the difference between ECS, EKS and Fargate?" difficulty="medium" topic="Containers">
**ECS** is AWS's own container orchestrator — simpler, deeply integrated with IAM, ALB and CloudWatch, no control plane to manage or pay for.

**EKS** is managed Kubernetes. You get the standard Kubernetes API and its entire ecosystem — Helm, operators, Spark-on-Kubernetes, Airflow's KubernetesExecutor — at the cost of a control plane fee and real operational complexity.

**Fargate is not an orchestrator.** It's a *launch type* for both ECS and EKS that removes the EC2 layer: you specify CPU and memory per task and AWS

title: AWS Compute for Data Workloads
description: AWS compute interview questions for data engineers covering EC2 instance families and purchasing models, Lambda, ECS, EKS, Fargate and AWS Batch — and choosing between them for ETL, streaming and orchestration workloads.
content:
runs it. No nodes to patch or scale.

Choosing: **ECS** if you're all-in on AWS and want simplicity. **EKS** if you need portability, the Kubernetes ecosystem, or already run Kubernetes elsewhere. **Fargate** on either when you don't want to manage nodes and can accept the price premium.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="awscm-cnt-02" number={2} question="When is Fargate the wrong choice?" difficulty="medium" topic="Containers">
- **Cost at scale.** Fargate carries a meaningful premium per vCPU-hour over EC2. For a large, steadily-utilised fleet, EC2 with Savings Plans is significantly cheaper.
- **No GPU support** — ML training needs EC2.
- **No instance store** — everything is network-attached, so a shuffle-heavy Spark job loses local NVMe.
- **Limited CPU/memory combinations** — you c

title: AWS Compute for Data Workloads

content:
an't pick an arbitrary ratio, and there's a per-task ceiling.
- **Slower task startup** than a warm EC2 node with the image cached.
- **No daemonsets** on EKS Fargate, which breaks some logging and monitoring agents.

The instance-store point is the data-specific one: Spark on Fargate spills shuffle to network storage and pays for it in performance.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="awscm-cnt-03" number={3} question="How do containers on AWS get permissions to reach S3 or a database?" difficulty="medium" topic="Containers">
Through **IAM roles**, never static keys.

- **ECS** — a **task role** (permissions for your application) distinct from the **task execution role** (permissions for ECS itself to pull the image and write logs). Confusing these two is a common setup error.
- **EKS** — *

*IRSA** (IAM Roles for Service Accounts) maps a Kubernetes service account to an IAM role via OIDC, so each pod gets scoped credentials. **EKS Pod Identity** is the newer, simpler alternative.

Both deliver short-lived, automatically-rotated credentials through the SDK's default provider chain, so your code needs no credential handling at all.

Scope tightly — one role per pipeline, with S3 policies restricted to specific prefixes. A shared role with `s3:*` is the finding that shows up in every security review.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="awscm-cnt-04" number={4} question="How does EKS fit a data platform?" difficulty="hard" topic="Containers">
It's increasingly the substrate for the whole platform:

- **Airflow** with the KubernetesExecutor or KubernetesPodOperator — one pod per ta

description: AWS compute interview questions for data engineers covering EC2 instance families and purchasing models, Lambda, ECS, EKS, Fargate and AWS Batch — and choosing between them for ETL, streaming and orchestration workloads.
content:
sk, so each task brings its own image and resource limits, and dependencies can't collide.
- **Spark on Kubernetes** — `spark-submit` creates driver and executor pods directly, replacing YARN. Now the direction of travel for new deployments.
- **Flink, Trino, Dagster, dbt runners** — all have mature Kubernetes deployments.

The benefits are consistent packaging, per-task isolation, and cluster autoscaling with **Karpenter** provisioning right-sized Spot nodes on demand.

The honest cost is complexity: you now operate Kubernetes — upgrades, networking, IRSA, resource quotas — which is a real platform-engineering burden. For a small team, EMR Serverless or Glue delivers most of the value with none of it.
</QuestionCard>

## AWS Batch

<QuestionList topic="AWS Batch" storagePrefix="aws-compute-batch">

<QuestionCard id="awscm-bat-01" number={1} question="What is AWS Batch and what problem does it solve?" difficulty="medium" topic="Batch">
A managed batch scheduler. You define **compute environments** (managed capacity, EC2 or Fargate, On-Demand or Spot), **job queues** with priorities, and **job definitions** (a container image plus vCPU and memory). Batch provisions capacity to match the queue and tears it down when it drains.

It fills the gap between Lambda and a permanent cluster: work that runs **longer than 15 minutes**, is **containerised**, and arrives in **bursts** — so you don't want a cluster sitting idle between runs.

Typical data engineering uses: a nightly transform too long for Lambda, per-f

title: AWS Compute for Data Workloads
description: AWS compute interview questions for data engineers covering EC2 instance families and purchasing models, Lambda, ECS, EKS, Fargate and AWS Batch — and choosing between them for ETL, streaming and orchestration workloads.
content:
ile processing over thousands of files, model scoring batches, and genomics-style parallel workloads.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="awscm-bat-02" number={2} question="What are array jobs and job dependencies in Batch?" difficulty="medium" topic="Batch">
An **array job** submits N copies of the same definition with an index available as `AWS_BATCH_JOB_ARRAY_INDEX`. Each child processes its own shard:

```python
index = int(os.environ["AWS_BATCH_JOB_ARRAY_INDEX"])
process(input_files[index])
```

One submission, thousands of parallel tasks, no orchestration code.

**Dependencies** let you express order — `N_TO_N` pairs array children one-to-one with a downstream array, and `SEQUENTIAL` runs children in order. A `dependsOn` on the parent job gives you a fan-out then fan-in shape.

For an

title: AWS Compute for Data Workloads
description: AWS compute interview questions for data engineers covering EC2 instance families and purchasing models, Lambda, ECS, EKS, Fargate and AWS Batch — and choosing between them for ETL, streaming and orchestration workloads.
content:
ything more complex than a simple DAG, use **Step Functions** or Airflow to orchestrate Batch jobs rather than encoding the graph in dependencies.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="awscm-bat-03" number={3} question="How does Batch compare with EMR and Glue?" difficulty="medium" topic="Batch">
- **Batch** — runs *your container*, whatever it does. No opinion about the framework. Best for arbitrary code, single-node parallel work, and non-Spark tooling.
- **EMR** — a managed Hadoop/Spark cluster. Best for genuinely distributed processing where the framework does the coordination and shuffling.
- **Glue** — serverless Spark plus a catalog and crawlers. Best when you want Spark with no infrastructure at all and can live with its abstraction.

The deciding question: **is the work distributed,

title: AWS Compute for Data Workloads
description: AWS compute interview questions for data engineers covering EC2 instance families and purchasing models, Lambda, ECS, EKS, Fargate and AWS Batch — and choosing between them for ETL, streaming and orchestration workloads.
content:
or just parallel?** A thousand independent files is *parallel* — Batch handles it with an array job, cheaply, no cluster. A single 5 TB join is *distributed* — it needs Spark, so EMR or Glue.

Using EMR for embarrassingly parallel single-node work is a common and expensive mismatch.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

<QuestionList topic="Choosing Compute for Data Workloads" storagePrefix="aws-compute-choosing">

| Workload | Choice |
|---|---|
| Event-driven, seconds, small payload | **Lambda** |
| Scheduled, minutes to hours, single node | **Batch** or **ECS/Fargate task** |

Decide with three questions: **how long does one un

it of work run** (over 15 minutes rules out Lambda), **is it distributed or merely parallel** (Spark versus containers), and **what's the duty cycle** (bursty favours serverless, steady favours reserved capacity).
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="awscm-ch-02" number={2} question="How do you right-size and control compute cost?" difficulty="medium" topic="Cost">
In rough order of impact:

1. **Spot for interruptible work** — up to 90% off, and the largest single lever for batch processing.
2. **Savings Plans for the steady baseline** — up to 72% off what you'd run anyway.
3. **Turn things off.** Non-production clusters running overnight and at weekends are pure waste. Auto-terminate EMR clusters on idle.
4. **Right-size from metrics** — CloudWatch and Compute Optimizer routinely show inst

description: AWS compute interview questions for data engineers covering EC2 instance families and purchasing models, Lambda, ECS, EKS, Fargate and AWS Batch — and choosing between them for ETL, streaming and orchestration workloads.
content:
ances at 10% CPU.
5. **Graviton** — typically 20–40% better price-performance for an architecture change, if your dependencies support ARM.
6. **Fix the data, not the compute** — a job scanning 10× more data than necessary because of bad partitioning is a storage-layout problem that no instance choice fixes.

Tag everything by pipeline and team, so cost is attributable and someone owns it.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="awscm-ch-03" number={3} question="A nightly Spark job on EMR takes 6 hours and costs too much. How do you approach it?" difficulty="hard" topic="Choosing">
Diagnose before changing instance types.

1. **Read the Spark UI.** Is it skew (a few tasks running far longer), shuffle-bound, or genuinely CPU-bound? Skew is the most common answer and no amount of hardware fixes i

t.
2. **Check how much data is actually read.** Poor partitioning or CSV instead of Parquet often means scanning 10× what's needed. Fixing the layout is usually the biggest single win.
3. **Then tune compute** — memory-optimised instances for shuffle-heavy work, instance-store types so spill goes to NVMe, and enough executors to use the cluster.
4. **Move executors to Spot**, keeping the master On-Demand.
5. **Consider EMR Serverless** if the cluster sits idle much of the night.
6. **Question the schedule** — does it need to be a full reload, or would an incremental run on new partitions do?

The strong answer leads with data layout and skew, not instance types.

## Common Interview Scenarios

**"Files land in S3 irregularly and need transforming. What do you build?"** — S3 event → Lambda for small files, or S3 event → Step Functions → Glue/Batch when files are large or the work exceeds 15 minutes. Mention that batching many small files first usually beats invoking per file.

content:
## AWS Databases: Picking the Right Store for the Access Pattern

**AWS has more database services than most people can name, and interviewers rarely want a feature list. What they want is whether you can match a workload to a store and defend the choice: why DynamoDB rather than RDS for a high-write event log, why Redshift rather than Aurora for analytics, and what happens to your pipeline when you read from a production database at full speed during business hours.**

title: AWS Database Services
description: AWS database interview questions covering RDS and Aurora, DynamoDB data modelling and capacity, ElastiCache and MemoryDB, DocumentDB, Neptune and QLDB, plus Redshift and Redshift Serverless for warehousing.
content:
## Key Concepts

The organising distinction is **OLTP versus OLAP**. Transactional stores — RDS, Aurora, DynamoDB — are optimised for many small, fast reads and writes against individual rows, usually row-oriented and heavily indexed. Analytical stores — Redshift, and Athena over S3 — are columnar, optimised for scanning and aggregating billions of rows. Running analytics on a transactional database is the most common architectural mistake in this space, and it degrades the application that database exists to serve.

The second is **relational versus purpose-built**. AWS's stated philosophy is a database per workload: key-value (DynamoDB), document (DocumentDB), in-memory (ElastiCache), graph (Neptune), ledger (QLDB), relational (RDS/Aurora), warehouse (Redshift). In practice most teams ne

title: AWS Database Services
description: AWS database interview questions covering RDS and Aurora, DynamoDB data modelling and capacity, ElastiCache and MemoryDB, DocumentDB, Neptune and QLDB, plus Redshift and Redshift Serverless for warehousing.
content:
ed two or three, and the interview value is knowing which access pattern justifies leaving relational.

For a data engineer, the third idea is **how you get data out**. Reading from a production OLTP database with a full-table `SELECT` is disruptive. The mature answers are a **read replica**, a **snapshot export to S3**, or **CDC via DMS** — and knowing which to use when is a recurring interview question.

title: AWS Database Services
description: AWS database interview questions covering RDS and Aurora, DynamoDB data modelling and capacity, ElastiCache and MemoryDB, DocumentDB, Neptune and QLDB, plus Redshift and Redshift Serverless for warehousing.
content:
## RDS & Aurora

<QuestionList topic="RDS & Aurora" storagePrefix="aws-databases-rds">

<QuestionCard id="awsdb-rds-01" number={1} question="What is RDS and what does it manage for you?" difficulty="easy" topic="RDS">
Managed relational databases — PostgreSQL, MySQL, MariaDB, Oracle, SQL Server and Aurora.

AWS handles provisioning, patching, automated backups, point-in-time recovery, Multi-AZ failover, monitoring and read replicas. You keep responsibility for schema design, query performance, indexing and capacity choices.

What you give up versus self-managing on EC2: **no OS access**, so no custom agents or filesystem tuning, and only the extensions and parameters AWS exposes. For most teams that's a good trade — the operational burden RDS removes is substantial, and the restrictions ra

title: AWS Database Services
description: AWS database interview questions covering RDS and Aurora, DynamoDB data modelling and capacity, ElastiCache and MemoryDB, DocumentDB, Neptune and QLDB, plus Redshift and Redshift Serverless for warehousing.
content:
rely bind.

For a data engineer, RDS is usually the **source** system, not the platform: it's where the application's data lives, and your job is extracting from it without hurting it.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="awsdb-rds-02" number={2} question="What is Aurora, and how does it differ from standard RDS?" difficulty="medium" topic="Aurora">
A cloud-native reimplementation of MySQL and PostgreSQL that keeps the wire protocol but replaces the storage engine entirely.

The key architectural difference: Aurora separates compute from a **distributed storage layer** that replicates six ways across three AZs and handles replication at the storage level. Consequences:

- **Faster** — commonly cited at 3–5× MySQL, 2–3× PostgreSQL.
- **Storage auto-scales** to 128 TB with no provisioning.
- *

title: AWS Database Services
description: AWS database interview questions covering RDS and Aurora, DynamoDB data modelling and capacity, ElastiCache and MemoryDB, DocumentDB, Neptune and QLDB, plus Redshift and Redshift Serverless for warehousing.
content:
*Up to 15 read replicas** sharing the same storage, so replica lag is typically milliseconds rather than seconds.
- **Fast crash recovery**, since redo is applied at the storage layer.
- **Backtrack** (MySQL) — rewind the cluster in place, without a restore.
- **Aurora Serverless v2** — scales capacity in fine-grained increments.

It costs more per hour than equivalent RDS, so the justification is performance, replica lag, or the operational features.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="awsdb-rds-03" number={3} question="What is the difference between Multi-AZ and read replicas?" difficulty="medium" topic="RDS">
They solve different problems and are frequently confused.

**Multi-AZ** is for **availability**. A standby in another AZ receives synchronous replication and is **not readable**. O

title: AWS Database Services
description: AWS database interview questions covering RDS and Aurora, DynamoDB data modelling and capacity, ElastiCache and MemoryDB, DocumentDB, Neptune and QLDB, plus Redshift and Redshift Serverless for warehousing.
content:
n failure, AWS fails over automatically and the DNS endpoint points at the new primary. You're paying for resilience, not capacity.

**Read replicas** are for **read scaling**. They're asynchronous, readable, can be in other regions, and can be promoted manually. Because replication is async, they can **lag** — so a pipeline reading a replica may see stale data, which matters if you're joining against something written seconds ago.

For data engineering, **read replicas are the standard extraction target**: run your heavy analytical reads there, so a long scan doesn't compete with production traffic. Just account for lag in any freshness guarantee you make.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="awsdb-rds-04" number={4} question="How do you extract data from RDS without impacting production?"

title: AWS Database Services
description: AWS database interview questions covering RDS and Aurora, DynamoDB data modelling and capacity, ElastiCache and MemoryDB, DocumentDB, Neptune and QLDB, plus Redshift and Redshift Serverless for warehousing.
content:
difficulty="hard" topic="RDS">
Options, roughly in increasing order of sophistication:

1. **Query a read replica** — simplest, and sufficient for scheduled batch extraction. Watch replica lag.
2. **Export a snapshot to S3** — RDS can export an automated or manual snapshot directly to S3 as Parquet, with **zero load on the live database**. Excellent for full-table refreshes.
3. **DMS with CDC** — reads the transaction log (WAL/binlog) and streams changes with minimal overhead. The right answer for near-real-time replication.
4. **Aurora zero-ETL to Redshift** — a managed integration that continuously replicates into Redshift without you building a pipeline.
5. **Federated query** — Redshift or Athena querying RDS live. Convenient for small lookups, dangerous for large scans.

The bad answe

title: AWS Database Services
description: AWS database interview questions covering RDS and Aurora, DynamoDB data modelling and capacity, ElastiCache and MemoryDB, DocumentDB, Neptune and QLDB, plus Redshift and Redshift Serverless for warehousing.
content:
r is a nightly `SELECT *` against the primary during business hours. Snapshot export and CDC exist specifically to avoid it.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="awsdb-rds-05" number={5} question="How do backups and point-in-time recovery work in RDS?" difficulty="medium" topic="RDS">
**Automated backups** take a daily snapshot plus continuous transaction log capture, retained 1–35 days, enabling **point-in-time recovery** to any second in that window. They're deleted when the instance is deleted (unless you take a final snapshot).

**Manual snapshots** persist until you delete them and can be shared or copied across accounts and regions.

Two details that matter operationally: a restore creates a **new instance** with a new endpoint — you can't restore in place, so cutover requires a DNS or

title: AWS Database Services
description: AWS database interview questions covering RDS and Aurora, DynamoDB data modelling and capacity, ElastiCache and MemoryDB, DocumentDB, Neptune and QLDB, plus Redshift and Redshift Serverless for warehousing.
content:
config change. And Aurora's **Backtrack** is the exception, rewinding in place in minutes, which is genuinely useful after a bad migration.

For a data platform, snapshot copies to a separate account are the standard protection against a compromised or mistakenly-deleted production account.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

title: AWS Database Services
description: AWS database interview questions covering RDS and Aurora, DynamoDB data modelling and capacity, ElastiCache and MemoryDB, DocumentDB, Neptune and QLDB, plus Redshift and Redshift Serverless for warehousing.
content:
## DynamoDB

<QuestionList topic="DynamoDB" storagePrefix="aws-databases-dynamodb">

<QuestionCard id="awsdb-ddb-01" number={1} question="What is DynamoDB and when should you choose it?" difficulty="medium" topic="DynamoDB">
A fully managed, serverless key-value and document database with single-digit millisecond latency at effectively any scale, and no servers or capacity planning in the traditional sense.

Choose it when:
- Access patterns are **known and simple** — lookups by key, not ad-hoc queries.
- You need **predictable low latency** at high request rates.
- Write volume is very high — event ingestion, session state, IoT telemetry.
- You want **serverless operations** with automatic scaling.

Don't choose it when you need ad-hoc queries, complex joins, aggregations, or analytical s

title: AWS Database Services
description: AWS database interview questions covering RDS and Aurora, DynamoDB data modelling and capacity, ElastiCache and MemoryDB, DocumentDB, Neptune and QLDB, plus Redshift and Redshift Serverless for warehousing.
content:
cans. Those are exactly what it's bad at, and a `Scan` over a large table is slow, expensive, and consumes the capacity your application needs.

The mental model: DynamoDB is a **fast, infinitely scalable index** you design *around your queries*, not a general-purpose database you query however you like later.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="awsdb-ddb-02" number={2} question="How do partition keys and sort keys work, and what is a hot partition?" difficulty="hard" topic="DynamoDB">
The **partition key** is hashed to choose a physical partition; the optional **sort key** orders items within it. Together they form the primary key, and a `Query` can efficiently fetch a range within one partition key.

A **hot partition** happens when traffic concentrates on one key value — partitioning eve

title: AWS Database Services
description: AWS database interview questions covering RDS and Aurora, DynamoDB data modelling and capacity, ElastiCache and MemoryDB, DocumentDB, Neptune and QLDB, plus Redshift and Redshift Serverless for warehousing.
content:
nts by `date` puts an entire day on one partition, which throttles regardless of how much capacity the table has, because per-partition throughput is bounded.

Fixes:
- **Choose a high-cardinality partition key** — `customer_id` rather than `status`.
- **Write sharding** — append a suffix (`2026-01-15#7`) to spread a hot key across N partitions, then query all N and merge.
- **Adaptive capacity** helps automatically but doesn't rescue a genuinely single-key hotspot.

This is the most common DynamoDB design failure and a very common interview question.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="awsdb-ddb-03" number={3} question="What is the difference between a GSI and an LSI?" difficulty="medium" topic="DynamoDB">
| | **GSI** (Global Secondary Index) | **LSI** (Local Secondary Index) |
|---|---|--

title: AWS Database Services
description: AWS database interview questions covering RDS and Aurora, DynamoDB data modelling and capacity, ElastiCache and MemoryDB, DocumentDB, Neptune and QLDB, plus Redshift and Redshift Serverless for warehousing.
content:
-|
| Partition key | **different** from the base table | **same** as the base table |
| When created | any time | **only at table creation** |
| Consistency | eventually consistent only | strongly consistent available |
| Capacity | its own | shares the table's |
| Size limit | none | 10 GB per partition key |

**GSIs are what you actually use**: they enable a completely different access pattern, can be added later, and scale independently. The eventual consistency is rarely a problem for read paths.

**LSIs** are constrained by the create-time-only rule and the 10 GB limit, so most teams avoid them.

Note GSIs cost extra writes — every base-table write that changes indexed attributes also writes to each GSI, so ten indexes means roughly ten times the write cost.
</QuestionCard>

<Question

title: AWS Database Services
description: AWS database interview questions covering RDS and Aurora, DynamoDB data modelling and capacity, ElastiCache and MemoryDB, DocumentDB, Neptune and QLDB, plus Redshift and Redshift Serverless for warehousing.
content:
Card id="awsdb-ddb-04" number={4} question="Explain DynamoDB capacity modes." difficulty="medium" topic="DynamoDB">
**Provisioned** — you specify read and write capacity units, optionally with auto-scaling. Cheapest for steady, predictable traffic, and eligible for reserved capacity discounts. Exceeding capacity causes throttling.

**On-Demand** — pay per request, scales instantly, no planning. Roughly 5–7× the per-request cost of well-utilised provisioned capacity, but far cheaper than provisioned capacity sitting idle.

The decision: **On-Demand for unpredictable, spiky, or new workloads** (you don't yet know the pattern) and for anything with a low duty cycle. **Provisioned with auto-scaling for steady, high-volume** production traffic where the savings are real.

You can switch modes,

title: AWS Database Services
description: AWS database interview questions covering RDS and Aurora, DynamoDB data modelling and capacity, ElastiCache and MemoryDB, DocumentDB, Neptune and QLDB, plus Redshift and Redshift Serverless for warehousing.
content:
though only once every 24 hours. Many teams start On-Demand, observe the pattern for a month, then move to provisioned.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="awsdb-ddb-05" number={5} question="How do you get data out of DynamoDB for analytics?" difficulty="hard" topic="DynamoDB">
Not with `Scan` — it's slow, consumes table capacity, and competes with production.

Better options:
1. **Export to S3** — a point-in-time export straight to S3 (DynamoDB JSON or Ion) with **zero consumed capacity**. The standard answer for full-table analytics.
2. **DynamoDB Streams + Lambda/Kinesis** — a change stream of item-level modifications, for incremental replication into the lake.
3. **Kinesis Data Streams for DynamoDB** — the same change data into Kinesis, then Firehose to S3.
4. **Glue connector** — reads

title: AWS Database Services
description: AWS database interview questions covering RDS and Aurora, DynamoDB data modelling and capacity, ElastiCache and MemoryDB, DocumentDB, Neptune and QLDB, plus Redshift and Redshift Serverless for warehousing.
content:
with a configurable capacity percentage so you can bound the impact.
5. **Zero-ETL to Redshift** — a managed continuous integration.

The design principle worth stating: DynamoDB is an **operational** store. Analytics belongs in S3 or Redshift, fed by exports or streams — not by scanning the serving table.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

description: AWS database interview questions covering RDS and Aurora, DynamoDB data modelling and capacity, ElastiCache and MemoryDB, DocumentDB, Neptune and QLDB, plus Redshift and Redshift Serverless for warehousing.
content:
## Caching: ElastiCache & MemoryDB

<QuestionList topic="Caching: ElastiCache & MemoryDB" storagePrefix="aws-databases-caching">

<QuestionCard id="awsdb-cache-01" number={1} question="What is ElastiCache, and how do Redis and Memcached differ?" difficulty="medium" topic="ElastiCache">
Managed in-memory caching, in two engines.

**Memcached** — a simple multi-threaded key-value cache. No persistence, no replication, no rich data types. Scales by adding nodes and sharding client-side. Good when you want a plain, fast cache.

**Redis** — richer: lists, sets, sorted sets, hashes, streams, pub/sub, Lua scripting; supports replication, automatic failover, snapshots and cluster mode.

**Redis is the usual choice** because the extra capability costs nothing meaningful and the replication and pers

title: AWS Database Services
description: AWS database interview questions covering RDS and Aurora, DynamoDB data modelling and capacity, ElastiCache and MemoryDB, DocumentDB, Neptune and QLDB, plus Redshift and Redshift Serverless for warehousing.
content:
istence options matter as soon as a cache becomes load-bearing.

For data engineering, Redis appears as a **lookup cache** in enrichment pipelines (avoiding a database round trip per record), a **dedup set** for exactly-once-ish processing, and occasionally a **rate limiter** in front of an API.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="awsdb-cache-02" number={2} question="What is MemoryDB, and how is it different from ElastiCache for Redis?" difficulty="medium" topic="MemoryDB">
MemoryDB is a **Redis-compatible durable database**, not a cache. It writes to a multi-AZ transaction log, giving **durability and strong consistency on primary reads**, with microsecond reads and single-digit millisecond writes.

ElastiCache for Redis is a **cache**: data loss on failure is acceptable because the source

title: AWS Database Services
description: AWS database interview questions covering RDS and Aurora, DynamoDB data modelling and capacity, ElastiCache and MemoryDB, DocumentDB, Neptune and QLDB, plus Redshift and Redshift Serverless for warehousing.
content:
of truth is elsewhere. Its persistence options are backups, not a durability guarantee.

So the choice is about whether Redis is your **system of record**. If losing the data means losing information — a session store you can't rebuild, a real-time leaderboard that is the truth — MemoryDB. If it's a cache in front of a database, ElastiCache, which is cheaper.

Most data pipelines want ElastiCache; MemoryDB shows up when someone needs Redis semantics with durability.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="awsdb-cache-03" number={3} question="What caching strategies should you know?" difficulty="medium" topic="Caching">
- **Cache-aside (lazy loading)** — the application checks the cache, and on a miss reads the database and populates it. Only requested data is cached, but every miss pays the fu

title: AWS Database Services
description: AWS database interview questions covering RDS and Aurora, DynamoDB data modelling and capacity, ElastiCache and MemoryDB, DocumentDB, Neptune and QLDB, plus Redshift and Redshift Serverless for warehousing.
content:
ll latency, and stale data persists until evicted.
- **Write-through** — write to cache and database together. The cache is always fresh; writes are slower, and you cache data that may never be read.
- **Write-behind** — write to the cache and flush to the database asynchronously. Fast writes, risk of loss.
- **Read-through** — the cache itself loads on a miss, hiding the pattern from the application.

Combine cache-aside with a **TTL** as the default: it bounds staleness without needing explicit invalidation, which is the hard part.

The classic failure is a **cache stampede** — a popular key expires and a thousand requests hit the database simultaneously. Mitigate with jittered TTLs, a lock so one request repopulates, or refreshing slightly before expiry.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

content:
## Purpose-Built Databases

<QuestionList topic="Purpose-Built Databases" storagePrefix="aws-databases-purpose-built">

<QuestionCard id="awsdb-pb-01" number={1} question="What is DocumentDB and when would you use it?" difficulty="easy" topic="DocumentDB">
A managed document database with **MongoDB API compatibility**, storing JSON-like documents with flexible schemas. It separates compute from a distributed storage layer, like Aurora, and scales to 15 read replicas.

Use it when you have an existing MongoDB workload you want managed, or genuinely document-shaped data with variable structure and query patterns that suit document indexes.

The caveat to name: **it is not MongoDB** — it implements a subset of the API, and version and feature gaps have historically caught teams out. Check the

title: AWS Database Services
description: AWS database interview questions covering RDS and Aurora, DynamoDB data modelling and capacity, ElastiCache and MemoryDB, DocumentDB, Neptune and QLDB, plus Redshift and Redshift Serverless for warehousing.
content:
specific operators and features your application needs before committing.

For new work on AWS, DynamoDB is often the better fit unless you specifically want document queries or MongoDB compatibility.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="awsdb-pb-02" number={2} question="What is Neptune, and what problems suit a graph database?" difficulty="medium" topic="Neptune">
A managed graph database supporting **property graphs** (Gremlin, openCypher) and **RDF** (SPARQL).

Graph databases win when the **relationships are the query**: fraud rings, "customers who bought this also bought", entity resolution across sources, network and dependency topology, recommendation traversal, and knowledge graphs.

The technical reason: a multi-hop traversal in SQL becomes a chain of self-joins whose cost explodes

title: AWS Database Services
description: AWS database interview questions covering RDS and Aurora, DynamoDB data modelling and capacity, ElastiCache and MemoryDB, DocumentDB, Neptune and QLDB, plus Redshift and Redshift Serverless for warehousing.
content:
with depth. A graph engine stores adjacency directly, so traversal cost scales with the results, not the table size.

For data engineering specifically, the realistic uses are **data lineage** and **entity resolution** — both naturally graph-shaped. It's a specialised tool, so justify it with a traversal-heavy access pattern rather than because the data "has relationships."
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="awsdb-pb-03" number={3} question="What is QLDB and when is it appropriate?" difficulty="medium" topic="QLDB">
A ledger database with an **immutable, append-only journal** that is cryptographically verifiable — you can prove a record's history hasn't been altered.

Fits where an audit trail must be provable rather than merely present: financial transaction records, regulatory complianc

title: AWS Database Services
description: AWS database interview questions covering RDS and Aurora, DynamoDB data modelling and capacity, ElastiCache and MemoryDB, DocumentDB, Neptune and QLDB, plus Redshift and Redshift Serverless for warehousing.
content:
e, supply chain provenance, and systems of record where "who changed what, when, and has it been tampered with" is a formal requirement.

The distinction from just adding an audit table: an audit table can be modified by anyone with write access. QLDB's journal is append-only and hash-chained, so tampering is detectable.

Worth knowing that **AWS has announced QLDB's deprecation**, recommending Aurora PostgreSQL with a verifiable ledger approach instead — so mention it as a concept rather than proposing it for a new build.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

content:
## Redshift

<QuestionList topic="Redshift" storagePrefix="aws-databases-redshift">

<QuestionCard id="awsdb-rs-01" number={1} question="What is Redshift and how is its architecture different from RDS?" difficulty="medium" topic="Redshift">
A petabyte-scale **columnar MPP data warehouse**. A leader node parses and plans; compute nodes hold slices of the data and execute in parallel.

Differences from a row-store like RDS:
- **Columnar storage** — a query touching 3 of 200 columns reads only those, and per-column compression is far more effective.
- **MPP** — work is distributed across node slices and executed in parallel.
- **No indexes** — distribution and sort keys replace them.
- **Optimised for scans and aggregations**, not point lookups or high-concurrency single-row writes.

**RA3 no

title: AWS Database Services
description: AWS database interview questions covering RDS and Aurora, DynamoDB data modelling and capacity, ElastiCache and MemoryDB, DocumentDB, Neptune and QLDB, plus Redshift and Redshift Serverless for warehousing.
content:
des** separate compute from **managed storage in S3**, so you scale them independently and pay for what you use — a significant change from the older DC2 model where storage was tied to node count.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="awsdb-rs-02" number={2} question="What are distribution and sort keys, and how do you choose them?" difficulty="hard" topic="Redshift">
**Distribution style** decides which node slice each row lands on:
- **KEY** — rows with the same value co-locate. Set it on the **join column of large fact-to-dimension joins** so the join happens locally rather than redistributing data across the network.
- **ALL** — a full copy on every node. Right for **small dimension tables**, since it makes every join to them local.
- **EVEN** — round-robin. The fallback when there's no

title: AWS Database Services
description: AWS database interview questions covering RDS and Aurora, DynamoDB data modelling and capacity, ElastiCache and MemoryDB, DocumentDB, Neptune and QLDB, plus Redshift and Redshift Serverless for warehousing.
content:
dominant join key.
- **AUTO** — Redshift chooses and can change it as the table grows. A reasonable default now.

**Sort keys** determine physical row order, letting Redshift skip blocks using zone-map min/max values. Choose the column you **filter on most**, usually a date.

The failure mode to name is **distribution skew**: a KEY distribution on a low-cardinality or skewed column puts most rows on one slice, so one node does all the work.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="awsdb-rs-03" number={3} question="How do you load data into Redshift efficiently?" difficulty="medium" topic="Redshift">
**`COPY` from S3** is the answer — it loads in parallel across all slices, which single-row `INSERT`s cannot.

```sql
COPY orders FROM 's3://lake/curated/orders/'
IAM_ROLE 'arn:aws:iam::123456789012:

title: AWS Database Services
description: AWS database interview questions covering RDS and Aurora, DynamoDB data modelling and capacity, ElastiCache and MemoryDB, DocumentDB, Neptune and QLDB, plus Redshift and Redshift Serverless for warehousing.
content:
role/redshift-load'
FORMAT AS PARQUET;
```

Practices that matter:
- **Split input into multiple files**, ideally a multiple of the slice count, so every slice works.
- **Prefer Parquet or gzipped files**; avoid a single huge uncompressed file, which serialises the load.
- **Never load row by row** — `INSERT` per record is orders of magnitude slower.
- **`ANALYZE`** after significant loads so the planner has current statistics.
- **Use staging tables** and swap, so consumers never see a partial load.

`UNLOAD` is the reverse, writing query results to S3 in parallel — the standard way to push data back into the lake.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="awsdb-rs-04" number={4} question="What is Redshift Spectrum?" difficulty="medium" topic="Redshift">
It lets Redshift query data **in S3** dir

title: AWS Database Services
description: AWS database interview questions covering RDS and Aurora, DynamoDB data modelling and capacity, ElastiCache and MemoryDB, DocumentDB, Neptune and QLDB, plus Redshift and Redshift Serverless for warehousing.
content:
ectly, without loading it, using external tables defined in the Glue Data Catalog. A single query can join a Spectrum external table to a native Redshift table.

Why it matters architecturally: you keep hot, frequently-joined data in Redshift for speed and leave cold historical data in S3, querying across both. That avoids loading years of history you rarely touch.

Pricing is **per terabyte scanned**, like Athena — so the same optimisations apply: partition the data, use Parquet, and select only needed columns. An unpartitioned Spectrum table scanned repeatedly gets expensive quickly.

It's slower than native Redshift storage, so it complements the warehouse rather than replacing it.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="awsdb-rs-05" number={5} question="What is Redshift Serverless and when

title: AWS Database Services
description: AWS database interview questions covering RDS and Aurora, DynamoDB data modelling and capacity, ElastiCache and MemoryDB, DocumentDB, Neptune and QLDB, plus Redshift and Redshift Serverless for warehousing.
content:
would you choose it?" difficulty="medium" topic="Redshift">
Redshift without provisioned clusters: you set a base capacity in **RPUs** and a maximum, and it scales automatically, charging per second of use with no cost when idle.

Choose it for **intermittent or unpredictable** workloads — a warehouse used heavily during business hours and idle overnight, development environments, or a new project where you can't yet size a cluster.

Choose **provisioned** for steady, high-utilisation workloads, where reserved-instance pricing is substantially cheaper than serverless RPU-seconds, and where you want fine control over node type and WLM.

The practical caution: serverless can be more expensive than expected if a badly-tuned query pattern keeps scaling capacity up. Set the maximum RPU limit de

title: AWS Database Services
description: AWS database interview questions covering RDS and Aurora, DynamoDB data modelling and capacity, ElastiCache and MemoryDB, DocumentDB, Neptune and QLDB, plus Redshift and Redshift Serverless for warehousing.
content:
liberately, and monitor usage rather than assuming it's automatically cheaper.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

## Common Interview Scenarios

**"Your nightly extract from the production database is slowing the application."** — move to a read replica, or better, snapshot export to S3 for full loads and DMS CDC for incremental. Explain that the primary should never serve analytical scans.

**"Design storage for an event ingestion system at 50,000 writes per second."** — DynamoDB with a high-cardinality partition key, On-Demand capacity initially, DynamoDB Streams or Kinesis feeding S3 for analytics. Address hot partitions explicitly, since that's the failure the question is probing.

**"Queries against your Redshift cluster got slow after a data growth spurt."** — check distribution skew and whether the sort key still matches the filter pattern, look for unsorted regions needing `VACUUM`, confirm st

title: AWS Database Services
description: AWS database interview questions covering RDS and Aurora, DynamoDB data modelling and capacity, ElastiCache and MemoryDB, DocumentDB, Neptune and QLDB, plus Redshift and Redshift Serverless for warehousing.
content:
atistics are current, and check whether concurrency is queueing in WLM.

**"Why not just use RDS for everything?"** — it works until the access pattern diverges: analytical scans need columnar and MPP, extreme write throughput needs a distributed key-value store, and sub-millisecond lookups need memory. Say plainly that a single Postgres is the right answer more often than AWS's marketing suggests, and the burden of proof is on leaving it.

content:
## AWS Integration: Wiring Pipeline Components Together

**Once you have more than one processing step, something has to connect them — and the choice between a queue, a topic, an event bus and a workflow engine determines how your pipeline behaves when a step fails at 3am. These questions test whether you understand delivery semantics and retry behaviour, because "the message disappeared" and "we processed it twice" are the two failures every integration design has to answer for.**

content:
## Key Concepts

The three messaging primitives differ by **fan-out and consumption model**. A **queue** (SQS) delivers each message to exactly one consumer, which then deletes it — point-to-point work distribution with buffering. A **topic** (SNS) pushes each message to every subscriber — one-to-many notification. An **event bus** (EventBridge) adds content-based **routing rules**, so subscribers declare which events they want rather than the publisher deciding.

**Orchestration** is a different concern from messaging. Step Functions and Airflow don't move data — they decide *what runs next* and handle failure, retry and branching. The distinction matters because teams frequently build a fragile orchestrator out of queues and Lambdas when a workflow engine would have expressed it in a pag

title: AWS Integration & Orchestration
description: AWS integration interview questions covering SQS, SNS and EventBridge, Step Functions, Amazon MQ, AppFlow, and Managed Workflows for Apache Airflow — plus event-driven pipeline patterns.
content:
e of configuration.

The property to reason about throughout is **delivery semantics**. Nearly everything in AWS is **at-least-once**, so duplicates happen: a visibility timeout expires while a task is still running, a retry fires after a partial success. The correct response is designing idempotent consumers, not trying to eliminate duplicates.

---

title: AWS Integration & Orchestration
description: AWS integration interview questions covering SQS, SNS and EventBridge, Step Functions, Amazon MQ, AppFlow, and Managed Workflows for Apache Airflow — plus event-driven pipeline patterns.
content:
## SQS

<QuestionList topic="SQS" storagePrefix="aws-integration-sqs">

<QuestionCard id="awsint-sqs-01" number={1} question="What is SQS, and what is the difference between Standard and FIFO queues?" difficulty="medium" topic="SQS">
A fully managed message queue that decouples producers from consumers and buffers work.

| | **Standard** | **FIFO** |
|---|---|---|
| Ordering | best-effort | strict, per message group |
| Delivery | **at-least-once** (duplicates possible) | exactly-once processing |
| Throughput | nearly unlimited | 300 msg/s, or 3,000 batched (higher with high-throughput mode) |

**Standard** is the default for data pipelines — the throughput is effectively unbounded, and you handle duplicates by making consumers idempotent.

**FIFO** matters when order within a key is sema

title: AWS Integration & Orchestration
description: AWS integration interview questions covering SQS, SNS and EventBridge, Step Functions, Amazon MQ, AppFlow, and Managed Workflows for Apache Airflow — plus event-driven pipeline patterns.
content:
ntically required: applying CDC events for one customer in sequence, or financial transactions. Note that ordering is **per `MessageGroupId`**, not globally, so choosing a high-cardinality group ID preserves both ordering where it matters and parallelism across groups.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="awsint-sqs-02" number={2} question="What is the visibility timeout, and what goes wrong with it?" difficulty="hard" topic="SQS">
When a consumer receives a message it isn't deleted — it becomes **invisible** to other consumers for the visibility timeout (default 30 seconds). The consumer deletes it on success; if it doesn't, the message reappears for another attempt.

That's how SQS survives a consumer crash, and it's also the source of the classic bug: **the timeout is shorter than the pro

title: AWS Integration & Orchestration
description: AWS integration interview questions covering SQS, SNS and EventBridge, Step Functions, Amazon MQ, AppFlow, and Managed Workflows for Apache Airflow — plus event-driven pipeline patterns.
content:
cessing time**, so the message reappears and a second consumer starts the same work. The result is duplicate processing that looks random and scales with load.

Fixes: set the timeout above the p99 processing time, call `ChangeMessageVisibility` to extend it for long tasks (a heartbeat), and make the consumer idempotent regardless — because a consumer can always die after doing the work but before deleting the message.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="awsint-sqs-03" number={3} question="What is a dead-letter queue and why does every queue need one?" difficulty="medium" topic="SQS">
A separate queue that receives messages which failed processing more than `maxReceiveCount` times.

Without one, a **poison message** — malformed, or triggering a bug — retries forever. It consumes capacity, f

title: AWS Integration & Orchestration
description: AWS integration interview questions covering SQS, SNS and EventBridge, Step Functions, Amazon MQ, AppFlow, and Managed Workflows for Apache Airflow — plus event-driven pipeline patterns.
content:
ills the logs with the same error, and in a FIFO queue **blocks everything behind it in its message group** indefinitely.

With a DLQ, the message is moved aside after N attempts, the pipeline keeps flowing, and you have a queue of exactly the failures to inspect.

Operational practices: **alarm on DLQ depth** (a non-empty DLQ is an incident, not a curiosity), keep retention long enough to investigate, and use **DLQ redrive** to replay messages once the bug is fixed. A DLQ nobody monitors is just a slower way to lose data.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="awsint-sqs-04" number={4} question="What is long polling, and why use it?" difficulty="easy" topic="SQS">
`ReceiveMessage` with `WaitTimeSeconds` up to 20 holds the connection open until a message arrives or the wait expires, instead of

title: AWS Integration & Orchestration
description: AWS integration interview questions covering SQS, SNS and EventBridge, Step Functions, Amazon MQ, AppFlow, and Managed Workflows for Apache Airflow — plus event-driven pipeline patterns.
content:
returning immediately.

Two benefits. **Cost** — short polling returns empty responses constantly, and you pay per API request; long polling eliminates almost all of them. **Latency** — the message is delivered the moment it arrives rather than at the next poll.

Short polling also has a subtle correctness quirk: it samples a subset of servers, so an empty response doesn't mean the queue is empty. Long polling queries all of them.

There's essentially no reason not to enable it. Set `ReceiveMessageWaitTimeSeconds` to 20 on the queue so every consumer gets it by default.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

content:
## SNS & EventBridge

<QuestionList topic="SNS & EventBridge" storagePrefix="aws-integration-sns-eventbridge">

<QuestionCard id="awsint-sns-01" number={1} question="What is SNS, and what is the fan-out pattern?" difficulty="medium" topic="SNS">
A pub/sub notification service: publishers send to a **topic**, and SNS pushes each message to every **subscriber** — SQS queues, Lambda functions, HTTP endpoints, email, or Kinesis Firehose.

The **fan-out pattern** is SNS to multiple SQS queues:

```
S3 event → SNS topic ─┬→ SQS → indexing consumer
                      ├→ SQS → analytics consumer
                      └→ SQS → archival consumer
```

Why insert queues rather than subscribing consumers directly: each queue **buffers independently**, so a slow or broken consumer doesn't affect the

title: AWS Integration & Orchestration
description: AWS integration interview questions covering SQS, SNS and EventBridge, Step Functions, Amazon MQ, AppFlow, and Managed Workflows for Apache Airflow — plus event-driven pipeline patterns.
content:
others, and each gets its own retry behaviour and DLQ. Subscribing Lambdas straight to SNS loses that isolation.

This is the canonical way to let several pipelines react to the same event without the publisher knowing about any of them.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="awsint-sns-02" number={2} question="What is EventBridge, and how does it differ from SNS?" difficulty="medium" topic="EventBridge">
A serverless **event bus** with content-based routing. Events are JSON; **rules** match on their content and route to targets.

Differences from SNS:
- **Filtering by content** — rules match on any field, so a subscriber receives only relevant events. SNS filtering exists but is attribute-based and more limited.
- **Many more targets** — Step Functions, Glue, ECS tasks, API Gateway, and cross

title: AWS Integration & Orchestration
description: AWS integration interview questions covering SQS, SNS and EventBridge, Step Functions, Amazon MQ, AppFlow, and Managed Workflows for Apache Airflow — plus event-driven pipeline patterns.
content:
-account buses.
- **AWS service events** — every service emits state changes (an EMR step finished, a Glue job failed), which you can react to without polling.
- **Schema registry and discovery** for event shapes.
- **SaaS partner sources** — Datadog, Shopify, Zendesk publish directly.
- **Scheduler** — a managed cron replacement.
- **Archive and replay** of past events.

SNS is optimised for **high-throughput fan-out**; EventBridge for **routing and integration**. EventBridge has higher per-event latency, so use SNS when throughput matters most.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="awsint-sns-03" number={3} question="How would you build an event-driven ingestion pipeline?" difficulty="hard" topic="Patterns">
```
S3 (file lands)
  → EventBridge rule (matches prefix and suffix)
    → SQS queu

e (buffer, DLQ attached)
      → Lambda or ECS task (validate, register)
        → Step Functions (orchestrate transform)
          → Glue/EMR job
            → EventBridge event on completion → downstream consumers
```

The design points worth defending:
- **A queue between the event and the worker** absorbs bursts. A thousand files landing at once would otherwise hit the Lambda concurrency limit and start dropping.
- **A DLQ on the queue**, alarmed.
- **Idempotent processing**, keyed on the object key plus version, because at-least-once delivery guarantees eventual duplicates.
- **Emit a completion event** rather than having downstream poll — that's what keeps the architecture decoupled.
- **Batch small files** before processing rather than invoking per object, or per-file overhead domin

## Step Functions

<QuestionList topic="Step Functions" storagePrefix="aws-integration-step-functions">

<QuestionCard id="awsint-sf-01" number={1} question="What is Step Functions and when would you use it?" difficulty="medium" topic="Step Functions">
A serverless workflow engine. You define a **state machine** — a JSON/YAML graph of states with transitions, choices, parallelism, error handling and retries — and it executes it durably, with full visual history of every run.

Use it when a pipeline has **multiple steps with dependencies, branching, or failure handling**: start a Glue job, wait for it, branch on the result, run three transformations in parallel, then notify.

Its advantage over chaining Lambdas by hand is that **retry, timeout, error handling and state are declarative and v

**Long-running tasks** use one of:

- **Map state** for fan-out; **Distributed Map** processes millions of S3 objects with high parallelism.

<QuestionCard id="awsint-mwaa-01" number={1} question="What is MWAA and what does AWS manage?" difficulty="medium" topic="MWAA">
Amazon Managed Workflows for Apache Airflow — Airflow with AWS running the scheduler, web server, metadata database and workers.

AWS handles provisioning, patching, autoscaling workers, and integration with CloudWatch, IAM, S3 and VPC. You supply **DAGs in an S3 bucket**, plus `requirements.txt` for Python dependencies and an optional plugins archive.

DAGs sync from an S3 bucket — you upload, and MWAA picks them up within a minute or two.

A sound pipeline: on merge to `main`, CI **validates** the DAGs, then syncs the folder to S3.

## AppFlow & Amazon MQ

<QuestionList topic="AppFlow & Amazon MQ" storagePrefix="aws-integration-appflow-mq">

<QuestionCard id="awsint-af-01" number={1} question="What is Amazon AppFlow and where does it fit?" difficulty="easy" topic="AppFlow">
A managed integration service that moves data between **SaaS applications** — Salesforce, ServiceNow, Zendesk, Slack, Google Analytics, SAP — and AWS services like S3 and Redshift, with no code.

You configure a flow: source, destination, schedule or event trigger, field mapping, filters and simple transformations.

Where it fits: the **long tail of SaaS ingestion** that would otherwise be a bespoke API client per system, each with its own auth, pagination and rate limits. AppFlow handles those, and supports incremental pulls.

Its limits: only sup

ported connectors, limited transformation, and less control than a custom extractor or a tool like Fivetran or Airbyte. It's the pragmatic choice when the connector exists and the requirement is straightforward; write your own when the API is unusual or the volume is large.

<QuestionCard id="awsint-mq-01" number={2} question="What is Amazon MQ and when would you choose it over SQS or SNS?" difficulty="medium" topic="Amazon MQ">
Managed **ActiveMQ** or **RabbitMQ** — traditional message brokers supporting standard protocols: JMS, AMQP, MQTT, STOMP and OpenWire.

You choose it for **compatibility**, not capability. If you're migrating an existing application that speaks JMS or AMQP, Amazon MQ lets it keep working unchanged; rewriting it against the SQS API would be a project

It also provides features SQS lacks: message routing with exchanges and bindings, message priorities, request/reply patterns, and transactions.

The trade-off is that Amazon MQ is **broker-based** — you provision instances, and it scales vertically rather than being effectively unbounded like SQS. For new AWS-native work, **SQS and SNS are the default**; Amazon MQ is a migration and interoperability service.

## Common Interview Scenarios

**"Messages are being processed twice."** — visibility timeout shorter than processing time is the first suspect, followed by a consumer dying after the work but before the delete. The real answer is that at-least-once delivery makes this inevitable, so the consumer must be idempotent.

**"One bad file stops the whole pipeline."** — no dead-letter queue, so the poison message retries forever. Add a DLQ with `maxReceiveCount`, alarm on its depth, and use redrive after fixing the bug.

**"Design a pipeline that runs when a file arrives, transforms it, and notifies three downstream teams."** — S3 event → EventBridge → SQS → processor → Step Functions for the transform → SNS fan-out to three queues on completion. Justify the queues as isolation between consumers.

title: AWS Integration & Orchestration

content:
**"Step Functions or Airflow for our nightly ETL?"** — Airflow if you need backfills, dataset dependencies and Python-defined DAGs; Step Functions if it's event-driven AWS service orchestration and you'd rather not run a scheduler. Note that using both is common and reasonable.
