## AWS Migration: Moving Data Without Breaking Anything

**Migration questions test planning more than tooling. Anyone can name DMS. The signal is whether you can size a transfer against available bandwidth, explain how to cut over a live database with seconds of downtime rather than a weekend, and say what you'd validate before declaring the migration done — because the failure mode isn't a failed transfer, it's a successful transfer of subtly wrong data.**

content:
## Key Concepts

Every data migration decomposes into three phases: a **full load** of existing data, **change capture** for everything written while the load runs, and a **cutover** where writes switch to the new system. Skipping the middle phase is what forces a weekend outage — with CDC running, the target stays continuously in sync and cutover becomes a matter of seconds.

The transfer method is a **bandwidth arithmetic problem**, not a preference. A 1 Gbps link moves roughly 10 TB per day at realistic utilisation, so 500 TB is two months of saturated network — during which the business also needs that link. Past roughly 100 TB, physically shipping devices usually wins.

The phase people under-plan is **validation**. A migration that completes is not a migration that succeeded: row cou

content:
nts, checksums, and business-metric reconciliation between source and target are what let you actually cut over, and they need to be built before the migration, not after.

content:
## Database Migration Service

<QuestionList topic="Database Migration Service" storagePrefix="aws-migration-dms">

<QuestionCard id="awsmg-dms-01" number={1} question="What is AWS DMS and what can it move?" difficulty="easy" topic="DMS">
A managed service that migrates and replicates databases. You define a **source endpoint**, a **target endpoint**, and a **replication task** that runs on a replication instance (or serverless capacity).

It handles **homogeneous** migrations (Oracle to Oracle, PostgreSQL to PostgreSQL) and **heterogeneous** ones (Oracle to Aurora PostgreSQL, SQL Server to Redshift), where it converts data types on the fly.

Sources include most relational databases, MongoDB, DocumentDB and S3. Targets add Redshift, S3, DynamoDB, OpenSearch, Kinesis and MSK — which is wha

title: AWS Migration & Data Transfer
description: AWS migration interview questions covering Database Migration Service and CDC, DataSync, the Snow family, Data Transfer Terminal, and planning a database or data lake migration with minimal downtime.
content:
t makes DMS a **data engineering** tool and not only a migration one: streaming database changes into S3 or Kinesis is a first-class use.

The source stays online throughout; DMS reads the transaction log rather than locking tables.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="awsmg-dms-02" number={2} question="What are the three DMS task types?" difficulty="medium" topic="DMS">
- **Full load** — copy existing data once, then stop. Fine for a static source or a one-off snapshot.
- **Full load + CDC** — copy existing data, then continuously apply changes that occurred during and after the load. **This is the one that enables near-zero-downtime cutover.**
- **CDC only** — apply changes from a specified log position, assuming the target is already populated (perhaps by a snapshot restore, which is much

title: AWS Migration & Data Transfer
description: AWS migration interview questions covering Database Migration Service and CDC, DataSync, the Snow family, Data Transfer Terminal, and planning a database or data lake migration with minimal downtime.
content:
faster than a DMS full load for large databases).

The common pattern for a big migration is **snapshot restore + CDC only**: restoring a native backup is far faster than DMS reading and rewriting every row, and CDC then catches up the delta.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="awsmg-dms-03" number={3} question="What does DMS not migrate, and what is SCT?" difficulty="medium" topic="DMS">
DMS moves **data**, plus a minimal schema. It does **not** move secondary indexes, stored procedures, functions, triggers, sequences, views, or user permissions.

That surprises people mid-migration. The order of operations that works: create the schema on the target first (with **no** secondary indexes and triggers disabled, so the load is fast and triggers don't fire on migrated rows), run the load, the

title: AWS Migration & Data Transfer
description: AWS migration interview questions covering Database Migration Service and CDC, DataSync, the Snow family, Data Transfer Terminal, and planning a database or data lake migration with minimal downtime.
content:
n add indexes and re-enable triggers.

**AWS Schema Conversion Tool (SCT)** handles the schema side for heterogeneous migrations, converting DDL and procedural code between engines and producing an assessment report of what it couldn't convert automatically. That report is the real value — it tells you upfront how much manual work an Oracle-to-PostgreSQL move actually involves.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="awsmg-dms-04" number={4} question="How do you troubleshoot a slow or failing DMS task?" difficulty="hard" topic="DMS">
Common causes, roughly in order:

- **Undersized replication instance** — CPU or memory bound, or the swap file growing. Check CloudWatch metrics on the instance, not just the task.
- **Target indexes present during full load** — every insert maintains them. Drop a

title: AWS Migration & Data Transfer
description: AWS migration interview questions covering Database Migration Service and CDC, DataSync, the Snow family, Data Transfer Terminal, and planning a database or data lake migration with minimal downtime.
content:
nd rebuild after.
- **LOB handling** — large objects are slow. Use limited LOB mode with a sensible size, or exclude and handle them separately.
- **No primary key on a table** — CDC needs one to apply updates; without it, updates become inefficient or fail.
- **Source log retention too short** — if CDC falls behind and the logs it needs are gone, the task fails and must restart from a full load. Increase retention before starting.
- **Network throughput** between source and replication instance.
- **Latency metrics**: `CDCLatencySource` (reading) versus `CDCLatencyTarget` (applying) tells you which side is the bottleneck.

Enable **CloudWatch task logs** at a detailed level; the default logging hides most of what you need.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

content:
## Change Data Capture

<QuestionList topic="Change Data Capture" storagePrefix="aws-migration-cdc">

<QuestionCard id="awsmg-cdc-01" number={1} question="What is CDC and why is it better than batch extraction?" difficulty="medium" topic="CDC">
Change Data Capture reads the database's **transaction log** — the WAL in PostgreSQL, binlog in MySQL, redo in Oracle — to capture every insert, update and delete as it happens.

Advantages over a periodic `SELECT`:
- **Low source impact** — reading the log doesn't compete with queries or take locks.
- **Captures deletes**, which a timestamp-based incremental query silently misses.
- **Captures every intermediate change**, not just the final state at extraction time.
- **Near real time** rather than hourly or daily.
- **No need for a reliable `updat

title: AWS Migration & Data Transfer
description: AWS migration interview questions covering Database Migration Service and CDC, DataSync, the Snow family, Data Transfer Terminal, and planning a database or data lake migration with minimal downtime.
content:
ed_at` column**, which many legacy schemas lack or fail to maintain.

The cost: it requires log access and configuration (`wal_level=logical`, binlog format `ROW`), it's more moving parts than a query, and you must handle schema changes explicitly.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="awsmg-cdc-02" number={2} question="How do you land CDC changes in a data lake?" difficulty="hard" topic="CDC">
Two distinct patterns:

**Append-only change log** — write every change event as a row with its operation type and timestamp into a `raw` table. Nothing is ever updated, so it's cheap, auditable, and lets you reconstruct state at any point in time. This is the right shape for the landing zone.

**Merged current state** — periodically apply the change log into a table reflecting current values, using `M

title: AWS Migration & Data Transfer
description: AWS migration interview questions covering Database Migration Service and CDC, DataSync, the Snow family, Data Transfer Terminal, and planning a database or data lake migration with minimal downtime.
content:
ERGE` on the primary key with an **Iceberg, Delta or Hudi** table so upserts and deletes are possible on S3.

Doing both is standard: raw append-only for history and reprocessing, curated merged for consumption.

The details that matter: handle **deletes** (soft-delete flag or actual removal), **order by the log sequence number** rather than arrival time, and make the merge **idempotent** so a replay doesn't corrupt state.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="awsmg-cdc-03" number={3} question="What are the alternatives to DMS for CDC?" difficulty="medium" topic="CDC">
- **Debezium** — the open-source standard, running on Kafka Connect against MSK. More control, richer transformation, portable off AWS, and a large community. The usual choice when you already run Kafka.
- **Database-native log

title: AWS Migration & Data Transfer
description: AWS migration interview questions covering Database Migration Service and CDC, DataSync, the Snow family, Data Transfer Terminal, and planning a database or data lake migration with minimal downtime.
content:
ical replication** — PostgreSQL publications and subscriptions, for Postgres-to-Postgres.
- **Aurora zero-ETL to Redshift** — a fully managed continuous replication with no pipeline to build. Least effort where it applies.
- **Vendor tools** — Fivetran, Airbyte, Qlik Replicate. Fast to adopt, priced per row or per connector.
- **Trigger-based capture** — writes changes to an audit table. Portable but adds write latency to every transaction, so it's a last resort.

The decision usually comes down to whether you want a managed service with limited flexibility (DMS, zero-ETL) or the Kafka ecosystem with more control (Debezium).
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

## Bulk & File Transfer

<QuestionList topic="Bulk & File Transfer" storagePrefix="aws-migration-bulk">

<QuestionCard id="awsmg-bulk-01" number={1} question="How do you decide between network transfer and physical shipping?" difficulty="medium" topic="Transfer">
Arithmetic, then constraints.

Transfer time in days ≈ **size in TB ÷ (usable Mbps × 0.0108)**. A 1 Gbps link at 80% utilisation moves roughly 8–10 TB per day.

| Data size | Typical answer |
|---|---|
| < 10 TB | network (DataSync or S3 CLI) |
| 10–100 TB | calculate — depends on bandwidth and deadline |
| > 100 TB | Snowball Edge, in parallel |
| > 10 PB | Snowmobile |

The constraints that override the maths: **is the link shared with production traffic** (saturating it for a month is not acceptable), **is bandwidth metered** (

title: AWS Migration & Data Transfer
description: AWS migration interview questions covering Database Migration Service and CDC, DataSync, the Snow family, Data Transfer Terminal, and planning a database or data lake migration with minimal downtime.
content:
egress charges can exceed device cost), and **is there a deadline** tied to a data centre exit.

Also plan for the **delta**: whatever ships physically will be stale on arrival, so DataSync or CDC handles changes since the snapshot.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="awsmg-bulk-02" number={2} question="What does DataSync do that a script with the AWS CLI doesn't?" difficulty="medium" topic="DataSync">
DataSync is a purpose-built transfer service with an agent deployed near the source (or agentless between AWS services).

What it adds over `aws s3 sync`:
- **Parallelism and pipelining** tuned for throughput, typically much faster than a naive sync.
- **Incremental transfer** by comparing metadata, not re-copying unchanged files.
- **Integrity verification** — checksums on every file transfe

title: AWS Migration & Data Transfer
description: AWS migration interview questions covering Database Migration Service and CDC, DataSync, the Snow family, Data Transfer Terminal, and planning a database or data lake migration with minimal downtime.
content:
rred.
- **Metadata preservation** — POSIX permissions, timestamps, ownership.
- **Bandwidth throttling**, so it doesn't saturate a shared link.
- **Scheduling, monitoring and CloudWatch metrics** rather than a cron job nobody watches.
- **Protocol support** for NFS, SMB, HDFS and object stores, including other clouds.

For a one-off copy of a few gigabytes, the CLI is fine. For terabytes, recurring syncs, or anything needing verification, DataSync earns its place.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="awsmg-bulk-03" number={3} question="How does a Snowball Edge migration actually work?" difficulty="medium" topic="Snow Family">
1. **Order** through the console, specifying the destination bucket.
2. **Receive and connect** the device to your local network.
3. **Unlock** it with a manifest and u

title: AWS Migration & Data Transfer
description: AWS migration interview questions covering Database Migration Service and CDC, DataSync, the Snow family, Data Transfer Terminal, and planning a database or data lake migration with minimal downtime.
content:
nlock code obtained separately — the device is useless without both, which is the security model.
4. **Copy data** using the Snowball client, the S3-compatible endpoint, or by mounting it via NFS.
5. **Ship it back** with the E-Ink label AWS pre-configures.
6. **AWS imports** into S3; you verify with a job report.

Details worth knowing: data is **encrypted with KMS** and the device is wiped after import. **Snowball Edge Compute Optimized** can run EC2 instances and Lambda locally, so you can pre-process or filter *before* transfer — useful when only a subset is worth moving.

For very large migrations, order **multiple devices in parallel**; a single device's local copy speed becomes the bottleneck.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="awsmg-bulk-04" number={4} question="What is AWS Data Tr

title: AWS Migration & Data Transfer
description: AWS migration interview questions covering Database Migration Service and CDC, DataSync, the Snow family, Data Transfer Terminal, and planning a database or data lake migration with minimal downtime.
content:
ansfer Terminal?" difficulty="easy" topic="Transfer">
A physical AWS facility where you bring storage devices and upload directly over a high-speed connection into AWS, then take your hardware away.

It sits between shipping a Snowball and using your own network: you get very high throughput without waiting for device shipping round trips, and without consuming your own bandwidth. Useful when data is extremely large, time-sensitive, or when regulatory constraints make shipping storage devices unattractive.

It's a niche service and unlikely to be central to an interview — knowing it exists and roughly what problem it solves is sufficient. The main alternatives remain Snowball for bulk and Direct Connect for sustained high-bandwidth transfer.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

## Planning a Migration

<QuestionList topic="Planning a Migration" storagePrefix="aws-migration-planning">

<QuestionCard id="awsmg-plan-01" number={1} question="Walk through migrating a 5 TB production database to Aurora with minimal downtime." difficulty="hard" topic="Planning">
1. **Assess** — run SCT for schema conversion and a compatibility report. Identify stored procedures, triggers and extensions that need manual work.
2. **Provision** the target and create the schema **without secondary indexes**, with triggers disabled.
3. **Enable logical replication** on the source (`wal_level`, binlog format `ROW`) and **increase log retention** so CDC can't fall behind and lose its position.

Layered checks, cheapest first:

- **Row counts** per table — necessary, nowhere near sufficient.
- **Checksums or aggregates** on key columns — `SUM`, `MIN`, `MAX`, `COUNT DISTINCT` — compared between source and target.
- **DMS data validation**, which compares source and target rows continuously and reports mismatches.
- **Business metric reconciliation** — total revenue for last month, active customer count. This catches subtle problems the technical checks miss.
- **Type and precision checks** — the classic failures are numeric precision loss, timezone shifts on timestamps, character set and collation differences changing sort order and comparisons, and `NULL` versus empty string.

Collation and timezone are the two that most often produce a technically-complete migration with wrong behaviour, so call them out specifically.

<QuestionCard id="awsmg-plan-03" number={3} question="What is the 7 Rs migration framework?" difficulty="medium" topic="Planning">
AWS's taxonomy of migration strategies:

- **Rehost** — "lift and shift" onto EC2. Fast, no benefit from cloud-native features.
- **Replatform** — "lift and reshape", e.g. self-managed PostgreSQL onto RDS. Modest effort, real operational gain. **The most common choice for databases.**
- **Repurchase** — move to a SaaS product instead.
- **Refactor** — re-architect for the cloud. Most effort, most benefit.
- **Relocate** — move at the hypervisor level, e.g. VMware Cloud on AWS.

- **Retain** — leave it where it is, for now.
- **Retire** — turn it off. Assessments routinely find systems nobody uses.

For data platforms, the honest advice is **replatform first, refactor second**: get onto RDS or Redshift with minimal change, prove it works, then re-architect toward a lake or lakehouse incrementally. Attempting both at once is how migrations run over.

## Common Interview Scenarios

**"Migrate an on-premises Hadoop cluster with 800 TB of HDFS data to S3."** — at that size, Snowball devices in parallel for the bulk, DataSync for the ongoing delta and final catch-up. ## AWS Storage: The Foundation of the Data Lake

**S3 is the single most important AWS service for a data engineer — it's where the lake lives, and almost every other service reads from and writes to it. Interview questions here go well beyond "what is a bucket": storage class economics, why a `LIST` on a million-object prefix is slow, how consistency changed in 2020, and why your lifecycle policy is costing more than it saves. The block and file services matter less, but knowing when *not* to use them is part of the answer.**

content:
## Key Concepts

S3 is **object storage**, not a filesystem — and most S3 surprises trace back to people forgetting that. There are no real directories; the "folder" in the console is a prefix in a flat key namespace. There is no rename; a rename is a copy plus a delete. There is no append; you replace the whole object. Understanding this explains why Spark writes to a temp location and copies, why "small files" hurt so much, and why table formats like Iceberg and Delta exist.

The three levers that decide cost and performance are **storage class** (how much you pay to keep bytes and how much to read them back), **request volume** (you pay per `GET`, `PUT` and `LIST`, which is why millions of tiny files cost more than a few large ones), and **data transfer** (egress out of the region is th

e expensive direction).

For block and file storage, the rule is simple: **EBS for a single instance's disk, EFS for shared POSIX access, FSx for specialised filesystems, S3 for everything analytical.** A data lake on EFS is an anti-pattern; the analytics ecosystem is built around S3.

## Amazon S3

<QuestionList topic="Amazon S3" storagePrefix="aws-storage-s3">

<QuestionCard id="awsst-s3-01" number={1} question="What is S3, and what are its key characteristics?" difficulty="easy" topic="S3">
Object storage: you store **objects** (data plus metadata, up to 5 TB each) under **keys** in **buckets**, accessed over HTTP APIs rather than a filesystem.

The properties that matter:
- **11 nines of durability** — data is replicated across at least three Availability Zones in a standard class.
- **Effectively unlimited capacity**, with no provisioning.
- **Flat namespace** — keys like `orders/dt=2026-01-15/part-0.parquet` only look hierarchical.
- **Immutable objects** — no in-place modification or append.
- **Regional** — a bucket lives in one region; cross-region access costs

title: AWS Storage for Data Platforms
description: AWS storage interview questions covering S3 storage classes, lifecycle policies, performance and consistency, EBS volume types, EFS and FSx, plus Storage Gateway, Transfer Family and the Snow family for data migration.
content:
latency and transfer.

For data engineering, the crucial consequence is that S3 decouples **storage from compute**: EMR, Athena, Redshift Spectrum and Glue all read the same objects, and you can scale or destroy compute without touching data.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="awsst-s3-02" number={2} question="What is S3's consistency model?" difficulty="medium" topic="S3">
Since December 2020, S3 provides **strong read-after-write consistency** for all operations — `PUT`, overwrite `PUT`, `DELETE` and `LIST` — at no extra cost or performance penalty.

Before that, new objects were read-after-write consistent but **overwrites and deletes were eventually consistent**, and crucially `LIST` was too. That caused real correctness bugs: a Spark job would write output files and then list the dire

title: AWS Storage for Data Platforms
description: AWS storage interview questions covering S3 storage classes, lifecycle policies, performance and consistency, EBS volume types, EFS and FSx, plus Storage Gateway, Transfer Family and the Snow family for data migration.
content:
ctory to commit, missing files that hadn't appeared yet. Tools like S3Guard and EMRFS consistent view existed purely to work around it.

Why this matters in an interview: it dates a candidate's knowledge, and it explains why older architectures carry consistency-layer complexity that's now unnecessary. Note that **strong consistency doesn't give you atomicity across multiple objects** — that still requires a table format like Iceberg or Delta.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="awsst-s3-03" number={3} question="Why is the 'small files problem' worse on S3 than on HDFS?" difficulty="hard" topic="S3">
Several costs compound:

- **Per-request pricing and latency.** Each file needs at least one `GET`, with tens of milliseconds of latency. A million 10 KB files means a million requests; the sam

title: AWS Storage for Data Platforms
description: AWS storage interview questions covering S3 storage classes, lifecycle policies, performance and consistency, EBS volume types, EFS and FSx, plus Storage Gateway, Transfer Family and the Snow family for data migration.
content:
e data in a thousand 10 MB files means a thousand.
- **`LIST` is slow and paginated** at 1,000 keys per call. Listing a prefix with a million objects takes a thousand sequential calls before processing even starts.
- **No block locality.** Every read is a network call, so there's no equivalent of reading a local HDFS block.
- **Metadata overhead per file** in Parquet — footers and statistics are re-read per file, and tiny files make compression and column statistics ineffective.
- **Task overhead** — Spark launches a task per file, so scheduling dominates actual work.

Fixes: **compact** on a schedule, size output files at **128 MB–1 GB**, tune writer partition counts, and use a table format that tracks files in metadata so listing is avoided entirely.
</QuestionCard>

sst-s3-04" number={4} question="What is multipart upload and when is it required?" difficulty="medium" topic="S3">
It splits an object into parts uploaded independently (and in parallel), then assembled by S3.

- **Required above 5 GB** — that's the single-`PUT` ceiling.
- **Recommended above ~100 MB** for throughput, since parts upload in parallel.
- **Resumable** — a failed part is retried alone rather than restarting the whole upload.

The operational trap: **incomplete multipart uploads are billed** and are invisible in the normal object listing. A pipeline that fails partway repeatedly can accumulate significant hidden cost. Always add a lifecycle rule:

```
AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload: DaysAfterInitiation: 7
```

That one rule is a standard recommendation in every S3 cost review.

<QuestionCard id="awsst-s3-05" number={5} question="What is S3 versioning, and what should you watch out for?" difficulty="medium" topic="S3">
Versioning keeps every version of an object, so an overwrite or delete is recoverable. A `DELETE` inserts a **delete marker** rather than removing data.

Benefits: protection from accidental deletion and from a buggy pipeline overwriting good data — genuinely valuable on a curated zone.

The costs people miss: **you pay for every version**, so a job that rewrites the same partition daily silently multiplies storage. And a "deleted" object still costs money until the noncurrent versions expire.

Always pair versioning with a lifecycle rule expiring noncurrent versions after N days, and expiring delete markers. **MFA Delete** adds pro

The two catches to name: IA and Glacier classes have **minimum storage durations** (30, 90, 180 days) and are billed for the full period even if deleted early, and they have **minimum billable object sizes** (128 KB), so transitioning millions of tiny files can cost *more* than leaving them.

<QuestionCard id="awsst-cls-02" number={2} question="How do lifecycle policies work, and how do you design one for a data lake?" difficulty="medium" topic="Lifecycle">

staging/  → expire at 14d

The cost is a small **per-object monitoring fee**. That fee is trivial for a 100 MB Parquet file and ruinous across 500 million tiny objects, so it's a poor fit for buckets full of small files.

Start with **S3 Storage Lens** (free tier gives account-wide metrics) and **Storage Class Analysis** to see what's actually accessed.

Common findings, in rough order of frequency:
1. **Incomplete multipart uploads** — invisible, billed, often gigabytes.
2. **Noncurrent versions** accumulating on a versioned bucket with no expiry rule.

5. **NAT gateway charges** on S3 traffic that should use a **gateway VPC endpoint** — free, and a one-line fix.
6. **Cross-region reads** where compute and bucket ended up in different regions.

## S3 Performance & Security

<QuestionList topic="S3 Performance & Security" storagePrefix="aws-storage-perf-security">

<QuestionCard id="awsst-perf-01" number={1} question="What are S3's performance characteristics and how do you optimise for them?" difficulty="hard" topic="Performance">
S3 scales to at least **3,500 `PUT`/`COPY`/`POST`/`DELETE` and 5,500 `GET`/`HEAD` requests per second per prefix**, and prefixes scale horizontally without limit.

Optimisations:
- **Spread across prefixes** for very high request rates — partitioning by date already does this naturally.
- **Parallelise** — multipart upload and byte-range `GET`s use many connections.
- **Larger files** — fewer requests, better throughput.
- **Columnar formats with pushdown**, so you fetch only the byte ranges you need.
-

description: AWS storage interview questions covering S3 storage classes, lifecycle policies, performance and consistency, EBS volume types, EFS and FSx, plus Storage Gateway, Transfer Family and the Snow family for data migration.
content:
**Same region as compute**, and a **VPC gateway endpoint** to bypass NAT.
- **S3 Transfer Acceleration** for long-distance uploads over the CloudFront edge network.

The historical note worth knowing: randomising key prefixes used to be necessary for partition scaling. Since 2018 it isn't, so **date-ordered prefixes are fine** — and better, because they enable partition pruning.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="awsst-sec-01" number={2} question="How do you control access to S3?" difficulty="medium" topic="Security">
Layered, and evaluated together:

- **IAM policies** — what a principal can do. The primary mechanism.
- **Bucket policies** — resource-based; used for cross-account access, enforcing TLS, or restricting to a VPC endpoint.
- **Block Public Access** — an account and bucket-le

- **ACLs** — legacy; AWS now recommends disabling them via Object Ownership.
- **VPC endpoint policies** — restrict which buckets are reachable from your VPC.
- **Access Points** — named endpoints with their own policies, useful for granting per-team access to slices of a shared lake.
- **Lake Formation** — table- and column-level permissions layered on top for catalogued data.

Least privilege in practice means **prefix-scoped** policies: `arn:aws:s3:::lake/raw/orders/*`, not `arn:aws:s3:::lake/*`.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="awsst-sec-02" number={3} question="What are the S3 encryption options?" difficulty="medium" topic="Security">

- **SSE-S

- **SSE-KMS** — KMS keys, giving you an audit trail via CloudTrail and the ability to revoke access by disabling the key. **Watch the KMS request cost and throttling limits** on high-volume workloads; enable **S3 Bucket Keys** to cut KMS calls dramatically.

**In transit** — TLS. Enforce it with a bucket policy denying requests where `aws:SecureTransport` is false.

For a lake handling sensitive data, SSE-KMS with a customer-managed key plus Bucket Keys is the usual answer: auditable, revocable, and affordable.

Options, from least to most involved:

- **Pre-signed URLs** — time-limited access to one object, no AWS account required. Ideal for a one-off export.

## Block & File Storage

<QuestionList topic="Block & File Storage" storagePrefix="aws-storage-block-file">

<QuestionCard id="awsst-ebs-01" number={1} question="What is EBS, and what are the volume types?" difficulty="medium" topic="EBS">
Network-attached block storage for a single EC2 instance, persisting independently of the instance lifecycle.

- **gp3** — general purpose SSD; baseline 3,000 IOPS and 125 MB/s, with **IOPS and throughput provisioned independently of size**. The sensible default, and cheaper than gp2.
- **gp2** — older; performance scales with volume size, so people over-provision capacity to buy IOPS. Migrate to gp3.
- **io1/io2** — provisioned IOPS SSD for latency-sensitive databases; io2 Block Express reaches 256,000 IOPS.
- **st1** — throughput-optimised HDD; cheap s

equential throughput. Good for logs and big sequential scans.
- **sc1** — cold HDD; cheapest, for rarely-accessed data.

For data workloads: **gp3** for most things, **st1** for large sequential reads on a budget, **io2** only for a genuinely IOPS-bound database.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="awsst-ebs-02" number={2} question="What is the difference between EBS and instance store?" difficulty="medium" topic="EBS">
| | EBS | Instance store |
|---|---|---|
| Attachment | network | physically attached NVMe |
| Persistence | survives stop/terminate | **lost on stop or failure** |
| Performance | good, network-bound | very high, local |
| Snapshots | yes, to S3 | no |
| Resizable | yes | fixed with instance type |

The data engineering application: **Spark shuffle and spill belong on insta

nce store** — it's much faster and the data is disposable. Anything needing to survive belongs on EBS or, better, S3.

Choosing an instance family with no local NVMe for a shuffle-heavy job silently pushes all that traffic onto EBS and turns a CPU-bound job into an I/O-bound one.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="awsst-efs-01" number={3} question="When would you use EFS or FSx instead of S3?" difficulty="medium" topic="EFS & FSx">
**EFS** is managed NFS — a POSIX filesystem shared by many instances concurrently, elastic, multi-AZ. Use it when software genuinely requires a filesystem and shared write access: an Airflow DAGs directory shared across schedulers and workers, or a legacy tool that can't speak S3.

**FSx** is a family of managed filesystems:
- **FSx for Lustre** — high-performan

- **FSx for Windows File Server** — SMB shares.
- **FSx for NetApp ONTAP / OpenZFS** — enterprise filesystem features.

The default remains **S3**. EFS and FSx cost substantially more per GB, and the analytics ecosystem — Athena, Glue, Redshift Spectrum, EMR — is built around object storage.

## Data Transfer & Hybrid Storage

<QuestionList topic="Data Transfer & Hybrid Storage" storagePrefix="aws-storage-transfer">

<QuestionCard id="awsst-snow-01" number={1} question="What is the Snow family, and when is physically shipping data the right answer?" difficulty="medium" topic="Snow Family">
Physical devices AWS ships to you; you load data and ship them back.

- **Snowball Edge** — 80 TB usable, with optional on-board compute for pre-processing.
- **Snowmobile** — a shipping container on a truck, up to 100 PB. Genuinely exists, rarely used.
- **Snowcone** — small and rugged, 8–14 TB, for edge locations.

The decision is arithmetic. Over a 1 Gbps link at realistic utilisation you move roughly 10 TB per day. So 500 TB is about **two months** of saturated transfer — during which you

title: AWS Storage for Data Platforms

content:
're also consuming the bandwidth your business needs.

Rule of thumb: **beyond ~100 TB, or where bandwidth is limited or expensive, physical shipping wins.** Below ~10 TB, use the network. Between, calculate both.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="awsst-dsync-01" number={2} question="What is DataSync and how does it differ from Storage Gateway?" difficulty="medium" topic="Data Transfer">
**DataSync** is a **migration and replication** service: an agent moves data between on-premises NFS/SMB/HDFS and S3, EFS or FSx, with parallelism, integrity checks, incremental sync and scheduling. It's for **moving data**, one-time or recurring.

**Storage Gateway** is a **hybrid access** service: it presents cloud storage to on-premises systems through familiar protocols, caching hot data locally.
- **

title: AWS Storage for Data Platforms

content:
File Gateway** — NFS/SMB in front of S3, so files written locally become S3 objects.
- **Volume Gateway** — iSCSI block volumes backed by S3.
- **Tape Gateway** — a virtual tape library backed by Glacier, so backup software keeps working while tapes disappear.

The distinction: DataSync **relocates** data; Storage Gateway leaves systems in place and gives them cloud storage behind a local protocol.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="awsst-tf-01" number={3} question="What is AWS Transfer Family, and when is it still relevant?" difficulty="easy" topic="Data Transfer">
Fully managed **SFTP, FTPS and AS2** endpoints backed by S3 or EFS. Partners connect with a standard SFTP client; the files land as S3 objects and trigger your pipeline.

It's relevant because **SFTP remains ubiquitous in B2B d

ata exchange** — banks, insurers, healthcare and retail partners frequently cannot or will not use an API or an S3 bucket policy. Transfer Family lets you support them without operating an SFTP server, managing keys on a box, or patching it.

The typical pattern: partner uploads via SFTP → object lands in S3 → S3 event triggers validation → the pipeline runs. **AS2** support matters specifically for EDI workflows in supply chain and healthcare.

## Common Interview Scenarios

**"Your S3 bill doubled with no new data."** — check incomplete multipart uploads, noncurrent versions on a versioned bucket, request costs from a small-files explosion, and NAT gateway charges on S3 traffic that should use a gateway endpoint. Storage Lens shows all four quickly.

**"A Spark job over a million small files takes hours."** — the cost is per-request latency, `LIST` pagination and per-task overhead, not raw bytes. Compact to 128 MB–1 GB files, and adopt a table format so file discovery comes from metadata rather than listing.

**"Design the storage layout for a lake."** — zones (raw, staging, curated) as prefixes or separate buckets, partitioned by ingestion date, Parquet with sensible file sizes, lifecycle rules per zone, versioning plus noncurr

title: AWS Storage for Data Platforms
description: AWS storage interview questions covering S3 storage classes, lifecycle policies, performance and consistency, EBS volume types, EFS and FSx, plus Storage Gateway, Transfer Family and the Snow family for data migration.
content:
ent expiry on curated, SSE-KMS with Bucket Keys, and gateway endpoints so compute never traverses NAT.

**"Migrate 300 TB from on-premises."** — calculate transfer time against available bandwidth first. At that size, Snowball Edge devices in parallel usually beat the network; DataSync then handles the incremental delta and the final cutover.

## AWS: Amazon Web Services Data Solutions

**AWS is the most widely used cloud platform for data engineering, offering managed compute (EC2), storage (S3, EBS), networking (VPC, Route 53), and purpose-built data services (RDS, DynamoDB, Redshift, ElastiCache) that let teams build pipelines and warehouses without managing physical infrastructure.**

content:
## Key Concepts

AWS interviews generally test whether you understand the trade-offs behind each service category rather than raw trivia. **Compute** (EC2) comes in pricing flavors — On-Demand, Reserved, and Spot — each suited to a different workload shape. **Storage** splits between object storage (S3, with its own storage-class tiers for cost vs. access-frequency trade-offs), block storage (EBS, persistent) and ephemeral instance storage. **Networking** (VPC, subnets, security groups, Route 53) controls isolation and availability, while **IAM** governs who can do what. On the data side, AWS offers managed relational databases (RDS, with engines like Aurora, MySQL, and PostgreSQL), a serverless NoSQL store (DynamoDB) for single-digit-millisecond lookups at scale, a petabyte-scale columnar

title: AWS
description: AWS interview questions covering EC2, S3, VPC, IAM, RDS, DynamoDB, Redshift, and ElastiCache for data engineering and cloud roles.
content:
warehouse (Redshift) for analytics, and an in-memory cache (ElastiCache) for read-heavy workloads. Understanding *when* to reach for each — and how they combine into a real pipeline — is what separates rote answers from strong ones.

### Core Compute & Storage (EC2, S3, AMI)

<QuestionList topic="AWS Compute & Storage" storagePrefix="aws-compute">

<QuestionCard id="aws-compute-01" number={1} question="What is EC2?" difficulty="easy" topic="EC2">
EC2 (Elastic Compute Cloud) is a virtual machine in the cloud on which you have OS-level control. You can run this cloud server whenever you want — useful when you need to deploy your own servers in the cloud, similar to on-premises servers, and want full control over hardware choice and updates on the machine.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="aws-compute-02" number={2} question="Explain what T2 instances are." difficulty="easy" topic="EC2">
T2 instances are designed to provide moderate baseline CPU performance with the ability to "burst" to higher performance as required by

title: AWS
description: AWS interview questions covering EC2, S3, VPC, IAM, RDS, DynamoDB, Redshift, and ElastiCache for data engineering and cloud roles.
content:
the workload — a good fit for applications with variable, spiky CPU usage rather than sustained high load.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="aws-compute-03" number={3} question="What are the different types of EC2 instances?" difficulty="easy" topic="EC2">
- **Compute Optimized** — high-performance processors, for compute-bound workloads
- **Memory-Optimized** — fast performance for memory-intensive workloads
- **Storage Optimized** — high, sequential read/write access to large local datasets
- **Accelerated Computing** — uses hardware accelerators (GPUs) for tasks like graphics processing and machine learning
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="aws-compute-04" number={4} question="What are the different types of EC2 instances based on their cost model?" difficulty="medium" topic="EC2">
-

title: AWS
description: AWS interview questions covering EC2, S3, VPC, IAM, RDS, DynamoDB, Redshift, and ElastiCache for data engineering and cloud roles.

**On-Demand Instance** — created as and when needed, no upfront commitment. Cheap for short-term use, but not for the long term.
- **Spot Instance** — bought through a bidding model against AWS's unused capacity; comparatively cheaper than On-Demand, but can be reclaimed.
- **Reserved Instance** — reserved for a year (or more) in advance; ideal when you know you'll need an instance long-term, and saves heavily on cost.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="aws-compute-05" number={5} question="What are Spot Instances and On-Demand Instances?" difficulty="medium" topic="EC2">
When AWS provisions EC2 capacity, some blocks of computing power go unused — AWS releases these as **Spot Instances**, which run whenever capacity is available and are a good fit if your workload is flexible about timing

title: AWS
description: AWS interview questions covering EC2, S3, VPC, IAM, RDS, DynamoDB, Redshift, and ElastiCache for data engineering and cloud roles.

and tolerant of interruption. **On-Demand Instances**, by contrast, are created whenever needed at a static price, and stay available until you explicitly terminate them.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="aws-compute-06" number={6} question="What do you understand by stopping and terminating an EC2 instance?" difficulty="easy" topic="EC2">
**Stopping** an instance shuts it down like a personal computer — attached volumes are preserved, and the instance can be restarted later. **Terminating** an instance is equivalent to deleting it: all attached volumes are deleted, and the instance cannot be restarted afterward.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="aws-compute-07" number={7} question="Can you change the private IP address of an EC2 instance while it is running or stopped?" difficulty="medi

um" topic="EC2">
No. A private IP address is assigned to an EC2 instance at boot time and stays attached for the instance's entire lifetime — it can never be changed.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="aws-compute-08" number={8} question="What does an AMI include?" difficulty="medium" topic="EC2">
An Amazon Machine Image (AMI) includes:

- a template for the instance's root volume
- launch permissions controlling which AWS accounts can use the AMI to launch instances
- a block device mapping that determines which volumes to attach to the instance at launch
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="aws-compute-09" number={9} question="What is an Instance Store Volume and an EBS Volume?" difficulty="medium" topic="Storage">
An **Instance Store Volume** is temporary storage used for data an instance

needs while running — as soon as the instance stops, the volume and its data are deleted. An **EBS Volume** is persistent block storage: data stored on it survives even after the instance is turned off.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="aws-compute-10" number={10} question="Explain what S3 is." difficulty="easy" topic="S3">
S3 (Simple Storage Service) is Amazon's object storage service. You can use the S3 interface to store and retrieve any amount of data, at any time, from anywhere on the web, on a pay-as-you-go pricing model.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="aws-compute-11" number={11} question="What are the storage classes available in Amazon S3?" difficulty="easy" topic="S3">
- Amazon S3 Standard
- Amazon S3 Standard-Infrequent Access
- Amazon S3 Reduced Redundancy Storage
- Amazon

Each trades cost against retrieval speed and access frequency, so the right class depends on how often the data is actually read.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="aws-compute-12" number={12} question="How can you send a request to Amazon S3?" difficulty="easy" topic="S3">
S3 is a REST service — you can send a request using the REST API directly, or via the AWS SDK wrapper libraries that wrap the underlying S3 REST API.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="aws-compute-13" number={13} question="Is there a way to upload a file greater than 100 megabytes to Amazon S3?" difficulty="medium" topic="S3">
Yes — using the **Multipart Upload** utility. Larger files can be split into multiple parts and uploaded independently (and in parallel, to reduce total upload time). Once all parts fini

</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="aws-compute-14" number={14} question="What is SnowBall?" difficulty="easy" topic="Data Transfer">
Snowball is a physical data-transport appliance that enables you to move terabytes of data into and out of the AWS environment without relying on network bandwidth — useful for large one-time migrations.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="aws-compute-15" number={15} question="What is Elastic Transcoder?" difficulty="easy" topic="Media">
Elastic Transcoder is an AWS service that converts a video's format and resolution to support playback across different devices — tablets, smartphones, and laptops of varying screen resolutions.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="aws-compute-16" number={16} question="List

the different types of cloud services." difficulty="easy" topic="Fundamentals">
- **Software as a Service (SaaS)**
- **Data as a Service (DaaS)**
- **Platform as a Service (PaaS)**
- **Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS)**

<QuestionCard id="aws-compute-17" number={17} question="What is the relationship between an Availability Zone and a Region?" difficulty="medium" topic="Fundamentals">
An **Availability Zone** is a physical location where an AWS data center sits. A **Region** is a collection of Availability Zones. Spreading VMs across multiple Availability Zones within a Region means that if one data center fails, requests still get served from the others — keeping the service available even if a single data center goes down.
</QuestionCard>

### Networking, Security & IAM

<QuestionList topic="AWS Networking & Security" storagePrefix="aws-network">

<QuestionCard id="aws-network-01" number={18} question="What do you understand by VPC?" difficulty="easy" topic="VPC">
VPC (Virtual Private Cloud) lets you customize your own networking configuration. It's a network that is logically isolated from other networks in the cloud, giving you your own private IP address range, internet gateways, subnets, and security groups.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="aws-network-02" number={19} question="How many subnets can you have per VPC?" difficulty="easy" topic="VPC">
You can have up to 200 subnets per VPC.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="aws-network-03" number={20} question="How do you monitor Amazon VPC?" difficulty="medium" topic="VP

C">
You can monitor a VPC using **CloudWatch** (metrics and alarms) and **VPC Flow Logs** (records of the IP traffic going to and from network interfaces in the VPC).
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="aws-network-04" number={21} question="DNS and Load Balancer services come under which type of cloud service?" difficulty="easy" topic="Fundamentals">
DNS and Load Balancer services are part of **IaaS** (Infrastructure as a Service).
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="aws-network-05" number={22} question="How does Amazon Route 53 provide high availability and low latency?" difficulty="medium" topic="Route 53">
- **Globally distributed servers** — AWS runs DNS servers around the world, so a query from any region reaches a nearby server, reducing latency.
- **High dependability** — Route 53 is

title: AWS
description: AWS interview questions covering EC2, S3, VPC, IAM, RDS, DynamoDB, Redshift, and ElastiCache for data engineering and cloud roles.
content:
built to meet the reliability demands of critical applications.
- **Optimal routing** — requests are served from the data center nearest the client. Data can be cached across regions depending on configuration, and Route 53 routes each request to whichever server holding the required data is closest, minimizing response time.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="aws-network-06" number={23} question="What is Geo-Targeting in CloudFront?" difficulty="medium" topic="CloudFront">
Geo-Targeting lets you serve customized content based on a user's geographic location. For example, you might show news about local elections to a user in India but not a user in the US, and vice versa for content more relevant to a US audience.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="aws-network-07" number={24} question="Wh

at are Key-Pairs in AWS?" difficulty="easy" topic="Security">
Key-Pairs are the secure login credentials for your virtual machines, consisting of a public key and a private key, used to connect to EC2 instances.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="aws-network-08" number={25} question="What are the advantages of AWS IAM?" difficulty="medium" topic="IAM">
IAM lets an administrator grant granular, role-based access to different users and groups, since different users typically need different levels of access to different resources. It also supports **Federated Access** — granting access to users and applications without creating dedicated IAM roles for each.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="aws-network-09" number={26} question="What do you understand by a Security Group?" difficulty="medium"

topic="Security">
When you create an instance, you may want to control which networks can reach it. A Security Group is a rule-based virtual firewall for controlling access to instances — you define rules by port number, network range, or protocol to allow or deny access.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="aws-network-10" number={27} question="What is a Stateful and a Stateless Firewall?" difficulty="medium" topic="Security">
A **Stateful Firewall** tracks the state of connections and requires you to define only inbound rules — it automatically allows the matching outbound traffic. A **Stateless Firewall** requires you to explicitly define both inbound and outbound rules. For example, if you allow inbound traffic on port 80, a stateful firewall auto-allows the outbound response on port 80

<QuestionCard id="aws-network-11" number={28} question="What is a Power User Access in AWS?" difficulty="medium" topic="IAM">
An **Administrator** user is effectively the owner of AWS resources — able to create, delete, modify, or view resources, and grant permissions to others. A **Power User** has that same level of resource access, but cannot manage users or permissions for other people.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="aws-network-12" number={29} question="What policies can you set for your users' passwords?" difficulty="easy" topic="Security">
- Set a minimum password length
- Require at least one number or special character
- Require specific character types — uppercase, lowercase, numbers,

<QuestionCard id="aws-network-13" number={30} question="Explain Connection Draining." difficulty="medium" topic="Load Balancing">
Connection Draining lets a server that's about to be updated or removed finish serving its current requests. With Connection Draining enabled, the Load Balancer allows an outgoing instance to complete in-flight requests for a set period but stops routing new requests to it. Without it, the outgoing instance goes offline immediately and any pending requests error out.
</QuestionCard>

### Managed Databases (RDS, DynamoDB, ElastiCache)

<QuestionList topic="AWS Managed Databases" storagePrefix="aws-db">

<QuestionCard id="aws-db-01" number={32} question="What do you know about Amazon's database offerings?" difficulty="easy" topic="Fundamentals">
AWS offers managed relational and NoSQL databases, a fully managed petabyte-scale data warehouse, and in-memory caching as a service. There are four core AWS database services, and you can mix and match based on your needs: **DynamoDB**, **RDS**, **Redshift**, and **ElastiCache**.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="aws-db-02" number={33} question="Explain Amazon Relational Database Service (RDS)." difficulty="easy" topic="RDS">
RDS helps users operate, scale, and manage a relational database in the cloud. It automates admin tasks

title: AWS
description: AWS interview questions covering EC2, S3, VPC, IAM, RDS, DynamoDB, Redshift, and ElastiCache for data engineering and cloud roles.

like setup, hardware provisioning, backups, and patching, giving you resizable, cost-effective capacity so you can focus on the application instead of infrastructure — while still getting high availability, fast performance, compatibility, and security.

Supported RDS engines include:
- MySQL
- Oracle
- PostgreSQL
- SQL Server
- MariaDB
- Amazon Aurora
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="aws-db-03" number={34} question="What are the key features of Amazon's managed database services?" difficulty="easy" topic="Fundamentals">
- Easy to administer
- Highly scalable
- Durable and reliable
- Fast performance
- Highly available
- More secure
- Cost-effective
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="aws-db-04" number={35} question="What are the consistency models for modern databases offered by AWS?" d

ifficulty="medium" topic="Consistency">
- **Eventual Consistency** — data becomes consistent eventually, but not necessarily immediately. Serves requests faster, at the risk that some early reads see stale data. Acceptable where real-time accuracy isn't critical (e.g., not seeing the newest tweets for a couple of seconds).
- **Strong Consistency** — provides immediate consistency across all DB servers. Slower to propagate writes, but guarantees every response reflects consistent data.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="aws-db-05" number={36} question="Which AWS database service is a serverless NoSQL database that delivers consistent single-digit-millisecond latency at any scale?" difficulty="easy" topic="DynamoDB">
Amazon DynamoDB.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="aws-db-06" number={37}

A key-value store is a database service that facilitates storing, updating, and querying objects identified by a key, with a value holding the actual content associated with that key.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="aws-db-07" number={38} question="What is DynamoDB?" difficulty="easy" topic="DynamoDB">
DynamoDB is a fully managed NoSQL database service offering fast, predictable performance with seamless scalability. Because it's fully managed, users don't need to worry about configuration, hardware provisioning, throughput capacity, replication, software patching, or cluster scaling — AWS handles the operational burden of running a distributed database.
</QuestionCard>

- Very high throughput at low latency

`DynamoDBMapper` is the entry point for accessing DynamoDB programmatically. It lets you access data stored across various tables, then execute queries, run scans, and perform CRUD operations on the data items through a higher-level, object-oriented interface.

DynamoDB supports scalar, collection, and null data types.

**Scalar types:**
- Binary
- Number
- Boolean
- String

**Collection types:**

- Number Set
- String Set
- Heterogeneous Map
- Heterogeneous List

DynamoDB Auto Scaling automatically scales a table's (or global secondary index's) read and write capacity up or down in response to actual traffic patterns, so you don't have to provision for peak load manually.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="aws-db-13" number={44} question="What is the work of Amazon RDS?" difficulty="easy" topic="RDS">
When a user wants to set up a relational database, RDS provisions the infrastructure capacity requested and installs the database software. Once the database is running, RDS automates tasks like patching the software, taking backups, and managing synchronous data replication with automatic failover.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="aws-db-14" number={45} question="What is the purpose of a standby RDS instance?" difficulty="medium" topic="RDS">
A standby RDS instance protects against infrastructure failure — it's stored in a

<QuestionCard id="aws-db-15" number={46} question="Are RDS instances upgradable or downgradable as needed?" difficulty="medium" topic="RDS">
Yes — you can upgrade an RDS instance with the `modify-db-instance` command. If you're unsure how much CPU capacity you'll need, start with a `db.m1.small` instance class and monitor CPU utilization with CloudWatch before deciding whether to scale up.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="aws-db-18" number={49} question="What is Amazon ElastiCache?" difficulty="easy" topic="ElastiCache">
ElastiCache is a fully managed, zero-administration in-memory key-value store that supports two engines — Redis and Memcached. It's used both to build new high-performance applications and to speed up existing ones, with common use cases in gaming, healthcare, and other latency-sensitive fields.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="aws-db-19" number={50} question="What is the use of Amazon ElastiCache?" difficulty="easy" topic="ElastiCache">

- **Memcached** — a popular in-memory store for high-performance caching. By keeping data in memory rather than on disk, it retrieves values in under a millisecond, uniquely identifying each cached item by key.
- **Redis** — favored for its performance, simplicity, and feature set. It offers sub-millisecond latency and supports complex data types (strings, hashes, and more), along with backup and restore capabilities. Where Memcached caps key/value size at 1 MB, Redis supports values up to 512 MB.

### Data Warehousing, Analytics & Resilience

<QuestionList topic="AWS Data Warehousing & Resilience" storagePrefix="aws-warehouse">

<QuestionCard id="aws-warehouse-01" number={53} question="What is a data warehouse, and what role does AWS Redshift play in it?" difficulty="medium" topic="Redshift">
A data warehouse is a repository where data generated by a company's systems and other sources is collected and stored, typically in a three-tier architecture:

- **Bottom tier** — tools that cleanse and collect the data
- **Middle tier** — tools that transform the data via an OLAP server
- **Top tier** — front-end tools for data analysis and data mining

Running a data warehouse in-house gets expensive fast, since storage needs keep growing and servers need continual upgrades. Redshift solves

title: AWS
description: AWS interview questions covering EC2, S3, VPC, IAM, RDS, DynamoDB, Redshift, and ElastiCache for data engineering and cloud roles.
content:
this by letting companies store their data in a fully managed, cloud-based warehouse instead.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="aws-warehouse-02" number={54} question="What is Amazon Redshift, and why is it popular among cloud data warehouses?" difficulty="medium" topic="Redshift">
Redshift is a fast, scalable, cost-effective data warehouse, ranging from gigabytes to hundreds of petabytes of storage. No specific programming knowledge is required to use it — you launch a cluster and start querying with familiar SQL tools.

Redshift is popular because:
- **It's easy to use** — create a cluster from the console, fill in a few details, and launch; Redshift automates management, monitoring, and scaling.
- **Scaling is simple** — just resize the cluster by changing the number of compute nodes.

title: AWS

- **It's fast** — columnar storage and massively parallel processing deliver high throughput and low response times, often 10x faster than comparable setups.
- **It's economical** — no upfront setup cost, bringing costs down to roughly a tenth of a traditional data warehouse.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="aws-warehouse-03" number={55} question="What is Redshift Spectrum?" difficulty="medium" topic="Redshift">
Redshift Spectrum lets you run queries directly against petabytes of unstructured data without any ETL/loading step first. It scales to millions of queries and lets you store data wherever and in whatever format suits you.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="aws-warehouse-04" number={56} question="What is a Leader Node and a Compute Node in Redshift?" difficulty="medium" topic="Re

The **Leader Node** receives queries from the client application, parses them, and builds the execution plan, then sends the resulting steps to the compute nodes and returns the final result to the client. The **Compute Nodes** execute the steps assigned by the leader node, process the data, and send their results back to the leader node before it responds to the client.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="aws-warehouse-05" number={57} question="How do you load data into Amazon Redshift?" difficulty="medium" topic="Redshift">
Common sources for loading data into Redshift include DynamoDB, EMR, AWS Glue, and AWS Data Pipeline. Clients can also connect via ODBC or JDBC and issue standard SQL `INSERT` statements to load data directly.
</QuestionCard>

Use **DynamoDB** to collect and store e-commerce data — it's a fully managed NoSQL service well suited to unstructured data from e-commerce sites. From there, run analysis on the retrieved data with **Redshift**. EMR is also capable of analysis but is generally avoided here, since it's less suited to the real-time requirement.

<QuestionCard id="aws-warehouse-07" number={59} question="What is CloudWatch?" difficulty="easy" topic="Monitoring">
CloudWatch monitors AWS environments — EC2 instances, RDS instances, CPU utilization, and more — and can trigger alarms based on metrics you define.

<QuestionCard id="aws-warehouse-08" number={60} question="What are Recovery Time Objective (RTO) and Recovery Point Objective (RPO) in AWS?" difficulty="medium" topic="Resilience">
- **Recovery Time Objective (RTO)** — the maximum acceptable delay between a service interruption and its restoration; effectively, the acceptable window of unavailability.
- **Recovery Point Objective (RPO)** — the maximum acceptable amount of time since the last data restore point; effectively, the acceptable amount of data loss between the last recovery point and the interruption.
</QuestionCard>

## Key Concepts

Azure comparisons cluster on four axes. **Access shape** — object, block or file; document, relational or key-value. **Managed versus controlled** — PaaS convenience against configurability. **Elastic versus provisioned** — scale-to-zero with per-use billing, or reserved capacity that's cheaper when steadily used. And **integration depth**, which on Azure often decides the answer because first-party integration with Entra ID, VNets and Power BI is a real differentiator.

Two Azure-specific patterns are worth internalising because they recur across comparisons. First, several settings are **immutable after creation** — hierarchical namespace on a storage account, redundancy tier, a Cosmos DB partition key — so the comparison isn't just "which is better" but "which can I cha

nge later." Second, **pausing matters**: Synapse dedicated pools and Databricks clusters bill until stopped, so the cheaper option is frequently the one someone remembers to turn off.

The third thing to hold: Microsoft's portfolio is **actively consolidating into Fabric**. Being able to say which services are strategic and which are legacy-adjacent is often the differentiating part of the answer.

For a data lake, choose per zone by reproducibility: **ZRS or GZRS for raw** (often the only copy of what a source sent), **LRS for staging** (rebuildable), **ZRS for curated**. Redundancy is an account-level setting, which is a practical reason to use separate storage accounts per zone.

Rule of thumb for a lake: raw to Cool at 30 days and Archive at 90–180; keep curated Hot or Cool because it's actively queried.

**hierarchical namespace (HNS)** enabled — a checkbox at account creation, not a separate product.

What HNS changes:
- **Real directories**, so renaming or deleting a folder is one atomic metadata operation instead of N per-object operations.
- **POSIX ACLs** on files and directories, alongside Azure RBAC.
- **The `abfss://` driver** used by Spark, Databricks and Synapse.

Why it matters concretely: a Spark job's commit renames a temporary output directory to its final name. Without HNS that's a copy-and-delete per file — on a job writing 50,000 files, seconds becomes many minutes.

The critical practical point: **HNS cannot be enabled after account creation** without migrating. Always enable it for a lake, even if you're not sure you need it yet.

<QuestionCard id="azcmp-int-01" number={1} question="Event Hubs vs Service Bus vs Event Grid vs Queue Storage?" difficulty="hard" topic="Integration">
The four-way version of Azure's most-asked comparison.

- **Event Hubs** — high-throughput **event streaming**, partitioned, retained and **replayable**, consumed with offsets. Telemetry, clickstream, IoT. Kafka-protocol compatible.
- **Service Bus** — **enterprise messaging**: queues and topics, sessions for ordering, transactions, dead-lettering, duplicate detection, scheduled delivery. For business messages where each one matters.
- **Event Grid** — **event routing**: lightweight reactive notifications pushed to subscr

ibers with content-based filtering. For triggering, not data transport.
- **Queue Storage** — a basic, very cheap queue. No topics, sessions, dead-lettering or transactions. Legacy-adjacent; Service Bus supersedes it for anything real.

The heuristic: **many events where the stream matters → Event Hubs; individual messages that must not be lost → Service Bus; reacting to something happening → Event Grid.**

A real pipeline commonly uses three of them together.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="azcmp-int-02" number={2} question="Azure Functions vs Logic Apps?" difficulty="medium" topic="Integration">

## Common Interview Scenarios

**"Which storage redundancy for our lake?"** — decide per zone by reproducibility, not one setting for everything. Note that geo-replication is async (non-zero RPO) and the secondary isn't readable without RA-, and that redundancy is account-level, so zone-per-account is a reasonable structure.

**"Event Hubs or Service Bus for this pipeline?"** — ask whether you need replay and multiple independent consumers over a stream (Event Hubs) or per-message guarantees like ordering, dedup and dead-lettering (Service Bus). If the answer is "a file landed and something should react", it's neither — that's Event Grid.

## Azure Compute: What Runs Your Pipelines

**On Azure, most data engineering compute is consumed indirectly — through Databricks clusters, Synapse Spark pools, or Data Factory integration runtimes. But those all resolve to VM series, Spot capacity and reservations underneath, which is why compute questions still land in data interviews: understanding the layer beneath the managed service is what lets you explain a cost spike or a job that won't fit in memory.**

## Key Concepts

Azure organises everything into a **subscription → resource group → resource** hierarchy, with resource groups as the unit of lifecycle and access control. That matters for data platforms because it's how you separate environments and attribute cost, and it's the boundary most governance policies attach to.

Compute itself spans the same spectrum as any cloud: **VMs** for full control, **AKS** for containers, **Container Instances** for a single container with no orchestrator, **Functions** for event-driven code, and **Batch** for large parallel workloads. The Azure-specific wrinkle is that the data services you'll actually use — Databricks, Synapse, HDInsight, Data Factory — each provision compute on your behalf, so your lever is usually choosing the VM series and purchas

ing model rather than managing instances directly.

The cost levers are the familiar three: **Reservations and Savings Plans** for steady baseline capacity, **Spot VMs** for interruptible batch work, and **turning things off** — which on Azure means auto-termination on Databricks clusters and pausing Synapse dedicated pools, both of which are missed constantly.

<QuestionList topic="Virtual Machines" storagePrefix="azure-compute-vms">

<QuestionCard id="azcm-vm-01" number={1} question="What are the Azure VM series, and which suit data workloads?" difficulty="easy" topic="Virtual Machines">
Series are lettered by purpose:

- **B** — burstable, credit-based. Cheap, and a trap for sustained work because credits exhaust.
- **D** — general purpose, balanced CPU to memory. The common default.
- **E** — **memory optimised**, high RAM per vCPU. **The default for Spark and Databricks**, since shuffle and caching are memory-bound.
- **F** — compute optimised, high CPU per GB. Good for CPU-bound transforms.
- **L** — **storage optimised** with large local NVMe. Excellent for shuffle-heavy Spark and for Kafka.
- **M** — very large memory,

- **N** — GPU, for ML rather than ETL.

For data engineering the two to name are **E-series for Spark executors** and **L-series when local disk throughput matters**. Suffixes matter too: `s` means premium storage capable, `d` means a local temp disk, `a` means AMD.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="azcm-vm-02" number={2} question="What are the Azure VM purchasing options?" difficulty="medium" topic="Virtual Machines">
- **Pay-as-you-go** — per-second billing, no commitment. Baseline price.
- **Reserved Instances** — 1 or 3 year commitment to a VM series in a region, up to ~72% off. Can be exchanged or cancelled with a fee.
- **Savings Plans for compute** — commit to an hourly spend for 1 or 3 years, up to ~65% off, and **flexi

- **Spot VMs** — surplus capacity at up to **90% off**, evicted with **30 seconds' notice** when Azure needs it back. You set a maximum price or accept the current one.
- **Azure Hybrid Benefit** — reuse on-premises Windows Server and SQL Server licences, often a large saving.

For data platforms: **Reservations or Savings Plans for the always-on layer**, **Spot for Databricks worker nodes and Batch pools**. Note Spot's 30-second eviction notice is much shorter than AWS's two minutes, so draining must be quick.
</QuestionCard>

Separately, many VM series include a **temporary local disk** (the `d` suffix) which is **ephemeral** — wiped on deallocation. That's where Spark shuffle and scratch data should go, exactly as with AWS instance store.

## Azure Kubernetes Service

<QuestionList topic="Azure Kubernetes Service" storagePrefix="azure-compute-aks">

<QuestionCard id="azcm-aks-01" number={1} question="What is AKS and what does Azure manage?" difficulty="medium" topic="AKS">
Managed Kubernetes. Azure runs the **control plane free of charge** (you pay only for node VMs, unless you buy the uptime SLA tier), handles upgrades and patching of the control plane, and integrates with Entra ID, Azure Monitor and Azure networking.

You still own node pools, workload configuration, networking choices, and the upgrade cadence for nodes.

For data platforms AKS hosts the same things it does elsewhere: **Airflow** with the KubernetesExecutor, **Spark on Kubernetes**, Flink, Trino, and dbt runners. It's also the substrate for Azure's own con

content:
tainer-based services.

The free control plane is a genuine differentiator versus AWS EKS, which charges per cluster — it makes running several clusters (per environment, per team) noticeably cheaper.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="azcm-aks-02" number={2} question="What are node pools, and how should you configure them for data workloads?" difficulty="medium" topic="AKS">
A node pool is a group of identical VMs in the cluster. A cluster has a **system** pool (running cluster services) plus any number of **user** pools.

For a data platform:
- **System pool** — small, on-demand, never Spot. Cluster components must not be evicted.
- **User pools by workload shape** — an E-series pool for Spark executors, a smaller D-series pool for orchestration tasks, an L-series pool if shuffle needs l

content:

- **Spot node pools** for interruptible batch, with taints so only tolerant workloads land there.
- **Cluster autoscaler** per pool, with sensible min and max.

Use **taints and tolerations plus node selectors** so workloads land on the right pool. Without them, a Spark executor can be scheduled onto the system pool and destabilise the cluster.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="azcm-aks-03" number={3} question="How do pods on AKS authenticate to Azure Storage or a database?" difficulty="medium" topic="AKS">
**Workload Identity** — the current recommended approach. A Kubernetes service account is federated to an Entra ID **managed identity** via OIDC, so pods receive short-lived tokens automatically with no secrets stored anywhere.

It replaces the older **AAD Pod Identity**, wh

The alternatives, in descending order of preference: a **managed identity assigned to the node pool** (simpler, but every pod on the node shares it, so it's coarse), and **service principal credentials in a Kubernetes Secret** — which means a secret to rotate and leak, and should be avoided.

Then grant that identity **Azure RBAC roles** scoped narrowly: `Storage Blob Data Reader` on a specific container, not `Contributor` on the storage account. Over-broad role assignments are the most common finding in an Azure data platform review.

## Container Instances & Functions

<QuestionList topic="Container Instances & Functions" storagePrefix="azure-compute-aci-functions">

<QuestionCard id="azcm-aci-01" number={1} question="What is Azure Container Instances and when is it the right tool?" difficulty="easy" topic="Container Instances">
The simplest way to run a container on Azure: specify an image, CPU and memory, and it runs — no cluster, no orchestrator, billed per second.

It fits **short-lived, single-container tasks** with no need for scaling, service discovery or rolling deploys: a scheduled data transformation, a one-off migration script, a build agent, or burst capacity.

For data engineering the common pattern is **Data Factory or Airflow launching an ACI container** per task, so each task carries its own dependencie

content:
s without a Kubernetes cluster to operate.

Its limits are the flip side of its simplicity: no autoscaling, no built-in load balancing, no rolling updates, and limited networking. Anything needing orchestration belongs on AKS or Container Apps.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="azcm-aci-02" number={2} question="What are Azure Functions, and what are the hosting plans?" difficulty="medium" topic="Functions">
Azure's serverless compute — event-driven code with bindings to Blob Storage, Event Hubs, Service Bus, Cosmos DB and HTTP.

Hosting plans, which is where the interesting differences are:
- **Consumption** — true serverless, scales to zero, pay per execution. **5-minute default timeout, 10 maximum.** Cold starts.
- **Premium** — pre-warmed instances (no cold start), VNet integration, **

unlimited timeout in practice**, higher cost.
- **Dedicated (App Service)** — runs on your App Service plan; useful if you already have one underused.
- **Flex Consumption** — newer, combining scale-to-zero with VNet support and faster scaling.

The data engineering consequence mirrors Lambda: Functions suit **triggering and small per-event work**, not full transformations. The Consumption timeout is the constraint that pushes work to Batch, ACI or Data Factory.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="azcm-aci-03" number={3} question="How do Functions integrate with data services?" difficulty="medium" topic="Functions">
Through **triggers and bindings**, which remove most of the client code:

- **Blob trigger** — fires when a file lands. Note it polls by default and can be slow at scale; **Even

- **Event Hubs trigger** — consumes partitions with checkpointing, the standard streaming entry point.
- **Service Bus trigger** — queue or topic consumption with dead-lettering.
- **Cosmos DB change feed trigger** — reacts to document changes.
- **Timer trigger** — cron scheduling.
- **Output bindings** — write to Blob, Cosmos, Service Bus without writing SDK code.

The pattern worth naming: for high-volume blob events, use **Event Grid** rather than the polling blob trigger — teams routinely hit unexplained latency because they didn't know the difference.

## Azure Batch

<QuestionList topic="Azure Batch" storagePrefix="azure-compute-batch">

<QuestionCard id="azcm-bat-01" number={1} question="What is Azure Batch and what problem does it solve?" difficulty="medium" topic="Batch">
A managed service for large-scale **parallel and HPC** workloads. You define a **pool** of VMs (fixed or autoscaling, dedicated or Spot), a **job**, and **tasks** within it. Batch schedules tasks onto nodes, retries failures and scales the pool.

It fills the gap between Functions and a permanent cluster: work that runs **longer than a Function's timeout**, is **embarrassingly parallel**, and arrives in bursts.

Typical data uses: processing thousands of files independently, media transcoding, Monte Carlo simulation, and model scoring batches.

The distinction from

title: Azure Compute for Data Workloads
description: Azure compute interview questions covering Virtual Machines and series selection, Azure Kubernetes Service, Container Instances, Azure Batch, and Azure Functions — and choosing compute for Databricks, Synapse and Data Factory workloads.
content:
Spark-based services matters: Batch runs **your executable or container per task** with no distributed framework. If tasks are independent, that's simpler and cheaper than a Spark cluster. If they need to shuffle data between each other, you want Databricks or Synapse Spark.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="azcm-bat-02" number={2} question="How does Azure Batch handle scaling and cost?" difficulty="medium" topic="Batch">
Pools autoscale on a **formula** you write, evaluated periodically against metrics like pending tasks:

```
$sample = $PendingTasks.GetSample(TimeInterval_Minute * 5);
$targetDedicated = min(100, max(0, avg($sample)));
```

Cost control comes from three places: **Spot (low-priority) nodes**, which can be 60–90% cheaper and are ideal because Batch retries evicted tasks au

description: Azure compute interview questions covering Virtual Machines and series selection, Azure Kubernetes Service, Container Instances, Azure Batch, and Azure Functions — and choosing compute for Databricks, Synapse and Data Factory workloads.
content:
tomatically; **scaling to zero** between jobs so an idle pool costs nothing; and **right-sizing the VM series** to the task.

The common mistake is a pool with a non-zero minimum left running permanently — it looks like a small line item and accumulates. Set the minimum to zero unless startup latency genuinely matters.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

<QuestionCard id="azcm-ch-02" number={2} question="Where does Azure Databricks fit, and what compute does it use?" difficulty="medium" topic="Choosing">

## Azure Data Solutions: Synapse, Databricks, Fabric and the Pipeline Layer

**Azure's data stack has changed shape more than any other cloud's — HDInsight gave way to Databricks and Synapse, and Synapse is now being absorbed into Microsoft Fabric. Interviewers use this area to test whether you can reason about the current landscape rather than recite a service you used three years ago, and whether you understand what actually differentiates a lakehouse from a dedicated SQL pool.**
