content:
## Key Concepts

Azure's analytics story rests on **ADLS Gen2 as the storage layer** with multiple compute engines over it. Synapse brought SQL pools, Spark pools and pipelines into one workspace; Databricks provides the Spark and lakehouse platform; Data Factory moves and orchestrates. **Microsoft Fabric** is the current direction — a SaaS bundle unifying these behind **OneLake**, a single logical lake with Delta as the native format.

The distinction that matters most in interviews is **dedicated versus serverless SQL**. A Synapse **dedicated** pool is a provisioned MPP warehouse with data loaded into its own storage — fast, expensive, and billed whether you query it or not unless you pause it. **Serverless** SQL queries files in the lake directly, billed per terabyte processed, with not

title: Azure Data & Serverless Solutions
description: Azure data platform interview questions covering Synapse Analytics, Databricks, Data Factory, Event Hubs and Stream Analytics, Microsoft Fabric, Service Bus, and serverless patterns for data pipelines.
content:
hing running when idle. They solve different problems and the wrong choice shows up immediately in the bill.

The second is that **Delta Lake is now the common denominator**. Databricks, Synapse Spark and Fabric all read and write Delta, so the open table format — not the engine — is what gives you ACID transactions, time travel and upserts on the lake. Designing around Delta rather than around a specific product is the answer that ages well.

## Azure Synapse Analytics

<QuestionList topic="Azure Synapse Analytics" storagePrefix="azure-solutions-synapse">

<QuestionCard id="azsol-syn-01" number={1} question="What are the components of Azure Synapse Analytics?" difficulty="medium" topic="Synapse">
A workspace bundling several engines over ADLS Gen2:

- **Dedicated SQL pool** — the MPP data warehouse, formerly SQL Data Warehouse. Provisioned in DWUs, data loaded into its own columnar storage.
- **Serverless SQL pool** — query Parquet, CSV and Delta **in the lake** with T-SQL, no infrastructure, billed per TB processed.
- **Apache Spark pools** — managed Spark for data engineering and ML, with autoscale and auto-pause.
- **Pipelines** — essentially Azure Data Factory embedded in the workspace, for orchestration and copy activities

title: Azure Data & Serverless Solutions
description: Azure data platform interview questions covering Synapse Analytics, Databricks, Data Factory, Event Hubs and Stream Analytics, Microsoft Fabric, Service Bus, and serverless patterns for data pipelines.
content:
.
- **Synapse Link** — near-real-time replication from Cosmos DB, Dataverse and SQL into analytics with no pipeline.
- **Synapse Studio** — the unified web UI.

The pitch was one workspace for warehouse, lake and orchestration. In practice many teams pair **Databricks for engineering** with **Synapse serverless or dedicated for serving**, and Microsoft's own direction has since moved to Fabric.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="azsol-syn-02" number={2} question="What is the difference between dedicated and serverless SQL pools?" difficulty="hard" topic="Synapse">
| | **Dedicated** | **Serverless** |
|---|---|---|
| Data location | loaded into pool storage | queried in place in ADLS |
| Billing | per DWU-hour, **whether used or not** | per TB processed |
| Pause | must be paused manually |

nothing to pause |
| Performance | fast, predictable, tunable | variable, no indexes |
| Features | distributions, indexes, materialised views, workload management | read-mostly, `CETAS` for output |

**Dedicated** suits a high-concurrency BI serving layer where consistent sub-second response matters and the cost is justified by usage.

**Serverless** suits exploration, ad-hoc analysis, and lightweight transformation over lake files — you point it at Parquet and query.

The cost trap worth naming: a dedicated pool left **un-paused** overnight and at weekends bills continuously. Pausing it is the single most common Synapse cost saving, and it's routinely forgotten.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="azsol-syn-03" number={3} question="How do you design tables in a dedicated SQL pool?" diffi

Two choices dominate performance, and they mirror Redshift.

**Distribution** — how rows spread across the 60 underlying distributions:
- **HASH** on the join key for large fact tables, so joins happen locally rather than shuffling.
- **REPLICATE** for small dimension tables (under ~2 GB), giving every node a full copy.
- **ROUND_ROBIN** as the fallback for staging tables with no obvious key.

**Indexing**:
- **Clustered columnstore** — the default and right answer for large fact tables.
- **Heap** or clustered index for small tables and staging.

```sql
CREATE TABLE fact_orders WITH (
  DISTRIBUTION = HASH(customer_id),
  CLUSTERED COLUMNSTORE INDEX
) AS SELECT ...
```

The failure to name is **data skew**: hashing on a low-cardinality or unevenly distributed

column puts most rows on a few distributions, so one node does all the work. Check with `DBCC PDW_SHOWSPACEUSED`.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="azsol-syn-04" number={4} question="What is PolyBase and COPY INTO?" difficulty="medium" topic="Synapse">
Both load external data into a dedicated SQL pool in parallel across distributions.

**PolyBase** uses external tables — you define an external data source, file format and table, then `INSERT ... SELECT` from it. Powerful, and more setup.

**`COPY INTO`** is the newer, simpler statement and the recommended default:

```sql
COPY INTO fact_orders
FROM 'https://acct.dfs.core.windows.net/curated/orders/'
WITH (FILE_TYPE = 'PARQUET', CREDENTIAL = (IDENTITY = 'Managed Identity'));
```

Both are dramatically faster than row-by-row `INSERT`, beca

title: Azure Data & Serverless Solutions
description: Azure data platform interview questions covering Synapse Analytics, Databricks, Data Factory, Event Hubs and Stream Analytics, Microsoft Fabric, Service Bus, and serverless patterns for data pipelines.
content:
use they parallelise across all distributions.

Loading practices that matter: **split input into multiple files** so every distribution works, prefer **Parquet**, load into a **staging table** then swap so consumers never see partial data, and run `CREATE STATISTICS` afterwards so the optimiser has current information.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

## Databricks & the Lakehouse

<QuestionList topic="Databricks & the Lakehouse" storagePrefix="azure-solutions-databricks">

<QuestionCard id="azsol-dbx-01" number={1} question="What is the medallion architecture?" difficulty="medium" topic="Lakehouse">
Databricks' name for a layered lake design:

- **Bronze** — raw, as-ingested, append-only. Preserves history and allows reprocessing. Minimal transformation, maybe just added ingestion metadata.
- **Silver** — cleaned, deduplicated, conformed, joined into meaningful entities. Quality rules applied here.
- **Gold** — business-level aggregates and dimensional models, shaped for consumption by BI and ML.

Why it's a useful convention rather than just naming: it makes **reprocessing** tractable (you can always rebuild silver and gold from bronz

title: Azure Data & Serverless Solutions
description: Azure data platform interview questions covering Synapse Analytics, Databricks, Data Factory, Event Hubs and Stream Analytics, Microsoft Fabric, Service Bus, and serverless patterns for data pipelines.
content:
e), it puts data quality gates at a defined boundary, and it gives consumers a clear contract about which layer is safe to depend on.

It maps directly onto raw / enriched / curated in other vocabularies — the concept matters more than the names, and being able to say that is the better answer.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="azsol-dbx-02" number={2} question="What does Delta Lake add over plain Parquet?" difficulty="hard" topic="Lakehouse">
Delta is Parquet files plus a **transaction log** (`_delta_log`), and the log is what makes the difference:

- **ACID transactions** — a writer commits atomically, so readers never see a partial write. This is the fix for the "downstream job read a half-written directory" failure.
- **Upserts and deletes** — `MERGE INTO`, which plain Parquet can't d

title: Azure Data & Serverless Solutions
description: Azure data platform interview questions covering Synapse Analytics, Databricks, Data Factory, Event Hubs and Stream Analytics, Microsoft Fabric, Service Bus, and serverless patterns for data pipelines.
content:
o without rewriting everything. Essential for CDC and for GDPR erasure.
- **Time travel** — query the table as of a version or timestamp, and restore after a bad write.
- **Schema enforcement and evolution** — rejects mismatched writes rather than silently corrupting the table.
- **Efficient metadata** — file listing comes from the log rather than an expensive directory scan, which fixes the small-files listing problem.
- **`OPTIMIZE` and Z-ordering** — compaction and data skipping.

The one-line version: **Delta turns a directory of files into a table**. Iceberg and Hudi solve the same problem; the concept is what matters.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="azsol-dbx-03" number={3} question="What is Unity Catalog and what problem does it solve?" difficulty="medium" topic="Databricks">
A u

nified governance layer across Databricks workspaces: a three-level namespace (`catalog.schema.table`), centralised access control, automated **lineage**, auditing, and a searchable data catalog.

The problem it solves is that before it, permissions lived in **workspace-local** table ACLs and in storage-level credentials, so governance was fragmented — different workspaces had different views of the same data, and lineage had to be reconstructed by hand.

For interviews the points worth making: it enables **fine-grained access control** (row filters and column masks) enforced consistently across SQL and Spark, it supports **Delta Sharing** for governed sharing outside the organisation, and it makes **lineage** automatic, which is what you need when someone asks "what breaks if I change thi

</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="azsol-dbx-04" number={4} question="Databricks or Synapse Spark — how do you choose?" difficulty="hard" topic="Databricks">
**Databricks** — a more mature Spark platform: Photon for vectorised execution, Delta Live Tables for declarative pipelines, Unity Catalog, MLflow, notebooks and collaboration, and faster adoption of new Spark versions. Costs DBUs on top of VM cost.

**Synapse Spark** — integrated into the Synapse workspace alongside SQL pools and pipelines, single billing, and simpler if you're already committed to Synapse. Generally trails Databricks on Spark features and performance.

**Microsoft Fabric** is now Microsoft's strategic direction, absorbing much of Synapse into a SaaS model over OneLake.

The honest answer for a new platfor

description: Azure data platform interview questions covering Synapse Analytics, Databricks, Data Factory, Event Hubs and Stream Analytics, Microsoft Fabric, Service Bus, and serverless patterns for data pipelines.

m today: **Databricks for serious data engineering**, especially if the team lives in Spark. **Fabric** if the organisation is Power BI–centric and wants an integrated SaaS experience. Synapse standalone is increasingly a legacy choice, and saying so demonstrates current awareness.

content:
## Data Factory & Orchestration

<QuestionList topic="Data Factory & Orchestration" storagePrefix="azure-solutions-adf">

<QuestionCard id="azsol-adf-01" number={1} question="What is Azure Data Factory and what are its core concepts?" difficulty="medium" topic="Data Factory">
A managed data integration and orchestration service — Azure's ETL/ELT workhorse.

- **Pipeline** — a logical grouping of activities.
- **Activity** — a step: Copy, Data Flow, notebook execution, stored procedure, or control flow (ForEach, If, Until).
- **Dataset** — a named view of data in a store.
- **Linked service** — the connection definition and credentials.
- **Integration runtime** — the compute that actually does the work.
- **Trigger** — schedule, tumbling window, or event-based.

Its strength is the **Copy

title: Azure Data & Serverless Solutions
description: Azure data platform interview questions covering Synapse Analytics, Databricks, Data Factory, Event Hubs and Stream Analytics, Microsoft Fabric, Service Bus, and serverless patterns for data pipelines.
content:
activity** with 100+ connectors, which handles the tedious part of moving data between systems with parallelism and fault tolerance.

Its weakness is expressing complex logic — the visual, JSON-defined model gets unwieldy compared with code-based orchestration, which is why many teams use ADF for movement and Databricks or Airflow for transformation logic.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="azsol-adf-02" number={2} question="What are the integration runtime types?" difficulty="medium" topic="Data Factory">
- **Azure IR** — fully managed, serverless compute in a region. Used for cloud-to-cloud copy and Data Flows. The default.
- **Self-hosted IR** — an agent you install on-premises or in a VNet. Required to reach **private data sources** — an on-premises SQL Server, or a database behind a f

title: Azure Data & Serverless Solutions
description: Azure data platform interview questions covering Synapse Analytics, Databricks, Data Factory, Event Hubs and Stream Analytics, Microsoft Fabric, Service Bus, and serverless patterns for data pipelines.
content:
irewall. It makes **outbound** connections only, which is what gets it through security review.
- **Azure-SSIS IR** — a managed cluster for lifting existing SSIS packages into Azure without rewriting them.

The one that matters most in practice is **self-hosted**: almost every real migration involves on-premises sources, and understanding that it's an outbound-only agent (no inbound firewall rule needed) is the detail that shows you've deployed one.

For high availability, install it on multiple nodes — a single-node self-hosted IR is a single point of failure for every on-premises pipeline.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="azsol-adf-03" number={3} question="What is the difference between Copy activity and Mapping Data Flows?" difficulty="medium" topic="Data Factory">
**Copy activity** m

title: Azure Data & Serverless Solutions
description: Azure data platform interview questions covering Synapse Analytics, Databricks, Data Factory, Event Hubs and Stream Analytics, Microsoft Fabric, Service Bus, and serverless patterns for data pipelines.
content:
oves data from source to sink with minimal transformation — format conversion, column mapping, and simple filtering. It runs on the integration runtime and is highly optimised, with parallel partitioned reads. Cheap and fast.

**Mapping Data Flow** is a visual transformation designer — joins, aggregates, derived columns, pivots, slowly changing dimension patterns — that **compiles to Spark** and runs on a managed Databricks cluster behind the scenes.

The trade-off: Data Flows let non-coders build transformations, but they're **much more expensive** (you're paying for Spark clusters with startup time per run) and harder to test, version and debug than code.

The common mature pattern: **Copy activity to land data, then Databricks notebooks or dbt for transformation**, using ADF purely for

title: Azure Data & Serverless Solutions
description: Azure data platform interview questions covering Synapse Analytics, Databricks, Data Factory, Event Hubs and Stream Analytics, Microsoft Fabric, Service Bus, and serverless patterns for data pipelines.
content:
movement and orchestration. Data Flows make sense when the team genuinely can't write Spark.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="azsol-adf-04" number={4} question="How do you handle incremental loads in Data Factory?" difficulty="hard" topic="Data Factory">
Three patterns, in increasing order of fidelity:

1. **Watermark** — store the last processed high-water mark (a timestamp or ID) in a control table, query rows above it, then update the watermark after success. Simple and portable; **misses deletes**, and depends on a reliable `updated_at`.
2. **Tumbling window trigger** — ADF passes window start and end to the pipeline, so each run handles a fixed time slice. Supports **dependency chaining and automatic backfill** by re-running windows, which is its real advantage.
3. **Native CDC** —

title: Azure Data & Serverless Solutions
description: Azure data platform interview questions covering Synapse Analytics, Databricks, Data Factory, Event Hubs and Stream Analytics, Microsoft Fabric, Service Bus, and serverless patterns for data pipelines.
content:
ADF's change data capture connectors, or Debezium reading the log. Captures deletes and every intermediate change, with the least source impact.

Whichever you choose, make the load **idempotent** — write into a partition you overwrite, or `MERGE` into a Delta table on the key — so a retried run can't duplicate rows. That's the part that separates a design that survives retries from one that quietly corrupts the target.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

## Streaming: Event Hubs & Stream Analytics

<QuestionList topic="Streaming: Event Hubs & Stream Analytics" storagePrefix="azure-solutions-streaming">

<QuestionCard id="azsol-eh-01" number={1} question="What is Azure Event Hubs?" difficulty="medium" topic="Event Hubs">
A managed, high-throughput event ingestion service — Azure's equivalent of Kinesis Data Streams, and **Kafka protocol compatible**, so Kafka clients and tooling work against it unchanged.

Core concepts: an **event hub** (a topic) has **partitions** for parallelism and ordering; **consumer groups** give each downstream application its own independent view and offsets; **throughput units** (or processing units in Premium) provision capacity.

**Event Hubs Capture** is the feature to name for data engineering: it automaticall

title: Azure Data & Serverless Solutions
description: Azure data platform interview questions covering Synapse Analytics, Databricks, Data Factory, Event Hubs and Stream Analytics, Microsoft Fabric, Service Bus, and serverless patterns for data pipelines.
content:
y writes the stream to ADLS or Blob in Avro at a configurable time or size interval, **with no consumer code at all**. That gives you a durable raw landing zone for free.

Ordering is guaranteed **within a partition**, not across the hub — the same constraint as Kafka and Kinesis, and the same consequence for partition key choice.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="azsol-eh-02" number={2} question="How do Event Hubs, Service Bus and Event Grid differ?" difficulty="hard" topic="Messaging">
This is Azure's most-asked "which one" question.

- **Event Hubs** — **high-throughput event streaming**. Millions of events per second, retained and **replayable**, consumed by partition with offsets. For telemetry, clickstream and IoT.
- **Service Bus** — **enterprise messaging**. Queues and topics with

title: Azure Data & Serverless Solutions
description: Azure data platform interview questions covering Synapse Analytics, Databricks, Data Factory, Event Hubs and Stream Analytics, Microsoft Fabric, Service Bus, and serverless patterns for data pipelines.
content:
ordering (sessions), transactions, dead-lettering, scheduled delivery and duplicate detection. For business messages where each one matters and must not be lost.
- **Event Grid** — **event routing**. Lightweight reactive notifications ("a blob was created") pushed to subscribers with content-based filtering. For triggering, not for data transport.

The heuristic: **Event Hubs for many events where you care about the stream; Service Bus for individual messages where you care about each one; Event Grid for reacting to something happening.**

A typical pipeline uses all three: Event Grid fires on a blob landing, Service Bus carries the work item, Event Hubs carries the telemetry.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="azsol-eh-03" number={3} question="What is Azure Stream Analytics, and when wou

title: Azure Data & Serverless Solutions
description: Azure data platform interview questions covering Synapse Analytics, Databricks, Data Factory, Event Hubs and Stream Analytics, Microsoft Fabric, Service Bus, and serverless patterns for data pipelines.

ld you use it over Spark Structured Streaming?" difficulty="medium" topic="Stream Analytics">
A fully managed real-time processing service using a **SQL-like language** with built-in temporal operators — tumbling, hopping, sliding and session windows — reading from Event Hubs or IoT Hub and writing to Blob, SQL, Cosmos, Power BI and more.

Choose **Stream Analytics** when the logic is expressible in SQL, you want zero infrastructure, and latency requirements are seconds. Setting up a windowed aggregate to Power BI is genuinely a few minutes' work.

Choose **Spark Structured Streaming** or **Flink** when you need arbitrary code, complex stateful logic, machine learning inference in the stream, exactly-once semantics with custom sinks, or portability off Azure.

The honest limitation: Stream

Analytics is excellent within its box and awkward the moment you step outside it — custom deserialisation, complex joins and non-SQL logic all push you toward Spark or Flink.

## Service Bus & Serverless Patterns

<QuestionList topic="Service Bus & Serverless Patterns" storagePrefix="azure-solutions-servicebus">

<QuestionCard id="azsol-sb-01" number={1} question="What features does Service Bus offer beyond a simple queue?" difficulty="medium" topic="Service Bus">
- **Topics and subscriptions** — pub/sub with SQL-like filter rules per subscriber, so each gets only relevant messages.
- **Sessions** — FIFO ordering within a session ID, which is how you preserve per-entity ordering while still processing many entities in parallel.
- **Dead-letter queues** — built in, automatic on repeated failure or expiry.
- **Duplicate detection** — Service Bus discards a message with a repeated `MessageId` within a window, giving effective exactly-once ingestion.
- **Scheduled d

title: Azure Data & Serverless Solutions
description: Azure data platform interview questions covering Synapse Analytics, Databricks, Data Factory, Event Hubs and Stream Analytics, Microsoft Fabric, Service Bus, and serverless patterns for data pipelines.
content:
elivery** and message deferral.
- **Transactions** across multiple send and complete operations.
- **Peek-lock** — the consumer locks a message, processes it, then completes or abandons it.

For data pipelines, **sessions** and **duplicate detection** are the two that justify Service Bus over the simpler Queue Storage: ordered per-key processing and dedup are otherwise real work to build.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="azsol-sb-02" number={2} question="What does 'Azure Serverless' mean for a data pipeline?" difficulty="medium" topic="Serverless">
A set of services that scale to zero and bill per use, composed into pipelines with no infrastructure to manage:

- **Azure Functions** — event-driven compute with bindings to Blob, Event Hubs, Service Bus and Cosmos.
- **Logic Apps** — visual

title: Azure Data & Serverless Solutions
description: Azure data platform interview questions covering Synapse Analytics, Databricks, Data Factory, Event Hubs and Stream Analytics, Microsoft Fabric, Service Bus, and serverless patterns for data pipelines.
content:
, connector-driven workflows for integration and approvals.
- **Event Grid** — event routing.
- **Serverless SQL pool** and **Cosmos DB serverless** — query and store without provisioning.
- **Container Apps Jobs** — containerised tasks that scale to zero.
- **Data Factory** — orchestration billed per activity run.

The benefits are no idle cost and no capacity planning; the costs are per-execution limits (Function timeouts), cold starts, and cost that becomes unattractive at sustained high volume.

The mature pattern is **serverless at the edges** — triggering, routing, light transformation — with **provisioned compute for the heavy processing** in the middle.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="azsol-sb-03" number={3} question="What is Microsoft Fabric and how does it change the picture?"

difficulty="hard" topic="Fabric">
A **SaaS analytics platform** unifying Microsoft's data products under one capacity-based licence: Data Factory for movement, Synapse Data Engineering (Spark), Data Warehouse, Real-Time Intelligence, Data Science, and Power BI.

The architectural centrepiece is **OneLake** — a single logical data lake per tenant, with **Delta Parquet as the native format** for everything. Engines read the same tables without copying, and **Shortcuts** reference data in ADLS, S3 or elsewhere without moving it.

What changes: the emphasis shifts from assembling PaaS services to consuming an integrated SaaS product, with tight Power BI integration (**Direct Lake** mode reads Delta directly, avoiding both import refresh and DirectQuery latency).

The balanced view for an inte

**For a data engineer these are usually the systems you read *from* rather than run — so the questions that matter are about extraction without hurting production, change capture, and knowing when a workload has outgrown a transactional store. Cosmos DB is the exception worth real depth, because its partitioning and consistency model come up constantly and people get both wrong.**

content:
## Key Concepts

Azure's relational offerings come in **deployment models** that trade compatibility against management. Azure SQL Database is a single logical database with the most managed features and the least surface area; SQL Managed Instance gives near-full SQL Server compatibility for lift-and-shift; SQL Server on a VM gives complete control and complete responsibility. The same pattern repeats for MySQL and PostgreSQL as Flexible Server.

**Cosmos DB** is the purpose-built NoSQL store, and its defining characteristics are **global distribution**, **five consistency levels** rather than the usual two, and a **request unit (RU)** currency that abstracts CPU, memory and IOPS into one number you provision or consume.

The data engineering thread running through all of them is **how yo

title: Azure Database Services
description: Azure database interview questions covering Azure SQL Database and Managed Instance, Cosmos DB APIs and consistency levels, Azure Database for MySQL and PostgreSQL, Database Migration Service, and extracting data for analytics.
content:
u get data out**. A full-table `SELECT` against production is the wrong answer everywhere. The right answers are a read replica, a snapshot or export, or **change feed / CDC** — and Azure's managed options (Cosmos change feed, SQL CDC, Synapse Link) are designed precisely so analytics doesn't touch the serving path.

title: Azure Database Services
description: Azure database interview questions covering Azure SQL Database and Managed Instance, Cosmos DB APIs and consistency levels, Azure Database for MySQL and PostgreSQL, Database Migration Service, and extracting data for analytics.
content:
## Azure SQL

<QuestionList topic="Azure SQL" storagePrefix="azure-databases-sql">

<QuestionCard id="azdb-sql-01" number={1} question="What are the Azure SQL deployment options?" difficulty="medium" topic="Azure SQL">
- **Azure SQL Database** — a single logical database, fully managed. Automatic patching, backups, point-in-time restore, built-in HA. Most managed, least compatible: no SQL Agent, no cross-database queries, no CLR.
- **Elastic Pool** — many databases sharing a pool of resources, so their peaks don't coincide. Much cheaper for SaaS-style multi-tenant estates than provisioning each database separately.
- **SQL Managed Instance** — near-complete SQL Server compatibility including SQL Agent, cross-database queries, linked servers and CLR, deployed into your VNet. The **lift-and-

title: Azure Database Services
description: Azure database interview questions covering Azure SQL Database and Managed Instance, Cosmos DB APIs and consistency levels, Azure Database for MySQL and PostgreSQL, Database Migration Service, and extracting data for analytics.
content:
shift target**.
- **SQL Server on Azure VM** — full control, full responsibility. Only when you need OS access or an unsupported feature.

The decision: **Managed Instance** if you're migrating an existing SQL Server estate with dependencies on Agent jobs or cross-database queries; **SQL Database** for new applications.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="azdb-sql-02" number={2} question="What is the difference between DTU and vCore purchasing models?" difficulty="medium" topic="Azure SQL">
**DTU (Database Transaction Unit)** bundles CPU, memory and I/O into one opaque number, with tiers Basic, Standard and Premium. Simple, but you can't tune the mix, and you can't map it to on-premises hardware.

**vCore** exposes cores, memory and storage separately, in **General Purpose**, **Business Cri

title: Azure Database Services
description: Azure database interview questions covering Azure SQL Database and Managed Instance, Cosmos DB APIs and consistency levels, Azure Database for MySQL and PostgreSQL, Database Migration Service, and extracting data for analytics.
content:
tical** (local SSD, in-memory OLTP, a readable replica) and **Hyperscale** (storage to 100 TB, near-instant backups, fast scale-out of read replicas) tiers.

**vCore is the recommended model** — it's transparent, lets you size dimensions independently, and is the only way to use **Azure Hybrid Benefit** to reuse existing SQL Server licences, which is often a large saving.

**Serverless** compute on vCore auto-pauses after inactivity, making it well suited to dev and intermittent workloads.

**Hyperscale** is the one worth naming for data work — its architecture separates compute from a distributed storage layer, so it handles very large databases and near-instantaneous restores.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="azdb-sql-03" number={3} question="How do you extract data from Azure SQL for

title: Azure Database Services
description: Azure database interview questions covering Azure SQL Database and Managed Instance, Cosmos DB APIs and consistency levels, Azure Database for MySQL and PostgreSQL, Database Migration Service, and extracting data for analytics.
content:
analytics without hurting production?" difficulty="hard" topic="Azure SQL">
1. **Read a secondary replica.** Business Critical and Hyperscale offer readable secondaries — connect with `ApplicationIntent=ReadOnly` and heavy reads land there instead of the primary.
2. **Change tracking or CDC.** SQL Server change data capture reads the log and exposes changes, so incremental extraction doesn't scan the table.
3. **Azure Synapse Link for SQL** — managed near-real-time replication into a Synapse dedicated pool with no pipeline to build. Least effort where it fits.
4. **Data Factory copy with partitioned reads** — parallel range-partitioned queries, run in a maintenance window.
5. **Export a `.bacpac` or restore a copy** for a full snapshot with zero load on the live database.

The bad answer i

title: Azure Database Services
description: Azure database interview questions covering Azure SQL Database and Managed Instance, Cosmos DB APIs and consistency levels, Azure Database for MySQL and PostgreSQL, Database Migration Service, and extracting data for analytics.
content:
s a nightly unpartitioned `SELECT *` against the primary during business hours. Naming the readable-secondary option is usually the quickest way to show you've done this for real.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="azdb-sql-04" number={4} question="How do backups and high availability work in Azure SQL?" difficulty="medium" topic="Azure SQL">
**Backups** are automatic: full, differential and log backups giving **point-in-time restore** within a retention window of 1–35 days, extendable to 10 years with long-term retention. Restores create a **new database**, so cutover requires a connection-string change.

**High availability** is built in and differs by tier. General Purpose separates compute from remote storage and fails over by attaching new compute. Business Critical maintains an **Alw

title: Azure Database Services
description: Azure database interview questions covering Azure SQL Database and Managed Instance, Cosmos DB APIs and consistency levels, Azure Database for MySQL and PostgreSQL, Database Migration Service, and extracting data for analytics.
content:
ays On availability group** with local SSD replicas, giving faster failover and a readable secondary. Hyperscale uses page servers with a separate compute layer.

**Active geo-replication** and **failover groups** add cross-region readable secondaries with automatic failover — the latter also moves the listener endpoint, so applications reconnect without configuration changes.

For a data platform, the readable secondary is the feature that matters most day to day.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

title: Azure Database Services
description: Azure database interview questions covering Azure SQL Database and Managed Instance, Cosmos DB APIs and consistency levels, Azure Database for MySQL and PostgreSQL, Database Migration Service, and extracting data for analytics.
content:
## Cosmos DB

<QuestionList topic="Cosmos DB" storagePrefix="azure-databases-cosmos">

<QuestionCard id="azdb-cos-01" number={1} question="What is Cosmos DB and what APIs does it offer?" difficulty="medium" topic="Cosmos DB">
A globally distributed, multi-model NoSQL database with single-digit millisecond latency, elastic scale, and SLA-backed availability, throughput, latency and consistency.

APIs:
- **NoSQL (Core)** — the native SQL-like query API over JSON documents. **Use this for new work**; it gets features first and has the best tooling.
- **MongoDB** — wire-protocol compatible, for migrating Mongo workloads.
- **Cassandra** — CQL compatible.
- **Gremlin** — graph.
- **Table** — the successor to Azure Table Storage.

The APIs are compatibility layers over one engine, so they share

title: Azure Database Services
description: Azure database interview questions covering Azure SQL Database and Managed Instance, Cosmos DB APIs and consistency levels, Azure Database for MySQL and PostgreSQL, Database Migration Service, and extracting data for analytics.
content:
partitioning, RUs and consistency. Feature support varies, and the non-native APIs lag — which is the caveat to give when someone proposes Cosmos as a drop-in Mongo replacement.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="azdb-cos-02" number={2} question="Explain the five consistency levels." difficulty="hard" topic="Cosmos DB">
From strongest to weakest, trading latency and availability for guarantees:

1. **Strong** — linearizable; reads always see the latest committed write. Cannot span regions with multi-region writes, and costs the most in latency and RUs.
2. **Bounded Staleness** — lags by at most K versions or T seconds, and preserves order. The practical choice when you need near-strong guarantees globally.
3. **Session** — **the default**. Guarantees read-your-own-writes, monotonic reads a

title: Azure Database Services
description: Azure database interview questions covering Azure SQL Database and Managed Instance, Cosmos DB APIs and consistency levels, Azure Database for MySQL and PostgreSQL, Database Migration Service, and extracting data for analytics.
content:
nd consistent prefix *within a client session*. Covers most application needs at low cost.
4. **Consistent Prefix** — you never see writes out of order, but may see them late.
5. **Eventual** — no ordering guarantee, lowest latency and RU cost.

The point that shows understanding: **reads at weaker consistency cost fewer RUs**, so consistency is a direct cost lever, not only a correctness one. Session is the right default; move to Strong only where a specific read genuinely requires it.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="azdb-cos-03" number={3} question="How does partitioning work, and what makes a good partition key?" difficulty="hard" topic="Cosmos DB">
Data is distributed by hashing the **partition key** into logical partitions, which map onto physical partitions. Each logical partition

title: Azure Database Services
description: Azure database interview questions covering Azure SQL Database and Managed Instance, Cosmos DB APIs and consistency levels, Azure Database for MySQL and PostgreSQL, Database Migration Service, and extracting data for analytics.
content:
is capped at **20 GB** and shares its physical partition's throughput.

A good partition key has:
- **High cardinality** — so data and requests spread evenly.
- **Even request distribution** — avoiding a "hot partition" where one value takes most of the traffic.
- **Alignment with your most common query filter**, so queries stay within a single partition rather than fanning out.

Classic bad choices: a `date` (all of today's writes hit one partition), a low-cardinality `status`, or a `tenant_id` where one tenant dwarfs the rest.

Two hard consequences: **the partition key cannot be changed** without migrating the container, and **cross-partition queries cost far more RUs** and scale poorly. Synthetic keys (`tenantId_yyyyMM`) are the standard mitigation for skew.
</QuestionCard>

<Question

title: Azure Database Services
description: Azure database interview questions covering Azure SQL Database and Managed Instance, Cosmos DB APIs and consistency levels, Azure Database for MySQL and PostgreSQL, Database Migration Service, and extracting data for analytics.
content:
Card id="azdb-cos-04" number={4} question="What are Request Units, and how do you control cost?" difficulty="medium" topic="Cosmos DB">
A **Request Unit** is the normalised currency of throughput, bundling CPU, memory and IOPS. A 1 KB point read costs about 1 RU; writes cost more; queries cost according to how much they scan.

Provisioning models:
- **Provisioned throughput** — a fixed RU/s, optionally **autoscale** between 10% and 100% of a maximum. Cheapest for steady load.
- **Serverless** — pay per RU consumed, no floor. Right for dev, spiky and low-volume workloads.

Cost control:
- **Design for point reads** — they're the cheapest operation by a wide margin.
- **Avoid cross-partition queries**, which multiply RU cost.
- **Tune the indexing policy** — Cosmos indexes every property by

title: Azure Database Services
description: Azure database interview questions covering Azure SQL Database and Managed Instance, Cosmos DB APIs and consistency levels, Azure Database for MySQL and PostgreSQL, Database Migration Service, and extracting data for analytics.
content:
default, and excluding unused paths cuts write RUs significantly. This is a big and frequently-missed win.
- **Weaker consistency** where acceptable, since reads cost fewer RUs.
- **TTL** to expire old documents automatically instead of storing them forever.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="azdb-cos-05" number={5} question="What is the change feed, and how do you use it for analytics?" difficulty="hard" topic="Cosmos DB">
A persistent, ordered log of **creates and updates** per partition, readable from any point — Cosmos's equivalent of a CDC stream.

Consume it with the **change feed processor** library, an **Azure Function trigger**, or Spark. Typical uses: materialising a denormalised view, pushing changes into a search index, triggering downstream work, and replicating into the lake.

title: Azure Database Services
description: Azure database interview questions covering Azure SQL Database and Managed Instance, Cosmos DB APIs and consistency levels, Azure Database for MySQL and PostgreSQL, Database Migration Service, and extracting data for analytics.
content:
Two limitations to state: it does **not** capture deletes (the workaround is a soft-delete flag plus TTL), and by default you see the **latest version** of a document rather than every intermediate change.

For analytics, the better answer is usually **Azure Synapse Link** — it maintains an automatically-synced **analytical store** in columnar format with a separate cost model, so Spark and SQL can query Cosmos data **without consuming operational RUs at all**. That's the clean separation of operational and analytical workloads, with no pipeline to build.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

content:
## MySQL & PostgreSQL

<QuestionList topic="MySQL & PostgreSQL" storagePrefix="azure-databases-oss">

<QuestionCard id="azdb-oss-01" number={1} question="What is Azure Database for PostgreSQL Flexible Server?" difficulty="medium" topic="PostgreSQL">
The current deployment model for managed PostgreSQL on Azure, replacing the older Single Server.

What it gives over Single Server: **zone-redundant HA** with a standby in another availability zone, **stop/start** to save cost on non-production, **custom maintenance windows**, better performance and cost control, **VNet integration** by default, and support for more extensions.

For data engineering it also supports **logical replication**, which is what makes **CDC via Debezium or Data Factory** possible — the key capability if you need near-r

title: Azure Database Services
description: Azure database interview questions covering Azure SQL Database and Managed Instance, Cosmos DB APIs and consistency levels, Azure Database for MySQL and PostgreSQL, Database Migration Service, and extracting data for analytics.
content:
eal-time replication into the lake.

**Azure Database for MySQL Flexible Server** is the equivalent for MySQL with the same shape of features.

Interview-relevant point: if someone describes Single Server, that's the legacy model — Microsoft has been retiring it, and Flexible Server is the answer for anything new.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="azdb-oss-02" number={2} question="How do you set up CDC from Azure PostgreSQL into a data lake?" difficulty="hard" topic="PostgreSQL">
1. **Enable logical replication** — set `wal_level = logical` on the server parameters and restart. Create a replication slot and publication for the tables you need.
2. **Choose a reader**:
   - **Debezium** on Kafka Connect (with Event Hubs or a Kafka cluster) — the most control and the standard open-source pat

title: Azure Database Services
description: Azure database interview questions covering Azure SQL Database and Managed Instance, Cosmos DB APIs and consistency levels, Azure Database for MySQL and PostgreSQL, Database Migration Service, and extracting data for analytics.
content:
h.
   - **Azure Data Factory / Synapse Pipelines** CDC connectors — managed, less flexible.
   - **Fivetran, Airbyte** or similar — fastest to stand up.
3. **Land changes append-only** in ADLS as a raw change log, ordered by log sequence number.
4. **Merge into a Delta table** on a schedule, using `MERGE` on the primary key to apply inserts, updates and deletes.

The operational care point: **replication slots retain WAL until consumed**, so a stalled or forgotten consumer will fill the server's disk and take the database down. Monitor slot lag and alarm on it — this is the failure that turns a nice CDC design into an outage.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="azdb-oss-03" number={3} question="When would you choose Azure Database for PostgreSQL over Azure SQL or Cosmos DB?" difficulty="med

ium" topic="PostgreSQL">
- **PostgreSQL** — when the team knows Postgres, when you want portability off Azure, or when you need its ecosystem: PostGIS for geospatial, `pgvector` for embeddings, TimescaleDB-style time-series patterns, and rich JSON support. Open source, no licence cost.
- **Azure SQL** — when you have existing SQL Server skills or code, need T-SQL features, or are migrating an existing estate. Azure Hybrid Benefit makes it cheaper if you already hold licences.
- **Cosmos DB** — when you need global distribution with local write latency, effectively unlimited horizontal scale, or a schema-flexible document model with known key-based access patterns.

The honest framing: for most new workloads a managed **PostgreSQL is the strongest default** — capable, portable, familiar and

description: Azure database interview questions covering Azure SQL Database and Managed Instance, Cosmos DB APIs and consistency levels, Azure Database for MySQL and PostgreSQL, Database Migration Service, and extracting data for analytics.

cheap. Cosmos should be justified by a specific need for global writes or extreme scale, not chosen by default because it's Azure-native.

content:
## Database Migration Service

<QuestionList topic="Database Migration Service" storagePrefix="azure-databases-dms">

<QuestionCard id="azdb-dms-01" number={1} question="What is Azure Database Migration Service?" difficulty="medium" topic="DMS">
A managed service for migrating databases to Azure, supporting **offline** (one-time, with downtime) and **online** (continuous sync, minimal downtime) migrations.

Common paths: SQL Server to Azure SQL Database or Managed Instance, Oracle to Azure SQL or PostgreSQL, MySQL and PostgreSQL to their Flexible Server equivalents, and MongoDB to Cosmos DB.

It pairs with the **Azure Migrate** family and, for heterogeneous work, schema conversion tooling that translates DDL and procedural code between engines and reports what it couldn't convert.

Like AW

title: Azure Database Services
description: Azure database interview questions covering Azure SQL Database and Managed Instance, Cosmos DB APIs and consistency levels, Azure Database for MySQL and PostgreSQL, Database Migration Service, and extracting data for analytics.
content:
S DMS, it moves **data** — you handle indexes, procedures, triggers, sequences and permissions separately, and the standard sequence is create schema without secondary indexes, load, then add indexes and re-enable triggers.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="azdb-dms-02" number={2} question="How would you migrate a large SQL Server database to Azure with minimal downtime?" difficulty="hard" topic="DMS">
1. **Assess** with Data Migration Assistant — compatibility issues, deprecated features, and a sizing recommendation. Choose Managed Instance if there are Agent jobs or cross-database dependencies.
2. **Provision** the target and create the schema, without secondary indexes, triggers disabled.
3. **Start an online migration** — full load followed by continuous sync of changes.
4. **Add inde

title: Azure Database Services
description: Azure database interview questions covering Azure SQL Database and Managed Instance, Cosmos DB APIs and consistency levels, Azure Database for MySQL and PostgreSQL, Database Migration Service, and extracting data for analytics.
content:
xes and constraints** once the initial load completes.
5. **Monitor sync lag** until it's near zero.
6. **Validate** — row counts, aggregate checksums on key columns, and reconciliation of a few business metrics. Check collation and datetime precision explicitly.
7. **Cut over** in a short window: quiesce writes, let sync drain, repoint connection strings, resume.
8. **Keep the source available** for rollback.

The value of the online model is that downtime becomes minutes rather than a weekend, because the bulk copy happened while the source stayed live.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

## Common Interview Scenarios

**"Cosmos DB costs are far higher than expected."** — check for cross-partition queries, the default indexing policy indexing every property (a big write-RU cost), consistency stronger than needed, provisioned throughput sized for peak rather than autoscaled, and missing TTL on data that should expire.

**"Your nightly extract from Azure SQL is timing out and slowing the app."** — move reads to a readable secondary with `ApplicationIntent=ReadOnly`, switch to CDC or change tracking for incremental loads, and partition the copy activity. Consider Synapse Link to remove the pipeline entirely.

**"Design a store for a global application with sub-10ms reads in every region."** — Cosmos DB with multi-region writes, session consistency, and a partition key aligned

title: Azure Database Services
description: Azure database interview questions covering Azure SQL Database and Managed Instance, Cosmos DB APIs and consistency levels, Azure Database for MySQL and PostgreSQL, Database Migration Service, and extracting data for analytics.
content:
to the dominant query filter. Address hot partitions and the fact that the key can't be changed later.

**"Why not just use Cosmos DB for everything?"** — RU cost for scan-heavy or ad-hoc query workloads, no joins, and a partition key you must get right up front. For relational access patterns, managed PostgreSQL or Azure SQL is cheaper and more flexible.

## Azure Storage: ADLS Gen2 and the Data Lake

**The single most important thing to know about Azure storage for data engineering is that ADLS Gen2 is Blob Storage with hierarchical namespace turned on — one checkbox that adds real directories, atomic renames and POSIX ACLs. Get that wrong and every Spark job pays for it in slow directory operations. Most Azure lake questions come back to that setting, the access tier you chose, and the redundancy you're paying for.**

## Key Concepts

An Azure **storage account** is the top-level container, and its settings — performance tier, redundancy, hierarchical namespace — are chosen at creation and mostly can't be changed later. Inside it live the four services: **Blob** (objects), **File** (SMB/NFS shares), **Queue** (simple messaging) and **Table** (key-value). For data engineering, Blob is the one that matters.

**ADLS Gen2** is not a separate product. It's a Blob Storage account with **hierarchical namespace (HNS)** enabled, which converts the flat key namespace into real directories. That single change gives atomic directory rename, efficient directory listing and delete, and POSIX-style ACLs — all of which analytics engines depend on, because a Spark job's commit protocol renames a temp directory to the fi

The cost model rests on three dials: **access tier** (hot, cool, cold, archive — cheaper storage in exchange for higher read cost and latency), **redundancy** (LRS through GZRS, roughly doubling in price as you add zones and regions), and **transactions**, which is why millions of tiny files cost more than a few large ones.

## Blob Storage & ADLS Gen2

<QuestionList topic="Blob Storage & ADLS Gen2" storagePrefix="azure-storage-blob">

<QuestionCard id="azst-blob-01" number={1} question="What is the difference between Blob Storage and ADLS Gen2?" difficulty="medium" topic="ADLS Gen2">
ADLS Gen2 **is** Blob Storage with **hierarchical namespace** enabled at account creation.

What HNS adds:
- **Real directories** — so renaming or deleting a folder is a single atomic metadata operation rather than N per-object operations.
- **POSIX-style ACLs** on files and directories, on top of Azure RBAC.
- **Better performance for analytics**, because engines list and manipulate directories constantly.
- **The `abfss://` driver**, which Spark, Databricks and Synapse use.

Without HNS, "folders" are just key prefixes, and a S

title: Azure Storage for Data Platforms
description: Azure storage interview questions covering Blob Storage and ADLS Gen2, access tiers and lifecycle management, redundancy options, Disk, File, Queue and Table storage, and designing a data lake on Azure.
content:
park job's commit — which renames a temporary output directory to its final name — becomes a copy-and-delete per file. On a job producing 50,000 files, that's the difference between seconds and many minutes.

**Always enable HNS for a data lake.** It can't be turned on after creation without migrating the account, which is the mistake to avoid.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="azst-blob-02" number={2} question="What are the blob types, and which do you use?" difficulty="easy" topic="Blob Storage">
- **Block blobs** — the default and the one you use. Composed of blocks, optimised for upload and streaming, up to ~190 TB. All lake data is block blobs.
- **Append blobs** — optimised for appends, used for logging scenarios where writers add to the end.
- **Page blobs** — random read/write, up

description: Azure storage interview questions covering Blob Storage and ADLS Gen2, access tiers and lifecycle management, redundancy options, Disk, File, Queue and Table storage, and designing a data lake on Azure.
content:
to 8 TB; the backing store for unmanaged VM disks. Effectively invisible now that managed disks are standard.

For data engineering, block blobs are the whole answer. The only time the distinction surfaces is diagnosing a tool that chose an append blob, or reading old documentation about page blobs and VHDs.

Large uploads use **blocks staged then committed**, which is Azure's equivalent of multipart upload — and, like S3, **uncommitted blocks are billed**, so failed uploads can accumulate hidden cost.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="azst-blob-03" number={3} question="How should you organise a data lake on ADLS Gen2?" difficulty="medium" topic="Data Lake">
A common, defensible layout:

```
container: raw/        landing zone, immutable, as-received
container: enriched/   cleaned, confo

```

with paths inside each like `source/entity/year=2026/month=01/day=15/`.

Decisions worth defending:
- **Separate containers per zone**, so RBAC and lifecycle policies apply cleanly per zone rather than per path.
- **Date partitioning** in Hive style (`year=/month=/day=`) so engines can prune partitions.
- **Parquet or Delta**, never CSV, for anything queried.
- **File sizes of 128 MB–1 GB** — the small-files problem is as real here as on S3.
- **A separate storage account per environment**, since many settings are account-level and blast radius should be bounded.

Some teams use separate accounts per zone to get independent throughput limits, which matters at very high scale.
</QuestionCard>

A standard general-purpose v2 account has account-level ceilings — on the order of **20,000 requests per second** and tens of Gbps of egress, varying by region and configuration.

That matters because a large Spark cluster can saturate an account, and the symptom is **HTTP 503 throttling** appearing as intermittent task failures rather than an obvious quota error.

Mitigations:
- **Spread across multiple storage accounts** — by zone, by source system, or by environment.
- **Fewer, larger files** — the same request budget goes much further.
- **Premium block blob accounts** for latency-sensitive or very high transaction rate workloads (SSD-backed, higher

- **Retry with exponential backoff**, which the Azure SDKs do by default.

The general shape: throughput problems on ADLS are usually **transaction-count** problems, and the fix is file layout before it is infrastructure.
</QuestionCard>

## Access Tiers & Lifecycle

<QuestionList topic="Access Tiers & Lifecycle" storagePrefix="azure-storage-tiers">

<QuestionCard id="azst-tier-01" number={1} question="What are the Azure blob access tiers?" difficulty="medium" topic="Access Tiers">
| Tier | Storage cost | Access cost | Min duration | Retrieval |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Hot** | highest | lowest | none | immediate |
| **Cool** | lower | higher | 30 days | immediate |
| **Cold** | lower still | higher still | 90 days | immediate |
| **Archive** | lowest | highest | 180 days | **hours** (rehydration) |

Hot, Cool and Cold are all **online** — accessible immediately. **Archive is offline**: a blob must be **rehydrated** to Hot or Cool before it can be read, taking up to 15 hours at standard priority or under an hour at high pr

The two traps: **early deletion is billed for the full minimum duration**, so moving data to Archive and deleting it a month later costs more than leaving it; and archived data **cannot be queried in place**, so anything Synapse or Databricks might need must stay online.
</QuestionCard>

- **Snapshots** — manual, read-only point-in-time copies of a blob. You create them explicitly; you're billed for the differences.
- **Versioning** — automatic: every overwrite creates a new version, with the previous one retained. No action needed by the writer.

The cost warning is the same one as S3: **versioning plus a pipeline that rewrites the same partition daily silently multiplies storage**. Always pair it with a lifecycle rule expiring old versions.

For a curated zone, versioning plus soft delete is a reasonable default. For a large raw zone, versioning can be expensive and the data is usually immutable anyway, so soft delete alone is often the better trade.

## Redundancy & Availability

<QuestionList topic="Redundancy & Availability" storagePrefix="azure-storage-redundancy">

<QuestionCard id="azst-red-01" number={1} question="Explain LRS, ZRS, GRS and GZRS." difficulty="medium" topic="Redundancy">
| Option | Copies | Protects against |
|---|---|---|
| **LRS** | 3, one datacentre | disk and rack failure |
| **ZRS** | 3, across availability zones | datacentre failure |
| **GRS** | 3 local + 3 in a paired region | regional outage |
| **GZRS** | 3 zonal + 3 in paired region | zone and regional outage |
| **RA-GRS / RA-GZRS** | as above, **secondary readable** | adds read access during an outage |

Cost roughly doubles from LRS to ZRS to geo-redundant options.

Two important details. **Geo-replication is asynchronous**, so a regional failover can

title: Azure Storage for Data Platforms
description: Azure storage interview questions covering Blob Storage and ADLS Gen2, access tiers and lifecycle management, redundancy options, Disk, File, Queue and Table storage, and designing a data lake on Azure.
content:
lose recent writes — the RPO is typically minutes, not zero. And without the **RA-** prefix, the secondary copy is **not readable**; it only exists for failover, which surprises people who assume GRS gives them a read replica.

For a data lake, **ZRS is a common sweet spot**: zone resilience without paying for cross-region replication of data you can usually re-ingest.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="azst-red-02" number={2} question="How do you choose redundancy for a data lake?" difficulty="medium" topic="Redundancy">
Choose per zone, based on **whether the data is reproducible**.

- **Raw** — this is often the only copy of what a source system sent, so losing it is unrecoverable. **ZRS or GZRS** is justified.
- **Enriched / staging** — derived and rebuildable from raw. **LRS** is fin

title: Azure Storage for Data Platforms
description: Azure storage interview questions covering Blob Storage and ADLS Gen2, access tiers and lifecycle management, redundancy options, Disk, File, Queue and Table storage, and designing a data lake on Azure.
content:
e, and the saving is real at scale.
- **Curated** — expensive to rebuild and directly consumed. **ZRS**, or GZRS if a regional outage would breach an SLA.

The question that decides it: *if this region disappeared for a day, what would it cost us?* If the answer is "we'd re-ingest from source when it comes back", geo-redundancy is insurance you don't need.

Note that redundancy is an **account-level** setting, which is a practical argument for separate storage accounts per zone.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

## Security & Access Control

<QuestionList topic="Security & Access Control" storagePrefix="azure-storage-security">

<QuestionCard id="azst-sec-01" number={1} question="How do you control access to ADLS Gen2?" difficulty="hard" topic="Security">
Three mechanisms, and understanding how they combine is the interview point.

- **Azure RBAC** — role assignments at subscription, resource group, storage account or **container** scope. Roles like `Storage Blob Data Reader` and `Storage Blob Data Contributor`. Coarse-grained but simple, and the primary mechanism.
- **POSIX ACLs** — available only with hierarchical namespace, set per directory and file, with read/write/execute for owner, group and other, plus named principals. Fine-grained.
- **SAS tokens** — time-limited signed URLs for delegate

title: Azure Storage for Data Platforms
description: Azure storage interview questions covering Blob Storage and ADLS Gen2, access tiers and lifecycle management, redundancy options, Disk, File, Queue and Table storage, and designing a data lake on Azure.
content:
d access, especially to external parties.

They combine: **RBAC is evaluated first, and if it grants access, ACLs aren't checked.** So a broad `Storage Blob Data Contributor` at account scope silently overrides every carefully-set ACL underneath — a very common misconfiguration.

The workable pattern: RBAC at **container** level for broad roles, ACLs for fine-grained directory permissions, and **Entra ID groups** rather than individual principals so ACLs stay manageable.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="azst-sec-02" number={2} question="What are SAS tokens, and what are the types?" difficulty="medium" topic="Security">
A **Shared Access Signature** is a signed URL granting time-limited, scoped access without sharing account keys.

- **User delegation SAS** — signed with **Entra ID creden

title: Azure Storage for Data Platforms
description: Azure storage interview questions covering Blob Storage and ADLS Gen2, access tiers and lifecycle management, redundancy options, Disk, File, Queue and Table storage, and designing a data lake on Azure.
content:
tials**. The recommended type: it's tied to an identity, auditable, and revocable by removing the identity's permissions.
- **Service SAS** — signed with the account key, scoped to one service.
- **Account SAS** — signed with the account key, broader scope.

The problem with key-signed SAS tokens is that revoking one means **rotating the account key**, which breaks everything else using it. That's why user delegation SAS is preferred.

Best practice: short expiry, minimum permissions, restrict to an IP range where possible, require HTTPS, and **disable account key access entirely** (`allowSharedKeyAccess: false`) so only Entra ID authentication is possible.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="azst-sec-03" number={3} question="How do you secure network access to storage?" difficulty="medium"

topic="Security">
Storage accounts are internet-reachable by default, which is rarely what you want for a lake.

- **Private Endpoint** — a private IP for the storage account inside your VNet, so traffic never traverses the internet. The strongest option, and the standard for production data platforms.
- **Service Endpoint** — restricts the account to specific VNet subnets over the Azure backbone. Simpler than Private Endpoint, but the account still has a public IP.
- **Firewall rules** — allow specific IP ranges, plus "allow trusted Azure services" for platform integrations.
- **Disable public network access** entirely once private connectivity is in place.

The operational gotcha: locking down networking frequently breaks things you forgot depended on public access — Data Factory integr

</QuestionCard>

## Disk, File, Queue & Table Storage

<QuestionList topic="Disk, File, Queue & Table Storage" storagePrefix="azure-storage-other">

<QuestionCard id="azst-oth-01" number={1} question="What is Azure Files, and when would you use it over Blob?" difficulty="medium" topic="Azure Files">
Managed file shares accessible over **SMB** and **NFS**, mountable by VMs, AKS pods and on-premises machines simultaneously.

Use it when software genuinely requires a filesystem with shared write access: a lift-and-shift application expecting a network share, a shared configuration directory, or a tool that can't speak object storage.

Tiers run from transaction-optimised through hot and cool (standard, HDD-backed) to **premium** (SSD-backed, provisioned IOPS).

For data engineering it's rarely the right answe

title: Azure Storage for Data Platforms
description: Azure storage interview questions covering Blob Storage and ADLS Gen2, access tiers and lifecycle management, redundancy options, Disk, File, Queue and Table storage, and designing a data lake on Azure.
content:
r — it costs substantially more per GB than Blob and the analytics ecosystem is built around ADLS. **Azure File Sync** is the one genuinely interesting feature, caching a share on-premises while the authoritative copy lives in Azure, which suits hybrid file-server consolidation.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="azst-oth-02" number={2} question="What are Azure Queue Storage and Table Storage, and are they still relevant?" difficulty="medium" topic="Queue & Table">
**Queue Storage** — a simple, cheap message queue with at-least-once delivery, a visibility timeout, and up to 64 KB messages. It lacks topics, sessions, dead-lettering, ordering and transactions. **Service Bus** is the richer alternative, and the right choice for anything beyond basic decoupling.

**Table Storage** — a cheap No

title: Azure Storage for Data Platforms
description: Azure storage interview questions covering Blob Storage and ADLS Gen2, access tiers and lifecycle management, redundancy options, Disk, File, Queue and Table storage, and designing a data lake on Azure.
content:
SQL key-value store keyed by partition key and row key. Very low cost, very limited: no secondary indexes, no complex queries, limited transactions.

Relevance today: both are **legacy-adjacent**. Table Storage's API lives on as the **Cosmos DB Table API**, which gives the same programming model with global distribution and better performance — and Cosmos DB is where new work should go.

Know them for existing systems and cost-sensitive simple cases; don't propose them for a new data platform.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="azst-oth-03" number={3} question="What are the Azure disk types and where does the temp disk fit?" difficulty="medium" topic="Disk Storage">
**Managed disks** attach to a VM and persist independently of it:
- **Standard HDD / Standard SSD** — dev, test, light produc

title: Azure Storage for Data Platforms
description: Azure storage interview questions covering Blob Storage and ADLS Gen2, access tiers and lifecycle management, redundancy options, Disk, File, Queue and Table storage, and designing a data lake on Azure.
content:
tion.
- **Premium SSD** — production; performance tied to disk size.
- **Premium SSD v2** — IOPS and throughput provisioned **independently of capacity**. The current default.
- **Ultra Disk** — sub-millisecond latency, very high IOPS, for demanding databases.

Separately, many VM sizes include a **temporary disk** (the `d` in the size name) which is local, fast and **ephemeral** — wiped on deallocation or host migration.

The data engineering point: **Spark shuffle and scratch belong on the temp disk**, not on premium managed disks. Choosing a VM series without a local temp disk for a shuffle-heavy job pushes that traffic onto network storage and turns a CPU-bound job into an I/O-bound one.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

## Common Interview Scenarios

**"Spark jobs writing to ADLS are slow at the commit stage."** — most likely hierarchical namespace is off, so the commit's directory rename is a per-file copy-and-delete. Confirm HNS, and check output file counts, since committing 100,000 tiny files is slow regardless.

**"Design storage for a new Azure data lake."** — ADLS Gen2 with HNS enabled, separate containers for raw/enriched/curated, Hive-style date partitioning, Delta or Parquet, lifecycle policies per zone, ZRS for raw and curated with LRS for reproducible intermediates, Private Endpoint, and Entra ID groups over RBAC at container scope with ACLs beneath.

**"You're getting intermittent 503s from storage under load."** — account-level throttling. Reduce transaction count with larger files, spread a

content:
cross multiple storage accounts, consider a premium block blob account, and confirm the SDK's retry policy is active.

**"Someone set an ACL but the user can still read everything."** — RBAC is evaluated first and short-circuits ACL evaluation. A broad data-plane role at account or container scope overrides the ACLs entirely.

## Key Concepts

Azure's classic PaaS model organizes an application as a **cloud service** made up of one or more **roles** — a **Web Role** (a managed IIS web server for front-end applications), a **Worker Role** (for asynchronous, long-running background processing), or a **VM Role** (a fully customizable Windows Server image for workloads that need OS-level control). The **Fabric Controller** provisions and manages the underlying hardware, while the **compute emulator** lets you test locally before deploying. A cloud service is packaged as a **.cspkg** (service package, built by `cspack`) plus a **.csdef** (service definition — the role model) and **.cscfg** (service configuration — instance counts and settings), then deployed to a **staging** or **production** environment, which can b

title: Azure
description: Azure interview questions covering cloud service models, compute roles, autoscaling, blob/table/queue storage, deployment, and diagnostics for engineers.
content:
e promoted via a **VIP swap** with no redeployment. Reliability and elasticity come from running **multiple role instances** (Azure's SLA requires at least two per role) and from **autoscaling**, which adds or removes instances based on load. For data, Azure offers **Blob storage** (Block Blobs for streaming/large objects, Page Blobs for random read/write), **Table storage** (a schemaless NoSQL store partitioned for fast, atomic access), and two queuing options — simple **Azure Queues** and the richer **Service Bus Queues**, which add publish/subscribe and dead-lettering.

### Storage: Blobs, Tables & Queues

<QuestionList topic="Azure Storage" storagePrefix="azure-storage">

<QuestionCard id="azure-storage-01" number={27} question="What is Blob storage?" difficulty="easy" topic="Storage">
BLOB stands for Binary Large Object — a file of any type and size. Azure Blob Storage offers two types of blobs: Block Blobs and Page Blobs. Blobs are addressable using a URL of the form `https://<account>.blob.core.windows.net/<container>/<blob>`.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="azure-storage-02" number={28} question="What is the difference between Block Blobs and Page Blobs?" difficulty="medium" topic="Storage">
Block blobs are made up of blocks, each identified by a block ID. You create or modify a block blob by uploading a set of blocks and committing them by their

title: Azure
description: Azure interview questions covering cloud service models, compute roles, autoscaling, blob/table/queue storage, deployment, and diagnostics for engineers.
content:
block IDs — if the blob is no more than 64 MB, you can also upload it in its entirety with a single Put Blob operation. Each block can be up to 4 MB, and the maximum size for a block blob (in the 2009-09-19 version) is 200 GB, or up to 50,000 blocks.

Page blobs are a collection of pages. A page is a range of data identified by its offset from the start of the blob; you create a page blob by calling Put Blob and specifying its maximum size, up to 1 TB, and a single page write can be up to 1 TB.

Use block blobs for streaming scenarios like video. Use page blobs when the application needs random read/write access.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="azure-storage-03" number={29} question="What is the difference between Windows Azure Queues and Windows Azure Service Bus Queues?" difficulty="m

Windows Azure supports two queue mechanisms:
- **Windows Azure Queues** — part of the Windows Azure storage infrastructure, featuring a simple REST-based Get/Put/Peek interface that provides reliable, persistent messaging within and between services.
- **Service Bus Queues** — part of a broader Windows Azure messaging infrastructure that supports queuing as well as publish/subscribe, web service remoting, and integration patterns.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="azure-storage-04" number={30} question="What is a Deadletter Queue?" difficulty="medium" topic="Storage">
Messages are placed on the deadletter sub-queue by the messaging system in these scenarios:
- when a message expires and deadlettering for expired messages is set to true on a queue or subscription
-

when the max delivery count for a message is exceeded on a queue or subscription
- when a filter evaluation exception occurs in a subscription and deadlettering on filter evaluation exceptions is enabled
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="azure-storage-05" number={31} question="What is Table Storage in Windows Azure?" difficulty="medium" topic="Storage">
Windows Azure Table storage stores large amounts of structured data. It's a NoSQL datastore that accepts authenticated calls from inside and outside the Windows Azure cloud, and it's ideal for storing structured, non-relational data.
- **Table** — a collection of entities. Tables don't enforce a schema on entities, so a single table can contain entities with different sets of properties. An account can contain many tables.
- **Entity** — a

title: Azure
description: Azure interview questions covering cloud service models, compute roles, autoscaling, blob/table/queue storage, deployment, and diagnostics for engineers.
content:
set of properties, similar to a database row. An entity can be up to 1 MB in size.
- **Properties** — name/value pairs. Each entity can include up to 252 properties, plus 3 system properties that specify a partition key, a row key, and a timestamp.

Entities with the same partition key can be queried more quickly, and inserted/updated in atomic operations. An entity's row key is its unique identifier within a partition.
</QuestionCard>

## GCP Analytics: Dataflow, Dataproc and the Streaming Stack

**GCP's distinctive contribution to data engineering is Dataflow — a managed runner for Apache Beam, where the same code handles batch and streaming with genuine event-time semantics. Interviewers use it to test whether you understand windowing, watermarks and late data, which are the concepts that separate someone who has built a streaming pipeline from someone who has read about one.**

content:
## Key Concepts

The GCP streaming stack is **Pub/Sub → Dataflow → BigQuery/GCS**, and each piece has a clear role. Pub/Sub is a globally available, auto-scaling message bus with no partitions to size. Dataflow runs Apache Beam pipelines with autoscaling and dynamic work rebalancing. BigQuery serves the results.

**Apache Beam** is the model worth understanding properly. Its central idea is that batch is a special case of streaming — a bounded `PCollection` rather than an unbounded one — so the same transforms apply to both. That's why Beam separates four questions explicitly: *what* is computed (transforms), *where in event time* (windowing), *when* results are emitted (triggers), and *how* refinements relate to earlier output (accumulation mode).

The concept that generates the hardest q

title: GCP Analytics & Data Processing
description: Google Cloud analytics interview questions covering Dataflow and Apache Beam, Dataproc, Pub/Sub, Dataprep, Cloud Composer, Dataplex and building streaming and batch pipelines on GCP.
content:
uestions is **event time versus processing time**. Events arrive late and out of order; a **watermark** is the system's estimate of how far event time has progressed, and it decides when a window can be closed. Getting this right is the difference between correct aggregates and quietly dropped data.

content:
## Pub/Sub

<QuestionList topic="Pub/Sub" storagePrefix="gcp-analytics-pubsub">

<QuestionCard id="gcpan-ps-01" number={1} question="What is Pub/Sub and how does it differ from Kafka or Kinesis?" difficulty="medium" topic="Pub/Sub">
A globally distributed messaging service: publishers send to a **topic**, and each **subscription** delivers an independent copy of the stream to its consumers.

What's distinctive compared with Kafka and Kinesis:
- **No partitions or shards to provision.** It scales automatically, so there's no resharding operation and no hot-shard problem from a bad partition key. That's a genuine operational simplification.
- **Global by default** — a topic isn't bound to a region.
- **Push or pull** delivery; push means Pub/Sub calls your endpoint.
- **At-least-once** deliv

title: GCP Analytics & Data Processing
description: Google Cloud analytics interview questions covering Dataflow and Apache Beam, Dataproc, Pub/Sub, Dataprep, Cloud Composer, Dataplex and building streaming and batch pipelines on GCP.
content:
ery by default, with **exactly-once** available within a region.

The trade-off: because there are no partitions, **ordering is not guaranteed by default**. You opt in with an **ordering key**, which gives ordering per key at some throughput cost.

**Pub/Sub Lite** exists as a cheaper, zonal, partitioned alternative — closer to Kafka's model — for very high, predictable volume.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="gcpan-ps-02" number={2} question="How do subscriptions, acknowledgement and retention work?" difficulty="medium" topic="Pub/Sub">
Each **subscription** tracks its own position, so multiple consumers get the full stream independently.

A message is delivered, and the subscriber must **acknowledge** it within the **ack deadline** (default 10 seconds, extendable to 10 minutes, and cli

title: GCP Analytics & Data Processing
description: Google Cloud analytics interview questions covering Dataflow and Apache Beam, Dataproc, Pub/Sub, Dataprep, Cloud Composer, Dataplex and building streaming and batch pipelines on GCP.
content:
ents extend it automatically while processing). Unacknowledged messages are redelivered — which is why **at-least-once means duplicates happen** and consumers must be idempotent.

**Retention** is 7 days by default (up to 31), and **seek** lets you replay from a timestamp or a snapshot — the recovery mechanism after a consumer bug.

**Dead-letter topics** move messages aside after N delivery attempts, so a poison message can't retry forever. As with SQS, alarm on the dead-letter topic; one nobody watches is just a slower way to lose data.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="gcpan-ps-03" number={3} question="What are Pub/Sub subscription types, and what is a BigQuery subscription?" difficulty="medium" topic="Pub/Sub">
- **Pull** — the subscriber requests messages. Best for high throughput an

title: GCP Analytics & Data Processing
description: Google Cloud analytics interview questions covering Dataflow and Apache Beam, Dataproc, Pub/Sub, Dataprep, Cloud Composer, Dataplex and building streaming and batch pipelines on GCP.
content:
d back-pressure control.
- **Push** — Pub/Sub POSTs to an HTTPS endpoint (typically Cloud Run or a Function). Simpler, with less control over rate.
- **BigQuery subscription** — writes messages **directly into a BigQuery table**, no Dataflow job at all.
- **Cloud Storage subscription** — writes batched messages straight to GCS files.

The last two are worth naming because they eliminate a whole pipeline. If all you need is "land these events in BigQuery", a BigQuery subscription does it with no code, no Dataflow cost and no job to operate.

Use Dataflow when you need **transformation, enrichment, windowed aggregation or joins** in flight. Use a direct subscription when you just need the raw events landed — which is more often than people assume.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>
