## Dataflow & Apache Beam

<QuestionList topic="Dataflow & Apache Beam" storagePrefix="gcp-analytics-dataflow">

<QuestionCard id="gcpan-df-01" number={1} question="What is Apache Beam, and what is the Dataflow runner?" difficulty="medium" topic="Dataflow">
**Beam** is a unified programming model for batch and streaming. You write a pipeline once, in Java, Python or Go, and run it on any **runner** — Dataflow, Flink, Spark or the local direct runner.

Core abstractions:
- **Pipeline** — the whole graph.
- **PCollection** — a distributed dataset, **bounded** (batch) or **unbounded** (stream).
- **PTransform** — an operation: `ParDo` (per element), `GroupByKey`, `Combine`, `Window`.
- **I/O connectors** — sources and sinks.

**Dataflow** is Google's fully managed runner. It provisions worker

title: GCP Analytics & Data Processing
description: Google Cloud analytics interview questions covering Dataflow and Apache Beam, Dataproc, Pub/Sub, Dataprep, Cloud Composer, Dataplex and building streaming and batch pipelines on GCP.
content:
s, autoscales them, and — distinctively — performs **dynamic work rebalancing**, redistributing work from straggler workers at runtime rather than waiting for them. That directly addresses skew, which on Spark you usually handle manually.

The portability claim is real but caveated: connector support and performance vary between runners, so a Dataflow pipeline isn't always a drop-in Flink pipeline.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="gcpan-df-02" number={2} question="What makes Dataflow different from Spark?" difficulty="hard" topic="Dataflow">
- **Genuinely unified batch and streaming.** Beam's model treats batch as bounded streaming, so the same code runs both. Spark's Structured Streaming is micro-batch and the APIs diverge more than the marketing suggests.
- **Event-time semantics are f

title: GCP Analytics & Data Processing
description: Google Cloud analytics interview questions covering Dataflow and Apache Beam, Dataproc, Pub/Sub, Dataprep, Cloud Composer, Dataplex and building streaming and batch pipelines on GCP.
content:
irst class** — windows, watermarks, triggers and allowed lateness are core model concepts rather than bolt-ons.
- **Dynamic work rebalancing** — Dataflow reassigns work from slow workers mid-job, mitigating skew automatically.
- **Autoscaling** including **Streaming Engine**, which moves shuffle and state off worker VMs into a managed service, so workers scale without rebalancing state.
- **No cluster** — you submit a job, not a cluster configuration.

Where Spark wins: a far larger ecosystem, SQL and DataFrame APIs many teams already know, better interactive and notebook workflows, and deep integration with Delta and Iceberg.

The practical guidance: **Dataflow for streaming with real event-time requirements; Dataproc/Spark when the team knows Spark or you're porting existing jobs.**
</Qu

<QuestionCard id="gcpan-df-03" number={3} question="What are Dataflow templates and Flex Templates?" difficulty="medium" topic="Dataflow">
A **template** packages a pipeline so it can be launched without the development environment — from the console, `gcloud`, a REST call, Cloud Scheduler or Composer, with runtime parameters.

- **Classic templates** — the pipeline graph is staged at build time, so parameters are limited to what was declared.
- **Flex Templates** — the pipeline is packaged as a **container image** and constructed at launch, so parameters can change the graph itself. More flexible, and the current recommendation.

**Google-provided templates** cover many common jobs outright — Pub/Sub to BigQuery, GCS to BigQuery, JDBC to BigQuery, Pub/Sub to GCS. For a standa

title: GCP Analytics & Data Processing
description: Google Cloud analytics interview questions covering Dataflow and Apache Beam, Dataproc, Pub/Sub, Dataprep, Cloud Composer, Dataplex and building streaming and batch pipelines on GCP.
content:
rd ingestion path, you may not need to write a pipeline at all.

The operational value is separating **who builds** the pipeline from **who runs** it: analysts or an orchestrator can launch parameterised jobs without touching code or a build toolchain.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="gcpan-df-04" number={4} question="How do you optimise a Dataflow job?" difficulty="hard" topic="Dataflow">
- **Enable Streaming Engine** (streaming) or **Dataflow Shuffle** (batch) so shuffle and state move off worker VMs. This usually improves autoscaling and reduces cost, and should be the default.
- **Use `Combine` rather than `GroupByKey`** where possible — combiners aggregate partially before shuffling, cutting data movement dramatically.
- **Watch for hot keys** — Dataflow logs them. Fix with a two-st

title: GCP Analytics & Data Processing
description: Google Cloud analytics interview questions covering Dataflow and Apache Beam, Dataproc, Pub/Sub, Dataprep, Cloud Composer, Dataplex and building streaming and batch pipelines on GCP.
content:
age combine or key salting.
- **Right-size workers** — machine type and `maxNumWorkers`; too few caps throughput, too many wastes money.
- **Use FlexRS** for non-urgent batch, mixing Spot and standard VMs at a discount with delayed scheduling.
- **Avoid per-element external calls** — batch them in `startBundle`/`finishBundle`, or use side inputs for lookups.
- **Fuse-break deliberately** when fusion creates an unbalanced stage; a reshuffle can help.

The distinctive one is **hot key detection** — Dataflow tells you, which is more than most engines do.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

title: GCP Analytics & Data Processing
description: Google Cloud analytics interview questions covering Dataflow and Apache Beam, Dataproc, Pub/Sub, Dataprep, Cloud Composer, Dataplex and building streaming and batch pipelines on GCP.
content:
## Streaming Semantics

<QuestionList topic="Streaming Semantics" storagePrefix="gcp-analytics-streaming-semantics">

<QuestionCard id="gcpan-sem-01" number={1} question="What is the difference between event time and processing time?" difficulty="hard" topic="Streaming">
**Event time** is when the event actually happened, carried in the record. **Processing time** is when your pipeline saw it.

They diverge constantly — network delays, mobile devices offline for hours, upstream retries, a consumer catching up after an outage. A phone that was in flight mode uploads events with yesterday's event timestamps today.

Why it matters: aggregating by processing time gives **wrong answers that look plausible**. Yesterday's late-arriving events land in today's bucket, so both days are wrong, and no

title: GCP Analytics & Data Processing
description: Google Cloud analytics interview questions covering Dataflow and Apache Beam, Dataproc, Pub/Sub, Dataprep, Cloud Composer, Dataplex and building streaming and batch pipelines on GCP.
content:
thing errors.

Correct streaming aggregates almost always use **event time**, which requires the system to decide when a time window is "complete" despite not knowing what might still arrive. That's what watermarks exist for, and it's the reason event-time processing is harder than it first appears.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="gcpan-sem-02" number={2} question="What are windows, watermarks and triggers?" difficulty="hard" topic="Streaming">
- **Windows** divide an unbounded stream into finite chunks by event time:
  - **Fixed (tumbling)** — non-overlapping, e.g. every 5 minutes.
  - **Sliding (hopping)** — overlapping, e.g. a 1-hour window every 5 minutes.
  - **Session** — grouped by activity with a gap duration, for user sessions.
  - **Global** — one window, used with custom trig

title: GCP Analytics & Data Processing
description: Google Cloud analytics interview questions covering Dataflow and Apache Beam, Dataproc, Pub/Sub, Dataprep, Cloud Composer, Dataplex and building streaming and batch pipelines on GCP.
content:
gers.
- **Watermark** — the system's estimate that all events up to time T have arrived. When it passes a window's end, the window is considered complete and results are emitted.
- **Trigger** — when to actually emit. Beyond the default (fire at the watermark), you can fire **early** for speculative partial results and **late** when stragglers arrive.
- **Accumulation mode** — whether a late firing **replaces** the previous result (accumulating) or is a **delta** (discarding).

Together these answer *what*, *where*, *when* and *how* — the four questions Beam's model is built around, and naming them that way is the strong answer.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="gcpan-sem-03" number={3} question="How do you handle late-arriving data?" difficulty="hard" topic="Streaming">
Explicitly, becau

title: GCP Analytics & Data Processing
description: Google Cloud analytics interview questions covering Dataflow and Apache Beam, Dataproc, Pub/Sub, Dataprep, Cloud Composer, Dataplex and building streaming and batch pipelines on GCP.
content:
se the default is to **drop it silently**.

```python
beam.WindowInto(
    beam.window.FixedWindows(60),
    trigger=AfterWatermark(late=AfterCount(1)),
    allowed_lateness=Duration(seconds=3600),
    accumulation_mode=AccumulationMode.ACCUMULATING,
)
```

The choices:
- **`allowed_lateness`** — how long after the watermark passes to keep the window's state open. Longer means more correctness and more state to hold.
- **Late triggers** — emit an updated result when a straggler arrives.
- **Accumulation mode** — accumulating gives a corrected total the sink can overwrite; discarding gives a delta the sink must add.
- **A side output for dropped data**, so events beyond allowed lateness are captured rather than lost — worth doing for auditability.

The design tension worth articulating: **l

title: GCP Analytics & Data Processing
description: Google Cloud analytics interview questions covering Dataflow and Apache Beam, Dataproc, Pub/Sub, Dataprep, Cloud Composer, Dataplex and building streaming and batch pipelines on GCP.
content:
atency, correctness and cost**. Emitting early gives low latency but provisional numbers; long allowed lateness gives correctness at the cost of state and memory. There's no universally right answer, only one you've chosen deliberately.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="gcpan-sem-04" number={4} question="How do you achieve exactly-once processing in Dataflow?" difficulty="hard" topic="Streaming">
Dataflow provides **exactly-once semantics within the pipeline**: it deduplicates on record IDs from Pub/Sub, checkpoints state, and makes shuffle deterministic, so a retried bundle doesn't double-count.

The hard part is the **sink**, and that's what the question is really about:
- **BigQuery via the Storage Write API** supports exactly-once with stream offsets.
- **Files in GCS** are written to

title: GCP Analytics & Data Processing
description: Google Cloud analytics interview questions covering Dataflow and Apache Beam, Dataproc, Pub/Sub, Dataprep, Cloud Composer, Dataplex and building streaming and batch pipelines on GCP.
content:
temp locations and renamed atomically on commit.
- **An arbitrary external system** — a REST API, a non-transactional database — cannot be made exactly-once by Dataflow. You need an **idempotent write**: a deterministic key with an upsert, or a dedup table.

The point to make: **end-to-end exactly-once requires source, processing and sink to cooperate.** Dataflow handles the middle; you must design the sink. And a non-deterministic `DoFn` (using random values or wall-clock time) breaks the guarantee, because retried work produces different output.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

content:
## Dataproc

<QuestionList topic="Dataproc" storagePrefix="gcp-analytics-dataproc">

<QuestionCard id="gcpan-dp-01" number={1} question="What is Dataproc and when would you choose it over Dataflow?" difficulty="medium" topic="Dataproc">
Managed **Spark and Hadoop** — clusters that start in about 90 seconds, with Spark, Hive, Presto/Trino, Flink, HBase and Jupyter available.

Choose **Dataproc** when:
- You have **existing Spark or Hadoop code** to migrate. Lift-and-shift is straightforward.
- The team **knows Spark** and would be learning Beam from scratch.
- You need ecosystem components — Hive metastore, HBase, Trino.
- You want **notebooks and interactive** development.
- Deep **Delta or Iceberg** integration matters.

Choose **Dataflow** when the workload is streaming with real event-t

title: GCP Analytics & Data Processing
description: Google Cloud analytics interview questions covering Dataflow and Apache Beam, Dataproc, Pub/Sub, Dataprep, Cloud Composer, Dataplex and building streaming and batch pipelines on GCP.
content:
ime requirements, or when you want no cluster at all.

The pragmatic reality: many GCP teams use **Dataproc for batch Spark** (because that's what they already have) and **Dataflow for streaming** (because Beam's model is genuinely better for it).
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="gcpan-dp-02" number={2} question="How do you configure Dataproc cost-effectively?" difficulty="medium" topic="Dataproc">
- **Ephemeral clusters** — create per job, delete on completion. `--max-idle` auto-deletes idle clusters, which prevents the classic "cluster left running all weekend" bill.
- **Spot secondary workers** — secondary workers are compute-only (no HDFS), so losing one costs a recomputed partition. 60–91% off.
- **Dataproc Serverless** — no cluster at all for batch Spark; often the best default now

title: GCP Analytics & Data Processing
description: Google Cloud analytics interview questions covering Dataflow and Apache Beam, Dataproc, Pub/Sub, Dataprep, Cloud Composer, Dataplex and building streaming and batch pipelines on GCP.
content:
.
- **Store data in GCS, not HDFS** — decouples storage from compute so clusters can be disposable, and it's cheaper and more durable.
- **Local SSDs** for shuffle on shuffle-heavy jobs.
- **Right-size machine types** — highmem for Spark, custom shapes to avoid paying for unused memory.
- **Autoscaling policies** for variable workloads.

The single most impactful pair is **ephemeral clusters with auto-delete** plus **Spot secondary workers** — together they typically cut Dataproc cost by more than half.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="gcpan-dp-03" number={3} question="What is Dataproc Metastore and why does it matter?" difficulty="medium" topic="Dataproc">
A managed **Hive Metastore** service, decoupled from any individual cluster.

Why it matters: with an ephemeral-cluster architecture

title: GCP Analytics & Data Processing
description: Google Cloud analytics interview questions covering Dataflow and Apache Beam, Dataproc, Pub/Sub, Dataprep, Cloud Composer, Dataplex and building streaming and batch pipelines on GCP.
content:
, table definitions must survive cluster deletion. A metastore living on the cluster disappears with it, so every job would have to re-register its tables.

Dataproc Metastore gives a **persistent, shared catalog** that multiple clusters, Dataproc Serverless jobs and BigQuery (via BigLake) can all use — the same architectural role AWS's Glue Data Catalog plays.

It also integrates with **Dataplex** for broader governance and discovery.

The design point: an ephemeral-compute architecture needs a **persistent metadata layer**, otherwise the disposability you wanted becomes an operational problem. That's the reasoning worth stating rather than just naming the service.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

## Orchestration & Governance

<QuestionList topic="Orchestration & Governance" storagePrefix="gcp-analytics-orchestration">

<QuestionCard id="gcpan-orch-01" number={1} question="What is Cloud Composer, and how does it compare to Workflows?" difficulty="medium" topic="Orchestration">
**Cloud Composer** is managed **Apache Airflow**, running on GKE. You get standard Airflow — Python DAGs, the provider ecosystem, backfills, the familiar UI — with Google managing the infrastructure.

**Workflows** is a lightweight serverless orchestrator defined in YAML, chaining API calls and Google Cloud services with retries and error handling. It costs per step, scales to zero, and has no environment to run.

Choose **Composer** for data pipelines: many interdependent tasks, backfills, catchup, dataset d

title: GCP Analytics & Data Processing
description: Google Cloud analytics interview questions covering Dataflow and Apache Beam, Dataproc, Pub/Sub, Dataprep, Cloud Composer, Dataplex and building streaming and batch pipelines on GCP.
content:
ependencies, and Python-defined logic. Choose **Workflows** for simple service orchestration — call an API, wait, call another — where a whole Airflow environment is disproportionate.

The honest caveat: **Composer runs continuously and isn't cheap**, so a dev environment left running is real money. Workflows' scale-to-zero is its main advantage for lightweight cases.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="gcpan-orch-02" number={2} question="What is Dataplex and what problem does it solve?" difficulty="medium" topic="Governance">
A **data governance and management** layer over data spread across GCS buckets and BigQuery datasets. You define **lakes** and **zones** (raw and curated), attach assets, and Dataplex handles discovery, cataloguing, quality and access.

What it gives:
- **Automatic di

title: GCP Analytics & Data Processing
description: Google Cloud analytics interview questions covering Dataflow and Apache Beam, Dataproc, Pub/Sub, Dataprep, Cloud Composer, Dataplex and building streaming and batch pipelines on GCP.
content:
scovery** — scans assets, infers schemas and registers tables so they're queryable from BigQuery without manual definition.
- **A unified catalog** with metadata search and business annotations.
- **Data quality** — rule-based checks (AutoDQ) with scheduled scans and results as metrics.
- **Data profiling** — automatic column statistics.
- **Governance** — consistent policies across storage and warehouse, with lineage.

The problem it addresses is a lake sprawling across many buckets, projects and datasets where nobody knows what exists, whether it's trustworthy, or who owns it. It's GCP's answer to Lake Formation plus a catalog, and it now underpins the unified Dataplex Universal Catalog.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="gcpan-orch-03" number={3} question="What is Dataprep, and where do

es it fit?" difficulty="easy" topic="Dataprep">
A **visual data preparation** tool (built by Trifacta, now Alteryx) for exploring, cleaning and transforming data without code. You see a sample, get profiling and suggested transformations, build a "recipe" interactively, and it compiles to a **Dataflow** job for execution at scale.

Its audience is **analysts and data scientists** rather than engineers — people who need to clean a dataset but won't write Beam or Spark.

Where it fits: exploratory cleaning, one-off preparation, and letting domain experts do their own wrangling instead of queueing for engineering time.

Where it doesn't: production pipelines that need version control, code review, testing and CI. A visual recipe is hard to diff and review, so the mature pattern is to **protot

description: Google Cloud analytics interview questions covering Dataflow and Apache Beam, Dataproc, Pub/Sub, Dataprep, Cloud Composer, Dataplex and building streaming and batch pipelines on GCP.

ype in Dataprep and reimplement in code** once the logic stabilises. Being clear about that boundary is the answer an interviewer wants.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="gcpan-orch-04" number={4} question="How would you design a streaming pipeline on GCP end to end?" difficulty="hard" topic="Architecture">
```
Producers → Pub/Sub topic
              ├→ BigQuery subscription  → raw events table (no code)
              └→ Dataflow (Beam)
                    ├→ BigQuery (windowed aggregates, Storage Write API)
                    ├→ Bigtable (low-latency serving state)
                    └→ GCS (raw archive, Parquet)
```

Design points worth defending:
- **A raw landing path independent of processing** — a BigQuery or GCS subscription means the raw stream is preserved even if the Dataflow

title: GCP Analytics & Data Processing
description: Google Cloud analytics interview questions covering Dataflow and Apache Beam, Dataproc, Pub/Sub, Dataprep, Cloud Composer, Dataplex and building streaming and batch pipelines on GCP.
content:
job has a bug, so you can reprocess. This is the most valuable single decision.
- **Event-time windowing with explicit allowed lateness**, plus a side output for events beyond it.
- **Dead-letter topic** on the subscription, alarmed.
- **Idempotent sinks** — deterministic keys so replays don't duplicate.
- **Streaming Engine** enabled for better autoscaling.
- **Orchestration** with Composer for the batch reconciliation job that corrects the streaming aggregates.

That last point — a batch job reconciling streaming output — is the practical acknowledgement that streaming aggregates drift, and it's what a production design usually includes.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

## Common Interview Scenarios

**"Your streaming aggregates don't match the batch numbers."** — almost always late data dropped beyond allowed lateness, or processing-time windows used where event-time was needed. Check the dropped-data side output, and reconcile with a scheduled batch job.

**"Design ingestion for 100k events/second on GCP."** — Pub/Sub (no shard sizing needed, which is the advantage to name), Dataflow with Streaming Engine for processing, BigQuery for analytics, Bigtable if there's a low-latency serving requirement, plus a raw archive subscription for reprocessing.

**"Dataflow or Dataproc for this batch job?"** — Dataproc if it's existing Spark or the team knows Spark; Dataflow if it shares logic with a streaming pipeline or needs Beam's model. For pure batch Spark, Dat

title: GCP Analytics & Data Processing
description: Google Cloud analytics interview questions covering Dataflow and Apache Beam, Dataproc, Pub/Sub, Dataprep, Cloud Composer, Dataplex and building streaming and batch pipelines on GCP.
content:
aproc Serverless is usually the cheapest and simplest.

**"How do you avoid reprocessing everything after a bug in your streaming job?"** — that's why the raw landing path exists. Keep the unprocessed stream in GCS or a raw BigQuery table, then replay from Pub/Sub seek or from the archive rather than needing the original events again.

## Key Concepts

GCP comparisons resolve on three axes more often than not. **Access shape** — scan-and-aggregate versus point lookup versus range scan by key; object versus block versus file. **Latency requirement** — milliseconds for serving, seconds for interactive analytics, minutes for batch. And **who operates it** — fully serverless, managed cluster, or your own on GKE.

Two GCP-specific facts short-circuit many comparisons. **BigQuery removes the compute question entirely** for analytical SQL, so the first question to ask about any transformation is whether it can just be SQL in BigQuery — it frequently can, and that beats every cluster option on cost and simplicity. And **co-location is a hard requirement**: BigQuery can't load from a bucket in another region, and cross-region rea

ds cost money everywhere, so region choice constrains architecture rather than merely influencing it.

The third thing to hold: several choices are **immutable after creation** — a bucket's location type, a Bigtable row key, a Spanner primary key. So the honest comparison isn't only "which is better" but "which mistake can I recover from."

|---|---|---|---|---|

| Access | HTTPS, anywhere | one VM (or read-only many) | one VM | many clients |

| Latency | tens of ms | sub-ms | microseconds | low ms |

or VM boot volumes and database files. **Local SSD** for Spark shuffle and scratch, because it's fast and the data is disposable. **Filestore** only when software genuinely needs a POSIX share.

The data engineering shorthand: **GCS for data, Local SSD for shuffle, PD for the OS, Filestore rarely.**

<QuestionCard id="gcpcmp-st-02" number={2} question="Regional vs dual-region vs multi-region buckets?" difficulty="medium" topic="Storage">

- **Dual-region** — a chosen pair of regions with geo-redundancy and **strong consistency across both**, plus optional turbo replication for a 15-minute RPO. Resilience without a separate replication setup.

The constraint that usually decides it: **BigQuery load jobs require the bucket and dataset to be in compatible locations**, and Dataproc pays egress and latency reading across regions. So co-location with compute is a requirement, not a preference.

**Location type is immutable** — changing it means creating a new bucket and copying, which at petabyte scale is a project. Choose deliberately.

## Database Comparisons

<QuestionList topic="Database Comparisons" storagePrefix="gcp-comparisons-databases">

<QuestionCard id="gcpcmp-db-01" number={1} question="BigQuery vs Bigtable — how do you choose?" difficulty="hard" topic="Databases">
Despite the similar names, they solve opposite problems.

| | **BigQuery** | **Bigtable** |
|---|---|---|
| Purpose | analytics (OLAP) | operational key-value (NoSQL) |
| Query | SQL, joins, aggregations | key lookup and range scan only |
| Latency | seconds | **single-digit milliseconds** |
| Writes | batch or streaming append | very high-throughput random writes |
| Indexes | none needed (columnar scan) | **row key only** |
| Scaling | serverless | add nodes |

**BigQuery** when you're scanning and aggregating large volumes with SQL — dashboards,

title: GCP Service Comparisons
description: Head-to-head Google Cloud service comparisons for data engineers — BigQuery vs Bigtable, GCS vs Persistent Disk vs Local SSD vs Filestore, Dataflow vs Dataproc, Pub/Sub vs Kafka, and Cloud SQL vs Spanner vs Firestore.
content:
reporting, ad-hoc analysis. **Bigtable** when you need millisecond lookups by key at high throughput — serving user profiles, IoT time-series, ML feature serving.

They're complementary rather than alternatives: a common architecture writes the same stream to both, Bigtable for serving and BigQuery for analysis. The mistake is using Bigtable for analytics (no joins, no aggregation) or BigQuery for point lookups (seconds, not milliseconds).
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="gcpcmp-db-02" number={2} question="Cloud SQL vs Spanner vs Firestore vs Bigtable?" difficulty="hard" topic="Databases">
- **Cloud SQL** — managed MySQL/PostgreSQL/SQL Server. Relational, ACID, familiar, cheap. **The default** for transactional workloads, and sufficient far longer than people expect.
- **Spanner** — rela

## GCP Compute: Under the Managed Data Services

**On Google Cloud, most data engineering compute is consumed through Dataflow, Dataproc and BigQuery — all of which provision Compute Engine underneath. The compute questions in a data interview are therefore really about the economics: Spot VMs on Dataproc workers, sustained-use discounts you get automatically, and why a Cloud Function's timeout keeps failing your ingestion job.**

## Key Concepts

GCP's resource hierarchy is **organisation → folder → project → resource**, and the **project** is the key unit: it scopes billing, quotas, IAM and networking. Data platforms typically use a project per environment, which is how you get hard isolation between dev and production and clean cost attribution.

Compute spans the usual spectrum — **Compute Engine** VMs, **GKE** for containers, **Cloud Run** for serverless containers, **Cloud Functions** for event-driven code — but two GCP-specific pricing behaviours change the calculus. **Sustained use discounts** apply automatically when a VM runs a large share of the month, with no commitment required. And **custom machine types** let you specify exact vCPU and memory rather than picking from fixed shapes, which avoids paying

title: GCP Compute for Data Workloads

content:
for memory you don't need.

The lever that matters most for batch data work is **Spot VMs** (formerly preemptible). At 60–91% off, with a 30-second termination notice, they're the standard configuration for Dataproc secondary workers and any restartable processing — and using them is often the single largest cost reduction available.

## Compute Engine

<QuestionList topic="Compute Engine" storagePrefix="gcp-compute-gce">

<QuestionCard id="gcpcm-gce-01" number={1} question="What are the Compute Engine machine families?" difficulty="easy" topic="Compute Engine">
Families are named by purpose and generation — `n2-standard-8`, `c3-highmem-16`:

- **E2** — cost-optimised, general purpose. Cheapest, with no sustained-use discount.
- **N2 / N2D / N4** — balanced general purpose. The common default.
- **C3 / C4** — compute optimised, highest per-core performance. For CPU-bound transforms.
- **M1 / M2 / M3** — memory optimised, up to several TB. For very large in-memory workloads.
- **A2 / A3 / G2** — GPU, for ML.
- **T2D / C4A** — Arm-based (Tau, Axion), strong price-performance if your dependencies build for Arm.

Within a f

**Custom machine types** let you specify exact vCPU and memory, which is genuinely useful for right-sizing a Dataproc worker rather than rounding up to the next predefined shape.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="gcpcm-gce-02" number={2} question="What are the GCP pricing models for compute?" difficulty="medium" topic="Compute Engine">
- **On-demand** — per-second billing after a one-minute minimum.
- **Sustained use discounts** — **automatic**, up to 30% off, applied when an instance runs a significant portion of the month. No commitment, no action required. This is distinctive to GCP.
- **Committed use discounts (

- **Spot VMs** — 60–91% off surplus capacity, terminated with **30 seconds' notice** and always within 24 hours. Formerly "preemptible", which had a hard 24-hour cap; Spot removes that but can still be reclaimed.

For a data platform: **CUDs for the steady baseline**, **Spot for Dataproc secondary workers and any restartable batch**, and sustained-use discounts arriving automatically on whatever else runs continuously.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="gcpcm-gce-03" number={3} question="How do you use Spot VMs safely for data processing?" difficulty="hard" topic="Compute Engine">

- **Handle the shutdown signal** — GCP sends an ACPI G2 soft-off; a handler has ~30 seconds to drain and checkpoint. That's much tighter than AWS's two minutes.
- **Diversify machine types** where the service allows, reducing the chance of simultaneous reclamation.
- **Checkpoint long jobs** so a restart doesn't lose hours.
- **Never run stateful services on Spot** — a database, a Kafka broker or an HDFS NameNode is the wrong workload.

<QuestionCard id="gcpcm-gce-04" number={4} question="What are the persistent disk and local SSD options?" difficulty="medium" topic="Compute Engine">
**Persistent Disk** is network-attached and survives instance deletion:
- **pd-standard** — HDD, cheap sequential throughput.
- **pd-balanced** — SSD, the sensible default.
- **pd-ssd** — higher IOPS for demanding databases.
- **pd-extreme / Hyperdisk** — provisioned IOPS independent of size; Hyperdisk is the newer generation and the current recommendation for high-performance needs.

Note that PD performance **scales with size** on most types, so a small disk is also a slow disk — a common cause of unexpectedly poor I/O.

**Local SSD** is physically attached NVMe: very fast, and **ephemeral** — lost when the instance

## Google Kubernetes Engine

<QuestionList topic="Google Kubernetes Engine" storagePrefix="gcp-compute-gke">

<QuestionCard id="gcpcm-gke-01" number={1} question="What is GKE, and what is the difference between Standard and Autopilot?" difficulty="medium" topic="GKE">
Managed Kubernetes from the company that created Kubernetes, generally the most mature managed offering.

- **Standard** — you manage node pools: machine types, sizes, autoscaling, Spot. Full control, and you pay for nodes whether pods use them or not.
- **Autopilot** — Google manages nodes entirely. You deploy pods and **pay per pod's requested CPU, memory and storage**. No node sizing, no bin-packing to worry about, stronger security defaults.

Autopilot is the better default for most workloads because it removes an entire

operational domain and eliminates paying for unused node capacity. Standard wins when you need specific machine types, GPUs with particular configurations, privileged workloads, or DaemonSets that Autopilot restricts.

For data platforms, GKE hosts Spark on Kubernetes, Airflow (Cloud Composer itself runs on GKE), Flink and Trino.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="gcpcm-gke-02" number={2} question="How do pods on GKE authenticate to BigQuery or Cloud Storage?" difficulty="medium" topic="GKE">
**Workload Identity Federation** — the recommended approach. A Kubernetes service account is bound to a Google service account, and pods receive short-lived credentials automatically through the metadata server. No keys stored anywhere.

gcloud iam service-accounts add-iam-policy-binding \

## Cloud Run & Cloud Functions

<QuestionList topic="Cloud Run & Cloud Functions" storagePrefix="gcp-compute-serverless">

<QuestionCard id="gcpcm-run-01" number={1} question="What is Cloud Run and how does it differ from Cloud Functions?" difficulty="medium" topic="Cloud Run">
**Cloud Run** runs **containers** serverlessly — any language, any dependency, scaling from zero to thousands of instances, billed per request and per resource-second. It comes in two forms: **services** (request-driven, HTTP or event) and **jobs** (run to completion, for batch tasks).

**Cloud Functions** runs a **single function** with a managed runtime and event bindings. Its 2nd generation is in fact built on Cloud Run underneath.

Differences that matter: Cloud Run takes **any container**, so heavy dependencies

title: GCP Compute for Data Workloads
description: Google Cloud compute interview questions covering Compute Engine machine families and pricing, Google Kubernetes Engine, Cloud Run and Cloud Functions — and choosing compute for Dataproc, Dataflow and BigQuery workloads.
content:
(pandas, PyArrow, a JDBC driver) are straightforward; it supports **concurrency**, with one instance handling multiple simultaneous requests, which is dramatically cheaper for I/O-bound work; and **Cloud Run jobs have no request timeout**, running for hours.

The practical guidance: **Cloud Run is the better default now**, with Cloud Functions reserved for genuinely tiny event handlers where its bindings save real work.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="gcpcm-run-02" number={2} question="What limits should you know for Cloud Functions and Cloud Run?" difficulty="medium" topic="Serverless">
**Cloud Functions (2nd gen)** — up to 60 minutes for event-driven functions, 60 minutes for HTTP, up to 32 GB memory. 1st gen was capped at 9 minutes, which is what older documentation and many people'

title: GCP Compute for Data Workloads
description: Google Cloud compute interview questions covering Compute Engine machine families and pricing, Google Kubernetes Engine, Cloud Run and Cloud Functions — and choosing compute for Dataproc, Dataflow and BigQuery workloads.
content:
s memory reflect.

**Cloud Run services** — request timeout up to 60 minutes, up to 32 GB memory and 8 vCPU, and **concurrency up to 1,000 requests per instance**.

**Cloud Run jobs** — no request-timeout constraint; a task can run up to 24 hours, with array-style parallel tasks.

The concurrency setting is the one that's most under-appreciated: for a function waiting on a database or an API, setting concurrency to 80 rather than 1 means one instance serves 80 requests, cutting cost by a large factor. It's the single biggest Cloud Run cost lever, and defaults are conservative.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="gcpcm-run-03" number={3} question="How do serverless services integrate with GCP data services?" difficulty="medium" topic="Serverless">
Mostly through **Eventarc** and **Pub/Sub**:

- **Cloud Storage events** — an object lands, Eventarc triggers Cloud Run or a Function. The canonical ingestion trigger.
- **Pub/Sub push or pull** — Cloud Run can receive push subscriptions; a job can pull.
- **BigQuery** — a Function or Cloud Run service triggered on completion of a load job, or invoked as a **remote function** inside a query.
- **Cloud Scheduler** — cron triggering a Cloud Run job or Function.
- **Workflows** — orchestrating several services with retries and error handling.
- **Firestore and Cloud SQL triggers** via Eventarc.

The pattern worth naming for data engineering: use serverless as the **trigger and glue** — receive the event, validate, then start a Dataflow or Dataproc job — rather than doing heavy transformation in the function itself.
</QuestionCard>

</Q

content:
## GCP Databases: BigQuery and the Stores Around It

**BigQuery dominates this topic and deserves most of the preparation — it's the service that defines data engineering on Google Cloud, and its separation of storage from compute, on-demand pricing per byte scanned, and partitioning model generate more interview questions than everything else combined. Bigtable, Spanner and Cloud SQL matter for knowing when a workload doesn't belong in BigQuery.**

title: GCP Database Services
description: Google Cloud database interview questions covering BigQuery architecture, partitioning, clustering and cost control, Cloud Bigtable schema design, Cloud SQL, and Cloud Spanner's globally distributed relational model.
content:

title: GCP Database Services
description: Google Cloud database interview questions covering BigQuery architecture, partitioning, clustering and cost control, Cloud Bigtable schema design, Cloud SQL, and Cloud Spanner's globally distributed relational model.
content:
## Key Concepts

BigQuery's defining property is that **storage and compute are completely separate**. Data sits in Colossus, Google's distributed filesystem, in a columnar format called Capacitor; query execution happens on Dremel, a multi-tenant serverless engine that borrows slots from a shared pool. You never provision a cluster, and storage costs the same whether you query it daily or never.

That architecture produces the cost model everything else follows from: **on-demand queries are billed per byte scanned**. Partitioning, clustering and column selection aren't performance optimisations in the usual sense — they're direct cost reductions, and the difference between a query costing cents and one costing hundreds of dollars.

The other services exist for access patterns BigQuery han

title: GCP Database Services
description: Google Cloud database interview questions covering BigQuery architecture, partitioning, clustering and cost control, Cloud Bigtable schema design, Cloud SQL, and Cloud Spanner's globally distributed relational model.
content:
dles badly. **Bigtable** for very high-throughput key-based reads and writes at low latency. **Cloud SQL** for ordinary transactional relational work. **Spanner** for relational semantics with horizontal scale and global consistency. Knowing when to leave BigQuery — and being able to say *why* — is what these questions test.

---

title: GCP Database Services
description: Google Cloud database interview questions covering BigQuery architecture, partitioning, clustering and cost control, Cloud Bigtable schema design, Cloud SQL, and Cloud Spanner's globally distributed relational model.
content:
## BigQuery Architecture

<QuestionList topic="BigQuery Architecture" storagePrefix="gcp-databases-bq-architecture">

<QuestionCard id="gcpdb-bq-01" number={1} question="How does BigQuery's architecture work?" difficulty="hard" topic="BigQuery">
Four layers, connected by a very fast network:

- **Colossus** — Google's distributed filesystem, holding data in **Capacitor**, a columnar format with per-column compression and statistics.
- **Dremel** — the execution engine. A query becomes a tree of stages; leaf nodes read columns in parallel and results aggregate up through mixers.
- **Jupiter** — the petabit-scale network that makes separating storage from compute viable, because moving data to compute isn't the bottleneck it would otherwise be.
- **Borg** — the cluster manager allocating **s

title: GCP Database Services
description: Google Cloud database interview questions covering BigQuery architecture, partitioning, clustering and cost control, Cloud Bigtable schema design, Cloud SQL, and Cloud Spanner's globally distributed relational model.
content:
lots**, the unit of compute.

The consequences worth naming: **storage and compute scale independently**, so you pay to store cheaply and pay separately for queries; there are **no indexes** in the traditional sense, because it scans columns very fast in parallel; and since compute is a shared multi-tenant pool, a query can recruit thousands of slots momentarily without any provisioning.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="gcpdb-bq-02" number={2} question="What are the BigQuery pricing models?" difficulty="medium" topic="BigQuery">
**Storage** — priced per GB per month, with **active** (modified in the last 90 days) and **long-term** (untouched for 90+ days, roughly half price) tiers applied automatically per partition. There's also physical (compressed) versus logical billing, and physical

title: GCP Database Services
description: Google Cloud database interview questions covering BigQuery architecture, partitioning, clustering and cost control, Cloud Bigtable schema design, Cloud SQL, and Cloud Spanner's globally distributed relational model.
content:
is usually cheaper for well-compressed data.

**Compute** — two models:
- **On-demand** — billed **per TB scanned**, with a 10 MB minimum per query. Simple, no commitment, and the default.
- **Capacity (Editions)** — buy **slots** (Standard, Enterprise, Enterprise Plus) with autoscaling and optional 1- or 3-year commitments. Predictable spend, and immune to a single bad query costing hundreds of dollars.

The crossover: **on-demand suits variable, moderate usage; slots suit steady, heavy usage** — and slots also cap the blast radius of an accidental full-table scan, which is often the real reason teams switch.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="gcpdb-bq-03" number={3} question="What is the difference between native tables, external tables and BigLake?" difficulty="medium" topic="BigQuery"

title: GCP Database Services
description: Google Cloud database interview questions covering BigQuery architecture, partitioning, clustering and cost control, Cloud Bigtable schema design, Cloud SQL, and Cloud Spanner's globally distributed relational model.
content:
>
- **Native tables** — data loaded into BigQuery's managed Capacitor storage. Fastest queries, full feature support (DML, streaming, time travel, clustering).
- **External tables** — BigQuery queries files in GCS (or Sheets, Bigtable) in place. No duplication, no load step, but slower, with no clustering and limited optimisation.
- **BigLake tables** — external tables plus **fine-grained security** (row and column level) and **metadata caching**, which brings performance much closer to native. They support open formats including **Iceberg**.

The practical architecture: **load curated tables natively** for the serving layer where performance and concurrency matter, and use **BigLake** over lake data you want queryable without duplicating or losing the open format.

BigLake is the GCP lake

title: GCP Database Services
description: Google Cloud database interview questions covering BigQuery architecture, partitioning, clustering and cost control, Cloud Bigtable schema design, Cloud SQL, and Cloud Spanner's globally distributed relational model.
content:
house answer — it's what lets you keep data in Iceberg on GCS while still getting BigQuery's governance and near-native speed.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="gcpdb-bq-04" number={4} question="How do you load and stream data into BigQuery?" difficulty="medium" topic="BigQuery">
**Batch loading** — from GCS via `bq load` or the API, in Parquet, Avro, ORC, JSON or CSV. **Free** when loading from GCS in the same region, which is a genuine architectural incentive to co-locate.

**Streaming**:
- **Storage Write API** — the current recommendation. Higher throughput, lower cost, exactly-once semantics with stream offsets, and immediately queryable data.
- **Legacy `insertAll` streaming** — older, more expensive, and superseded.

**Managed alternatives**:
- **Datastream** — serverless CDC from

title: GCP Database Services
description: Google Cloud database interview questions covering BigQuery architecture, partitioning, clustering and cost control, Cloud Bigtable schema design, Cloud SQL, and Cloud Spanner's globally distributed relational model.
content:
Oracle, MySQL and PostgreSQL straight into BigQuery.
- **BigQuery Data Transfer Service** — scheduled loads from SaaS sources and other warehouses.
- **Dataflow** — for anything needing transformation in flight.

The point to make: prefer **batch loads from GCS** where latency allows, because they're free and simpler; use the Storage Write API when you genuinely need sub-minute freshness.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

title: GCP Database Services
description: Google Cloud database interview questions covering BigQuery architecture, partitioning, clustering and cost control, Cloud Bigtable schema design, Cloud SQL, and Cloud Spanner's globally distributed relational model.
content:
## BigQuery Performance & Cost

<QuestionList topic="BigQuery Performance & Cost" storagePrefix="gcp-databases-bq-performance">

<QuestionCard id="gcpdb-perf-01" number={1} question="What is partitioning in BigQuery, and how do you use it?" difficulty="hard" topic="BigQuery">
Splitting a table into segments so a query with a filter on the partition column reads only the relevant segments — directly reducing bytes scanned and therefore cost.

Three types:
- **Time-unit** — by a `DATE`, `TIMESTAMP` or `DATETIME` column, at hourly, daily, monthly or yearly granularity. The common case.
- **Ingestion time** — by when the row arrived, exposed as the `_PARTITIONTIME` pseudo-column.
- **Integer range** — by buckets of an integer column.

```sql
CREATE TABLE orders
PARTITION BY DATE(order_ts)
CLUS

title: GCP Database Services
description: Google Cloud database interview questions covering BigQuery architecture, partitioning, clustering and cost control, Cloud Bigtable schema design, Cloud SQL, and Cloud Spanner's globally distributed relational model.
content:
TER BY customer_id
OPTIONS (require_partition_filter = TRUE)
AS SELECT ...
```

**`require_partition_filter = TRUE` is the single most valuable setting** — it rejects any query that doesn't filter on the partition column, which prevents accidental full-table scans entirely. Set it on every large table.

The limit to know: **4,000 partitions per table**, so daily partitioning covers about 11 years.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="gcpdb-perf-02" number={2} question="What is clustering, and how does it differ from partitioning?" difficulty="hard" topic="BigQuery">
**Clustering** sorts data within each partition by up to four columns, so BigQuery can skip blocks that can't match a filter — the same idea as zone maps.

Differences from partitioning:
- Partitioning gives **hard pruning** with

title: GCP Database Services
description: Google Cloud database interview questions covering BigQuery architecture, partitioning, clustering and cost control, Cloud Bigtable schema design, Cloud SQL, and Cloud Spanner's globally distributed relational model.
content:
a known cost before the query runs; clustering gives **best-effort block skipping**, so the byte estimate in the UI doesn't reflect it (the actual bill does).
- Partitioning suits **low-cardinality** time columns; clustering suits **high-cardinality** columns like `customer_id` or `product_id`.
- Clustering has **no partition-count limit**, and BigQuery re-clusters automatically in the background at no charge.

Use them together: **partition by date, cluster by the high-cardinality columns you filter or join on most.** Column order in the `CLUSTER BY` matters — filters must use a prefix of the clustering columns to benefit.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="gcpdb-perf-03" number={3} question="How do you reduce BigQuery query cost?" difficulty="hard" topic="BigQuery">
Since on-demand bill

title: GCP Database Services
description: Google Cloud database interview questions covering BigQuery architecture, partitioning, clustering and cost control, Cloud Bigtable schema design, Cloud SQL, and Cloud Spanner's globally distributed relational model.
content:
ing is per byte scanned, every item reduces bytes read:

1. **Never `SELECT *`.** BigQuery is columnar — selecting 3 of 100 columns reads 3% of the data. This is the biggest and easiest win.
2. **Partition and filter on the partition column**, with `require_partition_filter` enforcing it.
3. **Cluster** on high-cardinality filter and join columns.
4. **`LIMIT` does not reduce cost** — the scan still happens. A very common misconception.
5. **Materialised views** for repeated aggregations; BigQuery maintains them incrementally and rewrites queries to use them automatically.
6. **Use the query validator** — it shows bytes to be scanned *before* you run it.
7. **Set custom quotas** per project or user so nobody can scan 50 TB by accident.
8. **Preview data with the table preview**, which is f

title: GCP Database Services
description: Google Cloud database interview questions covering BigQuery architecture, partitioning, clustering and cost control, Cloud Bigtable schema design, Cloud SQL, and Cloud Spanner's globally distributed relational model.
content:
ree, rather than `SELECT * LIMIT 10`.
9. **Consider capacity pricing** if usage is steady — it also caps runaway cost.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="gcpdb-perf-04" number={4} question="How do you diagnose a slow BigQuery query?" difficulty="hard" topic="BigQuery">
Start with the **execution details** in the console, which shows per-stage timing, rows in and out, and slot time.

What to look for:
- **Data skew** — one stage where the max worker time far exceeds the average. Usually a join key with a dominant value or many nulls. Filter nulls before joining, or salt the key.
- **Excessive shuffle** — large "bytes shuffled" between stages, typically from joining on a non-clustered high-cardinality column.
- **Repeated `SELECT *` in CTEs**, pulling columns nothing needs.
- **Cross joins o

title: GCP Database Services
description: Google Cloud database interview questions covering BigQuery architecture, partitioning, clustering and cost control, Cloud Bigtable schema design, Cloud SQL, and Cloud Spanner's globally distributed relational model.
content:
r unintended fan-out**, visible as an output row count far exceeding input.
- **Slot contention** — on capacity pricing, the query is queueing rather than running slowly.
- **`JOIN` ordering** — put the largest table first; BigQuery generally handles this, but it matters in complex queries.

The `INFORMATION_SCHEMA.JOBS` views let you find the most expensive and slowest queries across a project, which is where a cost investigation should start.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

title: GCP Database Services
description: Google Cloud database interview questions covering BigQuery architecture, partitioning, clustering and cost control, Cloud Bigtable schema design, Cloud SQL, and Cloud Spanner's globally distributed relational model.
content:
## Cloud Bigtable

<QuestionList topic="Cloud Bigtable" storagePrefix="gcp-databases-bigtable">

<QuestionCard id="gcpdb-bt-01" number={1} question="What is Cloud Bigtable and when should you use it?" difficulty="medium" topic="Bigtable">
A managed **wide-column NoSQL** database — the same system behind Search, Maps and Gmail, and the design HBase was modelled on.

It delivers **single-digit millisecond latency** at very high throughput, scaling linearly by adding nodes, with no downtime for resizing.

Use it for:
- **Time-series and IoT** telemetry at massive write rates.
- **User or device profiles** looked up by key.
- **Real-time serving** of features for ML.
- **Very high write throughput** — millions of operations per second.

Don't use it for ad-hoc queries, joins or aggregations —

title: GCP Database Services
description: Google Cloud database interview questions covering BigQuery architecture, partitioning, clustering and cost control, Cloud Bigtable schema design, Cloud SQL, and Cloud Spanner's globally distributed relational model.
content:
it has **no SQL, no joins, no secondary indexes**, and only one index: the row key. If your access pattern isn't "look up by key or scan a key range", it's the wrong store, and BigQuery is usually the right one.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="gcpdb-bt-02" number={2} question="How does row key design work in Bigtable?" difficulty="hard" topic="Bigtable">
The row key is the **only** index, and rows are stored **lexicographically sorted** by it. That single fact determines everything.

Good keys:
- **Enable your read pattern as a range scan** — `deviceId#reversedTimestamp` lets you fetch a device's most recent readings contiguously.
- **Distribute writes evenly** across the key space.

The classic failure is a **hotspot**: keys prefixed with a timestamp mean every write at a given moment

title: GCP Database Services
description: Google Cloud database interview questions covering BigQuery architecture, partitioning, clustering and cost control, Cloud Bigtable schema design, Cloud SQL, and Cloud Spanner's globally distributed relational model.
content:
targets the same tablet, so one node saturates while the rest idle. Sequential IDs do the same.

Mitigations: **field promotion** (put a high-cardinality attribute first), **salting** (prefix with a hash bucket), and **reversed timestamps** so recent data sorts first without concentrating writes.

Two hard constraints: the key **cannot be changed** without rewriting the table, and there are no secondary indexes — a second access pattern means a second table with a different key.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="gcpdb-bt-03" number={3} question="How does Bigtable fit into a data pipeline?" difficulty="medium" topic="Bigtable">
Usually as the **real-time serving layer**, with BigQuery as the analytical layer.

A common architecture: streaming data arrives via Pub/Sub, **Dataflow** writes i

title: GCP Database Services
description: Google Cloud database interview questions covering BigQuery architecture, partitioning, clustering and cost control, Cloud Bigtable schema design, Cloud SQL, and Cloud Spanner's globally distributed relational model.
content:
t to **Bigtable** for low-latency serving and to **BigQuery** (or GCS) for analytics. The application reads features or current state from Bigtable in milliseconds; analysts and models query BigQuery.

The complementary detail worth knowing: **BigQuery can query Bigtable as an external table**, so you can join operational state into an analytical query without building an export — useful, though slower than native storage and best kept to small lookups.

For a feature store, this pairing is the standard shape: Bigtable for online serving, BigQuery for offline training data, with Dataflow keeping them consistent.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

---

title: GCP Database Services
description: Google Cloud database interview questions covering BigQuery architecture, partitioning, clustering and cost control, Cloud Bigtable schema design, Cloud SQL, and Cloud Spanner's globally distributed relational model.
content:
## Cloud SQL

<QuestionList topic="Cloud SQL" storagePrefix="gcp-databases-cloudsql">

<QuestionCard id="gcpdb-sql-01" number={1} question="What is Cloud SQL and what does it manage?" difficulty="easy" topic="Cloud SQL">
Managed **MySQL, PostgreSQL and SQL Server** — provisioning, patching, automated backups, point-in-time recovery, replication and failover handled by Google.

You keep schema design, query performance, indexing and instance sizing.

**High availability** uses a regional configuration with a synchronous standby in another zone and automatic failover. **Read replicas** (in-region or cross-region) scale reads and can be promoted.

**Cloud SQL Enterprise Plus** adds better performance, near-zero-downtime maintenance and a longer data cache.

For a data engineer, Cloud SQL is t

title: GCP Database Services
description: Google Cloud database interview questions covering BigQuery architecture, partitioning, clustering and cost control, Cloud Bigtable schema design, Cloud SQL, and Cloud Spanner's globally distributed relational model.
content:
ypically the **source system** rather than the platform — the application database you extract from, which makes "how do you read from it without hurting production" the question that actually matters.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="gcpdb-sql-02" number={2} question="How do you get data from Cloud SQL into BigQuery?" difficulty="hard" topic="Cloud SQL">
Options, roughly in increasing sophistication:

1. **Read replica + scheduled export** — export to GCS, load into BigQuery. Simple, batch, and keeps load off the primary.
2. **Datastream** — Google's serverless **CDC** service, reading the binlog or WAL and streaming changes into BigQuery with a managed merge. **The recommended answer** for near-real-time, low-impact replication.
3. **Federated queries** — BigQuery's `EXTERNAL_QUERY` ru

title: GCP Database Services
description: Google Cloud database interview questions covering BigQuery architecture, partitioning, clustering and cost control, Cloud Bigtable schema design, Cloud SQL, and Cloud Spanner's globally distributed relational model.
content:
ns SQL directly against Cloud SQL. Convenient for small lookups; dangerous for large scans since it hits the live database.
4. **Dataflow** with a JDBC source, when transformation is needed in flight.
5. **Datastream to GCS** then Dataflow or Spark, when you want the raw change log in the lake.

The bad answer is a scheduled full-table `SELECT *` against the primary. Naming **Datastream** shows current GCP knowledge — it's the managed CDC path most teams should use.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

---

title: GCP Database Services
description: Google Cloud database interview questions covering BigQuery architecture, partitioning, clustering and cost control, Cloud Bigtable schema design, Cloud SQL, and Cloud Spanner's globally distributed relational model.
content:
## Cloud Spanner

<QuestionList topic="Cloud Spanner" storagePrefix="gcp-databases-spanner">

<QuestionCard id="gcpdb-sp-01" number={1} question="What is Cloud Spanner, and what makes it unusual?" difficulty="hard" topic="Spanner">
A horizontally scalable, **strongly consistent, globally distributed relational database** — combining properties usually treated as mutually exclusive: SQL and ACID transactions **and** horizontal scale **and** external consistency across regions.

The mechanism is **TrueTime**, an API backed by GPS receivers and atomic clocks in Google's datacentres, giving bounded-uncertainty timestamps. Spanner uses it to order transactions globally without a coordination round trip on every read, which is what makes global strong consistency practical rather than merely pos

title: GCP Database Services
description: Google Cloud database interview questions covering BigQuery architecture, partitioning, clustering and cost control, Cloud Bigtable schema design, Cloud SQL, and Cloud Spanner's globally distributed relational model.
content:
sible.

It offers up to **99.999% availability** in multi-region configurations, with automatic sharding and rebalancing.

The trade is cost — it's substantially more expensive than Cloud SQL — and the need to design schemas for its distribution model. It's justified when you genuinely need global scale with relational semantics, not as a default relational database.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="gcpdb-sp-02" number={2} question="How do you design schemas and keys in Spanner?" difficulty="hard" topic="Spanner">
Spanner shards by **primary key range**, so key choice determines distribution — the same hotspot logic as Bigtable.

Avoid monotonically increasing keys (auto-increment IDs, timestamps); they concentrate all writes on the last split. Prefer **UUIDs**, or hash a sequential valu

title: GCP Database Services
description: Google Cloud database interview questions covering BigQuery architecture, partitioning, clustering and cost control, Cloud Bigtable schema design, Cloud SQL, and Cloud Spanner's globally distributed relational model.
content:
e into the key prefix.

**Interleaved tables** are Spanner's distinctive feature: declaring a child table interleaved in its parent physically co-locates child rows with their parent row, so a parent-with-children read is a single local operation rather than a distributed join. Modelling orders interleaved in customers is the canonical example.

Also mind the **transaction footprint** — a transaction spanning many splits requires two-phase commit and is much slower. Design so common transactions touch one split, which interleaving helps with directly.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="gcpdb-sp-03" number={3} question="When would you choose Spanner over Cloud SQL or BigQuery?" difficulty="medium" topic="Spanner">
- **Cloud SQL** — the default relational choice. Cheaper, familiar, and suffi

title: GCP Database Services

content:
## GCP Storage: Cloud Storage and the Lake

**Cloud Storage is where a GCP data lake lives, and it has two genuinely distinctive properties worth knowing: it has been strongly consistent since launch — no eventual-consistency workarounds ever needed — and its dual-region and multi-region buckets give geo-redundancy while still presenting a single bucket. Most GCS interview questions come down to storage class economics, the small-files problem, and how BigQuery relates to the files underneath.**

content:
## Key Concepts

Cloud Storage is **object storage** with a flat key namespace — the "folders" in the console are prefixes, and there are no real directories. That has the same consequences as on S3: no atomic rename, no append, and a directory listing is a prefix scan. It's why Spark commit protocols and table formats like Iceberg and Delta matter here too.

Two things differentiate GCS from its peers. It has offered **strong global consistency** for reads, writes, listings and deletes since the beginning, so the consistency workarounds that used to litter S3 architectures never applied. And **location type is chosen at bucket creation** — regional, dual-region or multi-region — which bundles geo-redundancy into the bucket rather than requiring separate replication configuration.

The cos

title: GCP Storage for Data Platforms
description: Google Cloud storage interview questions covering Cloud Storage classes and lifecycle, consistency and performance, persistent disks, local SSD and Filestore, plus designing a data lake on GCS.
content:
t model has the familiar three dials: **storage class** (Standard through Archive, trading storage price for retrieval fees and minimum durations), **operations** (you pay per request, which is why millions of tiny files cost more than a few large ones), and **network egress** — with the important GCP-specific note that **BigQuery reading from GCS in the same region is free**, so co-location is a design requirement, not an optimisation.

title: GCP Storage for Data Platforms
description: Google Cloud storage interview questions covering Cloud Storage classes and lifecycle, consistency and performance, persistent disks, local SSD and Filestore, plus designing a data lake on GCS.
content:
## Cloud Storage

<QuestionList topic="Cloud Storage" storagePrefix="gcp-storage-gcs">

<QuestionCard id="gcpst-gcs-01" number={1} question="What is Cloud Storage and what are its key properties?" difficulty="easy" topic="Cloud Storage">
Object storage: **objects** (data plus metadata) under keys in **buckets**, accessed over HTTPS.

Properties that matter:
- **Strong consistency** globally, for reads, writes, listings and deletes — from day one, unlike S3's history.
- **11 nines durability**, with redundancy determined by the bucket's location type.
- **Unlimited capacity**, no provisioning.
- **Flat namespace** — `orders/dt=2026-01-15/part-0.parquet` is one key, not a path.
- **Immutable objects** — no in-place edit or append; you replace the object.
- **A single global namespace for buc

title: GCP Storage for Data Platforms
description: Google Cloud storage interview questions covering Cloud Storage classes and lifecycle, consistency and performance, persistent disks, local SSD and Filestore, plus designing a data lake on GCS.
content:
ket names**, so names must be globally unique.

The architectural payoff is the same as any object store: **storage is decoupled from compute**, so BigQuery, Dataproc, Dataflow and Vertex AI all read the same objects, and compute can scale or vanish without touching data.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="gcpst-gcs-02" number={2} question="What are the bucket location types?" difficulty="medium" topic="Cloud Storage">
Chosen at creation and **immutable**:

- **Regional** — data in one region. Lowest cost and lowest latency to compute in that region. The default for a data lake.
- **Dual-region** — a specific pair of regions, with **geo-redundancy and strong consistency across both**, plus optional turbo replication for a 15-minute RPO. You get resilience without a separate replication set

title: GCP Storage for Data Platforms
description: Google Cloud storage interview questions covering Cloud Storage classes and lifecycle, consistency and performance, persistent disks, local SSD and Filestore, plus designing a data lake on GCS.
content:
up.
- **Multi-region** — spread across a broad area (US, EU, ASIA). Highest availability SLA and good for globally-read content, at higher storage cost and with less predictable locality.

The data engineering rule: **put the bucket in the same region as your compute.** BigQuery cannot query a bucket in a different region for load jobs, Dataproc pays egress and latency, and cross-region reads add cost to every job.

Dual-region is the pragmatic choice when you need DR without giving up co-location.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="gcpst-gcs-03" number={3} question="Why does the small-files problem matter on GCS?" difficulty="hard" topic="Performance">
The same reasons as any object store, and they compound:

- **Per-operation cost and latency** — every file needs at least one read reques

title: GCP Storage for Data Platforms
description: Google Cloud storage interview questions covering Cloud Storage classes and lifecycle, consistency and performance, persistent disks, local SSD and Filestore, plus designing a data lake on GCS.
content:
t with tens of milliseconds of latency. A million tiny files means a million requests.
- **Listing is a paginated prefix scan** — enumerating a prefix with millions of objects takes many sequential calls before processing begins.
- **Task overhead** — Spark launches a task per file, so scheduling dominates the actual work.
- **Ineffective compression and statistics** — Parquet footers and column statistics are re-read per file, and tiny files defeat both compression and predicate pushdown.

Fixes: **compact on a schedule**, target **128 MB–1 GB** output files, tune writer partition counts, and use a table format (Iceberg, Delta, or BigLake tables) so file discovery comes from metadata rather than listing.

One GCS-specific mitigation: **Autoclass** manages storage classes automatically, bu

title: GCP Storage for Data Platforms
description: Google Cloud storage interview questions covering Cloud Storage classes and lifecycle, consistency and performance, persistent disks, local SSD and Filestore, plus designing a data lake on GCS.
content:
t it doesn't solve small files — that remains a layout problem.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="gcpst-gcs-04" number={4} question="How do you optimise Cloud Storage performance?" difficulty="medium" topic="Performance">
- **Co-locate** bucket and compute in the same region. This is the biggest single factor.
- **Larger files** — fewer operations, better throughput per request.
- **Parallel and composite uploads** for large objects, and ranged reads for partial fetches.
- **Columnar formats with pushdown**, so engines read only the byte ranges they need.
- **Avoid sequential-only naming for extremely high write rates** — GCS auto-scales prefixes, but a sudden burst against a single hot prefix can throttle briefly.
- **Cloud CDN** in front of the bucket for read-heavy public content (not

title: GCP Storage for Data Platforms
description: Google Cloud storage interview questions covering Cloud Storage classes and lifecycle, consistency and performance, persistent disks, local SSD and Filestore, plus designing a data lake on GCS.
content:
relevant to lakes).
- **`gcloud storage`** rather than the older `gsutil` for bulk transfers; it's significantly faster.

The historical note: unlike early S3, GCS never required randomised key prefixes for scale, so **date-ordered prefixes are fine** — and preferable, since they enable partition pruning.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

## Storage Classes & Lifecycle

<QuestionList topic="Storage Classes & Lifecycle" storagePrefix="gcp-storage-classes">

<QuestionCard id="gcpst-cls-01" number={1} question="What are the Cloud Storage classes?" difficulty="medium" topic="Storage Classes">
| Class | Min duration | Retrieval | Use |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Standard** | none | free | frequently accessed, active lake data |
| **Nearline** | 30 days | fee per GB | accessed less than monthly |
| **Coldline** | 90 days | higher fee | accessed less than quarterly |
| **Archive** | 365 days | highest fee | long-term retention, rarely read |

The property that distinguishes GCS from S3 Glacier: **every class has millisecond access**. Archive data is retrieved immediately, not after a rehydration wait of hours. That's a genuine operatio

title: GCP Storage for Data Platforms
description: Google Cloud storage interview questions covering Cloud Storage classes and lifecycle, consistency and performance, persistent disks, local SSD and Filestore, plus designing a data lake on GCS.
content:
nal advantage — an archived partition is still queryable, just expensively.

The traps are the familiar ones: **early deletion is billed for the full minimum duration**, and **retrieval fees** mean a Nearline object read weekly costs more than leaving it in Standard. Calculate the crossover rather than assuming colder is cheaper.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="gcpst-cls-02" number={2} question="How do lifecycle policies and Autoclass work?" difficulty="medium" topic="Lifecycle">
**Lifecycle rules** are JSON conditions on a bucket that change storage class or delete objects:

```json
{"rule": [
  {"action": {"type": "SetStorageClass", "storageClass": "NEARLINE"},
   "condition": {"age": 30, "matchesPrefix": ["raw/"]}},
  {"action": {"type": "SetStorageClass", "storageClass": "ARCHIVE"},

s object versioning, and what should you watch?" difficulty="medium" topic="Lifecycle">
With versioning enabled, overwrites and deletes retain the previous object as a **noncurrent version**, recoverable later. A delete makes the live version noncurrent rather than removing data.

It protects against accidental deletion and against a buggy pipeline overwriting good data — genuinely worth having on a curated zone.

The cost point people miss: **you pay for every version**. A job that rewrites the same partition daily silently multiplies storage, and "deleted" objects keep costing money.

Always pair versioning with a lifecycle rule expiring noncurrent versions (`daysSinceNoncurrentTime`), and consider `numNewerVersions` to keep only the last few.

For a large immutable raw zone, versioning

title: GCP Storage for Data Platforms
description: Google Cloud storage interview questions covering Cloud Storage classes and lifecycle, consistency and performance, persistent disks, local SSD and Filestore, plus designing a data lake on GCS.
content:
often isn't worth it — the data doesn't change. **Soft delete** (a bucket-level retention window for deleted objects) is a lighter alternative.
</QuestionCard>

content:
## Security & Access Control

<QuestionList topic="Security & Access Control" storagePrefix="gcp-storage-security">

<QuestionCard id="gcpst-sec-01" number={1} question="How do you control access to Cloud Storage?" difficulty="medium" topic="Security">
- **IAM** — the primary mechanism, granting roles at organisation, folder, project or **bucket** level. Roles like `roles/storage.objectViewer` and `roles/storage.objectAdmin`.
- **Uniform bucket-level access** — disables per-object ACLs so IAM is the single source of truth. **Enable it**; mixed ACLs and IAM is a recurring source of confusion and accidental exposure.
- **ACLs** — legacy per-object permissions. Avoid.
- **Signed URLs** — time-limited access to one object without a Google account, for sharing with external parties.
- **IAM Con

title: GCP Storage for Data Platforms
description: Google Cloud storage interview questions covering Cloud Storage classes and lifecycle, consistency and performance, persistent disks, local SSD and Filestore, plus designing a data lake on GCS.
content:
ditions** — restrict a grant by resource path or time, which is how you scope access to a prefix.
- **VPC Service Controls** — a perimeter preventing data exfiltration to projects outside it. The strongest control for sensitive data.

For a lake, the working pattern is **uniform bucket-level access, IAM roles granted to Google Groups rather than individuals, and one bucket per zone** so permissions align with bucket boundaries.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="gcpst-sec-02" number={2} question="What are the encryption options?" difficulty="medium" topic="Security">
**At rest**, encryption is always on and cannot be disabled. The choice is key management:

- **Google-managed** (default) — zero configuration, no cost.
- **CMEK (customer-managed)** — keys in **Cloud KMS**, so you control ro

title: GCP Storage for Data Platforms
description: Google Cloud storage interview questions covering Cloud Storage classes and lifecycle, consistency and performance, persistent disks, local SSD and Filestore, plus designing a data lake on GCS.
content:
tation and can **revoke access by disabling the key**, with an audit trail in Cloud Logging. The usual requirement for regulated data.
- **CSEK (customer-supplied)** — you provide the key with every request. Rare, and you're responsible for key loss.

**In transit** — TLS always.

For a data platform, CMEK is the common answer where compliance requires demonstrable key control. Two operational notes: every service reading the bucket needs the **Cloud KMS CryptoKey Encrypter/Decrypter** role, which is easy to forget and produces confusing permission errors; and the key must be in a **compatible location** with the bucket.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="gcpst-sec-03" number={3} question="How do you prevent data from leaving your environment?" difficulty="hard" topic="Security">
**VPC Ser

title: GCP Storage for Data Platforms
description: Google Cloud storage interview questions covering Cloud Storage classes and lifecycle, consistency and performance, persistent disks, local SSD and Filestore, plus designing a data lake on GCS.
content:
vice Controls** is the distinctive GCP answer. It defines a **service perimeter** around projects, so even a principal with valid IAM permissions cannot copy data to a bucket or BigQuery dataset outside the perimeter.

That's a genuinely different control from IAM: IAM answers "may this identity read the data", VPC-SC answers "may this data leave". It blocks the exfiltration path that a compromised credential or a mistaken `gsutil cp` would otherwise open.

Supporting controls:
- **Organisation policy constraints** — for example, `storage.publicAccessPrevention` to make public buckets impossible, and `iam.disableServiceAccountKeyCreation` to eliminate long-lived keys.
- **Private Google Access / Private Service Connect** so traffic never traverses the public internet.
- **Retention policie

title: GCP Storage for Data Platforms
description: Google Cloud storage interview questions covering Cloud Storage classes and lifecycle, consistency and performance, persistent disks, local SSD and Filestore, plus designing a data lake on GCS.
content:
s and bucket lock** for immutable, compliance-grade retention.

Naming VPC Service Controls specifically is a strong signal in a GCP security question — it's the control most people miss.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>
