content:
## Block & File Storage

<QuestionList topic="Block & File Storage" storagePrefix="gcp-storage-block-file">

<QuestionCard id="gcpst-pd-01" number={1} question="What are Persistent Disks and Hyperdisk?" difficulty="medium" topic="Persistent Disk">
Network-attached block storage that persists independently of an instance.

- **pd-standard** — HDD, cheap sequential throughput.
- **pd-balanced** — SSD, the sensible general default.
- **pd-ssd** — higher IOPS for demanding databases.
- **pd-extreme** — provisioned IOPS.
- **Hyperdisk** — the newer generation, where **IOPS and throughput are provisioned independently of capacity**. The current recommendation for high-performance needs.

The important behaviour on classic PD types is that **performance scales with disk size** — a small pd-balanc

title: GCP Storage for Data Platforms
description: Google Cloud storage interview questions covering Cloud Storage classes and lifecycle, consistency and performance, persistent disks, local SSD and Filestore, plus designing a data lake on GCS.
content:
ed volume is also a slow one. Teams routinely over-provision capacity purely to buy IOPS, which is exactly what Hyperdisk fixes.

Persistent disks can also be attached read-only to multiple instances, and snapshots are incremental and global, so they can be restored into another region.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="gcpst-pd-02" number={2} question="What is Local SSD and when should you use it?" difficulty="medium" topic="Local SSD">
Physically attached NVMe on the host: very high IOPS and very low latency, attached in fixed 375 GB units.

It is **ephemeral** — data is lost when the instance stops, is migrated, or fails. That single property determines its use.

The data engineering application is **Spark shuffle and spill**. Shuffle data is large, write-heavy, latency-sensitive and c

title: GCP Storage for Data Platforms
description: Google Cloud storage interview questions covering Cloud Storage classes and lifecycle, consistency and performance, persistent disks, local SSD and Filestore, plus designing a data lake on GCS.
content:
ompletely disposable after the job — exactly matching Local SSD's profile. Dataproc lets you attach local SSDs to workers, and doing so on shuffle-heavy jobs is a standard tuning step that can transform runtime.

What must **not** go on it: anything that needs to survive — a database's data files, checkpoints you'd need after a restart, or job output. Those belong on Persistent Disk or, better, in Cloud Storage.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="gcpst-fs-01" number={3} question="What is Filestore, and when would you use it over Cloud Storage?" difficulty="medium" topic="Filestore">
Managed **NFS** file shares, mountable by Compute Engine VMs and GKE pods concurrently, in Basic, Zonal, Regional and Enterprise tiers.

Use it when software genuinely requires a **POSIX filesystem with shared

title: GCP Storage for Data Platforms
description: Google Cloud storage interview questions covering Cloud Storage classes and lifecycle, consistency and performance, persistent disks, local SSD and Filestore, plus designing a data lake on GCS.
content:
write access**: a legacy application that can't speak object storage, an ML training job needing fast random access to many small files, or a shared home directory for a research cluster.

For a data lake it's the wrong choice — it costs far more per GB than Cloud Storage, has fixed capacity you must provision, and the GCP analytics ecosystem (BigQuery, Dataproc, Dataflow) is built around GCS.

The realistic data engineering use is **ML training data** where the framework wants a filesystem and random small-file reads would be slow against object storage. Otherwise, default to Cloud Storage.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

description: Google Cloud storage interview questions covering Cloud Storage classes and lifecycle, consistency and performance, persistent disks, local SSD and Filestore, plus designing a data lake on GCS.
content:
## Designing a Lake on GCS

<QuestionList topic="Designing a Lake on GCS" storagePrefix="gcp-storage-lake-design">

<QuestionCard id="gcpst-lake-01" number={1} question="How would you structure a data lake on Cloud Storage?" difficulty="hard" topic="Data Lake">
Buckets per zone, in the same region as compute:

```
gs://org-lake-raw/       source/entity/dt=2026-01-15/
gs://org-lake-staging/   entity/dt=2026-01-15/
gs://org-lake-curated/   domain/table/dt=2026-01-15/
```

Decisions worth defending:
- **Separate buckets per zone**, so IAM, lifecycle rules, versioning and location type apply cleanly per zone rather than per prefix.
- **Hive-style date partitioning** so BigQuery and Spark can prune.
- **Parquet, or an open table format** (Iceberg via BigLake, or Delta) for ACID and upserts.
- *

title: GCP Storage for Data Platforms
description: Google Cloud storage interview questions covering Cloud Storage classes and lifecycle, consistency and performance, persistent disks, local SSD and Filestore, plus designing a data lake on GCS.
content:
*128 MB–1 GB files**, with scheduled compaction.
- **Uniform bucket-level access**, IAM to groups, and VPC Service Controls around the perimeter.
- **Lifecycle per zone** — raw tiers down and is retained; staging is reproducible so it expires quickly; curated stays Standard.
- **Regional or dual-region**, matching where BigQuery and Dataproc run.

Separate **projects per environment** gives hard isolation and clean cost attribution.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="gcpst-lake-02" number={2} question="How does BigQuery relate to data in Cloud Storage?" difficulty="hard" topic="Data Lake">
Three distinct relationships, and knowing which is which is the point of the question:

1. **Load** — copy GCS data into BigQuery's own managed columnar storage. Fastest queries, and you pay BigQuery sto

title: GCP Storage for Data Platforms
description: Google Cloud storage interview questions covering Cloud Storage classes and lifecycle, consistency and performance, persistent disks, local SSD and Filestore, plus designing a data lake on GCS.
content:
rage. The default for curated tables.
2. **External tables** — BigQuery queries the GCS files in place. No copy, no duplicate storage, but slower and without BigQuery's full optimisation or partition metadata.
3. **BigLake tables** — external tables with **fine-grained security** (row and column level) and metadata caching, so they perform much closer to native tables while data stays in open formats. This is the lakehouse story on GCP, and it supports **Iceberg**.

The practical architecture: land raw data in GCS, query it via BigLake or external tables for exploration, and **load or materialise curated tables into BigQuery** for the serving layer where query performance and concurrency matter.

Loading from GCS in the **same region is free**, which is a real reason to co-locate.
</Questi

<QuestionCard id="gcpst-lake-03" number={3} question="How do you move large volumes of data into Cloud Storage?" difficulty="medium" topic="Data Transfer">
- **`gcloud storage cp`** — the modern CLI, significantly faster than `gsutil` for bulk work, with parallel composite uploads.
- **Storage Transfer Service** — managed, scheduled transfers from S3, Azure Blob, another GCS bucket, or an on-premises POSIX filesystem, with incremental sync and verification. The right tool for recurring or large migrations.
- **Transfer Appliance** — a physical device shipped to you, for hundreds of terabytes to petabytes where the network would take months.
- **BigQuery Data Transfer Service** — scheduled loads from SaaS sources and other warehouses directly into BigQuery.

The decision is the sam

e arithmetic as anywhere: at roughly 10 TB/day over a saturated 1 Gbps link, past ~100 TB the appliance usually wins. Below that, Storage Transfer Service handles it with verification and scheduling you'd otherwise have to build.

## Common Interview Scenarios

**"A Dataproc job reading GCS is slow."** — check bucket and cluster are in the same region first, then file sizes (the small-files problem), then whether the format allows pushdown. Adding local SSDs helps shuffle, not read throughput.

**"Design a lake on GCP."** — regional buckets per zone co-located with BigQuery, Hive-style partitioning, Parquet or Iceberg via BigLake, lifecycle rules per zone, uniform bucket-level access with IAM to groups, CMEK if regulated, and VPC Service Controls as the exfiltration boundary.

**"How do you archive data but keep it queryable?"** — GCS Archive class has **millisecond access**, unlike S3 Glacier, so archived objects remain readable — you just pay a retrieval fee. That means an external or BigLake table over archived p

artitions still works, which is a genuine GCP advantage.

**"Your storage costs are climbing."** — check noncurrent versions with no expiry rule, whether Autoclass would beat your manual tiering, small-file operation costs, and cross-region reads from compute in a different region.

## GCP: Google Cloud Platform Data Services

**Google Cloud Platform gives data engineers a set of managed services — BigQuery for warehousing, Dataflow and Dataproc for processing, Pub/Sub and Composer for orchestration — built on top of IAM, VPC networking, and reliability primitives that span all of them.**

## Key Concepts

GCP's data stack splits cleanly by workload shape. **BigQuery** is the serverless, SQL-first data warehouse for large-scale analytics; **Cloud Storage** is the object store most pipelines land raw data in first; and **Cloud SQL**, **Cloud Spanner**, **Cloud Datastore**, and **Memorystore** cover relational, globally-distributed relational, NoSQL document, and in-memory workloads respectively. For movement and transformation, **Cloud Dataflow** runs serverless batch/stream pipelines, **Cloud Dataproc** runs managed Spark/Hadoop clusters, **Cloud Pub/Sub** handles asynchronous messaging, and **Cloud Composer** (managed Apache Airflow) orchestrates the dependencies between all of it. Across every service, **Cloud IAM** controls who can do what via fine-grained policies, **VPC

Reliability is a shared responsibility across regional/multi-regional deployment, automated backups, and data replication — the same primitives show up whether you're talking about high availability, disaster recovery, or redundancy, because they're solving the same underlying problem from different angles.

## BigQuery: Google's Serverless Data Warehouse

**BigQuery is Google Cloud's fully managed, serverless data warehouse — its interview questions center on how separating storage (Capacitor) from compute (Dremel) shapes partitioning, clustering, slot-based performance, and cost control.**

title: BigQuery

content:
## Table of Contents

title: BigQuery
description: Interview questions on BigQuery's serverless architecture, partitioning and clustering, query performance, slots, cost optimization, security, and BigQuery ML.
content:
## Key Concepts

BigQuery's defining trait is a serverless split between storage (**Capacitor**, a columnar format) and compute (**Dremel**, its distributed query engine), so users never manage clusters — they just query, and BigQuery scales both layers independently behind the scenes. Performance and cost both hinge on scanning less data: **partitioning** (typically by ingestion time or a date/timestamp column) and **clustering** (physical co-location by column values within a partition) let the query engine skip irrelevant blocks entirely. Compute is measured in **slots** — units of query processing capacity, billed either on-demand (pay per byte scanned) or via **flat-rate reservations** for predictable cost at scale. Data can land via batch loads, the **streaming API** (near-real-time,

title: BigQuery
description: Interview questions on BigQuery's serverless architecture, partitioning and clustering, query performance, slots, cost optimization, security, and BigQuery ML.
content:
buffered before permanent storage), or federated queries against external sources. BigQuery natively supports **nested and repeated fields** (structs and arrays), avoiding the joins a normalized relational schema would require. Governance rests on **IAM** roles, audit logs, and metadata tools like **INFORMATION_SCHEMA** and the Data Catalog, while **BigQuery ML** lets you train and evaluate models using only SQL.

## Key Concepts

The lakehouse idea is that **Delta Lake** — an open storage format built on Parquet — adds a transaction log, ACID guarantees, schema enforcement/evolution, and time travel directly on top of cheap object storage, closing the gap with traditional warehouses without giving up data lake flexibility. Compute is organized around **clusters** (all-purpose for interactive work, job clusters for scheduled runs, SQL warehouses for BI) and **Photon**, a native execution engine that accelerates SQL and DataFrame workloads. **Unity Catalog** provides the governance layer — a three-level namespace (catalog.schema.table), centralized access control, and lineage — spanning multiple workspaces. Delta Lake includes ACID transactions, schema evolution, data versioning, and a transaction log on top of Parquet, while plain Parquet is just a columnar storage format without these features — Delta tables are physically Parquet files plus a `_delta_log` directory that tracks every change.
</QuestionCard>

Managed tables store data in the Databricks-managed storage location and are dropped (data and all) when the table is dropped, while external tables reference data stored elsewhere and only remove the metadata reference when dropped — the underlying files remain.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dbx-lake-08" number={8} question="What are the data formats supported by Databricks?" difficulty="easy" topic="Data Formats">

</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dbx-lake-10" number={10} question="What is schema enforcement in Delta Lake?" difficulty="medium" topic="Delta Lake">
Schema enforcement ensures that data written to a Delta table matches the table's existing schema, rejecting writes that don't conform (unless schema evolution is explicitly enabled) — preventing silent data quality issues from mismatched columns or types.
</QuestionCard>

Table optimization involves reorganizing data layout, removing delete markers left by row-level deletes/updates, and compacting small files for improved query performance — primarily done through the `OPTIMIZE` command.

<QuestionCard id="dbx-lake-14" number={14} question="What is the VACUUM command in Delta Lake?" difficulty="medium" topic="Maintenance">
`VACUUM` removes old, no-longer-referenced data files from Delta tables (beyond a retention threshold, default 7 days), reducing storage costs while still preserving enough history for recent time travel queries.
</QuestionCard>

## How much Memory is required?
Although Impala is not an in-memory database, when dealing with large tables and large result sets, you should expect to dedicate a substantial portion of physical memory for the impalad daemon. Recommended physical memory for an Impala node is 128 GB or higher. If practical, devote approximately 80% of physical memory to Impala.
The amount of memory required for an Impala operation depends on several factors:
The file format of the table. Different file formats represent the same data in more or fewer data files. The compression and encoding for each file format might require a different amount of temporary memory to decompress the data for analysis.
Whether the operation is a SELECT or an INSERT. For example, Parquet tables require relatively little memory

title: Impala
description: Interview questions covering impala
content:
to query, because Impala reads and decompresses data in 8 MB chunks. Inserting into a Parquet table is a more memory-intensive operation because the data for each data file (potentially hundreds of megabytes, depending on the value of the PARQUET_FILE_SIZE query option) is stored in memory until encoded, compressed, and written to disk.
Whether the table is partitioned or not, and whether a query against a partitioned table can take advantage of partition pruning.
Whether the final result set is sorted by the ORDER BY clause. Each Impala node scans and filters a portion of the total data, and applies the LIMIT to its own portion of the result set. In Impala 1.4.0 and higher, if the sort operation requires more memory than is available on any particular host, Impala uses a temporary disk w

title: Impala
description: Interview questions covering impala
content:
ork area to perform the sort. The intermediate result sets are all sent back to the coordinator node, which does the final sorting and then applies the LIMIT clause to the final result set.
For example, if you execute the query:
select * from giant_table order by some_column limit 1000;
and your cluster has 50 nodes, then each of those 50 nodes will transmit a maximum of 1000 rows back to the coordinator node. The coordinator node needs enough memory to sort (LIMIT * cluster_size) rows, although in the end the final result set is at most LIMIT rows, 1000 in this case.
Likewise, if you execute the query:
select * from giant_table where test_val > 100 order by some_column;
then each node filters out a set of rows matching the WHERE conditions, sorts the results (with no size limit), and send

title: Impala
description: Interview questions covering impala
content:
s the sorted intermediate rows back to the coordinator node. The coordinator node might need substantial memory to sort the final result set, and so might use a temporary disk work area for that final phase of the query.
Whether the query contains any join clauses, GROUP BY clauses, analytic functions, or DISTINCT operators. These operations all require some in-memory work areas that vary depending on the volume and distribution of data. In Impala 2.0 and later, these kinds of operations utilize temporary disk work areas if memory usage grows too large to handle.
The size of the result set. When intermediate results are being passed around between nodes, the amount of data depends on the number of columns returned by the query. For example, it is more memory-efficient to query only the col

umns that are actually needed in the result set rather than always issuing SELECT *.
The mechanism by which work is divided for a join query. You use the COMPUTE STATS statement, and query hints in the most difficult cases, to help Impala pick the most efficient execution plan.

[Table of Contents](#apache-impala)

title: Impala
description: Interview questions covering impala
content:
## What are the main features of Impala?
A large set of SQL statements, including SELECT and INSERT, with joins, Subqueries in Impala SELECT Statements, and Impala Analytic Functions. Highly compatible with HiveQL, and also including some vendor extensions. For more information.
Distributed, high-performance queries.
Using Cloudera Manager, you can deploy and manage your Impala services. Cloudera Manager is the best way to get started with Impala on your cluster.
Using Hue for queries.
Appending and inserting data into tables through the INSERT statement.
ODBC: Impala is certified to run against MicroStrategy and Tableau, with restrictions. For more information, see Configuring Impala to Work with ODBC.
Querying data stored in HDFS and HBase in a single query.
In Impala 2.2.0 and higher, q

title: Impala
description: Interview questions covering impala
content:
uerying data stored in the Amazon Simple Storage Service (S3).
Concurrent client requests. Each Impala daemon can handle multiple concurrent client requests. The effects on performance depend on your particular hardware and workload.
Kerberos authentication. For more information.
Partitions. With Impala SQL, you can create partitioned tables with the CREATE TABLE statement, and add and drop partitions with the ALTER TABLE statement. Impala also takes advantage of the partitioning present in Hive tables.

[Table of Contents](#apache-impala)

title: Impala
description: Interview questions covering impala
content:
## What features from relational databases or hive are not available in Impala?
Querying streaming data.
Deleting individual rows. You delete data in bulk by overwriting an entire table or partition, or by dropping a table.
Indexing (not currently). LZO-compressed text files can be indexed outside of Impala, as described in Using LZO-Compressed Text Files.
Full text search on text fields. The Cloudera Search product is appropriate for this use case.
Custom Hive Serializer/Deserializer classes (SerDes). Impala supports a set of common native file formats that have built-in SerDes in CDH.
Checkpointing within a query. That is, Impala does not save intermediate results to disk during long-running queries. Currently, Impala cancels a running query if any host on which that query is executing f

title: Impala
description: Interview questions covering impala
content:
ails. When one or more hosts are down, Impala reroutes future queries to only use the available hosts, and Impala detects when the hosts come back up and begins using them again. Because a query can be submitted through any Impala node, there is no single point of failure. In the future, we will consider adding additional work allocation features to Impala, so that a running query would complete even in the presence of host failures.
Encryption of data transmitted between Impala daemons.
Hive indexes.
Non-Hadoop data stores, such as relational databases.

[Table of Contents](#apache-impala)

title: Impala
description: Interview questions covering impala
content:
## Does Impala support Generic Jdbc?
Impala supports the HiveServer2 JDBC driver.

[Table of Contents](#apache-impala)

title: Impala
description: Interview questions covering impala
content:
## Is Avro supported?
Yes, Avro is supported. Impala has always been able to query Avro tables. You can use the Impala LOAD DATAstatement to load existing Avro data files into a table. Starting with Impala 1.4, you can create Avro tables with Impala. Currently, you still use the INSERT statement in Hive to copy data from another table into an Avro table.

[Table of Contents](#apache-impala)

title: Impala
description: Interview questions covering impala
content:
## How do I Know how many Impala Nodes are in my cluster?
The Impala statestore keeps track of how many impalad nodes are currently available. You can see this information through the statestore web interface. For example, at the URL http://statestore_host:25010/metrics you might see lines like the following:
+ statestore.live-backends:3
+ statestore.live-backends.list:[host1:22000, host1:26000, host2:22000]
The number of impalad nodes is the number of list items referring to port 22000, in this case two. (Typically, this number is one less than the number reported by the statestore.live-backends line.) If an impalad node became unavailable or came back after an outage, the information reported on this page would change appropriately.

[Table of Contents](#apache-impala)

title: Impala
description: Interview questions covering impala
content:
## Are results returned as they become available or all at once when a query completes?
Impala streams results whenever they are available, when possible. Certain SQL operations (aggregation or ORDER BY) require all of the input to be ready before Impala can return results.

[Table of Contents](#apache-impala)

title: Impala
description: Interview questions covering impala
content:
## Why does my select statement fail?
When a SELECT statement fails, the cause usually falls into one of the following categories:
A timeout because of a performance, capacity, or network issue affecting one particular node.
Excessive memory use for a join query, resulting in automatic cancellation of the query.
A low-level issue affecting how native code is generated on each node to handle particular WHERE clauses in the query. For example, a machine instruction could be generated that is not supported by the processor of a certain node. If the error message in the log suggests the cause was an illegal instruction, consider turning off native code generation temporarily, and trying the query again.
Malformed input data, such as a text data file with an enormously long line, or with a deli

title: Impala
description: Interview questions covering impala
content:
miter that does not match the character specified in the FIELDS TERMINATED BY clause of the CREATE TABLE statement.

[Table of Contents](#apache-impala)

title: Impala
description: Interview questions covering impala
content:
## Why does my insert statement fail?
When an INSERT statement fails, it is usually the result of exceeding some limit within a Hadoop component, typically HDFS.

An INSERT into a partitioned table can be a strenuous operation due to the possibility of opening many files and associated threads simultaneously in HDFS. Impala 1.1.1 includes some improvements to distribute the work more efficiently, so that the values for each partition are written by a single node, rather than as a separate data file from each node.
Certain expressions in the SELECT part of the INSERT statement can complicate the execution planning and result in an inefficient INSERT operation. Try to make the column data types of the source and destination tables match up, for example by doing ALTER TABLE ... REPLACE COLUMN

title: Impala
description: Interview questions covering impala
content:
S on the source table if necessary. Try to avoid CASE expressions in the SELECT portion, because they make the result values harder to predict than transferring a column unchanged or passing the column through a built-in function.
Be prepared to raise some limits in the HDFS configuration settings, either temporarily during the INSERTor permanently if you frequently run such INSERT statements as part of your ETL pipeline.
The resource usage of an INSERT statement can vary depending on the file format of the destination table. Inserting into a Parquet table is memory-intensive, because the data for each partition is buffered in memory until it reaches 1 gigabyte, at which point the data file is written to disk. Impala can distribute the work for an INSERT more efficiently when statistics ar

title: Impala
description: Interview questions covering impala
content:
e available for the source table that is queried during the INSERT statement.

[Table of Contents](#apache-impala)

title: Impala
description: Interview questions covering impala
content:
## Does Impala performance improve as it is deployed to more hosts in a cluster in much the same way that Hadoop performance does?
Yes. Impala scales with the number of hosts. It is important to install Impala on all the DataNodes in the cluster, because otherwise some nodes must do remote reads to retrieve data not available for local reads. Data locality is an important architectural aspect for Impala performance.

[Table of Contents](#apache-impala)

title: Impala
description: Interview questions covering impala
content:
## Is the Hdfs Block Size reduced to achieve faster query results?
No. Impala does not make any changes to the HDFS or HBase data sets.
The default Parquet block size is relatively large (256 MB in Impala 2.0 and later; 1 GB in earlier releases). You can control the block size when creating Parquet files using the PARQUET_FILE_SIZE query option.

title: Impala
description: Interview questions covering impala
content:
## Does Impala use caching?
Impala does not cache table data. It does cache some table and file metadata. Although queries might run faster on subsequent iterations because the data set was cached in the OS buffer cache, Impala does not explicitly control this.
Impala takes advantage of the HDFS caching feature in CDH 5. You can designate which tables or partitions are cached through the CACHED and UNCACHED clauses of the CREATE TABLE and ALTER TABLE statements. Impala can also take advantage of data that is pinned in the HDFS cache through the hdfscacheadmin command.

[Table of Contents](#apache-impala)

title: Impala
description: Interview questions covering impala
content:
## What are the good use cases for Impala as opposed to Hive or Mapreduce?
Impala is well-suited to executing SQL queries for interactive exploratory analytics on large data sets. Hive and MapReduce are appropriate for very long running, batch-oriented tasks such as ETL.

[Table of Contents](#apache-impala)

title: Impala
description: Interview questions covering impala
content:
## Is Mapreduce required for impala and will Impala continue to work as expected if Mapreduce is stopped?
Impala does not use MapReduce at all.

[Table of Contents](#apache-impala)

title: Impala
description: Interview questions covering impala
content:
## Can Impala be used for complex event processing?
For example, in an industrial environment, many agents may generate large amounts of data. Can Impala be used to analyze this data, checking for notable changes in the environment?
Complex Event Processing (CEP) is usually performed by dedicated stream-processing systems. Impala is not a stream-processing system, as it most closely resembles a relational database.

[Table of Contents](#apache-impala)

title: Impala
description: Interview questions covering impala
content:
## Is Impala intended to handle Real Time Queries in Low latency Applications or is it for ad Hoc Queries for the purpose of data exploration?
Ad-hoc queries are the primary use case for Impala. We anticipate it being used in many other situations where low-latency is required. Whether Impala is appropriate for any particular use-case depends on the workload, data size and query volume.

[Table of Contents](#apache-impala)

title: Impala
description: Interview questions covering impala
content:
## How does Impala compare to Hive and Pig?
Impala is different from Hive and Pig because it uses its own daemons that are spread across the cluster for queries. Because Impala does not rely on MapReduce, it avoids the startup overhead of MapReduce jobs, allowing Impala to return results in real time.

[Table of Contents](#apache-impala)

title: Impala
description: Interview questions covering impala
content:
## Can I do transforms or add New functionality?
Impala adds support for UDFs in Impala 1.2. You can write your own functions in C++, or reuse existing Java-based Hive UDFs. The UDF support includes scalar functions and user-defined aggregate functions (UDAs). User-defined table functions (UDTFs) are not currently supported.
Impala does not currently support an extensible serialization-deserialization framework (SerDes), and so adding extra functionality to Impala is not as straightforward as for Hive or Pig.

[Table of Contents](#apache-impala)

title: Impala
description: Interview questions covering impala
content:
## Can any Impala Query also be executed in Hive?
Yes. There are some minor differences in how some queries are handled, but Impala queries can also be completed in Hive. Impala SQL is a subset of HiveQL, with some functional limitations such as transforms.

[Table of Contents](#apache-impala)

title: Impala
description: Interview questions covering impala
content:
## Can I use Impala to Query data already loaded into Hive and Hbase?
There are no additional steps to allow Impala to query tables managed by Hive, whether they are stored in HDFS or HBase. Make sure that Impala is configured to access the Hive metastore correctly and you should be ready to go. Keep in mind that impalad, by default, runs as the impala user, so you might need to adjust some file permissions depending on how strict your permissions are currently.

[Table of Contents](#apache-impala)

title: Impala
description: Interview questions covering impala
content:
## Is Hive an Impala requirement?
The Hive metastore service is a requirement. Impala shares the same metastore database as Hive, allowing Impala and Hive to access the same tables transparently.
Hive itself is optional, and does not need to be installed on the same nodes as Impala. Currently, Impala supports a wider variety of read (query) operations than write (insert) operations; you use Hive to insert data into tables that use certain file formats.

[Table of Contents](#apache-impala)

title: Impala
description: Interview questions covering impala
content:
## Is Impala production ready?
Impala has finished its beta release cycle, and the 1.0, 1.1, and 1.2 GA releases are production ready. The 1.1.x series includes additional security features for authorization, an important requirement for production use in many organizations. The 1.2.x series includes important performance features, particularly for large join queries. Some Cloudera customers are already using Impala for large workloads.

The Impala 1.3.0 and higher releases are bundled with corresponding levels of CDH 5. The number of new features grows with each release.

[Table of Contents](#apache-impala)

title: Impala
description: Interview questions covering impala
content:
## How do I configure Hadoop High Availability for Impala?
You can set up a proxy server to relay requests back and forth to the Impala servers, for load balancing and high availability.

[Table of Contents](#apache-impala)

title: Impala
description: Interview questions covering impala
content:
## What happens if there is an Error in Impala?
There is not a single point of failure in Impala. All Impala daemons are fully able to handle incoming queries. If a machine fails however, all queries with fragments running on that machine will fail. Because queries are expected to return quickly, you can just rerun the query if there is a failure.
The longer answer: Impala must be able to connect to the Hive metastore. Impala aggressively caches metadata so the metastore host should have minimal load. Impala relies on the HDFS NameNode, and, in CDH4, you can configure HA for HDFS. Impala also has centralized services, known as the statestore andcatalog services, that run on one host only. Impala continues to execute queries if the statestore host is down, but it will not get state updates.

title: Impala
description: Interview questions covering impala
content:
For example, if a host is added to the cluster while the statestore host is down, the existing instances of impalad running on the other hosts will not find out about this new host. Once the statestore process is restarted, all the information it serves is automatically reconstructed from all running Impala daemons.

[Table of Contents](#apache-impala)

title: Impala
description: Interview questions covering impala
content:
## What is the Maximum number of Rows in a Table?
There is no defined maximum. Some customers have used Impala to query a table with over a trillion rows.

[Table of Contents](#apache-impala)

title: Impala
description: Interview questions covering impala
content:
## On which hosts does Impala run?
Cloudera strongly recommends running the impalad daemon on each DataNode for good performance. Although this topology is not a hard requirement, if there are data blocks with no Impala daemons running on any of the hosts containing replicas of those blocks, queries involving that data could be very inefficient. In that case, the data must be transmitted from one host to another for processing by "remote reads", a condition Impala normally tries to avoid.

[Table of Contents](#apache-impala)

title: Impala
description: Interview questions covering impala
content:
## How are Joins performed in Impala?
By default, Impala automatically determines the most efficient order in which to join tables using a cost-based method, based on their overall size and number of rows. (This is a new feature in Impala 1.2.2 and higher.) The COMPUTE STATS statement gathers information about each table that is crucial for efficient join performance. Impala chooses between two techniques for join queries, known as "broadcast joins" and "partitioned joins".

[Table of Contents](#apache-impala)

title: Impala
description: Interview questions covering impala
content:
## How does Impala process Join Queries for large tables?
Impala utilizes multiple strategies to allow joins between tables and result sets of various sizes. When joining a large table with a small one, the data from the small table is transmitted to each node for intermediate processing. When joining two large tables, the data from one of the tables is divided into pieces, and each node processes only selected pieces.

[Table of Contents](#apache-impala)

title: Impala
description: Interview questions covering impala
content:
## What is Impala's aggregation strategy?
Impala currently only supports in-memory hash aggregation. In Impala 2.0 and higher, if the memory requirements for a join or aggregation operation exceed the memory limit for a particular host, Impala uses a temporary work area on disk to help the query complete successfully.

[Table of Contents](#apache-impala)

title: Impala
description: Interview questions covering impala
content:
## How is Impala Metadata managed?
Impala uses two pieces of metadata: the catalog information from the Hive metastore and the file metadata from the NameNode. Currently, this metadata is lazily populated and cached when an impalad needs it to plan a query.
The REFRESH statement updates the metadata for a particular table after loading new data through Hive. The INVALIDATE METADATA Statement statement refreshes all metadata, so that Impala recognizes new tables or other DDL and DML changes performed through Hive.
In Impala 1.2 and higher, a dedicated catalogd daemon broadcasts metadata changes due to Impala DDL or DML statements to all nodes, reducing or eliminating the need to use the REFRESH and INVALIDATE METADATAstatements.

[Table of Contents](#apache-impala)

title: Impala
description: Interview questions covering impala
content:
## What load do concurrent queries produce on the Name Node?
The load Impala generates is very similar to MapReduce. Impala contacts the NameNode during the planning phase to get the file metadata (this is only run on the host the query was sent to). Every impaladwill read files as part of normal processing of the query.

[Table of Contents](#apache-impala)

title: Impala
description: Interview questions covering impala
content:
## How does Impala achieve its performance improvements?
These are the main factors in the performance of Impala versus that of other Hadoop components and related technologies.
Impala avoids MapReduce. While MapReduce is a great general parallel processing model with many benefits, it is not designed to execute SQL. Impala avoids the inefficiencies of MapReduce in these ways:
Impala does not materialize intermediate results to disk. SQL queries often map to multiple MapReduce jobs with all intermediate data sets written to disk.
Impala avoids MapReduce start-up time. For interactive queries, the MapReduce start-up time becomes very noticeable. Impala runs as a service and essentially has no start-up time.
Impala can more naturally disperse query plans instead of having to fit them into a

title: Impala
description: Interview questions covering impala
content:
pipeline of map and reduce jobs. This enables Impala to parallelize multiple stages of a query and avoid overheads such as sort and shuffle when unnecessary.
Impala uses a more efficient execution engine by taking advantage of modern hardware and technologies:
+ Impala generates runtime code. Impala uses LLVM to generate assembly code for the query that is being run. Individual queries do not have to pay the overhead of running on a system that needs to be able to execute arbitrary queries.
+ Impala uses available hardware instructions when possible. Impala uses the supplemental SSE3 (SSSE3) instructions which can offer tremendous speedups in some cases. (Impala 2.0 and 2.1 required the SSE4.1 instruction set; Impala 2.2 and higher relax the restriction again so only SSSE3 is required.)
+

title: Impala
description: Interview questions covering impala
content:
Impala uses better I/O scheduling. Impala is aware of the disk location of blocks and is able to schedule the order to process blocks to keep all disks busy.
+ Impala is designed for performance. A lot of time has been spent in designing Impala with sound performance-oriented fundamentals, such as tight inner loops, inlined function calls, minimal branching, better use of cache, and minimal memory usage.

[Table of Contents](#apache-impala)

title: Impala
description: Interview questions covering impala
content:
## What happens when the data set exceeds available memory?
Currently, if the memory required to process intermediate results on a node exceeds the amount available to Impala on that node, the query is cancelled. You can adjust the memory available to Impala on each node, and you can fine-tune the join strategy to reduce the memory required for the biggest queries. We do plan on supporting external joins and sorting in the future.
Keep in mind though that the memory usage is not directly based on the input data set size. For aggregations, the memory usage is the number of rows after grouping. For joins, the memory usage is the combined size of the tables excluding the biggest table, and Impala can use join strategies that divide up large joined tables among the various nodes rather than tr

title: Impala
description: Interview questions covering impala
content:
ansmitting the entire table to each node.

[Table of Contents](#apache-impala)

title: Impala
description: Interview questions covering impala
content:
## What are the most Memory intensive operations?
If a query fails with an error indicating "memory limit exceeded", you might suspect a memory leak. The problem could actually be a query that is structured in a way that causes Impala to allocate more memory than you expect, exceeded the memory allocated for Impala on a particular node. Some examples of query or table structures that are especially memory-intensive are:
INSERT statements using dynamic partitioning, into a table with many different partitions. (Particularly for tables using Parquet format, where the data for each partition is held in memory until it reaches the full block size in size before it is written to disk.) Consider breaking up such operations into several different INSERT statements, for example to load data one ye

title: Impala
description: Interview questions covering impala
content:
ar at a time rather than for all years at once.
GROUP BY on a unique or high-cardinality column. Impala allocates some handler structures for each different value in a GROUP BY query. Having millions of different GROUP BY values could exceed the memory limit.
Queries involving very wide tables, with thousands of columns, particularly with many STRING columns. Because Impala allows a STRING value to be up to 32 KB, the intermediate results during such queries could require substantial memory allocation.

[Table of Contents](#apache-impala)

title: Impala
description: Interview questions covering impala
content:
## When does Impala hold on to or return memory?
Impala allocates memory using tcmalloc, a memory allocator that is optimized for high concurrency. Once Impala allocates memory, it keeps that memory reserved to use for future queries. Thus, it is normal for Impala to show high memory usage when idle. If Impala detects that it is about to exceed its memory limit (defined by the -mem_limit startup option or the MEM_LIMIT query option), it deallocates memory not needed by the current queries.
When issuing queries through the JDBC or ODBC interfaces, make sure to call the appropriate close method afterwards. Otherwise, some memory associated with the query is not freed.

[Table of Contents](#apache-impala)

title: Impala
description: Interview questions covering impala
content:
## Is there an update statement?
Impala does not currently have an UPDATE statement, which would typically be used to change a single row, a small group of rows, or a specific column. The HDFS-based files used by typical Impala queries are optimized for bulk operations across many megabytes of data at a time, making traditional UPDATEoperations inefficient or impractical.
You can use the following techniques to achieve the same goals as the familiar UPDATE statement, in a way that preserves efficient file layouts for subsequent queries:
Replace the entire contents of a table or partition with updated data that you have already staged in a different location, either using INSERT OVERWRITE, LOAD DATA, or manual HDFS file operations followed by a REFRESH statement for the table. Optionally, y

title: Impala
description: Interview questions covering impala
content:
ou can use built-in functions and expressions in the INSERTstatement to transform the copied data in the same way you would normally do in an UPDATE statement, for example to turn a mixed-case string into all uppercase or all lowercase.
To update a single row, use an HBase table, and issue an INSERT ... VALUES statement using the same key as the original row. Because HBase handles duplicate keys by only returning the latest row with a particular key value, the newly inserted row effectively hides the previous one.

[Table of Contents](#apache-impala)

title: Impala
description: Interview questions covering impala
content:
## Can Impala do User defined functions?
Impala 1.2 and higher does support UDFs and UDAs. You can either write native Impala UDFs and UDAs in C++, or reuse UDFs (but not UDAs) originally written in Java for use with Hive.

[Table of Contents](#apache-impala)

title: Impala
description: Interview questions covering impala
content:
## Why do I have to use refresh and invalidate Metadata and what do they do?
In Impala 1.2 and higher, there is much less need to use the REFRESH and INVALIDATE METADATA statements:
The new impala-catalog service, represented by the catalogd daemon, broadcasts the results of Impala DDL statements to all Impala nodes. Thus, if you do a CREATE TABLE statement in Impala while connected to one node, you do not need to do INVALIDATE METADATA before issuing queries through a different node.
The catalog service only recognizes changes made through Impala, so you must still issue a REFRESH statement if you load data through Hive or by manipulating files in HDFS, and you must issue an INVALIDATE METADATA statement if you create a table, alter a table, add or drop partitions, or do other DDL stateme

title: Impala
description: Interview questions covering impala
content:
nts in Hive.
Because the catalog service broadcasts the results of REFRESH and INVALIDATE METADATA statements to all nodes, in the cases where you do still need to issue those statements, you can do that on a single node rather than on every node, and the changes will be automatically recognized across the cluster, making it more convenient to load balance by issuing queries through arbitrary Impala nodes rather than always using the same coordinator node.

[Table of Contents](#apache-impala)

title: Impala
description: Interview questions covering impala
content:
## Why is space not freed up when I issue drop table?
Impala deletes data files when you issue a DROP TABLE on an internal table, but not an external one. By default, the CREATE TABLE statement creates internal tables, where the files are managed by Impala. An external table is created with a CREATE EXTERNAL TABLE statement, where the files reside in a location outside the control of Impala. Issue a DESCRIBE FORMATTED statement to check whether a table is internal or external. The keyword MANAGED_TABLE indicates an internal table, from which Impala can delete the data files. The keyword EXTERNAL_TABLE indicates an external table, where Impala will leave the data files untouched when you drop the table.
Even when you drop an internal table and the files are removed from their original locat

title: Impala
description: Interview questions covering impala
content:
ion, you might not get the hard drive space back immediately. By default, files that are deleted in HDFS go into a special trashcan directory, from which they are purged after a period of time (by default, 6 hours). For background information on the trashcan mechanism.

[Table of Contents](#apache-impala)

title: Impala
description: Interview questions covering impala

title: Impala
description: Interview questions covering impala
content:
## How do I load a big Csv file into a partitioned table?
To load a data file into a partitioned table, when the data file includes fields like year, month, and so on that correspond to the partition key columns, use a two-stage process. First, use the LOAD DATA or CREATE EXTERNAL TABLE statement to bring the data into an unpartitioned text table. Then use an INSERT ... SELECT statement to copy the data from the unpartitioned table to a partitioned one. Include a PARTITION clause in the INSERTstatement to specify the partition key columns.

[Table of Contents](#apache-impala)

title: Impala
description: Interview questions covering impala
content:
## Can I Do Insert Select Into a partitioned table?
When you use the INSERT ... SELECT * syntax to copy data into a partitioned table, the columns corresponding to the partition key columns must appear last in the columns returned by the SELECT *. You can create the table with the partition key columns defined last. Or, you can use the CREATE VIEW statement to create a view that reorders the columns: put the partition key columns last, then do the INSERT ... SELECT * from the view.

[Table of Contents](#apache-impala)

title: Impala
description: Interview questions covering impala
content:
## What kinds of Impala Queries or data are best suited for Hbase?
HBase tables are ideal for queries where normally you would use a key-value store. That is, where you retrieve a single row or a few rows, by testing a special unique key column using the = or IN operators.
HBase tables are not suitable for queries that produce large result sets with thousands of rows. HBase tables are also not suitable for queries that perform full table scans because the WHERE clause does not request specific values from the unique key column.
Use HBase tables for data that is inserted one row or a few rows at a time, such as by the INSERT ... VALUESsyntax. Loading data piecemeal like this into an HDFS-backed table produces many tiny files, which is a very inefficient layout for HDFS data files.
If the la

title: Impala
description: Interview questions covering impala
content:
ck of an UPDATE statement in Impala is a problem for you, you can simulate single-row updates by doing an INSERT ... VALUES statement using an existing value for the key column. The old row value is hidden; only the new row value is seen by queries.
HBase tables are often wide (containing many columns) and sparse (with most column values NULL). For example, you might record hundreds of different data points for each user of an online service, such as whether the user had registered for an online game or enabled particular account features. With Impala and HBase, you could look up all the information for a specific customer efficiently in a single query. For any given customer, most of these columns might be NULL, because a typical customer might not make use of most features of an online s

title: Data Warehouses
description: Data warehouse platforms and analytics engines (BigQuery, Redshift, Impala, Greenplum)
content:
# Data Warehouses

This section covers data warehouse platforms and analytical query engines designed for OLAP workloads.

title: Data Warehouses
description: Data warehouse platforms and analytics engines (BigQuery, Redshift, Impala, Greenplum)
content:
## Data Warehouse Technologies

- **Snowflake**: Cloud-native, fully-managed data warehouse with elastic scalability and data sharing
- **Databricks**: Unified analytics platform combining data warehousing, engineering, and ML on Apache Spark
- **BigQuery**: Google's serverless, fully-managed data warehouse
- **Redshift**: AWS's columnar data warehouse
- **Impala**: In-memory SQL query engine for Hadoop
- **Greenplum**: Distributed SQL database optimized for analytics

These platforms are designed for analytical queries over large datasets, OLAP operations, and business intelligence use cases. Modern platforms like Snowflake and Databricks offer cloud-native architectures with advanced features like data sharing, lakehouse capabilities, and serverless operations.

content:
## Key Concepts

Redshift runs as an MPP (massively parallel processing) **cluster**: a **leader node** plans and coordinates queries while **compute nodes**, split into **slices**, store data and execute work in parallel. Two settings drive most performance conversations: the **distribution style/key**, which controls how rows are spread across slices (minimizing data movement during joins), and the **sort key**, which controls on-disk row order within each node (enabling range-restricted scans via zone maps). Data typically enters through the **COPY** command, which loads in parallel from S3 (or DynamoDB/EMR/JDBC), and leaves through **UNLOAD**; both have many tuning options (manifest files, compression, error handling). **VACUUM** reclaims space and re-sorts rows after deletes, while **

title: Redshift
description: Interview questions on Amazon Redshift's cluster architecture, distribution and sort keys, query optimization, data loading, and AWS ecosystem integrations.
content:
ANALYZE** refreshes the statistics the query optimizer relies on. **Redshift Spectrum** extends queries directly onto data sitting in S3 without loading it, and **WLM (Workload Management)** governs concurrency and resource allocation across query queues. Redshift is built for OLAP, not OLTP — updates/deletes work but aren't its strength, and durability comes from automated snapshots to S3.

## Common Interview Scenarios

- **"A query against a large fact table has gotten slow — how do you approach it?"** Read the `EXPLAIN` plan for redistribution versus broadcast in joins, check whether the sort and distribution keys still match the query pattern, and confirm statistics are fresh (`ANALYZE`) and dead rows are reclaimed (`VACUUM`).
- **"Design a distribution and sort key strategy for a star schema fact table."** Distribute on the key most frequently joined against a large dimension (or use `ALL` for small dimensions), sort on the most common range filter such as a date column, and discuss the skew-versus-join-locality trade-off.

ult tolerance, staging-table-plus-atomic-swap patterns, and compression encoding.

## Snowflake: Cloud Data Warehouse Architecture

**Snowflake is a cloud-native data warehouse whose defining trait is the separation of storage, compute, and services into independently scalable layers — the source of most of its performance, concurrency, and cost-management interview questions.**

title: Snowflake
description: Interview questions on Snowflake's cloud architecture, virtual warehouses, query performance, data loading, and role-based security for data engineers.
content:
## Key Concepts

Snowflake's architecture splits into three layers: **cloud storage** (columnar data on S3/Blob/GCS), **compute** (elastic virtual warehouses that read that data), and **services** (SQL compilation, metadata, and access control). Because compute and storage scale independently, multiple warehouses can query the same data concurrently without contention — the basis for Snowflake's "unlimited concurrency" claims. Performance features build on this split: **result caching** and **metadata caching** avoid recomputation entirely, while **clustering keys** control the physical layout of micro-partitions so filtered queries scan less data. Operationally, **auto-suspend/auto-scaling** control cost, and **time travel**, **fail-safe**, and **zero-copy cloning** provide low-cost recov

description: Interview questions on Snowflake's cloud architecture, virtual warehouses, query performance, data loading, and role-based security for data engineers.
content:
ery and environment duplication because they operate on metadata pointers rather than copying data. Security follows a standard **RBAC** model (roles → privileges → objects) layered with encryption at rest/in transit, dynamic data masking, and row/column-level access policies.

### Architecture & Storage

<QuestionList topic="Snowflake Architecture" storagePrefix="snowflake-architecture">

<QuestionCard id="snow-arch-01" number={1} question="What is Snowflake?" difficulty="easy" topic="Fundamentals">
Snowflake is a cloud-native, fully managed data warehouse that supports structured and semi-structured data with elastic scalability and shared infrastructure. It's delivered as a SaaS product — there's no hardware or software to install or manage — and runs on top of AWS, Azure, or GCP.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="snow-arch-02" number={2} question="What are the key benefits of Snowflake?" difficulty="easy" topic="Fundamentals">
Key benefits include:

- Elastic scalability (compute scales independently of storage)
- Pay-per-use pricing (pay for compute you act

ually run and storage you actually use)
- Zero maintenance (no patching, tuning, or hardware management)
- Native data sharing capabilities
- Multi-cloud support (AWS, Azure, GCP)
- Strong out-of-the-box query performance
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="snow-arch-03" number={3} question="What is the Snowflake architecture?" difficulty="medium" topic="Architecture">
Snowflake uses a multi-cluster, shared data architecture that separates storage, compute, and services layers. All compute clusters read from the same central storage, so scaling one layer doesn't require scaling the others — this is the core architectural difference from traditional MPP warehouses where storage and compute are coupled to the same nodes.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="snow-arch-04" number={4} question="Wh

at are the three layers of Snowflake?" difficulty="medium" topic="Architecture">
- **Cloud storage** — persists data, in columnar format, on the underlying cloud provider's object storage
- **Compute** — virtual warehouses that execute queries against that data
- **Services** — SQL compilation, query optimization, metadata management, and security/access control

Each layer scales independently, which is what enables Snowflake's concurrency and elasticity.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="snow-arch-05" number={5} question="What is the cloud storage layer in Snowflake?" difficulty="easy" topic="Storage">
The cloud storage layer stores data in a compressed, columnar format on cloud object storage (S3, Azure Blob, or GCS), providing durability and high availability. Snowflake manages the ph

<QuestionCard id="snow-arch-06" number={6} question="What is the compute layer in Snowflake?" difficulty="easy" topic="Compute">
The compute layer consists of virtual warehouses — clusters of compute resources that execute queries against data in storage — scaling independently from storage. Multiple warehouses can query the same data simultaneously without competing for resources, since each warehouse gets its own dedicated compute.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="snow-arch-07" number={7} question="What is the services layer in Snowflake?" difficulty="easy" topic="Services">
The services layer handles SQL compilation, metadata management, access control, and query

optimization. It coordinates everything that isn't raw data storage or query execution — authentication, transaction management, and the metadata Snowflake uses to plan and optimize queries.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="snow-arch-08" number={8} question="What are virtual warehouses in Snowflake?" difficulty="medium" topic="Warehouses">
Virtual warehouses are compute clusters that process queries, with sizes ranging from X-Small to 6XL, sized based on concurrent users and query complexity. Each size roughly doubles the compute (and cost) of the size below it, and warehouses can be started, stopped, and resized independently of one another.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="snow-arch-09" number={9} question="How do you size a virtual warehouse?" difficulty="medium" topic="Warehouses">

Warehouse sizing depends on query complexity, concurrency requirements, and performance expectations. The general approach is to start conservative (a smaller size) and scale up only if queries are queuing or running too slowly — oversizing wastes money since larger warehouses cost proportionally more regardless of whether they're fully utilized.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="snow-arch-10" number={10} question="What is warehouse auto-scaling in Snowflake?" difficulty="medium" topic="Warehouses">
Auto-scaling automatically adjusts the number of warehouse clusters (multi-cluster warehouses) based on query queue depth and load, optimizing cost and performance. This is distinct from warehouse *sizing* — auto-scaling adds or removes parallel clusters of the same size to absorb concurrency

<QuestionCard id="snow-arch-11" number={11} question="What is warehouse auto-suspend in Snowflake?" difficulty="easy" topic="Warehouses">
Auto-suspend automatically stops a warehouse after a specified idle period, reducing costs when the warehouse is not in use. Since compute is billed per-second while running, tuning auto-suspend aggressively is one of the simplest cost-control levers available.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="snow-arch-12" number={12} question="How does Snowflake handle concurrency?" difficulty="medium" topic="Concurrency">
Snowflake supports high concurrency through its architecture, allowing multiple warehouses and queries to run against shared data without performance degradation, because

### Performance & Optimization

<QuestionList topic="Snowflake Performance" storagePrefix="snowflake-performance">

<QuestionCard id="snow-perf-01" number={19} question="What is query performance monitoring in Snowflake?" difficulty="medium" topic="Monitoring">
Query performance monitoring involves analyzing query statistics, execution plans, and metrics through the Query Profile and web UI (or `QUERY_HISTORY`/`ACCOUNT_USAGE` views), letting you see where time was spent — scanning, joining, spilling to disk, or waiting in a queue.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="snow-perf-02" number={20} question="How do you optimize Snowflake queries?" difficulty="medium" topic="Optimization">
Optimization techniques include using clustering keys on large, frequently filtered tables, materialized views

title: Snowflake

content:
for expensive repeated aggregations, relying on query result caching for identical repeated queries, and right-sizing warehouses so queries aren't starved for compute or spilling to local/remote disk.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="snow-perf-03" number={21} question="What are clustering keys in Snowflake?" difficulty="medium" topic="Clustering">
Clustering keys define the sort order and physical layout of data across a table's micro-partitions, improving query performance for filtered queries. They're most useful on very large tables where the natural insertion order doesn't align with common filter columns.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="snow-perf-04" number={22} question="What is the purpose of clustering in Snowflake?" difficulty="medium" topic="Clustering">
Clustering optimize

content:
s data layout for faster filtering and scanning, reducing the amount of data read during query execution through better "pruning" — Snowflake can skip entire micro-partitions that fall outside a query's filter range instead of scanning them.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="snow-perf-05" number={23} question="What is Snowflake result caching?" difficulty="medium" topic="Caching">
Result caching stores query results, returning cached results instantly for identical queries executed within a time window (up to 24 hours), without re-running any compute — provided the underlying data hasn't changed and the query text matches exactly.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="snow-perf-06" number={24} question="What are the benefits of result caching?" difficulty="easy" topic="Caching">
Benefits inc

lude faster query response times, reduced computation costs (no warehouse credits consumed for a cache hit), and improved user experience for dashboards or reports that re-run the same queries repeatedly.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="snow-perf-07" number={25} question="What is query caching in Snowflake?" difficulty="medium" topic="Caching">
"Query caching" is often used as an umbrella term combining result caching, metadata caching, and local disk (warehouse) caching — together these layers accelerate repeated or related query execution at different levels of the stack.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="snow-perf-08" number={26} question="How does Snowflake handle metadata?" difficulty="medium" topic="Metadata">
Snowflake maintains metadata in the services layer, tracking table str

ucture, micro-partition statistics (min/max values, row counts), and data distribution — this metadata is what the query optimizer uses to prune partitions and generate execution plans without scanning the raw data first.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="snow-perf-09" number={27} question="What is Snowflake metadata caching?" difficulty="medium" topic="Metadata">
Metadata caching stores information about table structure and statistics in the services layer, enabling faster query planning and optimization — some simple queries (like `COUNT(*)` on an unfiltered table) can even be answered from metadata alone, without touching a warehouse.

## Bigtable: Google's Wide-Column NoSQL Database

**Google Cloud Bigtable is a fully managed, wide-column NoSQL database built for massive, low-latency workloads — its interview questions center on how row-key design drives performance, since Bigtable provides no secondary indexes, no automatic query optimization, and no joins to fall back on.**

content:
## Key Concepts

Bigtable's data model is a sparse, distributed, **multi-dimensional sorted map**: every cell is addressed by a **row key**, a **column key** (grouped into column families), and a **timestamp** for versioning. Because rows are stored in row-key sort order and Bigtable has **no secondary indexes** and **no automatic query optimization**, the row key is the single most consequential design decision — it determines both read efficiency (range scans work only along the key) and write distribution (poorly chosen keys, especially monotonically increasing ones, create **hotspots**). Architecturally, a table is split into **tablets**, each served by exactly one **tablet server**, with a **master server** handling tablet assignment and load balancing while actual bytes live on **Col

title: Bigtable
description: Interview questions on Google Cloud Bigtable's row-key design, tablets, compaction, replication, access control, and integration with Spark and BI tools.
content:
ossus**, Google's distributed file system. Writes land in an in-memory **memstore** before flushing to immutable sorted files, and **compaction** periodically merges those files while **Bloom filters** skip unnecessary disk reads. Bigtable offers **no ACID transactions** beyond atomic single-row read-modify-write operations, replicates across clusters with **eventual consistency** and last-writer-wins conflict resolution, and delegates access control to **Cloud IAM**.

## Cassandra: Distributed Wide-Column NoSQL Database

**Apache Cassandra is a masterless, peer-to-peer wide-column database built for write-heavy workloads at massive scale — its interview questions center on how the write path, tunable consistency, and replication strategy trade off availability, consistency, and performance.**

title: Cassandra
description: Interview questions on Cassandra's peer-to-peer architecture, data modeling, tunable consistency, replication, and compaction for a wide-column NoSQL database.
content:
## Key Concepts

Cassandra has no leader or master — every node is a peer in a **ring**, communicating via gossip, which is what removes the single point of failure. Data is organized as **keyspace → column family (table) → row → column**, addressed by a **partition key** (determines which node owns the data) and optional **clustering columns** (order rows within a partition), and queried with **CQL**, a SQL-like language. Writes follow a fixed path: append to the **commit log** (crash recovery), write to the in-memory **memtable**, then periodically flush to an immutable **SSTable** on disk; **compaction** later merges SSTables, and **Bloom filters** avoid unnecessary disk reads. Deletes don't remove data immediately — they write a **tombstone** that's cleared during compaction. Cassandra

title: Cassandra
description: Interview questions on Cassandra's peer-to-peer architecture, data modeling, tunable consistency, replication, and compaction for a wide-column NoSQL database.
content:
's signature feature is **tunable consistency**: per-query read/write consistency levels (`ONE`, `QUORUM`, `ALL`, `LOCAL_*`) let you trade off latency against the strong-consistency condition `R + W > N`. This makes Cassandra an **AP** system under the CAP theorem — it favors availability and partition tolerance over strict consistency, and it deliberately has no joins or ACID transactions, pushing denormalization-heavy, query-pattern-first modeling onto the schema design.

## DynamoDB: Managed NoSQL Database

**DynamoDB is AWS's fully managed, serverless NoSQL database — its entire design (keys, indexes, capacity, consistency) is built around one constraint: you must know your access patterns before you model your data, not after.**

title: DynamoDB
description: Interview questions covering DynamoDB tables, partition and sort keys, capacity modes, secondary indexes, consistency, and access-pattern-first query design.
content:
## Key Concepts

Every DynamoDB table is built around a **primary key** — either a simple partition key, or a composite key combining a **partition key** (which determines physical data distribution via hashing) with a **sort key** (which orders items within a partition and enables range queries). This key design is the single most consequential modeling decision in DynamoDB, because unlike a relational database you can't easily bolt on new access patterns later — you address that with **secondary indexes**: Local Secondary Indexes (alternate sort keys within the same partition) and Global Secondary Indexes (alternate partition/sort keys across the whole table, with their own capacity). Reads come in two flavors, **`Query`** (efficient, targets a specific partition via its key) and **`Scan

title: DynamoDB
description: Interview questions covering DynamoDB tables, partition and sort keys, capacity modes, secondary indexes, consistency, and access-pattern-first query design.
content:
`** (reads every item, inefficient at scale), and in two consistency levels, **eventually consistent** (cheaper, may briefly return stale data) and **strongly consistent** (costs more, always current). Capacity is either **provisioned** (reserved throughput, cost-predictable) or **on-demand** (pay-per-request, better for spiky/unpredictable workloads), and both are vulnerable to **hot partitions** if the partition key doesn't distribute traffic evenly.

### Tables, Keys & Capacity Model

<QuestionList topic="DynamoDB Data Model" storagePrefix="dynamodb-data-model">

<QuestionCard id="ddb-core-01" number={1} question="What is DynamoDB?" difficulty="easy" topic="Fundamentals">
DynamoDB is a fully managed, serverless NoSQL database service provided by AWS that handles large-scale, high-performance distributed workloads.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="ddb-core-02" number={2} question="What are the key characteristics of DynamoDB?" difficulty="easy" topic="Fundamentals">
Serverless, fully managed, highly scalable, low latency, built-in replication across availability zones, automatic backup, and pay-per-request pricing.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="ddb-core-03" number={3} question="What is the difference between DynamoDB and relation

description: Interview questions covering DynamoDB tables, partition and sort keys, capacity modes, secondary indexes, consistency, and access-pattern-first query design.
content:
al databases?" difficulty="easy" topic="Fundamentals">
DynamoDB is NoSQL — flexible schema, horizontal scaling by design — while relational databases use a fixed schema and traditionally scale vertically. DynamoDB also requires you to design around known access patterns upfront, rather than querying flexibly with joins after the fact.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="ddb-core-04" number={4} question="What is a DynamoDB table?" difficulty="easy" topic="Fundamentals">
A DynamoDB table is a collection of items (records) with attributes (columns), identified by a unique primary key.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="ddb-core-05" number={5} question="What is a partition key in DynamoDB?" difficulty="easy" topic="Keys">
The partition key (hash key) determines which physical partition stores a

content:
n item, based on a hash of the key's value. It's the primary lever for how evenly data and traffic spread across DynamoDB's underlying storage.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="ddb-core-06" number={6} question="What is a sort key in DynamoDB?" difficulty="easy" topic="Keys">
The sort key (range key) orders items within a partition, allowing range queries (e.g., "all orders for this customer between two dates") on items that share the same partition key.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="ddb-core-07" number={7} question="What is the difference between partition key and sort key?" difficulty="easy" topic="Keys">
The partition key distributes data across partitions; the sort key orders data within a single partition. Together they form a composite key that supports both distribution and ri

content:
ch per-partition querying.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="ddb-core-08" number={8} question="What is a composite key in DynamoDB?" difficulty="medium" topic="Keys">
A composite key combines a partition key and a sort key, enabling efficient queries on both dimensions — items are distributed by partition key, then queryable and orderable by sort key within that partition.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="ddb-core-09" number={9} question="What is throughput in DynamoDB?" difficulty="easy" topic="Capacity">
Throughput measures a table's read/write capacity — how many read and write operations per second the table can handle, expressed in read and write capacity units.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="ddb-core-10" number={10} question="What is a read capacity unit in DynamoDB?" difficul

One RCU (read capacity unit) equals one strongly consistent read per second, or two eventually consistent reads per second, for items up to 4KB. Larger items consume proportionally more RCUs.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="ddb-core-11" number={11} question="What is a write capacity unit in DynamoDB?" difficulty="medium" topic="Capacity">
One WCU (write capacity unit) equals one write per second for items up to 1KB. Larger items consume proportionally more WCUs.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="ddb-core-12" number={12} question="What is on-demand billing in DynamoDB?" difficulty="easy" topic="Capacity">
A pay-per-request pricing model: you pay for actual reads/writes performed, without provisioning capacity upfront — well suited to unpredictable or spiky

traffic.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="ddb-core-13" number={13} question="What is provisioned billing in DynamoDB?" difficulty="easy" topic="Capacity">
You reserve read/write capacity upfront and pay a fixed rate for it. Better for predictable, steady workloads where you can forecast throughput and want lower, stable costs.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="ddb-core-14" number={14} question="How do you handle hot partitions in DynamoDB?" difficulty="hard" topic="Performance">
Use better partition key design (higher-cardinality, evenly-distributed keys, possibly with a random or calculated suffix to spread "hot" items), implement DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) as an in-memory cache to absorb read pressure, or switch to on-demand billing so the table can adapt to spikes automatically.

Auto scaling automatically adjusts provisioned capacity up or down based on actual traffic patterns, within limits you configure — it keeps provisioned mode responsive to changing load without manual intervention.

content:
### Indexes, Queries & Advanced Features

<QuestionList topic="DynamoDB Queries" storagePrefix="dynamodb-queries">

<QuestionCard id="ddb-query-01" number={16} question="What are secondary indexes in DynamoDB?" difficulty="medium" topic="Indexes">
Secondary indexes let you query on non-key attributes, providing flexible access patterns beyond what the table's primary key alone supports — DynamoDB offers two kinds: Local Secondary Indexes and Global Secondary Indexes.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="ddb-query-02" number={17} question="What is a Global Secondary Index?" difficulty="medium" topic="Indexes">
A GSI lets you query on a different partition key (and optional sort key) than the base table, across the entire table, with its own provisioned throughput independent of the base table

title: DynamoDB
description: Interview questions covering DynamoDB tables, partition and sort keys, capacity modes, secondary indexes, consistency, and access-pattern-first query design.
content:
's capacity.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="ddb-query-03" number={18} question="What is a Local Secondary Index?" difficulty="medium" topic="Indexes">
An LSI lets you query using an alternate sort key while keeping the same partition key as the base table, sharing that partition's throughput. It's limited to 10GB of data per partition key value.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="ddb-query-04" number={19} question="What is eventual consistency in DynamoDB?" difficulty="medium" topic="Consistency">
Eventually consistent reads return the most recent write in milliseconds in the common case, but might briefly return stale data if a read hits a replica that hasn't yet received the latest write. It's the default and cheaper read type.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="ddb-query-05" number=

description: Interview questions covering DynamoDB tables, partition and sort keys, capacity modes, secondary indexes, consistency, and access-pattern-first query design.
content:
{20} question="What is strong consistency in DynamoDB?" difficulty="medium" topic="Consistency">
Strongly consistent reads always return the most recent successful write, but consume twice the read capacity of an eventually consistent read and aren't supported on Global Secondary Indexes.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="ddb-query-06" number={21} question="How do you query DynamoDB?" difficulty="medium" topic="Querying">
Use the `Query` API to retrieve items matching a specific partition key value, with optional sort key conditions to narrow the range — this is the efficient, key-driven way to read from DynamoDB.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="ddb-query-07" number={22} question="What is a scan operation in DynamoDB?" difficulty="medium" topic="Querying">
`Scan` reads every item in a
