description: Apache Flume interview questions covering agents, channels, sinks, reliability, interceptors, and how Flume compares to Kafka for log ingestion pipelines.
content:
nel** — stores events in an embedded Derby database
- **FILE Channel** — writes the contents to a file on the file system after reading the event from a source; the file is deleted only after the contents are successfully delivered to the sink

MEMORY Channel is the fastest of the three, but carries the risk of data loss. The channel you choose depends entirely on the nature of the big data application and the value of each event.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="flume-reliability-03" number={11} question="Does Flume provide 100% reliability to the data flow?" difficulty="medium" topic="Reliability">
Yes — Apache Flume provides end-to-end reliability because of its transactional approach to data flow.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="flume-reliability-04" number={12} question="Explain

title: Flume
description: Apache Flume interview questions covering agents, channels, sinks, reliability, interceptors, and how Flume compares to Kafka for log ingestion pipelines.
content:
reliability and failure handling in Apache Flume." difficulty="hard" topic="Reliability">
Flume NG uses channel-based transactions to guarantee reliable message delivery. When a message moves from one agent to another, two transactions are started: one on the agent that delivers the event, and one on the agent that receives it. For the sending agent to commit its transaction, it must receive a success indication from the receiving agent. The receiving agent only returns a success indication once its own transaction commits properly first. This guarantees delivery semantics between every hop the flow makes.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="flume-reliability-05" number={13} question="Explain the replication and multiplexing selectors in Flume." difficulty="hard" topic="Channels">
Channel S

title: Flume
description: Apache Flume interview questions covering agents, channels, sinks, reliability, interceptors, and how Flume compares to Kafka for log ingestion pipelines.
content:
electors are used to handle multiple channels. Based on the Flume header value, an event can be written to just a single channel or to multiple channels. If a channel selector isn't specified for a source, the default is the Replicating selector, which writes the same event to all the channels in the source's channel list. The Multiplexing channel selector is used when the application needs to send different events to different channels.
</QuestionCard>

### Sinks, Integrations & Data Flow

<QuestionList topic="Flume Sinks and Integrations" storagePrefix="flume-sinks">

<QuestionCard id="flume-sinks-01" number={14} question="How can Flume be used with HBase?" difficulty="hard" topic="Sinks">
Apache Flume can be used with HBase using one of two HBase sinks:
- **HBaseSink** (`org.apache.flume.sink.hbase.HBaseSink`) supports secure HBase clusters and also the newer HBase IPC introduced in HBase 0.96.
- **AsyncHBaseSink** (`org.apache.flume.sink.hbase.AsyncHBaseSink`) has better performance than HBaseSink, since it can make non-blocking calls to HBase.

**HBaseSink** converts a Flume Event into HBase Increments or Puts: a serializer implements `HBaseEventSerializer`, which is instantiated when the sink starts. For every event, the sink calls t

title: Flume

content:
he serializer's `initialize` method, which translates the Flume Event into the HBase increments and puts sent to the HBase cluster.

**AsyncHBaseSink** implements `AsyncHBaseEventSerializer`. Its `initialize` method is called only once, when the sink starts. The sink invokes `setEvent` and then calls `getIncrements` and `getActions`, similar to HBaseSink. When the sink stops, the serializer's `cleanUp` method is called.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="flume-sinks-02" number={15} question="Differentiate between FileSink and FileRollSink." difficulty="medium" topic="Sinks">
The major difference is where the events end up: HDFS FileSink writes events into the Hadoop Distributed File System (HDFS), whereas FileRollSink stores events into the local file system.
</QuestionCard>

Yes. It supports multiplexing flows — an event can flow from one source to multiple channels and multiple destinations. This is achieved by defining a flow multiplexer.

## Data Ingestion Patterns: Choosing How Data Arrives

**"Should this be batch or streaming?" is one of the most common design questions in a data engineering interview, and the expected answer is almost never "streaming, obviously". Streaming costs more, is harder to reason about, and is harder to debug — so the strong answer starts by asking what latency the business actually needs, and only then picks a pattern. Candidates who reach for Kafka before asking that question are giving away the wrong signal.**

content:
## Key Concepts

The patterns sit on a **latency spectrum**, and each step down costs money and complexity: **batch** (hours to days), **micro-batch** (seconds to minutes), **streaming** (sub-second to seconds), and **real-time** in the strict sense (guaranteed millisecond response, which is an operational-systems property rather than an analytics one).

The distinction that matters technically is **bounded versus unbounded** data. A batch job knows its input is finite — it can sort, aggregate globally, and finish. A streaming job processes an unbounded sequence, so "the total" is never final, which is why streaming needs windows, watermarks and a decision about what to do with late data. That's the real source of streaming's difficulty, not the infrastructure.

The practical framing for i

title: Data Ingestion Patterns
description: Interview questions on batch, streaming, real-time, micro-batch and hybrid ingestion patterns — including Lambda and Kappa architectures, delivery semantics, backpressure and choosing the right latency for a pipeline.
content:
nterviews: **latency requirement drives the pattern, not the other way round.** A daily report needs batch. A fraud check needs streaming. Most things in between are served well by micro-batch, which is why Spark Structured Streaming and hourly incremental loads cover so much real-world ground.

title: Data Ingestion Patterns
description: Interview questions on batch, streaming, real-time, micro-batch and hybrid ingestion patterns — including Lambda and Kappa architectures, delivery semantics, backpressure and choosing the right latency for a pipeline.
content:
## Batch Ingestion

<QuestionList topic="Batch Ingestion" storagePrefix="ingestion-batch">

<QuestionCard id="ing-batch-01" number={1} question="What is batch ingestion, and when is it the right choice?" difficulty="easy" topic="Batch">
Processing data in bounded chunks on a schedule — hourly, daily, or triggered by arrival of a complete file.

It's the right choice when:
- **Consumers don't need fresher data.** A daily executive report gains nothing from second-level latency.
- **The source is naturally batch** — a partner's nightly file drop, a monthly billing extract.
- **The computation needs the whole set** — global ranking, deduplication across everything, a full reconciliation.
- **Cost matters** — batch uses ephemeral compute that scales to zero between runs, where streaming pays f

title: Data Ingestion Patterns
description: Interview questions on batch, streaming, real-time, micro-batch and hybrid ingestion patterns — including Lambda and Kappa architectures, delivery semantics, backpressure and choosing the right latency for a pipeline.
content:
or always-on infrastructure.
- **Simplicity matters** — reruns are trivial, debugging is straightforward, and backfills are just another run.

The honest default: **batch unless there's a stated latency requirement that batch can't meet.** It's cheaper, simpler, easier to test and far easier to operate, and a large proportion of "we need streaming" turns out to mean "we need hourly".
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="ing-batch-02" number={2} question="What are the common batch ingestion patterns?" difficulty="medium" topic="Batch">
- **Full snapshot** — copy everything each run and replace the target. Simple and self-healing; a bad run is corrected by the next one. Impractical past a certain volume.
- **Incremental by watermark** — pull rows where `updated_at` exceeds the last high-water

title: Data Ingestion Patterns
description: Interview questions on batch, streaming, real-time, micro-batch and hybrid ingestion patterns — including Lambda and Kappa architectures, delivery semantics, backpressure and choosing the right latency for a pipeline.
content:
mark, then advance it after success. Cheap; **misses deletes**, and depends on the source maintaining that column honestly.
- **Partition overwrite** — re-process and replace whole partitions (usually a date). Idempotent by construction, which is why it's the workhorse of most lakes.
- **Append-only** — add new immutable records, never update. Ideal for event data.
- **Snapshot plus CDC** — an initial bulk load, then change capture keeps it current.

The pattern to default to is **partition overwrite**: re-running a date replaces rather than duplicates, so retries and backfills are safe without any extra machinery.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="ing-batch-03" number={3} question="How do you handle late-arriving data in batch?" difficulty="hard" topic="Batch">
Data for Monday can arrive

title: Data Ingestion Patterns
description: Interview questions on batch, streaming, real-time, micro-batch and hybrid ingestion patterns — including Lambda and Kappa architectures, delivery semantics, backpressure and choosing the right latency for a pipeline.
content:
on Wednesday — a partner resends a corrected file, a mobile client uploads after being offline, an upstream job reruns.

The approaches:
- **Partition by event date, not ingestion date**, and re-process the affected partition when late data appears. Correct, and the reason partition overwrite matters.
- **A rolling reprocess window** — every run also reprocesses the last N days, so late arrivals are absorbed automatically at bounded cost.
- **Two timestamps on every row** — `event_time` and `ingested_at` — so consumers can distinguish "when it happened" from "when we learned about it", and so a reconciliation can find rows that arrived late.
- **Late-arrival alerting**, so a source that starts arriving days late is visible rather than silently distorting recent numbers.

The failure to av

title: Data Ingestion Patterns
description: Interview questions on batch, streaming, real-time, micro-batch and hybrid ingestion patterns — including Lambda and Kappa architectures, delivery semantics, backpressure and choosing the right latency for a pipeline.
content:
oid is partitioning by **ingestion** date and reporting on it — then Monday's late data appears in Wednesday's numbers and both days are wrong, with nothing erroring.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

title: Data Ingestion Patterns
description: Interview questions on batch, streaming, real-time, micro-batch and hybrid ingestion patterns — including Lambda and Kappa architectures, delivery semantics, backpressure and choosing the right latency for a pipeline.
content:
## Streaming Ingestion

<QuestionList topic="Streaming Ingestion" storagePrefix="ingestion-streaming">

<QuestionCard id="ing-str-01" number={1} question="What is streaming ingestion, and what does it actually require?" difficulty="medium" topic="Streaming">
Continuous processing of an unbounded sequence of events as they arrive, typically through a durable log — Kafka, Kinesis, Pub/Sub, Event Hubs — with consumers processing and committing offsets.

What it requires beyond a message bus:
- **A decision about time** — event time versus processing time, and windows to make an unbounded stream aggregable.
- **Watermarks and a late-data policy**, because events arrive out of order.
- **Idempotent sinks**, because delivery is at-least-once.
- **Checkpointing** so a restart resumes rather than

title: Data Ingestion Patterns
description: Interview questions on batch, streaming, real-time, micro-batch and hybrid ingestion patterns — including Lambda and Kappa architectures, delivery semantics, backpressure and choosing the right latency for a pipeline.
content:
replays everything.
- **Always-on infrastructure**, monitored continuously, with on-call implications a nightly batch job doesn't have.

The point worth making: the message bus is the easy part. The hard parts are **correctness under out-of-order and late data**, and the operational burden of a system that's never idle.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="ing-str-02" number={2} question="What are the delivery semantics, and which can you actually get?" difficulty="hard" topic="Streaming">
- **At-most-once** — send and forget. Fast, and messages can be lost. Acceptable only for disposable telemetry.
- **At-least-once** — retry until acknowledged. **No loss, but duplicates.** The default nearly everywhere.
- **Exactly-once** — each message affects the result once. Strictly impossible across a

title: Data Ingestion Patterns
description: Interview questions on batch, streaming, real-time, micro-batch and hybrid ingestion patterns — including Lambda and Kappa architectures, delivery semantics, backpressure and choosing the right latency for a pipeline.
content:
network in the general case.

What "exactly-once" means in practice is **effectively-once**: at-least-once delivery combined with **idempotent processing**, so duplicates don't change the outcome. Mechanisms: a deterministic key with an upsert or `MERGE`, a dedup table keyed on `stream+partition+offset`, or transactional checkpointing where the offset commit and the output write are atomic (Flink checkpoints, Kafka transactions).

The strong answer states plainly that you **design the sink to be idempotent** rather than trying to make delivery perfect — because retries, restarts and replays will happen regardless.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="ing-str-03" number={3} question="What is backpressure, and how do you handle it?" difficulty="hard" topic="Streaming">
When a downstream stage

title: Data Ingestion Patterns
description: Interview questions on batch, streaming, real-time, micro-batch and hybrid ingestion patterns — including Lambda and Kappa architectures, delivery semantics, backpressure and choosing the right latency for a pipeline.
content:
can't keep up with the rate arriving, work accumulates. Unhandled, it means growing memory, growing lag, and eventually a crash or data loss.

Handling it:
- **Pull-based consumption** — the consumer requests what it can handle, which is why Kafka and Kinesis consumers pull rather than being pushed to. This is backpressure by design.
- **Buffering in the durable log** — the broker's retention absorbs bursts, which is a large part of why you put a log in front of processing at all.
- **Autoscaling consumers** on lag, not CPU. Consumer lag is the correct signal.
- **Rate limiting or load shedding** where dropping is acceptable.
- **Framework-level backpressure** — Flink propagates it upstream automatically; Spark's `maxOffsetsPerTrigger` bounds each micro-batch.

The metric to monitor is **

title: Data Ingestion Patterns
description: Interview questions on batch, streaming, real-time, micro-batch and hybrid ingestion patterns — including Lambda and Kappa architectures, delivery semantics, backpressure and choosing the right latency for a pipeline.
content:
consumer lag**, and the alert should be on lag *trend*, not absolute value — steadily growing lag means you'll never catch up, which is the real failure.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="ing-str-04" number={4} question="When is streaming genuinely the right answer?" difficulty="medium" topic="Streaming">
When the **value of the data decays in seconds or minutes**:

- **Fraud and anomaly detection** — a decision after the transaction completes is worthless.
- **Real-time personalisation** — recommendations reacting to the current session.
- **Operational monitoring and alerting** on live systems.
- **Dynamic pricing and inventory** where stale numbers cause overselling.
- **IoT and telemetry** where the volume makes batching impractical anyway.
- **Event-driven microservice integration**,

title: Data Ingestion Patterns
description: Interview questions on batch, streaming, real-time, micro-batch and hybrid ingestion patterns — including Lambda and Kappa architectures, delivery semantics, backpressure and choosing the right latency for a pipeline.
content:
where the stream is the integration mechanism rather than an analytics choice.

And when it isn't: daily and weekly reporting, month-end finance, most ML training, and anything where a human looks at the number once a day.

The question to ask an interviewer — and a genuinely good move — is **"what decision is made with this data, and how quickly?"** That converts a technology debate into a requirements one.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

content:
## Real-Time & Micro-Batch

<QuestionList topic="Real-Time & Micro-Batch" storagePrefix="ingestion-realtime">

<QuestionCard id="ing-rt-01" number={1} question="What is micro-batch, and why is it so widely used?" difficulty="medium" topic="Micro-Batch">
Processing small batches on a short interval — seconds to minutes — so it looks continuous while retaining batch mechanics. Spark Structured Streaming works this way by default, as do frequent incremental loads.

Why it's the pragmatic middle:
- **Batch semantics** — exactly-once through atomic commits, simple reruns, familiar debugging.
- **Better throughput per record** than event-at-a-time, because per-record overhead is amortised.
- **The same code and engine** as your batch pipelines, so one skill set and one codebase.
- **Latency of s

title: Data Ingestion Patterns
description: Interview questions on batch, streaming, real-time, micro-batch and hybrid ingestion patterns — including Lambda and Kappa architectures, delivery semantics, backpressure and choosing the right latency for a pipeline.
content:
econds**, which satisfies the large majority of "real-time" requirements once you ask what they actually mean.

The trade is a latency floor set by the batch interval, and slightly more end-to-end delay than a true event-at-a-time engine like Flink. For most analytics that's irrelevant, which is why micro-batch quietly covers a huge share of production "streaming".
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="ing-rt-02" number={2} question="What does 'real-time' actually mean, and how is it different from streaming?" difficulty="medium" topic="Real-Time">
Strictly, **real-time** means a guaranteed response within a bounded time — a hard deadline, as in control systems. Missing the deadline is a failure, not a delay.

In data engineering the word is used loosely to mean "fast", which causes genuine c

title: Data Ingestion Patterns
description: Interview questions on batch, streaming, real-time, micro-batch and hybrid ingestion patterns — including Lambda and Kappa architectures, delivery semantics, backpressure and choosing the right latency for a pipeline.
content:
onfusion in requirements gathering. Worth separating:

- **Near real-time** — seconds. What most "real-time dashboards" actually need.
- **Streaming** — continuous processing; latency is typically low but not *guaranteed*.
- **Hard real-time** — a bounded guarantee. Analytics systems don't provide this, and shouldn't claim to.

The useful interview move is to **ask what latency the decision requires** rather than accepting "real-time" as a specification. Very often "real-time" means "not tomorrow", and an hourly micro-batch satisfies it at a fraction of the cost and complexity.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="ing-rt-03" number={3} question="How do you serve low-latency queries over streaming data?" difficulty="hard" topic="Real-Time">
Processing fast isn't enough — the serving layer mus

title: Data Ingestion Patterns
description: Interview questions on batch, streaming, real-time, micro-batch and hybrid ingestion patterns — including Lambda and Kappa architectures, delivery semantics, backpressure and choosing the right latency for a pipeline.
content:
t also answer quickly, and a warehouse usually can't at single-digit milliseconds.

Options:
- **A key-value serving store** — DynamoDB, Bigtable, Redis — written by the stream processor, holding current state for point lookups.
- **A real-time OLAP engine** — Apache Druid, Pinot, ClickHouse, or Azure Data Explorer — built for sub-second aggregation over recent high-cardinality data.
- **Materialised views** maintained incrementally by the stream job.
- **A hybrid**: recent data in the fast store, history in the warehouse, unioned at query time.

The architectural point: **the processing pattern and the serving pattern are separate decisions.** Streaming ingestion into a warehouse that takes ten seconds to answer hasn't delivered a real-time product — you need a serving layer designed for

title: Data Ingestion Patterns
description: Interview questions on batch, streaming, real-time, micro-batch and hybrid ingestion patterns — including Lambda and Kappa architectures, delivery semantics, backpressure and choosing the right latency for a pipeline.
content:
the query latency you promised.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

content:
## Hybrid Architectures

<QuestionList topic="Hybrid Architectures" storagePrefix="ingestion-hybrid">

<QuestionCard id="ing-hyb-01" number={1} question="What is the Lambda architecture?" difficulty="hard" topic="Hybrid">
Two parallel paths over the same data:

- **Batch layer** — reprocesses the complete historical dataset periodically, producing accurate, authoritative results.
- **Speed layer** — processes the live stream for low-latency approximate results covering the recent window.
- **Serving layer** — merges both, so queries get accurate history plus fresh recent data.

It solved a real problem when streaming engines couldn't be trusted for correctness: the batch layer guaranteed eventual accuracy while the speed layer provided freshness.

Its well-known cost is **maintaining the s

title: Data Ingestion Patterns
description: Interview questions on batch, streaming, real-time, micro-batch and hybrid ingestion patterns — including Lambda and Kappa architectures, delivery semantics, backpressure and choosing the right latency for a pipeline.
content:
ame business logic twice**, in two codebases and often two languages. They drift, and reconciling batch and streaming numbers that should match becomes a recurring tax. That duplication is precisely what Kappa proposed to remove — and why Lambda is now more a concept to explain than an architecture to propose.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="ing-hyb-02" number={2} question="What is the Kappa architecture, and did it win?" difficulty="hard" topic="Hybrid">
**One path**: everything is a stream. The durable log retains history, and "reprocessing" means replaying the log through a new version of the streaming job. No separate batch layer, no duplicated logic.

It requires a log with long or infinite retention, a stream processor whose semantics you trust for correctness, and enough throughp

title: Data Ingestion Patterns
description: Interview questions on batch, streaming, real-time, micro-batch and hybrid ingestion patterns — including Lambda and Kappa architectures, delivery semantics, backpressure and choosing the right latency for a pipeline.
content:
ut to replay history in reasonable time.

Did it win? **Partly.** The insight — don't maintain two implementations — was correct and is now standard. But few teams run pure Kappa, because replaying years of history through a streaming job is often slower and more expensive than a batch job over columnar files.

What actually emerged is a **third thing**: a lakehouse where the same engine and the same code run in both batch and streaming modes over the same tables — Spark Structured Streaming or Flink writing Delta or Iceberg. You get Kappa's single codebase with batch's efficiency for reprocessing, which is the practical answer to give.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="ing-hyb-03" number={3} question="What is a hybrid ingestion approach in practice?" difficulty="medium" topic="Hybrid">
M

title: Data Ingestion Patterns
description: Interview questions on batch, streaming, real-time, micro-batch and hybrid ingestion patterns — including Lambda and Kappa architectures, delivery semantics, backpressure and choosing the right latency for a pipeline.
content:
ost real platforms are hybrid, not by design purity but because different sources have different needs:

- **CDC streaming** from operational databases for freshness on core entities.
- **Batch file ingestion** from partners who send daily drops, because that's what they send.
- **Event streaming** for clickstream and telemetry.
- **Scheduled API pulls** for third-party SaaS, because their rate limits make streaming impossible.

They converge on a **common landing zone** in an open table format, after which everything downstream is uniform — one transformation layer, one serving layer, regardless of how data arrived.

That convergence is the design point worth articulating: **vary the ingestion pattern per source, standardise everything after it.** Trying to force every source into one pat

title: Data Ingestion Patterns
description: Interview questions on batch, streaming, real-time, micro-batch and hybrid ingestion patterns — including Lambda and Kappa architectures, delivery semantics, backpressure and choosing the right latency for a pipeline.
content:
tern produces either unnecessary streaming infrastructure or unnecessarily stale core data.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="ing-hyb-04" number={4} question="How do you decide the ingestion pattern for a new source?" difficulty="medium" topic="Hybrid">
Work through five questions, in order:

1. **What decision does this data drive, and how fast?** This sets the latency requirement, and it's the only question that genuinely determines the pattern.
2. **What can the source actually produce?** A partner's nightly SFTP drop cannot be streamed, whatever you'd prefer.
3. **What volume and shape?** Very high-volume telemetry may need streaming simply because batching it is impractical.
4. **Do you need deletes and intermediate states?** That points to CDC over a timestamp-based pull.
5. **What

title: Data Ingestion Patterns
description: Interview questions on batch, streaming, real-time, micro-batch and hybrid ingestion patterns — including Lambda and Kappa architectures, delivery semantics, backpressure and choosing the right latency for a pipeline.
content:
can the team operate?** Streaming infrastructure needs on-call coverage; a team of two may be better served by hourly batch that they can actually maintain.

Then default to the **simplest pattern that meets the latency requirement**. The strong candidate reaches for streaming only when questions 1 or 3 force it, and says so explicitly.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

content:
## Common Interview Scenarios

**"Should we build this as batch or streaming?"** — ask what decision the data drives and how quickly. If nobody acts on it within the hour, batch. Volunteering that streaming costs more in infrastructure, complexity and on-call is the part that signals experience.

**"Design ingestion for a system with a database, a clickstream and partner files."** — hybrid by source: CDC for the database, a streaming log for clickstream, event-triggered batch for the files, all converging on one landing zone in an open table format so everything downstream is uniform.

**"Your streaming numbers don't match the batch reconciliation."** — late data dropped beyond allowed lateness, processing-time windows where event-time was needed, or duplicates from at-least-once delivery

title: Data Ingestion Patterns
description: Interview questions on batch, streaming, real-time, micro-batch and hybrid ingestion patterns — including Lambda and Kappa architectures, delivery semantics, backpressure and choosing the right latency for a pipeline.
content:
into a non-idempotent sink. All three are worth checking in that order.

**"Explain Lambda vs Kappa."** — Lambda duplicates logic across batch and speed layers, which is its fatal cost; Kappa unifies on a replayable log. Then note that what actually won is a lakehouse running the same code in both modes over the same tables.

## NiFi: Flow-Based Dataflow Automation

**Apache NiFi automates the movement and light transformation of data between systems through a visual, flow-based programming model built around FlowFiles, processors, and connections.**

title: NiFi
description: Apache NiFi interview questions covering FlowFiles, processors, relationships, backpressure, templates, and clustering for data engineering interviews.
content:
## Key Concepts

Everything in NiFi revolves around the **FlowFile** — a unit of data made up of **content** (the actual bytes, stored separately in a content repository and only referenced by the FlowFile) and **attributes** (key/value metadata describing it). **Processors** are the workhorses that create, route, transform, and move FlowFiles; when a processor finishes with a FlowFile it emits a **relationship** (success, failure, or a custom outcome) that determines where the FlowFile goes next. Connections between processors have configurable **backpressure** limits (by count or size) so a fast producer can't overwhelm a slow consumer. Operationally, NiFi supports **templates** for reusable flows, **bulletins** for surfacing warnings/errors in the UI, a **variable registry** for externa

content:
lizing configuration, and a **zero-master clustering** model coordinated by ZooKeeper (a Cluster Coordinator and a Primary Node are elected, and failover is automatic).

content:
## Interview Questions

<QuestionList topic="NiFi" storagePrefix="nifi">

<QuestionCard id="nifi-01" number={1} question="What is Apache NiFi?" difficulty="easy" topic="Fundamentals">
NiFi is helpful in creating DataFlows. It means you can transfer data from one system to another system, as well as process the data in between.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="nifi-02" number={2} question="What is a NiFi FlowFile?" difficulty="easy" topic="FlowFiles">
A FlowFile is a message, event, or piece of user data that is pushed or created in NiFi. A FlowFile has two main parts attached to it: its content (the actual payload — a stream of bytes) and its attributes (key/value pairs attached to the content, essentially metadata for the content).
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="nifi-03" number={3}

title: NiFi

content:
question="What is a Relationship in a NiFi DataFlow?" difficulty="easy" topic="Processors">
When a processor finishes processing a FlowFile, it can result in a Failure, a Success, or another relationship. Based on this relationship, you can route data to a downstream/next processor or otherwise mediate it accordingly.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="nifi-04" number={4} question="What is a Reporting Task?" difficulty="medium" topic="Monitoring">
A Reporting Task is a NiFi extension point capable of reporting and analyzing NiFi's internal metrics, in order to provide that information to external resources or report status information as bulletins that appear directly in the NiFi User Interface.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="nifi-05" number={5} question="What is a NiFi Processor?" dif

content:
ficulty="easy" topic="Processors">
The Processor is the main component in NiFi that actually works on the FlowFile content, helping create, send, receive, transform, route, split, merge, and otherwise process FlowFiles.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="nifi-06" number={6} question="Is there a programming language that Apache NiFi supports?" difficulty="medium" topic="Extensibility">
NiFi is implemented in the Java programming language and allows extensions (processors, controller services, and reporting tasks) to be implemented in Java. In addition, NiFi supports processors that execute scripts written in Groovy, Jython, and several other popular scripting languages.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="nifi-07" number={7} question="How do you define the NiFi Content Repository?" difficult

y="medium" topic="Architecture">
Contents are not stored in the FlowFile itself. They are stored in the content repository and referenced by the FlowFile. This allows the contents of FlowFiles to be stored independently and efficiently, based on the underlying storage mechanism.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="nifi-08" number={8} question="What is Backpressure in the NiFi system?" difficulty="medium" topic="Flow Control">
Sometimes a producer system is faster than the consumer system, so messages are consumed more slowly than they're produced. All the messages (FlowFiles) that aren't yet processed remain in the connection's buffer. You can limit the connection's backpressure size either by number of FlowFiles or by data size. Once that limit is reached, the connection applies backpressu

re to the producer processor so it stops running — no more FlowFiles are generated until the backpressure is reduced.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="nifi-09" number={9} question="What is a template in NiFi?" difficulty="easy" topic="Templates">
A template is a re-usable workflow that you can import and export within the same or different NiFi instances. It can save a lot of time versus recreating a flow again and again each time. A template is created as an XML file.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="nifi-10" number={10} question="What is bulleting and how does it help in NiFi?" difficulty="medium" topic="Monitoring">
Rather than checking logs for anything interesting, it's much more convenient to have notifications pop up directly on screen. If a Processor logs anything as a WARNING

title: NiFi

content:
or ERROR, a "Bulletin Indicator" shows up in the top-right-hand corner of the Processor. This indicator looks like a sticky note and is shown for five minutes after the event occurs. Hovering over the bulletin shows what happened, so the user doesn't have to sift through log messages to find it. In a cluster, the bulletin also indicates which node emitted it. You can also change the log level at which bulletins occur in the Settings tab of a Processor's Configure dialog.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="nifi-11" number={11} question="Do attributes get added to content (the actual data) when data is pulled by NiFi?" difficulty="medium" topic="FlowFiles">
You can certainly add attributes to your FlowFiles at any time — that's the whole point of separating metadata from the actual data. Ess

entially, one FlowFile represents an object or message moving through NiFi. Each FlowFile contains a piece of content (the actual bytes); you can extract attributes from the content and store them in memory, then operate against those attributes without touching the content. This saves a lot of I/O overhead, making the whole flow management process extremely efficient.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="nifi-12" number={12} question="What happens if you have stored a password in a dataflow and create a template out of it?" difficulty="medium" topic="Security">
Password is a sensitive property. So while exporting the DataFlow as a template, the password is dropped — as soon as you import the template into the same or a different NiFi system, the password will need to be re-entered.

No — from NiFi 1.0 onward, a zero-master philosophy is used, and every node in a NiFi cluster is the same. The NiFi cluster is managed by ZooKeeper: Apache ZooKeeper elects a single node as the Cluster Coordinator, and failover is handled automatically by ZooKeeper. All cluster nodes report heartbeat and status information to the Cluster Coordinator, which is responsible for disconnecting and connecting nodes. Additionally, every cluster has one Primary Node, also elected by ZooKeeper.

## Key Concepts

Airflow models a workflow as a **DAG** (directed acyclic graph): a Python-defined graph of tasks with dependencies, where each task should be **idempotent** so it can safely be retried or backfilled. Four components make this run — the **webserver** (UI), **scheduler** (walks DAGs and triggers tasks), **executor** (decides how/where tasks run), and **workers** (run the tasks) — all backed by a **metadata database** that tracks DAG runs, task state, and configuration. The choice of **executor** (Sequential, Local, Celery, or Kubernetes) is largely a scalability-vs-operational-complexity trade-off. <QuestionList topic="Airflow" storagePrefix="airflow">

<QuestionCard id="af-01" number={1} question="What is Airflow?" difficulty="easy" topic="Fundamentals">
Apache Airflow is an open-source workflow management platform. It began in October 2014 at Airbnb as a solution for managing the company's increasingly complex workflows. Airbnb's creation of Airflow enabled them to programmatically author, schedule, and monitor their workflows via the built-in Airflow user interface. Airflow is a data transformation pipeline ETL (Extract, Transform, Load) workflow orchestration tool.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="af-02" number={2} question="What issues does Airflow resolve compared to cron?" difficulty="easy" topic="Fundamentals">
Cron is an old technique for task sched

content:
uling, and it has real limitations that Airflow addresses:

- **Scalability** — cron requires external tooling to log, track, and manage tasks, while the Airflow UI tracks and monitors workflow execution out of the box.
- **Dependencies** — creating and maintaining a relationship between tasks in cron is a challenge, whereas it's as simple as writing Python code in Airflow.
- **Reproducibility** — cron jobs aren't reproducible unless configured externally; Airflow maintains an audit trail of every task run.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="af-03" number={3} question="Explain how a workflow is designed in Airflow." difficulty="easy" topic="DAGs">
A directed acyclic graph (DAG) is used to design an Airflow workflow. That is to say, when creating a workflow, you consider how it can be divid

The overall logic of your workflow is based on the shape of the graph. An Airflow DAG can have multiple branches, and you can choose which ones to follow and which to skip during workflow execution.

Airflow can be completely stopped, and running workflows will then resume by restarting the last unfinished task. It's important to remember that Airflow tasks can be run more than once when designing them — each task should be **idempotent**, capable of being performed multiple times without causing unintended consequences.

There are four major components to Airflow:

- **Webserver** — the Airflow UI built on Flask, which provides an overview of the overall health of various DAGs and helps visualize their components and states. It also lets you manage users, roles, and configuration.
- **Scheduler** — every few seconds, the scheduler walks over the DAGs and schedules tasks for execution.
- **Executor** — an internal component used by the scheduler. Executors are what actually execute the tasks, while the scheduler orchestrates them. Airflow has different executor types, including `SequentialExecutor`, `LocalExecutor`, `CeleryExecutor`, and `KubernetesExecutor` — teams generally pick whichever is best suited to their use case.
- **Worker** — workers run the tasks that the executor hands them.

The webserver reads DAG state and run history from this database, and the scheduler is what keeps it updated.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="af-05" number={5} question="What are the types of executors in Airflow?" difficulty="medium" topic="Executors">
The executors are the components that actually execute tasks, while the scheduler orchestrates them:

A cron expression is composed of 5 fields separated by spaces:

Breaking down `schedule_interval='30 8 * * 1-5'`:

1. **`30` (Minute)** — the task runs at the 30th minute of the hour (e.g., `08:30` when the hour is `8`).
2. **`8` (Hour)** — the task runs during the 8th hour of the day, so `08:30 AM`.
3. **`*` (Day of Month)** — every day of the month; it doesn't matter whether it's the 1st, 15th, or 30th.
4. **`*` (Month)** — every month.
5. **`1-5` (Day of Week)** — Monday through Friday, skipping weekends.

So this schedule fires at **8:30 AM, Monday through Friday** — for example, Monday Jan 6 2025 at 08:30, Tuesday Jan 7 2025 at 08:30, and so on for every weekday.

## Operators, Hooks & Connections

The building blocks of a task, and how Airflow talks to external systems without hardcoding credentials.

<QuestionList topic="Operators, Hooks & Connections" storagePrefix="airflow-operators">

<QuestionCard id="af-18" number={18} question="What is an operator in Airflow?" difficulty="easy" topic="Operators">
An operator is a template for a single task — it defines *what* work gets done (run a Python function, execute a bash command, run a SQL query, copy a file to S3). A DAG is really a graph of operator instances wired together with dependencies; Airflow ships dozens of built-in operators (`PythonOperator`, `BashOperator`, `PostgresOperator`, `S3ToRedshiftOperator`, etc.) and providers add many more for specific systems.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard

title: Airflow

content:
id="af-19" number={19} question="What is a hook, and how does it relate to a connection?" difficulty="medium" topic="Hooks">
A **connection** stores the credentials and connection details for an external system (host, login, password, extra config) in Airflow's metadata database, referenced by a `conn_id` string rather than hardcoded values. A **hook** is the Python interface that uses a connection to actually talk to that system — `PostgresHook`, `S3Hook`, `SlackHook` — so operators are typically thin wrappers that call a hook under the hood.

```python
from airflow.providers.postgres.hooks.postgres import PostgresHook

hook = PostgresHook(postgres_conn_id="my_warehouse")
rows = hook.get_records("SELECT * FROM orders LIMIT 10")
```
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="af-20" number={20} que

title: Airflow
description: Apache Airflow interview questions covering DAGs, executors, sensors, hooks, the TaskFlow API, dynamic task mapping, branching, and scheduling.
content:
stion="How do you store and use a connection, like a database or S3 credential, in Airflow?" difficulty="easy" topic="Connections">
Connections are created through the Airflow UI (Admin → Connections), the CLI (`airflow connections add`), or environment variables (`AIRFLOW_CONN_*`) — never hardcoded in DAG files. Once stored, any task references it by `conn_id`:

```python
S3Hook(aws_conn_id="my_s3_conn").load_file(filename, key, bucket_name)
```

Storing credentials this way means rotating a password is a one-time change in the connection, not a search-and-replace across every DAG that uses it.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="af-21" number={21} question="How would you write a custom operator?" difficulty="medium" topic="Operators">
Subclass `BaseOperator` and implement `execute()`:

``

title: Airflow

`python
from airflow.models import BaseOperator

class DataQualityCheckOperator(BaseOperator):
    def __init__(self, table_name, min_rows, **kwargs):
        super().__init__(**kwargs)
        self.table_name = table_name
        self.min_rows = min_rows

    def execute(self, context):
        count = PostgresHook().get_first(f"SELECT COUNT(*) FROM {self.table_name}")[0]
        if count < self.min_rows:
            raise ValueError(f"{self.table_name} has only {count} rows, expected >= {self.min_rows}")
```

Write a custom operator when the same multi-step logic (a specific validation, a specific API call pattern) is repeated across many DAGs — it turns copy-pasted task code into one reusable, testable class.
</QuestionCard>

ow Variables, and how do they differ from XComs?" difficulty="easy" topic="Variables">
**Variables** are key-value settings stored in Airflow's metadata database, meant for configuration that's the same across runs — an environment name, a feature flag, a file path prefix. **XComs** are per-run data passed between tasks *within a single DAG run*. The distinction: Variables are static configuration read by (potentially) any DAG; XComs are dynamic data produced and consumed by specific tasks in one run.

```python
from airflow.models import Variable
environment = Variable.get("deployment_environment", default_var="dev")
```

Avoid stuffing large or frequently-changing data into Variables — they're read from the database on every access and aren't designed for that.

## Sensors

Tasks that wait for something to become true before the rest of the DAG proceeds.

<QuestionList topic="Sensors" storagePrefix="airflow-sensors">

<QuestionCard id="af-23" number={23} question="What is a sensor in Airflow, and how does it differ from a regular task?" difficulty="medium" topic="Sensors">
A sensor is a special operator that waits for a condition to become true — a file to land in S3, a partition to appear in a table, another DAG to finish — before letting downstream tasks run. Unlike a regular task that does work and finishes, a sensor's job *is* the waiting; it repeatedly checks (`poke`s) the condition on an interval until it succeeds or times out.

```python
from airflow.sensors.filesystem import FileSensor

wait_for_file = FileSensor(task_id="wait_for_export",

title: Airflow

```
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="af-24" number={24} question="What's the difference between poke mode and reschedule mode for a sensor?" difficulty="hard" topic="Sensors">
In **poke mode** (the default), a sensor occupies a worker slot for its entire wait, repeatedly checking on `poke_interval` — fine for short waits, wasteful for long ones since that slot can't run anything else. In **reschedule mode** (`mode="reschedule"`), the sensor gives up its worker slot between checks and reschedules itself, freeing that slot for other tasks while it waits — much better for sensors that might wait for hours.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="af-25" number={25} question="What is a deferrable operator/sensor, and what problem does it solve?" diff

title: Airflow
description: Apache Airflow interview questions covering DAGs, executors, sensors, hooks, the TaskFlow API, dynamic task mapping, branching, and scheduling.
content:
iculty="hard" topic="Sensors">
A deferrable operator (Airflow 2.2+) suspends itself entirely and hands the waiting off to a separate lightweight **triggerer** process, freeing its worker slot completely rather than just periodically — unlike reschedule mode, which still consumes scheduler/worker resources on each check. This lets a single triggerer process efficiently manage thousands of concurrent waits (for S3 files, external task completion, etc.) that would otherwise each tie up a full worker slot.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="af-26" number={26} question="What is an ExternalTaskSensor used for?" difficulty="medium" topic="Sensors">
`ExternalTaskSensor` waits for a task (or whole DAG) in a *different* DAG to reach a specific state before proceeding — the standard way to express a

## Control Flow: Branching & Trigger Rules

Controlling which tasks actually run, beyond a simple linear chain of dependencies.

<QuestionList topic="Branching & Trigger Rules" storagePrefix="airflow-control">

<QuestionCard id="af-32" number={32} question="How do you set task dependencies in Airflow?" difficulty="easy" topic="Dependencies">
```python
extract >> transform >> load          # extract, then transform, then load
extract >> [transform_a, transform_b] # both run after extract, in parallel
[transform_a, transform_b] >> load    # load waits for both
```

`>>` sets "runs after" (downstream), `<<` sets "runs before" (upstream) — both are shorthand for `.set_downstream()`/`.set_upstream()`. Dependencies can fan out to a list (parallel branches) or fan back in (a task waiting on multi

title: Airflow
description: Apache Airflow interview questions covering DAGs, executors, sensors, hooks, the TaskFlow API, dynamic task mapping, branching, and scheduling.
content:
ple upstream tasks).
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="af-33" number={33} question="How does branching work with BranchPythonOperator?" difficulty="medium" topic="Branching">
```python
from airflow.operators.python import BranchPythonOperator

def choose_path(**context):
    return "path_a" if some_condition else "path_b"   # must return a task_id

branch = BranchPythonOperator(task_id="branch", python_callable=choose_path)
branch >> [path_a, path_b]
```

The branching function returns the `task_id` (or list of ids) that should run next; every other downstream task in that branch point is automatically skipped, not just left unscheduled. This is how a DAG expresses "run path A or path B, never both" based on a runtime condition.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="af-34" number={34} questi

title: Airflow
description: Apache Airflow interview questions covering DAGs, executors, sensors, hooks, the TaskFlow API, dynamic task mapping, branching, and scheduling.
content:
on="What is a ShortCircuitOperator, and how does it differ from branching?" difficulty="medium" topic="Branching">
`ShortCircuitOperator` evaluates a condition and either lets execution continue (all downstream tasks proceed normally) or skips **everything** downstream if it returns falsy — it's an on/off switch for the rest of the DAG, not a choice between multiple paths like `BranchPythonOperator`. Use it for a "should this DAG even continue past this point?" gate (e.g., "were there any new records at all?") rather than routing between alternatives.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="af-35" number={35} question="What are trigger rules, and when would you use one other than the default?" difficulty="hard" topic="Trigger Rules">
A trigger rule decides when a task is eligible to run based o

title: Airflow
description: Apache Airflow interview questions covering DAGs, executors, sensors, hooks, the TaskFlow API, dynamic task mapping, branching, and scheduling.
content:
n the state of its upstream tasks. The default, `all_success`, requires every upstream task to succeed. Common alternatives: `all_done` (run regardless of upstream success/failure — useful for cleanup/notification tasks), `one_failed` (run if any upstream failed — useful for alerting), and `none_failed` (run if nothing failed, even if some upstream tasks were skipped by branching).

```python
notify = PythonOperator(task_id="notify", trigger_rule="all_done", python_callable=send_notification)
```
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

content:
## Scheduling, Backfills & Idempotency

The details behind "when does this actually run," and how re-running past dates is meant to work.

<QuestionList topic="Scheduling & Backfills" storagePrefix="airflow-scheduling">

<QuestionCard id="af-36" number={36} question="What's the difference between execution_date and data_interval in Airflow scheduling?" difficulty="hard" topic="Scheduling">
The older `execution_date` was confusingly named — a DAG scheduled `@daily` for "Jan 2" actually runs *after* Jan 2 ends (processing Jan 2's data), not at the start of Jan 2, which tripped up nearly everyone. Airflow 2.2+ replaced this with explicit `data_interval_start`/`data_interval_end`, naming the time range the run is actually processing, with `logical_date` as the modern (still slightly confusing

title: Airflow
description: Apache Airflow interview questions covering DAGs, executors, sensors, hooks, the TaskFlow API, dynamic task mapping, branching, and scheduling.
content:
but clearer) equivalent of the old term.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="af-37" number={37} question="What's the difference between catchup and backfill?" difficulty="medium" topic="Backfills">
**`catchup`** (a DAG-level setting) controls whether Airflow automatically creates runs for every interval between a DAG's `start_date` and now the first time it's turned on (`catchup=True`) or only starts from the current interval going forward (`catchup=False`, usually what you want). **Backfill** is a manual, on-demand action (`airflow dags backfill`) to (re)run a DAG for a specific past date range — for example, after fixing a bug, to regenerate historical outputs that were wrong.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="af-38" number={38} question="What is an SLA in Airflow, and what happens when

title: Airflow
description: Apache Airflow interview questions covering DAGs, executors, sensors, hooks, the TaskFlow API, dynamic task mapping, branching, and scheduling.
content:
one is missed?" difficulty="medium" topic="SLAs">
An SLA is a maximum expected duration for a task, set via `sla=timedelta(hours=2)`. If a task is still running (or hasn't started) past that threshold relative to the DAG's expected schedule, Airflow logs an SLA miss and can trigger a notification callback — but critically, it does **not** stop or fail the task; it's purely an alerting mechanism, not an enforcement one.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="af-39" number={39} question="What are pools and priority weights used for?" difficulty="hard" topic="Resource Management">
A **pool** caps how many tasks can run concurrently against a shared, limited resource (a database that can only handle 5 concurrent connections, an API with a rate limit) — tasks assigned to that pool queue once its sl

title: Airflow
description: Apache Airflow interview questions covering DAGs, executors, sensors, hooks, the TaskFlow API, dynamic task mapping, branching, and scheduling.
content:
ot limit is reached, regardless of how much broader worker capacity is free. **`priority_weight`** breaks ties among tasks queued for the same pool or worker slots, so higher-priority work (e.g., a time-sensitive report) jumps ahead of lower-priority backlog work competing for the same constrained resource.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

## Operations, Testing & Ecosystem

Running Airflow reliably in production — testing DAGs, alerting, performance, and where it fits among other orchestrators.

<QuestionList topic="Operations & Ecosystem" storagePrefix="airflow-ops">

<QuestionCard id="af-40" number={40} question="How do you unit test an Airflow DAG?" difficulty="medium" topic="Testing">
```python
def test_dag_has_no_import_errors():
    from airflow.models import DagBag
    dagbag = DagBag()
    assert len(dagbag.import_errors) == 0

def test_transform_task_logic():
    # test the underlying Python function directly — no need to run it through Airflow at all
    assert normalize_revenue({"revenue_cents": 1050}) == 10.50
```

Two layers are worth testing: DAG-integrity tests (does it parse without errors, does the expected

title: Airflow
description: Apache Airflow interview questions covering DAGs, executors, sensors, hooks, the TaskFlow API, dynamic task mapping, branching, and scheduling.
content:
task count/structure match) using `DagBag`, and unit tests of the actual business logic inside each task's callable — which, if written well, don't need Airflow at all to test, since they're just plain functions.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="af-41" number={41} question="How do you set up alerting when a task fails?" difficulty="easy" topic="Monitoring">
```python
def notify_slack(context):
    send_slack_message(f"Task {context['task_instance'].task_id} failed")

default_args = {"on_failure_callback": notify_slack}
```

`on_failure_callback` (and `on_success_callback`, `sla_miss_callback`) fire automatically on the relevant event, letting you push a notification to Slack, PagerDuty, or email without polling anything. Set sensible defaults at the DAG level (`default_args`) rather tha

title: Airflow
description: Apache Airflow interview questions covering DAGs, executors, sensors, hooks, the TaskFlow API, dynamic task mapping, branching, and scheduling.
content:
n repeating the callback on every single task.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="af-42" number={42} question="Why does DAG file parsing performance matter, and what's a common mistake that hurts it?" difficulty="hard" topic="Performance">
The scheduler re-parses every DAG file on a regular interval (to pick up code changes) — if a DAG file runs slow or expensive code at **import time** (a database query, an API call, a large computation outside of any task), that cost is paid on every single parse cycle, not once per run, and can meaningfully slow down the whole scheduler across all DAGs. The fix is keeping DAG files themselves lightweight — only DAG/task *definitions* at the top level, with any real work happening inside a task's callable, which only executes when the task actually runs.

title: Airflow
description: Apache Airflow interview questions covering DAGs, executors, sensors, hooks, the TaskFlow API, dynamic task mapping, branching, and scheduling.
content:
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="af-43" number={43} question="How does Airflow compare to Dagster or Prefect?" difficulty="medium" topic="Ecosystem">
Airflow is the most established and widely adopted, with the largest ecosystem of providers/integrations, but its DAG model is comparatively low-level about data (tasks pass small XComs, not first-class typed data assets). **Dagster** is built around "software-defined assets" — it tracks data products themselves, not just task execution, with stronger typing and local testability out of the box. **Prefect** emphasizes a more Pythonic, dynamic flow definition with less rigid DAG structure and easier local development. In practice, Airflow's maturity and ecosystem size are still the main reason it remains the default choice for many teams.
<

description: Apache Airflow interview questions covering DAGs, executors, sensors, hooks, the TaskFlow API, dynamic task mapping, branching, and scheduling.
content:
/QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="af-44" number={44} question="What can you do with the Airflow REST API or CLI that you can't easily do from the UI?" difficulty="easy" topic="Operations">
Both let you script and automate operations that would otherwise require manual clicks: triggering a DAG run with specific config from an external system (`airflow dags trigger` or `POST /dags/{dag_id}/dagRuns`), running backfills, managing connections/variables as part of infrastructure-as-code, and integrating DAG triggers into CI/CD pipelines — anything you want driven programmatically rather than by a person in the browser.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

- **"Walk me through how you'd design a DAG for a daily ETL pipeline."** Talk through breaking the pipeline into idempotent tasks, choosing a `schedule_interval`/cron expression, wiring dependencies, and how retries and backfills would behave given that tasks can run more than once.
- **"A task's output needs to feed into the next task's SQL query — how do you pass it along?"** Reach for XComs (`xcom_push`/`xcom_pull`) and Jinja templating to inject the pulled value directly into a templated field like a SQL statement.

a cluster and more nuanced docs).
- **"A DAG needs to process a variable, unknown-ahead-of-time number of files each run."** This is a dynamic task mapping signal — talk through `.expand()` over a list produced by an upstream task, versus the older workaround of a single task looping internally and losing per-item retry/visibility.

## Kubernetes: Container Orchestration Platform

**Kubernetes is the container orchestration platform that schedules, scales, and heals containerized workloads across a cluster of nodes — and for data engineers it's most often the substrate that runs Airflow's `KubernetesExecutor`, Spark-on-Kubernetes, or other per-task isolated workloads.**

## Key Concepts

Kubernetes schedules **pods** (one or more containers) onto **nodes**, using **requests** and **limits** to control resource usage and the scheduler's placement decisions. **Services** and **Ingress** solve networking: a Service gives a stable address for a set of pods (via a label selector), while Ingress handles L7 HTTP routing and TLS termination from outside the cluster into services. **Namespaces** partition a cluster for multi-team or multi-environment isolation, and **RBAC**, network policies, and admission control are the main security levers. Day-2 operations lean on constructs like **PodDisruptionBudgets** (safe draining), **init containers** (pre-work before the main container starts), **node affinity/nodeSelector** (pod placement), and **Operators** (custom con

trollers that encode operational knowledge for stateful applications). Monitoring and logging typically layer Prometheus and an EFK/ELK-style pipeline on top of the cluster.

## Interview Questions

<QuestionList topic="Kubernetes" storagePrefix="kubernetes">

<QuestionCard id="k8s-01" number={1} question="How do you perform maintenance activity on a K8s node?" difficulty="medium" topic="Cluster Ops">
Whenever security patches are available, the Kubernetes administrator has to apply them to the running containers to prevent vulnerabilities — an unavoidable part of administration. Two commands are used to safely drain a K8s node:

```bash
kubectl cordon <node-name>
kubectl drain <node-name> --ignore-daemonsets
```

`cordon` moves the node into maintenance mode (marks it unschedulable), and `drain` then evicts the pods from the node. Once `drain` succeeds, you can perform maintenance.

Note: if you only need to inspect nodes first, use `kubectl get nodes` to list

title: Kubernetes
description: Kubernetes interview questions covering pods, resource limits, networking, ingress, security, namespaces, operators, and cluster troubleshooting.
content:
all nodes, then `kubectl drain <node-name>` to drain a particular one.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="k8s-02" number={2} question="How do you control the resource usage of a pod?" difficulty="medium" topic="Resource Management">
Resource usage of a pod is controlled with `requests` and `limits`:

- **Request** — the amount of resources requested for a container. If a container exceeds its request, it can be throttled back down to that request.
- **Limit** — an upper cap on the resources a single container can use. If it tries to exceed this limit, it can be terminated if Kubernetes decides another container needs those resources. If you're sensitive to pod restarts, it makes sense to keep the sum of all container resource limits at or below your cluster's total resource capacity.

Exa

content:
mple:

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: demo
spec:
  containers:
    - name: example1
      image: example/example1
      resources:
        requests:
          memory: "256Mi"
          cpu: "250m"
        limits:
          memory: "512Mi"
          cpu: "500m"
```
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="k8s-03" number={3} question="What are the various K8s services running on nodes, and what is the role of each?" difficulty="medium" topic="Architecture">
A K8s cluster mainly consists of two types of nodes: executor (worker) nodes and the master (control plane).

**Executor node services:**
- **kube-proxy** — runs on every node and handles communication of pods within the cluster and to the outside network, maintaining network protocols as pods communicate.
- **kubelet** — a

title: Kubernetes
description: Kubernetes interview questions covering pods, resource limits, networking, ingress, security, namespaces, operators, and cluster troubleshooting.
content:
running service on each node that keeps the node in sync with its configuration (YAML/JSON). Note: kubelet only manages containers created by Kubernetes.

**Master (control plane) services:**
- **kube-apiserver** — the master API service that acts as the entry point to the K8s cluster.
- **kube-scheduler** — schedules pods according to available resources on executor nodes.
- **kube-controller-manager** — a control loop that watches the shared state of the cluster through the API server and makes changes attempting to move the current state toward the desired state.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="k8s-04" number={4} question="What is a PDB (Pod Disruption Budget)?" difficulty="medium" topic="Availability">
A Kubernetes administrator can create a `PodDisruptionBudget` for high availabili

title: Kubernetes
description: Kubernetes interview questions covering pods, resource limits, networking, ingress, security, namespaces, operators, and cluster troubleshooting.
content:
ty of an application. It ensures that the minimum number of running pods is respected, as defined by the `minAvailable` field. This is useful during a drain: the drain will halt until the PDB is respected, ensuring the application's high availability. The following spec shows `minAvailable: 2`, meaning at least 2 pods must remain available even during a voluntary disruption:

```yaml
apiVersion: policy/v1beta1
kind: PodDisruptionBudget
metadata:
  name: zk-pdb
spec:
  minAvailable: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: zookeeper
```
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="k8s-05" number={5} question="What's an init container, and when can it be used?" difficulty="easy" topic="Init Containers">
Init containers set the stage for you before the actual pod's main container(s) start running. Com

mon uses:

- Wait for some condition before starting the app container, with a command like `sleep 60`.
- Clone a git repository into a volume so the main container can use it.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="k8s-06" number={6} question="What is the role of a load balancer in Kubernetes?" difficulty="easy" topic="Networking">
Load balancing distributes incoming traffic across multiple backend servers, which helps ensure the application stays available to users. In Kubernetes, all incoming traffic lands on a single IP address on the load balancer — a way to expose your service outside the cluster — which then routes traffic to a particular pod (via a Service) using an algorithm like round-robin. If a pod goes down, the load balancer is notified so traffic isn't routed to that unavailable

title: Kubernetes
description: Kubernetes interview questions covering pods, resource limits, networking, ingress, security, namespaces, operators, and cluster troubleshooting.
content:
pod. Load balancers in Kubernetes are therefore responsible for distributing incoming traffic across the pods behind a service.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="k8s-07" number={7} question="What can be done to increase Kubernetes security?" difficulty="medium" topic="Security">
- By default, any pod can communicate with any other pod — set up **network policies** to limit this communication between pods.
- Use **RBAC** (role-based access control) to narrow down permissions.
- Use **namespaces** to establish security boundaries.
- Set **admission control policies** to avoid running privileged containers.
- Turn on **audit logging**.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="k8s-08" number={8} question="How do you monitor a Kubernetes cluster?" difficulty="easy" topic="Monitoring">
Prometheus is

commonly used for Kubernetes monitoring. The Prometheus ecosystem consists of multiple components:

- The Prometheus server, which scrapes and stores time-series data.
- Client libraries for instrumenting application code.
- A push gateway for supporting short-lived jobs.
- Special-purpose exporters for services like StatsD, HAProxy, Graphite, etc.
- An alertmanager to handle alerts across various support tools.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="k8s-09" number={9} question="How do you get centralized logs from pods?" difficulty="medium" topic="Logging">
This depends on the application and several other factors. Common logging patterns include:

- Node-level logging agent.
- Streaming sidecar container.
- Sidecar container with a dedicated logging agent.
- Exporting logs directly from the

application.

One common setup: `journalbeat` and `filebeat` run as a DaemonSet, dumping collected logs to a Kafka topic, which is eventually written into the ELK stack. The same result can be achieved with an EFK stack and `fluent-bit`.

<QuestionCard id="k8s-10" number={10} question="How would you turn the following Service into an externally accessible one, and what would the Ingress equivalent look like?" difficulty="hard" topic="Services">

```yaml

  selector:
    app: some-app
  type: LoadBalancer

<QuestionCard id="k8s-11" number={11} question="How do you configure TLS with Ingress?" difficulty="medium" topic="Ingress">
Add `tls` and `secretName` entries to the Ingress spec:

<QuestionCard id="k8s-12" number={12} question="Why use namespa

title: Kubernetes
description: Kubernetes interview questions covering pods, resource limits, networking, ingress, security, namespaces, operators, and cluster troubleshooting.
content:
ces? What is the problem with using only the default namespace?" difficulty="medium" topic="Namespaces">
Using only the default namespace makes it hard, over time, to get an overview of all the applications you manage in your cluster. Namespaces make it easier to organize applications into groups that make sense — for example, a namespace for all monitoring applications and a namespace for all security applications.

Namespaces are also useful for managing Blue/Green environments, where each namespace can hold a different version of an app while still sharing resources in other namespaces (logging, monitoring, etc.).

Another use case is a single cluster shared by multiple teams. Without namespaces, teams can end up stepping on each other — for example, if two teams create an app with the

same name, one overrides the other, since there can't be two apps with the same name in the same namespace.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="k8s-13" number={13} question="In the following ConfigMap, which service and namespace is being referred to?" difficulty="medium" topic="Namespaces">
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: some-configmap
data:
  some_url: silicon.chip
```

This value follows the in-cluster DNS pattern `<service>.<namespace>`, so it's referencing the service **"silicon"** in the namespace called **"chip"**.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="k8s-14" number={14} question="What is an Operator?" difficulty="medium" topic="Operators">
Operators are software extensions to Kubernetes that make use of custom resources to manage applications and their compon

ents. Operators follow Kubernetes principles, notably the control loop.

<QuestionCard id="k8s-15" number={15} question="Why do we need Operators?" difficulty="medium" topic="Operators">
Managing applications in Kubernetes isn't as straightforward for stateful applications as it is for stateless ones, where reaching the desired state and performing upgrades is handled the same way for every replica. In stateful applications, upgrading each replica might require different handling since each replica can be in a different state — traditionally requiring a human operator. A Kubernetes Operator is meant to assist with this, encoding that operational knowledge into software. This also helps automate a standard process across multiple Kubernetes clusters.
</QuestionCard>

onCard id="k8s-16" number={16} question="What is GKE?" difficulty="easy" topic="Cloud">
GKE is Google Kubernetes Engine, a managed service for managing and orchestrating Docker containers. With the help of Google Cloud, it also handles orchestrating the underlying container cluster infrastructure for you.

<QuestionCard id="k8s-17" number={17} question="What is an Ingress default backend?" difficulty="medium" topic="Ingress">
It specifies what to do with an incoming request to the Kubernetes cluster that isn't mapped to any backend — i.e., what happens when no rule matches the incoming HTTP request. If a default backend service isn't defined, it's recommended to define one so users see a meaningful message instead of an unclear error.

<QuestionCard id="k8s-23" number={23} question="How do you run a pod on a particular node?" difficulty="medium" topic="Scheduling">
Several methods are available:

- **`nodeName`** — specify the name of a node directly in the pod spec; it will try to run the pod on that specific node.
- **`nodeSelector`** — assign a specific label to a node with special resources, and use the same label in the pod spec so the pod only runs on nodes with that label.

number={24} question="What are the different ways to provide external network connectivity to K8s?" difficulty="medium" topic="Networking">
By default, a pod can reach the external network, but the reverse requires some setup. Options for connecting to a pod from outside the cluster:

- **NodePort** — exposes one port on each node to communicate with the service.
- **Load balancers** — operate at L4 (TCP/IP).

- **kube-proxy** — can expose a service that only has a cluster IP on the local system's port:

kubectl proxy --port=8080
```

Then access the service via:

```
http://localhost:8080/api/v1/namespaces/<namespace>/services/<service-name>:<port>/proxy/
```

content:
## Apache Flink: Stream Processing Framework

**Flink is a distributed engine built around one idea — that batch is just a special, bounded case of streaming — which is what lets a single runtime handle real-time event processing and large-scale batch jobs with the same execution model.**

title: Flink
description: Apache Flink interview questions covering the stream processing model, JobManager/TaskManager architecture, state, checkpointing, windowing, and watermarks.
content:
## Table of Contents
- [Key Concepts](#key-concepts)

title: Flink
description: Apache Flink interview questions covering the stream processing model, JobManager/TaskManager architecture, state, checkpointing, windowing, and watermarks.
content:
## Key Concepts

Every Flink program follows the same shape — **Source → Transformation → Sink** — executed as a distributed dataflow graph coordinated by a **JobManager** and run by **TaskManagers**, each offering a fixed number of **task slots** that bound how much work it can execute in parallel. Flink distinguishes three notions of time — **event time** (when something actually happened), **ingestion time**, and **processing time** — and uses **watermarks** to reason about how far event time has progressed despite out-of-order arrival, which is what makes **windowing** (tumbling, sliding, session) correct over unbounded streams. For reliability, Flink periodically snapshots operator **state** — held in a pluggable state backend (in-memory, filesystem, or RocksDB) — into **checkpoints**

title: Flink
description: Apache Flink interview questions covering the stream processing model, JobManager/TaskManager architecture, state, checkpointing, windowing, and watermarks.
content:
, using a barrier-based algorithm so a failed job can recover from a consistent point without losing or duplicating results. That checkpointing mechanism, combined with a two-phase-commit protocol at the sinks, is the basis of Flink's end-to-end exactly-once guarantee.
