<QuestionCard id="dbt-11" number={11} question="What are sources in dbt and how do you test them?" difficulty="medium" topic="Testing">
Sources declare upstream tables and their metadata in `sources.yml`. You can test sources with freshness checks and column-level tests (like `not_null`) to detect broken ingestion or schema drift early.

<QuestionCard id="dbt-12" number={12} question="What are snapshots in dbt and when would you use them?" difficulty="medium" topic="Snapshots">
Snapshots capture slowly changing dimension history by tracking changes in source records over time. They are useful when you need point-in-time analysis or to implement SCD2-style history from mutable source tables.

estionCard id="dbt-13" number={13} question="What are macros in dbt and when should you use them?" difficulty="medium" topic="Macros">
Macros are Jinja functions that generate SQL. Use them to avoid repetition (standardized column selection, reusable filters, dynamic SQL) and to keep business logic consistent across models. Overusing macros for complex logic can hurt readability and debugging.

<QuestionCard id="dbt-14" number={14} question="What is dbt state selection?" difficulty="hard" topic="CI/CD">
State selection runs only models that changed (and their dependents) compared to a previous artifact state. In CI, this reduces runtime by avoiding full rebuilds, while still validating that changes compile, run, and pass tests for affected parts of the DAG.

## Seeds, Sources & Project Configuration

The parts of a dbt project that aren't models — static data, environment config, and runtime parameters.

<QuestionList topic="Seeds, Sources & Config" storagePrefix="dbt-config">

<QuestionCard id="dbt-16" number={16} question="What are seeds in dbt, and when should you use one?" difficulty="easy" topic="Seeds">
A seed is a CSV file in the `seeds/` directory that dbt loads into the warehouse as a table via `dbt seed`. They're meant for small, static, rarely-changing reference data you control directly — a country-code-to-region mapping, a list of holiday dates — not for actual source data, which should come from a real ingestion pipeline instead.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dbt-17" number={17} question="What are environments and targets in

dbt (profiles.yml), and why do they matter?" difficulty="medium" topic="Configuration">
A `target` in `profiles.yml` defines a specific connection (dev, staging, prod) — its warehouse, schema, and credentials — and dbt commands run against whichever target is active. This lets the same model code build into a personal dev schema while developing and into the shared production schema when deployed, without changing a single line of SQL.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dbt-18" number={18} question="What are dbt variables, and how do you use them?" difficulty="medium" topic="Configuration">

```sql
{% if var('is_full_refresh', false) %} ... {% endif %}
```
```bash
dbt run --vars '{"start_date": "2024-06-01"}'
```
Variables let you parameterize model logic without hardcoding values — a cutoff date, a feature flag, an environment-specific limit — set as defaults in `dbt_project.yml` and optionally overridden per invocation with `--vars`.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dbt-19" number={19} question="What are exposures, and why declare them?" difficulty="medium" topic="Documentation">
An exposure declares a downstream consumer of dbt models — a BI dashboard, an ML pipeline, a reverse-ETL sync — as a first-class object in `dbt docs`, linked to the specific models it depends on. Declaring them means anyone changing a model ca

content:
n see, right in the DAG/docs, which dashboards or downstream systems that change might break, instead of finding out from an angry Slack message after the dashboard goes blank.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dbt-20" number={20} question="What is the purpose of dbt_project.yml, and what kinds of settings live there?" difficulty="easy" topic="Configuration">
`dbt_project.yml` is the project-wide configuration file — it sets the project name, declares folder paths (`model-paths`, `seed-paths`), and configures default materializations, tags, and variables per directory (e.g., all models under `models/marts/` default to `materialized: table`). Model-level `.yml` files can still override these project-wide defaults for a specific model.

## Materializations & Incremental Strategies

Going deeper than view/table/incremental — the fourth materialization type, and how incremental models actually apply changes.

<QuestionList topic="Materializations & Incremental Strategies" storagePrefix="dbt-materializations">

<QuestionCard id="dbt-21" number={21} question="What is an ephemeral materialization, and when would you use one?" difficulty="medium" topic="Materializations">
An ephemeral model isn't built as its own view or table in the warehouse at all — it's inlined as a CTE into every model that references it via `ref()`. Use it for a small, intermediate transformation step that exists purely to keep upstream models readable and DRY, but that nobody needs to query directly or that doesn't justify the overhead of its own databas

title: DBT
description: dbt interview questions covering models, seeds, materializations, incremental strategies, contracts, Jinja, packages, and the Semantic Layer.
content:
e object.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dbt-22" number={22} question="What incremental strategies does dbt support, and how do you choose between them?" difficulty="hard" topic="Incremental Models">
- **`merge`** (most warehouses) — upserts: updates matching rows on `unique_key`, inserts new ones. The most common choice when the warehouse supports it natively.
- **`delete+insert`** — deletes rows matching the incremental batch's keys, then inserts the new batch. Useful when `merge` isn't available or efficient for the target.
- **`append`** — just inserts new rows, no update/delete logic at all. Only correct when source rows are truly immutable and never revised (pure event logs).

The choice mostly comes down to what the target warehouse supports efficiently and whether source record

description: dbt interview questions covering models, seeds, materializations, incremental strategies, contracts, Jinja, packages, and the Semantic Layer.
content:
s can actually change after the fact.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dbt-23" number={23} question="When and why would you run a full refresh on an incremental model?" difficulty="medium" topic="Incremental Models">
```bash
dbt run --full-refresh --select my_incremental_model
```
A full refresh drops and rebuilds the entire table from scratch instead of processing only new/changed rows — needed when the incremental logic itself changes (a new column, a changed `unique_key`), when you suspect the incremental table has drifted from what the logic would now produce, or the first time a model is ever run.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dbt-24" number={24} question="What are dbt model contracts, and what do they enforce?" difficulty="hard" topic="Contracts">
```yaml
models:
  - name: ord

title: DBT
description: dbt interview questions covering models, seeds, materializations, incremental strategies, contracts, Jinja, packages, and the Semantic Layer.
content:
ers
    config:
      contract: {enforced: true}
    columns:
      - name: order_id
        data_type: string
        constraints: [{type: not_null}]
```
A model contract declares the exact column names, types, and constraints a model must produce — dbt validates the built model against this contract and **fails the build** if reality doesn't match, rather than silently letting a schema change flow downstream. It's the mechanism that turns a data contract (see [Data Quality](/level-2-core-concepts/data-quality/#interview-questions)) from a documented agreement into something dbt itself actively enforces.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dbt-25" number={25} question="What are pre-hooks and post-hooks used for?" difficulty="medium" topic="Hooks">
```yaml
{{ config(
    pre_hook="INSERT IN

description: dbt interview questions covering models, seeds, materializations, incremental strategies, contracts, Jinja, packages, and the Semantic Layer.
content:
TO audit_log (model, started_at) VALUES ('{{ this }}', current_timestamp)",
    post_hook="GRANT SELECT ON {{ this }} TO ROLE analyst"
) }}
```
`pre_hook`/`post_hook` run arbitrary SQL immediately before or after a model builds — common uses are audit logging, granting permissions on the freshly-built table, or refreshing a downstream materialized view. They're an escape hatch for warehouse operations that don't fit naturally into "define a `SELECT` and let dbt build it."

## Jinja & Packages

Templating and reusable code — how dbt generates SQL dynamically and shares logic across projects.

<QuestionList topic="Jinja & Packages" storagePrefix="dbt-jinja">

<QuestionCard id="dbt-26" number={26} question="How do Jinja control structures (if/for) get used inside a dbt model?" difficulty="medium" topic="Jinja">
```sql
SELECT
    order_id,
    {% for status in ["pending", "shipped", "cancelled"] %}
    SUM(CASE WHEN status = '{{ status }}' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS {{ status }}_count{{ "," if not loop.last }}
    {% endfor %}
FROM orders
GROUP BY order_id
```
Jinja `{% %}` blocks run at **compile time**, generating the final SQL text before it's ever sent to the warehouse — a `{% for %}` loop here writes out one `SUM(CASE...)` column per status without hand-typing e

</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dbt-27" number={27} question="What is dbt_utils, and what's an example of a macro from it you'd actually use?" difficulty="medium" topic="Packages">
`dbt_utils` is the most widely-used community package, providing macros for things nearly every project needs but dbt Core doesn't ship natively — `dbt_utils.generate_surrogate_key()` (hash multiple columns into one surrogate key), `dbt_utils.date_spine()` (generate a row per date in a range, useful for a date dimension), and generic tests like `dbt_utils.unique_combination_of_columns`. Reaching for it first avoids reinventing well-tested utility macros from scratch.
</QuestionCard>

number={28} question="How would you write a custom generic test?" difficulty="hard" topic="Testing">
```sql
-- macros/test_is_positive.sql
{% test is_positive(model, column_name) %}
SELECT *
FROM {{ model }}
WHERE {{ column_name }} <= 0
{% endtest %}
```
```yaml
columns:
  - name: amount
    tests: [is_positive]
```
A custom generic test is a macro following the `test_<name>` naming convention that returns a query — like any dbt test, it fails if that query returns any rows. Writing your own is worthwhile once the same non-standard business rule (positive amounts, valid enum-like values not covered by `accepted_values`) needs to be checked across many models.

## Documentation, Governance & Ecosystem

Generating docs, controlling test severity, access control, and where dbt is headed beyond SQL models.

<QuestionList topic="Documentation & Ecosystem" storagePrefix="dbt-ecosystem">

<QuestionCard id="dbt-30" number={30} question="How does dbt documentation generation work, and what does it produce?" difficulty="easy" topic="Documentation">
`dbt docs generate` introspects the project (model SQL, `.yml` descriptions, test definitions, and the warehouse's actual column metadata) and produces a static site with searchable model/column descriptions and an interactive DAG lineage graph — served locally with `dbt docs serve` or hosted for the whole team. Documentation quality is only as good as the `description:` fields authors actually fill in in each

content:
model's `.yml` file.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dbt-31" number={31} question="What's the difference between warn and error severity on a dbt test?" difficulty="easy" topic="Testing">
```yaml
tests:
  - not_null:
      config: {severity: warn}
```
An `error`-severity test (the default) fails the entire `dbt build`/`dbt test` run when it fails. A `warn`-severity test logs a warning but lets the run continue — useful for checks that are informative but not yet reliable enough (or not yet important enough) to block a deploy, without losing visibility into the issue entirely.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dbt-32" number={32} question="What are grants in dbt, and why configure them in code rather than manually?" difficulty="medium" topic="Governance">
```yaml
models:
  - name: reven

title: DBT

content:
ue_mart
    config:
      grants:
        select: ["role:analyst", "role:bi_tool"]
```
The `grants` config applies warehouse permissions (who can `SELECT` on a model) as part of the build itself, rather than someone remembering to run a `GRANT` statement manually after every deploy. Defining access in code means it's version-controlled, reviewed like any other change, and automatically reapplied if a table gets rebuilt from scratch.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dbt-33" number={33} question="What's the difference between dbt Core and dbt Cloud?" difficulty="easy" topic="Ecosystem">
**dbt Core** is the open-source CLI — you run it yourself, on your own infrastructure or orchestrator (often triggered by Airflow). **dbt Cloud** is the managed SaaS product built on top of it, adding a sch

eduler, hosted docs, an IDE, and the Semantic Layer, aimed at teams that don't want to build and operate that infrastructure themselves. The underlying model/test/macro code is the same either way — the difference is entirely in how and where it's run and managed.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dbt-34" number={34} question="What are dbt Python models, and when would you reach for one over SQL?" difficulty="hard" topic="Python Models">
On warehouses that support it (Snowflake, Databricks, BigQuery), a dbt model can be a `.py` file returning a DataFrame instead of a `.sql` file — it still participates in the same `ref()`/DAG/testing system as SQL models. Reach for one when the transformation genuinely needs something SQL is awkward at — a statistical/ML computation, a complex text-parsin

</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dbt-35" number={35} question="What is the dbt Semantic Layer / MetricFlow, and what problem does it solve?" difficulty="hard" topic="Semantic Layer">
The Semantic Layer lets you define metrics (revenue, active users) once in code, with their aggregation logic and dimensions, and have every BI tool and query pull a **consistent** value for that metric instead of each tool/analyst re-implementing the same calculation slightly differently. MetricFlow is the engine that compiles a metric query into the correct SQL against the underlying marts — it directly targets the classic "why do these two d

## Common Interview Scenarios

- **"A dbt model takes 40 minutes to build every night and it's only getting slower."** Talk through switching it from a table to an incremental materialization, choosing a reliable `unique_key`, and using state selection so CI doesn't rebuild the whole DAG on every PR.
- **"How would you catch a broken upstream schema before it reaches your marts?"** Discuss declaring the table as a dbt source, adding freshness checks and column tests (`not_null`, `relationships`), and failing the run loudly rather than silently propagating bad data downstream.
- **"You need point-in-time history for a dimension that only exists as a mutable table in the source system."** Explain dbt snapshots as the SCD2 mechanism, and how they differ from just re-running a model that alway

- **"Two BI dashboards show different revenue numbers, built from the same marts."** Point to the Semantic Layer/MetricFlow as the structural fix — a single defined metric every tool queries — rather than a one-off SQL reconciliation, and mention model contracts as the related mechanism for catching a schema mismatch before it causes the same kind of silent drift.
- **"A model change needs to not break a downstream dashboard nobody on the data team directly owns."** Talk through exposures (declaring that dependency explicitly in docs) combined with state-based CI selection, so anyone changing the upstream model sees the affected downstream consumer before merging, not after it breaks.

**Master cost optimization techniques for building efficient, scalable data platforms that remain sustainable at scale, rather than scaling cost linearly (or worse) with data volume.**

title: Cost Optimization
description: Interview questions on data platform cost optimization, covering cost drivers, partitioning, small files, skew, shuffle, materialization, and FinOps.
content:
## Key Concepts

Cost on a data platform is driven by a handful of levers: **compute time**, **bytes scanned and shuffled**, **storage growth**, **data movement**, and **operational overhead** like frequent backfills and retries. Most optimization work comes down to controlling those levers at the storage layer (partitioning, file sizes, avoiding small files), at the compute layer (reducing shuffle, fixing data skew, choosing the right join strategy), and at the process layer (deciding what to materialize, protecting the platform from runaway queries, and planning backfills deliberately instead of running them blind). None of this matters without visibility, which is what FinOps metrics — cost by team, cost per pipeline, bytes scanned per query — are for: they turn "the bill went up" into

"this dataset's cost went up, and here's why."

title: Cost Optimization
description: Interview questions on data platform cost optimization, covering cost drivers, partitioning, small files, skew, shuffle, materialization, and FinOps.
content:
## Interview Questions

<QuestionList topic="Cost Optimization" storagePrefix="cost-optimization">

<QuestionCard id="cost-01" number={1} question="Why is cost optimization considered a core skill for data engineers?" difficulty="easy" topic="Fundamentals">
Data platforms can scale costs linearly, or worse, with data volume and usage. Cost optimization ensures the platform remains sustainable while still meeting its SLAs. It requires understanding storage layout, compute behavior, query patterns, and operational practices like backfills and compaction — it isn't a one-off task, it's an ongoing part of running the platform.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="cost-02" number={2} question="What are the main cost drivers in a data platform?" difficulty="easy" topic="Cost Drivers">
- **Compute

title: Cost Optimization
description: Interview questions on data platform cost optimization, covering cost drivers, partitioning, small files, skew, shuffle, materialization, and FinOps.
content:
time** — clusters, warehouses, serverless slots
- **Bytes scanned and shuffles** — how much data queries actually touch and move
- **Storage growth** — raw plus derived plus duplicate data
- **Data movement** — egress and cross-region transfers
- **Operational overhead** — frequent backfills and retries

Most cost problems trace back to one of these five drivers.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="cost-03" number={3} question="How does partitioning strategy affect cost, and what happens when it's done poorly?" difficulty="medium" topic="Partitioning">
Good partitioning reduces scanned data by enabling partition pruning, so queries only touch the data they need. Bad partitioning creates too many small partitions, which increases metadata overhead and causes a small files problem. Partitioni

title: Cost Optimization
description: Interview questions on data platform cost optimization, covering cost drivers, partitioning, small files, skew, shuffle, materialization, and FinOps.
content:
ng should match common query filters and the actual data distribution, and it needs to be reevaluated as workloads evolve rather than set once and forgotten.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="cost-04" number={4} question="What is the small files problem, and why does it hurt performance and cost?" difficulty="medium" topic="Storage">
Small files increase scheduling and metadata overhead and reduce scan efficiency, since engines spend more time opening and planning files than actually processing data. Small files typically appear from streaming writes or overly granular partitions, and fixing them usually requires compaction or clustering to merge them into larger files.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="cost-05" number={5} question="How do you choose a target file size?" difficulty="medi

title: Cost Optimization
description: Interview questions on data platform cost optimization, covering cost drivers, partitioning, small files, skew, shuffle, materialization, and FinOps.
content:
um" topic="Storage">
You choose a size that balances parallelism and overhead. Too small increases file count and planning cost; too large reduces parallelism and can slow down selective queries that only need a fraction of a file. Many teams target hundreds of megabytes per file, but the right value depends on the engine, the storage layer, and the platform's actual query patterns.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="cost-06" number={6} question="How do you detect and fix data skew?" difficulty="hard" topic="Performance">
Skew happens when some partitions or keys have much more data than others, causing straggler tasks that hold up the whole job. You detect it via task duration distributions and partition size metrics — a few tasks taking far longer than the rest is the classic signature.

title: Cost Optimization
description: Interview questions on data platform cost optimization, covering cost drivers, partitioning, small files, skew, shuffle, materialization, and FinOps.
content:
Fixes include salting keys, using skew-aware join strategies, repartitioning, or broadcasting the smaller side of a join when possible.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="cost-07" number={7} question="What is shuffle, and how do you reduce it?" difficulty="medium" topic="Performance">
Shuffle is the redistribution of data across executors, needed for operations like joins, group-by, and distinct. It's expensive because of network IO and disk spills. You reduce it by using proper partitioning, avoiding unnecessarily wide transformations, filtering data early (before the shuffle-heavy step), broadcasting small tables instead of shuffling them, and tuning the number of shuffle partitions.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="cost-08" number={8} question="When should you materialize a dataset vs

description: Interview questions on data platform cost optimization, covering cost drivers, partitioning, small files, skew, shuffle, materialization, and FinOps.
content:
. keep it as a view?" difficulty="medium" topic="Materialization">
Materialize when many downstream queries reuse the same expensive computation, or when interactive BI needs low latency that a live view can't provide. Avoid over-materializing, since every materialized dataset adds storage and refresh complexity. A good default is to materialize stable, high-value marts and keep exploratory or rarely used logic as views.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="cost-09" number={9} question="How do you protect a platform from runaway queries and costs?" difficulty="medium" topic="Governance">
Use workload management: query timeouts, concurrency limits, resource quotas, and separate compute for heavy workloads so one bad query can't starve everyone else. Enforce best practices with guardrails like

title: Cost Optimization
description: Interview questions on data platform cost optimization, covering cost drivers, partitioning, small files, skew, shuffle, materialization, and FinOps.
content:
linting and cost alerts, and educate users with profiling tools so they can see the cost of what they're about to run. Multi-tenant platforms in particular need this kind of isolation to prevent one team from impacting another.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="cost-10" number={10} question="How do you optimize joins for cost and performance?" difficulty="medium" topic="Query Optimization">
You optimize joins by ensuring join keys are clean and well-distributed, filtering before the join rather than after, and choosing the right join strategy — broadcast for small tables, shuffle for large ones. You also reduce the size of join inputs by selecting only the columns you need, and consider pre-joining into curated marts when the same join gets repeated across many queries.
</QuestionCard>

content:
<QuestionCard id="cost-11" number={11} question="How do you plan and budget for a large backfill?" difficulty="medium" topic="Operations">
Estimate based on data volume, compute requirements, and expected scan and shuffle behavior. Run on a small sample window first to measure throughput and extrapolate to the full backfill. Backfills should be staged, monitored as they run, and preferably scheduled in off-peak windows, with a clear rollback plan if something goes wrong.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="cost-12" number={12} question="What FinOps metrics should a data platform track?" difficulty="easy" topic="FinOps">
Common metrics include cost by team or project, cost per pipeline, bytes scanned per query, cluster utilization, storage growth by layer, and the top expensive datasets or q

content:
ueries. You also want to track trend changes week-over-week and tie cost back to value — how much a dataset is actually used and how critical it is — rather than looking at cost in isolation.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

- **"You need to run a backfill across a year of historical data without blowing the budget or breaking current reporting."** Talk through sampling to estimate cost, staging and validating the backfill, running it off-peak, and iso

content:
## Machine Learning & MLOps for Data Engineers

**You won't be asked to derive gradient descent. You will be asked how you'd build a feature pipeline that doesn't leak future data into training, why the model that scored 0.94 offline performs badly in production, and who owns the pipeline when the data scientist has moved on. MLOps is largely a data engineering problem wearing a different name — reproducibility, lineage, pipeline reliability and monitoring — which is why these questions come up even for roles with no ML in the title.**

title: Machine Learning & MLOps
description: ML and MLOps interview questions for data engineers — the ML basics you're expected to know, feature stores and training-serving skew, model deployment and monitoring, drift detection, and where the data engineer's responsibility ends.
content:
## Key Concepts

An ML system is mostly **not model code**. The often-cited Google paper on technical debt in ML makes the point visually: the box labelled "ML code" is a tiny fraction of a diagram dominated by data collection, feature extraction, verification, serving infrastructure and monitoring. Nearly all of that is data engineering.

The property that distinguishes ML pipelines from analytical ones is that **they must be reproducible in two places at once**. The features used to train a model must be computed identically when the model serves a prediction — same logic, same data, same point-in-time semantics. When they aren't, you get **training-serving skew**, which is the most common reason a model that performed well offline fails in production.

The second distinguishing property

title: Machine Learning & MLOps
description: ML and MLOps interview questions for data engineers — the ML basics you're expected to know, feature stores and training-serving skew, model deployment and monitoring, drift detection, and where the data engineer's responsibility ends.
content:
is that **ML systems degrade silently**. A pipeline that breaks throws an error; a model whose input distribution has shifted keeps returning confident predictions that are increasingly wrong. That's why monitoring for **drift** is not optional, and why "the pipeline is green" says nothing about whether the model still works.

---

title: Machine Learning & MLOps
description: ML and MLOps interview questions for data engineers — the ML basics you're expected to know, feature stores and training-serving skew, model deployment and monitoring, drift detection, and where the data engineer's responsibility ends.
content:
## ML Basics for Data Engineers

<QuestionList topic="ML Basics for Data Engineers" storagePrefix="mlops-basics">

<QuestionCard id="mlops-basic-01" number={1} question="What are the main types of machine learning?" difficulty="easy" topic="ML Basics">
- **Supervised** — learn from labelled examples. **Classification** (churn yes/no, fraud/not) and **regression** (predict a number: demand, price, lifetime value). The overwhelming majority of production ML.
- **Unsupervised** — find structure without labels: clustering for segmentation, dimensionality reduction, anomaly detection.
- **Semi-supervised** — a small labelled set plus a large unlabelled one, when labelling is expensive.
- **Reinforcement learning** — learn from reward signals through interaction. Rare outside games, robotics and

title: Machine Learning & MLOps
description: ML and MLOps interview questions for data engineers — the ML basics you're expected to know, feature stores and training-serving skew, model deployment and monitoring, drift detection, and where the data engineer's responsibility ends.
content:
some recommendation systems.

What matters for a data engineer is the **data requirement each implies**. Supervised learning needs labels, and *where labels come from* is usually a pipeline problem — often derived from historical outcomes, which introduces a delay (you don't know if a customer churned until they have). That label latency shapes how often you can retrain and how you evaluate.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="mlops-basic-02" number={2} question="What are training, validation and test sets, and why does the split matter?" difficulty="medium" topic="ML Basics">
- **Training set** — what the model learns from.
- **Validation set** — used to tune hyperparameters and choose between models.
- **Test set** — held out entirely, touched **once**, to estimate real-world performance

title: Machine Learning & MLOps
description: ML and MLOps interview questions for data engineers — the ML basics you're expected to know, feature stores and training-serving skew, model deployment and monitoring, drift detection, and where the data engineer's responsibility ends.
content:
.

The reason a data engineer cares: **how you split is a data problem, and getting it wrong invalidates the result.**

For time-series or any data with a temporal element — which covers most business ML — a **random split leaks the future into training**. The model sees Thursday's data while predicting Wednesday, scores brilliantly, and fails in production. The correct approach is a **chronological split**: train on the past, validate and test on the future.

Similarly, splitting randomly when rows are grouped (multiple rows per customer) leaks across the boundary. Split by the **entity**, not the row.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="mlops-basic-03" number={3} question="What is data leakage, and how do you prevent it?" difficulty="hard" topic="ML Basics">
When information that wouldn't

title: Machine Learning & MLOps
description: ML and MLOps interview questions for data engineers — the ML basics you're expected to know, feature stores and training-serving skew, model deployment and monitoring, drift detection, and where the data engineer's responsibility ends.
content:
be available at prediction time gets into the training features. The model learns from it, scores extraordinarily well offline, and collapses in production.

Common forms, most of which are pipeline bugs:
- **Target leakage** — a feature that's a proxy for the outcome. Including `cancellation_date` when predicting churn, or an `account_status` field updated *because* of the event you're predicting.
- **Temporal leakage** — computing a feature from data after the prediction timestamp. Aggregating a customer's full-year spend to predict their behaviour in March.
- **Train-test contamination** — scaling or imputing using statistics computed over the whole dataset, so test-set information reaches training.
- **Duplicate rows** spanning the split.

Prevention: **point-in-time correct feature c

title: Machine Learning & MLOps
description: ML and MLOps interview questions for data engineers — the ML basics you're expected to know, feature stores and training-serving skew, model deployment and monitoring, drift detection, and where the data engineer's responsibility ends.
content:
omputation** (as-of joins), fitting all transformations on the training set only, chronological splits, and treating a suspiciously high score as a bug to investigate rather than a success.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="mlops-basic-04" number={4} question="What evaluation metrics should you recognise?" difficulty="medium" topic="ML Basics">
**Classification** — accuracy is misleading on imbalanced data (99% accuracy predicting "not fraud" always). Look at **precision** (of those flagged, how many were right), **recall** (of the real cases, how many did we catch), **F1** (their harmonic mean), and **AUC-ROC** or **AUC-PR**, the latter being better for heavy imbalance.

**Regression** — **RMSE** (penalises large errors), **MAE** (robust to outliers), **MAPE** (percentage, undefined at z

title: Machine Learning & MLOps
description: ML and MLOps interview questions for data engineers — the ML basics you're expected to know, feature stores and training-serving skew, model deployment and monitoring, drift detection, and where the data engineer's responsibility ends.
content:
ero), **R²**.

Why a data engineer should know these: the **precision/recall trade-off is a business decision with pipeline consequences.** A fraud model tuned for recall floods the review queue; tuned for precision it misses cases. That choice determines the volume your downstream systems must handle, and it's worth asking about rather than treating the model as a black box.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

title: Machine Learning & MLOps
description: ML and MLOps interview questions for data engineers — the ML basics you're expected to know, feature stores and training-serving skew, model deployment and monitoring, drift detection, and where the data engineer's responsibility ends.
content:
## Feature Engineering & Feature Stores

<QuestionList topic="Feature Engineering & Feature Stores" storagePrefix="mlops-features">

<QuestionCard id="mlops-feat-01" number={1} question="What is training-serving skew, and how do you prevent it?" difficulty="hard" topic="Features">
When features computed for **training** differ from those computed at **serving** time — so the model receives inputs unlike anything it learned from.

How it happens:
- **Two implementations** — features written in SQL for training and re-implemented in Python in the serving application. They drift, or were never identical.
- **Different data sources** — training from the warehouse, serving from an operational database with different values or freshness.
- **Time semantics** — training aggregates a full day; ser

title: Machine Learning & MLOps
description: ML and MLOps interview questions for data engineers — the ML basics you're expected to know, feature stores and training-serving skew, model deployment and monitoring, drift detection, and where the data engineer's responsibility ends.
content:
ving has only partial-day data.
- **Different preprocessing** — a scaler fitted on training data isn't applied identically at serving.

Prevention:
- **One definition of each feature**, computed once and reused by both paths. This is the core argument for a feature store.
- **Log the features actually used at serving time**, and compare their distribution against training. This catches skew you didn't anticipate.
- **Shared transformation code** as a library, not copy-paste.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="mlops-feat-02" number={2} question="What is a feature store, and what does it actually solve?" difficulty="hard" topic="Feature Store">
A system for defining, computing, storing and serving features, with two coordinated stores:

- **Offline store** — historical feature values (typica

title: Machine Learning & MLOps
description: ML and MLOps interview questions for data engineers — the ML basics you're expected to know, feature stores and training-serving skew, model deployment and monitoring, drift detection, and where the data engineer's responsibility ends.
content:
lly in the warehouse or lake) for generating training sets.
- **Online store** — the latest value per entity in a low-latency store (Redis, DynamoDB, Bigtable) for serving predictions in milliseconds.

What it solves:
1. **Training-serving consistency** — one definition materialised to both stores.
2. **Point-in-time correctness** — generating a training set with an **as-of join** so each label row gets the feature values as they were *at that moment*, not as they are now. Doing this correctly by hand is genuinely hard, and getting it wrong is temporal leakage.
3. **Reuse** — teams share features instead of each rebuilding "customer 30-day spend".
4. **Backfill** — computing history for a new feature.

Examples: Feast (open source), Tecton, Databricks Feature Store, Vertex AI Feature Store

title: Machine Learning & MLOps
description: ML and MLOps interview questions for data engineers — the ML basics you're expected to know, feature stores and training-serving skew, model deployment and monitoring, drift detection, and where the data engineer's responsibility ends.
content:
, SageMaker Feature Store.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="mlops-feat-03" number={3} question="Do you always need a feature store?" difficulty="medium" topic="Feature Store">
No, and saying so is the stronger answer.

It earns its place when you have **online serving with low-latency requirements**, **several models or teams sharing features**, or **complex point-in-time joins** across many entities.

It's overhead you don't need when models are **batch-scored** (predictions computed on a schedule and written to a table — no online store required), when there's **one model and one team**, or when features are simple aggregations already in the warehouse.

For batch scoring specifically, a well-tested dbt model producing a feature table, plus the same table used for training with a chron

title: Machine Learning & MLOps
description: ML and MLOps interview questions for data engineers — the ML basics you're expected to know, feature stores and training-serving skew, model deployment and monitoring, drift detection, and where the data engineer's responsibility ends.
content:
ological split, gives you consistency and point-in-time correctness without new infrastructure.

The mature position: adopt a feature store when the consistency problem is real and recurring, not because it appears on every MLOps reference architecture.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="mlops-feat-04" number={4} question="What is a point-in-time correct join?" difficulty="hard" topic="Features">
Joining feature values as they existed **at the timestamp of each training label**, rather than their current values.

The naive join is wrong:

```sql
-- WRONG: attaches today's feature values to a label from six months ago
SELECT l.*, f.total_spend
FROM labels l JOIN features f USING (customer_id)
```

The correct form takes the most recent feature value **at or before** the label's event time:

title: Machine Learning & MLOps
description: ML and MLOps interview questions for data engineers — the ML basics you're expected to know, feature stores and training-serving skew, model deployment and monitoring, drift detection, and where the data engineer's responsibility ends.
content:
```sql
SELECT l.*, f.total_spend
FROM labels l
ASOF JOIN features f
  ON l.customer_id = f.customer_id AND f.valid_from <= l.event_ts
```

(Written as an as-of join here; in engines without one it's a window function picking the latest qualifying row.)

Why it matters: the naive version leaks the future. A model trained on it learns from information that didn't exist at prediction time, looks excellent offline, and underperforms in production. **This is the single most valuable thing a feature store does**, and it's worth being able to write the query.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

---

title: Machine Learning & MLOps
description: ML and MLOps interview questions for data engineers — the ML basics you're expected to know, feature stores and training-serving skew, model deployment and monitoring, drift detection, and where the data engineer's responsibility ends.
content:
## MLOps & the Model Lifecycle

<QuestionList topic="MLOps & the Model Lifecycle" storagePrefix="mlops-lifecycle">

<QuestionCard id="mlops-lc-01" number={1} question="What is MLOps, and how does it differ from DevOps?" difficulty="medium" topic="MLOps">
Applying engineering discipline to the ML lifecycle: versioning, testing, automated deployment, monitoring and governance for models and the data behind them.

The differences from DevOps that generate the extra work:
- **You version three things**, not one — code, **data**, and the model artefact. Reproducing a result requires all three.
- **Behaviour depends on data**, so identical code can produce a different model. Testing must cover data properties, not just code paths.
- **Models decay** without any change to the system, because the

title: Machine Learning & MLOps
description: ML and MLOps interview questions for data engineers — the ML basics you're expected to know, feature stores and training-serving skew, model deployment and monitoring, drift detection, and where the data engineer's responsibility ends.
content:
world shifts underneath them. Software doesn't do this.
- **Testing is statistical** — you compare metrics against a baseline rather than asserting exact outputs.
- **Retraining is part of operations**, so the pipeline that produces the model is itself a production system.

The framing worth offering: MLOps is DevOps plus **data versioning, continuous training and continuous monitoring** — and the first and third are squarely data engineering responsibilities.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="mlops-lc-02" number={2} question="What does a model lifecycle look like end to end?" difficulty="medium" topic="MLOps">
1. **Problem framing** — what decision, what metric, what latency.
2. **Data collection and labelling** — often the longest and least glamorous stage.
3. **Feature engineering** —

title: Machine Learning & MLOps
description: ML and MLOps interview questions for data engineers — the ML basics you're expected to know, feature stores and training-serving skew, model deployment and monitoring, drift detection, and where the data engineer's responsibility ends.
content:
computed reproducibly, point-in-time correct.
4. **Training and experimentation** — many runs, tracked with parameters, data version and metrics (MLflow, Weights & Biases).
5. **Evaluation** — against a held-out set and against the current production model.
6. **Registration** — the artefact stored in a **model registry** with lineage back to the exact code and data.
7. **Deployment** — batch scoring, a real-time endpoint, or embedded in an application.
8. **Monitoring** — performance, drift, latency, data quality.
9. **Retraining** — scheduled or triggered by drift, and back to step 3.

The data engineer typically owns 2, 3, 7's data path, 8 and 9 — which is most of it. Being clear about that boundary is a good answer to "what would your role be".
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="mlops-

description: ML and MLOps interview questions for data engineers — the ML basics you're expected to know, feature stores and training-serving skew, model deployment and monitoring, drift detection, and where the data engineer's responsibility ends.
content:
lc-03" number={3} question="What are the model deployment patterns?" difficulty="medium" topic="MLOps">
- **Batch scoring** — predictions computed on a schedule and written to a table for consumers to look up. **Simplest and most common**, and sufficient whenever predictions don't need to reflect events from the last few minutes. No serving infrastructure, no latency budget, easy to reprocess.
- **Real-time endpoint** — a service returning predictions synchronously. Needed for fraud checks and personalisation; brings latency SLAs, autoscaling, and an online feature store.
- **Streaming scoring** — the model applied inside a stream processor as events flow.
- **Embedded** — the model runs on-device or in the client.

## Monitoring & Drift

<QuestionList topic="Monitoring & Drift" storagePrefix="mlops-monitoring">

<QuestionCard id="mlops-mon-01" number={1} question="What is model drift, and what types are there?" difficulty="hard" topic="Drift">
Degradation of a model's performance over time, without anything in the system changing.

- **Data drift (covariate shift)** — the input distribution changes. A new marketing channel brings a different customer mix; the model sees inputs unlike its training data.
- **Concept drift** — the *relationship* between inputs and target changes. What predicted churn before COVID stopped predicting it during, even with similar inputs.
- **Label drift** — the distribution of the target changes.
- **Upstream data changes** — a schema change, a unit change, a source system

title: Machine Learning & MLOps
description: ML and MLOps interview questions for data engineers — the ML basics you're expected to know, feature stores and training-serving skew, model deployment and monitoring, drift detection, and where the data engineer's responsibility ends.
content:
altering how it populates a field. Arguably not drift at all, but it presents identically and is the most common cause in practice.

The critical property: **none of these throw an error.** The pipeline is green, the model returns confident predictions, and the business quietly makes worse decisions — which is why drift monitoring exists and why it's a data engineering responsibility.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="mlops-mon-02" number={2} question="How do you detect drift?" difficulty="hard" topic="Drift">
Compare current production data against the training baseline:

- **Statistical distance per feature** — **PSI** (Population Stability Index), KL divergence, or a Kolmogorov-Smirnov test. PSI is the common industry choice, with rules of thumb around 0.1 for moderate and 0.25 for si

content:
gnificant shift.
- **Summary statistics** — mean, standard deviation, null rate, cardinality, min/max per feature, tracked over time.
- **Prediction distribution** — if the model suddenly predicts "churn" for 40% of customers when it used to say 5%, something changed even before you have labels.
- **Actual performance**, once labels arrive — the ground truth, but delayed by however long outcomes take to observe.

The practical setup: monitor **feature distributions and prediction distributions continuously** (available immediately), and **performance metrics when labels land** (delayed but authoritative). Alert on the leading indicators, confirm with the lagging one.

Tools: Evidently, WhyLabs, Arize, or the built-in monitoring in SageMaker and Vertex AI.
</QuestionCard>

"mlops-mon-03" number={3} question="When and how should you retrain a model?" difficulty="medium" topic="Monitoring">
Three triggers:
- **Scheduled** — weekly or monthly regardless. Simple and predictable, and either wasteful or too slow depending on how fast the domain moves.
- **Performance-triggered** — retrain when a monitored metric crosses a threshold. Responsive, but needs labels, which arrive late.
- **Drift-triggered** — retrain when input distributions shift materially. Fast, and can fire on a shift that doesn't actually hurt performance.

Most production systems combine a **schedule as a floor with drift or performance triggers on top**.

The engineering requirements matter as much as the trigger: retraining must be **automated and reproducible**, the new model must be **evaluat

<QuestionCard id="mlops-mon-04" number={4} question="What does a data engineer own in an ML system?" difficulty="medium" topic="MLOps">
Most of the surface area outside the modelling itself:

- **Data pipelines** feeding training and serving — reliability, freshness, quality.
- **Feature pipelines** — computed consistently for both paths, point-in-time correct.
- **Data versioning and lineage**, so a model's training data is reconstructable.
- **Infrastructure** for training and serving, and the pipeline that scores in batch.
- **Monitoring**

- **The retraining pipeline** as a production system.

What typically sits with data scientists: problem framing, model selection, feature *ideas*, and evaluation methodology.

The boundary worth articulating in an interview: **the data scientist decides what the feature should mean; the data engineer makes sure it's computed the same way, on time, everywhere it's needed, and notices when it stops being true.** That framing lands well because it's accurate and shows you understand the collaboration rather than either over-claiming or under-claiming.

**"The model scored 0.94 offline and performs terribly in production."** — leakage or training-serving skew. Check for target and temporal leakage first, then whether serving features are computed by the same code and from the same source. Logging serving features and comparing distributions to training is how you confirm it.

## Data Observability: Monitoring and Incident Response

**Data observability is the practice of monitoring, alerting, and diagnosing the health of data and data pipelines — catching silent failures before they reach a dashboard, and cutting the time it takes to find root cause once something breaks.**

content:
## Key Concepts

Data observability differs from application observability in what it watches: instead of latency and error rates for request/response services, it tracks dataset health over time — **freshness** (is data arriving on schedule), **volume** (are row/byte/partition counts within expected bounds), **schema** (did columns get added, removed, or retyped), and **quality** (nulls, uniqueness, referential integrity). These signals matter because data failures are often silent — a job succeeds, but the data is wrong, missing a subset, or duplicated — so detection depends on dataset-level checks and reconciliation rather than job exit codes alone. When something breaks, **lineage** tells you the blast radius (which downstream tables and dashboards are affected), and a good **runbook**

## Interview Questions

<QuestionList topic="Observability" storagePrefix="observability">

<QuestionCard id="obs-01" number={1} question="What is data observability?" difficulty="easy" topic="Fundamentals">
Data observability is the practice of monitoring, alerting, and diagnosing the health of data and data pipelines. It focuses on whether datasets are arriving on time, with correct volume and values, and whether downstream consumers can rely on them. The goal is to reduce "data downtime" and speed up root-cause analysis.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="obs-02" number={2} question="How is data observability different from application observability?" difficulty="easy" topic="Fundamentals">
Application observability focuses on service health (latency, error rates, traces) for request/re

</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="obs-03" number={3} question="What are the key signals you monitor for data pipelines?" difficulty="medium" topic="Signals">
Common signals include:

- **Freshness** — track max event/ingestion time to ensure data is arriving on schedule
- **Volume** — monitor row counts, bytes, and partitions for anomalies
- **Schema changes** — detect added, removed, or typed columns that may break downstream
- **Quality checks** — validate null rates, uniqueness, and referential integrity
- **Pipeline run status** — track job success/fa

<QuestionCard id="obs-04" number={4} question="How do you define and measure an end-to-end SLA for data?" difficulty="medium" topic="SLAs">
You define the SLA from source event time to availability in the final dataset or BI metric. Measure it with timestamps at each stage (ingest, transform, publish) and compute percentiles (p50/p95) as well as breach counts. SLAs should reflect consumer needs and include ownership and escalation paths.

This makes runs reproducible and speeds up debugging.

<QuestionCard id="obs-06" number={6} question="How do you detect silent failures?" difficulty="hard" topic="Failure Detection">
Silent failures happen when the job succeeds but data is wrong (missing subset, wrong join, truncation). Detect them with dataset-level checks: freshness, volume bounds, distribution checks, and reconciliations against sources. Monitoring key business KPIs for unexpected changes is also effective.

Alerts should be actionable, scoped, and owned. Use severity levels, suppression windows, and baselines that account for seasonality. Prefer multi-signal alerts (freshness + volume) over single noisy checks, and include runbooks with clear next steps.

<QuestionCard id="obs-11" number={11} question="What is a runbook and what should it contain?" difficulty="medium" topic="Runbooks">
A runbook is a step-by-step guide for responding to an alert or incident. It should include impact assessment, common root causes, validation queries, mitigation steps, rollback/backfill steps, and escalation contacts. Good runbooks reduce time-to-recovery for on-call engineers.

content:
## Metrics & Prometheus

<QuestionList topic="Metrics & Prometheus" storagePrefix="observability-prometheus">

<QuestionCard id="obsv-prom-01" number={1} question="What is Prometheus and how does it collect metrics?" difficulty="medium" topic="Prometheus">
An open-source metrics database and alerting system, and the de facto standard in the Kubernetes ecosystem.

Its defining choice is **pull-based scraping**: Prometheus periodically fetches a `/metrics` HTTP endpoint from each target rather than receiving pushes. Targets are found via **service discovery** (Kubernetes, Consul, cloud APIs), so a new pod is scraped automatically without configuration.

Data is stored as **time series** identified by a metric name plus labels, and queried with **PromQL**.

Pull has real advantages — you can

title: Data Observability
description: Data observability interview questions covering monitoring signals, SLAs, lineage, alerting, backfills, runbooks, and incident response for data pipelines.
content:
tell whether a target is *down* (a failed scrape) rather than merely silent, and there's no client-side buffering to lose. For short-lived batch jobs that exit before a scrape, the **Pushgateway** exists as the exception, though it's discouraged for anything else.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="obsv-prom-02" number={2} question="What are the Prometheus metric types?" difficulty="medium" topic="Prometheus">
- **Counter** — monotonically increasing; resets to zero on restart. For totals: rows processed, errors, bytes written. Always query it with `rate()` or `increase()`, never raw.
- **Gauge** — goes up and down. For current state: queue depth, memory in use, lag in seconds.
- **Histogram** — observations bucketed by value, plus a sum and count. For latency and size distributions; quant

title: Data Observability
description: Data observability interview questions covering monitoring signals, SLAs, lineage, alerting, backfills, runbooks, and incident response for data pipelines.
content:
iles are computed at query time with `histogram_quantile()`.
- **Summary** — quantiles calculated client-side. Cheaper to query but **cannot be aggregated across instances**, which is usually disqualifying.

The practical guidance: **prefer histograms to summaries** for latency, because you almost always want a p99 across the whole fleet rather than per-instance. And remember a counter's value alone is meaningless — the rate of change is the signal.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="obsv-prom-03" number={3} question="What is cardinality, and why does it break Prometheus?" difficulty="hard" topic="Prometheus">
Cardinality is the number of distinct time series, and each unique **combination of label values** creates one.

A metric with a `user_id` label and a million users creates a million

title: Data Observability
description: Data observability interview questions covering monitoring signals, SLAs, lineage, alerting, backfills, runbooks, and incident response for data pipelines.
content:
series. Prometheus holds series metadata in memory, so high cardinality causes memory exhaustion, slow queries and eventually an unusable server — the single most common way people break a Prometheus deployment.

Rules that prevent it:
- **Never label with unbounded values** — user IDs, request IDs, email addresses, full URLs, timestamps, or a raw error message.
- **Keep labels to bounded sets** — environment, service, status code, pipeline name.
- **Put high-cardinality detail in logs or traces**, not metrics. That's what those systems are for.

The related discipline for data pipelines: label by `pipeline` and `table`, not by partition or file name.
</QuestionCard>

content:
## Commercial Observability Platforms

<QuestionList topic="Commercial Observability Platforms" storagePrefix="observability-platforms">

<QuestionCard id="obsv-plat-01" number={1} question="What is Datadog and when would you choose it over Prometheus?" difficulty="medium" topic="Datadog">
A hosted, unified observability SaaS covering infrastructure metrics, APM and distributed tracing, log management, synthetics, RUM and security — all correlated in one UI, with 800+ integrations.

Choose **Datadog** when you want breadth without operating it: metrics, logs and traces already joined, long retention handled, and no Prometheus, Thanos, Loki, Jaeger and Grafana stack to run yourself. For a small team, the operational saving is real.

Choose **Prometheus + Grafana** when cost at scale matters

title: Data Observability
description: Data observability interview questions covering monitoring signals, SLAs, lineage, alerting, backfills, runbooks, and incident response for data pipelines.
content:
(Datadog's per-host and per-custom-metric pricing escalates sharply), when you want no vendor lock-in, or when you're already deep in Kubernetes where Prometheus is the native fit.

The honest framing: it's **cost versus operational burden**. Datadog bills are a recurring source of surprise — particularly **custom metrics**, where high-cardinality tags multiply the count and therefore the bill, the same cardinality discipline as Prometheus but with a direct financial signal.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="obsv-plat-02" number={2} question="What is Sentry, and what does it add over logging?" difficulty="medium" topic="Sentry">
An **error tracking** platform. Instead of errors being lines in a log, Sentry captures the exception with its stack trace, local variables, breadcrumbs leading

title: Data Observability
description: Data observability interview questions covering monitoring signals, SLAs, lineage, alerting, backfills, runbooks, and incident response for data pipelines.
content:
up to it, release version and environment — then **groups identical errors into a single issue** with a count and a trend.

That grouping is the point. A pipeline throwing the same `KeyError` 40,000 times is one issue with a count, not 40,000 log lines you have to notice among everything else.

For data engineering it's most useful in **long-running workers and services** — a streaming consumer, an API — where you want to know about a new exception type immediately, with the context to fix it, and to see whether a deploy introduced it (Sentry associates issues with releases).

It complements logs rather than replacing them: logs for the narrative, Sentry for "what's broken and how often".
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="obsv-plat-03" number={3} question="What is New Relic, and how do th

title: Data Observability
description: Data observability interview questions covering monitoring signals, SLAs, lineage, alerting, backfills, runbooks, and incident response for data pipelines.
content:
ese platforms overlap?" difficulty="easy" topic="New Relic">
A full-stack observability platform in the same category as Datadog — APM, infrastructure monitoring, logs, distributed tracing and dashboards, queried with **NRQL**. Its pricing is per-user plus per-GB ingested, which suits different shapes of organisation than Datadog's per-host model.

The honest answer to how they overlap: **substantially.** Datadog, New Relic, Dynatrace, Grafana Cloud and Splunk Observability all sell essentially the same three pillars — metrics, logs and traces — correlated in one place. Differentiation is in pricing model, UI, integration depth and specific strengths rather than in capability.

The interview-relevant point isn't which vendor, it's **what you'd instrument and why**: the four data-specific s

title: Data Observability
description: Data observability interview questions covering monitoring signals, SLAs, lineage, alerting, backfills, runbooks, and incident response for data pipelines.
content:
ignals (freshness, volume, schema, quality) that generic APM tools don't cover unless you emit them yourself.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="obsv-plat-04" number={4} question="What are the three pillars of observability, and what's missing for data?" difficulty="medium" topic="Fundamentals">
The conventional three:
- **Metrics** — numeric time series, cheap to store, good for alerting and trends. No detail about any individual event.
- **Logs** — discrete events with full context. High detail, high volume, expensive at scale.
- **Traces** — a request's path across services, with timing per span. Shows *where* latency comes from in a distributed call.

What's missing for data pipelines is that all three describe the **system**, not the **data**. A pipeline can be green on every one of t

title: Data Observability
description: Data observability interview questions covering monitoring signals, SLAs, lineage, alerting, backfills, runbooks, and incident response for data pipelines.
content:
hem while writing wrong numbers.

So data observability adds a fourth concern: **dataset-level signals** — freshness, volume, schema and quality — plus **lineage** to establish blast radius. That's the distinction worth making in an interview, because it explains why tools like Monte Carlo, Soda and Great Expectations exist alongside Datadog rather than being replaced by it.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

content:
## Common Interview Scenarios

- **"Freshness on a critical table breaches SLA at 3am — walk through your triage steps."** Tests signal literacy, runbook use, and escalation instincts.
- **"A BI dashboard shows revenue dropped 15% but nothing alerted — how did that slip through, and how do you prevent it next time?"** Tests silent-failure detection and multi-signal alerting.
- **"You need to backfill six months of a core fact table without breaking downstream dashboards — how do you approach it?"** Tests safe backfill strategy and raw/published layer separation.
- **"Design the logging and lineage you'd add to a new pipeline so the next on-call engineer isn't starting from zero."** Tests logging minimums and the practical value of lineage.

title: System Design
description: Data platform system design interview questions covering pipeline architecture, distributed systems, storage selection, scalability, fault tolerance, and governance.
content:
## Key Concepts

Data system design questions test whether you can turn a vague business requirement into a concrete architecture. Most answers draw from a small set of recurring building blocks: a **layered storage model** (raw/silver/gold) that separates immutable ingestion from cleaned and business-ready data; a **batch vs. streaming** decision driven by latency needs versus complexity and cost; **reliability patterns** — idempotent writes, retries, dead-letter queues, checkpointing — that make pipelines safe to rerun; and handling for the messy realities of production data, like **late-arriving events**, **schema evolution**, and **backfills**. Around all of that sit platform-level concerns — **multi-tenancy**, **observability**, and **cost vs. SLA trade-offs** — that turn a single pip

title: System Design
description: Data platform system design interview questions covering pipeline architecture, distributed systems, storage selection, scalability, fault tolerance, and governance.
content:
eline into a platform other teams can build on safely.

Underneath those pipeline-level decisions sit **distributed systems fundamentals** — the CAP theorem, consistency models, replication topologies, partitioning, and consensus — that explain *why* the tools you use behave the way they do, plus a **storage and database selection** framework (SQL vs. NoSQL, lake vs. warehouse vs. lakehouse, OLTP vs. OLAP, indexing and caching trade-offs) for choosing the right backend instead of defaulting to a familiar one.

At platform scale, interviews also probe **scalability and capacity planning** (partitioning strategy, back-of-envelope estimation, backpressure, auto-scaling), **fault tolerance and disaster recovery** (RTO/RPO, multi-region failover, backup validation), and **governance and securit

title: System Design
description: Data platform system design interview questions covering pipeline architecture, distributed systems, storage selection, scalability, fault tolerance, and governance.
content:
y by design** (access control, PII handling, lineage, audit logging, data contracts) — the concerns that separate a working pipeline from a platform other teams can safely depend on. The Interview Questions section below closes with applied **case studies** — designing the data pipeline behind a fraud detector, a recommendation engine, a feature store, and similar systems — since real interviews often frame these concepts as one open-ended "design X" prompt rather than isolated definitions.

### Pipeline Architecture & Reliability Fundamentals

<QuestionList topic="Pipeline Architecture & Reliability Fundamentals" storagePrefix="sysdesign-fund">

<QuestionCard id="sysdesign-01" number={1} question="How would you design a batch analytics pipeline?" difficulty="medium" topic="Batch Design">
A typical design ingests data into a raw layer (immutable), transforms it into curated datasets (cleaned and modeled), and publishes it into marts or BI-serving datasets. You define SLAs, data quality checks, and clear ownership for each dataset along the way. Batch pipelines are usually scheduled daily or hourly and optimized for correctness and cost rather than latency.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="sysdesign-02" number={2} question="How would you design a near-real-time ingestion pipe

title: System Design
description: Data platform system design interview questions covering pipeline architecture, distributed systems, storage selection, scalability, fault tolerance, and governance.
content:
line?" difficulty="hard" topic="Streaming">
You typically use an event log or CDC stream (Kafka, Pub/Sub, Kinesis) and write to a raw, append-only store with durable offsets. Downstream, you materialize current-state tables and metrics using windowing and deduplication. The hard parts are designing for replays, ordering guarantees, and late-arriving events, since streaming systems don't get a second batch run to fix mistakes.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="sysdesign-03" number={3} question="How do you ensure idempotency in data pipelines?" difficulty="medium" topic="Reliability">
Idempotency means retries don't change the final result. Common strategies include writing with deterministic keys (upserts or merges instead of blind appends), using exactly-once features where the engine sup

title: System Design
description: Data platform system design interview questions covering pipeline architecture, distributed systems, storage selection, scalability, fault tolerance, and governance.
content:
ports them, and keeping raw data immutable while rebuilding derived layers from it. You also need to store checkpoints and watermarks consistently with the writes they correspond to, so a retry replays from a known-good point.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="sysdesign-04" number={4} question="How do you handle late-arriving events and backfills?" difficulty="hard" topic="Data Quality">
You define an allowed lateness window and design tables keyed by event time, not just ingestion time. For late events, you reprocess the affected windows or partitions and update derived outputs deterministically, so reprocessing produces the same result regardless of when it runs. Backfills specifically should be incremental, validated, and isolated so they don't corrupt current reporting while they're i

title: System Design
description: Data platform system design interview questions covering pipeline architecture, distributed systems, storage selection, scalability, fault tolerance, and governance.
content:
n flight.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="sysdesign-05" number={5} question="When would you choose streaming over batch processing, and vice versa?" difficulty="medium" topic="Architecture">
Streaming is chosen for low latency and continuous updates, but it adds real complexity — state management, ordering, exactly-once semantics. Batch is simpler and often cheaper for many analytics use cases where near-real-time freshness isn't a hard requirement. Many real systems end up hybrid: streaming ingestion into a raw layer, with batch modeling on top to build marts.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="sysdesign-06" number={6} question="What is the raw/silver/gold layering pattern, and why use it?" difficulty="easy" topic="Data Modeling">
Raw (or bronze) is immutable ingestion with minimal tra

content:
nsformation. Silver is cleaned, standardized, and deduplicated data with consistent schemas. Gold is business-ready marts and aggregates designed for BI and applications. This layering helps with reprocessing (you can always rebuild silver/gold from raw), governance, and giving each layer a clear contract with its consumers.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="sysdesign-07" number={7} question="How do you design a multi-tenant data platform?" difficulty="hard" topic="Platform Design">
You need isolation — separate compute or quotas per tenant — clear ownership, and strong governance. Provide shared standards for naming, testing, and documentation, plus a catalog for discovery so tenants can find and trust each other's datasets. Multi-tenancy also requires controlling cost and preventing one

title: System Design
description: Data platform system design interview questions covering pipeline architecture, distributed systems, storage selection, scalability, fault tolerance, and governance.
content:
team's workloads from impacting others, which usually means resource quotas and workload separation.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="sysdesign-08" number={8} question="How do you handle schema evolution in a data platform?" difficulty="medium" topic="Schema">
You define compatibility rules, version schemas or contracts, and enforce them in CI and at ingestion. Downstream transforms should tolerate additive fields but fail fast on breaking changes rather than silently producing wrong data. You also maintain backward-compatible outputs wherever multiple consumers depend on a stable schema, since you can't force every consumer to upgrade at once.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="sysdesign-09" number={9} question="What reliability patterns do you use for production data pipelines?" diffi

culty="medium" topic="Reliability">
Common patterns include idempotent writes, retries with backoff, dead-letter queues for records that repeatedly fail, exactly-once or effectively-once processing, and separating raw from derived layers so derived data can always be rebuilt. You also rely on checkpointing and consistent watermark management to avoid gaps and duplicates across restarts.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="sysdesign-10" number={10} question="What does platform observability look like for a data system?" difficulty="medium" topic="Observability">
You monitor freshness, volume, quality, and lineage, plus pipeline runtime and failure rates. Alerts should be actionable and tied to runbooks, not just noise that gets ignored. Observability should be end-to-end — from source system

title: System Design

content:
s all the way through to the final BI datasets and the metrics stakeholders actually look at.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="sysdesign-11" number={11} question="How do you manage cost vs. SLA trade-offs in system design?" difficulty="medium" topic="Cost">
You optimize storage layout (partitioning, file sizes), avoid unnecessary recomputation, and use selective materialization rather than materializing everything. You also schedule heavy jobs off-peak, enforce resource quotas, and track cost per dataset or pipeline so spend is visible and attributable. Cost has to be part of the design from the start, not an afterthought bolted on once the bill is too high.
</QuestionCard>
